I want to love it, but got literally nothing out of this film. The combination of cinematography styles involving a handheld camera and normal camera were irritating. While saying this, I went with 3 female friends and they all left sobbing and experienced a deep emotional connection with the film. I tried asking them what about the film they enjoyed but it was such an intense engagement with the film that none of them felt comfortable verbalizing their emotions in the moment. I wish I could see and experience what they felt but I guess it wasn’t a film for me. Watching this in theaters was the only thing keeping me from turning it off halfway or leaving. Had a super cool Q&A experience afterwards when BARRY JENKINS CAME OUT AS THE INTERVIEWER FOR THE WRITER/DIRECTOR!!! They focused a bit too much on the process of directing and casting this film for me as a writer to enjoy the conversation. (This reminds me of Eighth Grade, except no where near as good or impactful)

A slog of a film. There are moments of genuine sincerity that comes through, but the film as a whole has little that actually resonates. Alrighty then. Aftersun... it's nothing much. Sure, it's tender a little psychological but there's not much worth digging into here. It's a solemn, minimal film; very few characters, brief interactions and a hazy, dream-like presentation. The whole thing plays out like a distant memory that, seemed happy once, but as you age, you see the sad undercurrents of it. Neat idea, but the execution was spacey and pretentious. Aftersun follows a recently divorced dad and his young daughter on vacation. He's depressed and doing his best to hide it from her. She is growing up, starting to feel attractions and is making real connections with other humans. As the vacation goes on, the daughter and father begin to relate to each other on a deeper level. That's it. Aftersun is good insofar as you relate to it. Most people my age on this site come from fucked up, divorced, miserable families so they have these decaying memories. They look back and realize when they started to realize the cracks. They remember discovering how flawed and broken their parents were; coming of age in a world of dysfunction. I can't really relate so this movie didn't have as much meaning for ol' D.W. The Rumsfelds have always been intact. For me, it was a plodding, gimmicky bore that should have just been a short film or something. I'll never forget the first time I saw my father cry... but that doesn't make this movie good. The characters were middling; mostly slates for the audience to project their sadness onto. Alot of the editing was stupid too, and only sometimes justified. I did like the cinematography and acting, though, Paul Mescal is promising and I have liked almost all of his theatrical performances thus far. Aftersun didn't hold much value for me. I felt like it wasted alot of time and tried to pull heartstrings. It had good focus and some intentionality but when all was said and done, I just kinda threw my hands up in frustration. Pithy abstraction, faux-cuteness, faint natalism, not for me. Two Mutzies and Odenkirk-grade singing

Words cannot fully describe just how disappointed I am that this film did not land for me. For the last sort of three to four years ‘ Aftersun’ has been talked about as one of the most successful directorial debuts ever, and in the same breath one of the most moving films of the decade yet, I’m utterly let down. There were only really a few scenes I was able to honestly resonate with and I don’t believe Charlotte Wells completely unlocks the deeply personal and stagnant emotionality she desires. Fairly dissatisfied with Paul Mescal’s performance in the film too, in fact I feel as though Frankie Corio even outperformed the then 26-year-old which is shocking. It also completely derailed any nuanced meaning for me because the way he acts is a causality and emotional anchor for Corio’s character, so for him to then not prevail in the role was an immediate disaster. I hope that this improves on rewatch, granted I give it a second chance, although I don’t see that being super likely.

Aftersun is sorely in need of another layer of cloud to give dramatic texture to its sky of wide and plain sunbeams.  Set in the time-drifting, picture-taking, memory-making period of a relaxed vacation, the film moves gradually with that dreamy aimlessness inherent to poolside holidays.  To complicate this drifting flow, a later perspective is introduced, years in the future, when the young daughter has grown into an adult and looks back to re-examine these memories without the lens of youth, which so often over-exposes the emotional image of those closest, in rosy brightness that reduces the deeper crevices of shadowed feeling. This complicating perspective, however, is severely underplayed, adding far too little to the sun-soaked spread of the main story.  ‘Story’ here is generous, for Aftersun works in the way of stringing together moments without narrative, similar to how its adolescent protagonist picks up her camcorder and films for the sake of filming, preserving, indulging in the novelty of the resort and the time it affords her with her father.  It is a time punctuated by play and lounge: games of pool and poolside pranks, evening balcony’s game of chess, afternoon’s non-time on beach chairs, gazing at the paragliders swaying soundlessly through the blue sky above.  Certainly such a meandering style can be successful, but here the film lacks the rhythm to sustain its floating drift, and lacks the poetic touch that would restore weight to its empty structure. The literal mode of characters reflecting upon the past blends into a cinematic motif of reflections, reflections within the curve of a dead TV screen, in the bathroom mirror, the camcorder viewer, the breakfast table, the rippled water’s surface.  Such angles underscore the film’s melancholic layer of perspectives, but accomplish little else, and occasionally feel forced or simply gratuitous.  Diffracting off of surfaces is carried further into the film’s themes, as its skips around ideas of how the daughter fits in with the older kids, is maybe beginning to feel self-conscious comparing herself to the older girls, and is certainly growing more aware of her father’s lower social class, evidenced in his inability to pay for all the resort’s options.  She inhabits the lowest section of maturity’s totem pole, glimpsing the romance of the teens, the completion of the other families around her, and the fractionally-visible life of her own father.  Yet the film never quite ventures into the deep end, unable to fully capture the threads of themes it invokes but doesn’t resolve. Aftersun moves to the pace of waves lapping in slow currents of something you do not yet have the experience to name.  It aims to be poetic and ambiguous— complete with the arthouse trope of overused abstract interludes (in this case, close-ups of dancing in obnoxiously disorientating strobe lights)— but ultimately, its vacation is too insubstantial to linger much longer after the sun has lowered for the darkness of night. CIFF 2022

why can’t we give ourselves one more chance? this isn’t the actual lyric, but i’ve always misinterpreted it as this and it makes more sense to me. a pretty stunning feature debut from wells, somewhere in between after yang and petite maman. oke moves the camera with all the measured physicality of claire denis and is almost yang-reminiscent in his interest in reflections. i love the confidence on display here and indulgence is great, but i do think that at a certain point, there are negative returns from the overuse of oke’s technique. the way hands and arms and interiors are framed is great at showing sophie’s curiosity at the unfamiliar and her burgeoning adolescence/independence, but i don’t think the composite character study is as successful at picking apart calum through her eyes. his empathy radiates in waves, and the inner turmoil is clear, but it’s missing something. god, the climax though. the kid is great and all hail paul mescal.

J'ai trouvé le film très lent et il manque, selon moi, de dynamisme. Pendant une grande partie du film, j'ai eu du mal à être réellement captivé, la seule scène qui m'a vraiment marqué est la séquence finale, lorsque le père et sa fille dansent ensemble avant la fin de leurs vacances. Les flashbacks qui s'entremêlent à ce moment donnent enfin tout son sens au film et apportent une forte charge émotionnelle. Le film montre avec beaucoup de subtilité comment le père cache sa souffrance pour préserver sa fille. En apparence, il essaie de lui offrir de belles vacances, mais on comprend qu'au fond il est profondément triste et terriblement seul. Il est père célibataire, confronté à des difficultés financières et sans véritable entourage, il porte un mal-être qu'il ne parvient plus à surmonter. La fin révèle également que l'on suivait en réalité les souvenirs de Sophie devenue adulte. Avec le recul, elle comprend enfin les signes qu'elle n'avait pas vus enfant et réalise à quel point son père allait mal avant son décès. Même si je n'ai pas été emballé par le rythme du film, je reconnais que cette conclusion est particulièrement touchante et donne une autre dimension a l’histoire .

I entered this with a fair bit of hype, so when I left rather confused about the hype, well... Yeah. There's a banger of a film here, but it only really became somewhat interesting past the halfway mark. Cut out 15-odd minutes of the first or 2nd act, then I think I would rate this movie higher. It's a coming-of-age tale about a father and his 11 year old daughter, on a holiday in turkey. We are given backstory about them as the film goes on, but again, only really after the halfway point. When it became really interesting, and I could tell the movie was wrapping up, I was rather sad as I wanted it to continue in the timeline of these characters, especially the daughter. I can accept the ending of the father as that was really well done, but the daughter? Naaaah, man, keep it going. At that point I was interested in the two leads, interested in the teasers we were shown in flash-forwards, and for sure I picked up on things that happened to Sophie that impacted the future, but again, I wanted more haha. So what did I like? It's really well shot, with a few "one perfect shot" worthy frames. For those who have seen it, two that instantly come to mind are the airport terminal with the father and the tv screenshot in the hotel room where the mirror is somewhat in frame. Plus, the writing of the two leads as mentioned before were great, I really did become interested in them after a bit, but it almost felt too little too late. There are some great character moments here, but besides that, felt like a film with... Not much. TL;DR: A great 85 minute movie here, and I wish it was a bit different in terms of pacing and the timeline of the movie. Seen at the Edinburgh International Film Festival.

Realistic. The hand-held camera is a distraction. The finale is powerful but does not explain the father's real physical, financial and mental condition adequately. Intriguing are a near-miss fatal accident with a bus, a possible suicide attempt, his fascination with Oriental meditation, the choice of the Turkish carpet, etc. Young Francesca Corio as the daughter is a delight to watch.

This film bummed me out. I sadly see myself in the character of the father played by Paul Mescal, I too have very little money and probably could not buy my daughter singing lessons. Many of us have not figured out how to make money and thrive within this system and so we cry on our hotels beds and fall asleep while our children wander around holiday resorts, drinking lemon Fanta. It is sad. This film inspires us to think, "can I afford to have children? And if I do, will they think I am a failure?" In the end though, its fine. Paul Mescals daughter has a nice flat with exposed brick work aplenty, plants for days and nice vintage lamps. Well done

75th Cannes Film Festival Day 3: Aftersun Section: International Critics’ Week I saw this within the last couple of weeks, but I’m only now getting around to actually reviewing the films I saw at Cannes now that I’m not going from screen to screen within such a short span of time. I’m honestly surprised that this film has gotten the traction it has both in terms of critical reception and word of mouth because WOW have people at Cannes been going super crazy over this film. It’s gained so much traction that A24 picked up the North American distribution rights for the film after its premiere at Cannes (which makes a lot of sense) I don’t know if I’ll end up in the minority on this film once it gets a wider release, but I thought it was good, but nothing super amazing thematically. It has a lot of interesting imagery and visual metaphors that gives audiences a lot to read into and I really loved the dynamic between the father and daughter. Honestly, I like the film more than I did after leaving the theater the more I think about that part of the film. Which is why it’s underwhelming to me that I found the story at the film’s core to be pretty average in comparison to everything else in the film. Maybe it’s because I’ve seen so many other indie films similar in style that also happened to have better stories, but this really didn’t leave that much of an impression on me on my first viewing in the way that it seemed to with a lot of other people and I don’t have a lot to say about the film in this review for that reason. That said, I’ll definitely check it out again when it gets a wider release to see if I was missing something and my opinion changes or something clicks as a result or if my opinion remains the same. Light To Decent 7/10

Ok, so this took a lot of thinking, but I think I finally made sense of this film. This film made me see that you only know the version of someone that they show to you. The memories you have with or of someone are probably not actually what happened or who they truly are and felt in those moments. Our memories, especially from childhood can often have a rose coloured lense over them because at that time, you weren't aware of things in the grand scheme. You had an innocent mind because you were a kid. Most of my personal childhood memories have gaps. These gaps could have been good events or not so good events, and I'll never know because there was no camera. My siblings probably share the same memories as me, but with less or more gaps, with different details and specifics. My parents probably remember every specific and have no gaps in the memories I have from being a kid. Its like we were all there, at the same event, where we experienced the same thing, but we all probably remember it a little bit different. I probably won't remember writing this review, the same way I don't remember writing most of my reviews after a few weeks. Memory is a weird thing when you think about it. And this movie really made me think about it.

Un recuerdo hecho película. Aftersun entiende la fortaleza que hay detrás de una sonrisa, de un abrazo, e incluso del amor. No necesita explicarte todo para que eventualmente lo entiendas. No dramatiza, pero sí transmite. Te muestra cómo hay gritos que no se escuchan, y cómo hay heridas tan grandes que al final terminan pasando desapercibidas. Te enseña que la vida es incluso irónica de una manera tan particular y nostálgica. Es una obra de arte genuina, real, cruda... pero sin dejar de ser extremadamente cuidada y linda. Dirigida de manera excepcional, te deja una marca en el corazón.

Much like through a foggy lens of a camera, it's a nostalgic reminiscence of that warm and fuzzy summer vacation, blissfully unaware of the realities of adult life, and the anxieties our loved ones can face. Only later on in life do we completely understand how significant these mundane interactions with our loved ones can be, how much meaning our words can have for them, and that we can understand what they once felt. Its emotional core is beautiful. It’s depiction of depression is one of the best I’ve ever seen in a movie, the final shot of Calum walking through the double doors into the night club to symbolize that his life was only ever heading in one direction after the time they spent together is soul crushing. Finally, it’s the lingering memory of a father's love that endures despite the crashing waves of loss and grief

“You can live wherever you want to live. Be whoever you want to be. You have time." I used to envy people who had a documented life when they were kids, pictures and videos of them living as if it was the proof of existence. To see them through the eyes of their parents on how much they love and care enough to capture those moments, something to look back on in the future. I think it stems from my hatred and shame that every time there is an activity in school that requires baby photos, I will always be the only one worrying, for I have nothing to show. Maybe it was due to poverty? Lack of love and attention? Maybe they don’t just see the point in taking photos? Or maybe a little bit of a mix of all? It kinda felt bitter and pathetic, just a child wondering why I am the only one in the room who lacks that experience…and weirdly enough, I would find myself imagining that I am the one in other children's shoes, fantasizing about what it feels like to be in their family? Throughout the movie I just kept on thinking and reflecting about my relationship with my Papa. Initially I had this realization that I’ve never had anything that I could look back to; we barely had any pictures nor memories since we never went on vacations, went on a trip, or even simply went out. But I thought it would be an awesome thing to do so…I do think he deserves to have fun and do trivial things and see life without always being in a survival mode worrying about spending money on what seems to fit in the ‘wants’ and not ‘need’ category. I’ve spent most of my life with him, and I think personality-wise I am more like him. I might not like him as a person with some of his questionable morals and beliefs, but I could pretty much say that he was a great dad who literally did everything just so that me and my brother doesn't have to worry going on an empty stomach and even provide things that might not be grand, but it was better than having nothing. Actually, I do think that my dad is a cool person; he experienced so much hardship in life and knows a lot of skills in order to survive. I sometimes wish that I knew him better or even bonded with him with life outside of the house. Other times, I imagine what would his life be if I hadn't existed? The sole reason why I want to succeed in life, to have money, is just to spoil them and return all the hard work they've put in raising me; growing up, I think my parents value money more than anything, and I do get why, so I thought that maybe giving back with money would be the best thing they would totally appreciate—so that they could finally live the life for themselves and experience what they truly deserve: pampering their own needs and not for the sake of other people.

When your parents are apart, by way of separation, death or any circumstance, I wonder if the way you split your love moves with it. I'm thinking if, before my mother's death, my love for my parents was carved down the middle, 50/50, or if it would change depending on who I was around at the time. In Charlotte Wells' Aftersun, Sophie's love for her father weighs so heavily towards him, so doting and special, it's almost as if her love for her mother stayed at home while she came with him on holiday. For the duration of this trip, and the film itself, there is only these two. And so we watch it pass by with familiar late-90s mundanity: shuttle coaches, sunloungers, lurid-coloured cocktails, tribute acts, Steps played on Walkman. This string of events is paired with – or interrupted by — conversations between Sophie and her father, identifying the traits that bind them so closely, observations of a father and daughter relationship that distance has somehow made stronger. I loved this. Sophie reminded me of my sister, how the character of Calum provided insight into the emotions of a father children seldom see. My dad is maybe the most mysterious person I know; often, I experience a deluge of emotion on the rare occasion he opens up. It's like seeing a rare painting out of its frame, vulnerable and likely to be damaged. It's funny how our memories of people are so often burned into celluloid or on digital files we store away; how our understanding of adolescence and who we were in our formative years leaves our brains but is easily returned to. But what it summons can be both gorgeous and heartbreaking, two perfect descriptors of AFTERSUN, a masterful debut in my eyes. A hugely important new filmmaker who successfully pins down what it means to love someone wholeheartedly, and to know that it's often not enough – and not possible – to always have them by your side.

It’s fun to try to figure things out, interpret what’s happening, and come up with theories. You’re given plenty of time to do so, too, since some conversations are long and some shots are even longer. For me, it all dragged on a bit too much and ended unsatisfactorily. I keep realizing that crime thrillers aren’t among my favorite genres.

c’est un film très lent, avec une atmosphère étrange et de très très très très longs dialogues. c’est un infini procès, avec une embrouille interminable, qui révèle une ambiance très sombre et des personnages tous plus bizarres les uns que les autres. on comprend pas tout et c’est très compliqué d’accrocher. certains plans sont filmées de façon original, et les scènes sont vraiment longues. c’est un film chargé en émotion, avec beaucoup de secrets enfouies. au bout d’un moment ça devient vraiment interminable, des faits surgissent, des hypothèses sont conjecturées, mais c’est jamais explicitement concret. bon ok la façon dont c’est réalisé est très intéressante. par contre, j’ai carrément détesté la fin, pcq tout le long on s’attend à une réponse concrète mais le but du film c’est justement de ne donner aucune réponse, du coup c’est super frustrant. toute l’histoire on peut l’interpréter seulement par des « peut être » et jamais par de véritables faits. chacun des personnages sont intéressants, avec des points de vus différents et des façons de subir la situation différentes, mais le spectateur est à la place des jurés, donc c’est très compliqué de savoir démêlé le vrai du faux. le film rappelle que le verdict ne coïncide pas forcément avec la vérité, et les hypothèses de la potentielle vérité restent plausible. cependant le lien avec le titre du film est très pertinent, en montrant la chute de chacun des personnages de façon disséquées. bon, en toute honnêteté je n’ai pas aimé. le fond du film est émouvant et bien recherché. MAIS, c’est lent + dialogues interminables + bcp de choses abstraites et surtout surtout surtout le film répond à rien, ça te laisse sur ta fin, c’est à toi d’interpréter et de trouver la vérité, la fin est ouverte et ne répond à aucune questions que tu te poses durant tout le film. c’est frustrant et c’est carrément ce que je n’aime pas.

J’en avais énormément entendu parler en bien, et certains le considèrent même comme un chef-d’œuvre. On me l’avait vraiment vendu comme un film incroyable, donc forcément, j’en attendais beaucoup. Et honnêtement, j’ai été assez déçu. Je comprend ce que dénonce le film et ce qu'il reflète de notre société et de la justice. Cependant j'ai trouvé ça long. Ce qui me gêne avec ce film c'est le côté élitiste de la communauté, comme si le fait de ne pas avoir une fin clairement expliquée rendait automatiquement le film plus intelligent. Personnellement, je trouve que ça peut vite donner une certaine prétention au film et à la manière dont il est présenté. Le fait de laisser le spectateur interpréter la fin peut être intéressant, mais ça ne signifie pas forcément que le film est meilleur ou plus intelligent. En soi, ça reste un bon film, je ne vais pas dire le contraire. Mais je pense que le principal problème, c’est que dès qu’un film sort un peu de l’ordinaire et propose quelque chose d’original, les gens ont tendance à énormément s’emballer. On lui attribue tout de suite une dimension exceptionnelle, voire de chef-d'œuvre. C'est dommage mais ça reste un bon film.

Me  pareció una película muy interesante. Desde el principio logró mantener mi atención, pero lo que más me gustó fue la actuación de Sandra Hüller. El hecho de que hable inglés, francés y alemán hace que su personaje tenga mucho más carácter y se sienta muy real, su personaje muestra inteligencia pero sabemos que es la actriz dándole vida y eso me encanta. Para mí, la película es una mezcla entre una historia fácil de seguir y el cine de arte. Aunque trata de un juicio, no solo busca resolver el caso, sino que te hace pensar en todo lo que pasa y en cómo cada persona puede ver la misma situación de una forma diferente. Al final, porque no te dice exactamente qué pasó. En lugar de darte una respuesta, deja que cada espectador saque sus propias conclusiones con las pruebas que fueron apareciendo durante la película.

Que decir, no supe a quién creerle nadota y mejor me quedo con la duda. Está comienza a parecer una historia de misterio, pero a lo largo de la película,  empece a ver los detalles familiares más íntimos, profundos y dolorosos. Y que bajo el escrutinio de extraños, con todos nuestros errores, fracasos y salud mental expuestos pues fácilmente  podemos ser juzgados como monstruos pero siento que al final  la verdad es que solo somos humanos. Es una película, limpia, supongo porque siento eso, siento que si es lenta y aburrida pero limpia, como que no hay mucho ruido para distraerme o algo por el estilo, y pues dos tres trucossss. Puntos por la reflexión.:))

Mettez du respect et de la lumière sur le cinéma féminin. Un film de procès qui ne cherche jamais vraiment le verdict, mais la faille. Triet construit son récit comme une dissection minutieuse du couple, où chaque certitude s'effrite à mesure que le tribunal (et le spectateur) croit avancer. Sandra Hüller y est habitée d'une opacité fascinante : on ne sait jamais si son intelligence est une armure ou un aveu. Mais au-delà du dispositif judiciaire, c'est une question bien plus vertigineuse que pose le film : connaît-on vraiment l'autre ? Son voisin, son frère, sa sœur, son ou sa compagne ? Aucune famille n'échappe aux secrets de polichinelle, à ces zones d'ombre qui persistent sans jamais être nommées. Chaque foyer a ses casseroles, ses non-dits tolérés en silence. C'est ce qui rend le film aussi dramatique que profondément humain. Il ne s'agit pas de juger un couple, mais de mesurer combien la connaissance intime de l'autre [ et de soi-même ] reste toujours partielle, négociée, parfois illusoire. Une leçon d'humilité face à la complexité des êtres. La mise en scène, souvent austère, presque clinique, épouse cette froideur alpine du chalet, comme si le décor lui-même refusait de trancher. C'est là toute l'ambiguïté du film : il ne raconte pas une mort mais l'impossibilité de connaître véritablement l'autre même après des années de vie commune. Les 2h30 pèsent par moments, notamment dans les longueurs procédurales qui, même si elles nourrissent le vertige du doute, testent aussi la patience. L'usage de l'anglais, pivot thématique plus que coquetterie, dérange certains. J'avoue que j'ai eu du mal avec ce yoyo entre les langues mais c'est à tort selon moi, tant il matérialise la distance entre les langues, les cultures, et finalement entre les personnes elles-mêmes. Une Palme d'or qui ne fait pas l'unanimité, et c'est peut-être normal. le film refuse lui-même toute unanimité sur ce qu'il raconte comme il refuse toute certitude sur ceux qu'on croit connaître. Pas le meilleur rythme mais très bon film.

Palme d’or 2023 et couronné de nombreuses récompenses, Anatomie d’une chute de Justine Triet mérite largement sa réputation. Derrière son apparence de film judiciaire se cache avant tout une dissection fascinante d’un couple en crise, où chaque détail du quotidien prend une importance capitale. Le suspense autour de ce whodunit atypique fonctionne parfaitement, mais le véritable sujet est ailleurs : les ressentis, les incompréhensions et les visions opposées que deux personnes peuvent avoir d’une même histoire. Sandra Hüller livre une prestation remarquable, parvenant à transmettre une multitude d’émotions d’un simple regard. Une réalisation subtile qui nous plonge au plus près des émotions des personnages. Un très bon film.

Ok, so firstly, this was a rewatch but I realised that like I had never really written a proper review for this film and honestly I feel like I do want to write about it. Firstly, stupendously brilliant acting performances(even Snoop) which honestly has always been one of the most appreciated aspects of this film and it deserves all of it and more. The brilliance in the cinematography and post production is easy to ignore due to its subtlety but it is never truly that easy when the primary locations are literally a courtroom, a house built out of wood and snow-capped mountains which require completely different palettes as far as grading and other visual aspects are concerned. bir köpek var filmde, hani al tüm oyunculuk ödüllerini ona ver inanılmaz iyi oynamış. Bir sabaha açılıyor film, bir aile. Anne, baba ve çocuk. Çocuğumuz görme engelli, Annemiz sahnede son derece sıcak fakat babamız öyle mesafeli ki kadraja girmeye bile yeltenmiyor. Sadece açtığı müziğin sesiyle varlığından haberdar ediyor bizi. Bu tanıtımdan sonra, bir düşüş gerçekleşiyor. Çocuğumuz evde değilken, baba pencereden düşüp ölüyor. O sırada evde bulunan tek kişi olan Anne ise ileride gerçekleşecek duruşmaların baş şüphelisi konumuna geçiyor. Daha sonra, filmimiz ilerledikçe bu düşüşü derinlemesine analiz ediyor, bir bakıma anatomisini çıkarıyor. Bu düşüş yalnızca  ölüme yol açmış bu kaza/cinayetin değil; bir aşkın, bir ailenin ve en önemlisi kişilere dair kafamızda oluşturduğumuz portrelerin de düşüşü. Onlara atfettiğimiz her bir iyi özelliğin, birlikte yaşadığımız her bir güzel anının bambaşka bir bağlamda nasıl bir silaha, korkunç bir eylemin kanıtına dönüşebileceğinin anatomisi. İşte bu film, tam olarak bununla ilgileniyor. İki saat otuz dakika boyunca filmimiz bunu anlatıyor. Gerçekte ne oldu? Aslında daha doğrusu, gerçekte ne olduğunu düşünüyorsun? Bu soru, izleyiciye düzenli olarak soruluyor ve  verdiğimiz cevaplar çoğu zaman (en azından benim verdiğim) bir öncekinden farklı oluyor. Spoiler olmayacak merak etmeyin, sadece ufak bir sahneden örnek vermek istiyorum. Bana kalırsa film başlangıçta sıkıca annemizin perspektifinden ilerliyor. Ortam onun açısından kuruluyor, onun gözlerinden şahit oluyoruz. Haliyle çoğumuz bu davada Annemin tarafını tutmuş oluyor. Sonra duruşmalar başlıyor ve bir sabah bir ses kaydı dinliyoruz. Ses kaydı bir tartışma hakkında. Önce ufak gerginlikler çıkıyor, sonra saygının sürdürüldüğü bir tartışmaya dönüyor. Fakat ne zamanki bu tartışma fiziksel şiddetin de dahil olduğu bir kavgaya dönüyor, görüntü kesiliyor ve aynı karakterlerimiz gibi sadece ses kaydıyla tanık oluyoruz geçmişe. Burada artık ne olduğunun kararı bize düşüyor. Ve o ana kadar her zaman tek bir açıya güvenmiş olan biz, kendimizi şüphe ederken buluyoruz. Film, bu tarafsız anlatımını soğuk atmosferi ve karakterlere mesafeli duruşuyla güçlendirmiş. Aynı zamanda ara ara kameranın el çekimi, handheld bir tarza geçmesiyle de sizi olan olayların içine bırakıyor. Kimi zaman kamera yaşananlara ayak uyduramıyor, sahne pozlamasında hatalara yer veriyor ve olanları olduğu gibi sergilemekte başarısız oluyor. Bu sayede anlattığı temayı da ustalıkla desteklemiş oluyor. Oyunculuklar gerçekten de efsane. Yazdığım birçok incelemede oyunculukları övüyorum, ben de bunun farkındayım. Fakat bana sorsanız en iyi oyunculuklar hangi filmdeydi diye, şüphe bile etmeden Anatomy of a Fall derdim. Sandra Hüller, kendi ana dili olmayan iki dilde konuşmasına rağmen destansı bir performans vermiş. Milo Machado-Graner unutulmaz bir oyunculuk sergilemiş. Hem çocuk oyuncu, hem görme engelli bir karakter hem de yas sürecini anlatan senaryo. Aktörümüz aleyhine olabilecek tüm durumların üstesinden ustalıkla gelmiş. Kadrodaki diğer oyuncularsa ortalamın çok üstünde performanslar vererek bu iki başrolümüzün emeğini boşa çıkarmamış. Son olarak, filmi sıkıcı bulan insanların olduğunun farkındayım. Hatta bunlardan birisi ablam. Dürüst konuşmam gerekirse beni bir an bile sıkmadı. Hatta film beni içine almakta o kadar başarılıydı ki bir sahnede karakterin sigarasından gelen dumanın benim odamda dolaştığını sandım. Zevk meselesidir diyip filmin temposu hakkındaki kararı size bırakıyorum. Benim için kusursuza çok yakın bir filmdi. Duygusal bağ kurmakta zorlanmış olsam da bunun bir sonraki izleyişimlerimde gerçekleşebileceğine hâlâ daha inanıyorum. Ayrıca, bir noktada bu duruma bilerek yapıldığını düşündüğümden çok da büyük bir problem olarak bakamıyorum. Şiddetle tavsiye ediyorum.

As the end marker for a long running generation of marvel movies, Endgame unfortunately drops the ball in all ways that matter. A lame attempt at reconciling irreversible character and wider plot choices, this film not only disrupts long established character growth and progression, but it also abruptly cuts off any opportunity for what many would call a “happy ending.” Multiple beloved characters are given the “tortured male existence trope,” wherein their wider personality and moral identity are swept to the wayside in order to justify a new generation of characters to swoop in following their exit. For example, by both butchering Peggy Carter and Steve Rogers emotional maturation and individuality in order to manufacture a “romantic reunification” following Steve’s travel back in time, Marvel has essentially removed both Peggy’s autonomy outside of being “Captain Americas love interest,” as well as Steve’s long established faithfulness to Bucky Barnes and his dedication to serving the weak. In no world would Steve rogers abandon a freshly reintroduced to society Bucky, nor a disrupted world reeling with the sudden re-appearance of 50% of the world’s population. In his decision to abandon his shield and interrupt Peggy’s progression towards an accomplished life as a shield founder and agent, as well as her pursuit of future love and motherhood as expressed in the original timeline, Steve is making an exceptionally selfish decision—which as any Marvel fan is aware—is the antithesis of his character. This is just one of the irreconcilable changes made to a central character that insults years of character establishment and development, which is then followed by yet again a female character being fridged for the greater plot. First starting with Gamora in Infinity war and now Natasha in Endgame, it is clear to see that the writers find no use for these strong female characters in these last plot stages other than as a motivation for male suffering and lament. Gamora, both present and past iterations of herself (as featured in this film), have much more worth as a character representing long building abusive deprogramming and female strength and endurance in the face of tragedy, than as a “sad she’s different than my girlfriend” trope—as presented by Peter Quills reaction to her appearance. Prior to this, viewers are slapped in the face with the sacrifice of Natasha for the soul stone, where her death is framed as a noble sacrifice in order to allow Clint Barton to return to his family once the snap is reversed. While faithful to Natasha’s character, one can only reconcile so much with the fact that it had to be only female character of the original Avengers to lose her life first. This is especially exasperated by the emphasized female power scene in the final battle, where every female hero on scene band together to fight, almost as an attempt by the writers to apologize for killing off the woman who pioneered female superhero-dom in modern media not 40 minutes earlier. All in all, these are just some of the many faults within this movie—which in its essence is a blatant attempt to slap a crooked bandaid on Marvels obvious (and clumsy) transition to a newer generation of actors and characters. As entertaining as a battle packed, time travel action movie can be, Avengers Endgame is a lazy attempt at hopefully pushing viewers towards future projects as they kill off their favorite characters one by one. We can only hope that these new superhero’s will be given the opportunity to grow into characters of their own and establish a storyline outside of the shadow of their predecessors.

"There was an idea, Stark knows this, called the Avengers Initiative. The idea was to bring together a group of remarkable people, see if they could become something more. See if they could work together when we needed them to fight the battles we never could." Sam Jackson's Nick Fury hit us with that way back in 2012's The Avengers. At the time, that movie seemed to be the fulfillment of the promise of a shared universe. It was groundbreaking in its own right and was proof that this could actually work. What resulted was a seismic shift in how studios approached making money. All of a sudden, setting up things to come became more important than the film itself and Marvel was no less guilty in said predisposition. It seemed like Kevin Feige's all-pervading control over every aspect of every film would, ultimately, lead to the death of the MCU. Somehow, it didn't. Audiences (me included) flocked in droves to watch the same movie (albeit with different characters and plot) over and over again. We sat through some real abysmal shit too. The "Marvel Formula", however, did not change much. My main issue was always how the film you were watching was always indebted to the next film in the pipeline to fulfill its promises. It seemed like a cycle that would never stop (and probably won't) but then, I watched Endgame. After the "space trash" (to quote David Ehrlich) that we all know as Avengers: Infinity War, Endgame really knocks it out of the park. For once, something had real consequences in the MCU. The sense of loss and grief is palpable. Don't get me wrong, this also a hodgepodge of random character moments structured around a plot that, if you think about it long enough, makes absolutely no sense but what happens to be Endgame's biggest weakness is also its biggest strength. This mish-mash works because its a mish-mash of much fewer characters. They have, and I can't stress this enough, time. The editing, while much tighter than Infinity War's, holds shots much longer than one would expect from a summer blockbuster studio tentpole and this is why, for once, I cried (more than once) in a Marvel film. Imagine the scene where Peter Parker turns into vacuum cleaner food in Tony's hands. Now imagine if an entire 3 hour film was like that. There is one cut that's absolutely ridiculous and doesn't work at all but it'll probably go unnoticed by the majority (pretty much everyone) of the people that watch this film. As you've probably read in other reviews, “fan service” is a huge part of the film. While that isn’t untrue, I prefer to think of these moments as homages and also, the fulfillment of character arcs and sub-arcs. Despite being 3 hours long, there’s very little to the film that I would call unnecessary. It’s almost as if Feige’s plan was to feed us a staple diet of horseshit (no disrespect to the artists that made those films but they were always tied down by the involvement of Feige and, sometimes, the military) for 11 years so that, when they finally did make a great film, we’d know it. And they have. Additionally, both Alan Silvestri’s score and Trent Opaloch’s cinematography happen to be, at least in my opinion, the best in the MCU. Here, Silvestri, unlike in Infinity War, creates a soundscape that builds upon previously established character themes satisfyingly while introducing new, moodier and much more effective pieces into the mix. He no longer has the burden of scoring for Thanos in almost every scene owing to the fact that this film is more The Avengers than The Avengers. A stride was also made towards embracing Joss Whedon’s influence and that pays off in heaps. The lighting gets a little experimental at times and you can see Opaloch’s Disrict 9 come through a little which is honestly great. The CGI is, well, Marvel CGI; rushed, everywhere, and, at this point, it seems like most major studios have stopped caring about the fact that CGI isn’t supposed to look computer generated in almost every case. Despite all its shortcomings, I laughed, I cried, and, on more occasions than I would like to admit, I got goosebumps. This was the endgame all along and it was worth it. Edit: didn't touch my original review because it's nice, if misguided, but this film is truly just imperialist propoganda

If Infinity War was, as @kernetcetera so eloquently described, ‘television’, then Endgame is the TV finale, the send-off show, the goodbye episode that wraps it all up with a nice little bow and gives the fans an opportunity to pay their respects to characters that had been a part of their lives for so many seasons. On that note, it’s certainly not the type of film that was made for someone like me, and I was a fool for thinking it may otherwise have been. I have highlighted my preference for the more singularly focussed storylines in the MCU within previous reviews, with IW being somewhat of an exception. Infinity War surprised me with its acute balance of multiple character threads and plot lines with the fast-paced and action-packed spectacle of superhero powers punching up against the Mad Titan, Thanos. It felt lean and muscly, where the added padding and lethargic pace of Endgame serves as a complete, and for me, unwelcome juxtaposition to what had preceded it. This, admittedly, is down to personal preference. I had wretchedly hoped for an escalation of the Infinity War saga, and was instead handed exactly what franchise fans had asked for all along. Endgame is fan-service through and through, and I have no doubt that day one MCU faithfuls will be absolutely delighted with what’s served up. Where I see po-faced and heavy-handed self-importance, Marvel’s fanbase will instead see earnest and earned tributes to the characters they love and themselves as supporters. And you know what? We’re both right. We’re just coming at it from different directions. If you’re like me, someone who is far more interested in self-contained stories that can stand on their own two feet and are concerned about only what is delivered within a film’s runtime, not what’s outside of it... you’ll probably walk away feeling a little ripped off. If, however, you have completely invested yourself in the 10 years worth of movies that the Marvel Cinematic Universe consists of, you’re unlikely to be disappointed. Enjoy it.

Well this is it. 22 films all leading to this moment. The final film in this massive cinematic universe. Finally we have arrived. Well what is the verdict from this viewer? It is better than Infinity War. That's a start right? This film ultimately succumbs to the same things that Infinity War fell under. The film, like many other MCU films, falls into a very drawn out final showdown between the Avengers and Thanos's army. Just like the battle of Wakanda in Infinity War, the battle for the Infinity Stones lacks creativity. And imagination. And suspense. It is mostly incoherent action that people will mistake for being good. The thing about MCU films though is that the ones that fall into the category of "good" or "great" is that they have an emotional core to tie them down and hold you over. Think the first Captain America or Black Panther. Those films are so good because they have something at the core. In Endgame, there isn't much there. That's not to say that the film doesn't have any emotional moments that hit. In fact, the first hour of the film I think is genuinely great. But once we get to the midway point most of that is gone. Then everything devolves into the rinse and repeat nature that we have come to expect of the MCU. A shame because like I said that first hour is excellent. Can I also say that the Russo’s continue to not impress me with their eye for visuals? Why is everything that isn’t green screen so dull and dour? How could anyone watch this movie and say it looks good? Even from just an aesthetic POV. Not even on a technical level or psychological level in regards to what these shots mean in relation to what’s happening. Did we all not watch Into the Spiderverse last December? The film is entertaining enough I suppose but I have to be honest, most of the fan theories you read on reddit were a lot more enjoyable than this film. But still better than Infinity War so that's good right?

„that is americas ass!“ Edit: So, here is my attempt on writing a proper review explaining my feelings for this movie. Yesterday, when I told one of my “““friends“““" that Avengers: Endgame didn’t blow my mind, that specific someone started insulting one of my favorite movies, La La Land, as „shitty arthouse rom-com“, so I am preparing myself to get hurt again after publishing this. But please leave La La Land out of this, guys. First of all: two stars is not a bad rating. It is slightly lower-than-average. Nothing more or less. Second of all: I haven’t seen every single movie leading up to this one. I would say that I’ve seen all the ones that are really necessary, but I definitely missed some along the way. So, one could argue that I am not as emotionally involved into the storyline as the specific target audience. Now that all of that’s said, lets get into it. Disclaimer: Spoilers! Avengers: Endgame starts off very weird. We get to see what happened after Avengers: Infinity War. Our heroes travel to a distant planet that Thanos is hiding on to get the stones back and to make everything undone. As they find out that the stones have been destroyed, they kill Thanos and return to earth. A, in my opinion, very bumpy beginning. The first 30 minutes just seem very unstructured and repetitious. Maybe they should have ended Infinity War with Thanos destroying the stones and getting killed instead of starting Endgame with that. Or maybe don’t show it at all. Endgame could have startet with Scott coming back from the particle world. He walks around the town just like he really does, sees all those weird monuments, and then goes on to the head quarter. That is where Steve explains what has been going on and that Scott has been missing for 5 years. Scott could be all like „What? That can’t be right! I’ve only been gone for like 5 hours!“ and they figure out this whole time-travelling thing together. That way you safe the shitty „5 years later“-card, 15 minutes of explaining how humanity has been doing these last years, and the incredibly long introduction. And can we please take a moment to talk about how a rat (????) is the reason that Scott comes back in the first place? I can’t possibly believe that this is the best thing they could come up with. How about one of the Avengers, possibly Natasha, still can’t let go and is searching for every clue she can find. Maybe she could be the one saving Scott? I don’t know if that would be any better, I just can’t believe that they are putting humanity’s fate in the hands (or paws?) of a rat. But that is not the only thing that seemed a little dubious to me. There are many things happening that don’t seem to have an real impact on the story. For example: Thanos dies, but the second Thanos from the past just travels to the future to take his place. The head quarter is being blown up, but still nobody gets hurt. The Avengers seem to be losing the war, but Captain Marvel is right around the corner to save their asses. Thanos manages to get the gold glove, but the stones have already been removed. And those are just a few examples. I mean, I know that those are the plot twist that everyone loves so much, but they just didn’t work for me. Making something like this one or two times would have been fine, but they pulled this „something-happens-but-not-really-because-tada-surprise!“-card so many times that i just couldn’t take anything that was happening in the movie seriously. It was just too much for me. But, as one might expect, not only those puns were a bit over-the-top, but also everything else in this movie. I know that this is supposedly the most epic movie in human history, and that if any movie would have the allowance to go all the way it would be this one, but guys…. too much is too much. Every single sentence was implemented as the most dramatic thing that has ever been said. Everyone knows that I love myself a good dramatic scene, but a slow-mo zoom to the person talking ahead of every sentence is a bit exaggerated even for my taste. I know that this film serves the sole purpose of making the fans cry tears of joy and anger, but that is no excuse for the level of epical slow-mos featured in this film. Especially scenes that would have been sad on their own like Tonys funeral are being destroyed for me because of the dolly shot through the crying crowd. I don’t need to see those crying faces to understand the impact of this scene. It is just a pointless way of saying: „Look, that guy’s also there! Do you see this one??? It’s your childhood hero crying! Hah!“. Yes, i get that this is the end of an era and that the fans deserve a way to say goodbye, but the films quality massively suffered due to scenes like this in my opinion. Yes, it was very sad and all, but still not needed to get the message across. I know, it sounds like i am only seeing the bad sides again. But it’s not like that. I actually really liked the framework plot of time travel. That was a solid foundation and executed nicely. The thing that bothered me is that instead of making this movie stand for its own and create something new and inspiring, it seems like it was just created to be closing ceremony for the fans that stuck around the past 11 years. If that is what you are looking for in a film, fine. I accept that, and I am definitely not judging anyone for rating this with 5 stars. It is just not what i had hoped to see. I would have needed something a little more demanding and challenging, not something that is only mend to satisfy my need of a happy ending to this long story. And before you say it, yes, i know that this movie is not meant to stand alone and that it is the product of 11 years of build-up. But more than that, it is also one of the movies with the highest budgets for story development, a huge milestone in film history and a one-of-a-kind crossover that has never been there before. And from a movie like that I would have expected a lot more than „just“ a long and bumpy farewell from my generations heroes. I’m really sorry if my opinion upsets you, but that is just the way I see it. As I said, two stars is not a bad rating. Is a little below average, and that is really that way I am feeling about this movie. So no, this is not a „i hate this because everyone loves it“ kind of thing, this is just my honest opinion. And if you don’t like it, please let me know why. I’m open for discussion. But please don’t hurt my baby La La Land. Second Edit: Now, a few days later, I just have to admit that they almost had me crying in the end. I can’t help it, I am a sucker for love and nothing gets me like reunited lovers do. I am weak.

Infierno en el espectáculo más grande sobre la Tierra Una de las películas más taquilleras de 1974 fue The Towering Inferno : un drama de cine catástrofe (y un poco catastrófico) cuyo título resume todo el argumento. En la tradición de The Greatest Show On Earth , The Towering Inferno es un desfile de cameos de actores famosos y dinero: todo es un aparato que fue acompañado por récords en ventas de entradas y hasta nominaciones al Oscar. Pero, pese a tantas entradas vendidas y noninaciones, ambas son películas que parecen haber sido relegadas al olvido hoy en día. El espectáculo (que se traduce en un juego de identificar los segundos de caras famosas cuando aparecen) se opone a la narración: hoy puede resultar más épico sobrevivir a las 3 horas de duración de cada uno de estos títulos que los desafíos que sus respectivos personajes enfrentan. El problema no es el "qué": es el "cómo" se muestra lo que se cuenta. Avengers: Endgame sufre un problema similar. No se trata de cuestionar decisiones argumentales. Hay una idea vertebral dando vueltas que recorre los laberintos del tiempo: ahí es cuando la película se vuelve más interesante. Cuando se aleja de los guiños para fanáticos que establecieron un contrato de lectura previo y de los planos generales de ejércitos incomprensibles sobre un fondo gris, cuando se centra más en los conflictos de los personajes que en las piruetas de héroes, sin peso ni alma, hechos por computadora. El pasado no se olvida pero tampoco puede repetirse: el Capitán América dice "we move forward". Hay una contradicción ontológica dentro de esa misma propuesta que funciona como espejo de las teorías de la imagen tiempo. Pero todo amenaza con diluirse en cameos y malabares logísticos (que tienen que ver más con los nombres que aparecen en pantalla que en innovaciones visuales o estéticas) para cerrar una historia que, con más torpezas que aciertos narrativos, lleva más de una década. La primera unión de los Avengers en la película de Joss Whedon conserva su energía: era la primera vez y estaba claro. Cada vez que se intentó replicar ese "momento" parecía perder más fuerza en la pantalla, aunque el leitmotiv sonara más alto y se amontonaran más y más personajes. A veces menos es más. La cacofonía visual no es sinónimo de emoción y lo que alguna vez fue novedoso ya se convirtió en rutinario. A esta altura uno puede identificar una estructura narrativa definida que incluye referencias pop (en especial, de la década del '80) y algún chiste inocente que contrasta con añadidos serios y dramáticos subrayados por música y encuadres solemnes que desentonan con el espíritu que los precedía. Más triste es que algunos personajes queden relegados a ser un Deus ex machina y que parezcan la representación simbólica no irónica del famoso "debo irme, mi planeta me necesita" de Los Simpson . ¿Por qué forzar personajes interesantes a estar solo para la foto cuando podían ocupar roles más interesantes? Son decisiones artísticas, y algunos no tendrán problema con ellas, pero Endgame no tiene la cohesión narrativa de historias corales tipo Nashville , City Of Angels o Magnolia , aunque lo intenta y eso no es un detalle menor. Infinity War funcionaba porque entendía que los héroes se definen en acciones antes que en palabras. A las piñas: como también sucedía en The Avengers . Tenía un personaje con un arco dramático definido y dividía el tercer acto en tres espacios distintos para darle lugar a cada línea dramática. El montaje en paralelo estaba justificado y adquiría sentido de urgencia. Ni el villano quedaba diluido en el medio del caos ni los héroes se amontonaban. Si todo es épico, nada es épico. Pasaron apenas diez años pero el cine de superhéroes se convirtió en algo tan despersonalizado y homogeneo que, en contraste, películas de estudio como Iron Man , The Dark Knight , Watchmen o Hellboy II muchos las reconocen ahora como productos artesanales que tenían algo para decir sobre el estado del arte y del mundo. Quizás todo se vuelva tan prefabricado y difícil de diferenciar que digamos lo mismo de Endgame en 10 años.

It's the culmination of a decade's worth of buildup that we will likely never see again regardless of how DOOMSDAY or SECRET WARS turn out. Ouais. Ok. Cool. Franchement ce film a cette note car c'est un film charnière, sinon je lui aurais mis 2 étoiles en terme de kiffe. Je n'ai ressenti aucune émotions, cela ne m'a pas fait rire et je n'étais pas ébahi ni ému. Le début est sympathique, voir Thor gros alcoolo c'est étrange, de même voir Tony Stark avec un enfant m'a surpris, mais c'est tout. Déjà je n'apprécie pas le fait de remonter le temps à l'aide de la technologique quantique. Ensuite je ne pense pas que les pierres permettent de refermer la branche d'univers créée (donc il existe trois univers distincts, le premier est celui dans lequel l'histoire se passe, le second est celui dans lequel on a prit les pierres et le dernier est celui dans lequel on a pris les pierres puis on les a restitués). Enfin Steve Rogers devrait avoir plus de 100 ans donc comment est-il en vie à la fin pour transmettre le costume et le bouclier ?? Cela étant dit c'était sympathique de revenir dans les précédents films, mais bon moi ce ne m'a pas trop touché vu que je les ai vu pour la plupart il y a moins de dix jours. Captain America est symbole et non un super-héros classique, il représente l'Amérique mais aussi la loyauté, le courage, le charisme, il est donc impersonnel et tout le monde qui est en digne peut être Captain America, c'est pour cela que je ne suis pas gêné par le fait que Steve Rogers ne soit plus Captain America à présent. D'ailleurs en parlant de dignité, j'ai trouve ça hyper classe que Steve Rogers ait pu maîtriser Mjöllnir. J'ai trop le seum que Black Widow soit morte c'est une de mes préférées. Elle aurait dû être présente pour l'une des meilleurs scènes du film : Toutes les super-héroïnes combattant côte à côte. La scène du sacrifice entre Hawkeye et Black Widow est bien je trouve et aussi un peu émouvante. A three hour epic conclusion to nearly two dozen films with hundreds of characters? Yeah it was alright. This will mostly be poorly constructed and random thoughts as I'll update when I think about it more. Avengers: Endgame really is a proper part 2 to Infinity War. Everything left off from there is picked up here. People are now dust bunnies and everyone else is packing a sad. The inevitable goal is to undo all this and of course they succeed. I don't know if anyone on Earth thought the great ending from the last film would stick. The trick to all this? Time travel. It's pretty bold to properly introduce it this late in the game, but this is sci-fi/fantasy fare, so whatever. The time travel doesn't really make any sense, even after several scenes where the characters poorly explain it. It especially gets confusing when tying into Captain America's ending, but at least that is satisfying on a character level. Just about everyone in the core cast gets some continuing or conclusive step in their story. Some work well like Iron Man's ending (plus dad talk), though some are confusing. I don't get Thor's arc right now. Why make him go through tragedy and vengeance to make him a comical bum? Then everything gets fixed so he can fuck around with the Guardians? Hadn't he finally accepted being a leader at the end of Ragnarok? Also they kill off Black Widow and it just reminded me that they never gave her any character outside of not being able to have babies in Age of Ultron. What a waste. The ending battle was the biggest thing a bunch of computers have ever made. AN endless mash of CGI and noise. It was mostly fun because I actually liked most of the characters. It was a pretty breezy three hours. Was there trimming to do? Absolutely, maybe even 20 minutes could've been scrapped here and there. I'm just glad there's some sort of conclusion here. I'll still watch these films, but I don't think anything that comes close to this scale will make me feel anything other than tired. Hopefully they just make small character-driven pictures that take a few more risks. It's not likely, though nonetheless I hope.

READ THE REVIEW IN FULL HERE Eleven years in the making, Avengers: Endgame is the finale to Marvel’s epic cinematic universe, one which has consistently broken box office records and won vast critical praise, combining its blockbuster might with the delicate storytelling and sociocultural consciousness of auteur-led cinema. It is unequivocally the series’ crowning achievement. It’s been twenty-one days since Thanos snapped his infinity gauntlet-clad fingers, evaporating half of all living beings to ash. Such massive existential trauma lays the groundwork for an initially sombre tone, the Avengers wallowing in despair. But once the tragic effects of Avengers: Infinity War have been explored, Endgame establishes its own story, one appropriately saturated with action set-pieces while never ignoring vital and deep character development. Unlike other ensemble pieces within the genre, Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely’s screenplay is precisely paced. Each character – and there are a lot of them – is given the perfect amount of screen time. Markus and McFeely know exactly where to subvert natural expectations; thus, while plot twists consistently surprise, they never feel shoehorned. And despite the largely existential themes explored – death, sacrifice, individual meaning – they find balance for the trademark quips and signature humour which have come to define the series. The MVP of the ensemble is Robert Downey Jr., who puts in the best performance of his career as Tony Stark, aided by a gorgeous script which gives his stony-faced character an edge of sensitivity, upholding an already cathartic climax. And let’s be clear here: Avengers: Endgame is saturated with catharsis. You’ll come away weeping. Style and content almost perfectly coalesce in Endgame, combining a well-structured narrative and rich characterisation with grand set pieces. This epic close to the biggest cultural phenomenon of our time is a resounding triumph for Kevin Feige, the Russo Brothers, and Marvel Studios. Follow us on Twitter!

As vésperas de completar 11 anos de seu primeiro lançamento, a Marvel Studios finaliza no dia 25 de abril, todos os arcos apresentados ao longo da última década. ‘That's the endgame' Tony Stark previu o título do filme lá em Era de Ultron, se referindo ao perigo que viria do espaço eventualmente. Vingadores Ultimato, título que foi dado no Brasil, vem para quebrar recordes, seja na bilheteria ou no número de pessoas chorando simultaneamente. Um filme que chega com status para se tornar maior de todos os tempos no seu gênero e permanecer nesse patamar por um bom tempo. Ao longo dos quase 11 anos de estúdio, foram 22 filmes, nem todos agradaram o público que é fanático, mas havia uma história maior sendo contada a cada filme. Em Vingadores Ultimato vemos tudo culminar em um filme grandioso, que amarra todas as pontas soltas e usa isso como alavanca para um roteiro excepcionalmente bem escrito. A direção mais uma vez impecável, é como se eu estivesse lendo um quadrinho realmente, a estética ,design de produção e até a fotografia, são retiradas diretamente das páginas. O filme tem um ritmo bom para o número enorme de personagens e para a história que os irmãos Russo querem passar. As cenas de ação são de tirar o folego e te deixar extremamente tenso na poltrona, principalmente a batalha final. As piadas e o clima leve da Marvel estão presentes e dão a quebra necessária de humor para o filme que carrega muita dramaticidade em cada um dos núcleos e personagens da história. Vemos personagens antes coadjuvantes ou que nem deram as caras em Guerra Infinita, agora ganhando seu protagonismo e mais tempo de tela, Scott Lang e Clint Barton são exemplos disso e tem papel fundamental na trama. Nebulosa é uma das estrelas do filme, a complexidade da personagem é mostrada de forma mais ampla e ela se torna o ponto chave para o enredo. Todo mundo tem seu protagonismo, seja ele de forma rápida ou não, todos tem seu tempo para brilhar, o que com certeza traz cenas que levarão os fãs a empolgação máxima na sala de cinema. (GRL PWR representadíssimo em uma cena maravilhosa) Mais uma vez os irmãos Russo entregaram o que prometeram e muito mais, então, melhor se prepararem para sentir um misto de emoções dentro de 3h00m57s que encerram uma era do cinema.

PINK ! 💓🎀 Film super entraînant avec une atmosphère enivrante et des messages philosophiques presque bien abordés ! C’est très années 80, les décors sont évidemment sublimes et de très haut niveau. Les costumes, le maquillage sont tout autant maîtrisés. La bande-son est vraiment superbe, ça s’inscrit dans la vibe disco du film tout en gardant assez de diversité pour coller à chaque passage. J’ai beaucoup aimé les moments où Lizzo chantait et conversait avec Barbie pendant la chanson. Par contre le Real World est moche, mais vraiment. Tout est gris, je peux comprendre la logique de faire une transition radicale entre le monde coloré des Barbie et le vrai monde mais on passe juste d’un monde magnifique à un monde morne et gris. Le film ne prend pas le temps de bien développer ses personnages et le rythme du récit est trop rapide, on ne s’attarde pas plus de quelques minutes sur une scène. Ce qui fait qu’il est difficile de s’attacher aux personnages, surtout Barbie parce qu’elle a un arc émotionnel intéressant. L’arc de Will Ferrell et de Mattel est très oubliable et pas forcément nécessaire au film. Le plot d’America Ferrara et sa fille : quel gros ronpiche, je n’en avais rien à cirer du début à la fin. Seule sa tirade finale sur la dissonance cognitive sur ce qu’est être une femme dans notre société est mémorable. Certains sujets sont traités un peu maladroitement mais ça n’était pas trop un problème pour moi. C’est justement ce que j’attendais le plus de Greta Gerwig, une des mes valeurs sûres : un bon traitement émotionnel. Je peux dire que celui qu’on a eu est très brouillon et ne marche pas toujours. On ne fait pas dans la finesse, on frôle même la grossièreté sur quelques passages. Certaines blagues sont remplies de buzz-words et faites pour cibler la Gen-Z ce qui donne un air faux mais ça ne concerne encore une fois que quelques répliques donc ça va. Margot Robbie est Margot Robbie, sans trop de surprises, elle est talentueuse mais rien de particulier ici. Par contre, Ryan Gosling se dépasse, il est vraiment amusant et ridicule, ça cimente sa réputation d’acteur comique pour moi. C’est lui qui a le plus retenu mon attention. D’autant plus que je ne l’avais jamais entendu chanter comme ça, pas même dans La La Land (2016), il pousse bien la chansonnette ! Sa séquence de transformation en comédie musicale à la fin est remarquable ! J’ai passé un bon moment, j’ai ri, les références sont intelligentes, des blagues justes et certains passages sont bien pensés. Je pense aussi qu’ils ont dévoilés trop de passages du film, pas les plus importants pour l’intrigue mais des blagues majeures qui font plus le même effet une fois qu’on les entendues une première fois. Pour résumer, c’est un film divertissant que j’ai pris du plaisir à regarder mais avec quelques défauts non négligeables qui ont un peu limé mon appréciation.

One thing that always brings a smile to my face is the memories of our children playing in our home. To have three daughters who all had long blond hair and the natural beauty of their mother, it came to be a natural consideration that they would receive Barbie dolls as gifts. Our girls had a pink carry case filled with these dolls, clothing, and accessories. We didn’t overthink what message this sent to them as they travelled into their teen years, where body image would become a significant issue. Ultimately, these dolls provided hours of joy for our girls, and to think I would be talking about these toys as adults hadn't occurred to me. Except the world has been taken over by a pink wave of Barbie-mania with the upcoming release of the live-action film starring Margot Robbie (Babylon) and Ryan Gosling (La La Land) as Barbie and Ken, respectively. Granted, it makes you wonder how two Academy Award-nominated actors could be involved in the Mattel-sponsored film project. That is until you see that the filmmakers are the exceptionally talented wife/husband team, Greta Gerwig (Little Women), and Noah Baumbach (Marriage Story). This surprising choice to helm this film has led to much speculation about the satirical messaging and artistic style of Barbie’s journey into self-awareness and purpose. Unlike the animated films that have defined this blond icon to generations, Gerwig’s adaptation has the central character living in the idyllic world of Barbieland. A world where everything seemingly is perfect with there being a balance of cultural representation and the ‘Barbies’ rule the community. The Kens of the community primarily serve as eye candy and try to impress the Barbies of this land. Until the central Barbie (Robbie) begins to have thoughts connected to the real world, such as death and cellulite. After a counselling session with weird Barbie (Kate McKinnon), Barbie decides to travel by toy-generated montage to the real world to find her true owner, and she is unexpectedly joined by Ken (Gosling). Yet, upon arrival, she realises that the real world is not the utopia she had expected when she left her life behind. Let's get it out of the way, I'm not the target audience for this film. I will admit this up front, but I do appreciate good entertainment regardless of the package it might be delivered in. Despite the indulgent use of pink, the over-the-top antics of the cast, and the obviously satirical nature of the humour, I did my best to enjoy this movie. Alas, I failed to find much that I enjoyed about this Barbie adventure. At first, it was difficult to put a finger on what it was about this story that didn’t sit right with me, since the initial tone of the film was manufactured joy that comes from movies about toys. Yet, nothing seemed quite right within this plasticine world despite the yearning to honour the fond memories of my daughters' youth. Also, throughout the years, I have appreciated the artistry of Greta Gerwig and Noah Baumbach, even though much of their work tends toward a darker and biting depiction of the human condition. Then it hit me that amongst this tale of fabricated dreams, the filmmakers are trying to redefine the image of the iconic doll from a poor example of body image and femininity into a potential poster child for feminism. Yet, as they attempt to dismantle the vicious nature of this world's definition of toxic masculinity and women’s self-identity, they managed to create an atmosphere of toxic femininity. Instead of offering an alternative to many of the world’s issues with gender division, they chose to replace the problems by mirroring the points on the opposite end of the sexual identity scale. They could have provided a balanced, heart-warming world where Barbies and Kens could exist in equilibrium and harmony. Yet, all they do is replace one form of oppression with another. As they unpack this messaging, something that does stand out in this screenplay is the message that men and women are different. Gerwig and Baumbach show that there is no middle ground between the sexes and despite their sardonic view of these worlds, they show that there are only two genders. Not even the Alan (Michael Cera) character can admit to being anything other than male. In this current media climate, it is fascinating to see this portrayal within the discussion of sexual politics. This might be one of the few things that I agree with about this film, but this gets me to the real challenge with this movie. Barbie (The Movie) is not for children. Unlike The Lego Movie’s mocking manner that appeals to adults and little ones, Barbie is meant for adults only. Yes, it does have a PG rating, but the filmmakers push this system to the limit with innuendo and clever wordsmithing. Despite being an unapologetic advertisement for the doll and the world that she represents, Mattel has greenlit a story that is only meant for the women who played with the dolls as children. Initially, this film feels like it is designed for all, but eventually proves to be a divisive and unappealing view of Barbieloand and reality that isn’t intended for the target market of the doll. For the sake of my family, I truly wanted to give this film the love that comes from a lifetime of adoring memories. Still, in the end, Barbie offers very little for little girls or their parents to enjoy. Reel Dialogue: The value of mothers There are many topics we could hash out about Barbie in this section, but the one I would like to highlight is the value of mothers. The most endearing character in the film is Gloria (America Ferrera), a Mattel employee struggling to connect with her teenage daughter. Her speech about the plight of women in the real world is one of the best parts of this screenplay. Within it, she unpacks the value of women, how they are uniquely created, and that each has value in the roles at home and at work. As she redefines her relationship with her daughter, this working mother shows her importance as a mentor, example, and, most notably, as a mom. In this world that places more importance on the woman outside of the home, this glimmer of hope within the overwhelming pink display shows how women are needed in their children's lives. Not that every woman in this world will have offspring of their own, but they can know that they do have an essential role in the investment of future generations. As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem. - Isaiah 66:13 God created and designed mothers to be a beautiful representation of His love for the world. This shows the importance and value of this role to humanity, and these women must be celebrated. Take some time today and show your mother how much you appreciate her today.

Embora seja um filme dirigido por Greta Gerwig (que no roteiro compartilha os créditos com o marido Noah Baumbach), a sua missão aqui nada mais é do que auxiliar a Mattel a vender uma Barbie que pode servir aos nossos tempos com a consciência do mundo que habita hoje - vire um copo com cerveja cenográfica todas as vezes que a palavra "patriarcado" é dita por algum personagem. E ainda me fez pensar como seria a "Barbie" de Amy Schumer, que ao menos tem a capacidade de despertar na gente um ódio genuíno.

Stellt euch den grandiosen LEGO Movie vor und ersetzt alle durch den Cast von Sex Education in einem viel zu lang gezogenen SNL-Sketch. Man spürt die Spielfreude. Die Meta-Jokes sind oft brillant. Vieles davon wird sich jetzt für immer in unsere Popkultur brennen. Nur alles dazwischen ist die gender-geswapte Version von Tom Gerhardt auf dem Ballermann. Und so präzise und so witzig die sozialkritischen Beobachtungen sind, so haarsträubend sind die Schlussfolgerungen daraus: Ein Geschlecht unterdrückt das andere Geschlecht. Also tyrannisiert dieses Geschlecht dann wiederum das andere - nur um als Lösung doch wieder ein Geschlecht das andere unterdrücken zu lassen. Als Lösung! Jetzt ist alles wieder gut. Wenn man wirklich darüber nachdenkt, ist das ist in der Konsequenz einer der toxischsten Filme des Jahres. Und wären die Geschlechter vertauscht, würden wir jetzt alle auf die Straße gehen. Aber hey, es ist ja nur Barbie , oder? ------------- Und weil das alles völlig falsch mansplained von dem LEGO-spielenden Typen ist, hier ein paar nachträgliche Ergänzungen nach der Eskalation in den Kommentaren: - Ich sage, dass die sozialkritischen Beobachtungen richtig und wichtig sind. Ich finde sie richtig und wichtig, weil wir alle die Benachteiligungen von Frauen sehen. - Ich interpretiere nur die Aussage am Ende als kontraproduktiv. Das ist meine Interpretation der Aussage. Das kann jeder anders sehen oder als nicht so gewichtig erachten. Für mich hinterlässt das nunmal einen faden Beigeschmack. - Das ist nicht der alleinige Grund für die 2 Sterne. Ich sage ja, dass ich mit dem restlichen Humor abseits der Meta-Jokes wirklich gar nichts anfangen kann. Und das ist bei 2 1/2 Stunden länge halt nicht meins. - Das ist eine Meinung. Die kann man richtig scheiße finden. Vielleicht sogar toxisch. Aber dass die Antworten darauf dann Todeswünsche und Entmenschlichung in jeder Art und Weise sind, ist nicht der Spiegel, den mir einige vielleicht vorhalten wollen, sondern nur selbstentlarvend. Und wie ich in dieser Review versuche auszudrücken: Unrecht mit Unrecht auszugleichen, bringt niemanden weiter.

Un film qui m’a plutôt surpris par ce qu’il cherche à raconter derrière son apparence de comédie colorée et légère. Barbie est évidemment très drôle et possède une identité visuelle vraiment réussie. Les décors, les costumes et la direction artistique donnent au film une personnalité qu’on reconnaît immédiatement. Margot Robbie et Ryan Gosling sont également excellents, avec un Ryan Gosling qui vole presque la vedette à chacune de ses apparitions. J’ai surtout apprécié le fait que le film ne se contente pas de faire une simple adaptation de la poupée Barbie. Il aborde des sujets plus sérieux sur les attentes liées aux hommes et aux femmes, l’identité et la place qu’on cherche à trouver dans la société. Cependant, malgré toutes ses qualités, je n’ai pas été aussi touché que je l’aurais voulu. Certains messages sont parfois un peu trop appuyés et le film m’a semblé perdre un peu de son charme lorsqu’il devient plus sérieux. Une comédie originale, drôle et très bien réalisée, avec de bonnes idées et d’excellentes performances, mais qui ne m’aura pas totalement convaincu.

Ryan Gosling! Filmin tek yıldızı o. Yoruma geçelim. Greta Gerwig o kadar fazla şey denemiş ki bu filmde tam olarak ne anlatmak istediğine kendisi de karar verememiş.
