Margot Robbie yine oyunculuk yapmamayı tercih etmiş ve kendisini sergilemiş. Uzun zamandır bunu tercih ediyor. Bana kalırsa bu film içerdiği onca eleştiriyle birlikte çocuklara da hitap etmiyor. Sıkılıp salondan çıkmak isteyecekler bence. Hitap ettiği kitle daha çok genç kesim olmuş. Genele hitap etmesiyle çok gişe yapacak, çok kazanacak ama bunca pr kampanyasından sonra öyle akıllarda bir efsane olarak kalacağını da düşünmüyorum. İzle ve unut. Öyle bir film olmuş.

Bu film çıkmadan önce film hakkında o kadar sert düşüncelere sahiptim ki kendi kendime “sanırım ben bu filmi asla beğenmeyeceğim” tarzı düşüncelere kapılmıştım. Çünkü filmin tanıtım süreci en azından bence o kadar kötü yapıldı ki filmin ciddiyetini ortadan bir anda kaldırdı ve çok gereksiz büyük bir beklenti oluşturdu. Hatta filmin fragmanları bizlere filmin aşırı ciddiyetsiz bir Barbie filmi izleyeceğimizin sinyallerini adeta bağırarak veriyordu ve ben de bundan dolayı filmle alakalı pek olumlu fikirlere sahip değildim. Ancak filmi izledikten sonra kendi kendime yarattığım bu ciddiyeti kırmam gerektiğinin farkına vardım ve filmi daha güzel değerlendirebildim. Barbie, bir Barbie filmi nasıl olması gerekiyorsa o havayı sizlere gayet iyi veren, eğlenceli, komik ve düşündüren bir yapım olmuş. Özellikle filmin 2. Yarısı anlatı yönünden epey güçlü ve hayatını Barbie oyuncakları ile geçirmiş insanlar için oldukça kıymetli sahnelere sahip. Bu açıdan filmi her ne kadar beklediğim derecede kötü bulmasam da çok gözüme batan birkaç gereksiz sahnesi ve yer yer kendi beceriksizliğinden doğan ton tutarsızlıkları nedeniyle filme çok bayılmadım. Ki zaten film başta çok tuhaf bir ton ile açılıyor ve ilk yarım saatinde olayları çok plastik bir hale sokuyor. Bu da doğal olarak sizi filmde yaşananları hiçbir şekilde ciddiye almamanız gereken bir psikolojiye sürüklüyor ama film 2.yarısında olaylarını öyle bir noktaya getiriyor ki Barbie’nin temsil ettiği bir takım klişe şeyler filmin çok ciddi birer teması haline gelmeye başlıyor. Özellikle Barbie’nin popüler kültüre ve insanlara kattığı şeylerin farkına vardığı sahneler filmin en vurucu anları ve film buralarda anlatı olarak çok sağlam bir temele sahip. Daha da üstüne günümüzün çok klişe sayılan bir takım bakış açılarıyla film çok güzel bir dil ile dalga geçiyor ve seyircisini epey eğlendiriyor. Bu yerlerde de film hem kendi seviyesini hem de espri anlayışını çok iyi bir noktaya taşıyor ve hayranlarını en azından bence çok memnun etmeyi başarıyor. Ayrıca Margot Robbie ve Ryan Gosling rollerine öyle yakışmışlar ki izlerken epey hoşuma gitti ve beni epey eğlendirdi. Özellikle Ryan Gosling Ken rölünü o kadar benimsemişki kendi başına filmin bazı noktalarını çok güzel sırtlamış. Aynı cümleleri Margot Robbie için de söylemek oldukça mümkün. Özellikle filmin kendisiyle ilgili dalga geçtiği kısımlar filmde epey eğlenceliydi. Zaten filmin genel oyunculuk performansları ve tercihleri epey başarılı. Herkes üstüne düşüne fazla fazla yerine getirmiş. Ancak filmin ilk yarısı çok sinir bozucu bir takım kararlara sahip olduğu için film tam potansiyeline ne yazık ki benim gözümde ulaşamıyor. Özellikle açılış sahnesinin tonu o kadar sinir bozucu ki öykündüğü filmin hayranı olan ben bu sahneye epey sinir oldum. Çünkü film esinlendiği eserin hem bütün ciddiyetini bozuyor hem de onun sayesinde kendine çok güzel bir temele sahip bir sahne katıyor. Yani filmin çok ikon olmuş olan açılış sahnesi bildiğiniz çalıyor ama esinlendiği eserin ciddiyeti kadar ciddi bir ton sunmadığı için bu kullanım çok yalan olmaya başlıyor. Filmin ilham aldığı filmi özellikle söylemek istemiyorum çünkü bence bu olay filmi izlerken deneyim edildiği zaman daha kıymete binecek bir sunum. Ki buna benzer filmde çok fazla gönderme hakim ve bunların neredeyse hepsi espri amaçlı. Bunun dışında film arada sırada tonunu tam ayarlayamıyor ve bir yandan çok ciddiyken aniden komedi yönünü çok gereksiz derecede yüksek açıyor. Bu da filmin hangi noktasının ciddi hangi noktasının komedi olduğunu biraz bozuyor ve izleyiciyi arada bırakıyor. Bunun dışında filmin çok büyük bir eksisi benim açımdan bulunmuyor. Özet olarak Barbie hem kendi hayranlarına hem de genel izleyiciye gayet güzel, eğlenceli ve anlamlı bir eser sunuyor. Filmin öncesinde çok korktuğum bir takım konuları film gayet iyi kotarmış ve bir Barbie filmi nasıl güzel olabilecekse ona yakın bir ton tutturmayı başarmış. Ancak bence bazı yönlerden çok daha iyi olabilirdi ve üstüne bi kademe daha konulabilirdi. Yine de bu haliyle de sinemada keyifli vakit geçirmek ve bir takım şeyleri küçük de olsa sorgulamak adına güzel bir tercih. Filmin yönetmeni Greta Gerwig beni hayal kırıklığına uğratmadığı için ben oldukça memnunum. Bu hafta Barbie mi Oppenheimer mı sorusunun cevabı ise bence net bir şekilde Oppenheimer çünkü ben basın gösterimi olmasa sanırım bu filme sinemada gitmezdim. Sizler de eğer sadece bir tane filme gidecekseniz tercihinizi bence bu yönden yapın çünkü internete düştüğü zaman keyif anlamında pek bir kaybınız olmaz. Ancak karar burada tamamen sizin. Görülmeye değer gibi. 6.5/10

Spirited, inherently hopeless effort to reconcile all the competing imperatives of making a live-action Barbie movie in the year 2023. It's knowing prefab camp that both revels in and loudly interrogates the retro appeal of Barbie. It's representationally inclusive while gently acknowledging that Mattel's forays into diversifying Barbie were, of course, financially motivated. It bites the hand that feeds (plays?) by pointing out the gender disparity within a company with a predominately female consumer base, while also covering for that company by making it look hip and self-aware enough to cop to its disparities. It nods to everything bad that's ever been said or written about Barbie as an iconic product even as it essentially gives everyone permission to forget all that and have fun. (Apropos the Kubrick reference of the opening scene, its subtitle could be How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bombshell .) It's practically the textbook definition of corporate feminism, but it knows that too, of course, and is earnest in using the platform of a big-budget toy commercial to speak to the audience about the patriarchy; there's a big speech that recalls the one Laura Dern delivers in Marriage Story , which makes me wonder if Baumbach counterintuitively wrote this one or if Gerwig helped him write that one. Even its lionization of the woman behind Barbie comes with an asterisk. The whole thing is animated by neurosis more than joy, which is what I found most interesting about it: Is there a little of Gerwig's offscreen wrestling with the assignment in Barbie's onscreen existential crisis? Wish it was a little funnier.

Gün saydığımız Barbenheimer seferinin ilk yarısını bu sabah tamamladım. Alışılagelen eleştirel söylevimden bir nebze saparak film hakkındaki düşüncelerimi; olumlu & olumsuz kısımlarını maddeler halinde sayarak, anlayacağınız direkt artı/eksi tablosuyla ele alayım dedim. Öyleyse pozitif başlayalım. + İçinde envai çeşit Barbie, Ken (ve bir adet Allen)’ı barındıran Barbieland dudak uçuklatan bir prodüksiyon dizaynına sahip. Barbie’lerin evlerindeki minik detaylara bayıldım; setler, hayali bir Barbie dünyası yerine gerçektende çocukların evlerindeki oyuncaklara benzetilmiş. Bu nedenle buzdolabındaki materyaller basit bir çıkartmadan, havuz ise yer kaplamasından ibaret. Arabalarda motor bile yok. Karakterler yemek/ içecekleri gerçekten mideye indirmektense tüketiyormuş gibi yapıyorlar. Bu hayali dünyanın fizik kuralları her ne kadar gerçeküstü olsa da; mekanlardaki her ayrıntı, yalnızca gerçek bir Barbie oyuncağında bulacağınız unsurlarla dolu. Kostüm tasarımında da muazzam bir iş çıkarılmış. Her Barbie’nin, zamanında satışa çıkan gerçek bir oyuncağın kıyafetini giymesi ve elbiselerin sahneler boyunca sürekli değişiklik göstermesi takdir edilesi bir çalışma olmuş. Aktörlerin kusursuz saçından bahsetmiyorum bile. Şüphesiz ödül sezonunda bu dallardan en az birisinde rakiplerini yerle bir edecektir. - Vizyona adım atmadan öncesinde seyirciye merak aşılayan aktörler; filmin basit bir oyuncak bebeğin hikayesinden ziyade çok daha derin anlamlar içerdiğinden, yaşam & ölüm konseptini felsefik bir perspektifle incelediğinden bahsetmişlerdi. Hatta Ryan Gosling, Barbie ’nin kariyerinde okuduğu en iyi senaryo olduğunu dahi belirtmişti. Yani, o kadar da uçmaya gerek yokmuş. Barbie her ne kadar mevzubahis konulara parmak bassa da, temasını belirtme şekli hem silik hem de oldukça bariz. Biraz daha açmak gerekirse; film, varoluş krizine değinerek bizlere ölümü hatırlatırken sonrasında ise küçük bir kızın mutsuzluğuna zıplayarak insaoğlunun kapitalist çıkarları gereği kendini mahvetmesine ışık tutuyor. Hemen ardından kadın olmanın ne demek olduğuna ve bu etiketin getirdiği mazur görülemez beklentilere değinerek kadınların çektiği zorluklara parmak basılıyor. En sondaysa kadınlardan da öte, insan olmanın ne olduğu sorgulanıp bir kişiyi tanımlayan olgunun ne olduğu araştırılıyor. Anlayacağınız bukalemun gibi perde başına tema değiştirmekte; ilk önce yaşamak , sonra kadın olmak , en son ise insan olmak irdeleniyor. Yalnızca bununla da kalmayıp odaklandığı mevzuları da kör göze parmak bir şekilde işlemekte. Örneğin kadın olmanın zorlukları; dünyamızdaki toplumların davranış biçimlerinden değil, doğrudan bir insan tarafından bu zorlukların haykırılmasıyla dile getirilmekte. Üçüncü perdedeki Ruth sekansı (spoiler vermeden), her ne kadar duygusal ve manâlı bir an doğursa da, aynı zamanda o esnada verilen mesajlar fazlasıyla göze sokuluyordu. + Fragmanlarda gösterildiği için rahatça bahsetmek gerekirse, Ken’in dünyaya geldikten sonra ataerkilliği keşfettiği sahneler ağız dolusu kahkahalar attıracak noktalarla doluydu. Feminen bir dünyada geçirdiği onca zamandan sonra bizim dünyamızdaki erkeklerin dominasyonunu ve masküleniteyi öğrendiği anlar, belki de filmin en komik parçalarından birisi olabilir. Drama janrasında bolca kol gezen Ryan Gosling, umarım bu yapımdan sonra daha fazla komedide yer almaya başlar. Fazlasıyla satirize edilmiş karakterine kazandırdığı kişilik, paha biçilemezdi. Meme lorduna dönen Beyciğimin sunduğu performans sayesinde, internet birkaç ay daha meme lerin ekmeğini yer herhalde. - İki saatlik süresine rağmen ikinci perdeden itibaren birçok kez esnediğim ve gözümü ovaladığım anlar oldu. Bir noktadan sonra tempo yönetiminde topallamaya başlayan Barbie , ikinci yarısında fazlasıyla kestirilebilir bir kapanışı takip ediyor. İlk yarıya doğru ilerlerken Barbie ile Ken’in yollarının ayrıldığı bir sahneye şahit oluyoruz, bu sahneden itibaren filmin geri kalanı, en azından benim gözümde oldukça barizdi. Bu noktadan sonra tek yapmam gereken şey, tahmin ettiğim olayların yaşanmasını beklemekti. Sürpriz faktörünü yitirmesinden ötürü son perde sakız gibi uzamaya başladı. Nihayetinde film, beni bitişe doğru oldukça yormayı başardı. + Barbie ’nin iki sinefil tarafından yazıldığı, sahneler boyunca durmaksızın maruz kaldığımız film göndermeleriyle rahatlıkla anlaşılıyor. İlk önce 2001: A Space Odyssey , ardından The Godfather , sonrasında The Matrix … derken bir anda Zack Snyder’s Justice League ! Filmin sinemaya duyduğu saygıya şapka çıkartıyorum. - Film başlamadan önce Mattel bu fırsatı kaçırmayarak yapımdan bağımsız reklamlar sıkıştırmış araya. TLC’nin Barbie programından tutun oyuncağın apaçık tanıtımına kadar onca anlamsız reklam izledik. Filmle pek alakası olmayabilir ama bu durum, beni uyuz etmedi desem yalan olur. + Salondan çıktıktan sonra hemen Spotify listesine saldırmasam da, müzikler fena değildi. Dua Lipa ve Billie Eilish’in parçalarını gayet beğendim, sahnelerle oldukça uyumlu ve duyusal tesiri arttıracak niteliğe sahip. Nicki Minaj’ın parçası ise… eh işte, Anaconda ablam yine kendi kulvarında yapmış bir şeyler. Peki film sinemada izlenmeli mi? Bu soruyu cevaplamak inanın bir hayli zor. Çünkü okuduğum eleştirilere göre azınlıkta görünüyorum. Bu nedenle direkt “Gitmeyin!” demek, izlediği takdirde beğenecek arkadaşlara haksızlık olur. Sadece bilin ki, bu film bahsedildiği kadar derin anlam içeren veya bir yetişkinin zihnini gıdıklayacak unsurlara yer vermiyor. Hatta bütününe bakacak olursak, çocuk filmi olduğu gerçeği daha ağır basıyor. Filmi bu Cuma bir daha izleyeceğim; eğer puanım 6/10’un üzerine çıkarsa, bilin ki filme olan bakış açım bir nebze değişmiş ve Barbie ’ye daha çok ısınmışımdır. Şu anda Barbenheimer yarışmasında ikinciliği elde tutuyor, hangi rakibin galibiyeti elinde tutacağını hem yarın Oppenheimer izlediğimde hem de Cuma iki filmi de tekrardan izlediğimde belli olacak. Barbie ’nin ‘Yılın En İyi Filmleri’ listesinde kaçıncı sırada olduğunu merak edenleri de buraya beklerim: boxd.it/lPB7U Yarın ki Oppenheimer incelemesinde görüşmek üzere 🙂

Fui ver esse filme hoje. Nem sei como começar a falar sobre ele. Fazia um tempo que eu não ia ao cinema e ir justamente pra ver esse filme foi uma experiência única! Sair toda de rosa e ver várias pessoas da mesma forma, como se um vírus extravagante e rosa tivesse contaminado 2/3 das pessoas daquele Shopping, isso definitivamente precisa acontecer mais vezes. Entretanto, não foi nem de longe um dos meus filmes favoritos de críticas ou o melhor sobre empoderamento feminino, pelo menos não na minha opinião. É um filme bom, em geral, diálogos engraçados, músicas envolventes e uma construção visual muito bonita. Não considero ter perdido meu tempo ou dinheiro vendo esse filme, não sei se veria novamente, mas afirmar que o filme é horrivel e inassistivel, eu não diria. No fundo todos nós sabemos que a maior partes desses "críticos" são pessoas com a mentalidade fechada que não entendem e nem querem aceitar a mudança, os filmes antigos irão continuar ali para você os rever, embora, é preciso aceitar a mudança! As coisas mudam e agora é uma nova geração que não agem e nem pensam da mesma forma, não é sobre gosta, e sim, respeitar a mudança. Francamente não entendo a crítica imensa em cima, é simplesmente um filme voltado para o público infanto juvenil feminino em tom de sátira e rosa, não tinha como esperar um filme estilo Christopher Nolan que batesse de frente com a intelectualidade de Opphenheimer. Outra coisa extremamente insuportável, é a comparação entre ambos os filmes que são totalmente diferentes e abordam assuntos divergentes, não tem lógica compara-los só por saírem no mesmo dia, fora que vai muito de gosto pessoal. Enfim, é um bom filme com uma tentativa de mensagem super interessante que a acabou falhando em algum pontos, mas em geral foi um filme divertido. Sendo bem sincera eu nem estava esperando muito de Barbie e acho que por isso não me decepcionei tanto. E por último vou deixar claro que só fui assistir Barbie por causa do Ryan Gosling que aparece 70% do filme sem camisa. I'm Just Ken!!!

Bold, disruptive, and piercingly relatable. Co-writer and director Greta Gerwig has cemented a grounded pattern with her style of filmmaking and even in the midst of a massive and universally known brand such as Barbie, she doesn’t waver from what she does best which is highlighting topics that are relatable to the viewer on the simplest terms of humanity. The premise is imaginably quirky and the performances are exaggerated at the highest level, creating a parodic energy that evolves into an emotional journey. The cast is incredible on paper and even better on screen with three standout performances representing the major emotions that are portrayed throughout this film. Margot Robbie captures the energy of reality and discovery through heartbreak and triumph while Ryan Gosling is complementary in his unexpected performance of perfect comedic timing. America Ferrera balances the ensemble with honest dialogue and a powerful monologue to reveal the underlying message that is buried until the third act. With additional attention to the music, the set design, and the fourth wall, this ambitious and HEAVILY marketed project lives up to the anticipation that viewers have had since the day it was announced.

i try to go into movies without any expectations, but i am only human, just as ryan gosling is only ken. this has been my most-anticipated release ever since greta gerwig became attached to the project. the review embargo has dropped so i can finally speak my mind! spoiler free, for now. i spent a lot of time thinking about what this film could be before i got the chance to see it last week. if you’re familiar with gerwig’s filmography, then you know the themes that take up space inside of her and shine through all of her work, and you’ll find them here as well. the meditation on what home is and where one really belongs, or if they ever truly belong anywhere, is present, as it was in lady bird and mistress america. so is, of course, the focus on the complicated inner lives of women, particularly in regards to the relationships that they have with other women, and how those relationships change them, as seen in everything she’s ever played a part in making, but most notably in frances ha and little women (2019). there’s also the certain kind of spirituality that gerwig always brings — barbie in particular almost feels mythic somehow, like the hot pink-doused, glittery, fringe-pants-and-sparkly-cowgirl-hat wearing younger second cousin of homer’s the odyssey . everything thematic about the film was satisfying to me. the specific physical journey that is taken, and the way that it plays out, however, was surprising. and, at first, in the moment, while sitting in the screening room at the warner bros. discovery office in hudson yards on the afternoon of july 12, i wasn’t sure if it was surprising in a good way. it took me a moment to get on board with the specific way it was being told. this must be because i’ve spent much too long thinking about how i would make this movie, and that is my own fault. i was definitely not surprised in a bad way, but it’s taken me a week to get used to what the movie is and not what i wanted it to be. and what it is is something really beautiful — something i will revisit again and again and that i know will resonate and deservedly delight a massive audience. and, if we’re destined to live in an IP-driven cinematic landscape, i hope barbie makes a billion dollars and that all my favorite girl-coded (whatever that means) childhood-nostalgic properties have mature, extremely fun movies made about them. more than that, i hope movies stay this colorful and silly and heartfelt and entertaining and original. and now i am really looking forward to seeing it again in theaters with new eyes that know what exactly is coming next 💖

Hi Barbie, I'm embargoed 💖 EDIT: I don't want to start with the discourse, especially as I saw this at the UK premiere before there was even a whisper of the film's quality, and I only brought my own hesitance over anything girly, but I truly can't see what would draw people's ire. Except maybe in the same way EEAAO did for those who couldn't find its wavelength, no crime, but a difficult fate when this film is going to define the summer as EEAAO also did. And that relates to my own opinion on Barbie . A film that is not going to change the face of the feminist cinema, nor is it a radical takedown of consumerism. But still can have fun with both ideas, an old style comedy almost in the style of those absurd IPs we got in the late 90s. Robbie and Gosling are at the top of their comedic game, and Gerwig keeps her hand on the wheel despite the jump to Hollywood proper. It's not a film for everyone, but if even my reluctant, pink hating self can find something worthwhile, it's highly likely others will. All other thoughts I'll save, as I'm due to see this at least four more times.

Devemos dizer que queremos ser saudáveis, mas também temos que ser magras. Devemos ter dinheiro, mas não podemos pedir dinheiro, porque é grosseria. Devemos ser chefes, mas não más. Devemos liderar, mas não detonar as ideias dos outros. Devemos adorar ser mãe, mas não falar dos filhos o tempo todo. Devemos ter uma carreira, mas também cuidar sempre de outras pessoas. Barbie is directed by Greta Gerwig and stars Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling as the main leads. I am so excited to give you this review early, so here is my thoughts on the highly anticipated movie Barbie. I’ve been a fan of Gerwig’s work since Lady Bird which is an absolute one of the best coming to age films in the last couple of years and Little Woman is definitely one of the better literature work in the last decade. This is Gerwig’s first time directing a full on pop culture property on a toy franchise that has been going on for 70 + years. Going in for this movie I was extremely excited and had really high expectations, after the movie finished I have confidence that Greta Gerwig is a 3 for 3 director and proves to be one of the strongest  young female voices in Hollywood today. Margot Robbie gives one of her best performances as Barbie and her character study is absolutely needed for female characters in films today. Early Test Screenings for this film has been praising Ryan Gosling Ken’s Performance calling it the best performances yet and I absolutely agree. Ryan Gosling as Ken is gonna be memed heavily and will recieved a cult following of his performance and hopefully snag a nomination for supporting actor because he’s incredible and stole the show and of course his performance is based on me. Other performances in this film including America Ferrera as Gloria is very good and there is an important scene in this film in which she delivers on her performance. Other performances like Emma Mackey, Simu Liu, Hari Nef, Kate McKinnon, Issae Rae, Dua Lipa and all of the performances in the film gives their characters a lot of personality and Will Ferrell’s best performance in almost a decade. The Costumes and Production Design captures the imagination as if you were playing a Barbie doll with a doll house and with Rodrigo Prieto cinematography makes this one of the most colorful and vibrant colors inspired by 1960s fashion and films that is heavily inspired by the projects from Jacques Demy from the French New Wave and of course The Wizard of Oz. The 2nd half of the film I absolutely loved and the way how Gerwig and Baumbach’s amazing screenplay gives a lot of risks on its ambitions that I think it’s not really for everyone so it will be mixed on but I absolutely think it contains one of the best scenes for a comedy film in a very long time with a 3rd act that has a lot of emotions yet contains one of the best sequences of the year. Gerwig’s complete reimagining of Barbie gives what we love about the late 90s and early 2000 comfort chick flicks but also delivers a serious deep message that will definitely not leave the audiences mind when the film is over. Barbie is one of the best movies of the year and probably the best feel good comedy in a very long time. Please support Barbenheimer and Oppenheimer when it hits theaters July 21st. Break it down to its constituents and we’re left with a largely asinine riff on the drug film. Junkies on the road, relapsing, rationalizing, self-destructing (and then mutually destructing); lost innocents in revolt against the world. Guadagnino twists it by making the addiction hereditary – he leans very much on the image of sexuality, to such a degree that this film sometimes takes on the image of a crude queer metaphor; he twists it further by making his addicts sadistic flesh-eaters. Despite some early pains in establishing a ‘grounded’, even ‘ethical’ approach to an obviously impossible problem (how can one eat the flesh of others without causing inexcusable harm?), Guadagnino will revel in vulgar and indulgent images of suffering: he will have his young lovers eat the body of a man not yet dead, who did nothing to deserve a torture so completely depraved. The film will later situate the blue Chalamet on a picturesque hillside, wondering if maybe he’s a bad person. His teenage-bride is quick to sooth him: of course not. This is a film whose stylistic credentials are so far removed from any kind of ethical compass that is can – in full earnest character – pose such a scene in almost direct sequence with the aforementioned brutality: and it should be noted that the moral problem faced by Chalamet is not that he brutally feasted on a man still breathing, but that he picked a man who happened to have a wife and family. (Which again becomes a rueful connexion to the queer reading: as though this pseudo-sexual encounter has broken up the model family.) The situation of the film becomes vapid: if we are to reduce it entirely to metaphor, it deals almost exclusively in soft-focus banalities; if we are to take it for its substance, it becomes indefensibly repugnant and entirely self-satisfied. Chalamet and Russell acquit themselves reasonably well (as they sit watching the cows, noting that they all have mothers and fathers); Rylance, on the other hand, turns in another insipid performance as a muttering, stuttering (stop me if you’ve heard this before) oddball, who later shifts into an unedited template of the incel rager. Rylance remains a capable actor – his recent run of Jerusalem is proof enough – but his screenwork has been dogged by a series of performances that lurch and die in the field of ‘guess the accent’. The film generally may resemble, in vague structural arrangement, Badlands ; and it may follow the rhythm of Bonnie & Clyde ; and then the visceral sensuality of Trouble Every Day but it is – much alike Gaudagnino’s Suspiria – an object almost wholly devoted to a certain kind of aesthetic presence. These people become pretty icons to situate before beautiful American vistas; their violence is represented in a kind of vulgar delight. The irony such a story would require – even buttressed against a genuine emotional register – is absent; a prime Jarmusch would have made of this material something funny and something moving. Instead we are faced with a grotesque display of beautiful people doing terrible things, and finding the heart to forgive themselves.

I was curious about this movie because of a ridiculously enticing trailer that had Leonard Cohen 's " You want it Darker " playing over it. The lyrics seemed perfect for the images I was seeing on screen : "There's a lover in the story, but the story's still the same - There's a lullaby for suffering and a paradox to blame - I didn't know I had permission to murder and to maim - You want it darker ? We kill the flame." Well, I wish I had never seen that trailer. Because, truly, nothing was remotely as good as what those 2 minutes teased and suggested. [Spoilers ahead] ( Before I start - I know that this is adapted from a book, and I've seen, as always, people say that the book was better, but know that I am not aware of the differences bewteen the original story and its adaptation.) THE PLOT : Against her father's rules, Maren, 18, sneaks out of the house to join a slumber party with 3 other girls. She must go back ' before 6AM ' she says, just in case. We barely have any time to get to know any character, our protagonist included, that she bites off her friend's finger. She comes back home, bloodied, banging on the front door. Her dad, instantly, gives her a " You didn't ", confirming this wasn't a first. " You have 3 minutes to pack before we leave and the police comes ". This clearly isn't a first. Maren and her father flee, and start a new life, all over again. But soon enough, her dad disappears. Maren is left all alone with her 'issue', with, as a goodbye, a message on a cassette to listen to, and a birth certificate with her estranged Mother's name. Here starts the girl's journey to find the latter, and herself alongside. THE CAST : Probably my very first problem with this movie - None of the characters I felt invested in, and the second roles shone way more than the 2 protagonists, Maren ( Taylor Russell ) and Lee ( Timothée Chalamet ). They are lifeless, boring, unconvincing. They have about as much chemistry as water and oil do. We're somehow supposed to believe those two love each other to death in such a short time, and while I know young love can be intense, this is not what's accurately represented here. Lee and Maren are together by default , because ' they're the same '. That's all. We don't see them having any real meaningful conversations, we just see them be . Which again, would be fine if they had that spark, but they just do not. THE SFX : The very few gory scenes are very well executed and I honestly wished there would have been more. For a movie which the literal main theme is cannibalism, there is almost none of it on screen (or off, for that matter). THE SOUND : Oh man, that fucking acoustic guitar. Those damn 4 accords we keep hearing all throughout the movie just about drove me crazy. Every time a conversation ended, or an important scene did, we had those zoom outs accompanied by that guitar trying to be melancholic. Of what , exactly ? I couldn't tell you. This movie desperately tries to be mellow, bittersweet and contemplative, but it fails in all regards. It's just slow and vapid. You should have seen the face I made when I recognized Trent Reznor 's voice at one point (in what I learned was the title song). I still cannot believe this literal genius of a composer did this score. If it wasn't for (obviously) hearing his voice; I would have never associated Reznor (nor Atticus Ross) to this movie. THE CINEMATOGRAPHY : This is the only good part of this movie, the way it looks. If you look at the trailers, it is absolutely beautiful, the dialogue sounds heartfelt, the feelings of the characters seem intense, it looks so good. Sadly, when spread accross two excruciating hours and eleven minutes, the cinematography isn't going to be enough. Despite it being gorgeous, I still have some gripes with it; to me, the filming lacked any kind of dynamism - it actually does feel like a 2h music video at times. And believe me, I love contemplative films. This one just wasn't it for me. IN THE END : Bones and All seems like a failed promise. From the moment Maren meets Lee, the movie ironically goes downhill. It wants to be controversial but just doesn't go far enough, then take that back and tries throwing us off with disgusting, shocking  characters, but they're never an actual threat. It all falls short. And every time the protagonists do something reprehensible, they are excused, justified by their ' nature ' and the very quick and basic remorse Maren sometimes shows. Their personal set of morals is discussable too; as the only person we see the couple feeding on together is a gay guy that Lee kills in a cornfield (only after sex, for some reason), but when Maren discovers he was married to a woman with a kid, suddenly, she freaks out. Ok girl. In the end, what bothers me most probably is the parallel this film obviously tries to make, using cannibalism as an analogy. The poster says " You can't run from who you are ", pretty much making them being cannibals their whole identity, making it unquestionnable, while the movie itself fights tooth and nails to make them appear desperately human. Final note : 2/10 . Bones and All had -everything-, and I truly mean everything , on paper, to appeal to me. But I found nothing enjoyable aside from the visuals, and then again, not for 2+ hours. As I often say to myself, " This would have been a great 40min short ".

The memes will lose the fact that this Taylor Russell's movie though. And while it doesn't all work. Every part that does belongs to her. Allow me to explain... Russell stars as Maren and Bones and All is her story. She is shy at school. Her father (André Holland) locks her up at night. We soon learn why. In the world of this film, based on a 2016 novel by Camille DeAngelis, being an “eater” of human flesh is a hereditary condition. It comes with a keen sense of smell which allows the eater to find others like them but for the most veteran eater, an eater can also use their sense of smell to locate homes where someone inside does not have much longer in this world. Because Maren knows nothing of her mother, she thinks maybe this necessary hunger afflicted her, too. And she traverses all over the Great Plains and Great Lakes to find her. First, she meets Sully (Mark Rylance) an older, polite eater whose sense of smell gives him the vibes of a stalker. Despite Sully’s kismet feeling, it’s those stalker vibes (he keeps his victim’s hair to braid into a rope) that puts her back on the road where she eventually meets and falls for Lee (Chalamet). The flesh of the story is the growing fondness and love between the two young eaters. Lee takes Maren on the road to find her mother and she learns more about his former life, too. Back in Kentucky, Lee has a younger sister (Francesca Scorsese) who begs for him to come home. The lovers’ road trip follows a world-building section that is full of tension and well-executed mood. The world-building is the bones of the story. The bones are eerie, and the flesh is twee. It’s a mix that doesn’t always work but the chemistry between Russell and Chalamet is so strong that each cameo (including Michael Stuhlbarg’s) feels extraneous and disruptive. (Of all the cameos in Bones & All, Suspiria’s Jessica Harper fares best as Maren’s grandmother who cannot bring herself to openly talk about her daughter.) Russell portrays Maren as guarded but warm, with a good read on others. And Chalamet has punk swagger that goes beyond his pink hair and torn jeans. Like many young punks, he’s lashing out at a self-centered world until he’s understood and forgiven. In the end, Bones and All starts to run out of gas because—while people are killed and eaten— the film never becomes a lovers-on-the-lam movie so the tension, which was so pronounced at the start, dissipates. The love story is pleasant and will surely be memed with care and admiration (so too will a cornfield rendezvous where Chalamet takes his fresh prey). But it weirdly removes a sense of urgency that they could get caught. The two sides of the story also carry different looks. The opening is full of shadows and darkness, punctuated gorgeously by streetlights and bedroom lights—the places where Maren is escaping and plunging into the unknown. Once it becomes a love story, the look of Bones and All becomes more hopeful with blue skies and open roads. There is a message about needing to accept yourself in order to love someone else, which is tried and true. But, even though there is bloodshed on the screen and gnashing teeth in the sound design, the light overtakes the darkness too much. Perhaps this is due to almost every character we meet being an eater and so the societal structure that they’ve all run away from doesn’t ever make a threatful appearance. Vampire movies, which often incorporate a love story, are usually driven by the threat of discovery. The absence of that in Bones and All, despite leaving evidence all over the Great Plains, makes it a beautiful-looking movie that becomes too devoted to repeating the same note. There is no “all,” just bones.

Es ist nicht recht erklärlich, wie, aber auf irgendeine Weise hat Luca Guadagnino es geschafft, einen ausreichend großen Teil der Welt davon zu überzeugen, dass er ein ernstzunehmender Filmemacher ist. Vielleicht, weil er selbst so verdammt überzeugt davon ist. Man lädt ihn nach Venedig ein und zeichnet ihn auch noch aus. Immerhin versucht der selbsternannte Auteur diesmal nicht Filmgeschichte neuzuschreiben, sondern begnügt sich damit, ein Buch zu bebildern. Bei "Call Me by Your Name" hat das ja immerhin ganz gut geklappt. Und Teenieschwarm Chalamet hat er auch wieder im Gepäck. Aber leider nicht James Ivory. Stattdessen diesmal wieder David Kajganech, dem wir "Suspiria" und "A Bigger Splash" zu verdanken haben. Gott, steh uns bei. "Bones and All" ist eine Verfilmung des gleichnamigen Jugendromans von Camille DeAngelis und erzählt Marens Weg ins Leben. Die junge Frau sieht sich alleine auf der Welt, nachdem nun auch ihr Vater plötzlich entschwunden ist, weshalb sie nun nach ihrer Mutter suchen will, die sie bereits nach der Geburt verließ. Das Ziel ist dabei nicht ganz klar, doch kauft sich Maren ein Busticket und beginnt die Spurensuche. Auf ihrem Trip durchs amerikanische Hinterland trifft sie allerlei Gestalten, darunter den etwa gleichaltrigen Lee, ebenfalls ein Außenseiter und Einzelgänger. Er begleitet sie auf ihrer Odyssee und die beiden einsamen Wölfe kommen sich näher. Außerdem sind beide übrigens auch noch Kannibalen, das nur für die Akten. Ja, die Geschichte braucht ein bisschen lustvolles Knabbern, um immerhin ein paar Nervenenden zucken zu lassen. Denn ansonsten ist die Coming-of-Age-Fabel hier so sehr nach der Lehrbuchschablone gestanzt, dass man vor Déjà-vus fast einen Anfall erleidet. Die beiden einsamen Seelen finden einander auf dem langen Roadtrip, kämpfen zusammen gegen ihre Traumata, doch zusammen können sie stark sein. Tolles Anderssein, Selbstakzeptanz, Emanzipation von den Eltern. Man kennt es. Auch Mark Rylance als schräger Antagonistenvogel wirkt so literarisch, dass seine Vorhersehbarkeit fast eine unglückliche Art Suspense erzeugt. Die einzige interessante Figur ist Michael Stuhlbargs Hillbilly, die große originelle Idee der Adaption, der mit seinem eigentlich Nicht-Kannibalen-Freund den Titel gibt: Sie essen ihre Opfer mit Knochen. Das ist zugegebenermaßen wirklich unheimlich, vor allem durch die aufgekratzte Ruhe des wie immer brillanten Stuhlbargs. Hillbillys sind und bleiben der größte Horror Amerikas. Wobei sie auch das Einzige sind, was einen hier überhaupt an den Handlungsort erinnert. Denn ansonsten ist Guadagninos Amerika so sonnendurchflutet, als wäre man im mediterranen Sommerurlaub. Selbst die abgewracktesten Staaten des Mittleren Westens und die düstersten Südstaaten flirren so grün wie die Toskana oder ergießen sich als malerisches Sizilien. Aber wie schon in "Call Me by Your Name" muss man es Guadagnino lassen: So deplatziert dieses Gefühl hier auch sein mag, er formt es großartig. "Bones and All" macht tatsächlich über weite Strecken Spaß, einfach weil alles so schön anzusehen ist und der Sommer einen bis ins schmackhafte Knochenmark dringt. Der Handwerker Guadagnino ist nun einmal begabt und hat zauberhafte Ideen, wie etwa ein Nachtbad im Fluss, dass nur von buntem Feuerwerk beleuchtet wird. Hätte er mit dem unerträglich prätentiös-ödem "The Staggering Girl" für Valentino Haute Couture nicht schon das Gegenteil bewiesen, könnte man in dem Mann einen der großen Mode- und Werbefilmemacher unserer Zeit vermuten. Dennoch steckt in "Bones and All" ein unleugbarer Charme der Lebendigkeit, sodass man sich durch die nicht zu peinlichen Standardsituation sorgenlos treiben lassen kann. Und dann ist da halt eben noch der Kannibalismus. Ja, was soll man mit dem machen? Natürlich kommen jetzt die großen Deutschleistungskürsler und erzählen einem was von Körperlichkeit, fleischlicher Leidenschaft und Gefahr eines verzehrenden Begehrens. Das mag ja alles auf dem Papier schön und gut sein und man spürt förmlich Guadagninos eifriges Nicken. Aber alles, was Gudadagnino fabriziert, sind Gore-Effekte. Viel Blut gibt es, natürlich, und gerade zum Finale werden die Bilder durchaus albtraumhaft. Aber das ist alles nur Geisterbahn. Guadagninos Coming-of-Age-Romanze passiert in einem völlig anderen Kosmos als die saftige Knabberarie. All der sogenannte Körperhorror ist ein weiter Sprung zurück hinter alles, was ein David Cronenberg und Clair Denis über Jahrzehnte im Kino kultiviert haben. Man denke "Trouble Everyday", an "Crash". Bei Guadagnino fühlt man nichts. Die sensuelle Vermählung von Fleischeslust und Lust nach Fleisch, von Küssen und Beißen bleibt eine bloße Behauptung. Ironischerweise wird der Film in seinen blutigsten Momenten am blutleersten. Der ganze Kannibalismus ist nicht mehr als ein Gimmick für einen sonst eher banalen Film. Dass ein solcher Budenzauber noch begeistert, verwundet wenig in einer Welt, die Ducournaus zahme Kinderei "Titane" als verstörendes Wagnis feiert. Am Ende will einem noch jemand erklären, wie wahnsinnig progressiv eine junge emanzipierte schwarze Frau als Protagonistin ist. Es ist ein Kino der Rückschritte, das Ideenlosigkeit mit angeblicher Extreme kaschieren will. "Bones and All" ist ein konventioneller Teeniefilm, den man sich mal antun kann, der aber in keiner Form das coole, anarchische Lebensgefühl vermitteln kann, das er vermitteln will. "Bones and All" ist der uncoole kleine Bruder von "Near Dark". Aber immerhin ist er noch in der besseren Hälfte von Guadagninos Filmografie. Herzlichen Glückwunsch.

It's not quite explainable how, but in some way Luca Guadagnino has managed to convince a large enough part of the world that he is a filmmaker to be taken seriously. Maybe because he himself is so damn convinced of it. He's invited to Venice and even given an award. After all, this time the self-proclaimed auteur is not trying to rewrite film history, but is content to illustrate a book. After all, it worked quite well with "Call Me by Your Name". And he's got teenycrush Chalamet in his luggage again. But unfortunately not James Ivory. Instead, this time it's David Kajganech, to whom we owe "Suspiria" and "A Bigger Splash". God help us. "Bones and All" is a film adaptation of the young adult novel of the same name by Camille DeAngelis and tells Maren's journey into life. The young woman finds herself alone in the world now that her father has also suddenly disappeared, which is why she now wants to search for her mother, who abandoned her at birth. The destination is not entirely clear, but Maren buys a bus ticket and begins her search for clues. On her trip through the American backcountry, she meets all kinds of characters, including Lee, who is about her age and also an outsider and loner. He accompanies her on her odyssey and the two lone wolves become closer. They are also both cannibals, by the way, just for the record. Yes, the story needs a bit of lusty nibbling to make a few nerve endings twitch, after all. Because otherwise, the coming-of-age fable here is punched so closely to the textbook template that one almost suffers a seizure from déjà-vu. The two lonely souls find each other on the long road trip, fight their traumas together, but together they can be strong. Great differentness, self-acceptance, emancipation from parents. You know that stuff. Even Mark Rylance as the quirky antagonist seems so literary that his predictability almost creates an unfortunate kind of suspense. The only interesting character is Michael Stuhlbarg's Hillbilly, the adaptation's big original idea, who gives the title with his actually non-cannibal friend: They eat their victims with bones and all. It's admittedly genuinely creepy, especially with the chirpy calm of the as always brilliant Stuhlbarg. Hillbillies are and remain America's greatest horror. And they are the only thing here that reminds you of the location at all. Otherwise, Guadagnino's America is as sun-drenched as if you were on a Mediterranean summer holiday. Even the most washed-up states of the Midwest and the gloomiest Southern states shimmer as green as Tuscany or paint themselves as picturesque Sicily. But as in "Call Me by Your Name", you have to hand it to Guadagnino: as out of place as this feeling may be here, he shapes it magnificently. "Bones and All" is actually fun for long stretches, simply because everything is so beautiful to look at and the summer penetrates you to the tasty marrow of your bones. The craftsman Guadagnino is talented and has magical ideas, such as a night bath in the river that is only illuminated by colourful fireworks. If he hadn't already proved the opposite with the unbearably pretentious and boring "The Staggering Girl" for Valentino Haute Couture, one might suspect the man to be one of the great fashion and advertising directors of our time. Nevertheless, there is an undeniable charm of liveliness in "Bones and All", so that one can drift carefree through the not too embarrassing standard situation. And then there is the cannibalism. Yes, what can you do with that? Of course, now the eager English students come and tell you something about physicality, carnal passion and the danger of a consuming desire. That may be all well and good on paper and you can literally feel Guadagnino's happy nod. But all Gudadagnino fabricates are gore effects. There is a lot of blood, of course, and especially towards the finale the images become quite nightmarish. But it's all just a ghost train. Guadagnino's coming-of-age romance happens in a completely different cosmos than the juicy munchies. All the so-called body horror is a far leap behind anything a David Cronenberg and Clair Denis have cultivated in cinema over decades. Think "Trouble Everyday", "Crash". With Guadagnino, you feel nothing. The sensual marriage of carnality and lust for flesh, of kissing and biting, remains a mere assertion. Ironically, the film becomes most bloodless in its bloodiest moments. All the cannibalism is no more than a gimmick for an otherwise banal film. The fact that such hype still inspires is hardly surprising in a world that celebrates Ducournau's tame kindergarten play "Titane" as a disturbing venture. For sure, someone still wants to explain to you how insanely progressive a young emancipated black woman is as a protagonist. It is a cinema of regressions that wants to conceal a lack of ideas with alleged extremes. "Bones and All" is a conventional teen film that one can enjoy, but which in no way can convey the cool, anarchic attitude to life that it wants to convey. "Bones and All" is the uncool little brother of "Near Dark". But at least it's still in the better half of Guadagnino's filmography. Congratulations.

Cannibalism is one of my absolute favorite subgenres of horror, but considering how much it has been tackled over the decades, it has never really been definitively defined. There's lots of different takes on the practice of consuming human flesh. There's the tribal approach like in "Cannibal Holocaust" and its use as a survival tactic, featured in films like " Ravenous ." There's the ghoulish variety, such as backwoods families often found in Texas and prone to murdering victims efficiently with motorized weaponry. Then you have the stealthy suburban cannibal, which is sometimes used in cheeky satyrical horror that is attempting to draw out some sort of metaphor about conformity, as in Bob Balaban's "Parents." All of these different types come with the same horrific fear that their victims are consumed and, with most of the remains housed in satisfied tummies, are never heard from again, which I always found rather chilling. But there's something else that all these types of cannibals have in common, and that is that their eating habits are always choice. They don't have to eat people, but they want to. What makes Luca Guadagnino's BONES AND ALL so unique is that it attempts to offer a purpose for these beings, giving them rules and a mythology much like vampires and other supernatural creatures that Hollywood loves to draw from. Although the characters in this film are driven by a genetic hunger that they can't ignore, there's otherwise not much supernatural about them, as Luca presents an ensemble that are a lot like us and people we may know. The film centers around Maren (Taylor Russell), an 18 year old girl who goes on the run after the latest in a string of compulsive incidents that make it difficult to make friends at school. She's searching for a family and it isn't long before others of her kind find her. There seem to be a lot of "eaters" out there in the world, and they sometimes are able to literally sniff each other out. After an introductory encounter with Mark Rylance (really making a meal out of his role), she continues on her road trip before coming across Lee, played by Timothée Chalamet. This actor who seems to be well on the path to superstardom had somewhat failed to impress me in the years following his astounding arrival in Luca's "Call Me By Your Name." It's not that he had been doing bad work since then, but perhaps I'm not as responsive to his "over it" style that so many find so compelling. But here he has something to be angsty about, and his performance works as both dangerous rebel and depressed soul searcher. He and Russell make a great pair, and the two go out into the world trying to find a home while occasionally satiating their hunger. Along the way they'll meet a bunch of colorful characters, including a memorable fireside chat with Michael Stuhlbarg and David Gordon Green. I was very happy to see a small role for Jessica Harper, who Luca coaxed out of semi-retirement for what I thought was an obligatory and respectful cameo in his "Suspiria" remake. Here she gets a quality scene which leads to an even better one with Chloë Sevigny, which is right around when the film peaked for me. This road trip movie, which frequently feels like a parody of Malik's "Badlands" but with more flesh-eating, does spin its wheels after a while and you get the sense that it's not really going anywhere. Perhaps I would have liked it more if it had leaned even more abstract and arty, rather than delivering violent thrills when we've all gotten more comfortable the love story elements. A little of Mark Rylance goes a long way here, and he can't decide if he'd rather chew Maren or the scenery. I appreciate that this film goes for some grisly gore, but it doesn't always feel like it has a purpose other than to shock us. I would have liked more discussion between characters about what they like about the taste of us. We must be pretty good if we are best consumed raw and unseasoned. (who has time to cook?) This definitely has some nasty images of body munching, which were a bit too graphic for some attendees at Alice Tully Hall to handle tonight, triggering some of the meaner audience members to giggle at the sight of the squeamish waddling down the rows towards the aisles. I feel like the film either needed more or less of its violence, because what's there feels a little matter of fact and sometimes a distraction once the film has decided the characters have been developed enough and now they need something to happen to them. For all the facts and history we get about characters early on, that goes away after a few weepy monologues but I longed for a bit more discussion that attempted to cope with how they might manage to function in society while giving into their urges. I had a lot of fun with this film up to a point, but I feel like it changes what it purports to be about and never fully recovers. Still, this is going to be a great way to avoid Thanksgiving leftovers come late November. Gobble gobble gobble.

Venezia 79 Coverage - DAY 3 Shy cannibals make for a strange and provocative piece from director Luca Guadagnino. Bones and All takes an unexpected moral step, with regret bleeding into torn flesh and skin. Taylor Russell’s understanding of the prose on hand is just as important as her portrayal of Maren Yearly, a begrudging cannibal attempting to understand her need to feed. A desire to figure it all out is at the heart of Maren’s journey, but it is up to Guadagnino to show restraint in his storytelling. An adaptation that comes through as far removed from the text it hopes to understand – Bones and All may as well be its own, unique piece that muses not on veganism but on the freaks at the feast, those looking for their individuality with the cards stacked against them. In doing that, Guadagnino prepares a littering of graphic horror elements. They are as bloody and real as the feelings Yearly has for her condition. Is it a condition? Bones and All never reveals the inner workings, just the outcome. An explanation would be futile for Maren, whose mannerisms are like a polite infected member of the 28 Days Later population. Instead, the campfire cannibal chats between Lee (Timothée Chalamet) and Yearly provide ample qualities that describe conditional impact and outcome, not cause or correlation. Their need to feed is opened well with a lingering, brief commentary from Mark Rylance, who sets out such few details that they too may as well be shrouded in mystery. But they are enough to cling to, Guadagnino has given enough detail to hold onto. To hope for more is understandable, but impossible. Rylance, with a button-clad lapel and a Foghorn Leghorn accent, provides a haunting rendition of what could happen to Chalamet and Russell. His whispered, whistling voice and provocations are lingering despite his few sightings throughout. Rylance finds a love for the role, a challenging performance that provides some clarity to the chilling moments Chalamet attempts to bring to the table. His performance is impossible to remove from this blur of Martin Sheen’s work on Badlands. A whiny and troubled character whose conditions and issues never transcend how entitled he appears. Chalamet’s work is fine enough, but it is Russell who steals the show and uses the ample work Chalamet provides as a base for her own soul-searching performance. Michael Stuhlbarg provides a brief and exceedingly creepy role too. Surplus to requirement? Maybe so. But that is Guadagnino in motion. It would not be enough to adapt, he must overcome. So much to change and so many variables to experiment with. Acoustic tracks lingering underneath horrific details. A cannibalistic cameo from Chloë Sevigny amps up the horror inevitably tied into Bones and All, which is both sparing and overwhelming with its relation to the horror atmosphere. Guadagnino attempts to rely on technical flashes and keen wordplay to build tension, but they feel bloated and move away from the thriller at the core of this. Is there a thrill in going bones and all? His adaptation and cast move toward the mental strain of coming to terms with beliefs and needs out of our control, why does his direction not follow suit? Bones and All is a functional piece that has infrequent, spotty moments to it. If you liked this review, you can read more of my work on my website, Cult Following . Can’t wait for the Timothèe Chalamet fans to eat this one up and miss the point entirely by romanticising it.

Bones and All got all the ingredients for a delicious movie meal, with Russell & Chamamlet in this coming-of-age, cannibal road trip film. Arguably, the rawness and messy nature of the plot might have been the intention after all Video Review: www.youtube.com/watch?v=7YJZskUdxzY Bones and All comes from director Luca Guadagnino, known for Call Me By Your Name, and the 2016 Suspiria remake. It stars Taylor Russel of Waves and the Escape Room films as well as Timothy Chalamet, who I probably don't have to introduce any further. Bones and All is mainly a coming-of-age road trip story with the added spice of cannibalism mixed in with a romance story and the quest to find yourself. Not having read the base material of the novel… of the same name, I can't comment on how well Guadagninoadapted the story. But at times, the characters felt quite constrained with certain moments we have to build towards whilst at other times the CMBYN energy of just floating in the present came through too. But Guadagninois really great at capturing that lost teen type of story and whenever the more plot-based story elements come into play, the film loses a bit of its quality. A big part of the film is dedicated to the proportionally frequent run-ins with other cannibals, which sometimes felt a bit overbearing, but connected to the theme of finding your own way in and outside of a new community as you grow up. Maybe idk… they also ate a bunch of people. Bones and All is not for the faint of heart with lots of blood and gore. But is somehow innocent, kind, and gentle with its characters. Giving them room to be vulnerable - maybe not with each other on-screen - but with the audience as we get to see them go on a very unique journey. Now like I mentioned before, there are a couple of moments where the plot is given a higher priority than the characters, which happens to be especially noticeable towards the end of the film and made it a considerable amount less enjoyable to me and left a bit of a twisted, sour aftertaste of the film in my mouth. Certain parts of the film are also a bit rushed but might have been part of the novel so they had to fit in here. Again, haven’t read the novel so I can’t say for sure, but just the impression I got from the pacing. BONES AND ALL is a simmer pot of teenage angst with cannibalistic tendencies and is fine entertainment, but if you are looking for a more tame, romantic version of a boy falling in love with a cannibal, you’ll have to stick with Call me by your Name.

Beautiful film. Luca did such a good job at balancing romance and horror, which are two polar opposites. The feeding scenes of the eaters were disgusting and incredibly gruesome, but watching it still felt warm somehow. Maybe it’s the muted colors and the strings that recurred throughout the film. My God, it was beautiful. I can’t believe I didn’t appreciate it as much before as I do now. Whatever they’re doing, killing and eating people, is morally wrong and just blatantly evil, but I can’t help but root for Maren and Lee. Whatever they had felt so calm and true, and they were really only like that with each other. ‘Di ko magets mga nagsasabing wala silang chemistry, to be honest kasi … kita niyo ba mga halikan scenes nila hahaha? I wanted the film to end when they had normal lives. They looked so happy. But the ending just made everything so much more painful to watch, andddd I’d watch it over and over again. It was so beautiful. What they had was bound to end eventually. Sabi nga nila, “Let’s be them for a while .” It wasn’t meant to last because they were pretending all along. I do wonder if they really had a choice, though. Maren actively decides not to eat people, but she eventually succumbs to it. Maybe cannibalism is intrinsic to them. Maybe they can stop for a while, eat their hands or whatnot in hopes of saving the people they love, but it all surfaces eventually, which is heartbreaking because it gets in the way of so many beautiful things. Or maybe… maybe they had a way out; they just didn’t know how. Siguro dito hindi magiging applicable ‘yong “if he wanted to, he would” hahahah. Ano ‘yun, final act of love niya ay ipinakain sarili niya para maging part siya ni Maren forever? From the terrifying first trailer to the scathing reviews, I knew at some point in my life I was going to watch Cats. It was too much of an anomaly, too high-budget a disaster for me to ignore, I didn’t want to watch it, I HAD to see just how bad it was. And fuck me was this an absolutely terrifying fever dream filled with an uncomfortable amount of drugs, sex and music without having any drugs or sex and too much music. I’m genuinely scarred for having seen it all the way through. Let’s start with the plot. There isn’t any. And I’m not just saying that to be funny, this entire film is 90 minutes of introductions, 10 minutes of actual story and the other 10 minutes is weird panting and gyrating. Here I’ll give you a rundown of what happens; we open with our lead Victoria being abandoned by her owners, she’s introduced to the Jellicle Cats with their Jellicle Ball – and sidenote, they never explain what a Jellicle is and why it’s important to be one despite them saying Jellicle about 587 fucking times in the first five minutes – who take her to see the cats hoping to become the Jellicle choice and live a new life in the fucking sky or something. I swear to Christ, the little plot I can recognise as a story makes me think this is about a fucking suicide cult. From there Victoria meets Rebel Wilson’s hairy cooch, Jason Derulo’s CGI bulge, James Corden’s fat arse, a couple thieving twins who I couldn’t tell if they were related or not because of the fuck me eyes they were flashing at each other, Judi Dench’s old face and Ian McKellen making Meow noises before we actually get to the Jellicle Ball in which the contestants are STILL being introduced since the bad guy – Idris Elba and his unnervingly smooth fur body – has been stealing all the contestants with magic – oh by the way there’s fucking MAGIC in this film, they kinda dropped that on you without warning – so anyone who’s still taking part in the Ball we’ve never fucking seen before, making their musical numbers an exercise in futility because I don’t know them and I don’t want to fucking know them. Those two paragraphs cover around 80% of the story, all this film has is cats introducing themselves through song for an hour and a fucking half and then getting lucky if they have anything to say afterwards. It’s not a plot, it’s a fucking 2 hour montage of people we’ve never seen before and it doesn’t stop, new characters are still being introduced with their own numbers with over half the film already done. The only time it actually works is with Mr Mistoffelees who, despite a fairly low amount of screen-time, has been shown to be a cowardly magician and needs confidence to do Big Magic, that works but it comes so late into the game that it couldn’t save the rest of this train wreck. And before anyone dares defend this film, I know it’s based on a musical and I know it’s a different medium, but Hamilton managed to tell an entire historical story with only singing, this is just cats singing about themselves without a story to give them a reason to sing about themselves. The cast is absolutely stacked with big names who are given nothing to work with, and the ones that have something are the weakest actors in the film, I feel kinda bad for Francesca Hayward who plays Victoria because she’s suppose to be our lead, our surrogate into this bizarre, fucked up world of the Jellicle Cats and she’s given nothing, out of all the speaking parts she has probably the fewest amount of lines, every face she makes has this big wondrous smile about EVERYTHING, no matter how benign, and sure she dances well but in a film where everyone is dancing that doesn’t stand out. This is Hayward’s big theatrical break and she’s the most forgettable element in the film, which ironically might save her career. Out of everyone Victoria meets during the many MANY introductions she has to suffer through, not one of them make it worthwhile to sit through their number. Jason Derolo  - who I just hate in general anyway – sings about how Rum Tum Tugger  is a fussy little cunt then screams for milk, Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer were the thieving twins who looked like they wanted to do a furry version of a Bratty Sis video, and I didn’t know they were twins until writing this review so that just knocks the film even lower for me. There was also a tap dancing train conductor who serves no fucking purpose, Ray WInstone hissing and wondering where the fuck his career has gone and Taylor Swift who even in a film filled with unnecessary sexual energy, gave off too much sexual energy. Seriously man, I got Lola Bunny flashbacks during her number. Worst of the lot was Rebel Wilson and James Corden as Jennyanyfots and Bustopher Jones respectively, I already dislike these two before going into the film and having them both talk the most out of almost any other character was a kick in the fucking dick. Wilson’s introduction was this disturbing piece where she did the most unsexy sexy poses while the camera focussed on her naked hairy body before bringing in singing mice and marching cockroaches with human faces which Jenny proceeds to eat several of when she’s not singing. Corden meanwhile sings for five minutes about being a fat fuck and eating a lot, that’s the entirety of his character, he’s fucking fat, and the fact that both of them are just allowed to skit and makes shitty jokes is simultaneously distracting from the actual plot while adding nothing to the plot either. Both of them were just playing themselves in fur suits and like I said I think both are fucking overdone anyway so I didn’t give a shit about them either way. The only people I see coming out of here unscathed are Ian McKellen and Judi Dench who both have strong enough careers to look past this blip, although Dench’s monologue at the end where she looks at the camera goes on WAY too long about how a cat is not a dog (the fuck?) and every pause makes you think that it’s finally over but no, she keeps fucking going. Jennifer Hudson as Grizabella should also be ok, despite being important to the film she only has three scenes but among those three is her version of the famous ‘Memories’ number which is unironically good, hell I’d say too good for this turd of a film. I’m also hoping that Idris Elba comes out of this unaffected, his villain Macavity is suitably villainous and his motivations generically evil enough – he wants to be the Jellicle Choice because Fuck You I guess – that Elba can work something out with the material but between nobody being able to recognise the most wanted cat in town and his own horrifying nude cat-body, I doubt he’s getting away from this thing clean. Director Tom Hooper has done a few things of note over the last few years, namely his last three films were all Oscar winners and he brought Les Mes to the big screen so I can see why he’s be chosen for this. But holy hell does he fuck this up, this has to go down as one of the biggest fuck-ups of direction of the 21st Century because while Hooper doesn’t do anything technically wrong, nothing he does is done right. Let’s get the big one out of the way; the cats look fucking weird, I knew the cats looked weird, I saw the trailer, I saw the memes, but nothing prepared me for the seeing them in full CGI horror, the first time I saw a Cat-Man clamber down a brick wall, looking like a human being contorting their body into some kind of fucking Cronenberg nightmare with a tail I realised that this was so much worse than I thought it was going to be. It’s the deepest level of the uncanny valley I’ve seen since The Rock in The Mummy Returns and that was 18 fucking years before this, nobody looks human but they don’t look like a cat either, they’re a disgusting hybrid of the two, these vaguely human looking faces pasted onto what looks like skin-tight cat-suits made with actual cat flesh, it NEVER sits right with you. What makes it even more uncomfortable is that there seems to be no rhyme of reason to the clothing, a few cats wear clothing but most of them are nude and some of them even take off their clothes making them nude and I’m left wondering if this is just a nudist colony with lax rules or if everyone is suppose to be naked and we’re just suppose to accept it. I know I shouldn’t be this focussed on naked cat people but I can’t help it, this movie has forces naked cat people into my fucking brain and given me no fucking logic about why they’re naked, hell I haven’t even touched upon the Rebel Wilson scene where she unzips her naked fur-body, as  in literally takes off her skin, to reveal a dance outfit underneath. It’s the tightness as well, I don’t know why they went out of their way to make the cats sexy but it just feels wrong, all the naked cat actors have all their curves pronounced so that every breast, every bulge, every butt covered in fur is on full display but without any form of genitals. Elba gets the worst of it because his fur colour is identical to his skin colour leaving him looking like a fucking Ken Doll with ears but not one person looks good like this. And that’s not even talking about how horny this film is, I heard the stories, I read the reviews that talked about how sexual the film was but it’s not until you’re seeing this cat people twist their bodies together, panting in unison and nuzzle into each other that you have to take a step back and realise that humans doing cat actions is trying way too hard to be sexy whilst not trying to be sexy. The Jellicle Ball is the most horrific example, it’s the hissing, the panting, the Judi Dench hairy leg spread, I honestly couldn’t tell you if the film was trying to be this sexual and went way too far or if it wasn’t trying at all and just came off that way by accident. I haven’t even touched upon the fucking music because I don’t know how to, the visual disaster overpowers the audio so much that I can’t tell if anyone actual sung during this film or not. Ok, over exaggeration, a few songs worked but only a few, the aforementioned Memories hit well and I was fine with the Mr Mistoffelees number but outside of them I really can’t remember any of the songs being any good. The opening introduction to the Jellicle Cats was upbeat I guess, I was too distracted by the CONSTANT use of Jellicle, Jennyanydots was too distracting with the human cockroaches and under-skin dress change for me to even remember what the song was. Tugger and Bustopher were both boring, end of discussion, McKellen’s small number as Gus felt like a lot of build-up for a limp-dick crescendo and Swift’s piece of Macavity trying to big him up almost worked as a villain song if I wasn’t distracted by the complete lack of Idris Elba penis. Before this film the only knowledge I had of Cats was hearing Memories here and there and the rape story from Team America, having now seen this film I know even less about Cats and I don’t want to know anything more about Cats. This is one of the strangest, most confusing, unsettling and fucked up pieces of cinema I’ve ever seen that wasn’t an intentional horror movie, I’ve never seen anything like Cats so 10/10 for uniqueness but just because nobody’s done it before doesn’t mean it’s a good idea and Cats the Movie was not a good idea. There’s no story, all we have is oversexed sexless Cat People introducing themselves for 2 hours before nothing happens and the film ends, nobody looks good, only a couple sound good, the CGI is a mess, the sexiness uncomfortable, the songs forgettable and the whole experience traumatising. I’d say you have to see it just to get the full picture yourself but honestly you’re safer avoiding this. 2/10

I watched this film three times in theatres. It was my sophomore year of high school and one of the first films I saw when the theatres reopened. Snowbanks piled outside of the theatre, making those tall industrial lampposts seem small by comparison. I begged my friends to join me to watch this film—, which I had been raving about. Not because I thought it was technically apt, not by any stretch would I make such an argument now or then. No, because I found it hypnotic. We ascended the crusted snowbanks and into the theatre. The final viewing there was only six people in the theatre. My two friends and I, and three grown men in the very back row. For the first twenty minutes or so they meowed at us, and naturally we meowed back. By the end of the film I was overcome by what I can only describe as a psychedelic euphoria. My friends and I, as well as the men danced in front of the theatre screen together—, meowing along to the music. We never spoke a word to those men, I don’t think we ever clearly saw their faces, only backlit silhouettes only further eroded by the joy of human connection. This is a moment that will flash before my eyes on my death bed. This is the high I will forever chase and nothing will ever compare. This is why I love Cats.

Im slightly biased towards cats. It was the musical that made me fall in love with musical theatre and why have such an appreciation for it. Which may sound strange since it is so hated. In my defence i was young so i was easily impressed. So i don’t hate this film. It’s not amazing either. I think its biggest problem for me is the visuals. The whole cgi human/cats plus the cgi back grounds are severely distracting. I think if the set felt more real and they were in costume like the stage musical it may have looked better. Although cats is difficult since they are cats… I think the stage costumes could have such potential and the movie’s costumes could have been a strong point. Along with the costuming, the music and dancing are strong points for this musical. I wish it allowed more space for the dancing, less close up shots. The dancing cant be fully appreciated since the cgi cat/humans are distracting. I think the better visual would help highlight this, along with hiring strong dancers and ballerinas. The plot of cats is weak. I think the movie could have taken the opportunity to add a conflict to move the plot further. Maybe adding another song or two, along with beautiful ghost. A little more about victoria and how abandoned she is, her need to fit in with these cats she has met. Another point is the script/jokes which are also weak. If the writers/director were wanting to make a cats movie, i think expanding on it rather than a straight up adaptation would make more sense. The musical itself is weak in many areas. So the movie is weak and doesn’t exactly work because what works on stage does not guarantee it works on film. I think they should have made some serious changes. My review of Cats (or A Stoner's Journey Into The Heart of Darkness) DISCLAIMER : This review is in no way an endorsement of the movie, please view at your own risk. (Mild Spoilers Ahead) So I finally find did something I had been considering for some time now. I got high and watched Cats and it nearly broke me. To preface, the choice to watch this movie on that very nigjt wasn't exactly random. If you follow me you might know that, immediately before this, I had watched a weird little gem of French cinema called Car Cemetery, a surreal punk rock "musical" mixing grimy, torturous and explicit sexual acts with messianic parable all while taking place in a post-apocalyptic junkyard. In my review of the movie I joked that it was "queerer than Cats." Not having seen Cats before and having an appreciation for strange and queer cinema, naturally I decided to put my money where my mouth is and challenge my assumptions on the matter. From the opening and throughout the first 10-15 minutes of the film I was engaged in an uncontrollable fit of hysterical laughter that seemed unstoppable despite my will to breathe. So early into the film, yet, had I already gone mad? How could this have been made with any intention other than to create a lovecraftian nightmare of fur and surreal landscapes. I believe the terror really set it about the time the Rebel Wilson Cat was concluding her number and began making unmistakeably suggestive petting motions. It was then I began to realized that all of these characters were trapped in an existential race towards death. The performers vying for the coveted "Jellical Choice" for their own reasons wanted to die. They were competing to prove which cat has suffered the most in whichever iteration of their 9 lives this was. Fear then turned to despair and however weird it was staring at Jennifer Hudson's face mapped onto a cartoonish cat body was not enough to distract me from the pain of existence that floated on every vocalization of "Memory." And then, just as it always does, the pain and suffering led to apathy. Maybe I too in some small way wanted to die, to move on from this nightmarish jest. Or maybe my hightened state of consciousness was just wearing off and I was getting bored. By the time the feline personification of Jennifer Hudson started floating off into the sunrise destined for reincarnation, I began foolishly searching for a deeper meaning to the whisical chaos of the film. Do cats experience God like humans are known to do? Does time exist as an infinite line or does it loop-de-loop over and over again until our astral bodies fade from existence. But alas the revelation in the form of Dame Judy Dench(s face on a cats body) staring into the camera and singing about addressing your cat with respect. A message which to me hearkens back to the theme of universal suffering, itself a strangely fitting echo of the words of the Great Buddha and the 4 Noble Truths, simplified to express an even more basic truth. We are all here in this reality together, and as we suffer and fight to mold our existence into something a little less distressing, we should always remember to treat all creatures with the respect they deserve. I shockingly rated this film 3 stars, because despite the unintentionally laughable moments, the uncomfortable character design, and all the many WTF moments, I still found myself in appreciation, if for nothing else, than the sheer insanity that resulted in this film. ...Oh yea, and the fact that it's queer as Fuuuuuck!
