É, eu sei o que você está pensando... "como assim???" Apenas me escute Quando o trailer de Cats saiu, eu nao tive interesse nenhum nessa bomba, mas aí um dos meus melhores amigos disse que a gente ia ver no cinema. Eu disse a ele: "-Por que você quer fazer isso??? Esse filme claramente vai ser uma chacota, uma vergonha ridícula" "-Eu sei, você não quer muito conferir esse desastre ao vivo???" E de fato, eu não tive resposta pra essa fala, então, um dia depois do Natal fomos a uma vazia sala de cinema pra assistir um filme que já nasceu morto. E foi umas das experiências mais inesquecíveis de cinema na minha vida. Por ter ido sem nenhuma expectativa de que esse filme pudesse ser bom, eu fui capaz de me divertir bastante sem levar nada a sério. A lógica irrealista (e incoerente) de Cats faz com que literalmente qualquer coisa na cena possa ficar muito engraçada por simplesmente estar ali, é como estar vivenciando um delírio de alta definição. Eu ri absurdamente de várias cenas... mas o que é engraçado mesmo é que eu pude sentir um genuíno charme no meio de toda aquela esquisitice. Eu já reassisti Cats várias vezes e os primeiros 30 minutos realmente me entretém, porque são num ritmo muito dinâmico de música e dança que, se você puder desligar o senso crítico, vai só te carregando nessa gracinha de cenas que não tem absolutamente nenhuma história a não ser gatos cantando. Mais pro meio do filme, realmente começa a ficar enfadonho e cansativo, pois o filme começa a se levar a sério, e quando ele tenta se levar a sério aí é realmente só um desastre mesmo. Tecnicamente, é um filme que de fato merece todo o chapisco. O diretor foi um maníaco que quis fazer caprichos técnicos que dificultaram a vida de todos os profissionais que trabalharam na pós-produção do filme, então esse cara merece mesmo ser avacalhado e ter seu trabalho chamado de o pior filme de todos. E é realmente curioso pensar como nomes tao pesados toparam estar no elenco desse filme. Mas sendo muito sincero, assistir Cats no cinema me trouxe uma epifania de que eu me sentia tão envolvido por aquele filme que não importava de nada que ele fosse um desastre. A sua autenticidade ressoou em mim de uma forma que no final, eu quase me convenci de que era um filme bom. Estou frisando isso para que você entenda que eu não estou defendendo a qualidade de Cats. Estou apenas dizendo que não importa ele ser ruim Às vezes, nós deveríamos só assistir mais filmes ruins e nos entregar à liberdade de não esperar nada do que estamos assistindo. Praticar o exercício de apenas nos entregarmos na experiência de uma obra, e assim percebermos que talvez, um filme ruim também possa te oferecer uma coisa boa. Um filme ruim pode ser engraçado pra caralho. No pior dos casos você ainda vai treinar mais o seu senso crítico. Hoje em dia é tão fácil ser exigente e crítico com tudo, que eu sinto que a coisa mais saudável a se fazer seria realmente, não assistir todo filme do mundo esperando que ele seja bom, mas que seja pelo menos interessante. E isso vai de encontro a uma coisa que eu quero ressaltar: A MAIORIA DAS PESSOAS JULGA ESTE TIPO DE FILME SEM NEM TER SE DADO AO TRABALHO DE VER PRA FALAR MAL. A ESTAS PESSOAS O MEU DESPREZO QUER FALAR MAL???? ASSISTA E TENHA PROPRIEDADE PARA FALAR MAL Pois Cats é um filme horrível mesmo, mas se você se permitir aceitar que ele é horrível, pode talvez conseguir deixar ele te envolver numa experiência lúdica e engraçada, ao fim da qual você vai perceber que ele é um filme ruim de fato, mas nem tanto assim pra criar caso..... Assistam mais filmes ruins, e sejam mais felizes

In the year 2026, in a world increasingly filled with fucking generative A.I. bullshit, Cats is more important than ever. It is a uniquely human piece. It is the product of decades of weird, blank check-level artists iterating on and interpreting each other's bizarre art in ways that frankly make no fucking sense. It is a film built on incredible artistic hubris. It is full of baffling choices. It is absurd that it exists at all, especially that it took so many years and so many versions of Cats for it to finally be so soundly rejected by people. I love it. I love sharing it with people, watching their reactions, explaining to them why this movie has my heart and reflects my soul. I love it. What you say of Cats , you say of me, of my family, my loved ones. I am not a believer in the existence of the butthole cut. But the mere idea that it could exist, that people might believe that it's something that Tom Hooper would've done if given the chance—the older I get, the more beautiful I think that is. There are still original artistic ideas, even amidst "safe" Hollywood choices, adaptations of adaptations, art can be made that is so unlike anything a human mind has conceived that it makes people believe in the butthole cut. Cats is so mind-blowing that it makes the inconceivable become conceivable. Thank you, Cats . Thank you to everyone in my life who is willing to watch it with me. We know each other better because of it. Thank you for caring enough to look directly into my heart.

Rebel Wilson and James Corden do improvisational comedy with all the ardor and skill of drama club kids whose families have just been taken hostage at gunpoint. Yet, everything else in this film has the feeling of watching a two hour cutaway gag from prime seasons of The Simpsons; it takes very little imagination to picture Troy McClure starring in this. When I saw this in theaters for the first time, I kept leaning over to my best friend and whispering, with unbridled exhilaration, "They made this into a movie!" Tom Hooper is not a talented director, which makes him perfect for this movie as a workmanlike, or even well made, version of this material would be forgetable to all but a handful of the most debased musical theater perverts. In Hooper's other pictures, he has a baseline level of competence more-or-less sufficient to overcome his penchant for deeply strange choices. Choices like like throwing dutch angles into his period prestige films-- or having the section of the John Adams miniseries where the title characeter goes to France mostly revolve around an elderly woman in clown make up jack off Benjamin Franklin in a tub (to be fair she could've also been milking his prostate; we don't get to see what's going on under the water). Here, however, the adulation Hooper received from his previous movies fried his brain; his hubris is archetypal. Every creative choice he makes big or small, is not merely off-- or sub-optimal-- they are objectively wrong. And that’s what makes Cats so special. There are many bad films, but they usually do some things right-- or alternatively they display a childlike lack of technical ability that reads as charming. Cats, inextricably, lands in neither category. It’s shaped like a movie. It has the bones, sinew, structure, and grammar of a movie in the way something like Birdemic or The Room never would. But despite its (mostly) quite talented cast, it's a series of wildly incorrect miscalculations that immediately begin to compound on one another and do not stop until the credits roll. I have never seen another movie like it and I watch it every chance I get. #Skimblegang

i think i have reached a point where i simultaneously find this film absolute catshit and a MASTERPIECE OF MODERN HORROR. the very thing(s) that Cats was able to achieve is something that i personally feel only its VFX team can take credit for, and maybe Tom Hooper. what Hooper and his team accomplished here was not only using VFX to generate an environment where the audience could be immersed in together with the film's characters, but also create visually stunning, unsettling and sometimes downright haunting imagery that stays in the viewers head for the days to come after a screening. the images that are produced make you feel like you're in a surreal state, almost similar to that of the work from David Lynch, and sometimes even surpassing that level of surrealism. a great example would be the scene with mice and cockroaches with human faces plastered over their bodies. the feeling of horror that this film evokes is one that is continuingly multiplied, as Rebel Wilson, Judi Dench, James Corden and many others of the cast present their immense talent at horrendous singing that sounds like a rat getting squished by a foot every 5 seconds (apparently Judi Dench can actually sing but no evidence of that could be found in this). it sounds unpleasant, yes, but it ultimately does a great job at making the audience squirm and curl up in fear in their seat (it happened to me). the cinematography is also one of the best in the cinema history, with (insert DP name here) being able to capture the film's surreal aesthetic. so is the production design, which takes audience immersion to a whole new level. sets are designed to make the audience feel as if they are at the same height of the cats, adding to the incredibly surreal experience of the film. to end my review, i would like to mention that Cats could be viewed as a terrible film, even the worst of the decade. there are plenty of reasons to think that, and it is totally up to you. but when you look at a film's intention, and at the final product, and realise that the film accomplished exactly what it set out do, in this case to cause discomfort, you know for a fact that it is truly a masterpiece. please give this underrated gem the money it lost at the box office by purchasing it on Blu-ray.

Oh, how I loathed CITY OF GOD's hypocrisy, its reliance on whizzbang visuals to thrill, all the while insisting -- quite obviously, mind you -- that guns and gangsta-life are bad, that violence begets violence. Now, were the film to glamorize the violence et al. in such a way as to woo us spectators into this life, were it to show us this life's allure rather than simply blitzing our senses with flashy, impersonal imagery, perhaps then I wouldn't find the film's pretty well-intentioned ethics so dishonest and offensive. What so many contemporary filmmakers keep refusing to acknowledge is that the individualization and humanization of all things morally abhorrent actually makes for a much more recognizable and truthful and scary reality than presenting some sort of tautological reality in which hoods are just hoods because they're hoods.

Can we actually find value in a film that while yes shows the violence people go through when their material needs aren’t met, but doesn’t actually fully call out the cause of the violence? I don’t think so. Especially when the violence towards the men, women, and children is shown as just a symptom and not actually done tactfully. To not have any discussion about the cause of the violence is because of state and police violence, because of class systems, racism, and sexism is irresponsible. Vague pointing at police is not enough. This film says violence begets violence and that right there is the most violent part of this film. These people deserve more. And if all we do is witness the violence can we say we are any better? I don’t think so.

I can’t imagine many of the people who live in The City Of God at the time actually saw this theatrically. And I imagine they would find this distasteful. This is all quite gauche and feels exploitative of real poverty and the trap of poverty. The film deals with race quite strangely as well in a way that made me feel a little bit uncomfortable. Im not really a fan of the style of this either, it’s all very flashy but it kind of makes the characters never feel fully realised. They don’t feel like real people because the movie is more interested in being stylised poverty porn exploitation than a story about people. The idea of gazing at disproportionally black poverty and violence and killing is not interesting to me. Especially when it isnt made for or by the community it is depicting the suffering of. The way death and dead bodies are handled in this film intentionally lacks a level of weight i think to alienate people and upset them. But an image  containing only viscera  divorces the humanity of death and turns it into a spectacle to gaze at. If this came out in an English speaking environment i think people would be more critical of this. Most English speaking audiences don’t really watch films in other languages. I think there is an element of this being an incredibly easy to understand narrative and stylistically familiar enough that more people would give this a shot as a “foreign film”. Which i think lends to a level of exoticism to how some people interact with and engage with the film. Of the few negative reviews i have bothered glancing at a lot of them seem to come from Brazil. There are other crime films i share this criticism with. However there are still several crime films that feel connected enough to the communities depicted in them, to where I feel they are less problematic. The gaze and regard in which this film is held in to me reads as somewhat colonial. The Auteurs and audience domination and extraction of respect, life and humanity in exchange for a narrative that allows people to have their “Harrowing” movie where they get to watch vicariously through an audience surrogate. Where is the framework of media analysis with the response to this film? I genuinely think audiences collectively should scrutinise this film so much more. During my film course at uni there have been several films we have seen where we interrogate how we felt about the film we just watched, we process what it was saying, what it meant, and even at times analysed where the point of view of its conception came from. And sometimes this encompassed the ethics of a film’s conception. And oftentimes this inherently led to the concepts of class dynamics and racism. This is a film that is quite frankly begging for this level of interrogation. And the overwhelming majority of people simply don’t care enough to analyse how the film made them feel the way it did or what it has to say about the context in which the film was made in.

City of God (2002) is a Brazilian crime film directed by Fernando Meirelles & Kátia Lund. Written by Bráulio Mantovani. Based on the novel of the same name by Paulo Lins. Loosely based on real life events. Academy/Oscar nominations: Best Director, Best Original Screenplay, Best Cinematography, Best Film Editing. It follows the story of a bunch of boys becoming gangsters & criminals in the slums of Rio called Cidade de Deus aka City of God. I'm probably getting shit for the negative review but I didn't like this film. If I knew what it was about I wouldn't have seen it. I already hate seeing white men gangsters in all those mafia gangster films & seeing little boys holding guns are a whole new level & it discomforts me. Its a scary depiction of the people who live in City of God. Personally can't comment on the realism of the depiction but I've seen some negative criticism from Brazilians themselves who say that the film brought a negative image towards City of God. I guess it did cause after seeing this, I do not wanna visit Brazil. The cinematography & editing were both nominated & to me, they were inconsistent with both aspects. The lighting was perfect in some scenes & really terrible in others. Same for editing. I don't see why it was nominated. The performances were great from everyone but none really stood out for me. Its an ensemble cast & the film didn't have a clear focus on anyone. I wasn't a fan of the narration by one of  the characters because how the fuck does he know everything? The pacing is fast but there is a lot happening & the film crammed too much characters & background on each of them in 2 hours. It really felt like a documentary instead. I was literally begging for the film to end by the time I hit the 1 hour mark but there was another hour to go. This would work better as a TV series or a documentary where viewers can actually connect with the characters on an emotional level. Fun Fact: The film was not actually shot in Cidade de Deus slum, as it was too dangerous. It was shot in a neighboring, less dangerous area. No quote. eddictionz rating: 3/10 = Bad/Just Don't Bother.

To be perfectly honest I'm currently unsure how to write this review because I'm still utterly baffled as to how City of God has been elevated to, pardon the joke, a god-like status. I can respect Meirelles for the brutal reality he's shown on screen and I found a few of the performances decent, but for the most part I found the film completely unwatchable for both it's disjointed narrative and obnoxious visuals. To begin I hated the way City of God handled it's multiple story lines. The film opened with a half an hour segment that features the protagonist's brother, a segment of the film that doesn't actually affect the rest of the story besides setting up the Lil' Dice character. Seeing as later in the film Lil' Dice gets reintroduced to us as Li'l Zé, with a whole little montage of Lil' Dice's experience in the hood, that rendered the opening 30 minutes completely pointless from a narrative point of view. The two biggest things I didn't like about the multiple narratives would be the constant narration from Rocket and how abruptly the stories would intertwine. First off, character narration is my biggest gripe about any movie, and it's got all the traits I hate about it in this film. Characters are introduced to us via an impersonal freeze-frame voice over monologue, rather than giving us a natural introduction through dialogue. Narration is used to mask progression in time, rather than simply showing us a montage of events. The narration is delivered in an extremely dry and emotionless manor, which becomes very annoying to listen to. Exposition is frequently delivered to us via voice over, like the character introductions, rather than just giving it to us subtly through dialogue. I feel like I have to write this in every review that features narration. A character's voice over just feels like a cheap way of feeding the audience information without utilizing the language of film. On top of that voice over is a very formal and impersonal way of presenting a story, making us feel disconnected from most characters besides the person consistently talking in our ear. If you're writing a script and it doesn't make sense without having someone literally explain the story to the audience, you have to re-write your script, which is something that should have been done with City of God . The other big thing I didn't like about the narrative was the intertwined stories. Take what was titled the "Knockout Ned story" for instance. In the middle of Ned's story, there were multiple scenes of Rocket working at a newspaper and taking photos in the hood. I don't really understand why the film went through all the effort of even giving us a subtitle for every chapter, when they're just going to freely inter-cut different stories along with it. I actually liked the ambition with the film and I really enjoyed all the character based stories, but I don't feel such a diverse story works if they try to simultaneously split up all the narratives while also editing them together. It made for a film that was inherently difficult to follow because they're attempting to build a kind of formality with the structure while also being very loose about when they told each story. Probably my least favourite thing about the film would be the visuals. I just felt everything was thrown at the camera without any attempts at properly constructing a scene. The camera darting and shaking so frequently that when there was a rare still moment I felt I could finally enjoy watching the film again. I'm not exaggerating when I say I found the film extremely challenging just to watch, which is made even more difficult with the straight-up ugly orange filter everything has. If the visuals were made intentionally unbearable I would understand, maybe the director was attempting to create a film that visually matches the lives of the people on the street, but this doesn't make the film any less disorientating to watch. There was one scene that I felt was impressive visually, and that would be the story of the apartment where we went through all the minor drug dealers that inhabited the same apartment. Not coincidentally that scene was also shot completely still, using cross-fades and overlays to construct the story rather than using multiple camera angles. Unfortunately that scene is an example of my problem with the voice over, because the story could have easily just been shown to us but rather there was a non-stop narration throughout. What the film did have working for it was a handful of decent performances. The lead, Alexandre Rodrigues as Rocket, gave a very enjoyable performance, I especially liked his character during the relationship scenes. I was very disappointed with Rodrigues's vocal performance, to be honest I found his voice very dreary and tiresome to listen to, making him the worst person to choose for the narrator, but my gripe with his voice is probably just because of how much I had to listen to it. I also liked Seu Jorge, who played Knockout Ned. Jorge should have been given a lot more time on screen. I found his character the most understanding and was extremely disappointed when his transformation into a hoodlum was brushed over in a couple of scenes. I also thought Matheus Nachtergaele, who played Carrot, was given far too little time on screen. Especially considering how big a role Carrot played in the story, I don't see why Nachtergaele wasn't given his own segment. The only gang leader that was properly represented was Li'l Zé, who happened to be my favourite character. I liked Lil' Dice's climb to the top, I really liked the child actor who played Lil' Dice, Douglas Silva, I liked his spiritual sub-plot. I liked his relationship with Benny, a character and performance (Phellipe Haagensen) that is given too much credit. I think the best thing this film does is tell the story of Li'l Zé from start to finish, and it shows that if the film wasn't so bogged down with multiple narratives and side-characters that don't amount to anything, it can actually tell a competent story. If a film ends and I don't care what happened to the protagonist, the film has failed. City of God manages to rip all of the character and humanity out of a film based around the lives of people. I wouldn't call it my favourite Paul Thomas Anderson film, but if you want to watch a movie that has as complex a conjoined narrative structure as well as a very emotional story, watch Magnolia . City of God was just obnoxious and difficult for me to watch from start to finish. That doesn't take away the good performances and occasional interesting visual, but those two things are far away from saving this film. I'm in the minority with this film and I'm sure plenty of people will strongly disagree with me, so I recommend you give it a watch yourself, but personally I didn't enjoy it and wouldn't go out of my way to watch it again.

City of God is a glitzy and glamorous Hollywood movie masquerading as a revolutionary foreign language indie. People are so impressed (at least based off my film class) to see the country of Brazil pornographically shot in a Tarantino, MTV-esque fashion that fetishizes violence, drugs and sex with outrageous vigor. No surprise that this was directed by somebody in the advertising field because it is a great looking film that is nonetheless empty of heart and soul. It's Brazil n' tha Hood, a pantomime of popular American films without even a tinge of visual realism or relevance to the real slums of Brazil. Not to say I know a damn thing about how it actually runs but I found very little to find believable among the pretty lighting and eye catching editing. I suppose I understand why this is so highly rated because City of God might be a good movie but it's also one that lies or at least blinds the audience to the non-sensational reality. The movie has many shocking moments but it doesn't earn them because of how it doesn't even bother to make a point out of anything, since again, this is a wildly slick picture interested in the surface and not much else. I can't say I'm a fan, and ignoring the technical merits of it, I feel largely nothing about this shell of "neorealist" cinema.

“I honestly don't understand the overwhelming praise for City of God. While the film has impressive camera work and a fast-paced style, I found it exhausting rather than engaging. The constant violence, brutal characters, and endless cycle of crime make it feel more like a long sequence of shocking moments than a meaningful story. The characters are difficult to connect with because so many of them are defined by cruelty and survival, leaving little emotional depth for the audience to hold on to. The movie seems more interested in showing chaos and brutality than exploring the people behind it. The storytelling style, with its rapid editing and nonstop narration, can also feel distracting and overcomplicated. Instead of creating a powerful emotional experience, it sometimes feels like the film is trying too hard to prove how gritty and intense it can be. Although it has technical strengths, City of God was not an enjoyable watch for me. It is violent, overwhelming, and far too focused on misery to be the masterpiece many people claim it is.”

I've wanted to watch this for years and years, and yet I never did. Maybe there was a reason for that. City of God brims with flair and technique, and there is nary a moment when the image and sound presented aren't well rendered and constructed. But therein lies the issue with this film. It feels too constructed, too amalgamated. The result of a heap of story material set ablaze specifically to hide from sincerity. Is the story true? To a turn, as many of these kinds of stories are. I think where this one falters is that it never seems to stop to consider that it's got one foot in the door of stylized imaginings of a roughly relatable cinematic narrative, and the other in the door of gritty depiction of the lives of the sub-altern. It tends to choose style more than anything else, and in doing so leaves a lot on the table. The flair and flash of its photography, cutting and acting lose quite a bit of their impact by the time you see the 15th or so callous murder--a weightlessness that it feels like the film encourages after a fashion. Simply put: there isn't enough story behind the pomp and circumstance to keep the style engaging. The narrative feels less like a cohesive tableau and more like a series of loosely connected vignettes that are united by violence and excess and not by character presence or investment. Glad I watched it, but I can't say I'm happy with what I watched.

City of God is executed with such technical skill that it almost feels like exhibitionism on the filmmakers’ part. We get split-screens, we get sharply edited montages, we get scenes shown twice from different perspectives, and we get some long, magnificent tracking shots, often through crowds, that must have been almost impossible to pull off. It’s really slick. But what is it? Is it a brutal gangster flick, or a social drama about degradation that carries genuine anthropological weight? The easy answer would be to say it’s both, and the vast swathes of critics and fans who think the movie’s terrific would be sure to express such a sentiment. I’m not so sure. Especially in its second hour, I felt the movie leaned more heavily toward the first description than the second, as its plot became denser and its level of sensationalist violence intensified. Thematically, and often in execution, too, it’s very similar to the TV show The Wire, and I can’t be the first to point that out, though contemporary critics would not have had the luxury of such a comparison. Inevitably, it is not able to say as much in two hours as The Wire was able to say over five seasons and fifty episodes. But, for one thing, The Wire breathed human life into its antagonists, and showed us that their actions are not always motivated by greed or viciousness. This cannot be said for City of God’s principal villain Lil Ze, who laughingly dispatches crying children on-camera and for whom passing jealousy is a perfectly good motive to rape a stranger while making her boyfriend watch. Sympathetic characters- Benny, for example, or Rocket, are conveniently never shown engaging in violent acts at all; we are left in no doubt which characters we are supposed to like and which characters we aren’t. Subsequently, it lacks The Wire’s more complex, incisive dynamics. On a cinema screen in 2002, when here in the UK I was still technically not old enough to watch it, it might have been pretty wild. Oldboy too. But though I did prefer it to Oldboy, ultimately I felt that, with its swathes of characters, its whip-smart edits, its proliferating abundance of death and carnage, the film was using sensory overload in an attempt to steamroller me into exhilaration. As it is, on a small screen 20 years later, I don’t feel the film had the kind of power that it appeared to be striving for. It’s not a bad film- far from it. It’s actually a very good one if the material happens to resonate with you. But what does it have to tell us, really, other than that the slums of Rio are terrible beyond belief, where the police have no power, and where the most amoral of a given generation tend to be the ones that rise up through the ranks and end up essentially running the place? I don’t know, really. That does seem to be the main heft of the piece. And there’s a titillating aspect to City of God that sits uncomfortably with its apparent status as a social document, a ‘message from the front line’. City of God is a film based on the true story of life in the Brazilian slums. It has a little coming-of-age drama, and tells about some boys who grow up and take very different paths in their lives. It seems to be a real struggle for kids to lift themselves out of this difficult place to live, and to escape the dangers of the drug trade. As a result of the atmosphere in the City of God there are no perfectly pure heroes, or even perfectly evil villains. In fact, one of the most interesting aspects of this movie is the way they manipulate the audience into rooting for different people at different times. Even Lil Ze, who starts out as the clear-cut villain, actually brings peace to the slums for a time and we sympathize with him when he experiences loss. I also loved how they gave such distinct nicknames to all the characters. Where it could be easy to get lost in the sea of faces, we are easily able to tell everyone apart because they have such unique names. I did struggle to stay invested in the film, however. I wasn't finding a consistent story arc. It almost felt like a historical film or something because we are just shown events in one era, then we move on to the next without any change in our protagonist or his situation. In fact the entire theme of City of God was basically the cyclical nature of violence in the slums. So by the end the entire story starts all over again. This is one of those films that was interesting to watch, but not something I would recommend to most viewers.

From its very first scenes, in which our young photographer-protagonist finds himself trapped in the midst of a Mexican (ok, Brazilian) standoff between a street gang and the corrupt cops, City of God makes no bones about its debts to Scorsese and Tarantino. In fact, for much of the film, I was reminded of Guy Ritchie’s Lock, Stock, and Two Smoking Barrels, which brought to London much of the same snappy, experimental camerawork, “funny” gunplay, and street gangster-chic that’s on display here in Rio. But that metaphor only goes so far — this increasingly dark film ultimately feels very different than the breezy Lock Stock. In fact, while Scorsese, Tarantino, and Ritchie gangsters all generally find themselves on the wrong side of the law as a calling, the Brazilian youths here are born into it — crime, violence, and murder are an inescapable part of the Cidade de Deus. Or is it? I know this movie is based on a novel based on real events, but at a certain point, right after the strobelight-marked murder of one of the film’s most likable characters, City of God just gets lost in its own cycle of violence. When L’il Ze, the cruelest hoodlum we meet on our travels, brutally rapes the girlfriend of Knockout Ned (we never see her again — she’s a plot point, not a character), a gang war ensues that drastically escalates the already considerable levels of death and carnage the audience has to deal with. In this final third, the film derails…it’s just too much. (Ken Turan aptly summed it up as “overkill.”) One goes from avidly following the travails of individual characters to watching most or all of them go down in a hail of gunfire. Like I said, I know that much of this tale is based on a real gang war, and that the ridiculously high body count at the end of the film may have a solid grounding in fact. But at times City of God wants to have it both ways. When innocent bystanders are mowed down or child gangsters are forced to make extremely grisly life-and-death choices, we’re shocked sullen by the events depicted here. But when L’il Ze blows away his stooge Tuba in a fit of frustration, it’s a sight gag. In sum, with swooping camerawork, great performances across the board, and a well-crafted narrative, City of God bridges the gap between Tarantino-cool gangsterism and shocking acts of violence reasonably well for its first two-thirds. Alas, it falters in the final act, and I found myself spending the last thirty-five minutes of a movie I’d quite enjoyed up til then keeping my head down and waiting for the last reports of gunfire to die away. Well worth seeing if you’re a fan of the hyperkinetic gangster genre, but ultimately City of God just can’t quite close the deal. Film #26: Around the World in 30 Days (May 2014 Challenge) Country : Brazil Violence is one big, long, grueling, and—most importantly—circular chain of events. Once you pull a trigger, the bullet eventually ricochets back to you, and unless you never shoot a gun at all, there’ll be no escaping the destruction that violence leaves in its wake. Welcome, my friends, to the world of City of God , a pulsating crime drama that chronicles the rise of organized crime in the titular Brazilian favela since its inception in 1960. Told from the perspective of a young man named Rocket, we see the unrelenting cycle of gangs, guns, drugs, vendettas, victories, defeats, corpses, cops, and cash repeat itself time after time; the scenarios play out differently, but the core elements all remain the same. While there is some mild humor mixed in at times, for the most part Fernando Meirelles keeps things dark and grim, and by the end of it all the body count is so high that it would be pointless to keep track of or tally. Let’s just say that this is A Very Serious Movie, and if you’re not prepared for the level of violence it serves up, you might as well look elsewhere. What’s especially notable about the film is its emphasis on its characters, most of whom are greatly fleshed out with the help of backstories and exposition. I liked this attention to the characters because it really drove the motif of circularity home, as well as gave the amateur actors a real chance to shine as individuals. The cast list is fairly large, but that never becomes an issue due to how to the narrative weaves the disparate character threads together to form an intricately-composed whole. And without this character-driven approach, there’s no way someone like Lil Zé would have been nearly as compelling (and I think it’s pretty much agreed upon that Zé is one hell of a villain). While some films are sorely lacking in believable characters, City of God is teeming with them… and, for me, that may be its saving grace. For, you see, I did not especially enjoy City of God . I won’t deny that it’s an accomplished and no-holds-barred take on the tragic realities of slum life, but I have to admit all the same that I struggled to get through it. I wasn’t big on Meirelles’ shaky camerawork for one, and the use of voiceover for both narration and exposition was a tiresome device after a while. I’m also still trying to work out what I gleaned from the film at the end of the day; aside from its cyclical (not to mention cynical) treatment of violence and retribution, it was all so morbid that not thinking about it too much seems like the best course of action. I know Rocket’s arc ends on a hopeful note, but everything else in the film is so plagued with dire consequences and ill-fated decisions that it never registers as powerfully as it should. Sure, the film is entertaining to a point (anything that gets your adrenaline rushing is), and it’s put together with great skill and flourish, but I’m having trouble seeing why it’s so acclaimed. Am I not its intended audience, or is there something I’m missing? Maybe I’ll just wait for the day when I run into someone who worships this film and they can make their case for it. I don’t think I ever want to sit through it again, but I’m always open to hearing a well-crafted argument. Until then, I’m going to have to side-eye City of God ’s high placement on IMDb’s Top 250 list and wonder what all the fuss is about.

Not quite for me. This Brazilian film, firmly entrenched in the coveted top-25 highest rated films on IMDB, is the true-story about two boys growing up in the violent "City Of God" neighborhood outside of Rio De Janiero in Brazil - one becomes a photographer, the other a murderous drug-dealer. The 130-minute story feels like a Portuguese version of Scorsese's "Goodefllas" - except with delusional and hopeless children, rather than Ray Liotta and Robert DeNiro. Perhaps it was because of the subtitles, or because all the children looked so similar, or perhaps it was the non-linear and sporadic narrative, but I found myself struggling to follow the complicated plot and character paths for most of the first half of this film. When things finally settled in, and after most of the supporting cast had been killed off - I was pleasantly surprised by "City Of God" - which finally started to come into its own, rather than a string of familiar scenes of people getting murdered. The immensely large cast of local amateurs all did a terrific job, but none of them really stood-out, and I found it difficult to really connect to any of the main characters. I will say this though: the cinematography and editing in this film were absolutely outstanding - keeping things moving at a blistering pace, all while maintaining a very stylized, almost music-video look to some of the shots. The dirty slums of Rio are portrayed with gritty and striking realism that really immerses you in the sounds and sights of this hellish neighborhood. And although this film, and all of its characters are closely based on a true-story, I couldn't help but feel like it was poor-man's version of much better gangster films that had come before. Although beautifully shot, written, and acted - I quite honestly wasn't that impressed with "City Of God", I'd go so far as to say I was even bored at times. Going in with high expectations was probably a mistake, but I really didn't think this movie was anything special. That being said however, I did enjoy the film, especially the last hour - and I can certainly appreciate it for what it was trying to accomplish - so it wins back some points from me there. There were aspects I thoroughly enjoyed, and thought were quite deserving of a higher ratings, while at other times, I found myself disconnected and uninterested with the plot... I thought it was GOOD.

City of God is a Brazilian movie that has received rave reviews since it was released and is often called 'The Brazilian Goodfellas'. Unfortunately, I don't think the film is as good as it has been praised to be, and I do not understand how it is compared to Goodfellas when the films are so far apart in quality. The film follows Rocket and L'il Dice, two young boys from the titular City of God, a Brazilian slum, and their adolescent and early adulthood exploits. The main problems the film has its plethora of characters, all with similar names. A various mix of characters are introduced and their story is told, and while they may have a significant impact on the overall story, most are never used again. This element could've been done away with as it messes up the pacing and draws the viewer out of the film. While many films, including Goodfellas, have a wide cast of characters and deal with them well, City of God does not. It's a good looking film and for the most part, the acting is decent. But the Brazilian Goodfellas it is not. 3/5.

O filme retrata o crescimento do crime organizado na Cidade de Deus, uma favela que começou a ser construída nos anos 1960, e se tornou um dos lugares mais perigosos do Rio de Janeiro no começo dos anos 1980. Para contar a trajetória deste lugar, o filme narra a vida de diversos personagens e eventos que vão sendo entrelaçados no decorrer da trama, tudo pelo ponto de vista do narrador, Buscapé, um menino que cresceu em um ambiente muito violento, porém, encontra chances de não ser fisgado pela vida do crime.

Kids with guns Kids with guns Taking over But it won't be long They're mesmerized Skeletons Kids with guns Kids with guns Easy does it, easy does it, they got something to say no to One of those movies that makes me feel awkward to about. Because on the one hand, it's based, in part, on true stories. On the other, while fiction and non-fiction aren't mutually exclusive, it comes across as a bit of a crime-story cliche. Not to mention, I'm slowly phasing out of gangsta movies in general as I find them increasingly harder to connect to, so this is not coming to me at the time to see it favourably. It's that thing gangsta movies do, too, where they pump a lot of cool music and fashion when depicting the lifestyle that constantly feels more like a celebration, despite all the death. I don't know. Formally it's never boring or dull and there's a real swagger to everything but it ultimately rings hollow to me.

In a way I want to be like "fuck this movie." I just hate gang movies, I have no sympathy for any of the characters whatsoever (except for ol' Knockout Ned but even he wears thin). Where as a movie like The Godfather was more interesting to me because it was about a person fighting tooth and nail to not be sucked into his inevitable downward spiral, City of God is full of people who are too stupid to subscribe to anything other than instant gratification... and the modern fast paced editing and interwoven story is made for that same type of viewer. That said, I can't hate this movie because it /is/ skillfully shot, deftly edited and the story is planned out flawlessly, leaving no loose ends. There's also a skillful use of suggestion which at least keeps it from exploiting its audience.

City of God brilliantly captures what it is like living in Brazil full of danger and terror. Any day there’s a risk of getting shot in the streets by local gangs. The protagonist tells his story and his experience of living amongst these people, trying to survive. His dream is to become a photographer, which is why during the film he starts capturing the “real” life in the ghettos.  I specifically enjoyed the part where the film begins at the end and goes back to the protagonist’s childhood to explain his whole story, giving details and information about each character that plays an important role in his life.

I think I was expecting something different. I wanted to follow Rocket much more than the rival gangs. I’m also not a huge fan of the late 90’s/early 2000’s film style of jarring cuts and shakey cam. I understand that they were going for a documentary style aesthetic, but I’m a grandpa and I like things to be calmer. It’s a pretty good film, but I wish we got more popular movies about Latin America that aren’t about crime and poverty.

Welcome to City of God. Welcome to the harsh reality of the favelas in Rio de Janeiro, the kingdom of drugs, the empire of organized gangs who run the entire cities, imposing a reign of terror that is very easy to fall and it is virtually impossible to get out? Unlike what you have seen in American-made gangsters films set in Chicago or Boston, City of God is ruled by young people who are in their early twenties, but have gained enough experience, misery and hatred passed from one generation to others for quite long. This is a great movie about violent gang-wars and drug-trafficking that clearly depicts blood and violence as commodity. City of God was Brazillian director Mereilles' feature debut film that was nominated for 4 Academy Awards nominations (Best Cinematography, Directing, Editing and Screenplay), City of God was also based on a 1997 semi-autobiographical novel by Paulo Lins, about three young men (The Tender Three) and their lives in Cidade de Deus, a shanty area in Western Rio de Janeiro where Lins grew up. This film nominated for Best Cinematography because it was able to portray the harsh life of Rio de Janeiro, its shanty towns, its drug-dealing activities and also the emotions of each character in the film through the use of high contrast lighting throughout the film. It's a fantastic fast-paced action drama, simply adorable!

Vivid and colorful depiction of the short lifes of several inhabitants of the so called "City of God". The film uses innovative techniques and visuals to draw the viewer into the hectic atmosphere without ever indulging in it's own visual overkill. The movie refrains from becoming too depressing and the use of the protagonist as a narrator gives the whole thing a more positive and natural feel, as to the kid everything that happens around him is normal. It is up to the viewer to make up his mind about what is happening, it is never dictated how you should feel about what you should see.
A really good movie that explores the concept of crime as a self-perpetuating cycle. A bit bleak, but the characters and cinematography are fantastic and well worth the watch.

[AV Club #40 of decade] I was expecting a more depressing look at the harshness of Brazilian life. It turns out the movie is much more of a crime story of crazy low level crime bosses. The movie was good, maybe not top 40 of the decade good, but good. Particularly the cutting, timeline jumping and storytelling of the beginning was great. Once I realized this was a relatively true story, it became a little less interesting. Being a true story limited the options for how the movie would likely end. A good crime movie.

A great drama with many great perspectives of lives in Brazil slums. Film about drugs, murders, shooting, gangs, love, and finding one's passion in this madness. Colourful and dynamic film. A true picture of tragic lives.

Really cool movie. I really liked it and it gave me a unique kind of feeling I don’t really get with most other movies. It’s rough, down right appalling and hard to watch at some points but for all the right reasons. I liked the fact that, while displaying some genuinely shocking things that most people would’ve never experienced or been exposed to, it didn’t glamorise them, focus too much on them or use them simply as shock value. It treated them as completely typical time and time again which I think is how most people growing up in that area (and the inspiration for the movie) saw these things. After a while, you started seeing things the same way. The cinematography was also really cool and effective. Particularly liked the club scene. Why not 5 stars? I mean I just didn’t ‘wow’ me as much as some of the 5 star movies I have. The thing is, I won’t see gang films or films about poverty the same after this, because I think it’s the most accurate portrayal of those themes ever (that also happens to be entertaining). Anyways I digress

After years of people telling me this film was good I finally sat down two nights ago to watch it. I was furious. Furious that it had taken me this long to see it. It was nothing like I had expected. It was warm and funny and terrifyingly violent. It made you feel like you could empathise with the main character despite the fact that no one I know lives in conditions or circumstances like this. It was that rarest of film. One that is a universal story set in a world that couldn’t be more specific. My favourite character was the tragi-hero Knockout Ned. It wasn’t until the movie finished that I realised where I knew him from. He was the wicked Brazilian guitar player, Pele dos Santos from “The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou”. The vibrant cuts and hyper realistic violence felt like a mixing pot between Scorcese, Tarantino, Aronofsky and Ritchie but never actually felt like it was ripping off any of them but rather developing it’s own style. The scene where Cabeleria is running away from the police after trying to push start the car was one of the most beautiful things I have ever seen. Buscapé: It was like a message from God: “Honesty doesn’t pay, sucker.”

This Brazilian film presents an intricate, absorbing account of the rise of organized crime in the “Cidade de Deus” slum of Rio de Janeiro. The story takes place across several years during which the main character grows up to become a photographer, while most of his friends become gangsters. It is a chilling, but very human, depiction of the vicious cycle formed by corruption and poverty in the Third World.

This movie reminded me a bit of The Infierno, where the cycle of violence never truly ends—it just gets passed on to the next generation. In City of God, though, the city was literally lawless, so the violence didn't have to wait for one generation to die before continuing. The ambition and brutality were simply passed from one group of kids in the favela to the next. Li'l Zé is one of the most despicable, disgusting, and pathetic characters I've ever seen in a movie. The fact that the film reveals at the end that it's based on a true story hit me hard. People like that are out there. Even though he's a victim of the environment he grew up in, I don't feel any sympathy for him—not even when he was a child. He seemed to have the personality of a psychopath from the very beginning. It's incredible that Bené genuinely enjoyed the company of someone as pathetic as Zé. Not even his death made me feel any better because that rain of bullets wasn't nearly enough punishment for all the pain and terror he caused. Talking about the movie itself, I understand why it's considered a masterpiece. It certainly was for me too. I'm not new to this kind of non-chronological storytelling, but saving the opening scene until the last 15 minutes of the movie felt incredible. I thought it was going to be a Casino situation, where the opening scene doesn't come back until about an hour and a half into the film.

Nunca me había dado la oportunidad de conocer parte de la historia de Brasil, ahora comprendo mucho más el por qué de su situación actual. ¿Por qué no es una película más famosa? Incredible movie. Emotional, funny, intense, brilliant. Cinematography was marvelous, dialogue was clever and powerful, story was well-narrated and well-presented, and the characters felt like real people living real lives. I was totally engrossed in the movie the whole time. I was initially shocked to find out it was based on a true story because of how cinematically perfect the plot was, but then it immediately made sense to me why everything in the movie felt so real. Terrific watch, contains every element of a perfect story.

Proof that the cameraman really never dies… LMAO On a real note, this is an absolute masterpiece. From the cinematography to the acting to the pacing, it is as close to perfection as a film can get. I spent a good 45 minutes after finishing it trying to come up with a single complaint, and not one thing came to mind. From the opening sequence with its incredible 360° transition and beautifully composed still shots to the emotionally devastating ending framed from behind, City of God is one of the best movies I’ve ever seen and, dare I say, the most creatively executed. There are so many things to love about this movie, but after doing my due diligence and learning that roughly 70% of the cast consisted of local children with little or no acting experience, I appreciated it even more. It makes the performances feel that much more authentic. It’s hard to write a review when there are so many aspects deserving of praise, but one thing I have to highlight is how interconnected the story is. There are at least 25 meaningful characters, yet somehow every single one leaves an impression. It doesn’t matter how much screen time they have—their presence is remembered and their role in the story feels important. I’d compare it to The Godfather , another film with an enormous cast, but I actually think City of God handles its ensemble even better. Every storyline feels purposeful, and none of the characters get lost in the chaos. I could easily write four more paragraphs about this film, but to keep it short, if you asked me to describe it in one sentence, I’d simply say it’s as close to a perfect film as I’ve ever seen. “Wanna get shot in the hand or the foot?” 9.9/10

The ensemble cast is flawless with each character leaving an impact and the vibes are HIGH the entire time. Brutal gang violence never seemed so fun! The story sucks you in with characters you love and root for and characters you want to get turned into swiss cheese, stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you wanna look away, but it’s also just lowkey a vibe. It feels like this could be a great movie to hangout to, and because so much is going on at once it could be amazing on a rewatch. This movie literally has it all I can’t recommend it enough. I kept saying it felt like the Brazilian Goodfellas. A stylish crime epic with timeless performances, characters, vibes, and one hell of a score. 5 stars check it out 🇧🇷

‘Cidade de Deus’ (City of God) is a Brazilian crime drama chronicling the lives of a group of Brazilian street kids & the growth of organised crime in a suburb of Rio de Janeiro. The film itself is brutal and has a frightening realism that you can only find by casting locals who have lived this life, there is little wonder that these youngsters descend into this life as they are pretty much damned either way. Only one of the boys ‘Rocket’ has no desire to be a criminal, he likes hanging out with his friends & develops a keen interest in photography, but staying out of the circle & staying alive are not certainties, even if you decide to live within the law. Driven by the local and completely unknown cast, this film is breathtaking from start to finish, brilliantly acted, beautifully shot and more than deserving of the plaudits directed towards it at the time of its international release. Which only makes be wish that I’d seen it earlier. Highly recommended viewing.

Fernando Meirelles electrifying portrait of favela life is the Brazillian equivalent of Martin Scorsese's Goodfellas but holds a much greater power. In Meirelles' film, everyone feels the effects of crime and disorder especially the kids - many of whom perpetrate the most disturbing crimes on show, such as L'il Dice/L'il Z who seems like the embodiment of evil...until you see everyone else and realise that he doesn't really differ from the norm.

The term masterpiece gets thrown around a lot often to films that don’t deserve. That mantra is often used when describing this film and it deserves it. The style is awe-inspiring but never overwhelming. The drama is thick but never enters into melodrama. The pace is quick and never ending causing the story to flow masterfully. Easily one of the best films of the 00’s.

Fantastic!  So many storylines.  So many characters.  All of them enhanced this movie. Nothing unnecessary. Nothing wasted.  It was captivating. And despite the tension building pace, all of the many characters were easy to connect to and the storylines were so easy to absorb. Beautifully shot.  So many techniques implemented.  But all with a purpose. Had this movie come out today with social media and streaming services, it would be massive. Maybe I underestimate its impact back in 2004, and it obviously garnered much critical acclaim, but I feel like a subtitled foreign film that probably wasn’t in a typical number of theaters and that you had to rent at the video store to be able to see, probably flew under most people’s radar.  It was certainly under mine. I cannot believe that I waited until 2026 to watch this masterpiece. 9.8/10

City of God is more than just a detailed look at life in the slums, and more than a fierce play on the Gangster genre. It's a morality plague for the mind, but only in the best way. If you don't get sucked up in the story  then there's plenty for your thoughts to chew on here. But what truly gives it that place in our minds as one of the greatest pieces of modern cinema is the way in which the two genres compliment each other. It doesn't set out to be shocking and nor does it try to set up many obvious connections to the gangster genre. Even when it isn't subtle, it's inventive and when it's subtle it opens out to be stimulative and embracing. But its ambition for being truly realistic allows it to leave an impression much grander than any scene purely designed for shock value ever could.

Okay this rambling of mine doesn’t make sense I’m warning you, I’m happy to have my mind changed. Very unpopular take, I think. Unfortunately, I probably was a bit too incapacitated for this movie, it did not click with me at all. I understand the intention of the long scenes and timed dialogue or actions but it was like I could hear a director in my head calling the cues for the characters, it unimmersed me frequently. Takabe also isn’t really showed to be burdened by his wife (what happened to in sickness and in health?), we don’t see the caretaker role in him at all, he just seeks a sort of liberation from social responsibility (looking after the person you love, who you made vows to). He feels burdened by the expectation that he should be a good partner to his wife, despite her becoming ill. We are not really shown the actual load that could be him having to look after her, the impact is detached and sterile (which thematically goes with the rest of the film) but his wife isn’t a true person, even in his story, she exists purely to illustrate his hardship . I’m sure I’ll attempt this movie again with a bit more respect, but for now my misandry hat has crept back on. Can’t even truely rate this movie upon this watch.

7/22/26 This movie leaves a lot to be desired. For one, there is almost no story to speak of. At the start of the movie we see that Mamiya can use supernatural powers to make people murder others. At the end of the movie we have no further clarification on that. We see the books, the video, and still we have no idea what is happening. Beyond just the lack of narrative there is a lack of character development. Mamiya does his bit the whole time and then dies. Takabe begins and ends the movie unable to control his emotions killing Mamiya. By the end of the movie I felt like I had just watched Seven, but vague. There was no one and nothing to really care about in the end. The thing I was most confused about were the reviews for this movie. It is not scary. There are a couple moments, but with the lack of sound it's never terrifying and it doesn't try to be. I also realized like with other movies the being vague is great for a movie. You can attribute as many things as you want to this film without ever being wrong.

this film did not work for me. the social commentary only really works, i think, if you bought into it ahead of time and are actively looking for it in the text. the (uncharismatic, irritating) hypnotist's victims aren't sufficiently fleshed out to support the idea that through subtle manipulation he's dredging up murderous misanthropic desires simmering beneath the surface of our alienated modern culture. it just looks like magic brainwashing. there's the implied horror, i suppose, of the fundamental unknowability of other people and even your own self, of what you are capable of thinking and doing under the right circumstances, but i just don't think the film actually conveys that in a compelling way. the first half drags. it's repetitive and kinda boring, showing the hypnotist's "method" over and over in a way that doesn't really build up to much. the second half is more entertaining to watch, but it's both too concrete to leave much up to interpretation and too abstract to set up and resolve the mystery, such as it was, in a satisfying way. the depiction of hypnosis stretched my suspension of disbelief thin, all in service of something that wasn't terrifying enough to instinctually scare or relatable enough to evoke a more conscious, intellectual dread. the film does some interesting stuff from a technical perspective, but that wasn't enough to hook me. tbh reading through the reviews i got the impression that either i watched a different film to everyone else, or the audience is 95% film students

The influences that contributed to this and also what came from it are very apparent, but unfortunately, this just did not work for me. I found it to be unbearably slow and uninteresting, and that’s coming from someone who often times appreciates a slower pace in film. What lost me on this was mainly the story; it was confusing and subtle in a way that the vagueness just made me continuously stay more and more unengaged as it went on. I found the character of Mamiya to be very frustrating and the long, drawn out scenes of his repetitiveness over and over again I really just disliked. I don’t know, I know a lot of people praise highly of this film and while I went in truly wanting to love it, I just never had that moment of connection. Kurosawa’s 2024 film “Chime” (which I was told was a spiritual successor this film) I think worked a lot better with its condensed runtime and modern filmmaking techniques. Although from a technical perspective, I found the production quality to be high and I also enjoyed the performances from the cast. This isn’t going to be something I revisit because I don’t see myself having a better experience but I’m glad those that get it, get it.

i liked the surrealism in certain scenes; felt like the movie was drifting in and out of the characters’ consciousness. the movie felt like it was in a fog, and that accurately represents the state most of the characters were in at times. i enjoyed the cinematography, sound, scenery, etc. there were direct nods to violence against women; a doctor carrying a lifetime of being told she’s not good enough to be one because of her gender, a murdered housewife institutionalized for mental strain because her life was shaped by the patriarchy/her “husband,” a woman murdered by yet another woman-hating man/“husband”, and.. you guessed it.. another woman murdered by a woman-hating man. lots of gender based violence being depicted, yet the focus of the movie is supposed to be two emotionally unstable men who obsess over one another and some mystical ability to hypnotize. i don’t have anything good to say about the premise of the villain’s hypnotism. the movie focused so much on this smoke screen instead of actually diving into the why behind violence (why men kill women). the villain felt too on the nose for me. the “mysterious” aspects of his character were repetitive and predictable after the first introduction to us. the theatrical nature of the villain kept creating a bigger and bigger disconnect between the violent themes of the movie that actually had something real and serious to explore. the feeling the villain and the detective evoked in me about 1/3 of the movie in was the same - there wasn’t really any differentiation between the two characters. the movie kept focusing on things that don’t have much substance (hypnotism, ambiguity, mystery, how the killer influences others, etc..) than focusing on the very real nature of male violence towards women and the psychological structure the patriarchy conditions both men and women into. there was something rich to explore here, but they missed the mark for me

This opens with a bang. It wastes no time at all ensnaring you in this whatthefuckery. The delightfully grimy atmosphere drips through every frame, and the lead performance is outstanding. But while both the lead performance and atmosphere never let up, the story ran out of steam after 40 minutes or so. Every conversation with the villain was the same conversation over and over again, and while it worked really well the first time, it got really repetitive and uninteresting after the 8th time. And by the time you get to the final act, the story really has nowhere to go except for where you expect it to. I love the bursts of violence, I love the cold drone that simmers on the soundtrack, and I think it’s occasionally pretty effective. But it’s more of a repetitive slog than anything else. I’m intrigued enough by it to want to read up about it a bit, so I guess that says something. I think it’s alright. It’s far from awful but it’s far from great either.

They don’t make sweaters like they used to. The primal urge to kill; just a flicker away. The terror of losing control and hurting the ones you love. The psychological as inseparable from the supernatural. Hypnotic, haunting, deeply unsettling. One of those movies that feels cursed to watch. Unfolds slowly, with a cold sense of inevitability. The assurance that you will snap someday; not a matter of ‘if’ but ‘when.’ The fire awakens something within you, an urge that has existed since the dawn of mankind. Maybe its influence is demonic in nature, maybe it’s baked into our DNA. A film too blackly intelligent to offer any easy answers or explanations; and besides, you know the truth anyway, don’t you? You’re just terrified to admit it to yourself. Kiyoshi Kurosawa is surely one of the best living writer-directors, a fact I am certain of even with this being my first film from him. A master of tone, pacing, storytelling; complete confidence in shot length, thematic subtlety, and a respect for the viewer to piece together information on their own. Beautiful, uneasy cinematography. Uses angles, windows, doorways, and distance to keep the viewer from the characters. You feel the urge to lean in, as if you’re an eavesdropper who just caught a glimpse of a strange conversation from across the beach. Long shots to prolong tension and deny release; to invite speculation, to sit with characters in moments of illogic and bewilderment. Koji Yakusho is one of the best living actors, full stop. He knows how to internalize his character’s emotions, convey changes in subtle ways, and go “big” and fully external when the story calls for it. Seeing him in a leading role is almost a seal of quality that the movie is going to be superb. This is not to discredit the work of his costars, whose work is on equal footing with his own, especially Masato Hagiwara, who gives one of the most skin-crawling performances I’ve ever seen in horror. As I was watching this, I didn’t want it to end. I know for a fact I’m going to rewatch this movie many times again, and I bet that I’ll get more out of it with each successive viewing. Its terrifying questions and insights into human psychology will stay with you long after the credits roll. This is unquestionably one of the greatest masterpieces in horror film history. Essential viewing. Mesmerizing.

Kurosawa lavora di pura sottrazione, appoggiandosi a un montaggio privo di sbavature e a interpretazioni di agghiacciante naturalezza per incollare lo spettatore allo schermo e mutarne radicalmente la prospettiva. Il vero orrore non risiede nell'ostentazione della violenza, ma nello spazio vuoto, in un gioco di luci e ombre gestito con l'autorità dei maestri. È un'opera che scava dritta nelle pulsioni più inconfessabili del nostro inconscio, lasciando un'impronta indelebile nell'immaginario di chiunque si esponga al suo sguardo. Un thriller psicologico ipnotico e viscerale, sconsigliato nelle ore notturne: la certezza che possa insinuarsi nella mente e non lasciarla più è fin troppo reale.

"All the things that used to be inside of me… now they are all outside." Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Cure is one of the most quietly disturbing films ever made... an absolute masterpiece of psychological horror, existential dread, and suffocating restraint. On the surface it’s a serial‑killer procedural, even sharing DNA with Fincher’s brilliant Se7en, but Kurosawa uses the genre only as a skeleton. What he builds on top of it is a bleak, nihilistic examination of human vulnerability, the erosion of identity, and the terrifying idea that violence isn’t imposed from outside circumstance, but awakened from within. The story follows Detective Takabe (Kōji Yakusho), a man already stretched thin by his wife’s worsening mental illness and the emotional exhaustion of his job. His life is a fragile balancing act, and Kurosawa uses that instability as the perfect entry point for the film’s central horror: a series of murders committed by everyday ordinary people who have no motive, no memory, and no explanation. Their only connection is a wandering drifter named Mamiya (Masato Hagiwara), whose vacant stare and fragmented speech seem to hollow out the minds of everyone he encounters. Mamiya doesn’t kill... he just removes the part of people that resists killing. Kurosawa’s direction is astonishingly controlled. The pacing is glacial, the dialogue sparse, the atmosphere suffocating. Every scene feels slightly askew, as if reality itself is losing structural integrity. The cinematography is incredible: long static shots, oppressive negative space, and a washed‑out palette that makes Tokyo look like a decaying Silent Hill‑esque purgatory. Kurosawa weaponizes emptiness... rooms feel too large, hallways too long, silence too loud. The sound design is equally unnerving, filled with distant hums, mechanical drones, and the constant threat of nothing happening at all. It’s a film where the absence of action becomes the source of tension and dread. Yakusho’s performance is extraordinary. He plays Takabe with a brittle mix of intensity and (seeming) restraint... a man whose sense of self is eroding under the weight of responsibility and despair. His exhaustion becomes the emotional anchor of the film, making his slow descent into obsession and madness terrifying. Hagiwara’s Mamiya is the perfect counterpoint: airy, spacey, disturbingly serene. He’s not a villain in any traditional sense: he’s a void, a philosophical black hole that strips people down to their most primitive impulses. His presence evokes the same chilling inevitability as Anton Chigurh in No Country for Old Men, but filtered through a soft, almost childlike haze. The horror Kurosawa taps into feels even more potent today, where cycles of copycat violence (especially in the wake of high‑profile school shootings) show how fragile the boundary is between suggestion and action. Mamiya’s vacant presence unlocking buried impulses mirrors how real‑world perpetrators often inspire others not through ideology, but through a kind of psychological permission structure: the realization that someone else has crossed the line makes the line feel permeable. It’s deeply disturbing to recognize how prevalent violent urges are in humanity, how easily they can be awakened, and how quickly they spread when people see their own private darkness reflected in someone else’s public act. Cure forces us to confront the terrifying possibility that the capacity for violence is a dormant part of the human condition waiting for the right fracture. What makes Cure so remarkable is its refusal to offer answers. Kurosawa isn’t interested in explaining Mamiya’s methods or providing a neat psychological theory. Instead, he suggests something far more unsettling: that identity is fragile, morality is performative, and the boundary between self and suggestion is terrifyingly thin. The film becomes a meditation on how ordinary people justify extraordinary horrors, how violence blooms in the cracks of everyday life, and how the desire for meaning can lead to annihilation of self and others. It’s a worldview so depressingly bleak... and its quiet repression fits the late‑90s Japanese cultural landscape far more poignantly than the loud, chaotic spectacle of the modern American out-in-the-open bumfight/rainbet/pump.fun/Kalshi slop-filled attention economy. Cure works because it fuses philosophical horror, exquisite procedural mystery, and methodical atmospheric filmmaking into a hypnotic descent into existential terror. It’s deeply unsettling, thought‑provoking, and instantly one of the best films I’ve ever seen. Kurosawa understands that the violence lurking inside all of us (whether it ever emerges or not) is far scarier than any sort of monster or demon.

Review by David Ehrlich In the end, Denis Villeneuve was all too right: Your television isn’t big enough for the scope of his “Dune,” but that’s only because this lifeless spice opera is told on such a comically massive scale that a screen of any size would struggle to contain it. Likewise, no story — let alone the misshapen first half of one — could ever hope to support the enormity of what Villeneuve tries to build over the course of these interminable 155 minutes (someone mentions that time is measured differently on Arrakis), or the sheer weight of the self-serious portent that he pounds into every shot. For all of Villeneuve’s awe-inducing vision, he loses sight of why Frank Herbert’s foundational sci-fi opus is worthy of this epic spectacle in the first place. Such are the pitfalls of making a movie so large that not even its director can see around the sets.

Shocked to know that a good artisan like Villeneuve is behind one of the worst turds of 2021, an astonishingly dull and amorphous film without an ounce of ambition where each character seems emptied of their soul, wandering in a setting of incredible ugliness (send that DP and the whole art department to the gulag). The linearity of the story and the action is unheard of, and never in my life have I witnessed a less engaging universe being set for 150 fucking minutes. Longest teaser you’ll ever watch

Lifeless and dull. Stripped of all the intricacy and depth that made the original novel so captivating in the first place, the focus instead lies on making everything as big as possible, and the end result is a generic and overlong modern sci-fi blockbuster devoid of subtlety or warmth. Monotonous and self-serious, yet paper-thin in pathos. 2.5 hours of setup and exposition. In a movie already lacking a proper climax, the final act drags. Everything is loud and bombastic, but the characters themselves ring hollow; Chalamet lacks any charisma in the lead role. The film is more concerned with displaying its massive world than it is filling it with something to care for. The city of Arrakeen looks cold and barren– the opposite of lived in. Duncan Idaho is effectively relegated to two lines of dialogue: COME HERE & MY BOY. The dream visions of Zendaya's Chani come across like bad parody of 80s perfume commercials. All the charm and weirdness is removed in favor of a brutalist, drab aesthetic that seeps into all aspects of the film; gone is the magic and sense of wonder I found in the books. Happy it’s found success as I want more ambitious sci-fi adaptations, but this was a miserable experience and I’m starting to think Villeneuve might just not be a filmmaker for me.

56 years after the publication of the novel of the same name written by Frank Herbert which started one of the most recognized and celebrated fictional cycles, and 37 years after the ramshackle but fascinating adaptation directed by David Lynch , here's again a movie adaptation of Dune , directed by Denis Villeneuve , which incorporates the vintage grandeur of the classic blockbuster, of those historical movies of the past, a combination of set pieces, CGI , sound design, a considerable cast in proportions and a monster lenght. The glittering audiovisual system, however, is not all that glitters is gold, on the contrary it's a way to mislead the viewer, give away desktop screensavers, daze and move away the viewer from the concrete problems of this production, which are many. First of all, Dune is basically the (bad and derivative) pilot of a TV series - or a miniseries - still in the process of being approved by the network, a long introductory chapter, with a tremendously staid rhythm that after an hour has yet to get into the heart of the story, directed towards a third act that waiting for a second part still to be defined, a way of doing far - and wrong - from that of other trilogies which in any case gave the single movie a shape and a limited meaning, will never materialize. In years like these in which the Marvel Cinematic Universe is defined as the transposition of the serial form in a cinematographic context, when instead it responds to the reasons, the ways, the structure of the comic universe, seeing Dune passed, which has many elements from a TV series pilot, like a work of art devoid of third-party reasons and ways, it makes me smile enough, but it's the rule of the game. And then despite the large budget used and the great action, especially when the narration arrives on the planet Arrakis , the sumptuousness doesn't always correspond to the epic as in this case in the continuous attempt to truly amaze, never concrete, even in the most ascetic moments (the expanses of the planet Arrakis , the Spice in the sand) or dreamlike, Villeneuve , despite everything, gives the feeling of not having interest and affection for the sense of adventure, of the space opera - and it's serious that this feeling comes from the director of Blade Runner 2049 . The expansion annihilates the whole, the implant is the formal excuse to give oneself a certain importance, an harmless serial project already seen in other more significante space opera variations, a wonderful empty gift box.
