Tudo em Todo o Lugar ao Mesmo Tempo (2022), de Daniel Kwan e Daniel Scheinert, é um filme cuja inventividade visual é inegável. A direção de arte, o uso das cores e a composição dos quadros sustentam um espetáculo imagético que raramente deixa a tela perder energia. O problema é que, conforme a narrativa avança e os conflitos centrais começam a aparecer, essa exuberância formal passa a competir com o próprio drama. Em vários momentos, o filme me lembrou um episódio estendido de Rick and Morty, insistindo o tempo inteiro em provar o quanto é "maluco" e "criativo", mas girando em torno da mesma dinâmica até ela perder o impacto. O excesso vira um fim em si mesmo, quase um exercício de estilo, e a montagem acelerada acaba produzindo uma sensação de clipe permanente. As discussões sobre família, identidade e aceitação existem, mas parecem sempre mediadas pelo humor e pelo absurdo, como se o filme não confiasse que essas ideias conseguiriam se sustentar sem um novo estímulo a cada poucos segundos. Isso enfraquece a construção psicológica dos personagens: muitas mudanças simplesmente acontecem, sem que a mise-en-scène ou o roteiro construam um percurso emocional convincente até elas. Soma-se a isso um niilismo já bastante desgastado, aquele discurso de que "nada importa porque o universo é infinito", tratado como se ainda fosse uma grande revelação filosófica. No fim, fiquei com a impressão de um filme que confunde complexidade estrutural com profundidade dramática. Multiplicar universos, referências e estímulos não torna uma narrativa automaticamente mais complexa; às vezes só faz mais barulho do que significado.

Start at zero and add a half star for each of the following: *You think it's a crime Michelle Yeoh has never headlined a movie before (this is the minimum half-star, if you don't pass this, sorry robot, go back to picking out pictures of traffic lights on concert ticket websites) *You definitely think that Michelle Yeoh should get to both kick ass and have fun in such a movie. *You think Jamie-Lee Curtis is underused as comedic talent. *You enjoy the idea of a multiverse movie with heavy dollops of absurdism. *You admire the aesthetics of Edgar Wright... *But think he should really try to cram a bit more into his movies. *You felt an emotion during Swiss Army Man that the filmmakers intended. *You are interested in the philosophical question "What if an everything bagel really had, y'know, everything ?" *You think things going in people's butts is intrinsically just incredibly funny. * You can come up with any reason this movie should be the same length as The Tree Of Life . I thought I'd be in the tank for this, and there's a banger of a 90 minute film trapped in here, but it's definitely from the team that brought you Swiss Army Man, and I think that should tell you everything you need to know, even if fanny-pack kung fu replaces a farting corpse. (Although not quite: unlike that film, this one is laden in exposition of its multiverse concept, one we haven't seen in a film since, like, December.) I am glad I saw it on the big screen (thanks for hosting, Letterboxd, don't hate me!) and there are real laughs, some terrific performances, one scene I consider absolutely a top ten of the year contender (I'll call it "a planet that failed to produce life") and a few great set pieces. And just even figuring out how this took less than a year to shoot staggers the brain. But it's emotional maximalism that fails to even stir me as it gets lost in whatever through line it's trying to cling onto, only to spend minutes of exposition in that through line telling us what to feel about this or that aspect. To paraphrase Lao Tzu: more stuff means less.

Midway through the film, people walked out of the theatre (people NEVER walk out of the theatre where I live) and, towards the end of the film, the guy in front of me started ignoring the film and using his phone instead. As we were walking out, a stranger also came up to me and quipped, “How do I get a refund? It was so shit.” There was, however, this one dude who clapped very enthusiastically when the film concluded and looked around when not a single other person did the same. I didn’t hate or love the film as much as any of these people but I can’t say I was impressed with the film. I went in expecting/ hoping/ thinking I would eat it up but I… didn’t. My problems with the film are that many of the scenes felt repetitive and dragged out and the direction was so over-the-top that the film became intolerable at some points. Its attempts to be comedic also often fell flat and made the film feel tacky (to me, this is what I imagine people who hate Don’t Look Up are describing.) On the flip side, the costumes, the visual effects and Michelle Yeoh’s performance are great.  I also appreciated the strong emotional beats in the final third of the film but even those got dragged out, I think. Maybe I’ve just seen too many films about the multiverse lately. I watched this and Spider-Man: No Way Home back to back, and I also recently watched the Family Guy “Road to the Multiverse” episode. I definitely need a multiverse detox but, objectively, I maintain that the film is too extravagant and has a disappointingly weak screenplay. Don’t get overhyped like I was going in. Maybe you’ll love it, maybe you won’t but just make sure your expectations are in check.

Charlie Kaufman’s multiverse- Tree of Life , if made for Adult Swim -or- The feminine urge to eat a bagel. Whatever it is it comes out like Scott Pilgrim vs. the World - an alive diversion that doesn’t hit the emotional notes and gets repetitive on the rest. I was absolutely giddy for the first hour, something I’d like to bottle for an energy drink. Everything Everywhere is overlong and reaching for some pathos that doesn’t feel genuine but more like an attempt to ground the insanity with spelled out motives (practice patience and kindness and everything shall pass). Everything Everywhere All at Once works best as a multiverse marriage of expansions and retractions - shared memories, disappointments, parallel lives - and then it becomes about mother-daughter bridges. In fact, the mother-daughter arc isn't too far removed from something like Inside Out — even though the daughter beats some people to death with huge, floppy dildos. But it is constantly inventive, ridiculous, and the sheer number of inserts/locations/costumes to pull off the concept are beyond commendable. Michelle Yeoh is great. TikTok is gonna eat this up with out-of-context usage. -so- See it on the big screen with a crowd. -because- There's a lot in this blender and it has lots of nutrients — even if they’re liquified by the end.

This movie already exists and it's called The Matrix Evelyn Wang (Michelle Yeoh) leads a boring life. She runs a failing laundromat with her meek husband Waymond (Jonathan Ke Quan) and fusses over her directionless, standoffish daughter Joy (Stephanie Hsu). During a meeting with IRS agent Deidre (Jamie Lee Curtis), Waymond suddenly changes, informing her that he is a version of her husband from an alternate universe and that she is the only one who can save the multiverse from an ultimate destructive force. If you've seen a sci-fi movie made in the last 20 years, then multiverses, body-swapping, and all the mumbo-jumbo those things entail will be pretty easy for you to understand. Unfortunately, the filmmakers don't think so. The Daniels' first film, Swiss Army Man is so comfortable not explaining itself. It presents the audience with a farting boner corpse whose body can be used in a myriad useful ways for wilderness survival, and it never takes a second to explain how all of it works. Because it doesn't need to. All of the people who complain about Christopher Nolan's films having too much exposition are going to love this, even though this movie is almost entirely explaining things that are already pretty clear. There is so much to love here: The Daniel's have a wonderful, kinetic visual style, Michelle Yeoh and Stephanie Hsu give fantastically funny and compelling performances, the action is uniformly fun and exciting (although not groundbreaking or physically impressive), and pretty much all of the jokes work. The alternate universe stuff is all really good. Almost all of them are basically one-note gags, but The Daniels' have a really good handle on how to draw emotion out of a world where people have frankfurters for fingers, or extended riffs on Ratatouille and the works of Wong Kar-wai. Once the movie is allowed to actually get going, there is so much to enjoy. If this was 20 minutes shorter and didn't treat its audience like slop drinking fools, it would pretty easily be one of my favourites of the year.

Full disclosure: AMC "We Make Movies Better" Theaters had the temperature set to a pleasant 85-90 degrees in the auditorium, and when I let an attendant know of the problem, they immediately offered me a refund and refused to actually do anything to make the theater less of a sauna. So this ended up being one of the more uncomfortable theater experiences I've had and likely impacted my enjoyment of the movie. The movie being, luckily, absolutely hysterical and one that plays so well in front of a crowd. The Daniels go for broke and release completely unrestrained insanity and it's truly a wonder to behold. The way they managed to get my audience screaming because of paper cuts is honestly nothing short of incredible. But I'm not quite sure EEAAO actually works as a film . Despite trusting their audience to be on board with their ludicrous sense of humor, the Daniels seem afraid to trust the audience to understand what's actually happening plotwise, causing the film to become more and more repetitive as we get scene after scene explaining that there's a multiverse out there and it's really big and anything can happen. I get the feeling that the Daniels just had too many ideas, too many jokes, too many scenes in their head that they couldn't bring themselves to cut any of them. It turns what should be a breakneck ride into one of the longest, slowest movies I've seen in a while, particularly when its entire narrative arc becomes clear within the first 30 minutes. Eventually I found it hard to really remain invested in the story, even if I was still laughing. This could have been 100 minutes long. Instead, it never ends. Also, honestly, this is visually darker than it needed to be. Must be said that every single actor involved is at the top of their game here. Ke Huy Quan is truly phenomenal. Addendum 1: It's truly a sadness that In the Mood For Love is from here on out going to be remembered as a disgusting green mush instead of the vibrant colors it originally had. Addendum 2: Seriously, what's the deal with the Absolutely (Story of a Girl) references? Such a strangely specific joke that it kind of took me out of the movie.

Utter maximalist chaos. While I definitely have some misgivings with the humor and a handful of redundant moments, I know there’s something really special here. This sensory overload of a movie exists outside of decorum and logic, and yet somehow manages to coalesce into an intimate, heartfelt narrative led by the excellent Michelle Yeoh. While it has a consistent refusal to be taken seriously, the movie is anchored in a human gravitas of (literally) cosmic proportions. The Daniels want us to feel all of Evelyn’s paralyzing overstimulation, with no hesitation to use every cinematic special effect at their disposal. I am so glad to have watched this in IMAX, as I don’t believe there many other movies that are more deserving of such a presentation. And as great as this movie is, I think it could have gone even farther. There were definitely times when the multiverses felt more redundant than expansive. I also would have loved to see the multiverses have more significance than being just another tool to fight with. Surely it’s concerned with liberating ourselves from the constraints of our own perceived limitations, and not merely “let’s just do weird shit! XD”

“What is it, exactly, that Yeoh and co-writer-directors Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert (they go by the collectively pseudonym “Daniels”) do in their new film, which premiered to the first in-person SXSW screening in three years Friday evening? What don’t they do? Daniels previously conjured up 2016’s surreal modern fable SWISS ARMY MAN, which, for all its farting-corpse feigning towards sincerity, might still leave some viewers wondering if they were the victims of a $3 million prank several years later. “That same audience can rest assured EVERYTHING EVERYWHERE ALL AT ONCE will have them feeling more confident that, yes, there’s a genuine humanity at the core of Daniels’ work, here taking the form of Yeoh’s Evelyn Wang facing down a tinderbox of familial and cultural ultimatums which will be set ablaze by the mother of all stressors: tax trouble. It just so happens that Daniels’ story is filtered through a kaleidoscope of prior cinematic innovation, cartoonish exaggeration and cosmic coincidence as Evelyn is drawn into a conflict against an all-powerful villain wherein she’ll have to unlock her true potential and fulfill a cross-universal destiny…or something. Truth be told, the blueprints of this particular war are a bit confusing. Hell, can any movie delving into the ramifications of a splintering multiverse afford not to be?” -full review on kens 5-

Multiverses are so hot right now. And why shouldn’t they be? At a time when people can’t even look at their phones without being confronted by a seemingly infinite number of competing realities — a time which everything seems close enough to touch, but almost nothing feels possible to change, and even the happiest people you know are haunted by the endless possibilities of who else they might have been — telling a story that only takes place on a single plane of existence might as well be an act of denial. That isn’t a problem for the filmmaking duo of Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert (better known as Daniels), who once created an interactive six-minute short that could be played in 3,618,502,788,666,131,106,986,593,281,521,497,120,414,687,020,801,267,626, 233,049,500,247,285,301,248 different ways. These guys aren’t just uniquely prepared to meet the present moment, they’ve been waiting for it to catch up with them for a long time. So it’s not much of a surprise that the project they’ve been working on since 2016’s “Swiss Army Man” sees the crisis of living with “Everything Everywhere All at Once” more clearly than any other movie like it. Not that there are any other movies like it. Here is an orgiastic work of slaphappy genius that doesn’t operate like a narrative film so much as a particle accelerator — or maybe a cosmic washing machine — that two psychotic 12-year-olds designed in the hopes of reconciling the anxiety of what our lives could be with the beauty of what they are. It’s a machine powered by the greatest performance that Michelle Yeoh has ever given, pumped full of the zaniest martial arts battles that Stephen Chow has never shot, and soaked through with the kind of “anything goes” spirit that’s only supposed to be on TV these days. “Everything Everywhere All at Once” is as overstuffed as its title implies, even more juvenile than its pedigree suggests, and so creatively unbound from the minute it starts that it makes Daniels’ previous efforts seem like they were made with Bressonian restraint by comparison (for context, their last feature was a sweet fable starring Harry Potter as an explosively farting corpse). It’s a movie that I saw twice just to make sure I hadn’t completely hallucinated it the first time around, and one that I will soon be seeing a third time for the same reason. I don’t ever expect to understand how it was (or got) made, but I already know that it works. And I know that it works because my impulse to pick on its imperfections and wonder how it might’ve been different eventually forfeits to the utter miracle of its existence. ~this review continues on IndieWire~

By balancing destructive nihilism with joyful absurdism, the film captures how small human connections can heal the deep wounds of generational trauma. This movie perfectly showcases the complexities of Asian cultural dynamics, as parental love is often masked as strict criticism and heavy expectations to protect the family’s future. This creates a painful cycle of conditional love, leaving a feeling unseen and burdened by the pressure to be perfect. Seeing this with my Asian mother was the cherry on top of this already deeply resonating experience.

SXSW 2022 , World Premiere:    That was…fucking phenomenal. Watching this film made me feel like I was on a rollercoaster, not really sure what was coming next. It’s not predictable, there’s no static narrative structure, and it is jam-packed with bizarre ideas. It’s an experience that completely engages all of your senses, and like the directors stated, “will keep you at the edge of your seats”. You’ll wince, burst out laughing, and maybe shed a few tears (especially if you’ve experienced your own generational trauma). If you particularly like action, comedy, drama, or sci-fi, I guarantee you that all of these genres will be covered. There is something for everyone, but there is also nothing out there quite like it. The editing/effects were INCREDIBLE. The fight sequences were extremely well-choreographed. There was a lovely score and superb performances from Michelle, Ke Huy, Jamie, and Stephanie. Don’t think too hard about it. Just sit back, relax, and enjoy the ride as you go through everything, everywhere, all at once .

Absolute Cinema. Dieser Film sprudelt nur so vor Kreativität und man merkt es be jeder Szene. Jede kleine Geschichte wird wunderschön ausgearbeitet (Raccacconie verdient einen eigenen Film) und ich kann mir gar nicht vorstellen wie schwer das Editing gewesen sein muss, hatte ein ähnliches Niveau von der Vielfalt wie der Spiderman Animationsfilm. Außerdem war die Story mit den Steinen auch richtig gut und die Kampfszene wo sie mit den beiden Typen kämpft, die was im Arsch stecken haben ist absolute Cinema. Das Worldbuilding ist auch richtig interessant und die Menge an verschiedenen Kostümen und Designs ist verrückt. Ich liebe dass sich dieser Film absolut nicht ernst nimmt und dann an den wichtigen Stellen es doch wieder macht. Dazu fand ich cool dass die Charaktere nicht durchgehend Englisch gesprochen haben, weil das ja nicht ihre Muttersprache ist, sondern immer so einen Misch-Masch gesprochen haben, so wie es im echten Leben mit zweisprachigen Familien wirklich ist. Ich kann diesen Film wirklich nur empfehlen, er ist wunderschön und sehr lustig.

Admit it—most people remember Friday the 13th (2009) for all the wrong reasons like the overwhelming amount of nudities. This is just another typical slasher film: an unstoppable killer hunting down a group of unintelligent teenagers, with some protected by plot armor and others serving as disposable victims. One thing that genuinely annoyed me was the death of one of the nicest characters, who deserved a much better fate.

Thus my Crystal Lake journey comes to an end (at least until October). I don't know if I just have Stockholm syndrome or if it was just anti-remake culture that was prevalent when I first watched this, but this movie isn't really that bad. It's still pretty mediocre, it's definitely not an Evil Dead (2013) situation, but in comparison to the following year's Nightmare On Elm Street reinvention, it might as well as be a masterpiece. This film has a real nasty edge with some properly gnarly gore, which does give it its own identity. It kinda surprises me that this is the only outing, which utilises a bear trap, especially because Part 2 sets up that Crystal Lake is bear country, however it does   lead to delightfully horrific results. I'm sure a lot of this is due to the filmmakers wanting to compete with the "torture porn" craze of the time, yet they do manage to hold their own well enough. The unfortunate over side to the grossness coin, it's how much aggressively juvenile misogyny is on display, leering at its female characters in a way only a Micheal Bay produced flick can. Similarly, the American Pie style sex comedy (outside of a few jokes) feels very tired and just unnecessarily unpleasant. The characters are a bit of a nothing burger, although not in a way significantly different than most entries and there's a few good performances scattered in. At first glance, the idea of combining story elements from the first four installments into one narrative sounds like a recipe for disaster, yet those movies are either a bit repetitive or rather simple, that it actually kind of works. The script wasn't gonna awards, the dialogue is far too clunky and there are dumb character decisions and contrivances galore, but some thought clearly went into it. Overall, if you stayed away from this because it's a 2000s horror remake, first of all... Fair. Nonetheless, you can do much much worse.

So we’ve got Dean Forester from Gilmore Girls, Kyle Bradway from Party Down, and Jonah Simms from Superstore. Essentially it’s Avengers Endgame for streaming binges. Watching this I can understand why young people say millennials are the worst generation. Be that as it may, I kind of enjoyed this. More so, admittedly, than most of the movies in this franchise.

You know what, I really love how aggressive Jason is here. Gone is the stiff stalker from the 80s, and instead, we get a rabid animal. He moves quickly and doesn’t hesitate to brutalize. I did feel it was somewhat disappointing, however, that despite how aggressive he is, the kills aren’t overly memorable. Rewatching this after my recent marathon was helpful just in helping me notice how they tried to piece together the various eras and foundational lore of the original films into one story. That progression mostly works. Despite it being a noticeably better-made film when compared to many of its predecessors, it still feels like a very mediocre slasher. While some of the older films were boring cash grabs, others had fun. Saw this in the theater when I picked up the His Name Was Jason DVD, which came with a free movie ticket for the remake. I wonder if sales of that disc counted towards the box office numbers? I only wonder because this thing had a historic second weekend drop-off that basically killed the franchise in the mainstream until the video game came out. I remember seeing trailers for Miss March and the remake of Last House on the Left before the movie started. Even at the time, Miss March felt like it was trying to ride some kind of American Pie wave that had long ago hit the shore and settled back into the seas - no wonder Zach Cregger pretended it didn’t exist when doing the Barbarian press tour. Last House ’s trailer featured a soft girly version of Sweet Child O’ Mine which admittedly felt unique in 2009 compared to the usual Let the Bodies Hit the Floor style nonsense that accompanied horror ads back then. Fast forward to 2026, and the soft-remix trope is one of the top items on my trailer shitlist. You may have noticed I’m not really talking about the movie much, that’s because like all the Platinum Dunes franchise cash-ins of this era, there’s not much to really say. It’s an early 2000’s reboot with that pukey CW Network sheen all over it. To its credit, it was nice to go back to the lake after several entries of goofy nonsense. Trent is one of the all-time douche characters of the entire franchise and Julianna Guill provides some of the best nudity. The kills really should’ve saved this, but aside from the wakeboarding scene, I always struggle to remember any of them even after repeat viewings. If Friday ‘09 (and my accompanying memories at the time of release) is notable for anything, it’s that it was one of the last gasps of the early millennium, and the transition away from things like Drowning Pool, physical media promotions, and raunchy comedies. Watching this feels like a eulogy for the aughts, but as we approach the premiere of a new Crystal Lake series, we know all too well that milking every drop out of a franchise is a timeless endeavor.

So here's the thing, most Friday the 13th films are average. As a series, it doesn't have incredible lows like The Curse of Muchael Myeys or Freddy's Dead, nor the spectacular rebounds like H20 or New Nightmare. It is a series that has remained consistently okay. And that's more or less what this is, another okay entry in the Friday the 13th series. It has all the sex and violence that you expect—actually, a bit more sex than you'd expect for 2009—but doesn't really do much to change up the formula. Ironically, not changing the formula is probably this movie's biggest strength. It's the 12th Friday the 13th movie, and it feels like a Friday the 13th movie. There are some changes that work, some that don't, but overall just an average slasher with a handful of memorable scenes makes for a fairly enjoyable experience if that's your thing. Which weirdly makes it possibly the best of the major horror franchise reboots. Friday the 13th never had the subtext of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, the quiet suspense of Halloween, or the playful creativity of Evil Dead or A Nightmare on Elm Street. To put it bluntly, there just wasn't really much to fuck up.

I don't think this quite reaches the heights of the best sequels, but it's undeniably a reboot that fundamentally understands the task at hand, and arguably the superior of both Marcus Nispel's 00's horror remakes. Essentially a smooshed-together rendition of the first four original films into a new narrative remix of sorts, after a bit of a ropey opening it skips straight to the good stuff, barrels through the mythology, and gives us Derek Mears' Jason absolutely ruling as a considerably more driven and vicious take on the Hockey Masked killer. I don't really buy the criticisms that it's "too horny", since that promiscuity and lure is kind of part and parcel with the series and its own bizarre detours. The final stretch loses some of the momentum that makes the opening hour such a blast, but the pacing overall is quite relentless, the kills are inventive and nasty, and it's packed with enough of why this series became an institution in the first place. It's a shame it never really spawned anything more, and I look forward to the day we finally get another one of these. Maybe Damien Leone would be a good shout?

KILLER CUT This movie is supposed to suck, but how hard can it be to remake FRIDAY THE 13TH? All you need is Jason slaughtering horny teenagers at Camp Crystal Lake. Should be an easy 8/10. Let’s find out… 🔪🔪🔪 The problem with this movie right away, is that teenagers and young people are portrayed so unnaturally these days. Back in the day, they felt more like real people. Awkward, weird, messy. A lot of it is you would have amateur or non-actors doing some level of improvisation. There is an attempt here to replicate the random weirdness of 80s horror, but it feels manufactured. The cinematography is very bad. The original was creepier because it was mostly natural looking. This remake looks so processed and edited, despite mostly taking place outdoors! It doesn’t look anything like real life. FT13th doesn’t need any of that shit. It’s a guy in a mask in the woods. I don’t want it to look polished into oblivion. By the way, how old are these people? I assumed they were young, but they all look at least 30. I guess it doesn’t matter, though, because they pull the old switcheroo and we get a whole new cast of characters. They also look pretty old. Trent is at least 47. This new group is slightly better, and I’m glad we’re not stuck with the first one. Something that should be commended is that they didn’t change Jason’s look. He looks like he could be from one of the original sequels. “Have you seen a guy carrying a dead body?” There is sufficient violence, I guess, but not any cool practicals. There is some choice nudity, though, which is cool. Julianna Guill is amazing! But yeah, the kills generally weren’t practical or creative. If you’re going to remake a classic slasher, you better have some cool kills in mind. Some of the suspense was successful, and I would probably be more lenient if it was an original property. It’s not terrible, it just doesn’t have enough personality. The end was acceptable. New Line DVD 📀

Friday the 13th (2009) was my first experience with the franchise, and honestly, I had a great time with it. It doesn’t try to reinvent the slasher genre, but it knows exactly what it wants to be, and it delivers an entertaining ride from start to finish. Clay was easily my favorite character. Unlike many slasher protagonists, he isn’t just trying to survive—he’s determined to find his missing sister, and I loved how he never gave up on her. I also appreciated how protective he was of Jenna, which made him someone I genuinely rooted for. Trent was easily my least favorite character. His arrogance and attitude made him impossible to like, so his fate felt well deserved. I also liked that Jason wasn’t portrayed as a completely mindless killer. He follows a distorted logic shaped by his obsession with his mother. Whitney survives because she reminds him of her, which helps explain his actions—but it never excuses them. Understanding a villain’s motives is very different from justifying their crimes. The film doesn’t introduce anything particularly new to the slasher formula, but I honestly didn’t mind. I enjoyed it for what it was, and as my first Friday the 13th film, it definitely made me interested in the franchise. Sometimes a classic formula is all you need when it’s executed with confidence.

About 6 months ago,  the world started seeing advertisements for a film that was touted as “a game changer” and “the scariest movie ever made”. People, myself included, started looking forward to the release of Hereditary. Recently, Letterboxd started filling with reviews for this much anticipated film - the most positive, enticing reviews I’ve seen. People I follow and trust gave 5 stars, a heart, and glowing reviews about holding back tears, almost passing out, being haunted by horrifying images. Tonight I finally saw this film that held so much promise and excitement. Two hours and change later, I’m absolutely shocked to find out that the past six months of hype and pointed, targeted advertising, along with the thousands of epic reviews on this site were actually all part of a very elaborate plot to punk me. It’s hard not to believe that this was all a Truman Show-esque experiment because otherwise that would mean that I really am this profoundly and inexcusably removed from the common consensus on what is good versus what is very, very bad. I’m sad and disillusioned. If this is the “future of modern horror” then I don’t think I can be a horror fan anymore. Boo

Very rarely do I do feel the kind of anger and hate towards a film with the kind of passion that Hereditary has. The human drama and the representation of guilt and grief could be channeled into a first-rate horror film such as the likes of The Babadook and It Comes at Night. Instead, the film muddies the message with a ton of misdirection, ludicrous introduction of supernatural elements and an ending that twists it's own logic into knots only to come off as two-bit Roman Polanski. I spent thirty minutes after seeing the film to piece together everything, figured out all the clues, then realized I spent more time making the movie make sense than its director had. That said, the film is gorgeously shot, Toni Collette gives one of her most passionate performances and there are a couple of really creepy moments (which are completely undermined by the end of the film). This is not a new classic in the making, it's a self-indulging, pretentious, hilariously tone-deaf thriller where nobody is likable because they all make mind numbingly bad decisions. This movie is good-looking garbage.

The entire movie has you sitting on the edge of your seat from the jump, constantly thinking, "Oh boy! This movie's about to get really good!" Aims for a home run, but strikes out before it can get past the first act. Man, this was a major disappointment. It’s clear Aster has watched indie horror films of late (hence what probably caught A24’s attention) and late 60s/70s classics. Yet unlike It Follows, The Babadook & The Witch, Hereditary lacks a desire to establish pathos that engages its themes, which are so haphazardly spelled out in every scene instead of letting them develop organically between characters. This will fall prey to the “scary” hype, but as we’ve seen recently, good horror doesn’t have to be traditionally scary — or “scary” by what 15-year olds want. Collette is fine, but hysteria — for me — doesn’t always make a performance stand out for the right reasons. Wolff is, at times, unwatchable. Shapiro is the real star. As Collette’s Annie says, “And what a waste.”

I’m actually kind of mad at how much I bought into this hype. A slow burn only works if there’s substance to sear, but this was like a brick candle doused in nothing but forced exposition, frail shock horror, and fatiguing stagnancy. I came in wondering if this movie would make me shit my pants, and I left wishing I did, so I could have had an excuse to walk out.

What does Hereditary have to say about literally anything? Does it comment on grief? Not really. We’re introduced to Annie who wears this guilt that the passing away of her mother isn’t as grieving as she expected or maybe even wanted it to be. Does it say anything about dysfunctional family dynamics— a disregard for healthy display of emotion? Not really. We’re shown that these characters bury their emotions and even punish others (and themselves) for being emotionally honest, but it couldn’t be bothered to expound on it because it’s more concerned with playing to it’s genre. Are we given any reason Annie wears guilt or that she “adds stress” to her family? Other than feeling the way she does about her mother, we’re given none whatsoever. So what is Hereditary ? An indulgent genre piece that’s not only missing an hour of family drama that would emotionally tie things together (as confessed by the director), it’s spiritually empty. For all it’s comparison to “The Exorcist”, Ari Aster’s first film pales in comparison. William Friedkin first of all never set out to make his film a “horror”. We’re met with a mystery of how things come to be and one priest’s crisis of faith. Hereditary is as depthfully honest as a tack compared to a sword.

The marketing's already begun and I'll admit I want to see it again. We heard whispers most of the festival about A24's hot new horror film, hearing many people say what's now in the marketing, that Hereditary is the new scariest film ever. While having that air of new horror I've written about before, Hereditary lacks the compelling story that truly would have had this grind my insides. This does a ton correctly that I'll praise. It builds up the tension immensely well, traversing at a deliberate pace that ramps up the dread perfectly. Something creepy looms on the horizon for a long time, daring the viewer that it will appear at any moment. But as a horror film going over two hours, that sense of loom ultimately gets to be too much. Hereditary doesn't give a release. It builds and builds, promising an explanation to the madness unfolding on screen only to drag on too long and not give any satisfactory answers. While effective in its horror, as the film gets to the truly terrifying moments, I had already lost faith that it would have any meaning. Hereditary does enough right to not be considered bad, but its also unbelievably frustrating in its attempts to mask the lack of a story with horror. Overall, I'll likely still see it again just to have a second opinion, yet I won't likely be able to forgive the problems riddling the film just because it builds the horror correctly.

It's the Michael Bay equivalent of a horror film, and about as incongruous as The Snowman, but gets by on shocking horror, and slick art direction. Hereditary is a narratively hollow culmination of ideas Ari Aster wrote on many napkins over a decade, stashed in a shoebox, then pulled out and scattered down a staircase to make a script. It bounces around various genres, concepts, plots, and themes, then haphazardly staples them together with elements of Rosemary's Baby. What it does well is evoke inventively disturbing imagery, underscored by immense dread. But then it takes all of it, and tries to stick it to its characters as well as sticking a slice of aloe to Teflon covered in motor oil. Its paper thin plot waffles between nebulous and overly expository. The characters are all one note, and underdeveloped. Whether it's Toni Collette who is crying or freaking out (nothing in between), Gabriel Byrne who's so skeptical, he doesn't even believe he's in the same movie, or Alex Wolff who plays a seventeen year old, but cries like a four year old. This is being treated as the second coming of The Exorcist (or insert whichever movie was seen as the scariest for its time). But it seems to really just be getting far off of its hype.

Okay A24--we're done. No more of these half-realized genre pics, technical exercise, calling cards. May Under The Skin remain the only great film you've released(okay and Spring Breakers). So what's wrong with Hereditary ? It's cynical but not so obviously at first. The first half begins with quite an unexpected plot point and builds upon it with an eerie, grief felt, and almost at the edge of tears/laughter kind of atmosphere. It is refreshing that the film doesn't cheaply go for jump scares(make of that whatever you will) and god damn, Toni Collette is great. She's perfect for this kind of role, too bad it's stuck in a movie that in turn, leads her character into one of the most tired resolutions. And really, that's where this film comes undone. It is easy to figure out what exactly is going on and the scariest thing is that it'll confirm your own presumptions that this film has nowhere new to go. In fact, it lamely falls back on the kind of final half hour that dissolves first, into absurdity, and second, into cynicism. What does that leave us with? A technical exercise and nothing more. What the film had set up was perfectly fine, and hilariously, its playing off well worn tropes of the horror genre by sheer force of will. But what the film fucks up, is that horror in one way or another, has to have more than just a bunch of creepy happenings and then the most routine, lame, and tired explanation to all those creepy happenings. Why does the director rely on dollhouses? Because the shots look cool. Why mine mental illness? Who cares. The big bad in this feels like a cheat. One in which I didn't have a single care or devotion to. And the film leaves it at that, which is so frustrating. The best kind of horror films leave us by confirming that our fears and emotions are justified, even if they are strongly ambiguous. What Hereditary does is try to explain why we should be afraid or why we were afraid before. It doesn't add up and it doesn't have the heart, nerve, or audacity to accept that. It would rather seem ambiguous and deep, as if it were pulling one over the audience, but its last trick is predictable, lazy, old news.

Way too much going on at once here for it to work as much of anything. In this sense, it becomes obvious that Hereditary is from a first time director in Ari Aster, as he throws in just about every horror trope that has gained critical and financial success in the past five years. The film really does have it all: the slow, brooding pace, the ambient soundtrack that becomes unsettling from the eclectic percussion, the long takes with smooth camera movement, haunted house spooks and scares a la James Wan, occultism, a weird looking kid, exploration of grief/guilt through horror, etc. If that seems like a lot it is because it is, and the film is unable to really commit fully to what it wants to be, resulting in a jarring tone. It probably would have worked well had it fully committed to one of the multiple films going on here, but as it stands we have a story of grief and regret that goes completely off the rails. It is all an exercise in excess, a mishmash of what is "in" right now in horror. The camerawork in particular is somewhat infuriating, I'm all for clever camerawork but this film just felt gimmicky at times. Specifically, a shot where Collette's character returns to visit Jeanie, and as she walks down the hall the camera is upside down, only to smoothly flip when she passes to go right side up. Maybe trimming unnecessary shots like this will make it so your horror movie isn't two hours long, brutal when there's not many scares to be had. To be quite honest, I think I'm about sick of the A24 art house horror/thriller style that all feel about the same, relying heavily on the art house style. This is fine if you actually make a compelling film around it, but recent busts like It Comes at Night and now Hereditary make it clear that the style is stale and the film needs to be ACTUALLY SCARY if it wants to work. Hereditary is too complex for its own good. The real bummer about this is there are parts that are really great in the film, which makes me think that Aster one day will make a good horror movie if he learns to have a more focused vision. Toni Collette gives a wonderful performance, honestly the family as a whole is pretty solid at capturing what it feels like to struggle with loss. And a certain car scene is one of the more shocking moments I've seen in a film, an incredibly powerful (and, perhaps exploitative moment given where the film goes) moment that genuinely left me stunned for a good few minutes after. Hereditary could've been great if it decided to be a drama focused on grief, a haunted house movie (because boy does this at the end want to be The Conjuring so fucking badly), a weird pulpy occult film, a more straightforward ghost flick, or about family dynamics following a complicated loss, but not all at once. What we get is a bloated horror movie that is light on everything scary and compelling, instead bouncing around from theme to theme resulting in a climax that feels so out of left field it is almost laughable. Am I missing something here? The praise is baffling to me. This movie does literally nothing better than other movies recently have, the grief as horror is probably better in The Babadook, the spooky house moments pale to Wan's work, the occultism feels like a lazy way to end a film, and the family drama is much better in a film like A24's own Krisha. There's a good movie in here somewhere, it's just got way too much going on to really see.

"I just don’t want to put any more stress on my family." Annie Graham (Toni Collette) makes miniature models for a living, including ones that reflect her weird relationship with her recently-departed mother. The effects of that relationship carry over to her interactions with her conflicting-avoiding husband Steve (Gabriel Byrne), her bong-hitting son Peter (Alex Wolff), and her clucking daughter Charlie (Milly Shaprio). Charlie, was particularly close to her grandmother, and finds it hard to accept the love of her mother. When Annie discovers her mother was heavily into the occult, her influence only grows from beyond the grave. Hereditary is a movie that has a distinct midpoint, with two very different movies on either side (think of the shooting scene in "Boogie Nights"). The first half is about a family's pain, and how they work hard not to address it. The second is about the terror created when those family members go to extremes to heal that pain. So the former is a slow-paced drama while the latter is a quickening horror film. And that's the main problem with this film. First-time writer/director Ari Aster had a strong  story idea and a distinct vision for telling it. However, he likely should have done one or the other. With the film's slow-burn beginning, the air is let out of the horror balloon, which made the second half less effective. This movie is being billed as this generation's "Exorcist," which creates high audience expectations. But without the continued building pace needed to scare the shit out of us, things that would likely have stood out as set pieces are lost. There are some things Aster does very well. Annie's model houses are a running metaphor, and he utilizes long shots that make the family look like they inhabit one of them. And there some great tracking shots I'm still trying to figure out how he did them. But we likely could have traded some brooding, quiet moments for illustrating parts of the backstory rather than telling it. With the grandmother discussed but not really seen, she's more concept than character. There's also a moment where a connection is noted in a line of dialogue that exposes a throughline of revelations all the way to third act (at least it did for me). A fresh set of eyes in the director's chair might have been able to find these flaws and corrected them to deliver a scarier film. Note that I'm being oblique in my story summary and discussion to avoid spoilers, which does mean there are some good twists that make the movie enjoyable. I was definitely shocked and got some good scares. Also the four main actors were all very strong, with Collette showing an insane amount of range. But even with that, I found I didn't care that much about what happened to this family, and finally figured out why. Being dropped straight into their grief over Annie's mother's set a sombre tone for every second of the movie. So there were no good times for this family. There was no bonding moments or even times when I thought anyone in the family liked anyone else. So by the second half when things got screwy, I just kinda shrugged. If you're a horror fan, go see this one in the theatre to get the full effect. But for everyone else, you can probably wait for it to show up on Netflix.

The recent surge of a particular brand of arthouse horror, favoring tension- and character-building over blood-fueled gonzo insanity, has found at a home in A24 with the likes of The Witch, It Comes at Night, and even Yorgos Lanthimos’ recent features. Their latest in the genre comes with Hereditary, the directorial debut from writer-director Ari Aster, which–as the title suggests–is less haunted house horror and more about the terror tied with psychologically-taut familial relations. Not unlike Robert Eggers’ Sundance sensation, Aster displays proficient skill in eerie tone-setting, elaborate production design, and the type of scares that will leave a pervasive imprint on the mind, even if the underlying mythology gets over-complicated by the finale. First of all, this film is not "this generation's 'The Exorcist.'" Nor is it "this generation's 'Rosemary's Baby'" for that matter. "Hereditary" doesn't come close to those classic horror films in terms of characterization or narrative coherence.  Toni Colette, Ann Dowd, and Alex Woolf all give very strong performances, and the film boasts some unusually creepy imagery, fabulous sound design (the doppler effect immerses us in the film, to the point that I swore I heard tongue clucking in the cab on the way home) and great sequences, rendering it a good, perhaps even very good, film. However, the story remains sketchy, and the ending in particular feels overwrought and unsatisfying, straining "suspension of disbelief."  There is not enough context for that resolution, as I saw it, so I felt stunned and a little let down. Which is really too bad, because the sequences leading up to it - directly after the "fire" scene - are extremely tense and quite frightening. The car scene with Peter and Charlie (I hope to see more of Milly Shapiro in future films!) is also brilliant & horrifying. It just doesn't come together **in terms of story.** Even the film's title is not clearly explained. There are intimations, but nothing is made clear. Don't get me wrong: ambiguity is fine; in fact, I usually love it. But "Hereditary" has too many loose threads to take it from very good to excellent. I will give it another watch, of course, to see if that changes for me. For now, I am glad I saw it in a theatre, and there is certainly lots to like, regardless of my critiques. I look forward to reading more reviews on here.

My guess is you'll see some best actor nominations from this movie - the performances are INCREDIBLE across the board. And it's a really well made movie with some interesting visual ideas and a relentless pace. It really is quite good - but I pretty distinctly did not like this movie. Without getting into details, this movie is an actual, living nightmare where all of our characters are reeling from various trauma in their lives. And for a long time the movie toils in this trauma and is absolutely heartbreaking and difficult to watch. It really fucked me up long before it got to the horror movie of it all. And I think that's kind of where I disconnected from this movie - once it moves into the horror movie elements, it gave me this very odd feeling. This isn't really a criticism of the movie, simply an explanation for how it made me feel and why that detracted from the experience of the movie for me - it almost insults the characters' very real trauma by becoming a horror movie. I couldn't shake the feeling that the movie was using all of these very real, awful predicaments it was putting the characters into simply to fuck up us, the viewers, with no concern for what any of that trauma actually means to the characters. This isn't entirely true, but I don't want to spoil any details and explain further why I think the movie operates like this, suffice to say that's absolutely how it made me feel. There's a particular shot about halfway through the movie that is horrifying and gruesome and ultimately doesn't come from any character's perspective - it's literally something the filmmakers force us and only us to see. I think that was the moment the movie started to lose me, and from there it only dug deeper into that kind of storytelling and it was just never able to get me back. There's definitely a lot to like here, but the feeling it gave me overall was one of manipulation and exploitation, and it made me very uncomfortable. And you could absolutely argue that it was supposed to - but that doesn't change how it ultimately made me feel, which was very uneasy with what this movie put both me and it's characters through.

Little bit of column A. Little bit of column Bad. This is the work of an adept technician with only a meager command of narrative and drama. Is ToniCollette-sploitation a thing? She's wild here. Hereditary possesses some impressive formal chops but the aesthetics have the misfortune of drawing attention to how lame the direction is when it's not trying to scare you. The mise en scene and uncanny dollhouse shots (especially those lateral tracks through walls!) I found to be aces, however, try to move the story along or do character work and you get hackneyed script or one dimensional direction. Note all the times a scene continues in an unmotivated slow zoom or begins on an object close up then pans to a character. These happen repeatedly and are more stylistic than revealing. Reaction shots are held beyond comfort although not in a gainful way; more in a way that has me asking 'is that all?'. Admittedly the camera movements contrast the stillness of the spooks for when they appear (frame movement vs movement in frames), but this technique communicates little more than its presence in the moment. The same can be said for the editing. Clipped scenes and dissolves, which seem more like choices made in conjunction with the score, a buzzing drone uniting mood and blurring time. Without spoiling anything, the film wants the audience to pendulate between two possible explanations up until the ending when it jettisons the more interesting (and fleshed out) of the two as more or less irrelevant. To this end, the narrative plays fast and loose with reality and portent, all the while whittling itself down to a literal but complex closure. Hereditary 's heart and head are in its play of light and shadows, but the interstitial tissue rots from neglect. (Edit. I have learned the original cut was much longer and contained elements I found lacking, so I could change my tune on the drama and narrative if I were to see it.)

I’m not saying that directors of horror films are better than other directors; I am saying that horror is a genre that is going to expose who’s got “it,” and who doesn’t. First-time feature director Ari Aster absolutely has “it” in this thriller about a woman named Annie (Toni Collette) who is dealing with the recent death of her mother when she begins to see spectral apparitions, and her family faces a variety of fresh terrors. Lurking around the edges of Aster’s story are possible metaphors for parents who fear what they might pass on to their kids—things like mental illness—but the thematic stuff is almost incidental. This is simply one creepy-ass piece of filmmaking, as Aster shows off an exquisite sense of where to put the camera so that an ominous glint of red light reflects in someone’s eye, or something unspeakable lurks in a dark corner of the frame. And he’s savvy enough at how to set up his narrative and his sound design so that a seemingly innocuous sound like a clucked tongue becomes a harbinger of doom. Hereditary gets a bit needlessly expository during its climax, part of an overall sense that there’s some pacing fat that could stand trimming. It’s absolutely worth that extra time, though, to put yourselves in the hands of someone who understands the way cinema can inspire profound unease.

Up until the final act, Hereditary offers up fantastically orchestrated terror.  Classic genre elements (e.g. seances, possessions) are blended with innovative horrific ideas, all anchored by engagingly complex and strongly portrayed characters.  Toni Collette and Nat Wolff show off impressive range as grieving family members, and the transition from psychological haunting to metaphysical is perfectly fluid.  Once my jaw initially dropped, it stayed down for much of the rest of the film.  Also of note is the welcome relegation of the patriarchal figure to the background.  Unfortunately, all the buildup is so strong that the shoddy, incongruously trite, and emotionally unsatisfying ending, which disregards psychological themes in favor of hokey folklore, is made all the more disappointing.  Still, Hereditary is a near-perfect horror treat. With: Matt Where: Egyptian Theater (Sundance)

Este filme representa, a meu ver, tudo aquilo que há de mais problemático no cinema nacional contemporâneo. É um insulto à tradição artística construída por cineastas que buscaram desenvolver uma linguagem verdadeiramente brasileira para a sétima arte. Saímos da ambição estética e intelectual de Glauber Rocha, responsável por obras fundamentais como Terra em Transe e Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol, passamos por realizadores como Nelson Pereira dos Santos e José Mojica Marins, que ajudaram a consolidar uma identidade própria para o cinema brasileiro, para chegarmos a produções como esta, inteiramente subordinadas à lógica do melodrama televisivo e da padronização estética importada do audiovisual norte-americano. O filme permanece preso ao nível mais superficial de apreensão estética. Qualquer sensação de profundidade surge menos de sua construção narrativa do que de expedientes psicológicos cuidadosamente calculados para provocar respostas afetivas automáticas. Tudo parece subordinado à lógica mercadológica: a identidade nacional, a riqueza cultural brasileira e a complexidade dramática são sacrificadas em favor da acessibilidade imediata e da rentabilidade, é o exemplo máximo do Brasil descartando seu cinema como arte para transforma-lo em mero produto e propagando fazendo uma representação porca de sua própria realidade, com um diretor de fotografia sem criatividade e atores que acham que estão em uma novela da globo.

Le film a la prétention de traiter un sujet « dur » mais il passe la pommade au spectateur pendant 2 heures. La folie et la douleur auxquelles les personnages devraient être sujets sont complètement reniées, tout est fait pour paraître plus doux (le gardien de prison qui est gentil mdrrr j’étais à deux doigts de couper le film). Ensuite, je n’avais jamais vu une famille aussi fonctionnelle, je pense que ça n’existe pas, c’est un fantasme, je n’y crois pas (surtout que les relations ne se fissurent jamais malgré les épreuves). En plus, le personnage principal, celui de la mère, n’existe apparemment qu’à travers son mari et ses enfants, elle n’a pas de personnalité, on ne ressent jamais la douleur et le vide qui pourraient la dévorer. Comme si ce n’était pas déjà assez insupportable, le spectateur est pris par la main constamment (ex : le coup du médicament contre le diabète). Enfin, encore un réalisateur qui filme un animal comme une poupée. Si c’était pour traiter le chien comme un doudou et ne pas en faire un personnage, ce n’était pas la peine (d’ailleurs, quand il meurt on ne sent aucune émotion puisqu’il n’a jamais existé dans le film). Les animaux sont souvent hyper mal utilisés dans les films, dommage. Je ne parle pas de la musique dégoulinante de bons sentiments qu’on se tape régulièrement. Bref, c’est typiquement le genre de films « sUr La rÉsiLieNce » qui donnent la nausée.

بنظر لحظه‌ی وداع تلخ خانواده با خانه‌ی گرم و محبوب‌شان، نقطه‌ی پایان قصه‌ی این خانواده‌ی دوست‌داشتنی در برزیلِ استبدادزده‌ی دهه هفتاد است و یک‌سوم پایانی و پرداختن به دو مقطع زمانی دیگر، کش دادن بیهوده زمان فیلم و تنزل اثر به گزارشی بی‌خاصیت از آینده‌ی این خانواده در جامعه‌ی جدید برزیل است که صرفا ادای دینی‌ غیرسینمایی/غیردراماتیک است به داستان واقعی مورد اقتباس اثر. ارزش فیلم در لحظه‌هایی‌ست که استبداد روح افراد و روحیه‌ی جمعی‌شان را ذره‌ذره به نابودی می‌کشاند (صحنه‌هایی چون انتقال مادر و دختر به بازداشتگاه با کیسه‌هایی روی صورت و یا بعدتر یک لحظه رد شدن مادر نگران از کنار دختر و شناختنش حتی با چشمان بسته). ایکاش پیوند‌های صمیمی و مؤثر پدر با تک‌تک اعضای خانواده و حتی دوستان خانوادگی در ثلث اول فیلم، در نیمه دوم و در خلأ هولناک پیش‌آمده از غیبت مرموزش، دست‌کم در ارتباط با فرزندانش، استمرار بهتری می‌داشت و جای خالی‌اش به اندازه کافی در روابط دیگران حس می‌شد بجای آنکه به مفروضات ظاهرا بدیهیِ عواقبِ یک حکومت مستبد، بسنده میکرد؛ این آثار دهشتناک و بشدت عمیق و پنهانی، در همان لحظات ظاهرا ساده‌ای ساخته میشود که حس میشود دیگر چیزی شبیه قبل نیست؛ زخم واقعی استبداد نه صرفا در بازجویی‌ها و شکنجه‌گاه‌ها که در همین لحظه‌های کوچک و خاموش زندگی روزمره خانه می‌کند؛ مثلا در نگاه دزدکی دختر به مادری که تازه از بازداشتگاه برگشته و در حمام مشغول شستشوی خود با چشمانی اشکبار است یا نگاه دخترک کوچکتر به خانه خالی‌شده‌شان که حرفهای ناگفته زیادی را با خود به همراه دارد.

Apesar de ter muitos méritos, como a atuação poderosa de Fernanda Torres, a bela cinematografia que acompanha todo o filme, a dor de ver uma família destruída por um fato que durou 21 anos no Brasil e a demonstração de como era a perseguição a dissidentes e críticos àquele regime imposto, I'm Still Here erra ao tentar ser um filme e, ao mesmo tempo, uma novela das 9:00 horas produzida pela TV Globo. Isso deve-se principalmente à forma pela qual Walter dirige, monta, cria e coloca os diálogos, constrói a trama e aplica filtros de cores ao seu filme, que remontam diretamente aos modelos e convenções novelísticas moldados por décadas pelas principais emissoras nacionais e internacionais, como as falas explícitas sem a construção do silêncio, as explosões de emoção dos personagens -- o que os faz parecerem um pouco irreais -- e o uso excessivo de meios dramáticos fáceis demais. Uma cena que exemplifica isso é o momento em que as crianças vão ao escritório do pai para mostrar o novo cachorro, pois embora seja uma cena de felicidade das crianças e, consequentemente, de seu pai com o novo cachorro, ela se assemelha muito à construção de cena de dramaturgia, graças aos diálogos, à reação do pai e do colega e à cor pastel que reforçam essa sensação durante todo o longa. A principal explicação desse estranhamento que atravessa a obra tem raízes na forma como o Brasil constrói e construiu suas artes. Desde a popularização do cinema nacional no meio internacional, muitas produtoras e distribuidoras têm escolhido o que é mais fácil e melhor para elas no sentido econômico e cultural: a contratação de atores de novelas para filmes, já que são rostos conhecidos pelo público e têm uma bagagem de atuação muito maior que um ator que está dando seus primeiros passos. Por isso, mesmo nascendo puramente como um longa-metragem, sua raiz pivotal está presa e ligada às novelas, e I'm Still Here sofre com essa dicotomia. Portanto, um dos maiores problemas do cinema nacional é o fato de sempre conversar e ter em seu âmago as regras e padrões da teledramaturgia, não obstante seja uma obra feita para o cinema. Por esse motivo, I'm Still Here , ainda que trate de um assunto pesado e espinhoso que permeia a sociedade brasileira, sofre com crise de identidade, não sabendo se é um drama televisivo ou um longa-metragem -- embora tenha muitos méritos que poderiam atingir seu auge caso se desprendessem das convenções de um meio do qual não faz parte.

In my opinion, this was a questionable choice to be the first Brazilian film to win an Oscar, considering how many stronger and way better films came before it. Like for example the movie "Central Station" by Walter Salles himself who even competed for the same category at the Oscars back in 1999. The performances, dialogues, and script leave a lot to be desired. There’s a lack of depth and good technique that makes it hard to fully connect with the story or its characters. For me, as a Brazilian who has seen so many outstanding films from our cinema, it felt like I was watching one of those generic Netflix movies. It’s not a terrible film, but it doesn’t feel nearly as impactful or deserving of that level of recognition.

"I'm Still Here" is a drama like many others, I'm a little unsure of what qualifies the film as to being so special, when it seems like almost every drama plays out in an all too similar fashion, was expecting a bit more from this one given the opening scene and being as highly acclaimed, now it may just be the case that I've seen one too many of these sorts of films, well, then in that case what makes this stand out amongst its peers? "Central Station" by the same director was a bit better and definitely better paced, so I'm a little unsure what all the hype is about besides it winning an award, perhaps it is a film for people who don't watch that many films or if they do they prefer to watch this, I'm unsure why you would prefer to watch something like this still? "I'm Still Here" has a couple of nice scenes, almost all of the scenes that hook us into the film appear within the first hour, after that happens the film slowly grinds to a complete halt in terms of how poorly paced it is, if we were to talk about a different aspect of the film it is the exact same story when it comes to being cinematically and visually appealing to the consumer et large, the first half upstages the latter on both fronts Marcelo Rubens Paiva's 2015 memoir shares the same name

Esse filme, nas suas escolha da cena em que em meio aos gritos, o policial diz pra Eunice que “ele não concorda”, ou a cena em que ela tá falando na faculdade que “agora as terras indígenas são demarcadas”, ficarem fazendo questão de falar que o Rubens Paiva não era um guerrilheiro, ou na cena final com ela já idosa observando com todo o rosto cheio afundado em saudade e melancolia a foto de seu esposo que nunca mais voltou (aliás uma das cenas, pra mim, mais impactantes), sendo assistida e cuidada minuciosamente por sua família branca, heterossexual, de classe média em um apartamento no rio/sp, todo mundo de branco indo tirar uma foto, todo mundo sorrindo menos Eunice…De fato há uma mensagem da falta que jamais será preenchida, de buracos que a ditadura realmente deixou, mas tudo me passa a mensagem que o Brasil realmente passou por uma redemocratização, de que além de o problema não ser a polícia enquanto instituição, e sim policiais especificos, que muitos só tinham que seguir ordens mas até “não concordavam com isso”, mas além disso, que agora é totalmente diferente do período da ditadura, que vivemos uma democracia. Acho inevitável deixar de comparar ele com outro filme recente sobre ditadura, é que também tem como escolha a cena final representar “os dias de hoje”, o Agente Secreto, que pra mim apresenta uma visão política, e portanto estética tbm, totalmente diferente da ditadura, comparando as cenas finais por exemplo, em vez de uma família que vive agora relativamente bem e feliz na “democracia brasileira”, temos um filho, agora adulto, sozinho em mais um prédio cinza gelado, que quase tudo de memória que tem do pai, são as fitas recém conquistadas, gravadas na época de sua perseguição por tentar resistir ao domínio empresarial, principalmente dos Estados Unidos sobre a produção de conhecimento, nas faculdades do Brasil durante a ditadura. Acho que o Agente secreto traz a tona a discussão de que não ouve ruptura e muito menos reparação com esse nosso passado tão recente, muito pelo contrário, perspectiva quase oposta ao filme do burguês dono da globo Walter Salles, onde temos a questão da violência policial apresentada quase como uma questão de cpf, não da instituição enquanto uma herança colonial e racista, e mesmo com esse buraco que fica no peito das pessoas que não voltam mais…a vida continua, e continua feliz, sorridente, muito melhor do que antes, enquadrada em uma foto de família feliz…uma perspectiva que nos coloca muito mais numa relembrança passiva, do que num incômodo ativo, uma pulga atrás da orelha sobre como o presente ainda é carregado de passado, de que não essa ruptura com quem nos domina, explora e mata. Enfim, acho ainda estou aqui o pior filme do mundo e muito menos um filme “feio”, ou que não tenha elementos importantes da nossa memória, mas acho que mostra tanto a ditadura quanto os dias de hoje numa perspectiva burguesa e pouco interessada na discussão da memória da classe trabalhadora da ditadura, muito menos na politização da mesma pra enfrentar os impactos desse período obscuro da nossa história no presente. (Também achei bem curiosa essa escolha de falar das terras indígenas hoje serem demarcadas como se fosse algo que hoje é tranquilo, sendo que no gov lula estão tento diversos embates, um seguido do outro, dos povos indígenas lutarem pra defender seu território sendo atacado por garimpeiro ilegal que mesmo assim entra ou lutarem arduamente um mês contra a iniciativa do gov lula de PRIVATIZAR um rio…)

Talvez «Ainda estou aqui» seja uma experiência que ressoe com mais força no público brasileiro. É sempre um desafio equilibrar o drama político sem cair no lugar-comum, especialmente para quem já consumiu o gênero antes. Embora seja um filme educativo e necessário, a obra se prende a uma narrativa previsível e a um ritmo que beira o letárgico. Apesar de composições visuais impactantes, o filme parece não querer arriscar, operando sob uma constante sensação de segurança estilística. Falta-lhe, talvez, um aprofundamento nas nuances ideológicas que cercam a trama; o conteúdo é sombrio, mas a abordagem carece de audácia. O brilho surge, porém, no desfecho. A cena final onde a mulher, que sofre de Alzheimer, encontra um fragmento de resposta é de uma melancolia cortante. É o retrato de uma reparação que chega tarde demais, transformando o encerramento em um momento genuinamente memorável. Disculpem brasileires, não gostei tanto.

Um filme fraco e claramente partidário, com um foco evidente em se posicionar contra a Ditadura Militar. A obra tenta prender o espectador de forma artificial, com cenas forçadas e atuações um pouco exageradas sem muitas "ações evidentes" numa tentativa pouco convincente de fazer o público sentir o que as pessoas daquela época viviam. Mesmo assim, o resultado é ruim. O filme se apoia quase exclusivamente na atuação e, ainda assim, não consegue entregar algo consistente ou impactante. Ou talvez eu não seja “culto” o suficiente para fingir que gostei de algo tão fraco e que não consegue transmitir nem mesmo a única proposta que se impõe. No fim, muitas pessoas se cegam por vieses políticos, independentemente de qual lado seja. E, por isso, relevam a decepção que o filme foi, tratando pontos fracos de roteiro, direção e construção emocional como se fossem virtudes

É meio cômico que queiram reconhecer esse como um filme "que respira Brasil" (como vi alguém dizer) sendo que ele é feito num molde super estadunidense. Se não fosse a história real que o inspirou e os nomes dos personagens e locais, daria pra fingir que é só mais um drama americano qualquer. Além desse molde estadunidense, o maior problema pra mim é que ele é extremamente apelativo em vários momentos ao mesmo tempo que entrega um texto que chega ser covarde de tão apolítico. Não chega nem perto da dimensão do que foi a ditadura, não tem pulso pra lidar com uma tragédia dessa, é como se fosse uma "revolta" branda, que sabe-se lá por que($$?) se recusa a botar o quão monstruoso tudo foi. Se assumisse ser uma história sobre superação do luto com a ditadura apenas como pano de fundo, seria um filme 10x melhor, mas por algum motivo os envolvidos (e os fãs deles e do filme) querem com todas as forças colocar "Ainda Estou Aqui" como um dos projetos definitivos sobre a ditadura. Não é. Nem de longe. A Fernanda Torres no geral tá ótima e salva muito o filme de ser mais oco que já é (como na cena da sorveteria ou na da entrevista), mas ainda assim tem alguns momentos que derrapa feio na atuação (a cena dela gritando e batendo no vidro do carro é constrangedora). Selton Mello tá fofo numa primeira assistida, mas depois fica soando só meio besta e sem personalidade (como quase tudo que ele fez nos últimos anos, aliás). Quem sai por cima do elenco, além da Fernanda quando a direção pasteurizada do Walter não esmaga ela, é a Luiza Kosovski, que tem algumas das cenas mais fortes junto com a Torres. O final é algo quase estúpido. Podia ser lindo, mostrando como o fascismo não destruiu aquela família e blábláblá, mas o tom e, principalmente, a fotografia parecem mais uma propaganda de final de ano do itaú que qualquer outra coisa. A Fernanda Montenegro é uma das melhores atrizes do país? Sem dúvidas, mas aqui ela não empresta nem 5% do talento e do magnetismo dela, parece que só aceitou fazer por que a filha é a grande estrela e é dirigido por um amigo que lhe deu o seu melhor papel anos atrás. De pontos realmente muito positivos tem todo o desing de produção e a ambientação da casa dos Paiva, que é praticamente uma co-protagonista. Tudo ali soa vivo, autêntico, real. É uma pena que quase todo resto do filme seja tão plástico, formulaico, quadrado.

Obviamente le tenía que dar una oportunidad a I'm Still Here por todo el bombo que hubo desde que arrasó en los Óscar, pero ya cuando vi Central Station me di cuenta que el estilo de Walter Salles quizás no era para mí. La memoria es un tema difícil de tratar en el cine y a mí simplemente no me encajó el enfoque que tomaron aquí. Salles camina por el sendero obvio con las largas tomas en los lugares de tortura, los niños sufriendo por su padre... Aún así, siento que no se mete en el lodo lo suficiente para profundizar lo necesario en los personajes y en lo que significa para ellos lo que está pasando. Consigue que el espectador se implique en lo que ocurre con una puesta en escena directa, pero en lo personal me costó que me importaran sus personajes por la distancia que adopta el director al contar una historia real tan impactante.

La película narra los horrores de la dictadura brasileña sin caer en la moralina ni en el sentimentalismo. Al enfocarse en los aspectos humanos y el dolor de quienes nunca obtuvieron respuesta sobre la desaparición de sus seres queridos, el guion se vuelve más impactante a medida que avanza. Las actuaciones de los jóvenes actores son excelentes. Torres ofrece una actuación sutil y conmovedora en la que sus ojos transmiten más que mil palabras. Delgada y elegante. Lo que hace que este film sea aún más significativa, es su profunda conexión con lo que sucede en el mundo actual. Es un fuerte recordatorio de los peligros de que los gobiernos tengan demasiado poder y de por qué es tan importante proteger la democracia. No es solo una película, es una historia importante que todos deberían ver y comentar.

I respect what I’m Still Here (Ainda Estou Aqui) is trying to do but I honestly struggled to stay fully engaged. Clocking in at over two hours and twenty minutes, personally for me the pacing felt painfully slow. This easily could’ve been trimmed down to under two hours without losing its core message. Because of the heavy, distant pacing, I couldn't fully connect with the family or the emotional beats the way I wanted to. You can feel the weight and importance of the real-life history and Fernanda Torres turns in a grounded performance but for me it felt more like watching a historical documentary than a compelling narrative that hooked me.

Mi sono commossa più di una volta ma la parte finale mi ha lasciata davvero perplessa. Eunice è una sostenitrice dei diritti umani delle vittime della repressione politica, ha lottato per tantissimi anni della sua vita per la campagna per aprire i registri chiusi della dittatura militare e ha sostenuto i diritti dei popoli indigeni del Brasile, eppure, di tutto il suo lavoro, e tanto meno del genocidio avvenuto, non si vede niente nel film se non una scritta alla fine,parte in cui c’è una fievole volontà di uscire dalla vita privata di Eunice e denunciare gli orrori della dittatura.E lo fa anche pateticamente con la classica frase che invita a non ripetere gli stessi errori che mi sa di insensibile, considerando che di come il Brasile sia diventato una dittatura non lo tocca mai. Per questo mi pare che al film importi davvero di mostrare la dittatura solo negli effetti che ha avuto sulla classe media, e ancora più specificamente su una famiglia a dir poco presentata come perfetta. Porta avanti una debolissima rappresentazione della causa rivoluzionaria, in cui puccia solamente i mignolini nel momento in cui decide di svegliarsi a riguardo negli ultimi 10 minuti rimanenti, cosa davvero paradossale considerando la donna che fu Eunice. Per il resto, nonostante mi renda conto che la biografia della famiglia possa essere stata romanzata, la loro storia il regista l’ha narrata davvero bene.

I'm Still Here es un drama histórico sólido sobre la dictadura militar brasileña, pero creo que exige una conexión emocional con ese contexto que, al menos en mi caso, nunca terminó de aparecer. Entiendo perfectamente la importancia que tiene para Brasil recuperar esta historia y poner rostro a las víctimas de un régimen que persiguió, secuestró e hizo desaparecer a quienes consideraba una amenaza. Precisamente por eso se entiende el enorme reconocimiento que ha recibido: ganó el Óscar a la Mejor Película Internacional y el Goya a la Mejor Película Iberoamericana. La película funciona muy bien mostrando la lucha institucional de Eunice Paiva por mantener viva la memoria de su marido frente a un Estado que pretende borrar cualquier rastro de sus crímenes. Es un relato sobre la burocracia, la resistencia y la dignidad mucho más que sobre la violencia explícita de la dictadura. Sin embargo, no terminé de conectar con ella. El ritmo es muy pausado, la historia avanza lentamente y la sensación de impotencia acaba pesando más que el propio conflicto. Entiendo que esa sea precisamente la intención del director, pero personalmente esperaba una propuesta con un desarrollo más intenso o un conflicto narrativo que me atrapara más. No me parece una mala película; al contrario, está muy bien hecha y comprendo perfectamente su relevancia histórica y política. Simplemente creo que pertenece a esa categoría de películas impecables en su ejecución, pero que difícilmente recordaré dentro de unos años. Para mí se queda en un 3/5: buena, necesaria y respetable, pero sin llegar a emocionarme tanto como esperaba.

A forma que a casa dos Paiva parece possuir vida e sentimento é perceptível assim que o Rubens deixa a casa, um ambiente aconchegante se torna um ambiente frio, escuro e sombrio, além da perfeita atuação da Fernanda Torres que expressou perfeitamente o que qualquer ser humano sentiria acerca de tal situação A única reclamação para esse filme é como o filme se limita a escolhas feitas no filme que geram contradição. O problema do filme ser mais um filme que retrata a ditadura militar aos olhos da classe média alta, uma elite intelectual fragilizada durante esse período, não está propriamente no filme em si, o problema é a falta de retratamento de pessoas como a empregada dos Paiva durante a ditadura, a falta de histórias de quem não tinha uma casa grande à beira da praia O filme no geral é talvez o filme mais bem trabalhado de Salles, emocionante e como filme funciona perfeitamente e transmite todas as emoções que o filme quer que você tenha A cena da Eunice vendo uma família feliz na sorveteria é uma cena que molha minha visão somente ao pensar
