Et voilà enfin le dernier Tarentino, normalement, d'après ses dires, le dernier, dernier! On verra s'il respecte ce qu'il a dit par le passé. Bref, revenons à nos moutons. La bande-annonce laissait présager du meilleur puisque elle laisse entrevoir une situation de huis-clos, avec une tripotée de personnages haut en couleurs et armés jusqu'aux dents, ce qui, dans ses précédents films nous offre toujours des scènes d'anthologie. Premier constat, 2h45, c'est un peu long. On attend un peu trop de temps pour que le film démarre vraiment, puis le rythme s'accélère, s'emballe carrément, pour partir en vrille totale dans la dernière demi-heure. Finalement, le rythme assez lent du début se comprend car on est scotché par cette accélération progressive qui, si elle avait pu tenir en 30' maximum, Tarentino a la classe et la maîtrise de le faire sur presque 3h. Une très bonne production qui est un plaisir à regarder, mais peut-être pas à revoir, ne serait-ce que pour découvrir d'autres détails supplémentaires liés à la résolution finale.

One of Tarantino’s more underrated films, which is sad because this is him at his peak. A bunch of dudes sitting around talking to each other for two hours as tensions slowly build, capped off with a rather violent ending sequence. What more could you want? The build here is great, I’m glued to my screen waiting for the first pin to drop. But once it does, I found less of a reason to stay invested before having to sit through 20 minutes of building up the backstory. Realizing that no one was going to make it out of this alive, I found myself not as worried about the outcome. I think it’d be cooler if there were a few more twists and turns along the way, maybe having half the group have the same end goal wasn’t the best idea. But, still a very solid film nonetheless. The winter theme and cottage vibes make for a surprisingly cozy watch. I’d love to watch this around Christmas time, hot cocoa in hand (minus the poison). I’m glad that in the end, a union and confederate soldier were able to come together and unite over their hatred for women (satire… slightly).

This was such a well-rounded story to watch. I think what made this movie stand out to me, and therefore Tarantino’s style to me, is his chapter by chapter presentation of the film. Well, it is easy to label things up to an episodic format throughout the movie, but Tarantino’s dialogue and cinematography are straight out of a book. I could literally imagine a novel being written as I watched the movie with the grand details that Tarantino’s shots offer in addition to the character dynamics and the insane performances the cast displays throughout the movie. Getting to know the characters and the setting was entertaining, although some monologues and sequences may feel a bit of a drag, it didn’t hamper my attention enough and the movie always kept me at bay. This is the fourth movie I have watched from Tarantino, and this is probably the best one so far.

Auf dieses Nachbartreffen kann man getrost verzichten, denn: Anstrengend, aber im negativen wie nervigen Sinne. Kein Vorwurf an den Cast: Alle Vier merkt man die Spielfreude sichtlich an und ist neben der flotten Inszenierung stellenweise auch ansteckend, nur bleiben ihre Figuren zu uninteressant bzw im Falle von Joe und Angela (Wilde, Rogen) fragt man sich, warum die Ehe bisher so lange gehalten hat und andersrum, die biblische Geduld von Piña und Hawk (Cruz, Norton), denn jede:r hätte nach spätestens 15 Minuten bei der (passiv-)aggressiven Stimmung das Weite gesucht. Aber Olivia Wilde setzt weniger auf Glaubwürdigkeit, sondern mehr auf Übertriebenheit und das von Beginn an: Kaum ein Dialog oder Gestik kommt in dem mit unzähligen Sticheleien versehenen Schlagabtausch ohne Hysterie und Theatralik aus. Subilität hat Sendepause und mit Authenzität hat das auch nicht mehr viel zu tun. Sinnbildlich der Score, der die Gefühlslagen stets (über-)präsent sowie penetrant mit schiefen oder sanften Klangteppichen ausrollt. Später, wenn Wilde den Fokus hinter der (bröckelnden) Fassade blicken möchte, bleibt dieser auch verschüchtert. Wer A sagt, muss auch B sagen: Wilde bleibt bei A brav hängen. Allein nur explizit über sexuelle Vorlieben sprechen, ist halt lange nicht mutig genug, provokant erst recht nicht. Entsprechend gestaltet sich Eskalation ernüchternd inkonsequent, noch weniger entlarvend. Stattdessen werden dabei doch wieder die platten Gags rausgeholt. Das ist nicht pointiert, sondern peinlich. Die Komplexität der Konflikte um verschiedene Beziehungsformen und Liebe, aber auch Kommunikationsunfähigkeit, entfaltet sich dadurch selten schlagkräftig, auch da der Film lediglich auf konstruierte Zuspitzung aus ist. Am Ende stehen dann doch wieder Luxusprobleme im Vordergrund und die Tatsache, dass bei aller Offenheit andere Partnerschaftsmodelle außerhalb der traditionellen Ehe, doch nur pervertiert sind und Unruhe reinbringen. Ahja... Aber dann, die letzten 5 Minuten: Die sind plötzlich zutiefst menschlich. Olivia Wilde findet in der Ruhe nochmal leise Töne, die stark beeindrucken! Gerade hier ist zu spüren, was für ein reizvolles Potenzial 'The Invite' besitzt. Hätte sich der Film in den vorherigen 100 Minuten doch mal mehr aus der zahmen (Hollywood-)Komfortzone getraut.

It’s not the single most important takeaway but I’ve seen all three Olivia Wilde directed films and I’m now convinced she’s had exclusively terrible sex. That’s in spite of how sweaty and performatively preoccupied with the female orgasm her films claim to be–either within the text of the films or as part of the messy promotional tours surrounding them–yet they’re constantly engaging in mortifying coitus interruptus or something that’s adjacent to assault (wouldn’t even begin to know how to classify what’s happening in Don’t Worry Darling ). Something a bit doth protest too much, methinks. Wilde’s involvement notwithstanding (and isn’t it precious how the film quotes a different O. Wilde before the opening credits) the more identifiable authorial voice here belongs to Jones and McCormack in the sense that if I immediately recognized the sensibilities which led me to  shutting off Celeste And Jesse Forever after 40 minutes. A grab bag of emotionally stunted, shrill quirks and indignant bellowing with Rogen and Wilde coming across like a more broadly comedic George and Martha, largely defined by a single grating personality trait each (gruff obstinance and try-hard neediness, respectively). Goes through the sitcom-y motions of a straight-laced couple having their horizons expanded by a couple of swingers who saw them across their apartment building lobby and dug their vibe (Edward Norton and Penélope Cruz, also saddled with nonsensical characters but at least they’re allowed to have a little fun with all the pseudo-bohemian touchy-feeliness) only for the film to abruptly pull up short for a, I fucking kid you not, therapy session with a *literal* psychoanalyst who is able to accurately make a snap diagnosis of their long-simmering dysfunction. I don't know why I thought the film would actually follow through on its attention-grabbing premise but sure enough it beats a hasty retreat to squishy social conservatism and a plaintive, maybe-kinda-sorta reconciliation to send the audience out on a hopeful note. At an utter loss to see people praising Wilde’s direction as I found this to be mostly visually incoherent with no innate sense of how to block actors or convey evolving character dynamics via their placement within the frame. Instead it’s a blitzkrieg of alternating singles of varying focal lengths (I regularly found myself questioning whether all four actors were on set at the same time for more than a couple days of shooting) with the occasional racked focus between foreground and background and back to foreground for variety. Particularly frustrating to see this exalted in most corners–flashbacks of Booksmart 7 years ago–in that Splitsville tackled, more or less, this same premise last summer and was mostly met with polite indifference and nonexistent box office despite having the benefit of genuinely engaging with the emotional fallout and trade-offs of polyamory while being form-forward in its approach (also, was actually funny).

“I’m the only one who fucks me currently.” This is  atavistic chamber piece that recalls the cinematic pleasures of watching beautiful people crash out and argue. It flirts with incendiary melodrama before settling into a more tragic, hopeless register. Centering on two couples who gather for dinner, only to end up spilling secrets, desires, and resentment about each other over immaculately plated charcuterie, each conversation feels like watching technicians try to diffuse explosives. There’s an inherently performative aspect to any given social situation, and The Invite finds great humor and awkwardness in characters who explore the tension between what they say and what they think. Viewers who suffer from second-hand embarrassment might find their tolerance tested by characters’ tendency to walk right up to the line of what’s socially unacceptable. Hilariously acted by its four leads, thanks to Wilde’s effective direction and Adam Newport-Berra’s immersive cinematography, The Invite always feels like it’s more than the sum of its parts — although its thematic reach is often frustratingly in conflict with the realistic story it’s attempting to tell. As the same kind of enthusiasm-to-cynicism cycle that followed the Summer Of Love plays out in the internet age, some of the topical filmmaking from that earlier time is too. “Sex positivity” has replaced “free love,” but the emotions are very much the same. Curiosity, jealousy, embarrassment, doubt—the feelings that crawl under the skin of relationships emerge, sometimes ugly and raw, when people are frank about their romantic and sexual needs, especially when they extend beyond tradition. For anyone whose dating life has led them to run up against ethical non-monogamy, where asking about acronyms opens up a philosophical can of worms about the nature of personal relationships, The Invite provides plenty of embarrassing, familiar relationship comedy. But it’s director-star Olivia Wilde’s tight, warm control of her ensemble that keeps the awkwardly horny dinner party moving forward through its clunkier courses. Full review @ The A.V. Club

Sundance Film Festival Presents: The Invite Directed By: Olivia Wilde Based on the Spanish film from 2020 called The People’s Upstairs directed by Cesc Gray. Joe and Angela is having a very tough time maintaining their relationship and one night in San Francisco their neighbors decided to come over of what could be a night to remember. Olivia Wilde wowed us in the 2019 film Booksmart which became an instant coming to age classic with one of the best comedic films in recent memory. Unfortunately I couldn’t say the same with her 2022 film Don’t Worry Darling which is a trainwreck of a movie and its production history behind it is a stuff of legends. After being in director jail for nearly 4 years, her next project is a smaller indie film is Based on the Spanish film from 2020 called The People’s Upstairs directed by Cesc Gray and it stars Seth Rogen, Olivia Wilde, Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton. So what do I think of the film, it’s a very provocative movie for adults that pays homage to the old school date movies. My only issue with the film is that the first 35-40 minutes didn’t find its footing yet and can feel a bit bloated at first but as soon as the comedy hits after those 35 minutes, the film eventually find its footing with some of the most silliest horniest scenes  during the film. Other than that issue, I do think this will be one of the most talked about films in the festival so far! Even though I like Seth Rogen and Olivia Wilde, it’s Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton’s show here that  I feel the film mostly worked because of their comedic timing and yet very horny character motives  that puts the film in insane situations. The film is also a one location film throughout the film and easily a very small cast but I feel the setting really create a far depressing tone that the film was going for and it worked for the most part. The Invite (2026) is easily one of this years Sundance’s better films so far! Even though it takes its time to get invested with the world and its characters, the film screenplay by Rashida Jones and Will McCormack gets better and gives uncomfortable horny jokes front and center and I feel Cruz and Norton understood the assignment the most. This is Wilde’s best film since Booksmart and easily the best directorial effort from Olivia Wilde that pays  homage to the old hangout films of the 1960s and 70s that managed to give the laughs and tears all throughout its official runtime.

THE INVITE is an uproariously funny yet profoundly sad dramedy about a deteriorating couple who invite their sexually confident, free-spirited neighbors over for what’s meant to be a pleasant evening, only for it to spiral into something painfully awkward, ugly, and brutally honest. Seth Rogen showcases remarkable range, blending his signature comedy with the finest dramatic work of his career. Olivia Wilde delivers a soul-crushing performance fueled by anxiety and secondhand embarrassment, while her precise, assured direction turns this intimate chamber piece into an astounding seamless balancing act between humor and heartbreak with something meaningful to say about marriage and relationships. Edward Norton and Penélope Cruz are the cherry on top of what is a delicious offering from Wilde and easily the best directorial work of her career so far.

The one-room film is certainly a rare breed, but certainly one of my favorites. With a stellar cast, raucously funny dialogue, and a fantastic script, it’s absolutely another win for Wilde. Plus, Seth Rogan twerks in this movie, so it gets some bonus points.

Contrary to some other film festivals out there, standing ovations don’t happen all of the time at Sundance. And, to be fair, getting one doesn’t mean the movie was necessarily great or will be a box office smash. But in the case of Olivia Wilde’s hilarious, rapid-fire marital comedy The Invite, I think both things are true. Wilde’s third time behind the camera, and a welcome return to comedy for the first time since Booksmart, the film is also a rebound from her polarizing suburban satire, Don’t Worry Darling. Underneath all of the witty one-liners, this is also a film that packs quite an emotional wallop, exploring love and sex between a longtime married couple that has lost that spark, and maybe needs a bit of neighborly advice to get it back. Full Review Here

There are rare moments when a film comedy hits a gear where the big laughs are coming so fast, one on top of the other, that it becomes absolutely euphoric, no matter what other minor slips might occur along the way. You get one such occasion about mid-way through this farce about a married San Francisco couple, Joe (Seth Rogen) and Angela (Olivia Wilde, who also directed), whose relationship difficulties come into focus when they host a dinner party for their upstairs neighbors, unconventional couple Hawk (Edward Norton) and Piña (Penélope Cruz). The script by Will McCormack and Rashida Jones adapts the 2020 Spanish feature Sentimental , and mixes farce with “comedy of remarriage” in a way that kind of rushes through the steps to figuring out whether Joe and Angela can work things out. But absolutely none of that matters at the peak of the gathering’s craziness, beginning with a wonderfully awkward search for a corkscrew and building to a conversation about Hawk and Piña’s sex life where the jokes come in a fusillade that barely lets you come up for air. All four of the performances are terrific while working in very different registers—Wilde’s reaction takes bouncing off Rogen’s ad-libs, with Cruz and Norton providing phenomenal straight-person counterpoint. The ending aims for a particular kind of sweetness, but really, nothing is sweeter than the sound of hundreds of people roaring in unison for several minutes straight.

The Invite is razor-sharp, as riotous as supremely tender. The sadness and anger that permeates it only makes it that much funnier. What a perfect quartet here, balanced and bouncing off each other flawlessly. Awkward, complex, hilarious. A beautiful tight-rope-walk of a film. Check out my full review over at Next Best Picture.

It’s one of the most electric theaters I’ve ever had the pleasure of being in. And as for the movie itself this is a genuine bonafide comedic masterpiece. In the Northman, the violence and evil doesn't stop, and it seems to serve only to shock and disgust the viewer. I think the biggest consideration of period pieces is that their programming of speech and behaviour is of a time where different things were at stake, largely because ritual and power were at the forefront of the status quo, rather than, for an easy example, the possibility of the static lifestyle one can live now, of which human expedition then would ensure seriousness and expectation be within every walk of isolated thought and shared interaction. It’s against this backdrop that the opening stages’ questionable editing choices become most apparent: establishing that kind of world demands relaxation of a viewer’s experience through integration methods that are timeless in human history, and the film stumbles slightly out of the gate in giving us our footing. It is then the filmmaker’s job to ensure a universal entry point for even the most unintelligent of audience members to understand what is going on. Whilst it doesn’t contain the outstanding personality of The Lighthouse, instead here chasing spectacle in the traditional, predictable form (against its own intended “wow” factor) of “thing happens, get ready for next thing happening!! NEXT THING ARRIVES,” it does unquestionably provide the same fly-on-the-wall approach to that earlier work, giving us full spectator view of a meticulously designed production whose scale no one could argue with, and it’s here that the texture, where production design meets framing, makes a big bang. Where I’m less convinced is the camerawork itself. Eggers leans mechanical: constant pans, deliberate moves, in a way that keeps reminding you it’s camerawork rather than photography. These are undeniably seamless and the level of choreography required is evident in the final product, which is arguably perfect in achieving its intended circuitry (THE SEIGE!), yet there are moments that would’ve landed harder as a single, cleverly framed image of directed blocking, as a still image instead of motion for revelatory sake.

" Rewatch ( non in questo caso ) delle opere di Robert Eggers " Episodio 1 Robert, mi dispiace dirtelo, ma il tuo tentativo di fare qualcosa di diverso dal film dell'orrore non è andato a buon fine. Il film in sè, penso sia uno dei migliori film a livello tecnico che eggers abbia mai fatto. Con bellissimi paesaggi e una grande regia, che già dal primo minuto di visione si può già riconoscere chi lo ha diretto. Non parliamo poi della maniacale accuratezza storica che Eggers DEVE dare ai suoi film. I combattimenti che si vedono sono fantastici, e il come vengono mostrate certe scene: realistiche e crude, con il giusto quantitativo di violenza e una rappresentazione del periodo storico molto azzeccata. Il problema per me sta sopratutto nella storia che viene narrata, più che mai come viene narrata. La trama in sè, seppur non proprio all'apice dell'originalità, aveva una buona premessa. Essendo che c'era Eggers che lo scrive e dirige, mi faceva presagire già al mio nuovo film preferito. Invece no, dopo averlo finito mi sono sentito come ricevere un nuovo telefono solo per scoprire che all'interno c'è un mattone. Tutta la storia è strutturata con scene che portano avanti la trama, e sono divise da altre che servono a poco, con scene oniriche e piene di rituali ecc. Avendo visto anche the VVitch, era abbastanza prevedibile con Eggers, ma in questo caso non le ho viste come qualcosa che facesse parte della trama apparte qualche eccezione, come qualcosa che caratterizza il film e in molte occasioni non le ho trovate necessarie con il suo andazzo. Sopratutto nella seconda metà succede varie volte. Nonostante non sia un film horror, di soprannaturale ce ne è anche troppo. The film looks great, and there is something here which could be a decently powerful story about lost innocence, a certain conceptualisation of masculinity/manhood, patriarchal violence unto women, a more metaphorical violence unto one’s identity, etc. The problem is that there’s basically no character work here. There is barely any humanity or life in this story which, on paper, should be very close to that humanity and life. I simply didn’t care about what was happening, especially with regard to the character relationships. As another user has already said, there’s also not much forward momentum: things just happen one after the other. The characters I most sympathised with were Olga and Gudrún, but that’s less because of their characters and more just because of the horrors they’re forced to endure with, by virtue of their status as women in such a patriarchal society, very little opportunity to do much about that. It’s probably the understated victimhood of the other characters - the ones who aren’t royal men - that the film gets to its most interesting themes (most notably the radical self-involvement/selfishness of the core character motivations that move the plot forward), but this is (seemingly intentionally) left as an understated part of the film and, even if it wasn’t, it wouldn’t counterbalance the issues I’ve already spoken about. I did want to like this film because I love Eggers’ work but this just didn’t work for me.

Not once does this movie stop to ask if you are ok. It forces you to accept Norse theology (although gruesome) in order to understand the characters. Even until the final scene, the movie does not once question the beliefs of those it is betraying. This makes the film feel like it is being told to you from a storyteller in 900 AD. That being said, one of the greatest rules of storytelling is broken. Amleth has no character arc, nor does he learn any sort of lesson. He is told at the beginning of his life what his fait is, and that is exactly what ends up happening to him. This feels natural, in fact the story wouldn't make sense if it were any other way. Amleth wouldn't truly be who he is portrayed as if it weren't for his adherence to his Norse ideologies. This got me thinking on The Oddesy. This story was told very differently and Odyseus almost feels out of place in his world. These two films represent the two different ways to tell an old story. The Oddysey is a modernized version of a story that feels relatable, while The Northman is a no-apologies telling of a story that stays honest (although not fully based on a historical story). It seems unfair to compare this to a Nolan film but boy does it hold its ground well.

I don’t think any review puts together what exactly this film is like, but imagine you mix Requiem for a Dream with Dorian Gray, give it a Cronenberg twist and then write and direct it like Cat in the Hat or Catwoman and you’ve got this. So many negative reactions I’ve seen relate to the film being misogynistic (I don’t necessarily agree) but not enough mention how it just fucking sucks. Hollow from beginning to end, stupendously trite in all it wants to say and extremely dragged out. Everything is lacking, especially the weirdly bland production design for how cooky it’s trying to be. It’s putting weird on weird on weird and in the end, it doesn’t work. But mostly, my distaste for this came from the fact that this moves, looks and sounds like a YouTube video, or even a TikTok. Like one of those terrible short films you find in the recommended tab with really corny messaging, except here it never ends and you’re stuck with it for an excruciatingly long runtime. I appreciate how this could almost be seen as a silent film, but my god you could tell this story in 20 minutes. I give it some credit for the ending, which was pretty hilarious. Otherwise, this is quite bad.

it’s interesting and it has A Concept, i guess! i’m glad it was made and got a big theatrical release. but i’m not sure it quite nailed down what it wanted to be saying. it has the trappings of a movie about how beauty standards and ageism are bad for women, especially celebrities, but in light of that being (at least theoretically) its core, it came off to me weirdly critical of Demi Moore’s character for taking The Substance. like, the movie knows that beauty standards are bad for women, but for some reason all of the criticism and disdain it seems to have is for the women who are forced to abide by these beauty standards rather than the corporations that sell them or even the broader culture that enforces them. I think the whole “remember you are one” angle could have led to a movie that was more tied together, but i never actually got the sense that they were really one consciousness (beyond the times it was literally written out or said in as many words). basically from the point that The Substance is taken it seems that the Moore and Qualley characters are different people and entities and there’s never really anything done with the idea of one consciousness inhabiting two bodies. there is also more minor stuff that’s stupid - Dennis Quaid is playing a sleazy exec Harvey Weinstein reference but for some reason playing him as The Gayest Guy Of All Time so i could never believe the lechery; the talk show that is apparently the top of the mountain in the entertainment industry is called ‘The Show’. and it’s sooooooooo annoyingly heavy handed at some points, it comes off like it thinks the audience are truly deeply stupid people. think the worst example is the stuff with the doctor who administers The Substance who is himself on The Substance - they show his prominent birthmark, and for people who know how to watch movies (or, like, people who know how to think thoughts), when a much older man appears and the same prominent birthmark is shown, it’s like oh ok. so that doctor was also using The Substance. but then it tells you that hey this old guy is the doctor from before like five more times in increasingly obvious ways and it’s like…come on. that really rankled me honestly.

My love for films literally stems from my obsession with the body horror genre, to this day the fly is one of my all time favourite films. So I love when movies embrace the ( feminine) grotesque, and see the body as something beautiful but incredibly disgusting. The body horror in The Substance is intoxicating, staisfying and camp. So I was totally all in with the gore, and seeing flesh being ripped apart. The problem is that the body horror is utilized in the most hollow attempt at satire, it fails to say anything of note  about youth, beauty and ageing. For all of its boundary pushing gore why is its commentary so one dimensional and bland. Its doesnt fully embrace the catharsis that is part of body horror. I absolutely adored her previous film Revenge in which that film successfully subverts the misogyny often a part of rape- revenge exploitation films and turns  her revenge against her abusers as a moment of catharsis and while  making it all feel incredibly visceral. I feel the Substance lacks that punch and brilliance that I was hoping for. I still had fun with it depsite my plethora of issues with its message. Everything is so god damn surface level while its purported hollowed out feminism is too reductive and regressive. Demi moore is decent enough throughout, and its nice to see her in all of her bloody glory on the big screen.

Sin embargo, conforme el relato avanza nos vamos encontrando con una suerte de retorno del espectro de "El hombre elefante", de "Carrie", de "Alien" y de otras múltiples tradiciones del cine norteamericano. Es contundente y celebratoria en el rumbo que toma y también divertida, e incluye una jocosa referencia a "Vertigo".

Unapologetically over the top, unsettling, gut-renching and excessive. At times it felt like never ending stimulation which was often overwhelming. Its strong Sci-fi element is enhanced by interesting designs and is complimented by a very well fitting score and visual aesthetic. All male characters were either hedonistic pigs or lame simps, the latter pretty much always being intolerable, though to its credit added to the unpleasantness of the world. Hyper-sexualisation served its underlying messages and aesthetic, however for me was excessive, although this perspective somewhat changed when I realised how exaggerated the rest movie was also. Denis Quade killed it. While I won’t be watching again, fans of body horror will surely be pleased, as this one takes the genre to new places in the craziest of ways. Well done, Coralie!

Era pra ficar com nojo ou libido? CINEMATOGRAFIA Esse é, na minha concepção, o melhor parâmetro do filme. Temos aqui um aspecto bastante sólido em como tudo se constrói e se forma dentro das suas proposições. A estética é bastante sólida e a câmera é usada ativamente para passar as mensagens do filme. Existe sim um defeito em como o filme é extremamente expositivo, e isso é tosco, mas claramente esse é um defeito do roteiro, não de como a cinematografia opera as coisas. As atuações são sólidas. É interessante como o filme seria sim uma coisa completamente diferente sem a Demi Moore, apesar de eu sinceramente não achar que a Margaret Qualley seja a “perfeita” para o papel. Ela desempenha bem, mas eu consigo enxergar uma dúzia de atrizes que fariam um trabalho igual ou até melhor. No geral, o filme acerta bastante e entrega bem tudo aquilo que se propõe. Não há nada de outro mundo, mas sim algo muito consistente. NOTA: 4.7/5 TRILHA SONORA O filme utiliza muito sons graves e pesados, sempre num tom mais pop. É quase uma mistura grotesca do pop eletrônico clássico com tensão e atrito. O filme trabalha muito bem esse aspecto na sua própria proposta de estética e ambientação. Tudo é bastante coeso aqui. NOTA: 3.7/5 ROTEIRO A escrita tem sim seus méritos, mas não é algo perfeito na minha perspectiva. Os problemas se concentram principalmente em como o filme aborda suas mensagens. A escrita em si é fraca. O filme se sustenta 100% nas suas mensagens e tentativas de profundidade, e mesmo nisso ele não é tão efetivo. Começando com o maior problema de escrita, na minha visão: a escolha horrível de relembrar várias vezes tudo, seja com flashbacks ou coisas na tela mesmo — como as instruções de uso da substância, ou o momento em que ela encontra o outro usuário da substância e o filme não só coloca o flashback como faz questão de fazê-lo derrubar tudo e revelar o número dele. O filme meio que insulta a inteligência de quem assiste diversas vezes. Além disso, o filme tem um problema meio crônico nas críticas dele, que é justamente o melhor aspecto dele: como ele aborda a crítica à indústria. Se você reparar, o filme somente aborda que a indústria lucra com a beleza e que, a partir do ponto em que a personagem de Elisabeth não está mais nesse padrão, ela é demitida. E assim, desculpa acabar com o sonho de quem quer que seja, mas qualquer indústria funciona assim: você é contratado por um motivo; se esse motivo não existe mais, você tecnicamente não serve mais para a vaga. Obviamente tem toda a caricatura do chefe daquela indústria, sobre como ele enxerga as mulheres de uma forma objetificada, mas nitidamente é só um viés de como o filme decide retratá-lo. Se você realmente para para observar os “pecados” dele e da indústria, tudo o que há é o fato de ele demitir Elisabeth por ela não estar mais no padrão de beleza. Isso seria um absurdo se ela fosse engenheira, mas não: ela é uma espécie de idol pop sexualizada. Eu estou pegando tanto no pé desse aspecto específico porque ele era pra ser o mais fácil. A indústria se aproveita das mulheres há décadas, especialmente a indústria pornográfica, que lucra através do trauma das garotas que se submetem a estar naquela posição exposta e lucra também com o vício e a deturpação doentia da humanidade das pessoas que consomem isso. Mas não: o filme só aborda como a indústria é malvada por demitir Elisabeth e para aí. Pra fechar a sessão da negatividade, eu pontuo também como a parte da profundidade e crítica do filme não se encaixa com a realidade do roteiro quando você o enxerga de forma mais literal — como quando Elisabeth mantém Sue consigo sem qualquer razão válida —, mas obviamente faz sentido quando você considera a trama subjetiva e a crítica. Apesar dos pontos negativos, é muito interessante como o filme trabalha toda a questão interna de Elisabeth. Esse é totalmente o destaque do filme: a forma como ela luta com Sue, que se torna uma persona com vontade própria, através da distorção de imagem que ela sofre, é realmente muito bem demonstrada. Todo o gore e body-horror tem uma função bastante emblemática justamente por isso. No geral, é uma escrita bastante disfuncional, na minha visão, que mais erra do que de fato acerta. Eu acabei nem comentando tanto sobre como a história se escreve em si, ritmo, storytelling etc., mas saibam que também é ruim: não tem muito para se extrair daqui. NOTA: -2/5 CONSIDERAÇÕES FINAIS Gosto muito da proposta do filme e, sinceramente, apesar do final extremamente arrastado e repetitivo que irritou um pouco a minha experiência, eu gostei do filme. Todas essas questões precisam sim de luz, mas a forma como o filme trabalha esses tópicos é nada mais que decepcionante. NOTA FINAL: 6.4/10

Writing this review at midnight so… I tried following along with Pump It Up as I watched it and dislocated my leg, this is ridiculous, I want a refund. 0/10. A grotesquely made satire, that can be best described as equal parts gross, depressing, funny, and raunchy. Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley brought a lot to this, playing Elisabeth/Sue playing the dual identities to feel like the same person (after all they are one) but different enough to feel distinct. Dennis Quaid is great at playing the most disgusting part of the movie, Harvey. The real star of the show here is Fargeat’s directing. A visual and audial treat of a movie. Not a treat like candy but the talent on display is stunning and I hope she continues making more movies (I also caught a bit of Revenge but not enough for a review). Stunning use of color and not to mention the creature and body horror effects. A lot of the creature stuff didn’t really freak me out but Elisabeth/Sue’s body mangling and decaying had mc flinching. There’s a bit to be said on the films similarities to the manga Helter Skelter and Oliver Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Grey. Which aren’t bad, nothing is original, and are distinct works but it’s interesting how they all handle the deterioration of self in search of beauty. How did Sue manage to build a small room in like, a few days. There’s a lot of heightened reality in this movie but that really took me out. I do think a few times the movie over explains its ideas, however that being said this is a thematically rich movie. The core is obvious, how women are treated within beauty standards, Elisabeth wants to maintain her youth and fame so she uses The Substance that’s the premise. The film shows that in a lot of ways how that’s enforced by men, Harvey’s introduction has him reference fertility ages, a note Elisabeth receives says “you WERE amazing, and when she interacts with the biker as Elisabeth and not as Sue, he yells at her. Harvey and the executives even say “pretty girls should always smile” before running off to chase dancers like dogs. Sue also enforces this. Giving Elisabeth an astronomically high standard, she cannot meet, although they are one. Both versions of Pump It Up are a good point here— Elisabeth’s show is mostly in a wideshot, instructions pretty clear. The leotard more of a cloth texture, though fitting, isn’t painted on. Then you have Sue’s… which is different. It’s a male gaze wet dream, a metallic bikini that’s practically spray painted on, is basically a thong on the bottom, and is cut to the point it can barely be considered athletic wear. It’s enforced on Elisabeth largely and more subtly on Sue. Funnily enough by the end, once everything goes wrong, that’s the only way the two could escape the cage of beauty standards. Two other threads I read in the film is within “respect the balance” is about self hatred and work life balance. Which going from male gaze to love yourself in theme is a leap but— Elisabeth and Sue hate eachother one considering her a “selfish bitch” the other an old woman who wastes her life. Yet they are the same person, they are one. Sue forces herself to work at Elisabteh’s expense, and Elisabeth does nothing in the meantime, just waiting for more Sue time. She buried herself in her career, and neglected any sort of relationships, that being familial, friendly, or otherwise. Her self-worth is her career, that’s all she has. And if she doesn’t have a career, she doesn’t have a self. Which she hates. While I just went on this whole thing about self hatred within the fact that though they are the same person Elisabeth and Sue hate eachother. I do think strangely enough, though it contradicts they have something that reads as a deeply messed up mother and daughter relationship. I think most of this comes from the interview scene. Elisabeth finds Sue spoiled, someone she gave life, someone who owes everything to her, and stealing away what she had. Sue thinks Elisabeth is jurassic, old, remarking she didn’t like the show but it was “inescapable”. Which does read a lot like a mother and daughters, not to so positive opinion of one another. It could be said that Elisabeth is exploiting the girl she created to extend her career, live through her, in this case literally. Though that does sort of ignore that Sue is defintley an extension of Elisabeth’s narcissism. Within that there’s two ways I see the Elisabeth/Sue fight. It’s either a manifestation of self hatred or a daughter trying to be her own person. Decide which one you like more, don’t debate in the comments. I do think the ending is far more campy than the first two hours but it’s not bad, a bloody wild climax. Anyways I’m glad to say The Substance has… The Substance in terms of theme and what it’s trying to say. Can’t wait to see whatever Fargeat does next, and though I’m not looking forward to it, I hope Demi Moore gets more work in the future, I’m sure Margaret Qualley will do great in the Posession remake.

I struggle to call this a mixed bag because the good is not nearly as present in quantity as the bad. The film is a bit too comfortable with it's source material I think. It most consistently preforms when it is working as closely to the stage show as possible, i.e. the famously good music is still good. However it does not manage to overcome any of the flaws of the original product, nor I think, particularly thrill in it's limited ability to translate stage to film. Choreography and set design are both at best, adequate which is a shame for a product which should shine in both areas. Costuming is a bit better, but is kept down by the Netflix gray smudge color grading. How can you produce a film in Oz and not have any color! A world of bright shades is reduced to smudgy pinks, dull greens, and little else that is not seemingly grey or earth tone. The film is far worse for not having put in the work to be as delightful to look at as the original Oz film. The story is not very good, there is basically no modification from the stage show to my understanding, and the show has always coasted by on the musical numbers over the story. The same structure remains here, made worse by the fact this is only part one and several more hours of story remain. Overall a pretty unremarkable thing, it managed to never make me consider stopping watching, but not much beyond that in terms of impact.

Pretty solid! This was certainly more up my alley than I expected it to be. Everything is very maximalist here, to the point of being visually overwhelming at times. There was clearly a great amount of care and detail put into the set design. The dialogue was fun and I was a big fan of all the words they came up with in here. It's a fun twist on The Wizard of Oz, which I'm ashamed to say I only generally know the story of. I also only just found out that Wicked is not, in fact, an original screenplay and was adapted from a play. Apparently I live under a rock. There are certainly some gripes I have here, with the biggest one being the music. Composition felt very flat and just unmoving to me despite all of its attempts at grandness. Mixing was horrible, you can't hear any of the instruments over the vocals half the time. Vocal performances are reminiscent of how I feel about TOOL and Angine de Poitrine; there's a high level of technicality and little to no feeling. Music can be a make or break thing in a MUSICAL, but this seems to be mostly genre-based personal taste whatever so I won't be too harsh. I also thought it looked very visually fake a lot of the time. My girlfriend pointed out that a lot of the sets were actually real, and a surprising amount of the movie was done practically, which I found difficult to believe cause, well... look!! It just looks CGI as all hell!! But apparently it's true, there was a lot of work on the set designs here, and maybe it's that they did TOO good of a job that my brain fills in that it must be fake. Even then, so many shots have this sort of saccharinity to them that feels very common in these high-budget blockbusters where everything is filmed in a green room. Speaking of green... I felt like they didn't know how to deal with the main character being green. I wanted them to either REALLY lean into her sticking out visually or actually coordinate the shots so that the colors all go together (bonus points for all the nature-y segments that are super green and she's sort of like camouflaged almost I thought that was kind of funny) but most of the movie seemed to be in this sort of awkward middle ground between the two. Maybe it's supposed to say something about her lived experience or whatever but I didn't get that from it either. It suffers from the same problem a lot of blockbusters with A-list actors do, which is that they spend all this money on the background and hardly have the characters interact with it! Maybe it's some shallow depth of field so we can't even see anything, or maybe there's a bunch of cuts so that they can split a complicated shot into more manageable chunks, or any number of other things, but it never feels like we're actually supposed to explore the frame!! Everything happens in the middle, everything is immediately apparent what it means and where you're supposed to look and the subtext always finds a way to rise to the level of text and yada yada yada yada boring pretentious stuff YES I KNOW ITS A CHILDRENS MOVIE YES I HAD THE SAME COMPLAINTS WITH STAR WARS YES THE PROBLEM IS PROBABLY ME but still!! Like I go on and on about, can we please just stop with the medium close up over the shoulder dialogue shots!? I guess through all the rambling what I'm really trying to say is that so much of the technical side of things is done right. It's got the budget, the sweeping sets, all the lighting equipment you could ever ask for, super high quality cameras, and yet... it feels like they just stopped there. You got the cameras, now USE them!! In all the grandiosity of the sets, it feels like there wasn't much thought put into visual language. I think this could have been a better movie if the budget was cut by 90%, because it would have forced people to think and get creative about how to film stuff! I think the whole writing a blank check is detrimental because creativity so often is fostered by limitation. But even after saying all that, it is undeniable that this movie is very fun to just sit back and watch. It's almost 3 hours but doesn't even feel like 2. Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande have wonderful chemistry, the writing here is very entertaining, and if I turn off the pretentious side of my brain, it's very easy to get swept away by all of the visual sugar here. I am even excited to see the second part!!

Okay, I am by no means a musical fan, I know blasphemy for a theater kid! Shoot me, but honestly I usually find them straight up just not interesting. So I'll start with the bad here and end with the good. The color grading is all over the place, some shots look phenomenal while others look incredibly bland or washed out. The pacing is also pretty rough, it's hard to care about the building of relationships when everything feels like it's happening within the same week, or even sometimes the same day. Like I don't give a fuck about the love triangle or Boq's lil romance suplot...most of the romance done in this is pretty wack. Finally the worst offender of it all...the fucking references towards the Wizard of Oz! Maybe it's not as egregious as I felt it was but like...it really feels like every little fucking thing needs to have a pointless explanation and cheeky little nod at the audience. The member berries are on crack and it made me roll my eyes every single time. Now the good, it's a fun watch, I was never bored. Maybe one scene had me slightly uninterested, but there's enough going on that it keeps your attention. The costumes and set design are really well done. Honestly, perfectly casted too, the characters are fun but the preformances are what stand out. For the most part the music is really good, Defying Gravity being the obvious stand out, I got straight chills in that scene. All in all, this is a fun but muddled concept, and obviously this isn't the films fault but the source material it is adapting. The conflicts are halfbaked and most of the time done in such a cartoonish manner you can't take anything seriously. While that is a huge blow to the entire plot...unfortunately the biggest blow is the relationship at the center of the film, the most important part, is just straight up not strong enough. I do not buy these two as friends. It feels like two people pretending to be friends or just keeping the peace because it's more work to be enemies. It's not tragic when the true goat of our story Elphaba loses her Glinda, cuz Glinda has always been a posh selfish person and one dance or the fact that she's not actively being an asshole is enough. There's no real growth or scenes of them being actual friends (besides a song of them at the Emerald City) to justify any of this crying. Maybe my mind will change when I get to the second part, but right now, it's a fine movie, an enjoyable time, but carries no real emotional weight for me.

Best moment: “Defying gravity”. That song and scene is the centerpiece of the musical and this (and the other) movie. It doesn’t disappoint. The song by itself already feels epic but the movie version puts a cherry on top. This small action interlude on the broom is a fun little break before it works toward that climax and note we have all been waiting for. Best quote: “I don’t cause commotions. I am one.” MVP: Cynthia Erivo. First, her voice is stunning. It is so crystal clear and she switches between emotional to powerful with the flip of vocal cord. Second, the acting matches the vocal performance. She gives Elphaba so much heart and a deep compassion but that fury beneath the surface is always brewing. It is an emotional performance in all areas. Best visual: The wizard’s room. The rest of the movie is so bright, colorful and joyful. That set, however, is darker and there isn’t any of the joy of the Emerald City. The design of the big head also looks really cool and ominous. Best showstopper: “Dancing through life” is just so much fun. The part in the library has so much cool choreography with the books and the spinning set. The ballroom looks stunning and also has some fun choreography. In all of this I ask myself one important question: How can someone be as charming as Jonathan Bailey? Rating: 9 out of 10 flying monkeys

Le film de Paul King sur le biopic de Wonka est une oeuvre orienté jeunesse. On sens une très grande inspiration cartoon de NOS jeunes années. Les chansons et danses omniprésentes parlent d'eux même mais ne sont pas les seuls points caractérisant ce coté cartoons. Les cadrages et décors colorés rappellent des prises de vue non habituelle du cinéma et une autre facon de retourner dans notre enfance. Le scénario va de paire avec cette idée, pas très elaboré ni très originale, cependant efficace. Le seul point noir de ce film est sa pâte graphique. Quelques manques de qualité de 3D se font ressentir. Surtout lors de deux scenes, les bonbons volants et la scène final de la fabrique. Malgré tout la girafe CGI fait très bien son effet. ❝ we are the music makers, and we are the dreamers of dreams. ❞ wonka felt like walking through a sweet shop at christmas — warm lights, colourful wrappers, and the smell of chocolate drifting through the air before you’ve even stepped inside. i went into it expecting something whimsical, and it certainly has that storybook charm. the film moves with a kind of cheerful optimism that feels very disney-coded, as though the world might become kinder if everyone sang at the right moment and shared a piece of chocolate. timothée chalamet brings a gentle sweetness to wonka that makes him easy to root for. this version of the character feels less eccentric genius and more hopeful dreamer, which gives the film a softer, more fairy-tale quality. what i enjoyed most was the atmosphere. there are moments that genuinely feel magical — little bursts of colour and wonder that reminded me of opening a childhood book and finding illustrations tucked between the pages. at the same time, i found myself wanting a little more of the strange edge that makes willy wonka such a fascinating character. the film is so determined to be charming that it occasionally feels a bit too safe, and some of the magic slips through my fingers before it can fully settle. still, there’s something comforting about it. it feels like a rainy-afternoon film: cosy, sugary, and easy to spend time with, even if it didn’t completely enchant me. a sweet, whimsical adventure that made me smile, even if it never quite became the golden-ticket experience i hoped for.

‘Tis the season for a sweet treat and, whilst not anything to do with Christmas, Wonka hits quite a lot of the festive buttons: fun, light-hearted, colourful and one for all the family. With much of the Paddington team behind this, it delivers that quintessentially English, quirky family film that its forebear (pun intended) achieved but sprinkled with a little bit of Cruella in its prequel backstory to a familiar character. It doesn’t present the titular chocolatier as a villain though, and rubs maybe just a little too much mystery off of the character, but does still feel very much a Roald Dahl tale. Wonka’s dream is to open a chocolate shop and he arrives in an alt-Paris (I think it’s meant to be Paris) to compete against the most famous chocolate makers of the time. From there, frolics, mishaps and big musical numbers ensue. Yes, this is a full musical like the OG Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory. Taking a couple of the songs but throwing in some excellent originals, this could well be destined for a stage run itself in the future. It’s cut through with a particularly English sense of humour and a brilliant ‘spot the famous person’ cast with a, hopefully intended, hat tip to Peep Show and yet another turn from Hugh Grant’s new comedy persona as an Oompa-Loompa. It’s just an utter delight, against all the odds, much like the aforementioned Cruella. A brisk and breezy one-for-all-the-family movie to smack a smile on your face. ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️

There’s either something I missed or I just wasn’t in the right mood, because this critically acclaimed ‘ masterpiece ’ was neither ‘ mesmerising ’ nor particularly ‘ powerful ’, and quite frankly I didn’t care for it all that much. Apparently kicking off the wave of late 90s J-Horror, I don't really see this as part of that canon, being a different beast entirely. I love a drawn out methodically psychological thriller, and this most definitely has those qualities in a not so short supply, but for me it borders on the miserable and gruelling with none of the chilling or foreboding tone able to pull me in, and a less than satisfying payoff, or lack thereof. I didn’t enjoy the directors later effort, the fiercely overrated Pulse, so obviously his style is just not working for me, but I’m truly surprised how much this one missed the mark in my opinion. There were elements of the cult 70s underground flick Blue Sunshine, but all it did was make me want to revisit that classic and forget about this entirely.

I watched this because I saw a TikTok saying that Martin Scorsese called this as Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s most terrifying film. It's really not a terrifying or even traditionally disturbing film. It's like a slow-burn detective story, but even so, it doesn’t fully grip either. It doesn’t have that usual pull, no strong sense of piecing clues together or being hooked by the mystery. The pacing is deliberately slow, almost hypnotic, but instead of drawing me in, I just felt bored. I know it's how easily people can be influenced into something darker. That violence isn’t always something external, but something already sitting beneath the surface. But even if I understood all the references, it still didn't resonate with me.

Though this may controversial, I did not enjoy this film at all. I feel like there’s something i’m missing. I can appreciate its approach in blocking, lighting, and general impact on J-Horror, but it felt like Kurosawa maybe relied too much on abstract storytelling to fully convey his message. Ambiguous endings can be used in very creative ways, but it almost felt like Cure left way too many questions unanswered (to the point where it was hard to interpret every single one). All the intentional “open ended” questions throughout this film almost left a bad impression- and it kind of ruined what could have been an incredibly unique form of storytelling.

Esse filme foi a segunda decepção do ano, logo depois de "La chimera" e realmente acho, que o grande problema para eu não ter gostado foi, novamente, ter criado muita expectativa. A ideia do filme é genial e as atuações em um geral são muito boas, principalmente do ator que faz o Mamiya, porém a construção dessa ideia e o decorrer da história simplesmente não me agradaram. Tudo é muito monótono, quieto e calmo, quase toda parte do filme. Além disso, é necessário ficar batendo cabeça do início ao fim do filme para entender coisas simples e básicas, que o diretor deixa solto ou apenas disponibiliza migalhas, para que possamos pensar e ligar os pontos, mas certas coisas passam do limite do normal e quando chega ao final do filme você não entendeu grande parte do filme. Não digo que não entendi, mas sim que é um longo caminho até chegar a mensagem que o diretor realmente quer passar. Acredito que o Kurosawa tentou fazer algo tão mirabolante, genial e místico, mas que no final se perdeu um pouco, na minha concepção. Ele quis trazer muitos detalhes e certas coisas que ficam em aberto, ou pistas pequenas, que são de extrema importância para a compreensão de determinados pontos, mas que no final fica difícil ligar tantas informações e tantas pistas para formular uma linha de pensamento. Penso que, talvez, se eu ver esse filme futuramente, posso mudar de ideia, até porque, como falei, a ideia do filme é promissora e bem interessante, mas para mim neste momento, foi mal direcionada e confusa.

Un thriller psicológico que avanza con mucha calma, pero utiliza ese ritmo para construir una sensación constante de inquietud. Más que resolver un misterio, parece interesado en explorar la fragilidad de la mente humana y lo fácil que una persona puede derribar las inhibiciones de otras cuando encuentra las grietas adecuadas. La violencia no surge de la nada, sino de impulsos que ya estaban ahí, esperando ser liberados. Su final ambiguo me pareció uno de sus mayores aciertos. La idea de que la manipulación y la violencia puedan reproducirse como un ciclo, más que como un hecho aislado, resulta inquietante y deja preguntas abiertas en lugar de respuestas cómodas. En conjunto, me pareció una propuesta muy interesante y bien construida. Su mayor virtud también puede ser su mayor defecto: confía tanto en la ambigüedad que, por momentos, deja demasiado a la interpretación. Para algunos eso será parte de su encanto; para otros, una fuente de frustración.

Atmospheric, quiet horror that never really gets too loud or in your face with how it puts you on edge. As pretentious as this may sound, it’s more so in the potential themes and ideas that are thrown around in your head. The more that I dug into what the story was trying to convey about evil, malicious harboring evil someone may have, the more creeped out I got about it. At the same time though, because of its approach in horror and how slow and methodical it is sometimes, some might find it boring or overrated, maybe overly pretentious which I can see as well. I also like how the atmosphere and genre feel like it smoothly transitions between each other. How it can go from an almost mundane, slow watch of a detective trying to solve a crime, something similar to maybe Memories of Murder, to something that feels like a horrific lucid, fever dream. Like your minds slipped and you can almost understand the descent into madness Takabe experiences. Great movie 👍

Tratto dal ponderoso romanzo di Paulo Lins (600 pagine), il film risulta fallimentare sotto tutti i punti di vista. Perché se è vero che le favelas di Rio de Janeiro rappresentano il luogo di un degrado sociale e morale certo profondo e di non facile soluzione, è altrettanto vero che non è con questa operazione che si può sperare di portare un minimo aiuto alla causa. Non risparmiando niente sul piano visivo per quanto attiene a brutalità e violenze e anzi lasciandole uniche, incontrastate protagoniste, il regista vorrebbe far passare l'idea che lui si limita a riprendere la realtà senza intervenire: ma l'eccesso di realismo scavalca il confine della credibilità e fa diventare il racconto più finto della finzione. Dominano allora personaggi come macchiette in mezzo ad un quadro di vita che non restituisce mai la complessità della situazione, essendo insisitito in una sola direzione, quella del crimine e della perdita della vita da adolescenti. Parziale e nichilista, il film accumula solo sconcezze e volgarità, compiacendosi di mostrare bambini sempre più piccoli in giro per le strade pronti ad uccidere, e così impedendo di mettere in piedi qualunque riflessione su quelle situazioni gravi che si vorrebbero (forse, ma non è sicuro) denunciare. Dal punto di vista pastorale, il film è da valutare come inaccettabile, e fortemente negativo.

I honestly don’t understand the overwhelming praise for City of God. While the film has impressive camera work and a fast-paced style, I found it exhausting rather than engaging. The constant violence, brutal characters, and endless cycle of crime make it feel more like a long sequence of shocking moments than a meaningful story. The characters are difficult to connect with because so many of them are defined by cruelty and survival, leaving little emotional depth for the audience to hold on to. The movie seems more interested in showing chaos and brutality than exploring the people behind it. The storytelling style, with its rapid editing and nonstop narration, can also feel distracting and overcomplicated. Instead of creating a powerful emotional experience, it sometimes feels like the film is trying too hard to prove how gritty and intense it can be. Although it has technical strengths, City of God was not an enjoyable watch for me. It is violent, overwhelming, and far too focused on misery to be the masterpiece many people claim it is. DONT RECOMMEND WATCHING

I was afraid this would be the case. Right from the start, we are introduced to the main characters, Goodfellas-style, Americanized and flashy. Fernando Meirelles stopped caring about being vocal about crime and poverty once he got the check, and I wouldn't have guessed otherwise. I find this film similar to La Haine in political and contextual terms, but one death in La Haine made me think for days, whereas there is a death every minute in City of God. It's not nearly as moving because the characters have no depth. Every person and the city are reduced to their worst, and it was painful to sit through this viewing. And of course, it doesn't pass the Bechdel test, why would it? It's disappointing that City of God is still so acclaimed. I guess the illusion of fatalism masquerading as social critique is too strong to break.

"City of God" is a technically good film that succeeds where many others fail in its ability to seamlessly connect stories, past and present into one cohesive timeline—though oversimplistically. The cinematography is strange, for better or worse, and the color grading or film (whatever it is) looks good at times, but bad in some scenes. Finally, the acting is mostly great. Unfortunately, "City of God" doesn't want to be anything more than this, instead it's an empty action film with pretty technicalities. What pisses me off the most is that that could have been it—a harmless action movie, it was okay, fun even. Sadly, it's based on a true story about a real town that was experiencing significant gang violence in a country where gang violence was and still is a major problem. The movie so badly wants you to care about the protagonist who's difficult life was largely glossed over in the prologue. I'm supposed to feel a dopamine release as both gangs fight to kill eachother faster, and eventually kill themselves too. This could have been interesting, but it's surface level. Back and forth, betrayal, murder, betrayal, murder. That's all it is—I've summed up the movie. What of the people who live in the city? I don't care about the dude who's family was slaughtered; the movie doesn't want to tell me about them. Instead I should focus on his half hearted revenge arc against the other gang. The movie tries to make you feel the brutality of everything, but you won't. It's all fake. And I just don't believe that the director wanted it to be any other way. He's too cool with it all, and I'm convinced that it's meant to be so—like a fairytale, not a real tragedy, or an on-going problem. An isolated story with an all too happy ending is what we get. Violence continues onto the next generation, but it feels half-hearted, like the director wanted to make a Hollywood blockbuster; small touches of artificial humanity are only put there to make the audience emotional. Characters are empty, blank slates. Poor characterization makes Rocket feel indifferent at times. Mega glorification of all that's bad.

Primeira revisão em anos, agora percebo que o Meirelles deve muito do sucesso de “Cidade de Deus” à sua experiência prévia com a publicidade. Isso funciona de momentos em momentos, o que realmente me pega e me faz odiar “Cidade de Deus” é o exotismo colonizador com o qual o olhar do Meirelles recai sobre essa realidade, que enxerga de uma perspectiva distanciada interessada em explorar (e, principalmente, vender) o sofrimento dos seus personagens sem nunca dar a dignidade para que eles se tornem seres humanos reais.

Assistindo para pesquisa. Acho impressionante o fenômeno de filmes do fim dos anos 90 para início dos anos 2000 nesse ciclo mais mainstream comercial. Claro que hoje tudo é mais padronizado que no passado, mas diria que existe uma forma muito mais explícita na maneira que vários desses filmes se emulavam em suas ideias de linguagem e escolhas narrativas. A ideia do que representava uma encenação de bom gosto tinha uma expressão muito mais clara, até porque existia uma menor quantidade de padrões a ser considerada. E não teria como não entender o grande projeto da retomada neste lugar. Definitivamente existe um primor no que se diz respeito à maneira que o filme se utiliza das personagens. Todos representam em algum lugar uma ideia muito única de si. Mas vejo isso apenas como um embrião que nunca nasce. A virtude se apaga no meio dessa formalização excessivamente programada. Cidade de Deus emula essa montagem ágil dos contemporâneos hollywoodianos. Isso enquanto tenta impor espetacularização em cima de uma banalidade que nunca parece se unir. Enquanto opta por uma narrativa cheia de tropos de outro lugar que não o engloba. Até a metade do filme, essa forma que é uma simbiose meio falha me incomoda menos do que quando decide transformar Leandro Firmino em um adolescente colegial norteamericano com dificuldades em chamar a garota para dançar no baile. Daí em diante a postura dele e do filme assume um caráter falso de infantilização, meio bobo. Eu poderia pensar na voz off didática que impede o filme de acontecer, ou na dramatização meio vazia do filme como um todo. À parte o momento em que Phellipe Haagensen sai de cena, pouco além disso impõe uma intenção dramática. Product of it’s time

There is a relentless, sun-drenched velocity to City of God that tricks you into thinking you’re watching a kinetic crime epic, right up until you realize every scene is quietly mourning. What hits hardest on a rewatch isn't just the breathless editing or the electric, samba infused soundtrack it’s how the film treats youth. Kids in the favela aren't given a grace period to just figure things out; they’re forced into adult archetypes before their voices even break. Rocket’s camera lens becomes his only real shield, a way to witness the chaos without letting it consume him entirely, while Lil Zé treats fear as the only currency that matters You could argue it occasionally risks hyper stylizing real world trauma at times, the late 90s post MTV sheen almost feels too sleek for the gravel and sweat it’s documenting. But underneath all that frantic, kinetic energy is a deeply human pulse. It barely lets you catch your breath, not just to thrill you, but because the kids on screen never got to catch theirs either

C’est définitivement un MOAT ( movie of all time ). J’avais des grandes attentes  envers ce film et il a livré la marchandise sur absolument tout les niveaux. Les personnages sont intéressants les dialogues donne la sensation d’être présent dans une scène de la vrai vie et c’est ce qui fait tout le charme du film. Plusieurs plans magnifiques et une cinématographie incroyable accompagné d’une bande sonore qui agit comme une colle entre les éléments de cette fresque. J’ai adoré la façon dont l’histoire est racontée à travers les différentes perspectives et l’utilisation de la narration tout au long du film est vraiment unique et j’ai adoré. Absolute cinéma / 10

Rogen and Wilde’s characters are miserable - but rogen’s character is evidently a more miserable and toxic partner. There might’ve been a “nobody’s perfect” insinuation but it was clear that Seth rogen’s character was far more imperfect than his wife’s. Usually with these type of relationship-character-driven single set dialogue movies you’ll see the narrative ask the viewer to fall on one side of a fence - but I don’t see what the fence was supposed to be here. This was a couple that probably should divorce. I didn’t see the complicated aspect since there was never a redeeming interaction between them in the brief 2 hours we shared with them. The sexually adventurous, risqué couple (that was more of a metaphor than anything, for what Rogen and Wilde wanted to be - “the grass is always greener”) didn’t shine a new light on the main characters to me. If anything they just told us more of what we already knew. I saw this with Zac and felt that I had to defend my disappointment because he quite liked it. And at its surface, it’s entertaining through its laughs and our wide eyed reactions to the sexual taboos. But on a deeper level I think Olivia Wilde wanted to reflect a sort of societal/romantic commentary. Perhaps on monogamy? On complacency? None of the commentary had an impact on me because it was rooted in a couple that no happy person would ever hope to relate to. At times I thought the movie would be an oddball, weird, shock factor sex comedy. It probably would have landed a better score if not for the “therapy” final act which had me constantly wondering why the second couple had not left an hour prior. I saw don’t worry darling twice and loved it but this one from Wilde tried to (maybe?)  encourage relationship perseverance but gave us no reason to root for them.

This movie is so Challengers coded to me. There’s comedy, there’s intrigue, and there’s this sick feeling you get in the third act. All people have vices (shortcomings). Whether it be physical, emotional, or mental, all people are living proof that there are mosaics that we will never fully understand. So when we do understand something, when it is tangible, and graspable, we hold onto it tightly, and attribute it to being us, something that is unmovable and unchanging. Any habit - good or bad - that one that sticks like glue, unmovable until something else shifts, and a new one is tacked on. What does that say about us? We limit ourselves to the known, and chain ourselves to monotony (at times) and get angry about the past and how we could be doing more instead of viewing it as a learning experience. Joe and Angela are falling apart. The movie feels like a blooming onion, where you can delve for the centre, but it focuses on peeling back savoury, witty, comedic layers before the core is hit. It was really funny that halfway through, the vibe completely shifted because Piña and Hawk’s secret was revealed, and then it took another dramatic turn towards the end. There is nothing shameful in wanting to be seen. There is nothing shameful in wanting to be heard. There is nothing shameful about trying!!!! There is tenderness in knowing anything intimately, but it only comes after you allow the technicolor of their world touch yours. It is a waste to live life in guilt, in shame, because you’re the only one who is white knuckled, and hard of fist. As pinkpatheress said, let it all go. (Lowkey need to watch this in theatres me thinks!)

Strange things are afoot in THE INVITE. I love movies that are basically just a play. The stacked cast -- Seth Rogen, Olivia Wilde, Penélope Cruz, and Edward Norton -- are all exceptionally locked in. Ed Norton was my saving grace, actually; he's always sweeping in with a random comment to help ease the tension. I hope this gets some Oscar noms (it would actually be so sweet to see Seth Rogen nominated in a serious acting category).

I wouldn’t be surprised if The Invite finds its way into multiple Oscar conversations. I already complimented my favorite aspects in my first review, but man, everything was so well done here. Today’s audience really liked the humor and I think Seth Rogen in particular balanced everything so well, including the humor and facial expressions. Being able to pull off a combination of one of the funniest and most tense movies of the year is special. The way they filmed it — the artsy opening sequence (which also perfectly comes full circle with the ending), the camera/lens choices, the color grading, and the way they framed the characters and utilized foreground and background blur — was so good. The color coordination too. I love how the opening scene goes from them being happy at an undisclosed time to the beautiful frames of Joe just being miserable. This film is an excellent psychological study on self and marriage — communication, opening up, your perspective on the things you have, and resentment. Joe had so many good things going for him, between his daughter, kids learning from him, his musical talent, a pretty wife, and a nice home in San Francisco. He chose to be hung up on the past and push people away. Angela just had communication issues and made Joe feel unheard. You also see that the seemingly perfect couple indeed had their own issues, but Hawk was able to apologize when he was wrong and it was easier for him to be vulnerable. It also just shows how someone like him — someone you could easily judge or put into a box because of his sex life — had his own life experiences that you could empathize with. The end is beautiful because music can really break down barriers and be a language of its own.

“Que pensabas que harías hoy cuando tenias 11?” Aftersun es una película que tenia guardada hace bastante tiempo, gente variada me la recomendaba porque parecía ser un film bastante crudo en cuanto a la relación parental y en simples palabras tocaba el corazón y te hacia llorar… no me pasó. Me parece interesante y precioso en verdad como la imagen y la paleta de colores que se ocupa te transporta realmente a la pre-adolescencia/niñez que Sophie concierne, me sentí en todo momento como si yo también conectara con mi niño interior. Sin embargo, creo que espere en toda la película a que sucediera algo sorprendente o que turnara la trama a algo más denso, a algo que me deje nervioso, o sea si, se logra, sobre todo ad portas del final de la película cuando la relación entre Sophie y Calum parece quebrarse la noche de su cumpleaños, pero sin más, se me hizo demasiado pretensiosa y lenta, es una trama tierna y triste, sobre todo por Paul Mescal interpretando a este padre que parece estar depresivo. Acotar que, aunque se me hizo esperable el que no se volverían a ver, fue un sentimiento ingenuo de pena el que la película finalice con quizás los recuerdos de la mini cámara de Sophie sobre las mejores vacaciones de su vida. Quizás no entendí el film, quizás no es mi tipo de genero al cual recurro para disfrutar, realmente la quería disfrutar pero simplemente no me llego… Cerrando, me parece increíble leer los comentarios sobre esta película, muchos de ellos replanteando la relación que cada individuo tiene con sus padres, porque si, la trama te hace replantearte, de forma implícita, sobre todo aquellas personas con padres separados, y en un punto sentí, que los roles se invertían, el padre parecía un niño y la hija la madre, muchas de las realidades pasadas y contemporáneas, en donde los hijos deben ser adultos responsables a temprana edad (y quizás, solo quizás, por eso Sophie se nos muestra como una niña de 11 que intenta entender la vida [un tanto arriesgada, incontrolable y placentera de la mayoría de edad]).

This feels like one of those movies that is purposely vague in key ways to allow the audience to imprint onto it, and that kind of film is never going to work for me. At its core, we have a father and daughter on vacation together. There are moments where they bond. There is obvious childhood tragedy for the father, which is probably why he seems to drink a lot, yet he's not one of those abusive drunks, so it's ok? We're never really given much depth beyond that. It's a girl growing up, having a first kiss, hanging with other kids on vacation. It's nice that there isn't any kind of bullying or any other overtly negative elements that usually make up these narratives. It's mostly just moments shared between father and daughter, mostly bonding. At the same time, not much actually happens for the entire runtime. There seems to be implied longing, but again, the narrative is kept vague on purpose so that we can somehow imprint on it. The thing is, I am not watching a movie to do its job for it. If there isn't much story there, I'm not going to fill in the blanks for it. If I want to do that, I will either work on one of my own stories or read a book. Is this supposed to be sad and reflective? I never got to vacation with my father before he died when I was around 8 or 9, I never got these moments with him... and to have it be such a positive experience... this girl is fortunate. All I know is real tragedy related to my father. Did the girl's father die right after this? Or was it years later? We see her as an adult, all reflecting and shit, but as I said, things are left mostly vague, so who knows? At least she has cherished moments with her father. More than a lot of us got. On top of that, I think people confuse realism for good. Yeah, it is shot very realistically, the performances are very natural, yet story wise, there isn't much there, and I really dislike the way this was shot, which is probably one of the main sticking points for me. Often badly framed, or where it often focuses on 'experiencing', rather than what they are experiencing, so for instance, they are playing pool, we see them take the shot, but not any of what's actually happening in the game. Or another instance, they play an arcade game, but we never really see what they are playing. As for the bad framing, at times people are talking and the frame is like whatever. Or like, the scene where there is a TV, a mirror behind it, and the whole scene is either shot from a camcorder feeding to the TV or later, when the camcorder is off, what we barely see in the reflection on the screen or in the fragment of exposed mirror is all we get. It is certainly a choice. Oh, I get it, being so 'artistic' in its reflection on what's happening with the character, but it goes on for too long and it's just badly framed, all of it. Or this repeated cutting to a dance club, flashing lights, to show this reoccurring element of the father dancing... but mostly, it is just hard to see anything. Too much of the film is like this. Extended scenes of someone laying around, or badly framed shots like this that are clearly intended to be artistic, but end up being that in a bad way. I remember reading positive comments about this film and it sounds like it should be a good one, right? I expect a level of crudeness from a documentary, because it is trying to capture something in a moment and bring it all together, but when it's a narrative film that looks mostly like a badly shot documentary, that seems to have less story than many documentaries... what are we even doing here?
