54/100 Haven't looked into how autobiographical this is, because that's not important: It feels, in every respect, like the writer-director's bittersweet memories of a vacation she took with her dad at age 11.  Which is to say that it's hyper-specific in detail but largely uneventful, seeking to evoke rather than to dramatize. That's the Terence Davies recipe, but where Davies compresses and magnifies, transforming the mundane into heightened shards of terror and exhilaration and communal spirit, Wells merely remembers (or has an impoverished imagination). Apart from Sophie herself, embodied by Frankie Corio with a thoroughly winning combo of guileless and astringent, nothing registered strongly with me; every filmmaker has this movie in them—we all have childhoods and at least one indelible experience from same—and I appreciate that most choose not to make it, recognizing that what's meaningful to them won't necessarily translate to total strangers. Not without significant formal and/or narrative embellishment, anyway. (Admittedly, Aftersun has many ardent fans, including the NYFF selection committee. But I have a hard time imagining a movie along these lines that they wouldn't love, so long as it's self-evidently heartfelt. Me, I'm enough of a Grinch to demand more.) Wells does ambitiously attempt to suggest an entire contrapuntal narrative, bridging the foregrounded party-like-it-was-1999(-because-it-was) quasi-idyll and a seemingly regretful present, from isolated moments spent with Dad alone, plus very brief glimpses of Sophie as an adult. Intriguing, but it's awfully skeletal, and Paul Mescal, judging from this surface-level performance and his similar work in The Lost Daughter (haven't seen any of Normal People ), just doesn't have the chops to communicate Calum's enigmatic inner torment in a way that would facilitate our understanding of what likely lies in store for the man, and for this relationship. A promising debut, but of the kind that makes you wonder whether there'll be a second film. NOTE: I liked it significantly more the second time .

At its best moments "Aftersun" is a tender and beautiful film about a separated dad spending holidays with his young daughter during the 90s'. For 2/3 of its time, "Aftersun" is filled with charming moments of perfect chemistry between Frankie Corio and Paul Mescal. The problem begins when Charlotte Wells pushes drama into her debut feature, unnaturally brought up, to break the built bonds. The so-called "reflection twenty years later" (from the description) works even less as the only few minutes of the adult Sophie's life do not cover the gap of " the man she didn't" knew.

This was a nostalgic watch that took me on this melancholic trip to the summer of my own childhood, a summer that would last forever before it's September and it's back to school again, before the 7 am alarm and the traffic jam and the lunch boxes. It's a summer full of long boring afternoons sitting in front of the tv watching whatever comes on. It's the swimming pool days with its fresh juices and short friendships that only last for a day. It's the sand in your hair and your flip-flops, the rosy sun-kissed cheeks, and the extra-defined curls due to the salty water. It's ice cream for breakfast and lunch, it's game nights and cold pizza for dinner, It's throwing off the sheets as the heat pours through your open window through that one long summer night. it's your mother looking young as ever, and your father while he was still doing his best. and your siblings as foolish and stupid as ever. This movie was all that to me, live footage of a life we all lived. I guess that's what makes it so special and hits this deep spot in anyone who watched it, it's how we all had those summers we long for now that we can't escape this adulthood world. My rating reflects my enjoyment of the movie, and in fact I was bored most of the time, I was never fan of those “nothing is really happening” movies.

Aftersun is one of those films that feels incredibly simple on the surface, yet completely devastating underneath. The performances are so natural that they never feel like acting, they feel like real people, which makes the relationship between Sophie and her dad (Callum) deeply personal and relatable. That ordinary, everyday quality is what makes the film so heartbreaking, because it captures the small moments we often overlook until they become memories. Rather than relying on dramatic events, Aftersun quietly builds an emotional weight that lingers long after it ends, leaving a sense of love, loss and regret that feels painfully human.

This was a movie which i didnt understand and definitely need to rewatch. Incredible acting from Mescal and Corio. Was clearly a movie which leans heavily on the bond between father and daughter and deals with the crippling depression which Mescal's character tries to hide from his daughter, Sophie. From the first sort of 20 minutes, you can tell that this film is showing and not telling , whether it's the very long shots focused on a single subject, or the use of solemn and dark composed music for the film within moments which do not warrant it, the film portrays depression in a much more subconscious way than ive seen other films and series manage. The use of the rave scenes, and lingering shots on what seems like random subjects are something I should analyse on a rewatch, as I am no film buff and therefore have not been able to pick up on the purpose of these scenes and what the intention of the cinematography is very well. The consistently sinister or sombre music being draped over the scenes in this film is representative of how depression consumes every waking minute of a person's life. I believe there was also a theme of a young person being introduced to the world of romance and sexual exploration, with lingering shots of teenagers kissing whilst Sophie was nearby, or that one scene of her overhearing some teenagers talking about a sexual experience. I initially assumed that the sinister and sombre music being used during these scenes was to represent how a young individual's introduction to sexual experiences from others educating said person could represent grooming. However upon research for this film's meaning, I found that this might not be the case? Sex as a theme isnt really a topic discussed online (or at least on reddit) So perhaps for that reason I dont think these scenes are about grooming but rather the coming-of-age experience of discovering romance, love and sex as an additional theme ALONGSIDE the depression Sophie's dad suffers from? If it's not clear, I havent fully understood what this movie is actually about. To really get a better understanding of the film I should rewatch it probably. I liked this film a lot, but oh wow I was very confused.

i just feel hollow, a slow melancholic dream with the highest highs and the lowest lows. it’s a fathers desperate attempts to create a happy memory for his daughter, young Sophie believes they’re both underneath the same sky. that’s the most heart breaking thing about this movie, scenes of Calum alone imagined by the adult Sophie to be so broken, sobbing furiously in his bedroom, his mask stripped by so many mentally and physically, it’s torturous. the experience of reliving her childhood memory now with adult sensibility, finding out what her father was through, must be devastating. the last dance, knowing its his last dance. the walk into the sea, tai chi on the balcony, big lavish purchase of £800 rug for Sophie that she said he can’t afford. gut wrenching.

I sat down and watched this twice consecutively tonight. I think part of the beauty of this film is that it takes a minute to get. it’s very beautiful and visually impressive, but the deeper meaning is definitely supposed to be lost to you on your first viewing, seeing as the whole thing happens in Sophie’s imagination. you are living it through her as she tries to piece together her memories of the trip and who her father really was. the symbolism here is insane. there’s definitely more to unpack, but the two that stood out to me were the “rave” scenes being a metaphor for Sophie’s incomplete memories of Calum, and the polaroid photograph that sort of made the movie’s meaning click for me: that the physical media is really all Soph can see when she delves back into her old memories. on my first viewing I didn’t really get it until that moment - I just thought it was very pretty and was unsettled by how clearly disturbed Calum was on his own. but the second time around I cried. this is perfect and takes levels of understanding, which is exactly what I look for in a movie.

Boah hat der mich eiskalt erwischt. In „Aftersun“ ging ich mit den Erwartungen rein, ein Drama über die Erforschung von Beziehung zwischen Vater und Tochter zu bekommen. Das gab mir der Film auch, aber auch noch so viel härtere Themen. „Aftersun“ fühlte sich für mich wie eine verlorene Erinnerung an meine Kindheit an. Diese Camcorder aufnahmen sind so dermaßen nostalgisch und schön, dass ich alleine da schon hätte heulen können. Das hier ist so toll gefilmt, die Umgebung und das Setting ist herrlich schön anzusehen und die Cinematographie zum dahinschmelzen. Oftmals erinnerte mich „Aftersun“ von der Erzählung und dem Vibe, an „Nowhere“ von Sofia Coppola welchen ich auch echt gerne mochte. Auch dort geht es ja um recht ähnliches, „Aftersun“ macht das aber nochmal ne ganze Stufe besser, meiner Meinung nach. Irgendwo ist „Aftersun“ ein richtiger feelgood-Film, besonders zu Beginn, die Figuren sind im Urlaub und haben einfach Spaß mit der Zeit die sie zusammen verbringen. Gleichzeitig umgibt den gesamten Film eine so bedrückende Atmosphäre und ein Gefühl von Schwere, Anspannung und Nervosität, was ich anfangs etwas seltsam fand, irgendwann aber so grandios für mich funktionierte. Was ich gehört habe, was vielen nicht gefällt, ist das pacing, weil ja, das ist wirklich sehr langsam. Dafür nutzt der Film diese Zeit und Ruhe um die Erzählung richtig aufzubauen und die Figuren uns nahezubringen, was für mich so gut funktioniert hat, wodurch der Film für mich nie langatmig oder gar langweilig war. Ich habe jetzt so viel Positives zu „Aftersun“ gesagt, ohne mein persönliches Highlight des Films zu nennen, Paul Mescal. Paul Mescal spielt wirklich phänomenal gut. Er und Frankie Corio haben erstmal eine 1a Chemie und sind zusammen so dermaßen süß, dazu spielt Paul Mescal diese Figur mit so einer Tiefe, man spürt bei ihm die ganze Zeit, dass er eine Last in sich trägt, welche im Film nie ausgesprochen wird, aber dennoch durch sein Spiel so deutlich ist, das ist unglaublich. „Aftersun“ hat mich mit seiner Thematik und Erzählung unfassbar gepackt, nicht mehr losgelassen und beinahe zu Tränen gerührt. Nur liebe für diesen Film.

Best Criterion purchase I made since Memories of Murder . ________________________________________________________ Anatomy of a Fall enticed me from the premise alone. A woman is blamed for her husband’s death and the only witness is her blind son. That in it of itself is enough to get my attention. The film is an amazing courtroom drama. It’s similar to A Few Good Men in that every single court sequence is riveting, filled with incredible dialogue and tense confrontations. The movie does a great job creating suspense and tension. I genuinely did not know how it was all gonna play out. What makes this movie stand out though is at its heart, it’s a family drama. It’s about a marriage on the brink of collapse, and how the couple’s issues are impacting their loved ones. It tackles very real topics like infidelity, sexuality, childhood, abuse, depression, and grief. I found myself caring about these characters and the struggles they endured throughout the movie’s runtime. Everything about this movie felt real. Never once did I feel like I was watching a movie. Anatomy of a Fall felt more like someone hid a camera inside someone’s house rather than actors reciting lines from a script (a very well written script I might add) in front of a camera. The authenticity of this film is thanks equally to the screen writer(s) and the actors. Sandra Hüller in particular is downright incredible. The realism of this movie is a bit of a blessing and a curse. I love that the director allowed certain scenes to “breathe.” It created a bunch of heartfelt moments and it gives the viewer the chance to sit with these characters and empathize with them. That being said, I felt like some scenes dragged on for a little too long, and it ruined the pacing in some parts. But once again, maybe on second watch, I’ll feel differently. Bottom line, I love Anatomy of a Fall . I can’t wait to watch it again. In fact I kinda have to watch it again. I watched it while my wife was at book club. When she returned and realized I was watching this movie, she was like “OMG I wanted to watch that too!” Sorry babe. 😜

In awe of just how much tension this film is able produce with essentially no score outside of Daniel’s piano and 50’s P.I.M.P. instrumental. I didn’t want to write this, I didn’t want to be the guy who sours all the love for the grand finale; the magnum opus. Nevertheless, as of ten minutes post- Endgame , I am profoundly disappointed. To be fair, I don’t honestly know what (if anything) could have satisfied me. My investment in this franchise was less tied to the ongoing character arcs, but rather more to it as a wildly successful experiment in storytelling; a structural marvel. Therein lies the genesis to my frustration. Narratively, the MCU does not play out as 22 films leading up to Endgame , but rather 21 to Infinity War , and 1 to clean them up. Clocking in at three fucking hours, it still felt aggravatingly rushed, and painstakingly formulaic. That formula plays out something like this: a dash of manipulative nostalgia, a hint of predictability, and a heavy dusting (pun intended) of unbelievable character decisions and clunky plot mechanics. Despite it’s recurrent moments of grandeur, Endgame serves as little more than the dotted-i and crossed-t of the MCU. Now, I’m not a complete Scrooge. Steve Rogers wielding Mjolnir; The battlefield return of The Dusted; Tony Stark’s climactic statement. These are undoubtedly some of the finest moments in the MCU, full-stop. But a handful of phenomenal moments don’t conclude a 22 film experience, and unfortunately Endgame left me wanting. I really hope that time and a potential revisit sway me into a more favourable camp. 60

Siguiente paso en la maratón Marvelita para estar un poco al día pre-Spiderman. Bastante sorprendido con que así sea el clímax final de 22 películas, porque realmente Infinity War sí se siente como tal y Endgame solo cumple la última hora y quizá en su planteamiento inicial. El histórico final de la anterior continua con un mundo casi post apocalíptico que me hubiera encantado que se explotara un pelín más. Tras ese inicio, la película claramente tiene el objetivo de llegar a una batalla final épica y falla clamorosamente en la manera de lograrlo. El planteamiento argumental es hacer viajes en el tiempo para robar las gemas del infinito, usarlas para revivir a todo el mundo y devolverlas a su lugar correspondiente para no generar líneas temporales caóticas. A las paradojas propias de las pelis de viajes en el tiempo no se le presta excesiva atención porque tampoco es el sitio, y así se permiten darle alguna patadita a la lógica. Eso funciona como excusa para hacer una especie de repaso a algunas pelis y personajes que se siente un poco liosa, anti climática y de una autorreferencialidad  que juega en contra de la épica de la peli. Esa vuelta a espacios de pelis anteriores sirve como excusa para traer a Thanos (el de la línea temporal actual está muerto) de vuelta, mucho menos desarrollado e interesante que la anterior. Además, lo más grave, es poco consistente con lo ocurrido ya que el personaje parece reaccionar a cosas que él no ha vivido. Por ejemplo, critica a los humanos por no haber sabido aprovechar su plan y por ello los condena a desaparecer para crear un nuevo mundo de cero. No queda natural y parece mucho más villano básico que en la anterior. La última hora vuelve a ser increíble, la batalla final es espectacular y el final con el sacrificio de Iron Man (que inició el MCU y acabó con él hasta ese momento) es muy emotivo.

Honestly, upon rewatching these movies, as decade-defining as it was to see the Avengers movies in theaters, they just don't hit the same on home release. Like they're plenty entertaining, and Infinity War is genuinely a great movie, but the payoff and subsequent downward trend of the MCU movies that directly followed this one (which has recently gotten better with additions like the last 2 Spider-Man movies and Thunderbolts) just feels a bit exhausting rewatching this one. I think this more negative approach I'm having with this rewatch stems from the anxiety of the upcoming Avengers movie being centered around my favorite comic book character of all time, Dr Doom, who is miles more powerful and methodical than a character like Thanos. As well as the MCU's portrayal of the character was, Thanos could and should never hold a candle. Before the MCU was celebrated for giving a new life and dedicated following to all the B-list characters Marvel had to settle with due to the big 3 (Spider-Man, F4, and the X-Men) being owned by Fox and Sony, there was a legacy of iconic comic heroes and villains that spanned over half a decade. And within the culture of comics, if you asked someone to name a comic book villain from Marvel Comics, 9/10 you're not going to hear Thanos, Ultron, or even Venom. They will say Dr. Doom. To the comic fan, Thanos is a nice can of RC Cola, but Doom... Doom is Coke from a glass. Despite this level of hype this character is known for, his film adaptations have been genuinely terrible, to the point of being disrespectful (I'm looking at you F4 2016). I guess the point I'm trying to make is that the luster is being lost for me in this film, along with the decisions of the past and present, which make me enjoy this film a little less and make me especially nervous for the film that, as a Doom fan, should leave me feeling excited but is instead making me feel the complete opposite way. All I ask for is a faithful adaptation of Dr. Doom in some facet, and I can die happy.

After being completely blown away by Infinity War , I have to say I’ve been left feeling a little bit disappointed in the saga’s conclusion. Infinity War is very well structured and executes all the beats it needs to hit to deliver something I felt was original and emotionally satisfying. Half of the universe’s population is gone, along with half of the heroes we love, and we’re left feeling hopeless, just like them. This is something we carry with us into the first 30 minutes of Endgame , which again subverted my expectations (positively) and dug the hole of wondering how they’d resolve this even deeper. When then, probably not even 10 minutes later, fucking time travel is thrown out there, it feels incredibly cheap. Instead of carrying the great momentum from the previous film, it becomes, from then on, a kids’ movie. Instead of the events leading the story, which I think made Infinity War so refreshing, it feels predictable, like the events are just following a path that will ultimately end in Marvel getting that big ensemble battle scene they wanted. From the moment time travel was mentioned, all the stakes disappeared. Though I don’t think it was done terribly, and it sets up the multiverse stuff in a good manner. Big spoilers if you somehow don’t know this, but Iron Man’s death hit me way less than I thought it would. Maybe it’s because I already knew it would happen. Maybe it’s because I didn’t watch every Iron Man film in theaters since they first started coming out. But still, I feel like a well-executed death should still do more for me emotionally, especially for a character of such significance. I think, along with a lot of what happens in this film, it was rushed. Yes, it had been foreshadowed—well, at that—but to me it felt like Marvel just thought, «Well, someone has to die. Who would make the most people cry?» And because it’s Iron Man, and Iron Man is Robert Downey Jr., they can just bring him back anyway, and people will eat it up. I don’t like what they did with Thor either. That is not the same fucking guy we saw being willing to give everything to save Asgard. I think Marvel dug themselves into a hole they hadn’t planned a way to get out of, which in the end makes for an overstuffed and rushed saga finale. Like Infinity War , it’s not particularly pretty to look at either, but now without the storytelling chops to make me look past most of it. I think it WOULD be a good film if it were written with a little more thought. Dangerously close to giving this 3 stars. It could easily be split into two films, honestly. It’s 5am now. I have more to say but can’t form any more thoughts. Good night . And bye MCU (for a bit) gonna watch Satantango now. Or dancing pig

" I love you 3000 ".                      "It's Been a Long, Long Time". El cierre definitivo de una era que cambió la historia del cine comercial para siempre. Después de 11 años, 22 películas y docenas de arcos argumentales entrelazados, Avengers: Endgame no solo logra estar a la altura de las colosales expectativas, sino que entrega una experiencia cinematográfica épica, nostálgica y profundamente emotiva. La película equilibra magistralmente la melancolía del duelo tras las pérdidas de Infinity War con la esperanza, la acción a escala monumental y el humor característico del UCM . El viaje en el tiempo no es solo un recurso narrativo, sino una hermosa carta de amor a toda la franquicia, permitiéndonos revivir momentos icónicos desde una nueva perspectiva antes del enfrentamiento final. El clímax y la batalla final es puro espectáculo visual y fan service ejecutado con brillantez, pero su verdadero corazón reside en las despedidas. Darle un cierre tan digno, humano y perfecto a personajes con los que crecimos — en especial a Tony Stark y Steve Rogers — es el mayor logro de los hermanos Russo. Un hito generacional que difícilmente se volverá a repetir. "Avengers... assemble." — Steve Rogers "I'm gonna need a dance raincheck."

Barbie wants to empower women while apparently believing women can’t understand subtext. I’m still trying to figure out who this movie is for. I’m apparently old enough to understand patriarchy but not old enough to recognize a metaphor without Margot Robbie explaining it to me. Enfin vu le film le plus populaire de Greta Gerwig (et mon premier film d’elle par ailleurs). Malheureusement j’ai pas été emballé par la proposition. C’est dommage parce que la propagande féministe est louable mais le message est entaché de dialogues un peu trop enfantins ou un peu trop débiles à mon goût même si je pense que c’est l’univers qui veut ça. Le fond est pas si mal mais la forme délivrée est pas subtile et trop gratuite. L’humour en général dans le film est lourd et certains tacles pas très biens sentis. Il y avait tout dans le film pour en faire quelque chose de réellement iconique et en faire un très bon blockbuster. Le côté monde alternatif, les côtés positifs et négatifs de Barbie avec ses stéréotypes sur le corps et l’esprit féminin, montrer qu’elle était, est et sera une figure de proue des jeunes filles mais surtout à l’avenir, une figure d’émancipation féminine dans une société patriarcale. The film is just as plastic and artificial as the source material it’s based on. I was severely disappointed after I finished the film. It has no nuance, no depth and for me, it’s just a vapid, virtue signaling mess. The problem isn’t the moral core of the film, which I do agree with, but how it’s dealt with. In my opinion it feels surface level and strangely disingenuous. This isn’t helped by the story, which has no twists and no particularly strong plot, it’s just filled with a bunch of underdeveloped characters that flash their fake smile at you as they wave the films message in your face like a great pink neon sign. That being said, the film has its moments, but most of these come from the more silly joke driven bits and are quickly overshadowed by the “I’m fourteen and this is deep” level existentialism. It’s like Gerwig was torn between making a film for young girls and a serious feminist film, and then from that inner battle rose this compromise, which fails to deliver on either. Still, thanks for all the silly goofs it’s not unbearable watch, at times it’s almost entertaining. Though, it’s a crime that the song Barbie Girl was not once played. Shame.

Aver.. por donde empiezo, en primer lugar, los escenarios no están tan mal montados y se ven bastante bonitos, y su mensaje sobre qué hay que crecer y afrontar la realidad tampoco es malo, pero no sé, todo lo demás me transmite la sensación de que está mal hecho y se han tomado las decisiones directivas incorrectas. Ya sabía desde un primer lugar que no me iba a gustar, pero es que como me iba a gustar, aparte que todo esto es de otro mundo opuesto para mí, me parece que hay demasiados agujeros en el guión, y el ritmo es MUY lento, por no decir lo polémica que es sobre el feminismo que puede llegar a transmitir, o lo clichés que son muchos personajes, que a mí me han llegado a dar vergüenza ajena a veces (repito que esto es mi opinión y no todo el mundo puede pensar igual), aunque sí aprecio como está la actuación, que no es para nada mala. También desprecio que por lo general parezca una película muy infantil, aunque tenga algunas escenas subidas de tono, es que a ver, ¿ A que tipo de audiencia se supone que va esta película dirigida? Ahora que estoy empezando a meterme más en el cine, estoy empezando a despreciar este tipo de películas de Hollywood que van dirigidas a atraer a un público muy amplio y ganar mucho dinero sin ni siquiera ser tan buenas, el cine genérico actual se está convirtiendo en una competición de ganar dinero más que en arte, pero bueno esa es mi opinión. Sigo sin entender, ¿Cómo es esto es la tercera película más vista en letterboxd? ¿Cómo esto superó en taquilla a Oppenheimer? ¿Cómo pasamos de tener películas tan perfectas como Stalker a slop como el que es Barbie? ¿Acaso el cine ha muerto? Bueno, por lo menos fue algo entretenida, hubo algunos momentos graciosos, y me gustaron las referencias a 2001, Matrix, El padrino y Los caballeros de la mesa cuadrada.

I think Barbie is one of those movies I wish every little girl could watch before the world gets the chance to tell her who she is supposed to be. Because underneath all the pink and glitter, it is a story about becoming a woman. About growing up and slowly realizing that there is no version of yourself that will ever be enough for everyone. Be beautiful, but not vain. Be smart, but not intimidating. Be strong, but still soft. Have ambition, but don't make anyone feel small. Be independent, but still be desirable. How exhausting it is to be a woman and constantly feel like you're failing at a set of rules that were never meant to be followed. And then Barbie asks you to let all of that go. To exist without having to be perfect. To be messy, uncertain, angry, joyful, ordinary. To grow older without believing you've become less valuable. To understand that your worth was never supposed to depend on how well you fit into someone else's idea of a woman. Maybe that's why this movie means so much to me. I wish little girls could see it before they learn to shrink themselves. Before they learn to apologize for taking up space. Before they learn that being loved sometimes means becoming smaller. I want them to grow up knowing that they don't have to be the prettiest, the smartest, the kindest, or the most accomplished person in the room. They just have to know that their life belongs to them. And maybe that's what Barbie really changed for me: Being a woman isn't about becoming the perfect version of yourself. It's about finally realizing you were never meant to be a version of anyone else.

Träumer Kino der schönsten und seltsamsten Sorte, das vielleicht gar nicht so das großartige Werk mit Metaphern aufgeladen ist, sondern eher eine kleine sympatische Kuriosität. Bones and All würde ist ein wenig bizarr und voller Gegensätze, aber im Kern würde ich sagen, es ist eine Außenseiter-Story, wie man ein Leben lebt mit einem let's call it "Lebensstil", der als problematisch angesehen wird. Dazu gehört sowas wie, dass sobald das Leben unerträglich wird, man Gleichgesinnte findet, die einem Halt geben, das Konzept fatalistischer Liebe und natürlich ganz viele Bilder, die ein Midwest-Roadtrip so gemütlich machen, wie man ihn sich nur vorstellt. Der krasse Gegensatz ist dann natürlich der Part, wo Maren und ihre vielen Bekanntschaften Menschen essen, aber auch das wird weirdly eklig faszinierend eingefangen und wirkt gegen Ende fast schon karthatisch. So ganz konnte ich mir keinen Reim auf diesen Aspekt der Geschichte machen, aber wie gesagt ist der Film sehr laid back und hat mir eher etwas Komfort mit dem Gefühl gegeben, wenn man im Leben einsam ist und sich anders und missverstanden fühlt. In gewisser Weise ist es auch ein Coming of Age Film. Aus Marens Perspektive beginnt ihr Leben erst so richtig, als ihr Vater sie zurücklässt und sie die Welt auf eigene Faust, ohne einen Vormund, entdeckt. Sie lernt noch viele andere Menschen wie sie kennen und irgendwann wird klar, dass im ganzen Land eine Art Community existiert, die ihre Dränge unterschiedlich ausleben, aber alle versteckt vor der allgemeinen Gesellschaft leben. An der Stelle geht der Lebensstil von Maren und Lee auch perfekt mit der im Midwest geprägten Armut einher. Man kann sich nirgends niederlassen, entwickeln, ist generell misstrauisch und kann morden und rauben wie es einem beliebt, weils eh kaum jemand nachverfolgt. Am Ende ist Bones and All für mich weniger Horror oder große Metapher als einfach ein stimmungsvoller Roadtrip über Einsamkeit, das Heranwachsen und das Bedürfnis, irgendwo dazuzugehören. Nicht jede Idee geht für mich komplett auf, aber Luca Guadagnino erschafft daraus so eine eigenartige Wohlfühlmelancholie, dass ich mich in der seltsamen Perspektive von Maren und Lee total verloren habe.

“The world of love wants no monsters in it.” Até os Ossos é um filme que eu gostei bastante, mas com um nó atravessado que demorei pra nomear. Ele é lindo de ver, tem duas atuações que me seguraram, tem uma metáfora potente, e ainda assim eu saí dele sentindo que faltou alguma coisa pra ele virar a obra que claramente queria ser. Eu gostei mas com ressalvas. A história acompanha a Maren e o Lee, dois jovens que compartilham a mesma condição, são canibais por natureza. Luca Guadagnino transforma isso em um road movie pelos Estados Unidos dos anos 80, os dois cruzando estradas vazias, cidades pequenas, motéis, tentando existir num mundo que jamais aceitaria o que eles são. É um romance sobre dois outsiders se encontrando, se reconhecendo, e descobrindo que talvez não estejam tão sozinhos quanto pensavam. E é aqui que mora o que eu mais gostei. O canibalismo, no filme, é metáfora de ser diferente, de carregar dentro de si uma coisa que a sociedade lê como monstruosa, de amar e desejar de um jeito que o mundo insiste em condenar. A fala de Janelle diz tudo, o mundo do amor não quer monstros dentro dele. É sobre não caber, sobre ser empurrado pra margem por uma natureza que você não escolheu, sobre procurar outra pessoa que carregue a mesma fome pra não ter que carregar sozinho. Essa leitura é o que sustenta o filme. Mas é também na metáfora que mora parte do meu incômodo, e é um incômodo dividido. Porque o filme nunca decide de tudo o que o canibalismo é. Ora é símbolo do outsider, ora é vício, ora é o amor absoluto de se entregar por inteiro a alguém, e ao mesmo tempo é uma coisa literal. Essa indefinição é meio faca de dois gumes pra mim, parte dela é exatamente o que me agrada, essa abertura pra ler o filme de vários ângulos, mas parte dela me deixa incomoda, com a sensação de que o filme não sabe direito o que quer dizer com a própria imagem central. Senti que Até os Ossos quer ser coisas demais ao mesmo tempo. Ele é road movie, é romance, é terror, é coming-of-age, e nem todas essas peças encaixam com folga. Tem horas em que ele parece uma sucessão de cenas belíssimas que não terminam de formar um quadro só. Cada pedaço isolado funciona, a fotografia é deslumbrante, os momentos de terror são bons, o romance convence, mas o conjunto fica disperso, sem a coesão que faria tudo isso virar uma coisa inteira. Até os Ossos é um filme que eu gostei de verdade, que me deu imagens interessantes, com atuações de Timothée Chalamet e Taylor Russell que merecem o crédito. Só não me pegou por completo, porque ele se espalha demais.

I really do love this movie more than I should. I know a lot of people find the visuals and some of the performances pretty detestable, and I understand that, but I think a lot of them are genuinely very good. The only truly awful performance is from Rebel Wilson, who manages to be intrusive in scenes dedicated to her. This is one of only two James Corden performances I defend, because I think he does a good job outside of the barge, where absolutely no one is doing their best work. It’s also fun to see the places where the visual style of the cats does work (mainly Old Deuteronomy and Gus) vs where it decidedly looks like a joke (think Macavity or Victoria). They seemingly removed a lot of the sexiness moving from the stage musical to Cats 2019, Id have to assume to appeal to as wide an audience as possible. Cats (1998) has a lot of the characters specifically play into things that are pretty widely considered hot, especially with someone like The Rum Tum Tugger being an amalgamation of Elvis and Bowie. There’s also this insane scene in the stage musical where they full body feel up Victoria for some reason. All of that has been removed and replaced with some light pawing and head nudges from some of the characters. The hottest thing in the movie is like, Taylor Swift cat doing cunty little dances or whatever.  Not to say this is either bad or good, just sort of interesting. I find this is inevitable when moving from sheer visual spectacle to like, trying to bring a coherent plot from cats. One thing I wasn’t too keen on watching these back to back was taking the songs from being sung about the cat by the rest of the Jellicles to being sung by the cat about themselves. It really goes from feeling like an introduction to these characters from a friendly face to being a railroading not dissimilar to a theme park. It also removes these ensembles that really are the heart and soul of Cats. Cats (1998) has so many moving bodies in every song and scene that the visual identity is never compromised. There’s never blank space if that makes sense. Cats 2019 eschews this in favor of taking on the styling of a 2010’s movie musical with all the various scenes. I’m just not certain it works. For as much as people whinge about the visual inconsistencies, be it size or fur or whatever I find it’s never really bothered me. The size being inconsistent is fine to me. I feel like people largely wouldn’t notice if it wasn’t pointed out to them. The biggest issue with the character design to me is their hands. They clearly don’t know how to give a Cat human hands and as such don’t even bother to try. It ends up being sort of distracting in a lot of scenes. Otherwise, which a few exceptions mentioned above, I actually found it to be unobtrusive after your brain has a second to adjust. Feels not dissimilar to the Navi from avatar to me. I love this movie dearly. Cats has always been THE peak musical to me. It’s got a little bit of everything and as such ends up feeling like this big silly romp. I love Skimbleshanks in this. I think his number in 2019 is maybe my favorite song across both variations (special mention to Growltiger’s Last Stand which I think also stands above) and I’m glad that the viewing populace tends to feel the same way. When I first started preaching about Cats 2019, nobody shared my sentiment that the film was good. Nowadays, it’s built a cult following especially amongst the online transgender crowd. It feels nice to find my people that way in much the same way Victoria does here.

A existência de arte para o consumo humano, vinda de forma americanizada e de holllywood raramente nos dará outras sequências de decisões incompreensíveis que resultem em um produto tão absurdo quanto cats. Eu aprecio filmes ruins, esse é um dos melhores dos piores. Ainda assim, por um motivo não posso dar 5 estrelas. Eu achava que única decisão imperdoável que qualquer filme pode tomar é colocar o James Corden na tela, mas há mais uma, colocar o James Corden cantando. Todo o resto consigo perdoar, mas desde a primeira vez que vi, a presença dele por alguns minutos na tela suga a aura camp que era construída e demora pra recuperar. De qualquer forma, vejam cats. É uma experiência única e é um dos filmes que eu mais queria ver pela primeira vez de novo.

December, 2019..right before the world went to hell in a kitty-basket... A few days after Cats opened (yup, that one), I headed to the Alamo Drafthouse in Downtown Los Angeles. The word was out....this is "The Room" bad. Hence...vapor trails to Alamo for me! Like so many of my fellow cinema lovers, I have a soft spot for gloriously misguided cinema. Give me The Room, Jaws 3-D, or Queen of the Damned, and I’m a happy man. Before the movie started, an Alamo employee stepped to the front of the theater. “Good news,” she announced. “Tomorrow Universal is sending us the fixed version. So tonight…you’re getting the butthole cut.” We all went nuts...and then could not stop cracking up. Like my sides hurt the next day and worth the Tylenol. All that being said...I’ve found myself feeling a little bad for director Tom Hooper. Yes, Cats is bizarre. Yes, it’s become a punchline. But this is also the filmmaker who gave us The King’s Speech and Les Misérables. One strange swing shouldn’t earn a lifetime sentence in director jail. The same goes for filmmakers like Martin Brest (BEVERLY HILLS COP, MIDNIGHT RUN) and John McTiernan (DIE HARD, THE HUNT FOR RED OCTOBER). Sometimes talented artists make masterpieces. Sometimes they make beautiful messes. Sometimes they make movies that become legendary for reasons nobody intended. And maybe that’s okay. What I remember most from that night isn’t the movie itself. It’s a packed theater in Los Angeles, filled with people from every background imaginable, sharing food, drinks, and uncontrollable laughter. For a couple of hours, nobody was arguing about politics, doom-scrolling, or yelling at each other online. We were just laughing. In this divided world, I’ll take joy wherever I can find it—even if it arrives in the form of digital cats and a legendary “butthole cut.”

Peut être que le film était trop attendu ? Peut être que le défi était tout simplement impossible à relever avec brio ? Toujours est-il que je suis sorti déçu du cinéma ce soir. Denis Villeneuve, à qui l’on doit Premier Contact, film plein d’intelligence et d’idées visuelles fortes et originales, nous amène tout un plateau de préjugés hollywoodiens fades et redondants. Tout d’abord, l’histoire : Paul Atréides est l’Élu galactique qui veut sauver les peuples opprimés. Il comprend son rôle d’Élu en ayant des visions de l’avenir. L’histoire se passe sur une planète désertique, sur laquelle évolue un Vers de sable géant… autant de déjà vus. Soit, l’histoire n’est pas de Villeneuve, puisqu’il s’agit d’une adaptation de roman. Pour autant, la mise en scène n’a rien d’original non plus : là où la planète désertique aurait pu offrir de sublimes lumières, on se retrouve la moitié du temps plongé dans une demi pénombre d’où aucune lumière ne sait émerger avec grandeur. D’ailleurs, ce désert ressemble trait pour trait à celui de Star Wars Rogue One. En allant dans ce sens, les costumes ont l’air tout droit sortis d’une penderie de chez LucasFilm; et si un ou deux vaisseaux ont des design atypiques et plutôt réussis au début du film, on se retrouve vite à cours de bonnes idées. Les antagonistes - en bon méchants qu’ils sont - évoluent dans des décors sombres, ont des voix bien trop graves pour être réalistes, et respirent très fort. Une bonne idée survient tout de même à la fin du film : le bain noirâtre du Baron, qui intrigue tant par sa couleur que par sa texture. Bien qu’anecdotique, ce détail détonne tellement dans le champ visuel qu’il nous fait prendre conscience d’un défaut majeur du film : il manque de texture. Les décors en intérieurs sont tous beaucoup trop épurés pour être réalistes, et la peau des personnages (même ceux vivant dans le désert) est tellement lisse que ça en devient ridicule. En un mot : l’univers de Dune, tel que représente par Villeneuve, n’a pas de vie. Quelle déception également de voir Hans Zimmer au générique ! C’est donc lui qui nous a pondu des basses vrombissantes vues et revues pendant les scènes d’action, à la seule originalité d’une cornemuse trop discrète ? Ajoutez à cela un jeu pas toujours juste de Timothée Chalamet, et vous avez de quoi décevoir toute la population d’un salon de SF en un seul film… Pour autant, je ne me suis pas ennuyé durant les 2h30 (tout de même…) que dure ce périple galactique. Sans avoir été pris spécialement en haleine, j’ai été facilement et efficacement immergé dans l’univers Dune, dont on m’avait pourtant dit qu’il était complexe. En somme, c’est un bon divertissement hollywoodiens, comme tout un chacun a déjà du en voir une vingtaine. Quelques bonnes idées disparates, des plans assez jolis, un sound design très bien ficelé, et le tour est joué. Mais je pense qu’il faut être difficile avec ce film. Très attendu, il n’a fait qu’être un divertissement de plus qui permettra, dans 5 ans, de faire passer un dimanche pluvieux. C’est sans doute de là que provient la plus grande déception : on ne veut pas voir l’univers de Dune traité de la même manière aseptisée et stéréotypée que Star Wars, les Gardiens de la Galaxy, et toutes la ribambelle de licences qui s’en suit. Pour conclure, je ne sais pas si Denis Villeneuve a échoué à adapter Dune au cinéma. Il n’empêche qu’il a fait un film quelconque là où Franck Herbert, avec son roman, avait su modifier en profondeur la face de la SF.

I really wanted to love Dune, but I didn't. Throughout the entire runtime I was waiting for one scene to hook me, to engage me in what's happening and allow me to immerse myself in the experience. But it never happened. For full transparency's sake, I read the book earlier this year and saw the Lynch film shortly after, so I went in knowing full well what the plot was and how another film adaptation handled the material. And while Lynch's Dune is riddled with problems in its pacing and plotting, there are things it suceeds in over Villeneuves latest endeavor. But we'll get there when we get there. The biggest problem in this newest adaptation of Herbert's seminal work is Villeneuves incessent gigantomania. When he said this film needs to be seen on a big screen, he was right, but I don't think any screen in the world will be able to make the size of this film look manageable. Every starship in this film is the biggest it can possibly be, Arrakeen, the capital of Arrakis, is an amalgamation of absolutely massive concrete buildings built almost on top of each other and the armies standing in formation seem endlessly big. Because everything is the enourmous size it is, none of it ever feels believable. When the courtyard of your palace is a massive concrete plain that stretches as far as the eye can see, but is entirely devoid of any markings, wells, walkways or any signs of life, they just look like computer-generated textures. When the ships are all huge grey blocks with no discernible characteristics or features, they just become big blocks that look artificially placed in an empty-looking environment. Dune is big because it is filled with literally huge structures and buildings and ships, but they never feel organic. Which is the next big issue. None of the sets the characters inhabit feel lived-in, or natural, or like they convey an actual world. Why Villeneuve opted for every building to be a grey slab with grey walls and nothing on them, I cannot for the life of me understand. None of its feels alive, vibrant, or remotely natural. It's all just copy-pasted textures that have nothing to them. Contrast this with Lynchs version and the lush round and gold features on the palace exterior and interiors, the beautiful ornaments and art-deco-looking elements. They have character to them, and they give a sense of personality to the area the characters are inhabiting. Villeneuves environments feel dead by comparison. Speaking of dead: To call the characters lifeless would be an overstatement, however, they do all have an air of imposed seriousness on drabness to them, that weighs down on the general atmosphere a lot. Never is there a sense of levity, of a character being content, and actually tender moments between characters are very sparse. The only actor that is allowed to have the slightest charisma is Jason Momoa, but even then he does not get the opportunity to let it shine much. Timothée is good at what he does, though he always looks like he's constipated. The rest of the cast has to abide by the general tone of the film, which is unflinchingly serious, to a fault. Again, Lynch was able to incorporate genuinely touvhing moments while condensing more story into less runtime, so why couldn't Villeneuve? All of these elements, the artifical scale, the lifeless set design, the one-note characters, it all leads to a very distant and cold experience. Never did I ever emotionally engage in anything onscreen, the film started and then it ended and I was left pretty unphased by everything. It's such a shame, because the book as well as Lynchs film both have spectacle and scale as well as emotion and very human moments. But Villeneuves Dune could have also taken place on an ice planet and it would have fit the tone of the film almost better. The main difference between the two films is that the newer really wants to take it's time and properly tell the story of Frank Herberts Dune. While Lynchs film tries to tell the entire story in two hours, essentially crippling it and leaving an overstuffed mess, the new Dune is intent on staying true to the details of what Herberts Dune is about. Except for the fact that there is still a lot missing. Not just details and single exchangeable scenes, but actual plot threads that fans liked (I know I'm not the only one upset over the plot line about the investigation into who the traitor is missing). So this new Dune is longer than the old one, and only tells half the story, but because the plot is decelerated so much the 150 mins feel like 240. The first hour of this film drags for very long, since exposition in reading is easier to digest than exposition in film, especially when in film it is just delivered through dialogue. At the same time, so much happens in this first movie already, that thinking about having to go see another one like this feels like a chore. It still feels overstuffed. Overall, this is definitely the better adaptation of the book Dune, though it is not finished yet. The second part is going to be far more interesting than the first, so I'm keeping my hopes up. In conclusion, while conceptually more mature and structured better than previous iterations, Villeneuves first Dune film can't help but bury its great base material under heaps of comically oversized imagery (Hans Zimmers oppressive and incredibly loud score only makes this film heavier and clunkier), an atmosphere that is way to stern and self-important for its own good and an approach to its base material that is taking its time, which has two sides, as it allows for more detail and clearer themes, but at the same time still seems like its barely managing to hit all the story beats before credits roll. This Dune needed more refining in a lot of places, and overall, its not bad. It's just not as good as everyone wanted it to be. I don't want to seem like I hated this film, so here are a list of things I liked: The cinematography largely supported the narrative quite well (though also succumbing to the aforementioned gigantomania) and generally looked pretty good. The CGI is entirely seemless (except for the artifical building exteriors and interiors). Everyone in the cast is sexy as fuck. The story of Dune is finally getting a worthy adaptation, though it is a flawed one. Might see this Dune again soon, might change my mind.

I remember back in the days, after the first few Game of Thrones seasons came out, I thought that this show was quite bloated, filled with unnecessary filler and a story that would probably work better as a movie series à la The Lord of the Rings . Eventually tho, I started to realize that there might be more to it and when I finally read the books between seasons 6 and 7, my previous assumption did a complete 180. The show wasn’t bloated, it was rather a condensed version of an even more detailed book series, books that explained a lot of the things I didn’t get in the show, because there they were only mentioned briefly or left out entirely. I retroactively developed a completely new appreciation for the show .. until season 7 came around, but I digress. The point is, when Dune was announced, I immediately wondered, given my previous experience, whether it would be useful to read the books first this time, but I still didn’t end up doing it. The main arguments being: a) It’s written and directed by one of the most accomplished filmmakers of our time. He will make it work. b) A movie is supposed/designed to work on its own anyway. c) I simply didn’t want to spoil myself knowing the story beforehand, possibly robbing myself of some amazing cinema experience and d) I didn’t assume Dune could be anywhere as complex as Game of Thrones . Well, after having seen the film, I totally wished I had read the books, at least the first one. The movie has to establish a whole new sci-fi world with all its rules and features and Villeneuve does in fact invest quite some time to setup persons, cultures, beliefs, ideologies, items and a whole lot of other things that seem to carry a lot of weight for the characters, yet I still felt like I’m missing something to fully grasp why this world is how it is and why the people are how they are. As a result, I could never fully connect to the movie and therefore I didn’t really care all too much about anything or anyone. It was almost ironic that when I finally started to become invested into the story .. it was over. If Dune: Part 2 will get made, it might retroactively clarify a thing or two that didn’t reveal themselves to me in this movie alone, but the solution to all my problems might simply be to just read the books. I’m quite certain this movie will grow on me either way. For now tho, I’m just not really feeling it.

他，回來了！Denis Villeneuve用熟悉的「慢條斯理」，來處理這份難以搞定的佳餚，手法幹練卻不失細膩之處，以一個沒看過小說的視角帶入，確實有難以消化的難處，但本片不至於像諾蘭那樣具有「干擾性」，而是可以輕易地貼近角色來了解架構的「引導」，然而，本片的弱點，也正是因受到原著及商業類型的束縛，導致成品流露出虛假與流於表面，最終成為另一部虎頭蛇尾的鉅作。題外話，如果你真要體驗到本片的壯觀，拜託去IMAX或ATMOS廳體驗，那種震撼與感動交織而成的「屏息」，難以形容。 《沙丘》算是維勒納夫中段班的作品，或許是因為有改編難度的壓力，整體看上來還是綁手綁腳的，不像《異星入境》與《銀翼殺手2049》那樣「放得開」，但他的導戲功力已達頂峰，大場面的調度讓人驚嘆連連，龐大的世界觀他也能處理得毫無匠氣、游刃有餘，從沙漠瀰漫的危險感，到室內空間的窒息感，都能捕捉到其深刻之處。劇情基本遊走在殖民與天選之子上，然而，劇本的空泛台詞與過度簡化，多少還是影響了兩個主題的力度，裡頭的傳承與戰勝恐懼的意象，則因為情節的不穩定，與兒戲般的轉折，讓這象徵意義變得薄弱，只剩「說出來」的表面意義。 說實話，如果沒了這群演員的表現，本片的角色塑造絕對會崩塌，裡頭我最愛Rebecca Ferguson的演出，她將眼淚化為角色的痛苦展現，母性的光輝清晰可見，隱忍與噴發的情緒拿捏得宜。漢斯季默，宛如為電影戴上一層淒美的面紗、穿上悲壯的戰衣，人聲總是能帶出電影最唯美的一面，可惜配樂的編排使整體情緒過滿，導致配樂干擾了劇情進行與情緒延展，人聲則因為頻繁的出現，給人煩躁的印象。聲音設計著實令人難忘，爆炸與打鬥的聲音富有層次感，衝擊力更是做得恰到好處，可惜，高亢配樂的過度氾濫，讓音效展現不了真正的實力。 《沙丘》在我看來，就是部相當適合大銀幕的作品，場面調度無懈可擊、音效特效傑出無比，創造出一場宛如《星際大戰》的視聽享受，可惜這場史詩，敗在劇情的單薄，支撐不了片長與大場面的輸出，《魔戒》之所以能支撐得了三個小時的打磨，就是因為劇本的可塑性及魅力，才能讓情緒持續延展下去，但《沙丘》犯了一個錯誤，就是用過多的篇幅來「介紹」，及彆扭的角色塑造，使電影少了收放自如的情緒，及大小場面切換的流利，更少了角色之間激盪的火花。 但這個缺點，仍無法改變本片是商業巨作的事實，Denis Villeneuve用極為藝術與富有情調的氛圍，讓影片既有沙漠的粗曠，也有人性的細緻，這，正是維勒納夫電影之所以吸引人的所在。然而，這只是《沙丘》的第一篇章而已，接下來，還有許多寶藏等著維勒納夫來挖掘，希望這告一段落的時間，能讓Villeneuve適應商業片的呈現。最後，一顆星給場景設計及特效的絕美，一顆星給眾星雲集的卡司，一顆星給Denis Villeneuve純熟的導戲功力。

Excellent cinematography and direction…however, this has to be one of the slowest and dullest movies I’ve ever watched for a franchise of this size. It’s easy to see why this story was long considered unadaptable for the big screen. The film has the difficult task of introducing multiple families, political factions, key locations, religious themes, and complex world-building, all of which are challenging to translate from the novel to film. Denis deserves credit for making such a dense and difficult story coherent, but I don’t think the pacing works. I understand that much of the film is dedicated to laying the groundwork for the sequels, but watching it often felt more like homework than an engaging introduction to this world. I admire the craftsmanship far more than I enjoyed the experience. 3/5

VENICE 78: There's a scene in Dune's first act where we are introduced to yet another faction of people and for a single moment I was taken out of the film, tearing myself away from the bombastic, ear-drumming score and larger-than-life visuals to wonder, so then who the hell are these people? The moment passed as swiftly as it came, but it's emblematic of a movie that almost buckles under the weight of its own worldbuilding as well as setup for things to come. Almost, I say, because it doesn't succumb completely, instead coming out on top to deliver an experience that thrills as well as awes, even in spite of its stumbling blocks. In that, it's not quite Blade Runner 2049, Denis Villeneuve's masterwork, but it's also far grander than that film, in scope as well as ambition. With Dune, there is a lot of ground to cover. The book has often been said to be "unfilmable", and it's easy to see why: its world is vast, its factions numerous, and its story incredibly dense. Because of this, the movie - billed as "Part One" on its opening title screen - only covers the first half of the book, opting to leave the latter half to a promised sequel. That's a gamble, because Dune spends so much time setting up its world and conflicts that if this doesn't get a follow-up, it would be infinitely frustrating: by the time the credits roll, the story's far from over. In many ways it feels like we're just getting started. This is where Dune will almost certainly divide people. Some may feel it's too much setup and not enough payoff; especially in the first half, viewers may experience the same thing I did in the aforementioned scene, to momentarily be taken out of it as they try to process this new influx of information. There's also the chance that people will feel disappointed by the end of the film, because it hinges a lot of itself on the promise of more to come: Zendaya, for instance, doesn't get all that much to do here, and the climax might be smaller-scale than some are hoping (though it really works on a narrative level). That's not to say the worldbuilding and setup are bad or unnecessary, in fact quite the opposite: there's just a lot of it. However, where Dune stumbles through these narrative shallows, if you allow it to find its footing as the sweeping political saga that it is - "Game of Thrones in space" as it's often called, though that comparison only applies insofar as it's about noble houses vying for control in a game of courtly intrigue, backstabbing, and all-out war - it absolutely wows, not just on a story level, but also visually as well as auditory. Rolling dunes, spaceships falling out of orbit, spice flowing through the air and sandworms filling the screen... its world of Arrakis and the noble houses of Atreides and Harkonnen are beautifully put to screen and sound, with a grandness to them that one so rarely finds in cinema anymore. The score by Hans Zimmer is terrific and cinematographer Greig Fraser has a beautiful eye on where to put the camera. The cast, too, gives it a Shakespearean feel: among others Oscar Isaac, Rebecca Ferguson, Stellan Skarsgård (in terrific make-up), and especially Timothée Chalamet and Zendaya (when she's in it) grace the screen beautifully. With this film it's clear that Villeneuve isn't afraid to give everything from its actors to its towering spacecrafts, to the grains of sand on Arrakis the attention they deserve. Looking back on the film now, a few days after I've seen it, I am strongly reminded of those history classes when the teacher starts telling a story, and at first you're not sure where it's going and there's a lot of information being thrown at you, but by the time the bell rings you're so invested that you don't want to leave, and you cannot wait for the next class - or, in this case, movie. I just hope Villeneuve gets to make it.

Sé que la calificación puede generar preguntas pero afortunadamente tengo bastante que decir de la que me parece una de las películas más sobrevaloradas de la historia. Vi la primer película en su momento y me pareció interesante pero nada espectacular, destacaba en el elenco y en los visuales pero nada que me llevaría a repetirla. Esa película planteó la adaptación un universo el cual pude ver que tiene como eje central la política, el problema de hacer historias sobre política es que se debe tratar con extrema atención el diálogo y el conflicto en cuestión, pues si ninguno de los dos puntos es interesante, no genera un gancho para ver horas de discusiones con el motivo de llevar un conflicto a una resolución contundente. En su momento no tomé tan en cuenta eso al ser solo la primera parte de Dune, pero cuando ves la segunda parte de esa historia sabiendo que es ya la mitad de una trilogía y el interés se siente vacío, ya es preocupante. Cuando Dune parte 2 salió vi gente alabándola como una de las mejores sino que la mejor experiencia cinematográfica de los últimos años, no podría estar más en desacuerdo y sostengo mi punto en base a su carencia de identidad. Es bien sabido que Star Wars plagió en muchos aspectos (aunque sean mínimos) a los libros de Dune, sin embargo, el reconocimiento a Star Wars viene de cómo a pesar de ello se logró crear un universo con identidad, el cual no viene de una obra previa sino que directamente nació en el cine, siendo que ahora su mundo es identificable al igual que sus personajes e historias, ya es un icono de la cultura pop. Ahora parece que los papeles se han invertido y Dune que en teoría es “la obra original” pareciera que quiere replicar a Star Wars, lo cual tiene sentido, la adaptación original de Dune fue un total fracaso. Dune parte 2 no parece que haga un trabajo por sacar a relucir su concepto y su mundo, más bien parece que quiere replicar lo que su supuesta copia “la venganza de los Sith” hizo años atrás para ser el éxito que fue y es lamentable pensar como la franquicia que en teoría es la copia me parece que tiene mucha más identidad que la obra original. No me quedo con los ambientes ni escenarios de la película, no me quedo con los nombres de los personajes, el conflicto no tiene lo suyo, solo parece que quieren convertir a Paul Atreides en otro Anakin Skywalker en vez de darle valor por ser su propio personaje. Y no, no es mala película, la disfrute, me emocione, estuve atento a ella y es una mejora absoluta de la 1 en todo aspecto, principalmente en el ritmo. Pero me parece desmedido el escándalo que en su momento se hizo al nombrar Dune Parte 2 como una de las mejores películas de la historia cuando me parece una buena película más del montón que destaca únicamente por su alto presupuesto. Personalmente tampoco siento que el elenco haya dado su mejor trabajo, sentí que igual hubo un hype desmedido por varios personajes y actores que tampoco son la gran cosa. Mi conclusión es que venimos de tantas películas malas que una película decente pareció una obra maestra a los ojos de todos, porque de lo contrario no me explico el hype.

I remember this age when everything felt so gargantuan and every small thing weighed so heavy. Its such a terrible time in life where everyone around you seems to be above you in a way and you’re so self conscious of every movement and every word. Im 21 now and I still sometimes see that really really weird awkward girl that couldn’t seem to find friends in the mirror. This movie brought me back to some of the worst moments in my life and im really grateful for it. I have the letterboxd of this boy I dated in 8th grade. I was going through a lot mentally at that time and I had a lot of anxiety and it was my first depression hole I really entered in. I looked at all these girls around that would make fun of me because I was so nervous holding this boys hand. I had a crush on him all year but rejected him twice because of my situation at home until we eventually started dating. I cut out so much of that time in my life from my brain but I still remember some really important moments. I read his review on this movie that was made a long time ago and it made me laugh out loud reading about myself. Its such a sensitive and tender time in life but he was a great memory from then. I thought he was the coolest guy in the world and he made these awesome drawings. Im studying engineering although I wanted to make movies, I still do. But he’s working his way into the film industry and to this day I cant wait to see what he does. I look back at that girl I was with a lot of embarrassment but a lot of love too. Its really interesting to talk to people i knew in middle school that i used to put on this pedestal because even as an adult its shocking to hear how unsure and weird they felt then too just like I did.

Oh, i expected to like this way more than i did. Bo Burnham huh? Honestly, i can't really say that i'm a massive fan of his in the way that yeah. I have heard about his songs here or there and did also enjoy them but i'm not really that knowledged in his general work and all. He is deffinetly talented as a musical artist but what about film? Let's see if he put out a good film or not! As usual, starting off with the positives: I really like how Kayla is characterized. The movie really does do a good job letting the viewer understand her psychological state and the type of stuff she is going through. The movie also has clever twists for itself, like when Kayla opens her "Time capsule" at the start of the movie we see her looking at what is seemingly a SpongeBob toy, and the viewer is led to thinking that the toy symbolizes childishness, but later down the movie we actually learn that actually no. It wasn't just a toy but rather an USB, in which she has a video on it that talks about generic expectations one has from life and honestly? It just feels very clever. Further more, the movie has a very respectful way of handling subject manners who are on the darker side of things. Like teenagers diving into flirting/other sexual manners and even SA. lastly, the cinematography is really effective in many ways. Let's be a negative nancy now: The videos Kayla films playing meanwhile she is going through things and those videos just EXACTLY about what she is going through is very very redundant. It is literally the exact opposite of, "Show not tell" it just feels so clunky. Further more, i think the movie's pacing during like the 30th munite to 40th munite period could've been a bit faster. I don't really mind a good slow pace but there are points where a slow pace works, and when it doesn't. The movie also has alot of cliches it has, and don't get me wrong: A certain thing being generic/cliche doesn't exactly mean it's mediocre. However, playing cliches straight forward is no good. I always preffered cliches being played with a clever twist, and for movie like this that has proven it to have some cool tricks up it's slevee it surely feels very dissapointing that it just feels so stupid and dumb. The last problem i have with this movie is kinda on the lighter side of things but i think the character dialogue feels kinda clunky at the first 30 munites or so. Overall, not a bad watch. It is very well made on some aspects but it has alot of problems too, not everyone has to be a polymath and that is fine. Bo Burnham even if i haven't lissened most songs of his is a really good musical artist and song writer from what i've seen. He should probably stick to it. 6/10

First off, I loved that Bo Burnham cast actual eighth graders. It made everything feel so much more believable. Honestly this was a hard for me to get through purely because of how accurate it was in portraying social anxiety and those painfully embarrassing moments in middle school. It made me think about a lot of not great memories I have. Even as a 27 year old, there were scenes with Kayla that I could still relate to. Elsie Fisher, given how young she was at the time, gave a great authentic performance. Captured all of the awkward, cringey moments in a way that felt incredibly real. The film also addressed the nuances of social media really well. Another thing of note was the awkward but genuinely loving relationship between Kayla and her dad, added a lot to the movie. An excellent coming of age movie that I probably will never watch again!

Penso sia uno dei film più realistici che io abbia mai visto. Di solito al cinema quando cercano di rappresentare un certo tipo di ragazza, lo fanno sempre attraverso il classico bullismo, quando in realtà in molti casi il vero problema è semplicemente il sentirsi invisibili. Mi sono rivista tantissimo in lei in molti momenti della mia vita. La difficoltà a farsi nuovi amici, ad entrare nei discorsi, il sentirsi sempre la persona fuori posto che non c’entra niente. È una cosa che mi è successa alle medie, al liceo e persino all'università, anche se fortunatamente non ai livelli di Kayla. Guardare alcune scene di questo film mi ha fatto venire dei flashback del Vietnam e sono felicissima che quel periodo sia ormai passato. Queste storie di solito si soffermano sempre e solo sul dramma o sulla tragedia, mentre molto spesso la verità dei fatti è esattamente quella raccontata qui. Mi è piaciuto davvero tanto come tutto questo non distrugga mai del tutto la protagonista, ma anzi lei cerchi sempre di uscire dalla propria comfort zone mantenendo un'attitudine positiva.

Went in with zero expectations. Didn't need logic, didn't need deep character work — just wanted something genuinely fun and entertaining. And honestly, I just ended up bored. The whole “genre-blending” thing isn't as wild as people say. Sure, it jumps between worlds and tosses in sci-fi, action, and some emotional moments, but none of it ever actually blends into something fresh or mind-blowing. It's just a movie that changes costumes without ever becoming genuinely entertaining. The multiverse stuff, which is supposed to be the big selling point, got repetitive fast. They create a couple of cool, weird worlds early on, but then keep revisiting the same handful over and over. “Everything Everywhere All at Once” quickly shrinks into “a few things, a few places”. That killed the sense of endless possibility and just made it feel small and monotonous. Also, people praise the relentless pace, but I honestly didn't feel it. The editing is busy, not fast — there's a difference. Especially the last hour dragged like crazy. So many slow-motion moments that didn't earn their weight, stretching out scenes that already felt emotionally repetitive. And the humor? The problem isn't that the jokes are random or dumb — it's that the movie never commits to real chaos. It gives you a couple of weird ideas, then just keeps circling back to them until they're completely worn out. A truly random, limitless multiverse should be throwing something new at you constantly, but instead the jokes become predictable, cliché, and as limited as the worlds themselves. That's really the core issue here: the movie runs out of ideas and then just stretches everything thin, repeating itself because it doesn't know what else to do. If you're going to be this narratively limited, you'd better have deep characters, sharp logic, or some real emotional weight to fall back on — and it has none of that. The emotional beats are so forced, practically holding up cue cards that say “care now” and “cry here”. Given how wild and limitless the premise is, the ending lands as preachy, cliché, and a total drag — exactly the kind of safe landing a film like this should have avoided. Honestly, it's not that different from plenty of other weak films that start with a decent premise and then fumble it. The only difference is this one got a sky-high rating and a pile of Oscars.

I won’t deny that the direction is ambitious and visually inventive, and the performances are solid, especially from the lead cast. However, none of that was enough to make it a great experience for me. My biggest issue was the core concept itself. It felt surprisingly simplistic, reminding me of ideas that had already been explored in older animated works, only with modern additions that I personally didn’t enjoy. I also found some of the themes and relationships in the film unnecessary and distracting rather than meaningful. In the end, this is only my personal opinion, but out of respect for my love of cinema and the films that truly leave a lasting impact, I have to say that this one simply didn’t work for me. Despite all the praise it received, I consider it a poor film.

Wild and warm and chock-full of just about everything you’d expect from cinema that isn’t bound to IP or convention of any sort. Swiss Army Man is one of my very favorite films, so it was a real joy to see the Daniels go sicko mode once again, yet I couldn’t help but feel that this didn’t quite come together the way it intends. There is a lot - and I mean A LOT - going on here: Hot dog fingers, rocks, a butt-plug brawl, the ultimate everything bagel, a frumpy Jamie Lee Curtis, chewing glue, and so much more, all branching from a multiverse guided by every possible scientific outcome and human decision ever dreamed of. Despite the film’s wholly original extravagance, the sheer scope of its visual and thematic ambitions prove to be a bit exhausting. The climax in particular becomes increasingly winded as the film sounds off on all its grand declarations about the messy contradictions life has in store for us. A flawed, but no less admirable marriage of the sacred and the profane as only the Daniels could conceive.

I’m glad I watched this film. It’s been on my watchlist for a very long time. It seems like it’s a bit of a love-it-or-hate-it kind of film, and I wasn’t expecting to land in the middle on it. But that’s what happened. I wasn’t disappointed, but I definitely wasn’t blown away. Okay, that’s a lie — I was blown away for parts of it, but I was checked out for other parts. This movie is beautifully shot, competently written, and there is very obvious artistic intent and passion that comes across in every scene. Even if I hated every second of it, which I didn’t, I would have to admire the sheer ambition and creativity that’s on display here. But ultimately the takeaway seems to be “everything is absurd, but we can still find truth in the chaos, form connections, and even be inspired by others despite life’s meaninglessness,” and to me, that’s just not a unique enough sentiment to warrant such a unique film. It was also just a bit heavy-handed in the way it was conveyed. There definitely wasn’t any room for interpretation. Everything Everywhere All At Once was clearly a passion project for everyone involved. I’m sure in the end they made the film they set out to make, and are very happy with the finished product. Obviously this film has an audience, and I wish I could say I’m a big fan, because good golly was this movie an experience, but sadly it left me feeling underwhelmed when the credits rolled. It ultimately amounted to spectacle — packaged as avant-garde but somehow failing to tap into something universal, which is ironic given the title. Then, I suppose this film is for everything, everywhere, but not necessarily every one .
