Friday the 13th and its main antagonist Jason Voorhees has been part of the American pop culture zeitgeist since I was a child. I knew about Jason and his murder sprees on Crystal Lake before I was allowed to watch, or wanted to watch, any of the movies. Jason hit a bit closer to home than other movie monsters like Freddy Kruger or Michael Myers because I grew up in rural Maine surrounded by forests and spent a lot of time on a lake at my Grandparent’s camp. The lake at night could be scary with its isolation, the occasional unrecognizable animal noises and limited visibility. If someone were to scream in the distance it’d be hard to pinpoint where it would be coming from because sound echoes off the water. On top of that, running at night in the woods is dangerous because of uneven ground and tripping hazards. It was easy for me to place myself in a “Friday the 13th” scenario. The lake also had its own kind-of-sort-of legend of a “crazy guy” who used to have a shack on one of the islands, the remains of the shack still visible. I don’t want say this is gospel truth as I’m going off of a vague memory and I don’t know what’s true and what’s exaggeration, but I remember thinking as a ten year old that if I did happen across an adult with ill intent out on the lake there isn’t much I could do except run and hide and I wasn’t that fast. My imagination built up the Friday the 13th movies so much there was no way they’d live up what I thought they were. When I finally entered the right of passage to watch horror movies at too young of an age…I was kind of relieved I didn’t find them that scary. Don’t get me wrong, I thought they were fun, but not the terror inducing experience I was expecting. My friends and myself would be cracking jokes the entire time. When we got to the original “Friday the 13th” (we watched them out of order) there was a running gag of going “Where’s Jason?” and died laughing when the killer turned out to be his mom (though the last scare was pretty good, highly influenced by Brian DE Palma's  Carrie’s ending I imagine). When it was announced that they were remaking Friday the 13th in 2008 I thought there was a chance they could make the Friday the 13th movie I wanted, but didn’t hold out much hope. While there are some absolute gems from the era, I consider the 00’s to be the weakest period for horror movies. They are typically sanitized by the studios for mass audiences appeal and can be cynically seen as resume padding for upcoming actors. I didn’t bother seeing it in theaters, but eventually caught it on VOD….and…I thought it sucked. Maybe I would have felt different if I was a teenager watching it with friends, but as an adult watching it by myself I was highly disappointed even with low expectations. Fifteen years later I happened to get a trial subscription for Cinemax because my daughter wanted to watch Kevin Smith’s “Tusk”  last Saturday night. Since I have access to a slew of movies for seven days I ended up watching “Poltergeist 2: The Other Side” and this movie yesterday. The reason being I knew I didn’t like it, but barely remembered it. The only elements I remembered was something about Jason growing pot and sex scene that was incredibly graphic, even by R-Rated horror standards. “Friday the 13th” is a paint-by-numbers slasher where a group of young and horny dummies get picked off one-by-one by a killer that just happens to be the champion of killing young and horny dummies. And my first complaint is about these characters we are stuck with. I understand there is a certain devilish glee in watching people with unpleasant personalities get murdered with creative kills, but I find myself unable to get fully invested in a movie if there is no one I care about. In this version of Friday the 13th the people are in two camps and neither of them are good. They are the people you’re not supposed to like being extreme jerks and the people you are supposed to care about are not jerks, but instead are f’n boring. The cast seems to be in their mid-twenties and there is no talk of them being either in high school or college, but still everyone is so immature I have a hard time believing these are supposed to be adults. Hell, even by High School and College standards they are vapid and shallow.. Take for example that there is a scene where Lawrence (Arlen Escarpeta) is at a party, but finds himself alone in the living room. He finds a clothing catalog, looks at a photo of an attractive model and starts the very beginning stages of…jerk’in it. In the living room. In the living room where people are still coming and going. And the model wasn’t even in underwear or lingerie. It’s just a lady in a nice sweater. He doesn’t end up cranking the yank because people come running into the living room to warn the others of the murders..but who thought this was a good idea?! Did they think the audience would be in the grips of suspense? And please keep in mind there is at no point prior where it’s established that Lawrence is like that. The whole sequence is just awkward and weird. The same can be extended for the aforementioned sex scene, which is worse than I remember and it’s not the sex itself. The intercourse happens between Bree (Julie Guill) and Trent (Travis Van Winkle) while Travs’s girlfriend Jenna (Danielle Panabaker) is out helping Clay (Jared Padalecki) find his missing sister Whitney (Amanda Rightetti). While we are guided by the movie to absolutely hate Trent it’s Bree who initiates the cheating. Nothing prior sets this up, as Bree was just a background character.It’s confusing why Bree would not only have sex with someone’s boyfriend at a party attended by the girlfriend,but record it on a camcorder. It’s also weird at no point did Trent object to having his infidelity recorded. It’s even weirder that this camcorder seems to come out of nowhere. It’d make more sense if Bree always had it on her, but she didn’t. And when Jenna and Clay do return to the cabin Trent and Bree’s betrayal is glossed over quickly and never addressed making me wonder what the point of it was. If there HAD to be a sex scene with Bree there were two other guys they could have used. Or at least imply beforehand that Bree and Trent were screwing behind Jenna’s back. While I have no evidence I can’t help but think that the group had done ecstasy prior, explaining everyone’s odd and hyper-sexualized behavior, but any reference to the drug was cut by the studio, but I may be giving the writers and director too much credit. I looked around and couldn’t find anything to back this theory up, so maybe the point is that everyone is an extremely stupid sexual deviant. And there is also a problem with the casting that I don’t think I’ve ever encountered with any other movie, most of the characters look the same. And I don’t mean everyone is just Hollywood beautiful/ possible Abercrombie & Fitch models, I was getting characters confused. Jenna and Whitney look exactly the same, so when Jason kills one of them I thought it was the other. Bree and Chelsea (Willa Ford) are interchangeable. Trent and Clay look like they’re related and early kill Wade (Jonathan Sadowski) looks like both of them. The only reason Wade stuck out is because he had on a stupid “F***K Christmas” shirt on (No explanation on why Wade hates Christmas is given). Even if the actors were good the script sucks with some of the clunkiest dialogue ever committed to the silver screen. Having recently gone through the rigamarole of script coverage and the demands for perfection getting your script made requires this script by Mark Swift and Damion Shannon makes me shake my fist at the sky at the unfairness of it all. The direction of Marcus Nispel is lazy and bad and he should be ashamed of himself. I tend not to be this harsh towards directors as movies are really hard to make, but Nispel just comes off as uninspired and bored. Granted, the past Friday the 13th movies are not exactly peak cinema, but the grit of their film stock and other signs of their low budgets makes the flaws palatable, if not fully forgivable. Even when they’re bad, they’re still fun. But this remake has a studio gloss that raises the expectations, its higher budget ending up being a weakness. It’s not a bunch of young filmmakers scraping together what they can to make a horror flick, using sex and violence as marketing gimmicks in hopes of getting a return. It’s a studio collaboration knowing no matter what they’ll make bank ( This movie made 93 million off of it’s 19 million budget) So when the acting is bad and the dialogue is bad and the characters suck and  the scares don’t  work, it really stands out. There is even one scene when two characters are running in the forest where you can tell it’s a soundstage. Despite my clear disappointment with the film there are two little things I can give the movie props for. The interpretation of Jason as a survivalist hiding in the woods is interesting and there is one scene with a character getting struck with a boat but not dying that was tense. It’s been over a decade since we’ve had an incarnation of Jason Vorhees on the silver screen. In 2025 we are going to be getting a television series called “Crystal Lake” from Television Producer Bryan Fuller (Hannibal, American Gods) which I have high hopes for given Fuller’s track record of quality content, but also reservations given Fuller’s track record of projects going sideways. We shall wait and see. If there is one thing that is clear, the mythos of Jason Vorhees and Crystal Lake is destined to endure even with all setbacks, failures, lackluster attempts and hollow studio cash grabs. As long as we know the fear of wandering too far from the campfire to engage in hedonistic acts, he’ll be there waiting. In conclusion….ch-ch-ch ah-ah-ah.

Honestly a pretty good adaptation of Friday the 13th. It takes inspiration mainly from the first three films in the series and translates it into a more modern, easily digestible version of the original movies. Also, the teenagers are pretty good, even if a bit one-dimensional, which is arguably appropriate. Aesthetically not the exact same, but it still looks good and has a distinct identity of its own. The teens are fairly decent this time around. They aren't great characters or anything, still lack depth, but they are at least fun to watch for the most part. It certainly helps that Jared Padalecki is in this movie, as he is the most interesting character besides Jason himself. He is searching for his sister, who plays the role of Ginny from Part 2, confusing Jason as his dead mother. Because of this, he kidnaps her and keeps her in tunnels beneath the camp, a new addition to the remake. Speaking of, Jason is portrayed quite well. This time, he is HAULING through the whole movie. I enjoy when Jason walks casually towards his victims, but seeing him sprint full speed is pretty scary too. He starts with the baghead from Part 2 and eventually gets the hockey mask from Part 3, found in a random barn. He also has some pretty brutal and efficient kills. I do wish the climax ended with him fully going into the woodchipper, or at least had an axe in his head to create that iconic top-right chip on the mask. Overall, not bad! It's a different story and a different kind of Jason. Definitely not a replacement, but a good interpretation. With this viewing, my Friday the 13th marathon is complete, aside from Freddy vs. Jason, which I plan to watch when I marathon the Nightmare movies. So, that will be coming soon!

I don’t care what anyone says, this movie fucking rips. It’s the best Friday the 13th movie of all time (not saying much but whatever). The direction is unique and tense, you root for the good guys to get out alive and root for the assholes to get sliced up, it’s a damn near perfect script. If they cut down the sex scenes just a little, this movie would’ve been better in the eyes of most people, but it’s also clearly very satirical in its excess. This is also the best portrayal of Jason in any of the movies. He’s not a zombie, he’s not a demon, and he’s not some random copycat killer. He’s a severely deranged person who witnessed traumatic events and has raised himself in the woods for 20 years, becoming an expert with the bow and arrow, axe throwing and the ol reliable machete. He’s basically RAMBO but with no sense of right or wrong. He’s an absolute menace and it is absolutely terrifying.

Am Ende des Tages, für uns, die die Reihe jedoch kennen, liefert der Film jedoch auch nur das, was wir schon kennen, nur in besserer Qualität, was ja nicht unbedingt schlimm ist. Was ich etwas komisch finde, aber das haben die anderen Filme auch, ist, das man Jason wie einen Hund rufen kann. Ich meine klar, er ist ja im Grunde ein Kind, aber manchmal ist das schon etwas albern. Looking at the Rotten Tomatoes score and other reviews for this Friday The 13th remake, it seems like most people pretty much hated it. But I actually really enjoyed this movie and had a fun time with it. I like how this remake wasn't just a complete copy and paste story of the original movie. They swiftly establish the lore and cover Pamela Voorhees' story in the opening credits which I really appreciate because whilst Pamela is the OG killer, with this franchise, everybody wants to see Jason . Also, the birth of the iconic hockey mask is shown nicely here. One of the most memorable things about this remake is that it doesn't waste any time getting to the action and kills and it sustains this energy throughout the movie. The opening sequence is one of the best I've ever seen in a horror movie. Just that sequence alone would make for a great Friday The 13th short film. It's absolutely brutal and incredibly effective. The rest of the movie continues like this. The kills are so brutal and gloriously nasty, especially that opening sleeping bag kill. Derek Mears as Jason Voorhees is probably my favourite portrayal of Jason in the franchise. He's brutally terrifying, aggressive and monster-like throughout the movie. I also like how this Jason is smart and adaptable. His whole underground tunnel system is pretty clever and it explains how he's able to get around so quickly. I will admit that the writing is very cheesy and sometimes just straight up silly and it can be a bit distracting from the fun, darker tone but it doesn't really bother me too much. Also, I think a lot of people's biggest problem with this film is just how annoying and cliche the characters are. But I think that works for this movie and I mean, have the characters in this franchise ever really been that likeable? Overall, this Friday The 13th remake is a really underrated and incredibly brutal entry in this iconic franchise. With the cliche characters, silly dialogue, brutal kills, cool lake house location and Jason going into full monster mode, this movie fully embraces Jason's cult iconography. It's just a damn shame that this never got a sequel and nearly 20 years later, we still haven't gotten a new entry to this iconic franchise.

I wish I could like Hereditary more. It attempts to tap into a fear not engaged with enough: that is, hereditable disease/mental illness. Formerly, such diseases were incorporated into horror in a mystical or religious way, birth defects being a prime example. Such defects were alternatively viewed as divine or a curse, either being an elevation from normal existence. Now (by that I mean at least since the modern synthesis), with the scientific comphrension of herediability, a new sort of horror has arose. The horror of potentially damning your offspring to a life of suffering, though by no personal fault of your own. In this film, some scenes capture this anxity brilliantly, both from the mom and her son's perspective. Unfortunately, these scenes are invariably undermined by less-than-great acting or by being retroactively neutured (e.g. made into a dream). Even if the individual scene was allowed to breath (rarely), the overarching themes (doll-house, A24 etc), which weren't pulled together well, hampered the cinematography. I did like that the family (namely the father) was supportive, the "curse" of disease can strike anyone. The ending was also provocative (especially when read through the lens of mental illness). Also, maybe its just me (or that I had this movie partially spoiled), but it really wasn't that scary! Probably because it felt so pastiche?

A family are grieving the death of their mother/grandmother who apparently had a strained relationship with her daughter, Annie (Toni Collette). A little while later the family's unusual 13 year-old daughter, Charlie (Milly Shapiro) is killed in a car accident driven by her teenage brother (Alex Woolf). Annie eventually takes solace in a medium (Ann Dowd). Not long after the family become haunted by dangerous supernatural forces. A very moody and atmospheric psychological horror that focuses on character rather than shock. Indeed, for much of the film it's a heavy drama about grief and family tension before the horror starts to leak in. A remarkable debut feature from Ari Aster who also wrote the script. A force to be reckoned with for sure. His touch and flair for the bizarre and the macabre is put to the fore here. Aster regular cinematographer Pawel Pogorzelski casts some incredible dark shadows and corners creating some uncanny and terrifying spaces in otherwise banal or ordinary spaces. Add to this the extraordinary sound design, some all round impressive performances (with Collette pulling off the performance of her career) in a truly impressive film.

Um banco que, durante a ditadura militar brasileira, beneficiou-se de políticas econômicas que favoreciam a concentração bancária e o crescimento de instituições privadas, expandindo significativamente durante o regime por meio de fusões e aquisições incentivadas pelos governos militares. Walter Moreira Salles Júnior, herdeiro neoliberal bilionário do Itaú, decidiu fazer um filme retratando os horrores causados pela ditadura militar. Me sinto repetindo a exata mesma crítica que fiz em "Barbie". Aqui nós temos mais um filme cínico feito da burguesia para a burguesia, onde a trama é centrada em uma família de classe média alta no Rio de Janeiro. Essa escolha possui seus méritos, a dor da família Paiva é real, profunda e incontestável, mas esse recorte social estreito não representa a complexidade do trauma coletivo causado pelo regime militar. Algumas pessoas argumentam que "Esse é um filme sobre a família", mas esse filme sobre família está inserido em um contexto político de um momento extremamente grave na história brasileira, onde o filme não abre espaço para uma verdadeira discussão politica, para confrontar o que está sendo narrado, para denunciar os horrores da ditadura. Esse é um filme despolitizante que quer passar a impressão de ser um filme político. A empregada da família Paiva, que provavelmente vivia sob vigilância, com medo e em condições precarias (diferente da família Paiva, ela advém de uma classe social que não tinha voz, educação ou qualquer capital simbólico) recebe um tratamento decorativo apenas. Ignorar figuras como ela em um pais onde a ditadura aprofundou desigualdades raciais e de classe, não foi uma escolha dramática artística do diretor, foi apenas silêncio político intencional. Isso vale também para os guerrilheiros urbanos que são apenas um detalhe implícito no filme, onde o filme evita confrontar essas figuras e realizar um embate ideológico, privilegiando o luto privado. Aqui a ditadura é representada de forma muito vaga, parecendo muito mais uma força abstrata e cruel do que um projeto de poder enfrentado ativamente por diferentes figuras históricas. Aquele momento totalmente jogado do soldado do bem que diz "saiba que eu não concordo com isso" é quase cômico. Nada do que escrevi diminui ou menospreza o sofrimento da família Paiva, já que a repressão destruiu sua rotina familiar. Porém, ao tratar a ditadura militar de forma tão vaga e ignorando outros recortes sociais, o filme torna-se um drama comum. Por fim, o filme adota a linguagem clássica com começo bem definido, desenvolvimento da história com conclusão emocionante, arco dramático da protagonista, fotografia perfeitamente satisfatória, figurino perfeitamente satisfatório e direção perfeitamente satisfatória com cortes suaves e uma trilha sonora que induz emoção nos momentos escolhidos. A escolha pouco inspirada de conceber a obra aos moldes de Hollywood, de retratar uma história num contexto político grave (mas sem levantar uma discussão política real) somada com todo o cuidado técnico, transforma esse filme em um típico filme de padrão internacional feito para ganhar prêmios em festivais e na cerimônia política de autopromoção dos EUA. Me parece que o filme foi realizado única e exclusivamente nesse intuito... Bem, ele conseguiu. No entanto, de longe esse filme representa toda a diversidade e criatividade artística que o cinema brasileiro pode proporcionar. A torcida pesada que esse filme teve para ganhar o Oscar reflete como estamos culturalmente colonizados.

Como brasileira, existe em mim um cansaço acerca dos filmes sobre a ditadura, mas porque eles geralmente fazem o caminho inverso ao que é feito por esse filme. O apelo à brutalidade fisíca geralmente reduz a mensagem dos filmes nesta temática a uma lembrança do passado violento, mas Ainda Estou Aqui esquece o excesso e explora o silêncio e vazio com sensibilidade. Além de Eunice, a protagonista da história é a violência invisível que sobrevive ao fim da ditadura. No recorte do filme, essa violência está na saudade de Rubens Paiva, mas existe em muitas outras camadas da sociedade brasileira, por isso senti um pouco a falta da escolha de abordar o trabalho social de Eunice com vítimas da ditadura de todo tipo, afinal, ela mesma sempre disse que a maior vítima era o Brasil como um todo e não uma família ou outra. Mas, de todo jeito, Ainda Estou Aqui é um filme especial por ser sobre o presente, mesmo sendo ambientando no passado que o país tenta esquecer e corre o risco de repetir.

Dentro del género fílmico dedicado a explorar las historias de quienes sufrieron los horrores de las dictaduras, esta pieza guarda una autenticidad única al contar la historia de quienes son dejados atrás, de aquellas familias, hijos, novias y nietos que quedan más allá del asesinado y desaparecido. "Aún estoy aquí" combina de una manera simple pero precisa ese desasosiego frente a la injusticia y la incertidumbre a la vez que se niega a renunciar a la esperanza innata al humano frente a las peores circunstancias; siendo fiel a lo expresado por Viktor Frankl: "La última de las libertades humanas es elegir nuestra propia actitud ante cualquiera de las peores circunstancias- la libertad de decidir el camino propio". Hermoso homenaje a la vida de Eunice Paiva por parte de una magistral Fernanda Montenegro que carga con todo el film. Tal vez hubiera deseado ver una mayor evolución de los hijos en correlación del contexto vivido.

Ele toca na ferida da ditadura militar brasileira, tanto por pensarmos que essa história é real, tanto pela atuação de Fernanda torres e Montenegro, quanto Selton Mello. A direção, feita por Walter Salles, nos traz o sentimento nacionalista, que é primordial quando pensamos que nosso país será representado pelos atores e produtores. as cores, as falas, o tempo, a montagem, a fotografia e o tempo nos traz arrepios de emoção e medo pelos personagens, e só de pensar que são pessoas reais, meus olhos se enchem d'água.

Apesar de achar que se estende um tanto quanto deveria e ter um final mais educativo, é inegável a qualidade deste filme. Um ótimo filme sobre a ditadura militar, com excelentes atuações para todos os lados, é um bom passo para dar mais visibilidade para o cinema brasileiro. Um filme que merece ser lembrado. Mas também um filme que parece tentar ser um pouco benevolente fazendo vários jogos de cintura para ter chance no Oscar, como na cena onde o militar diz que "não concorda com isso".

i think joker: folie à deux is one of the most misunderstood movies in recent years. before anything, i am NOT justifying arthur fleck’s actions. this man literally killed 6 people. understanding a character’s psychology does not mean excusing what they did. that’s what makes this movie so interesting to me. it isn’t asking us to forgive arthur, it’s asking us to watch him completely lose himself. the musical aspect was definitely a choice, and i understand why it didn’t work for everyone, but i think people missed what it was trying to do. i don’t think most of the singing is actually happening. i think it’s all inside arthur’s head. the songs are his fantasies, his escape, and another sign that he can no longer separate reality from the world he created. the movie isn’t about the rise of the joker. it’s about the death of arthur fleck. after the first movie, everyone wanted arthur to become the joker we know from the comics. the mastermind, the villain, the legend. but todd phillips almost feels like he’s challenging the audience by refusing to give us that. we wanted the myth of joker, but he keeps showing us the broken man underneath the makeup. and honestly, i think that’s the point. gotham didn’t love arthur. they loved joker. harley didn’t fall in love with arthur fleck, she fell in love with the idea of joker. everyone was obsessed with the fantasy, including the audience. lady gaga was also incredible. i just wish we got more of her as harley quinn because she can genuinely act her ass off. but maybe the reason we don’t fully understand harley is because arthur doesn’t fully understand her either. we only see the version of her that exists in his mind. this movie is messy, and i understand why people don’t connect with it, but i think there is so much more going on underneath the surface. the musical numbers, the courtroom, the relationship with harley, and the ending all feel like a reflection of arthur’s collapsing mind. not a perfect movie, but definitely a much deeper one than people give it credit for.

Great horror. One of the first in a very long time to actually unsettle me on a deep level. Sort of thing that has me looking over my shoulder when I walk home from the cinema. Love the new theme in horror where it makes you brutally uncomfortable rather than relying on cheap sound related jump-scares. Loved the theme of cat and mouse. First time I watched it, I thought the twist at the end was stupid. However, upon re-watch, its painfully obvious the whole time that this is not really about an FBI agent hunting a killer. It's about the devil being the devil for the sake of being the devil. Pure evil, good pacing, great sense of discovery as the movie moves throughout acts. Film really rewards you for noticing small details in scenes allowing you to piece the truth together before the protagonist does. Acting was top-notch, really has you on the edge of your seat. Everyone is a suspect, tension is so great throughout. Man that opening scene with the iconic longlegs intro makes me think this will be a cult classic in the future. Loved the constant lingering shots, the open doorways, the strange camera angles that left you not knowing what was round the corner. Appreciated the lack of shitty tropes and cliches. Would give it 5 starts if it didn't have such a significant twist that still feels abrupt in an otherwise nearly perfect film!

Franchement, quelle déception. S'attendre à une grande fresque sur l'une des figures les plus marquantes de notre histoire et se retrouver face à ça, c'est vraiment dommage. Le plus frustrant, c'est la façon dont le personnage est dépeint. Présenter un tel stratège et un esprit aussi complexe sous un jour aussi maladroit et réducteur, ça passe complètement à côté de ce qu'il était. Entre les erreurs historiques à la chaîne, les raccourcis et un récit qui rate totalement la profondeur politique, le contrat n'est clairement pas rempli. On a l'impression d'une vision extérieure biaisée qui cherche plus à démolir un mythe qu'à raconter une histoire avec la nuance et le respect qu'elle méritait. Bref, une grosse douche froide pour un film qui passe complètement à côté de son sujet. Si vous ne souhaitez pas perdre 2h30 de votre vie, passez votre chemin.

Director’s Cut I have really mixed feelings on this. While I have to say this is an outstanding production with stellar cinematography, amazing set and costume design and superb sound. The biggest issue for me was its uneven tone which treated the war time events with a dramatic seriousness, while the parts that focused on Napoleon’s personal life felt satirical. I have no idea whether this was intentional or not but it really threw me off. I also wasn’t the biggest fan of Joaquin Phoenix in this role due to the conflicting tone but I think that’s mostly down to the script which felt like Ridley Scott wanted to present Napoleon as a fragile pathetic character who hid behind his tactical genius, but I just found it to be jarring with it feeling like two separate characters and Phoenix was way too old for the majority of this role. I have heard criticism about the plot being shallow with it feeling like it quickly jumps to and from major plot points. I didn’t really think it did that but I must only presume this is due to the extra depth added within the Directors Cut. The action sequences in this were excellent and really showed Ridley Scott at his best with hard hitting brutality and authentic choreography creating some of the best large scale battles I’ve seen. The ending was also phenomenal. Vanessa Kirby was fantastic as Josephine who played a key role in Napoleon’s story. But, there are a lot of characters in this and while I don’t think anyone was particularly bad no one really stood out to me. I did enjoy this film with the full 3 and half hours feeling generally well paced. For me it doesn’t do much wrong apart from as I said the weird tone surrounding Napoleon but unfortunately that is a big deal considering the whole film surrounds him. This could have been an absolutely incredible film. I would love to know if the awkward portrayal of Napoleon’s personal life was intentional and maybe inspired by England’s historical propaganda that did show him as weak and childish. I would like to watch this again one day knowing what to expect.

Un deuxième visionnage bien rentable, cette fois-ci vu en version intégrale qui rajoute 48 minutes environ. Je me rappelle que la version cinéma de 2h40 donnait l'impression que les évènements s'enchaînaient bêtement et sans raison, ce qui n'est pas le cas dans la director's cut. Napoléon de Ridley Scott est indéniablement imparfait et inégal. La photographie est parfois sublime, parfois absolument infecte. Bien sûr, c'est plus souvent beau que laid... Mais je ne peux vraiment pas passer outre cette scène d'ouverture affreuse, qui annonce vraiment mal le film. Qu'est-ce que c'est moche pendant la première minute ! La musique aussi est pompeuse pendant une bonne heure avant de devenir bonne. Mais les scènes d'action sont particulièrement réussies : très belles, toutes uniques, on comprend bien ce qui s'y passe (pas comme dans un certain blockbuster récent que je ne citerai pas...), et durent globalement le temps qu'il faut. Il faut noter que le film s'essouffle un peu pendant la deuxième heure avant de repartir de plus belle. En terme de mise en scène, c'est à la fois subtil, maîtrisé, et parfois un poil grossier/burlesque, ce qui n'est pas nécessairement un défaut. Je pense que c'est le genre de films ou beaucoup de détails nous échappent et que l'on découvre au fur et à mesure des visionnages. Ensuite évidemment, là où le film ne prend pas tellement de risques en matière de costumes et de décors (ce qui me dérange un peu car la reconstitution historique ne m'intéresse franchement pas, et je n'aime pas tellement le style de cette époque), il en prend énormément sur le fond. Et cette prise de risque fondamentale, qui est de faire de Napoléon un personnage mauvais et comique, est géniale ! Elle porte franchement le film et lui donne un intérêt. Phoenix est excellent dans ce rôle (sous certains angles, la ressemblance avec le vrai Napoléon est frappante). L'idée de faire d'un Empereur que la tradition historique prend au sérieux un simple cocu immature en manque d'amour et qui a clairement des dizaines de manques à combler, c'est merveilleux. De quoi rendre fou tout morveux qui prétend être un patriote en adorant ce neuille de Napoléon. Qu'est-ce que je préfère un protagoniste de la sorte, absolument inattendu et presque dégoûtant, à un personnage historique qui répond simplement aux attentes d'un spectateur lambda qui s'attend à un film épique comme les autres, du style Pierre Niney dans le Comte de Monte-Cristo. Bien entendu, j'aime bien Pierre Niney malgré sa filmo douteuse, mais le comparer à Phoenix c'est comme comparer une panthère et un moustique. Aussi pour revenir sur le personnage de Napoléon, j'apprécie beaucoup l'idée d'en faire un mégalo matrixé par l'envie de devenir un des grands de l'histoire au point d'écrire sa propre histoire de son vivant. (Bien sûr Napoléon de la vraie vie était aussi quelqu'un d'intelligent, à l'origine de plusieurs avancées notables, un fin stratège etc... Ok, mais dans un film c'est pas intéressant de voir ça. Je considère également qu'une grande intuition n'empêche en rien qu'il fut une grosse merde humaine). Les deux motifs sur lesquels je devrai davantage me concentrer au prochain visionnage seront la possessivité de Napoléon à l'égard de Joséphine/La France, et la lumière céleste. Bref, un film imparfait mais pour lequel j'ai étonnement développé avec le temps une réelle tendresse. Inutile de préciser que tout ce qui est vérité ou crédibilité historique est pour moins un non-argument car il s'agit de fiction, et que Ridley Scott a bien raison de se torcher le cul avec les livres d'histoire.

I’ll preface by saying i only watched the director’s cut. That said, god, i hate that i liked this. Do i think it’s a good portrayal of how Napoleon was perceived by others? Perhaps not, but i do think it does a fantastic job in making you feel like how it would’ve been inside his mind throughout his life. Especially towards the end where failure was more and more common. The huge battles, sets, cavalry charges, all of it was a feast for the eyes. The actors did a good job, and i feel like Joaquin Phoenix and Vanessa Kirby were the quite obvious standouts. Although i must say i liked Edouard Philipponant portrayal of the tsar as well. It has a lot of flaws, as a film. But it’s enjoyable, and never boring which i see as the worst sin a film can commit. Made 3 hours and then some feel like an hour. Perhaps the last good Ridley Scott movie,  but of course i’d love to be proved wrong.

This movie sent me down a spiral into the French Revolution and the Coalition Wars! Visually, it’s stunning. It genuinely felt like being dropped into 19th century France. Also Joaquin Phoenix somehow went from looking like the cool uncle to looking like the creepy grandfather everyone just hates 😭 Knowing the man, the only annoying thing is that the movie spends so much time showing Napoleon’s flaws that it almost forgets he was one of history’s greatest military minds. My man had generals and army’s in Europe wetting their pants. It could’ve spent a bit more time showing how brilliant he was instead of giving us shots of him charging headfirst with a sword into an enemy line full of muskets. I've always thought that making a film about a great historical figure is one of the hardest things a director can do. Unless it's a TV series or a whole film saga, trying to fit an entire life into a single movie means leaving out a lot of important moments. And when that person is Napoleon Bonaparte—a man whose life was defined by politics, military genius, and an incredibly complex personality—the challenge becomes even greater. Any filmmaker has to balance historical accuracy with cinematic spectacle, and I think Ridley Scott only partially succeeds. The film follows the major milestones of Napoleon's life in chronological order and recreates some of his most famous campaigns. At the same time, it takes several dramatic liberties to make them more visually impressive. The cannon fire aimed at the Pyramids never happened, Napoleon wasn't present at Marie Antoinette's execution, and the famous frozen lake sequence at Austerlitz is a huge exaggeration of what actually took place. Those scenes are entertaining, but they prioritize spectacle over history. Honestly, those changes don't bother me that much because they're based on real events that have simply been dramatized. What I do miss are the omissions that make it harder to understand who Napoleon really was. The film barely touches on his background as a member of the Corsican minor nobility, something that was essential in allowing him to attend military school in France and begin the career that eventually led him to become Emperor. Joséphine also deserved a more nuanced portrayal. The movie mostly reduces her role to Napoleon's wife and his desperate need for an heir. While that was certainly an important part of their relationship, she was also a politically influential figure who navigated the highest circles of French society and played a significant role while Napoleon was away. The film turns a remarkably capable historical figure into little more than a romantic subplot. That said, I do think the movie succeeds in portraying Napoleon as more than just a military genius. We see an awkward, emotionally intense man whose love for Joséphine shapes much of his personal life. Joaquin Phoenix captures that contradiction between the vulnerable individual and the unstoppable conqueror surprisingly well. I also liked how the film hints at Napoleon's admiration for Julius Caesar and Alexander the Great. At times, Scott presents him as someone driven by an almost classical sense of duty—a man convinced that his destiny was to serve France above everything else. Whether intentional or not, that echoes the Roman ideal of devotion to the state and adds another layer to his character.

This cut is so much better than the original. While I was planning to save Ridley Scott’s Napoleon until I reached the next chapter of my director deep dive, the opportunity arose to watch it, so I took it. At three and a half hours, Scott’s director’s cut is a substantial expansion of the theatrical version. It doesn’t quite add the sense of scale I expected from an extra hour of runtime, but that’s easy to forgive when the film delivers on the level that it does. Napoleon certainly has its flaws, and some of them are significant, but in the grand scheme of things, it’s a great time. From the opening sequence, the film radiates a grit that seems to seep off the screen, steadily building throughout the runtime. That escalation culminates in several disturbing scenes of political violence that are incredibly effective. Scott captures the messiness of government, revolution, and monarchy with remarkable clarity, making it easy to understand the absolute chaos of France’s political climate during this period. The director’s cut is far more expansive and patient with its pacing, allowing these elements to breathe and making the atmosphere all the more effective. Much of that atmosphere is still rooted in the relationship between Josephine and Napoleon, just as it was in the original cut. What elevates it here are the expanded plotlines surrounding Napoleon’s rise to power, along with the greater focus given to key political and historical developments. These additions provide the film with far more depth and substance than its theatrical counterpart. My biggest issue with the film, both the director’s cut and the theatrical version, is its use of American accents in place of French ones. It’s a truly baffling decision that repeatedly pulls the viewer out of the film’s otherwise immersive atmosphere. It feels especially strange when you have a Russian character speaking with a Russian accent while a native Frenchman speaks with an American one. It constantly distracted me. I understand why Joaquin Phoenix was cast, he is excellent and perfectly suited to the role in many ways. However, I can’t understand why he doesn’t attempt a French accent at all. While his star power undoubtedly helped the film commercially, the decision to forgo an accent altogether may have avoided certain pitfalls, but it ultimately hurts the film’s authenticity and integrity.

The only reason this gets 2.5 instead of 1.5 is because the acting was incredible by Cilian Murphy and Robert Downey Jr and it was visually fun to experience in imax. I was disappointed at the theatre but thought it was fine. Upon re-watch, I conclude that this movie genuinely blows. Three hours and you feel nothing but sympathy for the “antagonist.” Seriously, no one with a brain would have trusted Oppenheimer. Depending on how you view this movie, it might even be apparent that Nolan disliked Oppenheimer and chose to tell a story that builds him up as a tragic hero who had to atone for his bomb. The reality is that Oppenheimer was psychotic and he was chosen for the job because he was a suspected communist Jew who could be blamed if things went south. Yes, he was also very smart. Turning Oppenheimer’s wife into a character is boring. It’s BBC television. That interrogation scene with the FBI is laughable. It’s basically a deposition. How is anyone meant to take that seriously? Some stories are not meant to be movies. This movie is so devoid of interesting themes that it had to do a sandlot style “get the band together” montage. That type of plot device is reserved for B and C movies. Don’t get me started on the cast. Matt Damon as a four star general hard ass? Give me a break. I would have bought Steve Buscemi in that role before Damon. What role does Florence Pugh play? She’s supposed to provide some kind of emotional connection and atonement for Oppenheimer. Actually, she’s just there to show off her tits. No one cares that Oppenheimer was a womanizer. That’s not something people are interested in. Maybe she’s meant to convince us that Oppenheimer really was a communist? Robert Downey Jr was awesome in his role. No notes. But the rest of the movie felt so ensemble that it took me out. Close up of Josh Peck at the climax of the bomb testing? What are we doing here? I maintain that this is a BBC drama with really good acting a huge budget. It’s a story no one cares about. Even if it’s all true, what point did this story serve? Each time it builds up to a pivotal moment, it falls dreadfully flat for me. There’s no reason to ever rewatch this.

J. Robert Oppenheimer, an amazing physicist, is given the job of leading the Manhattan Project, as the United States races to develop the atomic bomb during World War II. The movie follows Oppenheimer as pressure continues to build on him during the creation of the bomb (and in the years that follow). This movie came out in 2023 and for some reason I never came around to watching it until now. I regret delaying it until now as this movie lacked no action even thought it wasn’t an “action” movie. Christopher Nolan continued to make the story more and more interesting as more pressure was put on Oppenheimer, and I love how he made you feel stressed without barraging you with explosions of the bomb (I thought the movie would be like this in 2023). I also like when historical movies feel different than what you know or what you've learned, typically because they go into the little details; and bridge the gaps in between. This I felt like was done in the Odyssey too. Cillian Murphy gives an incredible performance and the entire movie does a great job showing the weight that came with what Oppenheimer helped create. The quote “And now I have become Death, the destroyer of worlds” is one of those sick movie quotes that will ping in my mind for awhile - I love how it was echoed throughout the movie. This is another movie that shows why Christopher Nolan is one of the best directors of all time.

This is my third time watching this film, and it gets better with every watch. From the moment the opening frame of raindrops shows, I was captivated. The rain being a motif for the consequences and troubles of Oppenheimer is a beautiful decision, and it executed perfectly throughout the entire film. It shows the weight that Oppenheimer has to carry with the decisions that he made, even if he appears to not be fully set on his emotions. Murphy absolutely deserved the Oscar for this masterful, career-defining performance. The way he able to play an anti-hero by showing regret through his voice and emotional restraint at times is done in a way only a few actors can do. I’d like to applaud the successful writing as well. Oppenheimer is one of the most complex characters Nolan has written. He has many moral flaws throughout, and even more contradictions to his actions, but yet the audience is made to feel for him emotionally, as we see the weight he carries, and the regret he holds, even if it’s too late. The cinematography in this film is also superb. The use of frequent, quick flashes throughout helps create the overall story, and sets the tone for what is going on. It allows for complex story telling, well-rounded characters, and sophisticated story telling. This helps create the great structure and pacing that this film has, which many argue is a problem in other Nolan movies. I can’t write this review without giving praise to Ludwig, and his amazing score for this film. It’s his best work, and I think he’ll have a hard time ever topping this string carried melody. I’d also like to shoutout Emily blunt. Her performance is already very famous for what she does with such little screen time, but the praise is warranted. Her face acting is a masterclass in show don’t tell. If she had more screen time, she’d have an Oscar for this role, which she might’ve deserved even with the little time she had to show off her talent. This is Nolan’s second best film. It has become very clear to me after debating this for a long time. This watch was necessary for me to determine where this ranks in his filmography. It is also the best film of the 2020s so far. There’s an argument for Dune 2, but Oppenheimer still clears. Now I am become death, destroyer of worlds.

Wanted to check that my perception of this film was not clouded by me being 17 and fairly new to IMAX at release. Those checks have cleared. The greatest lead acting performance ever. Greatest VFX and SFX ever, and would-be greatest score if Ludwig didn’t top it with Sinners. The perfection of Nolan’s exposition and weird editing of dialogue panning to everyone but the speaker’s face. Everyone involved in this film was born to play their role in it. The build and release of tension (much like how the movie presents fission) is masterful, using gorgeous visuals of subatomic warfare and sonic booms of egotism to represent the fractured genius of Oppenheimer’s mind and conscience in both the physical and moral sense in the lead-up, execution and conclusion of his most important moments. The Trinity Test remains my favourite scene ever crafted. What separates this from other biopics, or even The Odyssey, is the ambiguity that Nolan allows the viewer to cherish. Your view of Oppenheimer’s morality and consequentiality is entirely up to your reading of events - with clear view of the Red Scare, of America’s myths, of human history; you are the jury.

I remember when my Grandmother used to speak with me on the phone about Harry Truman's speech indicating the end of World War II. She would start to tear up when he spoke about how not one more American would be killed. It used to be very powerful to hear. There was, however, a missing part of this story I never knew about, the man who had to live with creating the bomb that ended the war. The film takes us from the opening credits to the kangaroo court of J. Robert Oppenheimer. Due to his past associations with communists, he never stood a chance. It was amazing to watch his brilliance be taken over by a man who was no more loyal to him than the communists he once befriended. Oppenheimer was the main architect who built the atomic bomb and he lived with the guilt long after it dropped. This guilt and a petty grudge gave Lewis Strauss all the ammunition he needed. Strauss got what he wanted from Oppenheimer. Strauss takes down Oppenheimer by sticking him in a kangaroo court. Afterwards, Strauss doesn't realize he's sitting in his own version of a kangaroo court until it's too late. I remember walking out of the theater and my friend and I both agreed how amazing it was. In The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan used IMAX cameras for the entire film. In Oppenheimer, he used them for a majority of the film. This made it a visual spectacle that looked as good on a 4K TV as it did when I saw it in theaters. Cillian Murphy was an actor I knew of before this film. As Oppenheimer, he became the emotional center of the film regardless of time or destination. I could look in his eyes and know the highs and lows of being the man who received far more credit than he wanted. Beyond Nolan's directing, my friend and I discussed Robert Downey Jr. as Lewis Strauss extensively. I thought he was going to have a good chance at winning the Oscar, but he stole the film in every scene he was in. I saw Oppenheimer 3 years ago on the anniversary of the bomb dropping in Hiroshima in 1945. It was a moment that hit me after I left the theater. A few weeks later, I watched the film again in theaters, and then a few months later again with my Mom. Each time I thought to myself about how Oppenheimer had to live with what he did. Lewis Strauss had to live with unnecessary pettiness that cost him what he worked so hard for. Harry Truman may have taken responsibility, but guilt has to fall on someone's shoulders. Oppenheimer wasn't wrong for taking on the guilt, but just like his other mistakes, decisions are very hard to take back once they've been made. I write longer reflections about life and film here: filmsthatstay.substack.com/

هستند. فیلم در نیمه‌ی اول از نظر موقعیت و اتفاقات باورپذیرتر است. فضای فیلم بیشتر شبیه یک کمدی اجتماعی است و ورود خانواده‌ی فقیر به خانه‌ی ثروتمند با ریتم قابل تحمل‌تری پیش می‌رود. اما حتی در همین بخش نیز مشکل اصلی شخصیت‌پردازی وجود دارد. شخصیت‌ها عمق کافی ندارند و بیشتر بر اساس جایگاه اجتماعی خود تعریف می‌شوند. نگاه فیلم به فقر برای من بسیار سطحی است. فقر در فیلم بیشتر با نشانه‌های ظاهری تعریف می‌شود؛ زیرزمین، خانه‌ی کوچک، بوی بد و شرایط زندگی پایین‌تر. اما فقر فقط این نشانه‌های بیرونی نیست. فقر تجربه‌ای انسانی است که شامل ترس، محدودیت، روابط، آرزوها و فشارهای روانی می‌شود. فیلم برای من کمتر به این جنبه‌ها نزدیک می‌شود و بیشتر با نمادهای ظاهری فقر کار می‌کند. همین مشکل درباره‌ی ثروت نیز وجود دارد. ثروت در فیلم بیشتر به خانه‌ی بزرگ، ماشین، فضای لوکس و بوی خوب محدود می‌شود. فیلم فاصله‌ی طبقاتی را بیشتر با تفاوت‌های ظاهری نشان می‌دهد تا تجربه‌ی واقعی زندگی انسان‌هایی از دو طبقه‌ی متفاوت. مشکل دیگر فیلم، نمادگرایی بیش از حد آن است. نمادپردازی به خودی خود ضعف نیست، اما زمانی که نمادها جای انسان‌ها را بگیرند، شخصیت‌ها دیگر به اندازه‌ی کافی زنده و باورپذیر نمی‌شوند. برای من در «انگل» شخصیت‌ها بیشتر نماینده‌ی ایده‌ها هستند تا انسان‌هایی واقعی. نیمه‌ی دوم فیلم برای من نقطه‌ی سقوط آن است. از زمانی که اتفاقات مربوط به زیرزمین شروع می‌شود، فیلم از فضای کمدی اجتماعی فاصله می‌گیرد و تبدیل به یک تریلر خشن می‌شود. مشکل این تغییر فقط تغییر ژانر نیست؛ مشکل این است که اتفاقات بعدی بیشتر بر اساس شوک طراحی شده‌اند تا منطق شخصیت‌ها. پایان فیلم برای من کاملاً غیرواقعی است. اتفاقاتی مثل حمله، قتل‌ها و واکنش شخصیت‌ها بیشتر برای ایجاد شوک و ضربه‌ی ناگهانی به مخاطب ساخته شده‌اند. رفتار شخصیت‌ها نیز در این بخش بیشتر تابع نیاز فیلمنامه است تا نتیجه‌ی طبیعی مسیر روانی آن‌ها. پایان مربوط به پدر خانواده نیز برای من باورپذیر نیست. تصمیم او بیشتر تحمیل‌شده به نظر می‌رسد و فیلم به اندازه‌ی کافی مسیر درونی لازم برای رسیدن به آن نقطه را نمی‌سازد. همچنین پایان مربوط به اینکه او در زیرزمین پنهان می‌شود و پسر خانواده می‌گوید روزی خانه را می‌خرد و او را نجات می‌دهد، برای من بسیار ساده و غیرواقعی است. از نظر کارگردانی، بونگ جون هو توانایی خود را نشان می‌دهد. میزانسن فیلم یکی از نقاط قوت آن است. طراحی خانه‌ی خانواده‌ی ثروتمند، فضای زیرزمین و تفاوت میان محیط‌های زندگی، با دقت ساخته شده‌اند. خانه به خوبی در خدمت ایده‌ی فیلم قرار می‌گیرد و فضای طبقاتی را منتقل می‌کند. قاب‌بندی‌های فیلم نیز قابل توجه هستند. کارگردان از مدیوم‌شات، کلوزآپ و لانگ‌شات استفاده می‌کند و از نظر ساختن فضا توانایی خوبی دارد. با این حال، این قدرت‌های فرمی برای من نتوانسته‌اند ضعف شخصیت‌ها و نگاه فیلم به انسان را جبران کنند. موسیقی فیلم برای من تأثیر زیادی ایجاد نمی‌کند. استفاده از موسیقی کلاسیک و برخی انتخاب‌های موسیقایی وجود دارد، اما بیشتر در خدمت ظاهر فیلم هستند و تأثیر احساسی عمیقی ایجاد نمی‌کنند. بعضی تصاویر اسلوموشن نیز برای من بیشتر کلیشه‌ای هستند تا تاثیرگذار. کمدی فیلم یک کمدی اجتماعی و سیاسی است و به موضوعاتی مثل جامعه‌ی کره، سیاست و مسائل اجتماعی اشاره می‌کند. ممکن است برای مخاطب کره‌ای ارتباط بیشتری داشته باشد، اما برای من بسیاری از این شوخی‌ها تأثیر زیادی نداشتند. ریتم نیمه‌ی اول از نیمه‌ی دوم بهتر است، اما به طور کلی فیلم برای من جذابیت انسانی کافی ندارد. مشکل اصلی این است که فیلم به جای نزدیک شدن به انسان‌ها، بیشتر درباره‌ی نمادهای اجتماعی حرف می‌زند. در نهایت، «انگل» از نظر میزانسن و ساخت فضای بصری فیلم قابل توجهی است، اما برای من در بخش مهم‌تر یعنی شخصیت‌پردازی، انسان‌سازی و نمایش واقعی طبقات اجتماعی شکست می‌خورد. فیلم زمانی که انسان‌ها را به نماد تبدیل می‌کند، ارتباط احساسی خود را از دست می‌دهد. نمره: ۲.۵ از ۵

This was the last of the three loosely connected slasher films starring Mia Goth that I watched, and easily the one that left the strongest impression on me. What captivated me most was its deliberately old-fashioned style - the theatrical performances, exaggerated emotions, and long takes that feel lifted straight out of classic Hollywood. The whole film plays like a dark version of Dorothy from Kansas, where dreams of stardom slowly give way to obsession, frustration, and madness. Mia Goth is unquestionably the film's greatest strength. Her extended monologue is emotionally devastating, but the ending lingers in my mind just as much - nearly two minutes of her desperately holding a smile as the end credits roll over cheerful, almost quaint music. It's the perfect closing note for a film built on the contrast between its bright, nostalgic aesthetic and its steadily growing psychological horror. It's rare to see a horror film that draws so confidently from cinema's past while using that style to tell such an unsettling character study. Mia Goth keeps marching toward the horror queen's crown with unwavering confidence -perhaps with just a touch too much arrogance, but it fits her well.

Dear Wim Wenders, I've tried, man. I really tried with this one. Your films, while esthetically pleasing, carry nothing in terms of substance, story, or attention. I'm not saying I need action packed, narrative expository, tiktok noise to keep me invested, but Jesus Christ, Wim, give me something to work with. Your films are flat. They engage with the lonely side of life and less about the slice of it - and that's something to be commended for. But not everyone is lonely. Not everyone feels that way. And sometimes a lonely day is not that engaging. If I wanted to see a lonely slice of life piece that's a little more engaging, I would rather just watch a documentary. I'm sorry Wim, but I feel you will never write anything that's neither engaging or worth my time. The closest you got to making a film that explores loneliness while keeping your audience somewhat entertained was 42 years ago and it definitely shows. Maybe you're a lonely man who wants everyone else to feel as lonely as you, and maybe that's the point of your films. But I don't to feel that way everytime I want to engage with your art. You'll never change and that's okay, but I don't think I'll invest in your talent ever again. Your fans are few but dedicated, and your quality speaks to them in ways that I will never comprehend. I'm sorry I can never be part of that dedicated community that sees the beauty of your world, and I'm sorry I can't see what you see. Maybe someday I might, but not banking on that anymore. But keep making your art anyway. Film as a whole needs voices like yours. Sincerely, A.F.X. Heller

MVFF 2023 #2 Maybe I haven't seen enough Wim Wenders yet but this was unexpectedly modest and wholesome. Yet, dare I say, not in a particularly earned manner? Hirayama could be an interesting character but the film does not probe him nearly enough, rather mainly showcases his content quotidian existence. I do generally like plotless slice-of-life films, and this is not quite an exception with its pleasant vibes and eschewing of narrative clichés. But I strongly prefer the genre to showcase some amount of complexity through their characters in lieu of much of a plot to lean on. Here, while there are a few small hitches via hints of Hirayama's past and being subjected to classist behavior, the film largely skates over them and feels too simple for my tastes. Hirayama appears to me as just a simple man with a simple job and simple hobbies. The film does ask ourselves why he is so content with his profession and quietude but without presenting even much of a hint, the answer(s) will not keep me up at night.

Magnifiques décors et cinématographie. Le film était tristement joyeux et paisible; on suis l’histoire d’un homme qui passe sa vie à nettoyer des toilettes et pourtant, elle n’est pas si ennuyeuse. Sa vie est répétitive , il fait toujours les mêmes activités en boucles ( laver les toilettes, aller au bain public et dormir ) et pourtant il réussi à l’apprécier. Et c’est justement ce que j’ai apprécié dans le film, le fait qu’il suffit juste de prêter attention à ce qui nous entoure pour réaliser la valeur de la vie. Car tout au long du film, le personnage principal fais des rencontres, des expériences, plus ou moins enrichissantes et longues, mais qui laissent toujours une marque dans sa vie. Et tout ce qu’il vis viens un petit temps et repars, en le laissant à sa vie routinière habituelle à la fin,  mais elles viennent, et le comblent de bonheur même pour quelques minutes. Et chaque mauvaise expérience qui va l’affaiblir amène toujours à quelque chose de plus beau. Le personnage ne se contente pas d’exister sans réellement vivre dans l’instant , il remarque chaque détails de son existence , et il est altruiste et humain. très peu de paroles sont dites , parce que ces moments là n’ont pas besoin d’être expliqués et je trouve ça cool. Cependant j’ai mis du temps à vraiment accrocher , et je suis pas trop film très lent, j’aurais quand même aimé qu’il sorte de sa routine et qu’il essaye de garder ou de relancer ce qui est venu dans sa vie, mais je conçois complètement qu’on puisse adorer le film pour les mêmes raisons qui m’ont fait un peu - l’aimer  ; j’aurais aussi aimé qu’il fasse des rencontres qui durent + longtemps et non uniquement des mots échangés de quelques minutes . J’aurais aimé voir des rebondissements, sa routine se déconstruire , mais je sais que ce n’était pas l’objectif du film et je trouve ça bien aussi. Je met seulement 3 ( j’aimerais mettre 3,25 si jpouvais) parce que perso la simplicité c’est pas mon truc, mais j’ai kiffé les messages du film Scène de fin superbe g kiffé J’ai passé un bon moment et le film m’a rendu triste autant qu’il m’a rendu heureuse.

No es para todos y pienso que dentro de esta especie de subgénero de películas "no pasa nada" hay mejores, pero aún así Perfect Days es una película bellísima que cambia tu forma de ver la cotidianidad de la vida, es una historia realmente sencilla, sin grandes giros ni pretenciones solo la vida de un hombre que limpia baños. Una película muy necesaria, muy contraria a lo que lo acelerado de la vida actual nos tiene acostumbrados. Me gusto mucho lo relajante que es ver está película, si bien no es la película más estímulante en cuanto a trama de la historia pues es que eso no es lo que busca daré está obra, entre la excelente dirección, la fotografía que hace que cada momento del film sea bello e incluso el sonido ambiental te transmiten muchísimo esa paz de Hirayama, de apreciar los pequeños detalles. Eso mismo los detalles son un gran acierto de Perfect Days, ver está obra por encima es un gran error, por más que sea una película en la que no pase mucho el verla de fondo es no entender lo que te está tratando de decir, cosas pequeñas como la nota del gato (#) que Hirayama dejaba en el baño, sus fotos, en indígente que siempre veía son las cosas pequeñas y fugaces que hacen en conjunto a Perfect Days una película tan especial sobre ver el mundo sin toda la prisa con lo que lo solemos ver. Un tema que me gustó como fue plasmado fueron lo choque generaciónales entre Hirayama con su sobrina y el wey que lo ayudaba a limpiar, un contraste entre la forma calmada y serena de vivir de alguien que alguien con su experiencia formó contra la forma apresurada y caótica que la juventud y la sociedad actúal tenemos. También me gustaron estás escenas intermedias surrealistas y en blanco y negro entre cada día que la película tiene, como si fueran solo instante de los recuerdos que las rutinas largas nos dan. En fin, este tipo de películas que usan un ritmo lento para resaltar los momentos pequeños siempre son las que más terminan renonando conmigo con el pasar del tiempo y Perfect Days siento que va a ser una de las que más me voy a quedar.

Perfect Days is only my second Wim Wenders film after Paris, Texas , and somehow he’s already given me two incredible films. I honestly feel like I may have peaked way too early with his filmography, because I don’t know how he tops either of these for me. There’s just something so beautiful about the simplicity of this film. Hirayama’s life is incredibly routine and on the surface there isn’t a huge amount happening, but Wenders makes that routine feel meaningful without ever forcing it to be. The pacing is absolutely brilliant. The film is more than happy to sit with Hirayama as he goes about his day, and I never felt bored or impatient. If anything, I found myself becoming more immersed in the rhythm of his life. The sparse dialogue works perfectly with this too. So much of Hirayama’s character is communicated through his expressions, his routines, the people he interacts with, the books he reads and especially the music he listens to. There’s very little need for exposition because the film trusts you to simply observe him and gradually piece together who he is. I also loved the visual style. The colour palette is gorgeous, the editing is really neat, and the Tokyo cityscapes are beautiful throughout. There’s something about the contrast between the busy, overwhelming city and Hirayama’s incredibly simple existence within it that I really loved. Wenders somehow makes cleaning public toilets, eating lunch in a park and driving around Tokyo listening to music feel almost meditative. It’s also interesting comparing this to Paris, Texas. They’re very different films, but there’s definitely a similar fascination with loneliness, human connection and people who have seemingly withdrawn from a previous life. Paris, Texas is much more emotionally heavy and dramatic, whereas Perfect Days feels far more content with simply observing life. It almost feels like Wenders has arrived at a more peaceful understanding of some of the same ideas. And Koji Yakusho is incredible. He does so much with so little dialogue, and the final sequence in particular is such a beautiful example of that. His face says more than pages of dialogue ever could. I think what I loved most is that Perfect Days never feels like it’s trying to convince you that Hirayama’s life is perfect. It’s just showing you that there can be something beautiful in an ordinary life if you actually pay attention to it. The repetition, the routine, the little moments of connection, the music, the trees, the photographs - all of these tiny things gradually become meaningful. This is easily the best thing I’ve seen from Wenders so far, although I’ve only seen two films, so maybe I’ve just started with an unfairly strong pair. Either way, absolutely beautiful from start to finish. 10/10 Top100

“Next time is next time. Now is now.” Wow. This film is truly a hidden gem I’m surprised it isn’t talked about enough mainstream, but I think it’s better this way. Perfect days has very little monologue yet there’s so much meaning behind every frame. This film teaches us to look for the beauty within our every day routines. Every small action makes a huge impact within our day to day lives which can drastically change it, no two days are the same even if we feel like we’re living the same day over and over again. However there are some days which aren’t so “perfect” and it’s those ones where we have to push past it to make it to the next one and the one after that and so on. I really wish I watched this film sooner as I feel like I’ve learnt a lot that will now broaden my future and my every day life going forward. Highly recommend.

A rotina não é uma prisão. É uma prática. Todos os dias Hirayama acorda antes do sol, limpa banheiros públicos em Tóquio, ouve fitas cassete e fotografa árvores. Muitos veem nisso uma vida depressiva, sem ambição. Mas Dias Perfeitos não fala só de rotina. Fala de maneiras de encontrar o infinito no repetitivo. Ele não aspira ser outra coisa. Não há drama, não há "um dia eu vou ser...". Ele simplesmente é. E o filme trata isso como quem reverencia algo grandioso. Simplicidade não significa falta. Significa escolha. Cada gesto de Hirayama é intencional, cada movimento econômico. Não é minimalismo estético. É minimalismo existencial. Hirayama está sempre olhando para cima, capturando a luz filtrada pelas folhas. Isso tem um nome em japonês: komorebi. Não é luz, não é sombra. É o que existe entre elas. Quando ele levanta a câmera, não procura a árvore. Procura outra coisa. Algo que tem a ver com pausa, atenção e a coragem de parar enquanto o mundo corre. [Não por acaso, komorebi é a palavra que dá nome ao meu canal.] Wenders não fez um filme sobre um homem que limpa banheiros. Fez um filme sobre um homem que encontrou paz. E a paz não está em mudar de vida. Está em habitar a vida que a gente tem. Mas o que é, exatamente, um dia perfeito? O filme não responde. Ele mostra. E você? Quando foi a última vez que olhou para cima? 🎬 Eu crio vídeo-ensaios onde gosto de falar sobre filosofia, fotografia, direção de arte, roteiro, montagem, etc., de filmes que gosto ou que causaram uma 'mudança' em mim. Mas tudo isso de maneira bem 'informal' e 'despretenciosa'. Se você chegou até aqui e tiver interesse em conhecer, fique à vontade pra assistir: 👉 www.youtube.com/watch?v=_HNYE311-kw&t=2s

A couple years ago I lost my religion and there was so much dread and uncertainty that came with that. Even years later sometimes I get worried. What if I’m wrong? There is SO much on the line if I’m wrong. After this life I may never see my family again. Milly and I may never be together again. The family Milly and I long for may be eternally damned because I chose myself. What am I doing this all for? I’ve had to really accept a reality where this life is truly all there is. After this life, there could be nothing. While I hope for more after I die, I found so much peace and purpose in this life being all there is. Because if that’s true, then my only responsibility is to love so fully and deeply that when I die I’m satisfied. To love Milly with everything I have, because if this is it and I die and don’t get to see her again, I want to be confident that I couldn’t have loved her more. I didn’t have an ounce more of love to give. I gave it all in this lifetime. I think that’s a real privilege. I get to be with trees, I get to listen to music, I get to create, I get to love people and I get to try and deepen how I do that every single day. If I’m wrong, then I guess I deal with whatever punishment god has, but if I happen to be right, I don’t need heaven or anything after this. This is good enough

A beautiful film about solitude, routine, melancholy and enjoying the little things. Hirayama’s solitude is beautiful and meaningful, but it may also be a protective shell he has built around himself. Short, sometimes wordless human interactions can be deeply meaningful, yet he has effectively cut himself off from his family for reasons we never fully understand. There is joy in listening to music alone in your car, but also in sharing that music with someone else. He has built a tiny world for himself inside an enormous Tokyo: his apartment, small izakayas and bookshops, the park, the bath house. I loved the way such a vast and sometimes impersonal city becomes intimate through these small spaces, where you encounter the same regulars and gradually become part of one another’s lives. He follows almost exactly the same routine every day, yet every day is slightly different: the light hits the leaves differently and creates new patterns of shadow, the homeless man strikes another absurd pose, a salaryman or a group of children passes through one of the toilets he is cleaning. Routine becomes a way of noticing change rather than escaping from it. A good life can contain both happiness and sadness, tears and a smile at the same time, as in that beautiful final shot.

Enjoyable as Spider-Man eye candy. It's amazing we get a Spider-Man movie where Miguel O'Hara plays such a huge role, me in the nineties never would've believed such a thing would ever happen. I enjoyed the first one well enough, it has the edge of being a self-contained movie, but O'Hara being in this one gives it a big boost. Spider-Man is a humorous, self-deprecating character, but after so many incarnations of Woody Allen in a lucha mask, getting a masculine presence like O'Hara is a welcome change. Of course, such a character can't be a good guy in a movie today, so he's presented as a villain. But he also happens to be right. Multiverses are a cheat and always suck. Even if the story does something clever with it, it's always just a device for lazy writers to worm their way out of the corners they paint themselves into. This movie explains a lot of rules for its multiverse to you, through Miguel O'Hara, who enforces said rules, only for the movie to tell you the rules don't matter and you can do whatever you want (a theme in society today, especially during the years when this film was being made). Ok pal, then I don't care about your plot. The way I stayed invested was hoping their supposed villain, the correct and true alpha chad O'Hara, gets to eventually execute the arrogant, insufferable main characters. It's not a movie with an actual ending, so I can hope it happened offscreen after the credits roll, at least until the next movie where nothing matters comes out.

Really wanted to like this one more than I did. After all, what better way to complete my Trolls Remorse arc than giving a favorable score to the Other Miles Morales movie. Sadly, this is a textbook case of chief creatives whose eyes are far, far bigger than their stomachs. The worst of the post Gunn, post Waititi “Comic Book Authenticity” is depicted here, and this time I truly do not believe that any of the 3 writers have any kind of fondness for the comics. The focus of Across the Spider-Verse is selling moviegoers on the importance of Spider-Man as a brand within Marvel, with a set of rules to be followed; a checklist of inciting traumas to be applied where the end result is a new Spider-Man. Conveniently, the film makes this subtext text by centering the film around the prevention of “Canon Events”, tragic deaths of loved ones that must happen because That’s Spider-Man. Mercifully, Lord and Miller rarely show our massive cast experience or be changed by said traumas — a film that thinks for itself, what a Marvel. Having read more comics than I think 99% of Letterboxd, Alternate Universe stories are among some of the laziest writing one can choose. The superior first film largely uses it for Family Guy cutaway tier gags; “Hey remember the Spider-Man Popsicle” novelty signaling to the adults in the room that this is Growing the Brand but fun. Now we must succumb to the Elseworlds Comic Story Effect: writing essentially a re-themed take on the platonic Spider Man second outing, each moment signposted through overt “meta” staging, and a complete wet fart of a 15 minute 3rd act after a 70 minute 1st to boot. One would hope that character could carry us through a lackluster script, but Lord and Miller and The Other One opt for a thin but wide approach instead. It feels as if character attributes were chosen at complete random. Jessica Drew is a strong black woman working while pregnant because… Ben Reilly is brooding because the 90s were grim and dark (yet nothing in the handful of Ben Reilly appearances I’ve read would even touch the vicinity of brooding). Like the aforementioned Cutaway Gags, characters who could be Sneakers O’Toolesian delightful non sequiturs overstay their welcome and confuse. The hired gun Lego commercial got an earnest laugh out of me, everything in the set pieces to follow would not. Once again the thankless job of creating something worth writing paragraphs about falls to the Animators. Eyes and stomachs in perfect alignment, they truly deliver on great leaps forward in mainstream animation. No minced words about it: this film can look gorgeous . However, due to the complete dearth of imagination from the top down everything feels off. I found myself getting genuinely overstimulated by the film at times; nothing moves right, scenes feel poorly timed, and not a single moment felt as effortlessly evocative as the sequence in the first film where Miles leaps off a building into a colorful void. Around the 50 minute mark, as we wind down on the prologue, Across starts to look legitimately ugly. Chromatic blurs fill the screen for no other reason than to exist, the camera rapidly adjusts itself throughout a scene, and your eyes struggle to find a place to rest while taking in the composition. Very few of the colorful compositions have meaning, I struggle to ascribe any real meaning to heavy decisions like a Trans Reading for Gwen because of how arbitrary the movie can look; the curtains are simply blue. It is creative flailing, masquerading as vision. People with little experience in either often call comics and film sister mediums. Both deal in the marriage of language and visual, and storyboarding kinda feels like a comic to the layman. The analogy can be allowed to continue to live regarding Across the Spider-Verse because the disconnect between animator and Director/Writer/Producer feels as if they couldn’t be any further apart — as if the worst instincts of American comics is a style to be worshipped and imitated. If you’ve ever read a bad comic with good art you’ll understand what I mean. If you haven’t, you can buy Kingdom Come for like 10 bucks now.

Muito descolado ser ficar chapado de falar com o outro plano. ... Fale Comigo não possui uma ideia original – nem mesmo ao jogar uma sessão espírita pro meio virtual – tampouco na sua temática, o seu mérito está na maneira em que a direção traz novas perspectivas no subgênero sobrenatural. O que entra também o recurso dos movimentos de câmera durante a possessão – conforme os personagens reagem em contato com a mão – com enquadramentos sufocantes, o que traz uma sensação de imersão e tensão. O ápice dessa construção – o que faz parecer que, uma vez que entramos no submundo, não saímos mais – é na montagem que transita com várias possessões no ritmo da faixa instrumental Le Monde e que vai intercalando com um remix de Edith Piaf – com um pesadelo se instaurando ao mesmo tempo que o caos das cenas se encerra ao som da música. Ter a narrativa centrada na perspectiva de Mia foi essencial para como a mudança de tom vai abraçando uma dissociação cada vez mais inconstante – e a sonoplastia é um elemento que acompanha os sentimentos conflitantes da personagem, a exemplo dos barulhos de água – porém, nesse tempo, é quando a narrativa passa a ser menos consistente e empolgante, e começa a seguir um caminho pessimista com a própria própria história em vez de buscar por resoluções criativas. Dessa forma, Talk to Me termina de modo cômodo, fugindo totalmente do ritmo alucinante e frenético que tinha iniciado, como se a mitologia tivesse sido pensada pela metade – mas que ainda assim consegue se relacionar com o tema de saúde mental.

Critiquing a movie with this much gravitas almost feels like internet suicide, but I’m gonna do it anyway. First of all, I’m happy this movie exists solely for the truckload of entertainment it has provided to me via all the media it has inspired. It is and always will be an absolute classic, and I’m honored to have finally seen it. But, judged on its own merits today, stacked up against a genre which it helped birth, I have to say, I didn’t like it. There are parts which I really liked, but they are too few and too far between. You know how some movies are three hours long yet they feel barely two? Well, The Godfather is a three-hour movie and feels like six. "Bloated" was the first thing that came to my mind when the credits rolled. Its insistence on showing you the mundane, dragging the hell out of it, and beating you over the head with it is truly something special. The plot points which should drive the story forward feel very unsatisfying. All the time that could have been spent on better character development is spent in the most inconsequential of all places, which hardly matters at the end of the day. And even though Al Pacino's presence and charisma is one of the few reasons why I stuck around until the end, his performance is still fairly plain—far removed from his best. Sadly, the biggest crime The Godfather has committed is that it must have been so good and influential when it came out that all the copycats have eventually caught up. All of the genre tropes have been done better a million times since, producing far more compelling stories than what the Corleone family has to offer today.

Overall good movie that I enjoyed watching. Most of the negative things I have to say about the film are a product of the era it was made. A lot of the acting seemed disingenuous, none of the female actors were very convincing in their roles. The foley work was very bad at times, and there were scenes with noticeable dubbing. Finally, I think many of the scene setting drew on too long (notably the wedding scene in the beginning, and the scenes of Micheal in Sicily). All that being said, it was a very enjoyable story. I can see how this movie clearly inspired a lot of media later on. There really aren’t many movies prior to 1990 that I have liked, but this was an enjoyable watch. The critical acclimation this film has received is - in my opinion - probably based a lot on how it compared to the other films of the period, and not based on all media from all time. This movie is ranked #2 movie of all time on IMDb. Without the nostalgia/bias I don’t think this movie could hold its own against many modern pictures
