Fails at being a western and fails even harder at being a mystery somehow. It's western genre tag is superficial and only goes as far as it's aesthetics and setting in history. The "mystery" is fed to you with information from left field that solves it artificially. The Hateful Eight tosses aside one of Tarantino's strongest senses as a director: that being his ability to instill a strong feeling of underlying menace throughout any given style of movie he makes. Just think of Jackie Brown, a movie essentially about a middle-aged romance, yet there is a scene of Samuel L Jackson's character in a car that genuinely strikes fear into my heart, and added another layer to every interaction with him going forth in the movie in spite of the character's many flubs and unforced errors. Hateful Eight feels sinister becuase the way it showcases evil is overt through nasty over the top violence and course language. It's stupid becuase the mystery that holds up this classic Tarantino menace fails if you're a prudent viewer and guessed that all the residents of the habedashery prior to the arrival of the Kurt Russell's stagecoach were the "bad guys". It fails because we have no scope for their wickedness apart from bounty rewards -- we have no reason to feel any sort of way about the antagonist, which is a shame as Tarantino has always rendered compelling and wicked ones in the past. Everything about this movie is just so self-indulgent from Tarantino. He narrated it with his annoying voice, his use of slow-mo, the amount of shots that last way too fucking long is maddening (think when the 4 passengers chapter starts for example); the jump back in time just for the events of the flashback to not give any new insight on the "mystery" that we already could have surmised the answer from Marquis' proselytizing theories; the split diopters on Walter Goggins near the end; the stupid voice distortion on Marquis that one time, and all the violence is turned up to 11 with people's heads being vaporized into a bloody mist with bullets (???) -- it's all so obnoxious. Also, what a weird message at the end. It's as if the movie is insinuating that racism can be mended if only we focused our efforts on destroying the true enemy: WOMEN. So dogshit. I look down on you as a person if you think this movie deserves any more that a 2/5 rating. Seriously.

This was my third to last Tarantino movie, and I was honestly surprised to still see him pulling out new tricks. It felt like Reservoir Dogs if I had dosed peyote before watching. The Hateful Eight was the complete opposite from the movie I was expecting, being the most cynical spaghetti western which revels in its simplicity and is a character piece through and through. I was pleased to find that, despite the runtime and despite the minimalistic approach, I was never bored. This is one of, if not Tarantino’s funniest movie, with some of his best dialogue. It has a really strong cast in general, but the three that shone the most for me was the master manipulator Major Warren, the oblivious Sheriff Mannix, and the feral opportunist Daisy Domergue. The catalyst of the conflict being a pot of coffee that sends a chain reaction of madness and killing is true Tarantino fashion. If I had to pull away one complaint, it would be that it’s a little too straightforward for its own good. While Reservoir Dogs actively had me pulling my hair out trying to connect the dots, here there was a mix of scenes I found predictable, and scenes that threw me for a loop. But then again, maybe that’s the point. Either way I found more enjoyment in the whacky characters and slapstick brutality than the whodunnit aspect.

Tension boils in the shelter of a blizzard, a gaggle of mysterious western icons, two bounty hunters with contrasting ethics, many racists on varying degrees of the hatred spectrum, a suave British hangman with an iron grip on justice, all packed into one perfect thriller. As obtuse and aggressive as Tarantino can be, in spite of his repugnant attitude, he compensates his behaviour with the sublimeness of his character creations. The Hateful Eight is a later instalment of Quentin’s, and it shows with the challenging dynamic of this whodunnit style thriller. The Hateful Eight is like a heartfelt serenade of the entire western genre, every moment is smothered in history and every actor wears their character in the snug confines of this time period. The ensemble are the familiar faces of Tarantino’s career, with Jennifer Jason Leigh joining the ride in her fantastically devilish outlaw Daisy Domergue. The dialogue of this film is filled with fantastic nuances and character quirks, the film is very much a masterclass in characterisation, with every character introduction playing off unique and grandiose. For a near 3 hour film, The Hateful Eight wastes no time, plowing through the snow and the plot slowly bubbling up to a chemical explosion of Tarantino mayhem. It’s as if his films have a promise, to get as bloody as possible after a long, intense grind of cake cutting tension. This film is a flawless concept with so many intricacies to digest. Samuel L Jackson is as funny as ever, Walton Goggins even more so, Jennifer Jason Leigh displays all her talents, and Kurt Russell demands your attention every second. The final chapter of this film is one of the most joyous experiences I’ve ever had in the cinema. Everyone laughed and cringed at all the right moments. The final chapter is truly a spectacular piece of dark comedy that signs the movie out on a bleakly humorous and then rounds everything with a truly sweet palate cleanser of an ending. This movie is absolute perfection. It’s a modern classic with all the trimmings of a pure Tarantino quest, lead down a red stained path, all the way to a trigger happy stand off.

I'm starting to think that the people who praise Eggers for historical accuracy are the same kind of people who think that photos are better than paintings because they "capture" the "reality" more precisely; that is to say: there is some perceived virtue in "depicting" the "past" as "accurately" as possible. I am sorry for all the quotation marks, but that's the quickest way to underline that all these ideas are... kind of dumb. I honestly don't care whether Eggers' movies are accurate and well-researched or not. It does not matter. There is so little intention behind the images on the screen that I can't bring myself to care about them. Also, the mask of "historical accuracy" kind of absolves the director of responsibility for any artistic decisions he makes; because, you see, that's how things were back then: violent, grey, boring, miserable. He's just showing things as true as possible! The weirdest part about the whole Eggers oeuvre for me is that I don't believe that he has any real interest or love for the eras he's depicting. It is paradoxical; he has built a reputation as this geek who is obsessed with the past, and yet it feels like they are just different Instagram filters for him. Puritanical 17th century New England? 19th century Germany? 10th century Scandinavia? Somehow, Eggers manages to make all of these look and feel the same. Ugh. We should all go read some Icelandic sagas (which are really fun and colourful and even humorous at times, by the way) instead of watching this.

More Art, with Less Splatter! So kann man, sich des Hamlets bedienend, diesen ebenfalls sich des Hamlets bedienenden Film wohl trefflich kommentieren, denn was Robert Eggers mit The Northman (2022) abliefert, ist im Grunde ein „Hamlet Light“, auch wenn es an schwergewichtigem Eisen und Blut keinesfalls mangelt. Wieder einmal gelingt es dem Regisseur, das Auge zu überwältigen, indem er die Kamera zahllose Bilder von dunkelumwölktem Unheil, nackter Brutalität, ungezähmter Kraft, aber auch betörender Schönheit zeichnen läßt, und auch sein Amlet könnte ein düsterer tragischer Held sein, denn er läßt sich unaufhaltsam von seinem Haß leiten, dem er Schuldige wie Unschuldige zum Opfer bringt. Ich sage hier bewußt: „Er könnte ein tragischer Held sein.“ In Wirklichkeit ist er es aber nicht, denn die Brutalität und Entschlossenheit, die er an den Tag legt, hat er mit allen Menschen, die um ihn herum leben, gemein, und mithin ist er eine gnadenlose Bestie unter vielen, und diese Gnadenlosigkeit ist es, die den Film letztendlich trotz all der Action, der Ausflüge in das Mystische und Übernatürliche, recht schnell langweilig werden läßt, gibt es doch nur einen einzigen Moment, in dem wir Amlet während eines inneren Kampfes erleben, nämlich dann, wenn er sich entscheiden muß, seinen Rachefeldzug abzubrechen, um mit der schwangeren Olga einer glücklicheren Zukunft entgegenzugehen, oder aber zurückzukehren, um seinen Onkel für sein Verbrechen zu töten. Dieser sehr kurze Moment wird jedoch schnell entschieden, wenn Amlet sich einredet, daß es für ihn und seine ungeborenen Kinder keine Ruhe geben würde, solange der Onkel noch lebt. Ungeachtet dessen, daß kaum ein Mann, der bei Trost ist und der mit Anya Taylor-Joy in einem Boot sitzt, ins Wasser springen würde, um jemanden anderen umzubringen, ist selbst dieser Augenblick einer, in dem Amlet keine eigene Entscheidung treffen muß. Schauen wir aber auf Shakespeares Hamlet, so sieht das schon anders aus: Eggers erzählt die Geschichte streng chronologisch und läßt den jungen Prinzen dabei auch zum Zeugen des Mords an seinem Vater werden. Mit eigenen Augen sieht er, daß sein Onkel die Meuchler anführt und danach den Befehl erteilt, den eigenen Neffen zu töten. Es gibt mithin keinen Zweifel daran, daß der Bastard-Bruder schuldig ist. Bei Shakespeare hingegen erhält Hamlet die Kunde, daß sein Vater keines natürlichen Todes gestorben, sondern ermordet worden sei, von einem Geist, der behauptet, der Geist seines Vaters zu sein, und ihm das Gelöbnis der Rache abnimmt. Im folgenden verwickelt sich Hamlet immer fester in ein Gewirr aus Zweifeln, denn er muß sich fragen, ob er tatsächlich dem Geist seines Vaters gegenüberstand oder einem bösen Geist, der ihn zu einem Mord verleiten will. Während Eggers‘ Amlet über weite Strecken des Filmes der Meinung ist, daß seine Mutter nur unter Zwang die Gattin des Onkels geworden ist, sieht Shakespeares Hamlet Gertrude freiwillig als Königin an der Seite des Claudius sitzen und sich so, nach dem 3. Buch Mose, des Inzests schuldig machen. Die solchermaßen komplizierte Situation läßt immer mehr den Zweifel an Hamlet nagen, der sich in einer aus den Fugen geratenen Welt wähnt, die er wieder ins Lot bringen muß, und diese Komplexität, sowohl die der Situation als auch die im Innenleben des Protagonisten, sucht man in Eggers‘ Verfilmung vergeblich. Selbst Amlets Liebesbeziehung zu Olga folgt dabei den 08/15-Regeln des Hollywood-Kinos, während der wahrhaft tragische Hamlet seine Ophelia, an der er auch zu zweifeln beginnt, mit seinem Verhalten zugrunde richtet. In The Northman mögen zwar die Landschaft und das Meer sehr oft nebelverhangen sein, aber eigentlich ist alles klar wie Kloßbrühe – und somit entsprechend langweilig und muß durch Sidequests wie den um das magische Schwert aufgepfeffert werden. Inszenatorisch und handlungsbezogen läßt sich The Northman mühelos in die Nähe von Wolfgang Petersons Hohl-Epos Troy (2004) rücken und ist für mich somit der, hoffentlich nicht nur bislang, schlechteste Film von Robert Eggers.

If you asked me for my favorite revenge story, I'd have to give it to Berserk. I consider that manga to be a fantastic achievement and a shining example of what a revenge story could be. Berserk is a story that invites you to grow close to it's characters, to understand their desires, and to understand what they have to lose and what loss would mean to them. Upon the moment of betrayal, that seething hatred was something I felt on a visceral level. I was upset alongside the characters, and I was desperate (and still am) to see revenge take form. Comparing Berserk to The Northman is admittedly unfair. Comics, as a medium, can be much longer than movies. We're able to spend so much more time with the characters, and we're given a more intimate understanding of who they are. But what can I really say? I was ultimately disappointed with how little The Northman urged me to care about it's protagonist. It's a fairly familiar revenge plot (reminiscent of Hamlet) along the lines of "you killed my loved one; now I'll kill you". Protagonist vows to kill the man who "made his life hel", but you never get an understanding of what that misery looks or feels like to him. He is stoic, hyper-serious, and emotionally distant from the audience. None of this was aided by some non-sequitur side-questy sequences that were largely uninteresting. Don't get me wrong, the visuals are great. If all you want is brutality, it's in there. It's got a vibe of raw, primal hyper-masculinity through the filter of a psychedelic haze. It's actually pretty neat. Unfortunately the story is too unfocused and detached. Definitely my least favorite from Eggers. Pretty sure Willem Dafoe's character hangs dong, though, and that's cool.

Why, because we’re given the truth behind Amleth's vengeance.  We're told of the horrors his father committed, the freedom his mother was afforded from his death and still Amleth continues his rage.  It sucks the air out of his hero's journey and reframes his rage as childlike ignorance. Which to an extent is fine. We’ve seen stories of children continuing cycles of anger started from their forefathers. It just kind of made his mother and uncle a bit more sympathetic than I expected. A beautiful film, nonetheless.  Anya Taylor-Joy playing a witch in this film was a tongue-in-cheek nod to her previous work with Eggers. While I grasped the message of our fates predestined (nature v nurture), I had hoped Amleth would’ve broken that cycle on that boat. He doesn’t and instead gives us a sick battle below a volcano. Sick visuals! Not my favorite film entry from Eggers, but he gave me a vengeful Nicole Kidman. I take what I can get.

To put things briefly, The Substance is a relatively sound film, although, it still comes with a fair share of issues. As films of this more thematic nature, and more broadly within the horror genre typically demand, you’re sort of supposed to just go with the plot, which I struggle with. It’s not necessarily poorly written, it’s just contrived, not implausibly, but I still feel the beats could’ve been better strung together. Speaking of themes, it touches primarily on our contemporary culture, our media, and on the treatment of women, particularly within the public sphere; although I do find that the film fails to boldly challenge our perception of these social facets, or issues. For example, the premise, alongside how the film is shot evidently wish to discuss the self-objectification of the individual, of which is intrinsically tied to social norms, and to capitalism; yet this is highly surface level, and largely visual, it isn't actually protested. Overall, it's quite straightforward in its messaging, quite literally infantilising a woman, and I don’t have any qualms with it, however, a bit of nuance, or development upon these themes would’ve made the piece a touch more grounding, connecting, perhaps it might’ve helped alleviate the disconnect created by the grotesque body horror. On that, yeah, uhm, the film excels in disgusting me, although, I expected as much and genuinely struggled to convince myself to watch it. More technically, I was pleased in that colour wasn’t shied away from, as is the case frequently in this genre, and in this era; and the camerawork was solid, if albeit a bit uninspired—I also found it notable that some shots were clearly added solely for the sake of evoking disgust, or discomfort, even if the details were irrelevant, most prominently in the opening scenes of the film.

SFF2024 #7 (Closing Night Film) Spends a surprising amount of its third act riffing on extremely specific images from a not very well-regarded Doctor Who episode. This gets a lot of mileage out of its excellent concept, which allows for both lots of squeamishly fun body horror and plenty of (definitely unsubtle but undeniably worthwhile) social commentary about how we view women’s bodies culturally & the speed at which we tend to discard those on our screens once they reach a certain age. To her credit, Fargeat handles the topic deftly without resorting to the self-seriousness that trips up many a horror movie that sets out to say something about a specific issue, though I did feel at times that the film’s camp tone was keeping me at a slight ironic distance from the emotions of the characters. Said characters are brought to life nicely by the cast, though. I don’t think this is quite as much of a Demi Moore showcase as some of the Cannes critics hailed it as (by plot necessity, she’s off-screen for large chunks of the runtime), but it’s certainly bold, electric work from her. There’s a sequence where her character is overcome by body image-related insecurities while getting ready to go out, and it’s made as viscerally heartbreaking as it is by Moore’s excellent work. Margaret Qualley’s material is a bit more one-note but, as usual, she sells it on her screen presence alone (also, at the risk of proving the movie’s point, it must be said that she is quite hot). Dennis Quaid’s turn would be way too much in almost any other movie but it works for this one’s camp sledgehammer of an approach. Fargeat’s cooking with all the right ingredients here, but I think she undercuts herself with self-indulgence. There’s no real reason for this to be 140 minutes long; the concept could have easily made for a brilliant, punchy 90-minutes. By the third act, the movie just keeps piling hats onto hats in service of a gorefest that strays too far from the original allegory. It’s not that it isn’t a natural escalation of the conflict, per se, but I think it’s possible to escalate things a little too much, to the point where it becomes more numbing than impactful. There were several great possible endings in the climax, but Fargeat just kept dragging it out for no apparent reason, and the whole movie - while never boring - is similarly just a bit flabby given the simplicity of its plot. The film’s issues are not big enough to entirely sink it, but they definitely made me feel a bit out of step with the hype from Cannes. As recent Cannes-awarded, women-directed body horrors go, I’m much more of a Titane man.

QUE FILME FILHA DA PUTA! Uma mistura de enjôo e deslumbre; UMA CRITICA DO CARALHO! A obra leva o "odiar a si mesmo" para a físico; Lize odeia a Sue e visce versa e se machucam diversas vezes durante o longa, talvez uma metáfora a bulimia e suas consequências psicológicas, porém nesse caso, físicas. A Sue extraiu toda a juventude de Lise, mas não podemos esquecer que a Sue nunca foi um ser humano independente. Ou seja, a pressão social para voltar a juventude e ter um corpo fino, pele lisa e rosto simétrico, trouxe (fisicamente) uma anorexia para a protagonista. Fazendo com que ela compulsóriamente, trocasse de corpo sem mesmo pensar nas consequências, como na cena do Fred em que a Lise finalmente tenta experimentar sua beleza natural (receosa com seu futuro), mas se rende após múltiplas comparações. Outra coisa muito interessante de se analisar nessa cena; é a forma que Fred conversa com Lise, ele é carinhoso, fofo, compreensível e verdadeiro. Ali, ela se sente amada, afinal, até aquele ponto ela era tratada como algo defasado, algo que já podia ser jogado fora, em contrapartida, Sue tinha um tapete vermelho estendido em seus pés. O menino da moto, o vizinho e o dono da empresa tiveram esse comportamento, e Fred fugiu desse padrão. Porém, críticas e inseguranças sempre entram mais na cabeça de quem não está satisfeito com o presente, por isso o final trágico. Isso fica evidente quando compramos cenas da Sue e da Lise. Ao se banhar, Sue ergue sua cabeça, passa a mão pelo corpo e sorri enquanto faz isso, agora, Lise banhava com uma postura fechada, encolhida, quase como se aquele corpo fosse uma vergonha para ela. Mas o choque vem no final, quando ela já drenou tanto sua matriz, que vê beleza no corpo que tanto odiava. O problema não era ela, nunca foi, o problema sempre foi homens que juram ser uma profecia cobrando perfeição mas esquecem que comem iguais animais famintos por 3 meses. "Me dê uma versão melhor de mim, POR FAVOR!"

Wicked tells the story of Elphaba, a young woman born with green skin—an outcast due to her difference—who arrives at Shiz University. There, she meets Glinda, her polar opposite: popular, privileged, and deeply concerned with her image. Despite their differences, a genuine friendship forms between them as Elphaba gradually discovers that the world of Oz is far less wonderful than it appears. What I found interesting was the way the film questions who gets to decide what is "good" or "bad." Elphaba is rejected before she has even done anything, simply because she is different. Conversely, Glinda fits the mold of the "perfect" girl: beautiful, popular, and well-liked. Yet, as the story unfolds, this contrast becomes far less clear-cut. The relationship between the two is clearly one of the film’s highlights. They represent two completely different ways of responding to how others perceive them: Elphaba ultimately accepts rejection rather than compromising her convictions, whereas Glinda is far more invested in validation and popularity. Visually, I really enjoyed the world-building. Oz is incredibly colorful, intricately designed, and almost fairytale-like, featuring a striking contrast between Glinda’s bright, pink aesthetic and the darker tones associated with Elphaba. The costumes and sets give the film a strong identity, and the musical numbers are clearly designed as full-scale spectacles. However, despite all this, I felt the film sometimes lacked the depth it seemed to promise. While certain themes—such as discrimination and propaganda—are interesting, they remain somewhat simplistic. The film spends a great deal of time establishing its world and characters, which can make the story feel like it is moving rather slowly at times. The fact that this is only the first part of the story also reinforces this impression. We reach the end just as several plotlines are barely getting started. This is understandable, given that the film is designed as the first chapter, but as a standalone movie, I find it makes the experience less satisfying. Spoiler (ending): Elphaba finally discovers that the Wizard and Madame Morrible are manipulating events in Oz—specifically using the plight of the Animals to consolidate their power. She refuses to be part of this system and flees, while Glinda remains in Oz. Elphaba is then publicly branded a threat. However, the "Defying Gravity" scene is brilliantly executed; it perfectly captures Elphaba’s choice: she would rather be seen as wicked than conform to others' expectations of her. Ultimately, I found *Wicked* interesting and visually stunning, with excellent chemistry between the two female leads, yet I was left wanting a bit more regarding the story and the depth of certain themes. There was immense potential, but I was more impressed by the world-building and the spectacle than truly moved by the narrative itself.

Interesting take on the character, but I much prefer Gene Wilder's bizarre, mysterious, slightly unsettling eccentric chocolatier who you don't know if you can fully trust. Chalamét is absolutely not a bad actor by any stretch, but the "young, sweet inventor we're meant to be rooting for as a feel-good origin story" is a whiplash turn from the OG movies. It might likely be a bias from seeing him in previous roles but he didn't quite shake off that vibe he always has to fully step into a musical, theatrical role of someone being loud and vibrant and filling the screen with performance. Also he spent the movie doing a huge balancing act between kind-hearted trickster and a naive, forgetful himbo at times, which didn't do a lot for a fully fleshed out character. It does leave you with a sense of his "young genius" being incongruous with his "bumbling his way through the plot" at parts. I can see how people who never watched the OG film might enjoy this one more than I did. Can see this dropping over time, honestly. Right now I’m carried by how great Inde is here (the rest of the acting is, by and large, mediocre) and the boldness. But the theming here gets pretty sloppy even with the simple premise. The film does a good enough job making Bear out to be “the bad guy” for the most part. He’s meek, cowardly, selfish, and irresponsible, to the extent that he is clearly a rapist by the film’s end. I think where I get a little frustrated with how clumsy the messaging here is, is that because the premise is still fantastical by nature, there’s still that lingering aspect of plausible deniability for too much of the film. Bear thinks it’s odd at first and he wonders if it worked (looks it up and originally the info actually suggests it DOESN’T work) but rolls with it. And initially he tries to be respectful in the face of odd behavior. And eventually he starts rolling with it. By the time it’s really confirmed for him, he’s ebbing between whether to kill himself to set her free and not caring about Nikki or her autonomy at all as long as wish Nikki can “perform” Nikki appropriately. The former would be near heroic and the other is downright monstrous. Everything is unequivocally Bear’s fault (though Ian certainly isn’t helpful) and yet the situation is so outrageous that the character’s condemnation accidentally becomes somewhat conditional. Unlike in the real world, Bear is never given a choice to just respect Nikki’s autonomy after the wish is made, before he begins to act intentionally. He immediately is locked into suicide or manipulation as his two options, and that’s where this basically fails as cultural critique. Technically there’s possibly a loophole with the wish and he actually attempts to exploit this, but there’s no clear indication as to how it would’ve panned out. The inherent issue here is that as pathetic as Bear is, there is probably a version of this film that gives him more reasonable opportunities to exit this situation cleanly and he still doesn’t take them due to his desire to possess “Nikki.” But that’s not really this movie and the messaging gets confused as a result. This thing is also very, very mean-spirited in general. I don’t really expect horror to be happy, but this whole thing really doesn’t have me rooting for anyone to make it through unscathed. I’m not sure any of the core four here totally deserves their fate, but I also think it’s telling that the two men are far closer to deserving it and the women go through, far, far worse, to the point of borderline directorial cruelty when they’ve functionally done very little wrong. Nikki is clearly the primary victim here and thinking about the film and how flimsy its messaging is, this reveals itself to be nearly torture porn for violence against women. I think about how easy Ian gets off, and maybe that’s “commentary,” but when I see interviews with Barker, he seems wholly unable to articulate any sort of genuine thematic intent. I think he just understands that watching women suffer feels bad, and decided to make that a movie. He’s right, but that doesn’t make this any good. The more I write this, the more I realize I do not like Obsession.

Inde Navarrette's spectacular performance reminded me of a golden retriever (it's important her performance is natural at the beginning and then as a stunted dog later) and I found myself think about why I'd never own a pet again. There is this perverted want from the owner to own a dog. It is captivity. Moreover the dog doesn't have a choice in loving who will ultimately feed them. While you live your life, their life is nearly paused (you should take them to a dog daycare) and you restrict what they can do when you're together. It's this weird, acceptable relationship where almost instantly you can be loved. Just because you chose this for her doesn't make it less real. It sounds to me you have a moral obligation to be there for her. But love is not meant to be instant. It's not even meant to be initially comfortable or gratifying. OBSESSION, which I don't really think is the right title, could be sold as the anti-Prince Charming and Disney fantasy. Horror elements are clearly inspired by the Forbidden Room scene in PULSE. What's actually provocative isn't a gun in a person's mouth but expecting the bullet to come as they fumble with the mechanics of killing themselves. I had just told Tony the other day I don't reflect anymore (I suspect because I'm just so focused now) then I put on Depression Cherry and listened to it three times on the plane to Spain. Levitation's lyrics "there is no right time" and Days of Candy's "the universe is riding off with you" just hit me. I think I realized after watching OBSESSION, which iterates on skipping the awkward asking part of starting a relationship, how I'd been keeping myself in limbo and protecting myself from any possibility for a little too long. I start thinking of apologizing to Ines 20 years ago for leaving her in the basement and having ignored it, I think I thought it was weird kissing a girl younger than me at the time, that you were supposed to kiss someone your own age. I lost a friend when she moved. I thought about Kat and writing back after she ghosted me for two years but I was probably coming up on my own anniversary. I thought about how Nate was someone I felt close to but never really made a strong enough effort to maintain that relationship (so I texted him). I thought about, again, how I need to be kinder to my dad. That being disappointed is not an excuse for being irritable or curt. I thought about getting a plane ticket to Biaritz. I thought about the four or so questions I want to ask this girl at the gym and how this past week would have been a good time to ask them but I skipped lifting because my elbows and wrist hurt but then asking those questions would have been fine to ask the last two years and next week too. I thought about how I feel like the ground underneath me is unstable, how I can't take a shower without feeling like the tub might split in half and I'd sink through the floor or how some parts of the house feel like I could put a leg through it if I jumped. I thought about how these coming months feel like a major infection point in my life where I've been riding on table stakes with this game and either the last five months of development and time and sacrifice (no one but me asked to do)—well, I'll be rich or I'll have been delusional. I thought about how I shouldn't take my side projects so seriously and then in the same train of thought how I should quit my job to pursue them fully and if I truly enjoyed what I did, I wouldn't have to worry about the money. I thought about financial situation and how far and close I was to $4 million dollars. I thought about the insane commitment I'd say to someone, that I'd spent 22 years of my life trying to fit in and then the last 8 years being comfortable with who I am, that my delusions of grandeur and creation will likely come up short, that my goals may change, that I wasnt looking to absorb someone and was happy with the status quo but if they added to my life, I'd be unwaveringly faithful and excited to see the world through their eyes. I thought about how I wouldn't use dating apps, it'd have to be an approach. I thought about how the end doesn't concern me anymore, it's the middle parts where there's choices being made. I thought about how I'm done with games. I thought about how I hope my brother outgrows his feelings of inconveniencing people over his own comfort.  I thought about how recently my eyes get really watery again when I'm out in public spaces that aren't the gym almost like I'm going to cry. I thought about writing again. Sigh coz I've been putting off logging this. I watched it twice to verify my suspicions and can say with absolute certainty that this is the work of a douchebag. Curry Barker is a douchebag. I have turned into a conspiracy theorist because of this film - the internet has decided it is a feminist masterpiece. My thesis is that Curry Barker's original premise was innately misogynistic and has only been altered to make it vaguely interpretable as feminist because he realised that is more profitable. I read an interview where Barker said the original inspiration for the film was seeing an actress play a character who shifted between emotions really quickly, and it freaked him out the idea of a woman who could switch emotions really fast. I will not insult my imaginary reader by explaining the misogynistic implications of this and tje historical demonisation of women's emotions and labelling them as hysterical yadda yadda yadda.  I will refer to the taboos still surrounding women's mental health and the dual fetishization / demonisation of "crazy women" which I think lies at the heart of this film. Barker also specifically stipulates that she isn't possessed, but is simply acting how someone who loves Bear "more than anyone in the world" would act. Okay, so the horror is not supernatural, but simply grounded in her acting mentally ill. Again, not gonna reiterate why that's an issue. But it also makes no sense, because she does things that objectively don't fit into that - moving in reverse for a start. Why would you write something that so clearly seems like a possession or an alternative entity, then deny its existence? Unless you have no clear idea of what you actually want to SAY and simply want to base a film of an aesthetic or concept, the concept here being crazy woman. It's just left open-ended enough that he has a get out of jail free. Yes, Bear is depicted in some ways as a villain. He is callous, lacks a firm grasp of the notion of consent, chooses to ignore Nikki's cries for help, and is selfish. For a woman watching Nikki's torment, the real horror lies there, and many women have stated that's why it's a good horror film. And I'm not going to undermine the positives in the way it depicts that selfishness, and there's definitely an argument to be made that he's playing with the clichés of how men view woman to create this film. But I do just think that's an intelligent viewer giving too much credit to a not that intelligent writer / director. Ultimately, that concept is not where the manufactured fear comes from, it all comes from Nikki carrying out clichéd versions of the crazy woman which are largely borrowed from films like Fatal Attraction and Misery even. Also, I'd argue the framing of the sex scene is still loaded with male gaze and the real fear being that a woman is being duplicitous but that's a whole other thing that I can't really figure out how to explain. And if he's so feminist, why is the naked defiled corpse of Sarah on display in the final sequence? Surely this undermines the whole imagined feminist thesis? What's the point of that? Why are we sexualising maimed corpses? Oh yeah because curry barker uses violence against women as a horror tool instead of something to genuinely dissect. Notice that the most gratuitous violence in the film is done to Sarah by Nikki, or to Nikki by herself. Both the men who die do so in relatively "clean" ways, no screaming or blood or mutilation and certainly no naked faceless corpse in fetish gear. Yes yes they'll argue that that's the point, is how Bear's passive selfishness and desire for control results in the destruction of women, but I still feel like the film's lens absolutely relishes the visual mutilation of women in a way I don't think should be interpreted as feminist. It's just more shock horror at the expense of women. I guess my question is: if Curry Barker is allegedly parodying the male gaze by embodying it, how is the actual product different onscreen? Also, when asked how they got Nikki's face to look so creepy and whether it was SFX or makeup or just her acting, he claimed it was a choice he'd made to use a special kind of makeup which is "called contour I think" (hate him). It's actually directly lifted from the Tiktok uncanny valley makeup trend which was started by Emilia Barth who he did not credit, so him taking credit for this idea pisses me off, and he also then removes credit from Inde Navarette, which also pisses me off. His other horror effects are just stolen from Tiktok horror shorts, like straight up putting it in reverse. I'm all for low budget cinema, but don't act like he is a genius for making a feature length Tiktok short. It's just cheap scares and self congratulating for ideas that aren't his own. Also the pacing is shit. She acts so insane on literally night one. There's no buildup. You're telling me he slowly realises she's not fine when she does that to his cat on night one. And I know you're going to say he chooses to ignore it and that's why he's the villain, but from a filmmaking pov it just makes no sense anyway. Also they're just screaming so much. It feels lazily explosive. I really really feel instinctively that this is a film about how men's biggest fear is a woman who is crazy, and the fear of being blamed for taking advantage of that. I believe Bear is still positioned as a victim, alongside Nikki. People are saying the point is that it seems like that but actually it's much deeper but I really think we're giving him too much credit. Curry Barker has made the premise and plot vague enough that it has been interpreted by emotionally intelligent viewers to carry that same emotional intelligence that they watched with, and he has piggybacked off that because it's more profitable. It's literally making me feel insane and no one seems to agree with me on this but seriously no one can tell me otherwise!!!!!! I know in my SOUL.

I can’t believe that the film community have been so vocal in their support for what’s, at best, an average, feature length episode of Black Mirror (main character discovers something that makes their desire a reality, but it spirals out of control rapidly). I’m all for a successful non-franchise film, which is why I’ll give Obsession some credit, but we can do better than this.

Add Nikki’s moves to Fortnite, 6.99 for the jitter in the corner emote It’s hard to give this an unbiased review with the discussion this provoked in culture, but I think people’s excitement about showing how men don’t value women’s autonomy is making them not see how this movie doesn’t say or do a whole lot else. Essentially we are starting with the premise of “what if pygmalion’s statue had some personality beforehand mixed with monkey paw antics”. It’s not a terrible idea but having the film be wholly in bears perspective loses most, if not all of the horror of Nikki’s side and diminishes any message trying to be put across. I get the idea, it was always superficial to him, so anytime she deviates from his ideal partner persona he starts being like “why am I here” only to be comforted by the touch and reassurance he bought and paid for. The idea that she is is fully under his control with no autonomy is mainly seen from his side (which doesn’t get talked enough about regarding the lacanian mirror philosophy of how she reflects bear back himself). And these ideas work fine but when here will the kernel of the movie be sprung: you can be a huge loser coward but don’t let being so pussillanimous hurt others. The conversation about this movie ends with “even the nice guys will rape you” which while true, isn’t going as far as the movie is even letting you step. We see bears cowardice and fear throughout the movie, and by only being able to judge what we see, he’s probably internalized some toxic masculinity from Ian if not also just from existence. Nikki doesn’t get possessed by any spirit, she gets possessed by bears spirit (maybe why you only get one wish) which is full of loser cowardice and will grovel at any push back to try to fix his mistakes. Obviously he gets worse as the movie goes on and he’s rightfully criticized and called a rapist but we need to interrogate why he did this and why he acted this way. He’s a person who wanted someone to love him. That’s not a crazy wish, I doubt even the most hardcore incel could claim they never wished to be loved nor the most attractive person in the world. It’s not a sin to want to ignore the rough parts of developing a relationship. We don’t know the backstory besides a few small fragments of any of the main crew which hurts everyone’s personhood and leads to a lot of flat moments from a filmmaking and thematic perspective; but what we can parse is that Nikki is nice, wants to write, and doesn’t like a high school nickname and that bear is indecisive and a coward. We aren’t going off a lot here. The “did she like him before the wish or not debate” is pointless because they both are withholding their honest feelings to each other. Bear is guessing because he’s a loser and can’t talk about his feelings while Nikki says she’s famously hard to read if she crushes on someone or not. There’s no fault on Bear for wishing she loved him in a normal seeming world where magic hasn’t shown to him to be real. Where we can criticize him though, is for his main trait through the movie of being a coward. This man is not in touch with himself, he said during the beginning monologue that Nikki was the first person he really felt he could open up to due to her being the only nice person when he moved there and couldn’t shake his feelings just from that. Buddy, go talk to a normal non fratty guy over beers and figure your shit out. You don’t need to wish and rape a mirror version of yourself who only gives into your worst desires as those consequences escalate. I would list the cowardice on display but then I’m citing the whole movie. But to take the pills in order to get the last little bit of bliss can be the cherry on top of what I don’t feel like writing out. It’s late and I’m ranting. Maybe I’ll clean this up at some point but I think we need to discuss the dirty heart, our Id (I don’t think bear has much super ego to provide morals, just an ego to stop from looking bad), rather than just cast the bad man down to the depths. We can see that from the online manosphere backlash of this movie that this is clearly a problem that resonates with men that they don’t want to look at. It’s hard to say “don’t just call it the male rape fantasy movie to protect the dumb dudes who don’t think he’s wrong” but I think there needs to be some other avenue to get people who don’t get it to approach it. And that’s no one persons responsibility. But at the end of the day our art should try to help us see ourselves better and not help to obscure the truth that we don’t wanna talk about. Watched this with my friends after we finished WABIAD, which was some fundraiser, and honestly… what a way to end the day 😭 This movie had us laughing, screaming, and getting genuinely freaked out at the same time. Watching something this psychological and gory at school probably wasn’t the smartest idea, but somehow being surrounded by my friends made the whole experience even better. Every disturbing moment became ten times funnier because of our reactions. From a horror lover’s perspective, I really enjoyed the overall plot. There was something genuinely smart about the way everything unfolded, and I liked that it wasn’t just relying on gore for the sake of being gory. The psychological side made it much more interesting, especially when you start questioning what’s actually happening and where things are going. That being said, the movie definitely felt a little too fast. I think some scenes could have been given more time to breathe, especially the moments that were building tension or developing the story. I wanted to sit with certain ideas a little longer instead of immediately being thrown into the next thing. Still, the combination of psychological horror, gore, disturbing moments, and the absolutely chaotic experience of watching it with friends made this such a fun watch. Definitely the kind of horror movie that becomes even better when you’re sitting next to your friends trying not to scream while also laughing at each other. Would I watch it again? Probably. Would I recommend watching it at school with your friends? Absolutely not… but also absolutely yes😭

Obsessão é um filme eu não entendo como o pessoal fala que é ruim, o único motivo plausível pra mim por pessoal não gostar é só questão de opinião mesmo, por que devemos concordar que o filme é muito bem feito. A fotografia é muito bonita e consegue criar uma sensação constante de desconforto, usando bem a iluminação e os enquadramentos para acompanhar o clima cada vez mais intenso da história. A trilha sonora talvez seja uma das melhores que eu já vi, principalmente pelo fato de tocar forever no final mas tirando isso as outras músicas também merece muito destaque. Ela ajuda bastante a construir a tensão e, em vários momentos, consegue deixar cenas comuns muito mais inquietantes. É aquele tipo de trilha que realmente contribui para a experiência do filme, em vez de simplesmente estar ali no fundo. A atuação da Inde Navarrette foi outro ponto que gostei bastante. Ela consegue transmitir muito bem as emoções da personagem, principalmente nos momentos em que a situação começa a fugir do controle. Para mim, é uma das melhores coisas do filme. Apesar disso, acho que o roteiro poderia desenvolver algumas situações e personagens um pouco melhor. Em certos momentos, senti que o filme poderia ir mais fundo nas ideias que apresenta, e o ritmo também oscila um pouco. Outro ponto que eu não gostei no filme é uma cena específica que o Ian deseja 1 bilhão de dólares e começa a cair rios de dinheiro, eu simplesmente odiei essa cena, pra mim acabou com clima da cena, considerando que o filme tava quase no final. Mesmo com esses problemas, Obsessão funciona muito bem como um suspense psicológico, principalmente por sua estética, sua trilha sonora e pela atuação da Inde Navarrette.
E é tão bom que chega ser nojento, doentio e perturbador. Me deu ódio. É sempre um homem. E esse filha da puta ainda fica perguntando “você gosta de mim?” Caralho, vsfd, olha a merda que você fez

I would give Obsession 2.5 out of 5 stars . Overall, I found the movie to be pretty strange, and while I thought the basic concept was interesting, I did not think the way the story played out worked very well. The idea behind the movie had a lot of potential and could have made for a really interesting psychological story, but I felt that the execution made the movie confusing and, at times, difficult to take seriously.One of my biggest problems was the story. I thought the plot had some interesting ideas, but the way everything developed felt somewhat forced and unrealistic. Instead of building tension naturally, some of the events felt like they were happening simply to move the story forward. I also felt that certain parts of the movie could have been developed more because the characters' decisions did not always make sense to me.The acting was okay overall, but it was not something that stood out to me. There were some good performances and believable moments, but I did not think the acting was strong enough to make up for some of the problems with the story. Because the movie relies so much on its characters and their relationships, I think stronger performances and more developed characters could have made the story much more effective.That being said, I do think the movie deserves some credit for its concept. There were moments where I could see what the filmmakers were trying to accomplish, and I think the idea could have worked really well with a different approach. The movie had the potential to be much more suspenseful and psychologically interesting than it ended up being.Overall, I wasn't a huge fan of Obsession . I thought the concept was cool, but the execution, story, and some of the acting kept me from really getting invested in the movie. There were definitely some interesting ideas, but I don't think they were developed as well as they could have been. For those reasons, I would give Obsession 2.5 out of 5 stars.

Obsessão é o básico bem feito. É o simples que funciona. Uma trama muito bem desenvolvida do início ao fim. Excelente atuação de Inde Navarrete (Nikki) e uma excelente direção de Curry Baker.

Curry Baker retira todo o aspecto mágico deste tipo de estória e leva-a para o mais puro desconforto e horror, com o auxílio da fotografia de Taylor Clemons que faz bom uso das sombras e do desfoque para criar a sugestão, apresentando uma "enfeitiçada" condenada a ser outra pessoa para servir ao desejo de um protagonista que aparenta ser um cara legal, porém, Curry consegue mostrar-nos uma perversidade neste tipo de comportamento que vai piorando a cada cena. Além disso, todo o encadeamento de eventos levam ao horror graças à interpretação da Inde Navarrette, sua variedade no tom de voz, suas expressões e sua fisicalidade causam um sério medo no telespectador. E o final é um dos melhores do gênero.

Deux flics de province tellement dépassés par leur enquête qu'ils préfèrent frapper des suspects au hasard et consulter une voyante plutôt que suivre une vraie méthode scientifique, l'académie de police coréenne n'a visiblement jamais entendu parler de la scène de crime qu'on ne piétine pas à dix personnes. Bong Joon-ho enchaîne les scènes qui devraient installer une tension glaçante mais qui basculent sans prévenir dans un comique presque slapstick, comme cette poursuite ridicule dans les champs de riz où l'un des flics dégringole une pente en pleine filature. La scène de l'interrogatoire musclé, censée être un tournant dramatique fort, se retrouve elle aussi parasitée par ce ton étrange qui hésite entre le grave et le grotesque. Et le twist final, où l'enquêteur revient des années plus tard sur les lieux sans jamais avoir eu de réponse claire, tombe complètement à plat après tant de tergiversations tonales. Bref, ce mélange volontaire d'humour et d'enquête criminelle ne m'a jamais permis de rentrer dans le film, ni par la peur ni par la tension, le tout m'ayant laissé complètement indifférent du début à la fin, 1 étoile.

Pissed me off. I get it, I understand why it ends the way it ends but it was so immensely frustrating it ruined the movie for me. And I get that that is the point!!! Admittedly, I didn’t know that this movie was based on a true story and that it was a cold case in 2003 until it ended and my brother told me, so know that I know that, I get it even more. And so I don’t necessarily dislike the idea of a no-answer (the final shot is amazing, yeah) — especially if that was the ‘truth’ at the time — and of course I get that the cops are meant to be corrupt and that the desperation of an unsolvable crime drives people to the brink, but I had a very hard time caring about men with power abusing it while women were being brutally murdered, seemingly in the background. I like Bong Joon Ho, and I didn’t think that this was a hyper misogynistic movie, but the brutality of the crimes felt so commonplace. The victims were consistently treated as a narrative afterthought and I just couldn’t bring myself to care about it at all. The cops torture men to get a confession for their own sake. Of course they don’t care about the women being raped and murdered with their own clothes, why would they? All they want is a confession, which is what the movie makes us care about. The women are an afterthought to the corruption. They are victims twice over, once in ‘practice’ (for lack of a better term), and for a second time when they are effectively forgotten about during the course of the investigation. And I get that that is sadly the way it almost always seems to be in real life, and perhaps the movie does it so well, it portrays that calloused, misogynistic corruption that seeps into everything so well that I couldn’t stand it. I felt like this meme while attempting to laugh at the dropkicks. How can I care about anything in the face of such brutality, especially when that brutality seems to be barely relevant? I don’t think it’s a bad movie, but I rarely write searching for objectivity, so I can only say that I hated it. Not for me at all. Once again, I understand why it does all that it does, and I guess I understand why it’s hailed as a Great, but I couldn’t look past how cavalier it was towards women being consistently brutalized. And I understand that perhaps that’s the way it’s meant to be, I guess it is a critique on that very calloused misogynistic corruption, but it feels a bit like the idea of an anti war movie. How can a movie not be misogynistic when most of its female characters are shown with their limbs splayed out on the ground? I’ve been very angry lately and I just can’t bring myself to ignore misogyny more than any woman does every day.

Let’s be honest: if you strip away all the pseudo-intellectual interpretations people have of this movie, it’s literally about nothing. It feels like everything that happens was made solely to build up to the ending. And yes, the ending is interesting in its own way, but it’s nowhere near as groundbreaking, revolutionary, or profound as people try to make it out to be. Movies like this existed before, were being made around the same time, and continued to be made afterward. There’s nothing particularly new here, other than the fact that this specific movie was made by Koreans. And if you take the ending away, there’s basically nothing left. The movie doesn’t stand out in any other way. There’s no particularly interesting detective element, no characters you actually want to follow, and no dialogue that’s especially engaging. Just exaggerated emotional reactions that start getting annoying after a while. It’s an incredibly boring movie. Yes, it has an idea, and yes, that idea is expressed reasonably well, but it’s hardly some extraordinary concept that magically makes up for everything else. It’s simply a mediocre movie about nothing that people seem to worship way too much — and, honestly, the only real reason I can see for that is that it was made in Korea. There just doesn’t seem to be any other explanation

I found out after that this was based on a true story, of a then still unidentified murderer. This movie does make many statements. Among other things, I think it was meant to highlight the unethical ways police at the time operated, but also the bad conditions people lived in, the violence in the everyday, blame laid on disabled people because it was convenient, and unending other problems which seem to build the violence to the point of murder, and the inadequacy of the police in catching the culprit. And you do feel the helplessness, yet another murder happens and you’re still not any closer to the answers. There are criminals among us in society and they could be anyone. The way the movie ends could be interpreted in different ways, but it implies that society is part of the problem, which includes you. I liked the color grading and the vibe of the film, definitely felt like the time period it was supposed to have taken place in, but not my first pick because of how crude it was. The first half was worse.

Au vu de ses excellentes notes, le film n'est sûrement pas mauvais, mais c'est un style que je trouve inintéressant au possible. J'ai bien compris l'intention : utiliser l'enquête pour inverser la morale des deux inspecteurs et critiquer une police incompétente qui doit absolument fermer une enquête pour garder une réputation. L'idée est bonne, mais je me suis profondément ennuyé. L'enquête est omniprésente, mais manque cruellement de tension. On enchaîne les interrogatoires sans suspense avec des suspects ridicules, comme le mec en slip à plumes roses suspendu au plafond ou le personnage autiste utilisé comme ressort comique. Cette ambiance tout sauf sérieuse, avec des flics qui lâchent des high kick sortis de nulle part, m'a totalement sorti de l'atmosphère sombre et mystérieuse que j'attends d'un thriller. Du coup, quand la fameuse évolution psychologique des personnages finit par arriver, il est trop tard, l'ennui m'avait déjà fait décrocher. C'est dommage : si le film avait associé ce développement intelligent à une vraie ambiance oppressante et des suspects intrigants, il m'aurait marqué. En l'état, il est complètement passé à côté de mes attentes.

Tratto da eventi storici realmente accaduti, ovvero gli omicidi seriali avvenuti a Hwaseong in una provincia rurale della Corea del Sud. "Memories of Murder" è stato uno dei maggior successi commerciali dell'apprezzato regista coreano Bong Joon-ho. Anche se l'incipit della narrazione e il modus operandi del serial killer vengono descritti in modo del tutto ordinario. Memories of Murder si discosta dal solito poliziesco per quel ricordo, un frammento di eventi autoctoni svaniti nel tempo che tornano alla mente solo nel finale, capace di trasportare lo spettatore occidentale in un mondo parzialmente estraneo. L'opera di Bong Joo-ho è dunque degna di interesse perchè porta alla superficie una concreta denuncia sociale, una pertinente e aspra critica alla società, nello specifico quella delle forze di Polizia, fondata sul concetto autartico dell'ego. Un ego smisurato che non si preoccupa minimamente del concetto di variabilità dell'ipotesi. Ciò che conta di più è portare a termine le indagini ad ogni costo, e insabbiare alla stampa certe pratiche ortodosse adottate a discapito dei sospettati. Tipiche pratiche fra l'altro molto diffuse nella cultura asiatica.. Il film cattura l'interesse già da subito grazie all'ottimo cast, Sang Kang-ho (Parasite), Park Ha-il, Kim Roi-ha, Kim Sang-Kyung, Jung In-sun etc, e all'ambientazione rurale piovosa e a una fotografia degna di nota. Aimé non mancano delle forzature per "incanalare" la sceneggiatura negli eventi voluti, e l'importante minutaggio evidenzia dei dettagli di trama superflui. Ma la soggettiva peculiarità della trama sta tutta racchiusa nel finale amaro quanto drammaticamente evocativo. La curiosità, e il rammarico di aver sbagliato scuotono i sensi del protagonista e dello spettatore.. Dove il cinismo del passato riemerge e si impadronisce di nuovo della ragione, ma quello che ne rimane e soltanto l'immaginazione di un volto comune. Troppo comune.. Visione consigliatissima. Voto: più che sufficiente.

Très sympa mais sans aller plus loin, Memories of Murder , c'est un Zodiac avant Zodiac mais qui ne se prend pas au sérieux. Une œuvre qui reprend l'histoire vraie d'un mystérieux tueur en série national aux manies étranges qui n'a jamais été démasqué. C'est un film d'enquête qui ne se prend pas au sérieux tout du long, sauf à la fin où il essaye de faire passer un message sur les stéréotypes de l'apparence d'un tueur en série dans l'imaginaire collectif (ce que Cure faisait beaucoup mieux avec beaucoup plus de poésie). Le film reste sympathique, bien présenté et cohérent. Mais bon sang pourquoi il est aussi vide et énervant tout du long ? Les personnages sont insupportables, et vu que le film ne propose rien d'autre on se retrouve seul face à eux. Cet aspect ridicule marche en tant que comédie à certains moments, mais le revirement sérieux à la fin offre au film une situation inconsistante inconfortable. On n'a pas un film hybride, on a un tout chimère. Relativement déçu même si le tout reste bien.

Terminei de assistir e fui procurar sobre o filme no Google, e simplesmente descobri que ele é superaclamado, considerado uma obra-prima do cinema sul-coreano. Mas, para mim, ficou longe disso. É aquilo: se a gente não gosta dos protagonistas, dificilmente consegue se envolver com a história. E aqui aconteceu justamente isso. A incompetência dos investigadores me dava agonia, principalmente por deixarem várias pistas passarem, como se não estivessem levando o caso a sério. Não é à toa que o caso não foi solucionado. Agora, uma coisa que gostei bastante foi a ambientação, mostrando a transição de um regime autoritário para uma democracia funcional e como esse contexto influencia a investigação. No final, senti como se o filme tivesse sido feito pensando justamente no serial killer. Quando o detetive quebra a quarta parede e olha diretamente para a câmera, dizendo que o assassino tem um rosto normal e que pode ser qualquer pessoa, parece quase um aviso à população: ele ainda está à solta e pode estar em qualquer lugar.

However, from the chase scene onwards, the tension ramps up significantly; it creates an incredible atmosphere that kept me completely gripped until the very end. That said, the ending left me feeling unsatisfied. I understand why the lack of resolution made sense—partly because the real-life case remained unsolved at the time, and partly to add depth and tragedy to the officers' desperation. The film is intelligent, and I find its message interesting and bold, but I still would have liked a compelling resolution to this mystery-crime thriller

When first watching Memories of Murder: I had heard that it was a masterpiece of True Crime filmmaking. I had watched many Korean horror films but this was the first drama/true crime foreign film. I'll admit, I didn't really get it the first time. All the detectives are kind of inept and do some pretty bad things themselves. So who do we route for? And that ending .... What!? But for years it stuck with me. So I started looking into it and realized "Oh, this was based on an actual serial killing in South Korea." And not just a serial killing, but what many would consider to be the first modern serial killer in South Korea. The director, Bong Joon-ho, probably remembered and experienced some of this growing up.  The police were actually pretty inept did infact torture confessions from people and were in over their heads. While creative liberties were taken, timelines shortened and some people involved changes: the telling is quite accurate. Knowing that now, Memories of Murder becomes much more engaging, interesting and poignant. All of our characters are shades of grey because the detectives were in fact torturing confessions from people, were incredibly under resources and frequently went off of feelings or hunches because of a lack of evidence. While being culturallydifferent from traditional American detective stories (Zodiac and Seven come to mind) once you get used to the Korean style and culture, with some added understanding of the true events that inspire the story, Memories of Murder really is a master piece in true crime filmmaking. It is also an interesting look at a director's early work that would carry them into greater future success.

Quand je l'ai regardé je lui m'étais 4/5. Mais après m’être renseignée sur la véritable histoire qui a inspiré le film et avoir regardé plusieurs interviews de Bong Joon-ho, je me suis rendu compte que c'est littéralement un chef d'oeuvre, ça en devient un 5/5 et sûrement un de mes films préférés parce que le réalisateur cherche vraiment à nous faire passer un message à nous et au coupable. J’ai beaucoup aimé la manière dont les personnages sont écrits. On n’a pas simplement des bons où des mauvais policiers qui cherchent à résoudre une affaire, là on voit leurs méthodes, leurs erreurs, leurs frustrations et même leurs limites. Le film montre la police entrain de chercher désespérément des réponses dans une situation où elle n’a pas les moyens scientifiques ou techniques nécessaires, ça a rend l’enquête beaucoup plus réaliste mais aussi beaucoup plus frustrante pour le spectateur. Car finalement c'est ce que les habitants et les enquêteurs ont ressenti à cette époque. Le fait que le film soit sorti alors que l’affaire n’était toujours pas résolue et que le coupable aurait bientôt plus eu le droit d'être condamné même s'il était retrouvé rend la création du film encore plus original. C’est pour ça que je conseille vraiment de se renseigner sur l’affaire après avoir vu le film, parce que connaître le contexte réel permet de réaliser à quel point Bong Joon-ho a réussi à transformer cette histoire en œuvre de cinéma tout en cherchant à adresser un message au coupable. En fait le film est incroyable d'un point de vu cinéphile (jsp pour qui je me prends). D'ailleurs le coupable à été retrouvés et apparemment il a vu le film et à dit qu'il ne l'avait pas trouvé terrible 😭 (la scène avec le petit garçon au début je vais jamais m'en remettre 🤣)

Gerade geguckt: „Memories of Murder“ ist ein Kriminal Thriller welcher 1986, in einer kleinen Provinz, im von der Militärdiktatur geprägten Südkorea spielt. Es geht um zwei ungleiche Kommissarre, die versuchen eine Reihe von Morden aufzuklären, welche immer an einem verregneten Tag und an rot gekleideten Frauen begangen werden. Allerdings ist der Film nicht nur ein einfacher Krimi sondern auch eine Nachricht an den echten Mörder, welcher erst 16 Jahre nach dem erscheinen des Films gefasst wurde. Abgesehen davon Thematisiert der Film die Inkompetenz der Polizei und den moralischen Verfall einer der Kommissare sowie Südkorea im Chaos des kurz bevorstehenden Umbruchs der Diktatur. Regisseur Bong Joon-ho zeichnet mit „Memorie of Murder“ ein atmosphärisches und immer düsterer werdendes Portrait einer traumatisierten Gesellschaft in wunderschönen aber dreckigen Bildern. Die letzte Szene ging mit einem einfachen aber tief gehenden Blick in die Kamera, nicht zu Unrecht in die Filmgeschichte ein. „Memories of Murder“ wird mir wahrscheinlich noch die nächsten Tage im Gedächtnis bleiben und motiviert mich weiter in Bong Joon-ho‘s Vita und das Koreanische Kino einzutauchen. Meiner Meinung nach einer der besten Filme seines Genres, die ich bis jetzt gesehen habe. Kann ich jedem empfehlen. (Btw noch nie so viele Dropkicks in einem ernsten Film gesehen)

There are many reasons why I particularly avoid Korean films, yet I do not detest them entirely. One of the biggest factors is their tendency toward exaggerated theatricality at the expense of a tighter logical structure in the plots they follow. Park-Chan Wook is the most classic example of this phenomenon of Korean cinema with his films such as Oldboy where he tries to tie out a similar moral tragedy like the Danish film Jagten (2012) through a stylistically elaborate revenge spiral, but the plot eventually moves beyond the boundaries of grounded internal logic. Devices such as hypnosis can feel like one-time narrative bandages, introduced primarily to connect pieces that otherwise resist being connected. My problem isn't simply that Oldboy is unrealistic, it's that, for me, certain revelations and mechanisms feel retroactively installed to preserve a plot that has already stretched beyond its own credibility. The Handmaiden is also a victim of a massive twisted theatrical presentation with an underwhelming logical ground for plot. So are many many films such as I Saw The Devil, A Bittersweet Life, Forgotten etc... Decision To Leave is what I consider the most perfect Park-Chan Wook film and what I consider the film where he establishes a perfect route between a top-notch presentation, poetic moral complexity and an established ground of logic that complements the plot. The Wailing is no stranger to this victimisation but deliberately worse. Here we follow the story of a dad, who is a police in a remote town, where the guilty, the misdeeds, the victims and even the apparent solutions reveal themselves so early, yet the plot repeatedly demands that its characters descend further into its catacombs of uncertainty, not necessarily because the logic requires it, but because the theatrical experience does with its top-of-the-class cinematography, set design and the quote-unquote "thriller" ride of Korean cinema which is deemed to be so extraordinarily unique. Even the 2 hour 40 minutes runtime serves the furthest from being a momentum of an intrigued continuity. Instead, the film repeatedly pauses, expands, and obscures itself in pursuit of an exhilarating theatrical experience, backed by extraordinary cinematography and production design, but without enough narrative momentum to justify the journey. It could be a brilliant concept film, if only it was told with a better expression of plot in mind, better attachment of all the fragmentations of the elements since they were so obviously present. Yet none clicks except until the final reveal becomes the most emphasized point of the film. In short, my utmost frustration is specifically with the film's prolonged withholding of decisive movement. Underwhelming is an understatement for The Wailing. Bong Joon Ho is the only Korean director to ever do Korean cinema the justice of the trio- cinematic experience, established complementary logic and an unique narrative statement of being a Korean foreign cinema. Lee Chang Dong also comes to mind. Burning is my most favorite Korean cinema of all time. I just want to say this phenomenon is of course not exclusive to Korean cinema only. Any film can become a victim of its own grandiosity when cinematic spectacle begins demanding sacrifices from the internal logic that is supposed to sustain it. I'm looking right at you Amadeus .

One of the things I like about Korean movies is that the stories are usually quite different from the usual stuff. Even when the movie isn’t particularly great, the ideas are often different enough to keep me interested. The Wailing has a really good opening. The mystery behind the deaths and the strange behaviour of the people really pulled me in. I kept watching because I wanted to know what was going on. Up until around the middle, it just kept getting stranger and stranger. But after that, everything starts becoming a complete mess. Is it a ghost? Poisonous mushrooms? Zombies? A demon? A curse? Black magic? Damn, my brain was getting tired trying to figure it out. 😂 Then there’s the shaman’s “healing ritual” with all that dancing and jumping around. And apparently the devil knows how to use a camera to take pictures for black magic too. OMG… this movie really went everywhere. The Korean mountain village setting is beautiful, but I just can’t get along with the story. For me, the beginning until the middle is good. After that, it completely falls apart. Not recommended.

In Asia il coesistere di giallo e paranormale nella stessa storia ha un carattere diverso da quello che possiamo trovare in Sherlock o altri racconti occidentali. Lo spiritismo spesso si assimila alle indagini come un dato plausibile e popolarmente creduto, almeno nei villaggi più rurali. Goksung parte molto bene, la prima parte è un crime a tinte mostruose, inspiegabili, che sono proprio l'aspetto più avvincente, perché spingono a voler sapere cosa ci può essere dietro gli efferati omicidi. Per tutta la durata del film, nel totale un po' troppo prolungata, la fotografia va migliorando, diventando pian piano più fredda, come se un'occulta entità diabolica si stesse impossessando della stessa atmosfera, mentre per quanto riguarda la storia la seconda parte vede incrinarsi  la componente misteriosa per schiaffarti in volto la verità. In questa parte prende vigore la parte religiosa del film, tra esorcisti, citazioni bibliche al canto del gallo e altro che giustifica la citazione evangelica a Luca all'inizio del film, ma con ciò si assiste anche all'indiscreto farsi protagonista del gore, all'indebolimento del ritmo investigativo, alla banalizzazione della storia, che di originale ha solo ciò che riguarda la tradizione coreana a noi sconosciuta, e a scene che non hanno l'impatto desiderato, come il rituale sciamanico per liberare la figlia, un costante battere di percussioni e grida senza climax ascendente. Il buon regista tiene in piedi l'impianto fino al termine, ma lo script a mio parere non fa altrettanto, non per difetti oggettivi ma per scelte talvolta imperfette.

Incredibly clunky, bloated, and loud. This is one of the most self-destructive films I’ve seen, and I mean that in the literal filmmaking, for better, but mainly for worse The only thing that I can really say that’s consistently great throughout the film, is the performances, every character is so fun to track, and follow, but because of how the tone hardens at the end of the movie, it kind of guts some of these characters, and turns their performances against them to an extent. That could be said about the entire movie to be honest. I think it had a very good first act, it was so damn funny, and I was so engaged in the horror that was going on, and then it started to get more over the top, and chaotic towards the middle of the movie, and it genuinely had me on the edge of my seat, questioning what could possibly happen next, and this shit just kinda hit the fan at the end of the film. when you have a film that sets itself up in such a perfect way, balancing humor and horror, and then you throw that balance out the window at the end of the film, and change the tone to be so much darker, and so much more self serious, it ends up, creating a film that completely guts itself. Not to mention the amount of random twists, and revelations thrown in at the last act, it was like the film kept changing, and rearranging just for the sake of saying that it could, just for the mirror shock value of the ride. Once again, I really love the first act of this thing, and by the halfway point, I was super excited to see what it was going to do next, but about 20 minutes after that second half, it took a complete nose dive, as it tried to breach into overly heavy, self loathing film territory, that contrast what it was setting up in the worst way possible Definitely not a bad film, though, I almost have to respect this type of filmmaking, I’ve never seen anything this clunky before, but this confident behind that clunkiness. It’s quite the experience, and I have respect for that alone.

An Atmospheric and Engaging Horror That Isn’t Quite Perfect I love what Na Hong-jin has to offer here, a kind of horror that is not only scary and terrifying, but also really engaging, i truly loved the atmosphere and the slow pace of the film, especially how it slowly builds up to the main conflict, i liked it a lot, and i think it's a unique, well-made, and engaging horror film, especially considering its runtime. Until the last 20 minutes or so, this is where i started to feel like the film was dragging, with all the twists, questions, assumptions, and one wild intense sequence after another, the movie started to feel like it was trying too hard to make the ending more open and leave more possibilities about what actually happened, i'm just going to be honest without spoiling anything, but i personally thought the earlier ending worked better than what they eventually revealed in those final 20 minutes, it almost felt like a bonus scene that was added after the movie had already reached a good ending. From there, the movie started to feel unnecessarily stretched out, and honestly, even a little boring and less interesting than everything that came before it, it's too bad, because i genuinely enjoyed around 80% of the film before that. Overall, i still think The Wailing is a good piece of work, it's a genuinely engaging horror story, especially considering its runtime, and i think that deserves to be appreciated, the performances are good, the filmmaking is great, and the atmosphere is one of the film's biggest strengths, it's definitely not perfect, and there are flaws here and there, but my biggest issue is still those final 20 minutes, without them, The Wailing probably would have been a much more satisfying experience for me personally, but as a whole, The Wailing is still a good movie for the most part. 7/10

Злодеем оказался Дьяво Ляо При могучем хронометраже в два с половиной часа и достаточно интересной завязке о чумной деревне кино не втягивает меня в по-настоящему неоднозначное расследование. Кино, казалось бы, говорит: «Оно!», а ты такой: «Оно!», а оно такое: «Точно оно?», чтоб по итогу оказалось: «Оно». Интересный мув, когда верное подозрение ещё не означает верного знания, а надёжного способа отличить веру от заблуждения нет. Но проблема в том, что здешние намёки слишком жирные, а попытки переобуться слишком неубедительны. Из-за этого наблюдать за происходящим попросту скучно. Хорошо поставленных, жутких сцен и эффектных задумок хватает, но чем глубже пытаешься во всём этом разобраться, тем более шаткой кажется конструкция. Ведь ключ к пониманию происходящего то ли в религиозных подтекстах, то ли в южнокорейской внутрянке, то ли в широкотрактовных метафорах. Сложно из-за этого проникнуться, хотя вайб, безусловно, присутствует.

Considering that this is sorta like if the detectives from Memories of Murder were investigating a more extreme possession/occult folk horror-procedural case (a la Cure , The Exorcist , Noroi: The Curse ), I kinda expected this to hit me a little harder... Pretty good though! Great muddy-rainy look, gross and grisly when it counts, good feel for ambiguous dread. But as it goes on it feels like less of a slow-burn than just unfocused and exhausting (really doesn't earn the epic length imo), and I guess what I like so much about the films it's riffing on is their sense of heavily controlled unease. Pay no mind to me though if this is your kinda thing, I recall feeling similarly about I Saw the Devil which everyone loves too. And still, it's not often you get a movie that goes as all-in on the literal evil descent-like structure where strangers turn into shaman and lead directly to satan, so I get why this has had some staying power, even if I don't know that I fully understood what happened or what it all means. I'm sure there's 10 years of THE WAILING - EXPLAINED videos I've missed out on.
