"O Lamento" é um suspense com potencial que se estende além do necessário. Esse é mais um longa sul-coreano de Na Hong-jin que mistura elementos do terror e suspense em torno de Jong-Goo, um policial de uma pequena cidade que investiga mortes misteriosas em seu vilarejo. O que parecia epidemia ganha contornos sobrenaturais e religiosos conforme sua filha apresenta sintomas estranhos. A premissa é sólida e o diretor faz questão de marcar presença, mas o filme carrega consigo um problema estrutural que o compromete: é longo demais para a ideia que sustenta. O filme possui um bom clima de suspense, porém a duração não ajuda, poderia ter sido mais enxuto, e se perde às vezes no roteiro deixando o espectador impaciente. Há momentos onde a câmera trabalha com precisão, onde o diretor demonstra sensibilidade visual genuína ao filmar os rituais e a tensão entre personagens. A estrutura religiosa do filme oferece camadas interessantes, mas Na Hong-jin não consegue contê-las adequadamente dentro de 156 minutos. O roteiro flerta com devaneio total em seus segmentos intermediários, explorando filosofia religiosa quando deveria intensificar a narrativa principal. Algumas atuações carecem de sutileza, especialmente em momentos que exigem nuance emocional, o que prejudica a credulidade de cenas críticas. O melhor que o filme oferece existe em seu final. A última meia hora confunde o espectador e o deixa cheio de dúvidas, com reviravoltas e um final surpreendente. É quando Na Hong-jin finalmente alinha visão e execução, permitindo que a ambiguidade moral do desfecho respire adequadamente. Nesse segmento, o diretor comprova que possui potencial genuíno para manipular emocões e conceitos complexos. Porém, tudo o que precede essa conclusão deveria ter sido trabalhado com maior economia narrativa. Certamente é um filme de ideias contidas demais numa estrutura que não sabe dizer não, logo, não entendo o alvoroço em torno dele.

And Ari wept Quite the wild romp upon an initial viewing, even now I still remember how distributed Jong-goo finding those photos made me feel. Regretfully though this wound up being less riveting  conceptually after a much delayed rewatch. Now in saying that I’m not claiming it's entirely void of any non-cinematic merit. With a much better understanding of Korea’s antipathy towards Japan due to their colonialist occupation during the early 20th century helps illuminate Gokseong’s central subtext ( or just text now ) in a very appreciated manner. This makes a lotta the “clues,” “hints” or actions of Kunimura Jun’s character, aptly named Japanese Man , click for me. Our character's treatment of him, however “justified” in the context of the film's spiritual battle between light and dark, is painted in a far more tragic light by the end. Jong-goo , the village, and by extension us are given divine punishment for blind discrimination. This helps make the ending, one which I found quite frustrating on a first watch, ring rather potent. What we see and what is actually there are two different things and believing that isn’t true is a dangerous belief to hold. The wider issue for myself is the film doesn’t always compel and thus my mind occasionally tends to wander here or there. Could this’ve been remedied by trimming it down a tad? Yea maybe but even then it’s so clearly a fully realized vision that I can’t help but still admire the ambition. Certain leaps in logic might be perplexing if not for the fact the film actively acknowledges them in a manner less irksome and more cheeky fudging of plausibility. I will say it helps that this film still looks euphoric. Splendid mountainscapes made of croaked bark and rough rock all doused in a healthy hue of blue and orange make their harboring of poisonous beasts feel all the more enticing. Again, not an all timer for me but far from being a foul film.

This heads in so many truly wild directions I wouldn't even know where to begin really. I feel like even the positive reviews of it on here (mine included) are mostly just throwing their hands up and rolling with the punches after a certain point. The mid-film exorcism scene - which is such a brilliant sustained stretch of filmmaking that it alone makes this film worth watching - kicks things into another gear and the film never really relents from there. While in some ways I find the structural shifts this movie undergoes a little disorienting and not as organic as they could be, those critiques are subsumed by the sheer amount of ground covered by this story. The slow burn opening - played for laughs as much as horror - is both a bit of a conceptual hurdle to navigate and also ultimately essential to charting the tragic scale of what this character goes through. As others have noted, this is kind of a shaggy dog joke of a horror movie, with the punchline coming at the main character's expense in extremely, irrevocably consequential fashion. It is also not often anymore that a horror movie manages to contain an image or a sequence that genuinely gets under my skin, and this one had several of those. The scenes of "the stranger" feasting on a deer carcass before turning to stalk his prey, eyes blazing red, in particular, register as even creepier in hindsight.

“I’ll take care of everything.” Highly do not recommend eating a meal while watching this. Certainly too long and Jong-goo’s incompetence throughout is rather annoying to watch, but I thought this still managed to be a damn good horror movie because it strips its characters and the audience of their confidence. The belief in truth, that what you’re seeing is real and that this person did this to that person, it all gets mixed up on the road to a finale full of second guesses. It’s so terrifying to cling onto truth like it will save you when it won’t. Like it will shield you from a nightmare, and all the suffering other people have faced. But it won’t. And it’s that insecurity that this taps into so well. Honestly do not get the complaints I’ve read about tone. There are different tones in this movie but to me it often felt clearly defined by where we were. And there’s one pocket in here where a tonal shift feels different in a very good way and that’s during the shaman’s drum-banging, fire-wielding, child-screaming ritual. Crazy scene.

“But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit. And he said to them, ‘Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.’ -Luke 24:34-37” Been a hot minute since I’ve watched a film and I got back into it with a banger. Imagine the father-daughter relationship in Train to Busan combined with the supernatural levels of horror and thrill from The Exorcist and mixed with the history and culture of Korean shamanism from Exhuma. Now give that steroids and you got The Wailing . Upon watching this film, I have way more questions than I had as I was watching it. To be honest, I actually don’t know what happened. For such a huge chunk of the film, I’ve been led to believe that the old Japanese man was some sort of demonic power that casted a sinister shadow over the Korean village (probably inspired by anti-Japanese sentiment from Koreans due to colonization, just like in Exhuma ). There were so many clues that hinted that that likelihood, especially when the dad cop barges into the Japanese man’s house and found those disgusting pictures and shrines. It was as clear as day that the old man was responsible. There was no other way around. Even the shaman confirmed that, as he describes the old Japanese man as a fisher, casting a line out into the water and baits anyone that fall for his schemes. And the pinnacle of this growing suspicion is the simultaneous rituals, which masterfully showcased a battle of spirits for the daughter’s life and essence (arguably my favorite sequence in the film. It was gripping, intense, and thrilling). And then all of a sudden, just like that, everything comes crashing down because the shaman is confronted by the woman in the white robes and then calls the dad cop, frantically telling him that she was responsible and that the old man was another shaman combating her. Then we’re in a standoff between the woman in white and the shaman, where she’s telling the dad cop that she set a trap for the demon at his house and that he needs to wait and the shaman is saying that she’s lying and that dad cop needs to get back. But the woman is wearing articles of clothing from the victims so that’s a clear giveaway. Meanwhile the priest goes on to find the Japanese man in a cave and he reveals that he’s the devil and responsible for terrorizing the village, to which he takes pictures of the priest. And just when it can’t get any more confusing, the shaman returns to the dad cop’s house to find everyone slaughtered but then takes out a camera, photographs the dead, and then puts the pictures in a box filled with the pictures of all the other dead victims. So there are 3 entities that are potentially responsible and the film ends on an ambiguous note that doesn’t resolve the conflict. Instead, the film ends on a happier note of the dad remembering the happy times with his daughter as he’s dying by her hand. Like what just happened 😂 I actually like and appreciate the fact that the truth never reveals itself. With every plot twist and then, our sense of reality and truth gradually becomes more distorted, completely and intentionally shattering any truth and objectivity that would remain as the film went on. And to be honest, I actually don’t want to know who was the real villain or not because I feel like it would diminish the objective the film, which is more than capably achieved. This was my firs t나홍진 film and the style is so right up my alley. Not only was the cinematography exquisite in capturing the beauty of the Korean countryside, but much of his style was cinematically intentional and exact. He guides audiences towards what he wants us to see and not see through frames within frames. Almost every focal point in each scene was enclosed in a frame within the actual frame, which makes us think about who to follow and how to follow the story. I thought that was executed very well. My only complaint is that the dialogue was almost to the point of being completely incomprehensible. Because this film took place in the Korean countryside, these are country folk and they have 사투리, which means accent/dialect and their vocab and dictation is completely different than that of city folk in Seoul and Incheon. So I actually couldn’t make out what they were really saying but that’s a minor nitpick in a major banger. Way more sinister than I was expecting. Gritty, disturbing, and aggressive, just the way I like films (sometimes).

Maybe it's because only "the best of the best" makes it over here to America, but it feels like Korean filmmakers really know how to make incredible detective stories (Memories of Murder) and horror movies (Train to Busan and Exhuma). The Wailing combines both and makes an incredible film noir, meets folk horror film. The wailing exceeds at making you feel uncomfortable, there are certainly movies that are more intense, more unrelenting and/or more brutal, but few movies make my skin crawl in the way The Wailing does. It's fast and intense when it needs to be and it lets you sit long and slowly with the disturbing material it's presenting you. Its folk horror aspects also take parts of Korean spiritualism and culture and makes them digestible to those of us who are unfamiliar. The police procedural and detective parts are engaging and keep you guessing throughout. The characters are handled very well, especially as we watch the family of our main protagonist struggle and then have to face suppernatural forces. The Wailing really balances things incredibly well when you consider it's a family drama, police procedural, folk horror. That's a lot for one movie to take on, but it does it phenominally well and parts of it will stick with you for years to come.

I've finally found it. My favorite horror movie ever made. This was not only stunning, it was deeply political and cultural. How they managed to so tastefully weave in criticism of religion, post-war trauma, and absolutely insane Biblical references together alongside cultural shamanism, black magic, and its unbreakable hold over generations was absolutely mindblowing. The terror went hand in hand with the tragedy. The atmosphere draws you in in the way so many horror movies have tried to do and failed. Just goes to show you don't need jumpscares in order to suffer from series upon series of mind-numbing chills for the duration of two and half hours. At some point the plot did begin to confuse me, but honestly? I didn't even care, the sinister beauty and the depth behind this piece surpassed everything else it might have lacked. I've seen my fair share of horror movies, but this one had something different about it, something very special that I will most definitely come back to time and time again.

I think I approached this film with the wrong expectations. I started watching it as a conventional mystery, and when almost nothing seemed to happen for quite a while, I found myself getting confused. Then, when the greenhouse came into the story, I realized that this was essentially Haruki Murakami’s “Barn Burning,” a story I had read a long time ago. From that point on, I shifted my perspective and watched it as a story in which ambiguity itself is the subject. The film scatters motifs such as plastic surgery, pantomime, cats, wells, and silent phone calls—things whose very existence becomes ambiguous as the point of view shifts. It leaves you feeling as though you’ve been told something profound, but in the end, I was left with an unsatisfying feeling of having been led down the garden path.

Muito estilo, pouco desenvolvimento. Poxa, até as coisas que mais curti no filme são meio largadas no meio… tem uma crítica meio socioeconômica, de classe, com as casas da mulher, pequenina sem sol, e a do cara, mais numa área rural (que é onde eles nasceram, mas mesmo essa ligação com o passado ou uma Coreia mais empobrecida é meio só jogada no roteiro) mas maior e que bate sol. Tem até o rolê da África, que poderia ser outro tipo de pobreza, desigualdade, mas pra mim ficou só uma coisa meio estereotipada e fetichizada, inclusive com a “dança da fome”. E tem a atriz, que é a melhor coisa do filme. Mostra alegria, frustração, vai atrás do que quer, toma iniciativa das coisas (até põe a camisinha no cara). Mas além de também ser meio fetichizada dançando com os peitos pra fora, some depois do meio do filme e é isso… É um drama sobre o casal/trisal ou sobre família? Não sei, o filme não desenvolve. É um estudo de personagem? Talvez. É um filme policial? A parte final até parece que sim, mas sei lá. Tem o lance da memória, do passado (tem poço ou não? Lembra de mim? E a mãe?). O personagem principal que parece que tem outro traquejo com a bezerra, mais a vontade (aliás, o protagonista mais apático que deixa de ser estilo e parece preguiça mesmo). Enfim, é um filme bom? Pode ser, mas não sei não…

Lee Chang dong's adaption of Murakami is a complete nothingburger. Murakami's whole trick of the cat that may or may not exist, the woman who evaporates mid sentence, the missing thing standing in for a missing meaning has never worked on me. It isn't mystery. It's vagueness borrowing mystery's coat. "Barn Burning," the story underneath this, is itself a riff on Faulkner, and Faulkner actually earned his ambiguity through prose density, through a kid caught between his father's violence and the world's contempt for both of them. Murakami just removes information and calls the hole where it used to be meaning. Lee inherits that hole, dresses it beautifully, and asks us to call it depth. Because nothing major happens here, not really. The entire back half is speculation stacked on speculation, and the film knows it, and dares you to mind. The only saving grace is Yoo Ah in. With him it's a performance you can't look away from.

In the Burning, Jong-su the main character wants to become a writer, but he almost never writes, his life seems to have a certain emptiness, And he doesn’t seem to really pay much attention or take much agency for most of the movie. Jong su meets a girl he knew from his childhood, Hae mi, and they start spending time together until she leaves for a trip to Africa, and she asks him to watch her cat while she is away. When she returns, she isn’t alone but with a new mysterious friend named Ben. He is apparently wealthy, and his life appears much more put together, a stark contrast compared to Jong Su. After spending some time together with Ben and Hae mi, one evening, Ben reveals his odd hobby to Jong Su. After the reveal of Ben's hobby, the movie starts feeling very sinister and at times eerie. And this reveal sets off a chain of events that consume Jong Su but also for the first time give him a certain meaning, and he starts taking some action but in the process also confusing both Jong Su but also us, the viewers, and with no real explanation to any of them, the movie remains purposefully vague, and it keeps us guessing as to what has really happened and hasn’t happened, keeping the burning truth obscured by smoke. The character of Hae mi plays an important role in translating the message of the movie, and how the characters interact with her might be one of the most important parts of the whole movie. We know from certain characters that her life is a mess, but she doesn’t really let us see this, or maybe Jong-su at first just wasn’t looking hard enough (just like the viewer being focused on the mystery), not really caring about her but mostly seeing her and her body as an object. Jong-su appears helpless to the competition from Ben, while maybe also feeling resentment towards him because of their class differences. Hae mi is concerned with her life’s meaning and purpose. Ben and Jong-su are more concerned over who will have “ownership” over her. 4/5

Solid neo-noir that I tried to connect with. I seemed well-equipped to enjoy Burning. I held an affinity for love triangles and mystery, I liked fire motifs, and I also had ample personal lore for the film to mean something to me. However, its impact never hit. Perhaps Burning would’ve had a stronger impact if it focused on Jong-Su and Haemi’s intertwined fates. Facing the same odds in life, the only differing factor was their sex. Unfortunately the film seemed preoccupied with making Haemi’s struggle picturesque and easy to consume. Her hopelessness was unconvincing, not in a way that strengthened the mystery either. She just seemed a little too objectified for my liking. Respectfully, I don’t think weed makes you do all that. When the film was recommended to me, much of the emphasis was on Steven Yeun’s acting. The praise felt contrived; his acting was stellar but the character wasn’t utilised to its full potential for it to be memorable. Burning introduces itself as a Murakami adaptation, but I learnt later that Murakami’s short story was adapted from Faulkner’s work. There’s a rich intertextuality that is missing from my assessment of the film, and I’m inclined to fill that gap. Doing so might distinguish it from Blow-Up, The Long Goodbye, Under the Silver Lake, quietly haunting films about intrigue and ennui. Complaints and praises alike, Burning spurred many subsequent discussions. When asked if the film was more of a window of discovery or a mirror for introspection, I jokingly likened it to a well. Perhaps that’s true. Refreshment and nourishment were there, but somewhat out of reach, drying up even 🫣 And the field of vision was narrow, but one could catch sparse insights if you stared long enough.

I have less to say about Burning than I thought I would. Perhaps I found it too slow or cold. I wanted it to grab me with emotion or mystery or provocation, but for the most part, Burning just simmers. Of course, I think this is the point. I suppose there’s any number of themes available for examination, but I interpreted Burning to be a study in main character syndrome. Lee Jong-su is more or less idled in life. By some combination of his social class and passivity, he is unable to find his footing. So, when Hae-mi (re)enters his frame, and subsequently offers a portal into a life of privilege and agency vis-à-vis Ben, Jong-su spirals. There’s too much ambiguity over the course of the movie for it to be unintentional; yet we watch as Jong-su haphazardly rushes to solve, villainize, and intervene. But it’s too late. In time, it becomes clear that he is leaping to conclusions because the potential for his life to finally develop some meaning is too intoxicating. These ideas are potent, even emotional. For that reason alone, I can recommend Burning with ease. I wish I had loved it, but I’m glad I at least found it great.

cerita perlawanan kelas pekerja terhadap orang kaya yang semena-mena itu selalu berhasil membeli (tidak dalam ruang kapitalisme) saya. belum lagi kini protagonisnya beresonansi dengan saya pribadi yang sama-sama penulis novel yang belum juga debut (bedanya naskah saya sudah diterima dan dalam tahap pengeditan) yang membuat film ini terasa begitu dekat dengan saya pribadi. sebelum masuk ke filmnya sendiri, perlu diketahui saya adalah pembaca sastra jepang yang tidak terlalu suka Haruki Murakami. di novelnya yang berjudul Norwegian Wood, saya sampai harus mencorat-coret satu halaman saking terganggunya dengan adegan seksual yang sebegitu eksplisitnya. bukannya saya anti dengan penggambaran seks dalam konteks sastra, akan tetapi menggambarkannya dengan mentah dan hanya berfokus pada “tata cara mengeluarkan sperma dalam dua halaman” bukanlah sesuatu yang menarik di mata saya. seks seharusnya dapat digambarkan dengan indah dan penuh dinamika kuasa. bisa kok adegan seks itu ditulis dalam rangka menunjukan seberapa telanjang seseorang di hadapan masalah yang ia hadapi atau seberapa kuat seseorang memegang peranan orang lainnya dalam menggerakan cerita. apapun itu, ini dapat diolah menjadi sesuatu yang punya nilai tambah dalam ceritanya itu sendiri. tetapi ya mungkin kebanyakan pembaca suka-suka saja dengan sajian yang seperti ini. di film ini saya tidak menemukan itu. Hae-mi berhasil dibuat sebagai gadis yang menggerakan Jongsu di adegan seks mereka. ada dinamika kuasa yang ditaruh di sana. ditambah bayangan di dinding selagai mereka melakukan itu juga yang memberikan petunjuk tambahan di filmnya sendiri. jadi adegannya tidak serta merta jadi penambah keseksian storytelling Lee Chang-dong. cerita dijalani dengan lamban tetapi tidak membosankan karena selalu ada yang terjadi. kamera dibuat seperti pena yang meliuk, menebar prosa di mana-mana. beberapa dibiarkan tanpa dialog. beberapa kali juga tanpa suara. seru sekali, seperti melihat seorang penyair sedang berpuisi dengan intonasi serta penekanan yang pas. iya, betul. yang pas. bukan yang seperti lomba puisi tingkat kabupaten yang semua pesertanya memakai intonasi yang sama padahal puisinya berkonsep jenaka. kita disuguhkan karakter bernama Ben, seorang kaya yang nggak jelas pekerjaannya apa. kurang lebih seperti orang-orang yang kita sering lihat di pagi hari sedang joging santai dengan kacamata hitam dan earphone di telinganya, ketika kita sendiri sedang berdesak-desakan di dalam transjakarta dengan para pekerja (dan pencari kerja) lainnya. kadang saya berpikir, “mereka kerjanya apa ya?” dan pertanyaan itulah yang ditanyakan Jongsu di awal pertemuan mereka. Haemi di sini ditempatkan sebagai hiburan untuk Ben dan teman-temannya (yang saya yakin bermasalah juga). Sama seperti yang terjadi dewasa ini, di mana kalangan menengah ke bawah disawer di platform digital selama mereka menari-nari tidak jelas di depan kamera ponselnya yang berkabut. di luar tampak seperti berkarya tetapi sejatinya kita memang hanyalah boneka hiburan kala mereka bosan saja. di sinilah yang memberakan Jongsu dengan Haemi. Jongsu menyadari itu. mereka tidak pernah benar-benar peduli dengan kita, mereka cuma melihat kita lucu. seperti anak-anak kampung yang melepas sendal saat masuk mall (saya sendiri hehe) dan ditertawakan oleh anak komplek. Haemi sama seperti itu, sedangkan Jongsu tidak. kenapa? karena dia terjamah pendidikan. pernah ada ungkapan dari seorang rusia yang hobi berceloteh, “penderitaan adalah untuk mereka yang intelek nan penuh empati.”. intelektualitas dibangun dari pendidikan. tidak melulu pendidikan formal kok. Jongsu diperlihatkan sebagai seorang yang gemar membaca (uniknya tanpa ada adegan dia membaca). rumahnya dipenuhi buku-buku yang berserakan, tipikal karakter lelaki yang ditulis Haruki Murakami. ini yang membuat kepekaannya lebih tajam melihat kondisi sosial mereka. hanya saja seorang intelek tidaklah mampu berbuat apa-apa ketika di hadapannya adalah seorang raja jahat yang memiliki segalanya. bagi saya, di akhir film, dan hanya di akhir film, film ini menjadi metafiksi. adegan terakhir adalah bagaimana kita bisa terus berkhayal (untuk suatu hari kejadian) bahwa kita juga punya kuasa di hadapan mereka. seperti Jongsu yang menulis ceritanya sendiri, kita juga suatu saat dapat membalikan keadaan di mana kita tidak lagi ditindas oleh mereka. tentu jika dan hanya jika kita semua bersatu, bukan seperti saat ini, yang kota saling meninju, membiarkan para kaya raya itu berlari pagi dengan hati dan hari yang penuh ketenangan, mengetahui mereka tidak perlu tersentuh apa-apa. eat the (bad) rich, soon.

What strikes me the most about Lee Chang-dong's Burning is that throughout its entire 2 hour and 28 minute runtime, nothing happens. This is partly untrue, Burning's second half concedes to some minute thriller conventions but never fully yields to being a standard, by the book thriller. Instead, much of it is this masculine ego war between two men. Two men from completely opposite social classes. The first of these two men is Jong-su, an aspiring writer unable to find employment in Korea's rigidly competitive job market. He's curious and always questions the world around him, and he's very well aware of his class standing. He's aware of the material conditions around him, and he seems to have some sort of knowledge on the issues of capitalism and imperialism (even if this is never outwardly revealed). And standing opposing to him is Ben. Ben is this mysterious figure who stands blissfully ignorant to the world around him. He gets to do so because he's one of the upper elites. And when the inciting incident about halfway into the film occurs, the film becomes a silent battle between the two, attempting to dominate the other, Jong-su channeling his jealousy of Ben's lifestyle while Ben attempts to use his status to elevate himself over Jong-su. However, it is almost impossible to talk about Burning without mentioning the most important character of the film (in my opinion at least), is Hae-Mi. If Jong-su represented the alienation and repressed anger of the lower class Koreans, Hae-Mi serves as an allegory for how women are stripped of their agency under capitalism and its brutal class system. Early on the film, Hae-Mi is introduced to the audience as an old friend of Jong-su, and they go for a dinner together. Here she explains two metaphors, "Little Hunger" and "Great Hunger". "Little Hunger", she says, is the immediate desires of humanity, to fulfill their literal hunger and to survive. However, she then elaborates that the "Great Hunger" is humanity's hunger for meaning in life, some objective truth to the absurdity we live in. Her story is one of the most important parts of the film, yet it is completely depicted through the eyes of Jong-su. It is established that he is completely obsessed over her, yet the film never highlights how much of that love is truly real, or is some infatuation. Through his gaze, she is completely stripped of her agency, mirroring the film's commentary on patriarchy in a Korean society as well. When Hae-Mi dances in the sunset, high on weed and naked from the top, the film drifts into its most hypnotic and stunning. The visuals are truly incredible during this scene, and I was utterly captivated throughout her ritualistic performance. Jong-sus jealousy of her and Ben turned into misogyny and here, as he angrily refers to her as a "whore", the audience begins to see the pent up anger spew out with uncomfortable misogyny, which boils into the final act of the film. Yet, as the end arrived, the film refused to provide any answers. Which is why the ending had more than a few people feel it was futile. There's no final answer, no twist to shock the viewers. Nothing. With this, Lee Chang-dong even questions the genre's conventions of objective finalities, that the final act of violence has any meaning in solving the mystery of the film. The film asserts the mystery isn't the point, the pointlessness IS the point. Whether an objective truth can ever be found is unlikely, all humanity can live on are interpretations of narratives and ideas we build in our heads.

Quando penso a un regista, con uno stile arrogante e privo di sostanza, mi viene sempre in mente Ryūsuke Hamaguchi. Drive My Car più che un film pare una presa per il culo di 3 ore, con scene al limite del cringe, lunguaggini inutili e soluzioni narrative scontate e involontariamente divertenti. È un film banalmente noioso, ripetitivo, e con una messa in scena piatta e televisiva. Sostenuto da attori che recitano come dei manichini e da una scrittura degna di un surreale libro di Federico Moccia. Chiunque consideri Hamaguchi un maestro del cinema moderno si è fatto abbindolare da un grande paraculo.

Such a pathetic old man bro 😭 This movie really did not need to be almost 3 hours long because this really wasn’t it for me. “Ohhh but he’s supposed to be like that because the movie is about how he deals with his grief.” Yeah, I fucking know that, bro. And because he’s supposed to be like that, I’m also allowed to fucking hate his sorry ass. His character development still made me mad as hell, and the way he handles his grief is giving LOSER ENERGY throughout the entire movie. And holy shit, the scene where he literally sees his wife cheating on him and then just fucking walks away? That was the real embodiment of a loser and a stupid ass man. Bro really stood there, processed the information, and decided, “Yeah, I’m just gonna leave.” I know the whole point is that he’s emotionally repressed and doesn’t know how to confront his feelings, but watching that shit still made me want to punch the screen. But despite how much I fucking hate this type of main character, I have to admit there are so many scenes here that are genuinely beautiful. Especially all those moments when they’re driving around in the car and the camera slowly zooms out, revealing the entire area around them. There’s something so peaceful and almost hypnotic about those shots. The movie can be painfully slow, but visually, I can’t deny that it knows exactly how to create an atmosphere. And the dinner scene with his coworker and his wife who can’t speak? That shit was genuinely moving. It’s one of those scenes where barely anything needs to happen, but the emotion just fucking lands. The way they communicate without being able to communicate normally was probably one of the few moments where I completely understood why people love this movie. My friend actually told me a few years ago that this movie was probably not for me, but I thought, “Nah, I’ve watched enough movies now. I’m ready to step outside my comfort zone.” And to be fair, I’ve actually managed to do that before. I used to hate Linda Linda Linda, and now I fucking love that movie. But this one? Nah man. I can appreciate the aesthetics, the quiet atmosphere, the beautiful cinematography, and some genuinely touching scenes, but spending almost three hours with this fucking loser was still not an experience I enjoyed 😭 I genuinely wanted to laugh in this old man’s face and punch him just because I fucking could. Bro is a loser anyway.

Drive My Car shares its name with a short and fun song by The Beatles , but it’s quite the opposite. Not short, nor fun. A long, quiet, slow-burn trauma bond that never fully clicked for me. Like a melodramatic play, ‘twas grade-A crapola. Critically acclaimed, subtitled snoozefest 😴 I’ll admit, I was already burnt out on slow burns, so seeing the 3-hour runtime didn’t help, but I didn’t realize how much that would be felt. I was confused by the opening; relationship dynamics felt unclear, emotional beats didn’t land cleanly, and by the time the “2 years later” card and intro credits hit (40 minutes in!), I was still trying to piece together that overlong prologue I just saw. After that, it settles into a slow moving, very talky, theatre folk drama with lots of subtlety, themes of infidelity, shared grief, and not ever truly knowing someone. It never felt impactful enough to justify the length. I struggled to stay engaged, and 3hrs of subtitles felt like work rather than immersion. Some foreign films completely absorb me to the point I forget I’m reading; this wasn’t one of them. This one made me feel very outside of everything. Not bad, just not for me. Maybe I’m missing some nuance, but from my POV it feels very overrated. Of course a movie about driving a car will have some nice sweeping shots and cinematography, but it wasn’t incredible, nothing I haven’t seen before, and that plot just wasn’t very captivating. It only finally begins to open up a bit in the last stretch, but by then it’s like… that’s it? A long road to a simple idea. This could’ve been a short film.

i did not like this movie. i do not think it is a very good movie. yes, it's well-crafted, yes, i suppose it is conceptually quite rich (i can see many potential essays about the role of voice in the movie, language, acting and known/unknown selves, etc), but when i watch a movie i'm looking to *feel* something, and drive my car left me feeling nothing. there is a real mismatch between the emotional weight of the experiences the characters have and how we see the character act. obv this is not a problem in and of itself. the problem is that the film sustains this mismatch for far too long, and the characters began, at some point, to feel not hurt/traumatized/in shock but simply flat. the ending scene in the snow, which is meant as a moment of catharsis, produced no real impact on me because i was so alienated from these characters. it was like watching robots have breakdowns. the film also failed, imo, to satisfactorily develop kafuku and misaki's relationship. i really think misaki's actress was robbed of screen time. did we really need all those rehearsal scenes? it was also extremely annoying to find the manic pixie dream girl trope rearing its head in BOTH of the main female characters, who seemed to only exist to accessorize kafuku's character. (i am so damn tired of these 'dead wife' movies. solaris. paris, texas. it's misogyny dressed up in a nice color grade.) i absolutely adore evil does not exist, hamaguchi's most recent film, so i came into this expecting to love it. i still think he's a really talented filmmaker, and there are some scenes in here i loved (the hands out the skylight w/ the cigarettes immediately comes to mind), but it just completely missed the emotional chords it was trying to hit.

Green Book for the arthouse crowd - Armond White Surely no masterpiece - David Stratton Reasonably happy that a 3 hour Japanese film with multiple meta-narratives which asks of some familiarity with Chekhov from the audience has proven so popular. I much preferred a very different film festival darling from 2021, the gritty and strangling Hive from Kosovo which ran a tight 80 minutes, but any increased appreciation for more challenging cinema is respectable. Whilst it would be nice for recent slow cinema diamonds like Long Day's Journey Into Night (2018) or Inside the Yellow Cocoon Shell (2023) to share in some of this success I much prefer to discuss this film over Don't Look Up or Squid Game which seemed to dominate cultural conversation that year. The strength of the film is this running theme that 'we are the love we have lost' and how that manifests in different ways for various personality types. On this, the text succeeds, it is humanist and relatable. There are moving moments, I like the smoking through the sunroof and the closing lines of Uncle Vanya delivered through sign language from a mute Sonya (Park Yu-rim) and particularly enjoyed the scene of Yūsuke (Hidetoshi Nishijima) observing his wife's infidelity then leaving quietly. I also love the Saab, great car choice. Length is not so much the issue, it is the inability for the film to stay focused which lets it down. A generation raised on meandering television series seems not to mind this but I still expect a level of purposeful refinement to writing and craft to pacing. The cinematography is also done in the modern adroit style, cuts to a still shot with an object entering the scene with speed or a slow dissolve between spinning wheels and spinning tape on a cassette. I don't mind when this style is used for intention over design ( Past Lives ) but too often the objective is the aesthetic. What to say about the connections to Chekhov? Burin described it as "both wide-of-the-mark and on-the-nose" which I like, the play material either feels abstract from the emotional malaise or stops still to show direct connection. I like that it took such a difficult shot at it though with the multilingual angle. Vanya on 42nd Street definitely handled the material better but it was a smart move to take a different approach here. Landscapes were beautiful.
Not really for me, but I was quite impressed by how this 3 hour long slow-paced film went by decently quickly. It had a rhythm. I just like movies that actually have something going on.

I like a lot of different parts of this film. But to quickly sum up my feelings, I feel as if “The juice is not worth the squeeze” with this one.. I hate to feel that way as there’s a lot of things to like about this film, it’s just the time it takes to get there. The film has a general slow pace which I don’t mind in films, it’s the execution. There’s a lot of scene developing subtext about characters and their emotions towards one another, not a lot of dialogue and usually if it is it’s not directly saying what is true to the moment. WHICH is the point of the film, but I just never found the dialogue itself and the issues at hand to always be interesting enough to warrant this technique or development to be so prominent throughout the runtime. Then there’s portions where you are getting somewhere and….it’s….getting…there….just….keeeep……waiting……we’re…..THERE. I actually loved those moments for what it’s worth, it’s just that the pacing is already slow as molasses and the better moments in themselves is slow as well. The opening credits rolled around the 45 min mark and that just mentally did something to me, when I realized how that opening portion of the film was meant to actually start the movie. Something that I feel could have been shortened from 45 minutes to about 15-20 with effective dialogue and pacing. It’s hard to really harp on a director on pacing when most of that is intentional in this case. You can feel it’s meant to be a slow grind to the finish line for the pay off to feel that much more emotionally rewarding to see, yet I felt like the finishing beats of the film are something you can read on the characters face the entire time and a lot of the “filler” I experienced was for something I expected the whole time. There’s a few good moments throughout this run time like I said earlier, I enjoy parts. I love most scenes with the driver, this is a character that I think has good interactions with the lead to really break Yūsukes walls down. Her story really came full circle at the end which felt good, yet sometimes in certain emotional moments there’s a point where the dialogue really gets on the nose with things like “AND THIS EMOTIONAL MOMENT IN MY LIFE CAN SERVE AS A LESSON TO YOU BTW….” For a film that’s subtle throughout its entire run, it sort of blows its figurative load randomly throughout the film and seems to have a hard time finding a balance between nuance and convenient dialogue. Something I did like about the film is some of the themes in particular the overhead theme of grief and how you can grieve someone you have complicated feelings about. How hard it may be to let go of certain ideas about this person, that there isn’t going to be a reconciliation. The complexities of human relationships, how one person can never truly be understood 100% even through years and years of a relationship. There are always different sides of us as we grow and change. It’s about adapting, growing, challenging yourself and coming to grips with hard truths. The car scene between Yūsuke & Takatsuki is probably the best directed bit and best written portion of the film. It’s a payoff inside about the last hour of the film. The performances across the board are good, especially the lead, if not a little drab seeing him almost never smile and just look melancholic almost the whole film. Overall I think this just felt like overly long for myself and that could it be cutdown at least half an hour at minimum and have its emotional effectiveness still hit.

Drive My Car no es una película sobre aprender a vivir con una pérdida. Es, quizá, una película sobre descubrir que nunca terminamos de conocer a las personas que amamos. Kafuku pasa buena parte de su vida intentando descifrar a Oto: sus silencios, sus infidelidades, las historias que inventa, aquello que calla. Pero cuando ella muere, descubre una paradoja devastadora: a veces la muerte no nos arrebata solamente a una persona, sino también la posibilidad de hacerle las preguntas que dejamos para después. Quizá amar sea convivir con esa clase de incertidumbre. La película parece decir que escuchar no siempre significa alcanzar al otro. Podemos conocer su voz, sus gestos, sus rutinas y hasta sus heridas, y aun así existir frente a una habitación interior cuya puerta nunca se abre del todo. Por eso el auto funciona como algo más que un escenario: es un espacio de confesión. Dos desconocidos avanzan durante horas sin mirarse directamente, y paradójicamente, en esa ausencia de mirada consiguen verse de verdad. Misaki y Kafuku no se salvan mutuamente; simplemente se reconocen en el lugar donde ambos están rotos. Y quizá ahí está lo más hermoso: no necesitamos resolver el dolor de alguien para acompañarlo. La película también cuestiona esa idea romántica de que amar significa conocer al otro por completo. Tal vez sea exactamente al contrario. Amar es aceptar que el otro siempre conservará una parte de sí mismo que no nos pertenece. Hay algo profundamente humano en nuestra necesidad de encontrar explicaciones: creemos que ponerle palabras a una herida hará que duela menos. Pero algunas heridas no se cierran cuando encontramos una respuesta, sino cuando dejamos de exigirla. Drive My Car me dejó pensando que el duelo no consiste solamente en extrañar a alguien, sino en aprender a vivir con todo lo que nunca sabremos de esa persona. Y quizás amar a alguien sea también hacer las paces con ese misterio. ¿Es posible conocer verdaderamente a alguien a quien amamos, o el amor exige abrazar la imposibilidad de comprenderlo por completo?

And I could talk for hours about the importance of the last “words” of the movie (pre epilogue) being the last of Uncle Vanya and signed. I think that a lot of people don't truly understand the power this has. Some scenes, which my memory obliterated, were a lit bit more cringe (the brain sometimes). This rewatch made me realise that this movie is clearly the reason why I'm so touch-starved for long powerful hugs full of emotions, and why I give them so much meaning and importance in my life. Because they say more than words. (Especially as I am aroace this is like the top thing I can manage/accept from/give to others) My own car, I also realise, is my home, I don't think I ever feel more myself, in my body and my thoughts, than when I'm in my car. I never feel at home anywhere. But everytime I'm in my car, I can breathe . My overthinking becomes clear, quiet. It all untangles . And now I'm crying because what am I doing with my life right now? I'm not meant to stay. It's a shame that I haven't read Uncle Vanya yet when this movie has such an importance to me. How can I pretend to truly understand it (even if the extracts of the text are perfectly inserted in the movie) if I haven't read what makes the main character so torn?

Drive My Car follows an actor and theater director, Yusuke Kafuku who get invited to direct a multilingual production of Uncle Vanya in Hiroshima, two years after his wife passed away. There, he meets Misaki, his quiet personal driver. Through long drives and theater rehearsals, he slowly confronts his grief, secrets, and inner healing. It’s a slow film, but it never feels boring to watch. The cinematography is outstanding the views of Hiroshima by the sea feel so fresh and beautiful, also the snowy scenes in Kutsukake’s hometown are stunning. I really liked how the film gives a long 40-minute prologue as background for the character, so there are no flashbacks for the rest of the movie. Even though it’s slow, the pacing feels just right. It’s interesting to follow the characters’ theater rehearsals and preparations, and how the play’s dialogues parallel the characters’ inner conflicts. The use of different languages by the actors is also very unique. The “dialogue” between Sonia and Uncle Vanya in the ending is incredibly powerful.

A film about grief, intimacy, guilt, and how little we can ever truly know another person. Loved how the red saab becomes this private space between solitude and connection, where Yusuke and Misaki slowly recognize the same guilt in each other without ever needing to completely explain themselves. Uncle vanya slowly becomes more than a play within the film. The multilingual rehearsals, repetition, sign language… all blur the line between performing and actually confronting yourself. Acting becomes another language for feelings you can’t say as yourself. Such an impressive way to weave a play through three hours where even the lines we understand seem to quietly serve the film’s message. So subtle. Grief lingers through the slow pacing and endless drives, which somehow gave me a bittersweet sense of peace. And that Hokkaido journey with the red car surrounded by snow finally gives them the space to say what they’ve been carrying. Not forgiveness, not closure, just acceptance. Then misaki inherits the saab. The same car that carried Yusuke through his grief, memories, and loneliness now carries her. Maybe that’s all there is to it sometimes. You carry what you’ve lost, you get behind the wheel and you keep the car moving.

A subtle yet rich work. The Saab too was a great addition to the cast. It seems remarkable that the switch to Hiroshima was a COVID workaround. Fitting, perhaps, that, in the end, that city of lost souls served as the backdrop for this tale of grief, regret, and rebuilding after profound loss.
I know there’s way more important stuff here but I have to point out that the 2-door red Saab is one of the best movie cars I’ve ever seen. Just a truly excellent car. Lots of character.

- Sr. Kafuku, me siento vacío. No hay nada dentro de mí. Sobre la conexión con el texto que comentó… creo que la sentí con los guiones que escribía Oto. Por eso vine aquí, porque quería volver a sentir eso. Así que… lo que dijo Ud. de que Oto nos unió… tiene toda la razón. Por fin lo entiendo. - […] Oto no tuvo interés por nada durante años, y un día de repente, empezó a escribir historias. Bueno, a contarlas. […] Existía un fuerte vínculo entre el sexo y todas sus historias, aunque no lo pareciera. […] esas historias nos ayudaron a los dos a sobreponernos […]. Como pareja creo que congeniábamos bien. Nosotros dependíamos el uno del otro. Yo pensaba que nuestra vida estaba totalmente completa, tanto en el día a día como en el plano sexual. Al menos así era para mí. […] jamás puse en duda su amor por mí […], no se me ocurriría. […] Aún así había algo oscuro en su interior, un lugar al que yo nunca conseguí llegar. - ¿Y a Ud. nunca se le ocurrió preguntarle por qué hacía todo eso? - Es que lo que más miedo me daba era que yo pudiera perder a Oto. […] - ¿No es posible que ella quisiera que simplemente Ud. la escuchara? - ¿Alguna vez Oto te contó algo a ti? Sé sincero. - [Procede a contarle la historia de la adolescente que era una lamprea, con el final]. Bueno, solo me contó hasta ahí. No sé si ese es el final del relato o quizá sea mucho más largo. Al contármelo, me dejó con un nudo en el estómago pero incluso así, al escucharlo de sus labios, me di cuenta de que Oto había compartido algo importante conmigo. Sr. Kafuku, por lo poco que sé, Oto era una mujer con un gran corazón, está claro que yo apenas la conocí, y que después de tanto tiempo Ud. la conocía infinitamente mejor. Pero lo que sí tengo es una cosa clara en este momento, compartió su vida con una mujer increíble durante 20 años, y debería sentirse agradecido por ello. Es mi humilde opinión. Aunque uno piense que cree conocer a alguien perfectamente, aun si ama a esa persona, nunca podrá saber lo que guarda en lo más profundo de su corazón. Solo conseguirá sufrir. Pero si pudiéramos esforzarnos un poco, lograríamos conocernos a nosotros mismos mucho mejor. Realmente creo que al final lo único que tenemos que hacer es ser sinceros con nosotros mismos, y seguir los dictados de nuestro corazón con honestidad. Si uno desea conocer el alma de los demás, no le quedará más remedio que conocer la suya primero. Un périple rempli à la fois de mélancolie et de chaleur humaine, une véritable balade à l'atmosphère oscillant entre la profonde tristesse provenant de passés douloureux, et un sentiment d'apaisement. À l'intérieur de cette voiture rouge difficile à rater, nous allons assister à la rencontre de deux êtres blessés et égarés. Dans cette sorte de cocon permettant au protagoniste d'échapper au dehors, cette espèce de symbole de son intimité, de son monde intérieur où il s'est renfermé sur lui-même, une chauffeuse viendra s'y introduire, cette deuxième âme esquintée qui deviendra progressivement pour le personnage principal une compagnie précieuse, une semblable avec laquelle il développera une relation de confiance, transformant petit à petit ce qui était un environnement de solitude et d'isolement en un refuge, un lieu de partage et de guérison pour deux individus aux plaies encore ouvertes, une voiture avec laquelle ils partiront vers un voyage introspectif. Avec Drive My Car, Ryusuke Hamaguchi démontre une nouvelle fois sa capacité à fluidifier et teinter d'authenticité ses métrages. Le film se déroule lentement, soigneusement, en laissant tout le temps à son spectateur de s'imprégner de son ambiance naturelle. Je me suis vraiment complètement senti absorbé par ces silences, ces instants de calme presque aérien, cette mise en scène utilisant les espaces, les environnements, les regards ou encore de simples gestes pour illustrer l'intériorité des personnages avec subtilité, mais aussi toutes ces discussions parfois chaleureuses, et à d'autres moments beaucoup plus lourdes, quand les fêlures étouffées refont finalement surface. Il y a une profonde humanité qui se dégage de ce film, notamment lorsque Hamaguchi va, autour d'une pièce de théâtre servant de fil conducteur, présenter des personnages d'horizons distincts, certains avec des origines différentes, s'exprimant avec d'autres langues, et même un autre ayant un handicap avec lequel il parvient à vivre. On sent que le réalisateur tient à dépeindre tout ce qui fait la richesse de l'humain, que ce soit en montrant les différences apparentes, mais aussi en explorant des vécus qui n'ont rien à voir entre eux. À travers cette pièce de théâtre et les récits gravitant autour, ayant comme le dit si bien le film le pouvoir de faire ressortir toute la subtilité et la profondeur des sentiments, ainsi que les interactions entre nos deux protagonistes qui sont parfois remplies d'échanges et parfois simplement silencieuses, Hamaguchi explore les différents chemins pour espérer franchir la terrible épreuve qu'est le deuil et tenter de soulager son mal-être, un moyen d'avancer malgré ce trou béant provoqué par la perte et la culpabilité, qui se trouverait donc dans le partage, l'introspection et l'extériorisation. Faire preuve d'honnêteté et faire la paix avec soi-même, accepter ses erreurs, ses regrets, ce qui ne peut être changé, et rester malgré tout ouvert au reste du monde, c'est pour moi ce que prône Drive My Car, cette sublime parenthèse de vie pleine d'humanité qui m'aura complètement transporté.

The first time I saw this was on release, and it remains one of my favorite moviegoing experiences. I caught a late showing in my college town, walked out around 1am, and still had time to grab a burger and a drink at one of my favorite bars. I gave it five stars then — it left me with a strange, specific peace I couldn't fully explain. About four years later, I hit play again and realized how much I'd actually forgotten. It felt almost like a first viewing, except this time I was older, a little wiser, and genuinely stunned by how good the script is. It would be easy to assume the film is simply "inspired" by Murakami's short story of the same name, but it's actually weaving together at least two more stories from the same collection — "Kino" and "Scheherazade" — alongside Chekhov's Uncle Vanya, which functions as the film's central framing device, mirroring the protagonist's emotional state and his relationship to his own grief. None of it feels clunky or bolted on — it's fully absorbed into the film's own language. What struck me most this time is how the despair on screen never too feel harsh toward the viewer — but the tension is there. It's life, distilled: that inevitable state of living and missing, of loss that doesn't resolve so much as scar over. And still — you move forward. Maybe that's the most human thing there is.

Not all three-hour movies are going to be GOATs. For every GODFATHER/GODFATHER PART II, you are going to get a MEET JOE BLACK. Happily, DRIVE MY CAR falls into the former category. The 35-minute prologue set in Tokyo is one of the greatest pieces of cinema I've ever seen. The complex relationship between Hidetoshi Nishijima's protagonist, and Reika Kirishima as his wife -- who features in three sensitive and nuanced explicit love scenes, something you don't find with 48-year-old actresses in Hollywood -- is well-written and well-directed, with a turntable playing Beethoven and a full-length hallway mirror, given Chekhovian introductions. Speaking of Chekhov, the remainder of the film involves NIshijima directing a multilingual performance of "Uncle Vanya" in Hiroshima, with young Toko MIura as a driver he didn't ask for. Six languages are utilized. The cast and theater staff (including Miura) are broken characters who use the play as therapy to explore or heal their wounds, but not every character finds their muse in Chekhov or achieves their happy ending. The three hours fly by. Long silences in a film can be deadly but here the silences invite you to think and reflect. A gorgeous work of art, and the fact that it was made during COVID, with an epilogue set at the height of the pandemic, only makes it more urgent and more interesting.

Hearing the hype around this movie for a while so i was excited to finally get high and dedicate a deserving 3 hrs to it. Hamaguchi, imo Japan's premiere contemporary voice on dramatic, ‘exploration of self’ movies, does what he normally does in creating a set of characters that are both understated and wholly captivating. We care about these people, the traces they leave behind, and the specters they follow. Hamaguchi’s impressive filmography might really be topped here; distinctly Japanese yet subtly critical of 21st century Japan, DMC just does so much to underline a ghostly collective Japanese consciousness, creating a deeply personal, heartfelt and beautiful sense of isolation. As an American person watching DMC it definitely aches; i get a sense of looking inward from the outside at a culture that I think I understand, but do not truly know. Its like touching something through a pane of glass. Then theres the monumental, and perfectly executed attempt at adapting and reimagining a Murakami novel. To take this legendary written voice and put it to screen such that it FEELS like we are truly being transported to several of his multi-realmed kami worlds is significant. Murakami has such fun with the concept of overlay and Hamaguchi doesnt disappoint in his exploration of it; who is Kafka? Who is Misaki? Who is Oto? Where are we? Are we here, or did we lose ourselves somewhere else, searching for answers that shouldnt have questions. How do we express the existence of others in the projections of ourselves and do we move on, or is a part of ourselves never actually with us, but left behind in a place beneath or above us, through a tunnel, unseen.

"And what you most can’t have is what you already had, and lost" sirens scene from The Odyssey is all i could think about throughout watching Drive My Car, and that line pretty much sum up most of my feelings. such a moving depiction of being grief-stricken, trauma and the weight of the guilt that comes along with it. a deeply personal and emotionally resonating story that will touch many lives on so many levels, without a shadow of doubt one of the finest films of 2020s. grief is the hardest emotion to ever process, to the point when you finally feel like you've come terms with, it just randomly hits you like a truck out of nowhere and you can't help but crumble, fall to pieces wishing how things would be different. time flies and we just learn to live with it, carrying fond memories. kafuku and misaki raising cigarettes out of sunroof while driving away into the night is definitely my favourite moment and also the whole final performance legit left me speechless.

Asks the essential human question on how do we continue to choose to live in spite of everything. Drive My Car is a film of reserved stillness that rewards the patient, really fell into this one. Ambient, slow and steady yet full of humanistic integrity, Hamaguchi’s rendition lifts Murakami's 20 or so page short story about an isolated man dialoging through his past and turns it into an incredibly ambitious project concerning art, personhood, grief, transference through creation, and acceptance. The creative liberties it takes with the initial story turns it from a compelling piece about two people conversing into an incisive and engaging treatise on the anatomy of melancholy and complex yet essential human truths. The words we leave unsaid end up corroding us from the inside out; sometimes all we need is someone not to fix anything for us, but simply to hear us out. Life changes when we move away from drifting inaction and decide to choose every second. To be heard is to feel connected, to be connected is to feel alive, and to feel alive is to save ourselves. Visually gorgeous and the soundtrack had me floating… sometimes films come to you at the right time when you need them, and this one did just that. Can feel myself returning to this one a lot in years to come.

But unfortunately, Happy Hour truly tried my patience, crawling at a snails pace with a story that is so stupidly lacking in any narrative drive whatsoever. Even the actors looked dreadfully bored here, exacerbating my complete lack of engagement with the worthless goings-on of this awfully disappointing film. For a director who had been so good at mesmerising me up till now (Drive My Car, Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy, Asako I & II), I'm rather sad I now have to be so scathing towards Hamaguchi.

I love movies about mundane lives of people, I love movies about (almost) nothing but the *feels* but this isn't it for me. I had no idea this movie was so focused on loveless marriages and affairs. I tried searching for some wisdom or interesting insights in the dialogues but they were...just boring and stiff like characters themselves. The cinematography was as simple as it gets. 5 hours of this on loop is too much. Disappointed.

Four thirty-something friends navigate love, marriage and personal growth while supporting each other through life's challenges. Unlike the previous films I've seen from this director, this film does have a sense of authenticity with characters, and chemistry, that feel genuine. However, the characters themselves are relatively uninteresting and the film fails to highlight anything meaningful about them. It often feels like a series of mundane small moments of their lives played out in real time--like a long workshop in trust exercises or an hour long reading of a dull book. As I'm generally not into slice of life type of stories, this may have been somewhat enjoyable had the characters been more layered or the film been more dynamic but as it is it's dull, lacks spark and is way too long for what little it has. 令人難受。 濱口的去戲劇化並不是為了某種布列松式的極簡主義或是像侯孝賢一般去突出時間的不感症（而其中工作坊一景可能才算得上是碰觸到了這種意圖），相反地，他的電影哲學似乎是在於「能用說的就不要用演的」，也因此煞盡苦心的把所有關於精神的荒漠、性格的碰撞還有道德焦慮都文縐縐的刻進了對白之中。 然而，它劇情的編排卻簡單降智到一個令人驚訝的地步，《歡樂時光》方便的為每個主要角色都設置了一個功能相似的恐慌按鈕以及講述他們如何利用做作的冷漠來逃脫；而事實上，我認為濱口龍介很聰明的把「生活化」的敘事作為這種逃脫的表象，但對於一部長達五個小時的電影而言，這樣的表象顯然遠遠不夠...還有它所呈現（並試圖辯證）的當代生活場景，過於理想化的程度而使其實際上比它想要指責（控訴？）的東西還來的空虛。 而怪異的地方在於，當我終於有辦法靜下來仔細聆聽那些talking heads對某些事情的看法的時候，那些理當可愛的角色卻都顯得如此令人生厭，幾乎是導演帶著惡意可以為之一樣...

C- I tried to like this one. I really did. Having seen Drive My Car (also by director Ryusuki Hamaguchi), I knew this was going to be slow, but as long as it was still investing like DMC I didn't think it would be a problem. But I never got invested, no matter how hard I tried. The first hour I found really tough to get through since more than half of that time frame is this session at a physical therapy class or whatever that was, and it wasn't like DMC where you could technically lose the first forty minutes but in doing so you would sacrifice some crucial and rich characterization, because during this session we learn nothing major about anyone. But since I had another four hours to go I wasn't judging it too harshly since I figured the pacing would pick up once the story kicked in. But sadly, even when the story did actually start, I was still unable to get into it. So for the past FIVE HOURS I've been bored out of my mind. I'm glad that this brought Hamaguchi into the international spotlight and that Drive My Car received major awards buzz which resulted in a Best Picture nomination, but that doesn't make me like THIS five hour slog any more then I do.

If this movie were a hamburger (I say this because I just ate two pepperoni and bacon hamburgers that my dad made and they were absurdly amazing), the moment this afternoon when I finally saw the credits would be the moment when, more than stuffed, feeling sick, I would lean back in my chair as if about to give birth, look up, turn my neck, sigh, and closing my eyes briefly, put my hand to my forehead as if in despair or regret for having eaten something bigger than I could handle. I think this comparison would be much better if I remembered exactly what I would say afterwards, today I'm not feeling well. "Happy Hour," being the Japanese classic that it is, was on my list and I randomly picked the name and went looking for it. I pressed play and damn, 5 hours of film made me think like it was a vital decision whether I would embark on this journey or live in peace, and perhaps fortunately (or unfortunately) I chose to watch, and now I just want to go home, sleep and make my mind think that this will regulate my sleep, but at least it will give me the rest I need. I should clarify that I didn't watch the whole movie in one sitting, not even in a single day, of course, and something tells me that some fanatics will comment that this was the reason I didn't like it so much, but damn, I'm not going to do that, I'm sorry. I watched about 3 hours of the movie today to finish it and I can't say if it was good or bad, but actually something in me makes me want to be sure that it wasn't enjoyable, and I agree with that something. I wanted to stop watching the movie several times and I don't know why I didn't. I think for some reason I expected it to be as good as "Eureka," which has a similar vibe, but this one is something much more distinct. Affairs, slice of life, the drama of constantly dissatisfied adult life and friendships—all of this makes up "Happy Hour" and the narratives of the four characters. I think this is an attempt to immerse us as much as possible in everyone's lives and the melancholy that pervades the entire film, which is why it's so long. In fact, the character development and the acting (including amateur performances, but still very good) are very good elements, but at the same time, I felt like I was traveling and traveling and didn't reach a destination with the plot. It's not that "Happy Hour" is necessarily bad; I understand that it's so acclaimed not only because cinephiles love a tediously long film (I say this respectfully, okay?) and, on top of that, a Japanese one, but because it's clearly a strong, well-made work with a unique approach; truly impressive. But personally, I can't like it. The story didn't grab my attention, I lost interest at numerous points, and despite appreciating several aspects like the well-done production, I couldn't connect with the film and I think I wasted my time watching the whole thing. I'm sorry.

Mis bout à bout, le projet impressionne : une narration audacieuse, un regard déjà singulier sur le monde, porté par une foi dans la puissance de la poésie, de l'écoute, des trajectoires personnelles. Comment se connaître et s'aimer soi-même, comment composer avec l'autre ? Hamaguchi est un cinéaste profondément philosophique, et qui l'assume — sa grâce est de rendre cette philosophie accessible. Il aime aussi inviter d'autres œuvres dans son cinéma, avec exigence : le théâtre dans "Drive My Car" ou "Soudain", et ici la lecture intégrale d'un texte intime signé d'une jeune romancière, suivie d'un débat avec elle. Postures clivantes, qu'on pourra juger anti cinématographiques, mais qui définissent son geste. Les moments les plus forts sont sans doute les affrontements. Je pense à cette soirée, après un atelier étrange où les quatre amies apprennent à écouter le corps des autres, où le divorce tenu secret de l'une d'elles finit par affleurer et fait éclater les tensions pour des raisons parfaitement inattendues, qui tiennent à la susceptibilité, à la jalousie. À partir de là, ce groupe qu'on imaginait uni vole en éclats, puis tente de se reformer sans jamais vraiment y parvenir. Beaucoup diront que le format tient davantage de la série ; je dirais simplement que "Senses" est un film trop long, parce que l'émotion s'y dilue sur une durée qu'il ne parvient pas à tenir. Les ramifications montent si haut qu'on finit par perdre de vue le tronc : l'amitié et ses perceptions divergentes au sein d'un groupe de femmes, la solidarité, l'amour, bref la vie, ou comment la reconstruire dans le Japon d'aujourd'hui, entre famille, amitié et travail. Dans ses œuvres suivantes, même plus courtes comme "Contes du hasard et autres fantaisies", l'artisan Hamaguchi devient orfèvre : l'émotion se densifie de film en film sans rien sacrifier des audaces de mise en scène. "Senses" n'atteint pas encore cette puissance. J'y vois pourtant la matrice de "Soudain", si différent dans son sujet mais si proche dans sa foi en la conversation comme événement : en resserrant sur deux personnages ce que "Senses" dispersait sur quatre trajectoires, Hamaguchi parvient enfin à tenir l'émotion sur la durée. Reste qu’il compose dans "Senses" avec une galerie de femmes complexes, autrement plus fines que les clichés dont se contentent la plupart des fictions, et touche à une vérité profonde dans la représentation de l'humain. On sent l'artiste au travail. Parler de brouillon serait injuste tant il contient de belles choses ; disons plutôt que les films qu'il signera ensuite, avec des ingrédients similaires, seront encore plus émotionnels, profonds, évocateurs.

I think it’s very unfair to compare the rich storyline of such a long movie with that of other films that are only about two hours long. In theory, if those two-hour movies also took the time to seriously develop their characters, their runtimes could easily stretch to over five hours as well. Therefore, in my view, calling the depth of this movie’s plot an “advantage” is essentially an unfair kind of cheating.

Happy Hour uses its runtime to give each member of the friendship group time to explore their own domestic dramas, but I came away from the film feeling that the script needed some sharpening given the repetition within those story lines.

There's an interesting heart to this film, but the characters are such awful self-centered people, I just ended up being annoyed more than anything else. I understand that to err is to be human, but some of the things these protagonists do and say is pretty irredeemable. I could not care for their lives, and I felt extremely bad for all the men in the film, which feels kind of misogynist? I found it very watchable nonetheless, just frustrated by what the film was actually trying to say.

While I love long films, there are times I'm daunted by the runtime depending on the film itself. 'Happy Hour' is a 5+ hour drama around the small lives of four women. That's right: just when you finished a 2 1/2 hour movie, you got another 2 1/2 hour movie to watch plus an additional seventeen minutes of your choice. Despite the praise, I'm rather mixed, but I can understand both opinionated sides, even if I lean a bit more on one. It's rather a visual novel: exploring their lives in full detail, every scene taking its time with its slower pacing, making sure the audience is living with them, details hidden till revealed, and really loves the leads by delaying the conflict till around the eighty-minute mark. My favorite would be Akari; she's a nurse and I found her more interesting in personality, although Sakurako's storyline kicks in gear around the three-hour mark, and Jun is the one with her conflict; Fumi's show comes in later. While I appreciate its commitment in itself, did it really need to be 317 minutes long? I don't think so. Cutting two hours or so would make it an abridged version, sure, but there were several times I felt unengaged and even bored because it felt rather dry and tedious, in my opinion. The length basically doesn't earn itself from its script, and I felt something rich and beautiful was missing. At least it wasn't sappy - far from it. 'Yi Yi' is almost three hours, but I never thought it was a bog as it manages to tell its epic slice-of-life story without sacrificing too much; 'Happy Hour', on the other hand, is too precious of its memories all the time. Some don't think it's a big deal, but I thought the cinematography was kinda boring. Let me say this: the framing and composition are well-done, but the lack of color grading and using only the white balance, I assume, got tiring and plain after a while. Also, the sound editing isn't amazing, but I imagine the budget was much smaller, and I've heard editing is expensive. I can see both sides defending for what they stand: either a reflective, human masterpiece or a bloated, self-indulgent movie. As for me, it's a risky experiment that doesn't fully pay off for me, where I see a great three-hour film hidden within what I thought was the editor's cut. A minor recommendation.

During the latter half of the expedition that is Happy Hour , there is a scene where a young author named Ms. Nose is criticized for having read her book to an audience in a monotone voice. She answers that since she knew the characters she wrote so well, and all of the emotions are on the page, no matter what vocal inflections she adds, the importance is found in the words. Happy Hour hinges on words and communication. For what's basically a five-hour-long monologue how could it not be about these things? The story follows four women who vocalize their anxieties to everyone except the people who these actual anxieties originate, mostly their husbands. The story becomes how communication gets lost in a marriage. Saying a couple of words as a husband and wife pass by each other around the breakfast table is not the kind of interaction that can sustain a marriage. Before long the important needs of these women go unaddressed and they realize they could do better. I like where Hamaguchi takes the story. In a very Bergman-esque fashion, he captures the female perspective with confidence. However, to draw on how Ms. Nose reads her book in a monotone way, the rest of the movie features the most unemotive acting I've ever seen. I believe this was done purposefully to show the true emptiness behind each woman's marriage. None of the cast are trained actors either for this reason. The scene I brought up basically literalizes the intent of emphasizing the dialogue. For my personal enjoyment of this film, I couldn't get compelled to care about any of these characters for the lack of them feeling like people I know or acting like actual people at all. A character would be told about how their partner wants a divorce and they would wear an awkward blank stare. Outside of the film's length showcasing an incremental decline of each character's relationship with their spouse, I did not see the need for a five-hour project. I would've settled for three. I think for anything dialogue-heavy, talented actors really go a long way to sell key emotional moments. A lot of the time I couldn't read what emotion a character was showing, rendering the point of the scene mute. Hamaguchi builds a believable world around its characters, but there was so much more to explore, things that were left unsaid, which makes me think that the five hour runtime could've been used more effectively.

This film is trying to do something different, which is to linger in the moments a lot longer than other movies. I don't mean long takes. I mean that instead of getting the essence of an experience it goes for the whole enchilada, so when the group goes to an encounter you get the whole thing. And you get the luncheon after and an analysis of the event. Which is an artistic risk and I applaud it. But it's not cinema verite either. Communication.  That was the main theme of this film.  While I liked the overall theme and plot points of this, I felt like there was a lot of filler that could have been cut out of it to make it a more tightly edited film.  After seeing Drive My Car a few months ago, I was interested to check out Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s work, as Drive My Car was a three hour long film, it didn’t feel that way.  I could definitely feel the running time on this as it felt like some of the conversations went on longer than they needed to.  Examples are: the communication exercise (which wouldn’t surprise me if it was an homage to Out 1 ) and the q&a also felt like it went on for too long. *Minor spoilers ahead* I did like the plot points revolving around the divorce court, underage pregnancy, and the dosing error that the nurse made, as it felt like all of these issues could have been prevented with better communication skills.  I also liked that the women began to question their respective relationships with both their significant others and with each other throughout the film. I still want to check out more of Ryusuke Hamaguchi as he seems to have his own style when making a film.  I personally feel that Drive My Car should be in the letterboxd top 250 over this.

I enjoyed this dialogue-driven flick in bursts and flashes -- more than I can say Hamaguchi's other big hit, Drive My Car -- whenever it really productively explored the ways we do or don't communicate with one another. I just wish it wasn't five-plus bloody hours. I know, I know: the entire movie is fundamentally about the ways we do or don't communicate, so my statement above can seem silly. The kick is that it does so with varying degrees of clarity or focus throughout its painful runtime, and I found myself rapt in those stretches where it really was tackling the concepts head-on. So yes, then this thing gets into the meaning of what it is to be in a relationship, and how we center ourselves while also supporting other people? Brilliant. I wasn't sold on its tactics at first, but the way Hamaguchi puts you through these trust exercises, seemingly without purpose, and then has a participant criticize the instructor with the same thoughts as I had, only to have the purpose hinted at a bit more firmly -- well, let's just say it helped crystallize the point of the film. It's not that I'm an idiot; I understand and appreciate some artistic metaphor and allusion. It's when people are staring in silence for five minutes, or moving into much less direct tangents that I find myself being pulled into areas of the film that work for me much less well, and that I think is where the majority of this thing spends its time. I don't need to be spoonfed, as I love when movies trust the viewer; but this also means the movie sometimes meeting me halfway. I value its quiet, austere, calm take, and that it's able to produce great tension in the most silent of conversations. I especially value the core concepts it's working with, and I was sucked into the movie when it really knuckled down. But as someone who cared a lot less for the meandering bits about infidelity, or gender roles in parenting, or career aspirations, I drifted in this thing a lot more than I'd like. In short, a bit too long and a bit too all-encompassing for the energy I was willing to put in. Still, an impressive beast, and one I'll be thinking about -- in pieces, at least.

I have never been in love which certainly limits my lens, but that’s precisely how I feel about every character here: none of them love anyone. Akari is amazing, but the rest I completely fail to understand on one level or another, anchored in their poor marriages. Of all the complex relationships, it’s the teen pregnancy plot with Sakurako’s son that I felt most invested in. They’re making it out like they’re trapped but if so it’s by themselves, none of them ever really talk or hang out with their partners. The degradation and perversion of relationships once full of life devolving into hollow routines imitating how they were when in love is a strong theme, and logically seems to fit, but I didn’t feel it conveyed that at all. There’s still a lot of tender moments, beautiful music and scenery, camerawork and writing that gets so close to every character, and acting that feels anything but despite my ultimate lack of empathy towards them.
