So, how do I represent the world, and not just myself? Happy Hour , more like Somber Five Hours . Hamaguchi, you madman. An over five hour movie that's more or less made up of conversation after conversation sounds like a death sentence for engagement. Instead, while I wasn't truly wowed by it like seemingly all of my mutuals on here were, I was at least impressed by it more often than not. It's conversational and almost scarily like watching genuine interactions between people that, despite how clearly so much effort is put into each exchange between its characters, the film with time starts to feel less like a narrative work and more like documentary. It's through these moments that the characters share, and what they talk about, that they are able to work through the woes of their lives. It is through talking that they will seemingly be taking a new path towards being better. Do I think Hamaguchi has portrayed that better in his other films at a much shorter length? Absolutely. I do also think that being able to make the ending to a film that's this long feel in some way cathartic, and it's not because you are in relief that it's finally over, that's still an achievement. I think also especially with intense family drama going on with myself currently, the moments reflecting on love and divorce had extra poignancy. I'll do my best to take from what Ryûsuke offers here and know that when darker feelings seem more fruitful, it's taking a breath and being able to communicate with others that's more valuable. 6/10

I was all in on the extensive runtime but if as a director you take the audience on a five-plus hour ride, you'd better have the internal logic of this world figured out before say, hour three. The first 180 minutes or so trade on the transfixing performances of the four leads, who add tremendous warmth and authenticity to their elliptically motivated characters. The last two hours though, never quite progress beyond those opaquely drawn character sketches, and it left me feeling stranded in a world where nothing quite connected together, where characters were mostly speaking at one another, delivering surprisingly rude personal judgments with extreme politeness and inertness, and little logical expression. It's mostly a shame, because the initial promise of the film is so tremendous.

A lot to like in Happy Hour but at over 5 hours in one sitting, I found it taxing on my attention span. It felt like it took a good two hours to even get going. The plot is quite compelling, a confrontation between Jun, Fumi, Akari, and Sakurako and the lives they have made for themselves. Most of the cast are non-actors from which Hamaguchi coaxes naturalistic performances. Especially given the long speeches the characters make, it’s impressive. But communication is the real key for these characters, and it’s the lack of communication between husbands and wives, parents and children, and dear friends which is the root of so much unhappiness. The film strips away structures and order, the detailed planners of the opening, to make room for the possibility of growth and fulfillment.

The story of four friends in Kobe and their disintegrating relationships amidst endless and varied attempts to communicate. Akari is divorced and outspoken, a strong nurse with an empathy deficit. Sakurako is a put-upon housewife with an ungenerous husband and a teenager (who in turn has a unexpectedly pregnant girlfriend). Fumi is a childless curator with a husband who's more a roommate than a romantic (or, at least, his romantic affections are directed elsewhere). And Jun is divorcing her spouse, a cold blooded scientist who hasn't harmed her but won't ever let her go, even if she has to fly into hiding with her unborn child. I've seen "Happy Hour" described as novelistic and that's true, but also a coded way of excusing its 317-minute run time. Just as much of a novel, however, the film reminds me of a workshop, and indeed two very long stretches of the movie are centered around performances of sorts at Fumi's arts space, PORTO (not to mention the extended, fractious discussions after both). Perhaps fitting as I understand that Ryusuke Hamaguchi developed the script through improvisational exercises with his non-professional actresses. Not entirely successful in its own right, as the dyads can feel a bit obvious and the pacing languorous, but I'm convinced that this work is a rehearsal for a compelling cinematic voice.

There were many times when a character would express a unique and nuanced thought or idea about life that resonated with me. Watched as part of my 5 Directors X 5 Unseen Films: Part 5 Challenge. Above all, Hamaguchi grants each protagonist the time, honesty, and care that are inimitable amongst his peers. An epic of the melodrama genre. Ironically, the sheer length of the film and the focus it gives the leading quartet still leaves them incomplete and granular (the point, no doubt). Fumi, in arguably the emotional climax of the film, walks home along those same bridges against the sunrise, alone.

The four main characters' lives form a parallel. If divorce is the mark that separates each character's own life, then Fumi and Sakurako are the before-divorce, Jun is the during-divorce, and Akari is the after-divorce. Neither Fumi and Sakurako legally divorced or even brought out divorce, yet they both experienced similar emotions and events that Jun and Akari went through that led to the end of their marriage. Between the last 1.25-1 hr, I was quite pissed to the fact that, so far, almost every character kept mingling in others' business, supported by what I understood as their sense of righteousness. It was only until later, after both Sakurako and Fumi couldn't stand their marriage anymore and fought back, that I realized they cared because they saw themselves in the couples they criticized. It's quite pessimistic that the writer of the movie decided for everyone to no longer stand their marriage. I don't have any data, nor am I familiar with Japanese culture or marriage life. So it could be a norm for most couple that, at some point, their love for each other diminishes infinitely to none, and all is left is the legal paper that binds them.

The book reading is one of the most accurate things I’ve ever seen in a movie, and that hurts. I hate readings! These four women are such finds. I want to see them in everything. Also, demand more from your men, folks!!

I ordered a region-free DVD player just so I could watch this intimate, five-hour-plus epic of domestic life from Ryusuke Hamaguchi, who’s quickly become one of my favorite working directors (and quite possibly my very favorite). Two discs, three viewing sessions, and one day of rumination later, I can say that Happy Hour is an essential part of Hamaguchi’s filmography, thoroughly imbued with the intelligence and humanity that mark his extraordinary recent work ( Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy , Drive My Car , Evil Does Not Exist ). I have a few hesitations about some recurring elements that, despite the massive runtime, feel less consequential than I’d like them to be (guy who runs the New Age workshop that we experience in full, I’m looking at you). But on the whole, I was happy to be immersed in a film that values the mundane but that, in its very form, departs so strikingly from ordinary moviegoing experience. A few areas of thought: * Loved how completely female friendship permeates the film, even through some long stretches in which Akari, Jun, Sakurako, and Fumi remain apart. I thought from time to time about Virginia Woolf’s The Waves , in which the friendship between six characters who meet as children and interact only intermittently as adults forms a vessel that gives life meaning, a structure of belonging that has no official sanction or force but remains a continuous source of identity. The slow pace of the film’s first two hours comes in part from how the women, preoccupied by and/or attempting to cover up unhappiness related to marriage, family life, and work, don’t communicate very openly with one another, but one senses how their bond might offer a framework for disruption or renewal. I found the middle hour, leading up to and immediately following the trip to the hot springs resort, most compelling for precisely this reason, as the women begin to prod each other—lovingly, but not always pleasantly—to speak beyond their learned inhibitions, to risk a more radical, unsettling kind of honesty with one another. * As for what the film has to say about gender, sex and sexuality, and Japan’s still conservative mores and laws around marriage and divorce: forceful stuff, appropriately stamped with the texture and complication of actual life. None of the heterosexual relationships in Happy Hour are satisfying in any way, and Jun’s refusal to submit herself to a marriage she’s come to experience as deadly—as she attests in court, he’s killed her by lack of conversation—acts as a catalyst for some of the other women to ask themselves questions about desire, need, and sacrifice that would otherwise remain encased in the “cotton wool” of the ordinary (I’m borrowing from Woolf again). Nevertheless, it’s not apparent that there are right or wrong choices for each of the women, merely that there are choices: whether one seeks a separation or a strategy for marital repair, one can do and say things beyond the routine and reassert a right to happiness, even when the path to happiness remains elusive. * On the related topic of expressivity: I understand that the stolid reserve of the women has a cultural element and that it makes key moments of breakdown or decisiveness all the more poignant. At times, though, the performances verge on illegibility, and in some of the more charged stretches of the last two hours, I couldn’t quite work out what the film was suggesting about self-possession under duress. It occurred to me that the restrained affect might be related to the film’s understanding of itself as a kind of literary text, too. The visiting writer who reads her short story aloud at the cultural institute where Fumi works is herself asked why she performs with so little emotion, and the answer is a fascinating one: she doesn’t want to pretend that she can inhabit all of her characters, and she thinks that a sort of presentational truth, one that simply delivers the words themselves, still carries all the requisite feeling. A version of this idea may apply to the film, too. In the relative absence of histrionics, perhaps we are better able to understand and internalize the accrued weight of what these women have carried in their lives, the unspectacular ways they have been subsumed into (but thankfully not consumed by) the everyday. * Lastly, about duration: yes, I do think this could be an hour or two shorter and it would work nearly as well. And yet, I think it’s important to say that this isn’t a miniseries in disguise. It’s a novelistic film, just as Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy is a filmic collection of short stories. Although I watched in installments, I felt the continuous logic of the film’s development, the way the friendship group’s warm, complex, fraught tangle shifted and reconstituted, and how it informed the dramas in the women’s individual lives. Though I found some parts of the film too languorous, a bit too repetitive or restrained, I also didn’t want to leave these characters in the end, with their understanding of themselves and the impact of some of their bolder, pattern-breaking choices still very much in progress. But that’s the truth in which I suspect Hamaguchi is most invested: whatever span of time one chooses for a story, markers like beginnings and endings are arbitrary impositions, creations dictated by narrative. Life doesn’t work that way, and neither does friendship. letterboxd.com/cinemapoodle/list/ryusuke-hamaguchi-ranked-so-far/

It has been a joy and quite a chance experiment to follow Hamaguchi’s career backwards from Evil Does not Exist, Drive my Car, to Wheels of Fortune and Fantasy, and Happy Hour. Recently got a sneak peak of All of a Sudden as well. I’m dying to watch his even earlier films like Passion and Asako, and I don’t know how he can surprise me more. As you get more into his filmography you tap on your forehead and have this realization that this is a director who knows what he’s best at and keeps mastering his craft. His talent of scene construction, script writing, character building, momentum continuity just shines through the screen from the beginning like no other. Massive thanks to French New Wave, to Kurosawa, and Locarno film festival for providing the inspiration and stage for Hamaguchi to leave marks in film history. I wonder if the title Happy Hour is the exact translation from the Japanese title or if there’s nuance. I hate that in American (?) culture it has a rather superficial meaning. The length of the film… I think I felt it was halfway after two hours ish, the typical length for an entire feature film, which was so surprising, you can’t resist your urge to check on time when the movie’s bad, and this one I even needed to calculate a bathroom break (when are they not talking!!? Haha). Hamaguchi has the ability of writing dialogue that run smoothly, you would speak like that in daily life, they can be philosophical but have the sprinkle of mundane. And when they are going they struck you, when they stop they linger. They are not fast words with volume like maybe Linklater films, and the characters speak in a flat tone, with breaks, it’s really interesting I wonder how much of it is directors decision. Cinematographer has easy time with Hamaguchi project maybe haha, shots are so simple not dreamy flowy etc, they can even be problematic by the industry standards? Especially in the workshop scene (much of time the window light overpower and you can’t see faces at all, it’s dark). But it serves Hamaguchi’s style so well. I like the framing, I like when the director stare into the camera moments are happening, I wonder how much style Hamaguchi developed already and carried forward from his documentary projects. After a Hamaguchi film, you are not so sure if humanity is good or bad, whether we should keep on having hopes or diving into despair. But you know for sure that humanity is there and it’s worth keeping looking into it and looking after it.

Clocking in at over five hours, Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Happy Hour (Happī Ā) is a quiet, monumental masterpiece of slow-cinema intimacy that feels less like watching a scripted movie and more like observing real lives unfold in unhurried, real time. Set in Kobe, the film follows a tight-knit circle of four women in their late 30s whose long-standing dynamics fracture when one of them suddenly reveals she is undergoing a messy divorce prompting the remaining three to re-examine their own stifled desires, marriages, and personal truths. What makes the film so uniquely captivating is Hamaguchi’s extraordinary process: developed through acting workshops with non-professional actors, the performances possess an astonishing, naturalistic grace (jointly earning all four lead actresses the Best Actress award at Locarno). Extended sequences like a fascinating body-listening workshop or a literary reading are allowed to breathe so fully that minor shifts in conversation carry the emotional impact of major plot twists. It’s an epic, exquisitely patient exploration of female friendship, emotional honesty, and the quiet compromises of adulthood.

can't quite decide if this or evil does not exist is hamaguchi's masterwork so far. one of them is going up to a 10 by the end of the year, trust you me. absolutely massive movie, but often in ways that are unexpected. compared to the slow pomposity of what i've seen of satantango or eureka, the oppressive trod of an elephant sitting still or the arch narrative construction of seven samurai, this movie is pretty airy. it feels its length but it's insanely hard to imagine what to cut. a lot happens here, and the trademark hamaguchi-ness of treating mundanity with the importance it deserves means that this lot of events needs a lot of time. one of my first film reawakening moments came with watching the juilliard scene in tar, and this movie clears that trick with the MASSIVE workshop and qna scenes, neither of which feel intrusive because it just... it'd feel weird to cut them away and edit them, ykno? sandwich a slice of life in between that's pretty breezy pacing wise and it creates this delightfully verisimilitudinous form. the character work is genuinely immaculate. there's a controlled mood here, hamaguchi's characters feel but it is so often deflected or stated without exaggerated movements or raised voices. when one of our four main ladies just thonks onto the floor in grief and overwhelmingness, you feel that in your bones. all of the characters feel lived-in; we see them fuck up and act in questionable methods, and simultaneously see them offering wonderful kindnesses to people. you see how these people might have become friends, and hope that the brief break they get can someday be had again in the future. if there is a tiny flaw, i don't think it's visually as beautiful as some of the work hamaguchi would go on to make. drive my car and especially evil does not exist both achieve a wonderfully intense yet controlled colour that this lacks, and while the editing is wonderful, the camera shots also feel the teensiest bit derivative of edward yang's work as compared to later works starting to become a bit more idiosyncratic. it's a nitpick because to even get a comparison to yang is high fucking praise from basically anyone.

Passei cinco horas do meu domingo imersa na vidinha de quatro amigas e que experiência confortante principalmente quando você não está com a menor vontade de viver a própria vida. O filme tem essa capacidade deliciosa de simplesmente deixar as coisas acontecerem, acompanhar o desenrolar espontâneo, coletivo e individual dessas mulheres, suas particularidades, relações, pequenos conflitos e a rotina, até que você sente que realmente passou aquele tempo convivendo com elas. E o melhor é como o melodrama vai surgindo aos poucos, em cada canto do filme. A amiga que está se divorciando da maneira mais dramática possível, a enfermeira despojada que quebra o pé, a mãe, esposa e dona de casa que passou a vida se reprimindo e a outra que assiste ao marido se apaixonar por outra sem poder fazer muita coisa. Tudo vai ganhando proporções cada vez mais dramáticas, mas sem que o filme abandone seu ritmo contemplativo. Narrativamente, ele trabalha muito com a duração, os silêncios e as conversas, deixando que os conflitos se desenvolvam organicamente das relações, em vez de conduzir a história por grandes viradas. É justamente essa estrutura paciente que faz tudo parecer tão espontâneo, quase como se estivéssemos apenas testemunhando pedaços da vida dessas mulheres. Cinco horas de filme que passam como cinco horas da vida de alguém. Filme lindo!

我心中最理想的配置，會是《在車上》跟《歡樂時光》交錯著看。這禮拜看《歡樂時光》，下禮拜看《在車上》，如果能一直反覆反覆著看就太好了。 五個半小時的《歡樂時光》，它不能切成五份，它不可能也不可以拍成影集，它是最特殊的觀影體驗。 從一開始的那個鏡頭，我們跟著女主角們坐在火車裡，搖搖晃晃的穿過綠色隧道。我們會發現，《歡樂時光》提供的不只是一個故事，它還邀請你一起跟主角們旅行、野餐、參加工作坊與朗讀會。我們不只是旁觀一個故事，還彷彿置身其中，跟著主角們一起煩惱，跟著主角們一起焦慮。 ★ 我讀了這部電影的電影書《在鏡頭前表演》，裡面提到，電影中的工作坊只跟表演者決議了流程，就用拍紀錄片的方式拍出來，但第一次沒有拍到需要的素材，大約兩個月之後再拍了一次。 這一段事實上沒有劇情，但我們的情緒被工作坊本身牽引，這兩個人背靠背能不能順利的站起來？四個人呢？全部人一起呢？這次會成功嗎？ 而整個後編都在呼應著前編工作坊的「倚靠」主題，四個女主角有時候互相倚靠，有時候摔倒，但大多數都能接住對方——即使沒有出現，也沒有真的缺席。 電影快結束時，向來很兇的明里給學妹一個擁抱，很深很深，很久很久。這部電影就是這樣，看完像是被擁抱了一樣，而且不是輕率的擁抱，是貫串過去現在未來的擁抱。 ★ 那到底什麼是「歡樂時光」？ 前編的工作坊結束時，帶領的鵜飼說： 「背對背站立、聆聽五臟六腑、貼額頭⋯⋯我不知道這些事有沒有意義。但平常我們不太有機會嘗試這些溝通方式。」 「如果人我之間能建立完美的平衡，那或許會是很幸福的一段時光。但我們也會不斷的在關係中失重，不斷的需要找回這種感覺。」 「希望大家把在工作坊學會的東西，帶回日常生活中。」

《歡樂時光》 因為《在車上》開始認識 濱口竜介 這位導演，從《偶然與想像》看見精巧的「對話」如何塑造電影的靈動感，但真正讓我愛上濱口電影的，則是《歡樂時光》。 《歡樂時光》講述四位友好女性的日常，劇情圍繞在看似平凡無奇的生活中，各自所面臨的情感困境。 《歡樂時光》的主題是「溝通」，也是濱口電影的主旋律。雖然有人認為濱口大量使用對話來推進劇情的電影風格，有點「話癆」。但這次在電影院欣賞《歡樂時光》，則讓我更加確定，濱口的電影不只是在對話上有獨到的設計外，同時鏡頭語言的掌握也很厲害。 電影好幾幕的對話，鏡頭都是正對著說話者，使觀眾彷彿在角色面前「聆聽」其講述。然後在多人交談的場景時，透過適當的剪輯調度，讓交叉紛雜的對話鮮活而不單調，且情緒轉折與氛圍改變時也很自然。 電影中除了可看到濱口擅長的「車內對話」外，在電車和某些移動場景，更可見其善於運用自然的光影明暗，來傳達角色幽微的心境變化。 而《歡樂時光》最吸引我的，還是在於演員們在鏡頭前真誠地袒露自我，表達那些生活中被壓抑已久的心聲，呈現了「語言」、「非語言」的溝通，以及溝通的「阻礙」與「抵達」，還有那試圖觸及他人內心的「意願」。

My first Edward Yang film, and while the story itself is relatively clear about Taiwan’s situation during the period it portrays, the aftermath of the Chinese Civil War, the migration to the island, and the way violence, prejudice, and social tensions shaped that society, the way the film chooses to tell all of this feels far more fragmented and disorienting. At first, it seems as though we will follow a single character in something close to a coming-of-age story, especially through his feelings for a girl. But over the course of its four-hour runtime, the film constantly branches out into teenage power disputes, gang rivalries, side characters, and parallel stories that do not always clearly converge with the main narrative. This also extends to Yang ’s mise-en-scène. Many of the film’s most important moments avoid the traditional shot-reverse-shot structure; the camera often remains static, refusing to follow reactions or decisive actions, leaving much of what happens outside the frame, almost as mere suggestion. It’s an interesting style because it forces the viewer to fill in the gaps through their own perception, yet at the same time it dissipates some of the dramatic weight of the events and weakens the emotional involvement with what the characters are going through.

How do you rate a movie that’s both amazing and terrible at the same time? There’s a terrific scene 42 min into the movie where Si’r’s brother, Lao Er, goes to play pool at the 217 gang’s hideout. Although we don’t actually see him playing pool, we hear him pocketing every shot and see the looks of surprise on a spectator’s face as he wins the game, and all of the money on the table. This is a great scene, but it’s also confusing: we never actually see Lao Er’s face, and have to intuit that it’s him based on a brief scene 20 minutes prior in which he picks up a cue ball at a party. You would also think this foreshadows him winning lots of money playing pool (given his incredible talent) but the next significant time we see him, it’s towards the end of the film when he’s being beaten over debt he’s accrued from gambling—something that feels inconsistent with his previous characterization. I mention this scene because it represents what I dislike so much about this film. It’s filled with scenes that are so great on their own, but within the context of the broader narrative, fail to coalesce into anything cohesive. Toward the end, it’s revealed that Si’r actually saw Ming kissing Sly, not Jade. This ultimately leads to the climax of the film, so it’s undoubtedly an important piece of information. But it was never clear to the audience that Si’r thought it was Jade who kissed Sly in the first place, so this detail really just adds confusion. And that initial kissing scene is briefer than the pool scene I mentioned earlier, so it’s narrative weight isn’t clear either. I wanted to enjoyed this movie more than I did, but instead found myself constantly pausing and rewinding to understand what was happening in the story, and because of this, I never forgot that I was watching a movie. And after it was over, I wished that I could forget it.

三年前和劉一起去北美館看了楊德昌的回顧展覽，三年後的今天終於看了我的第一部楊德昌的電影，想都沒想過會是在布魯塞爾吧，竟然剛好在花毯節期間遇到台灣駐歐盟辦事處協辦的楊德昌專題（在這之前在同間電影院還有台灣電影專題，可惜沒機會看到） 牯嶺街少年殺人事件，將近四小時的片長，觀影前三天都熬夜還睡超少，導致當天精神狀態蠻差的，看電影前就覺得不妙，果然睡著好幾次。看完還是不知道為什麼會是一部評價如此好的電影，可能因為年代久遠，六十年前的台灣與現在差異太大了，很難共感。為什麼這樣的背景下會需要組織幫派，武裝自己呢？看著電影覺得都是一些小情小愛，壓垮駱駝的最後一根稻草也只是情侶間的吵架，某種程度上其實也就是情殺吧，只是本來應該是和小馬互相廝殺的。 意外的是張震原來從這麼小就在演戲了，看電影分心的時候都在看張震，試圖從那稚嫩的臉龐拼湊出現在的他，莫名有種時空穿越的感覺。 另外很多角色的口音都聽不太懂，即使是中文發音的電影也不得不看字幕，然而人名都是什麼Si’r, Ma, Airplane, Ming，英文字幕真的是看得我好痛苦，而且感覺翻譯的也不是很到位，我需要中文字幕⋯⋯ 不過總之也算是看過楊德昌的電影了，希望有機會可以在精神好的狀態下重看一次這部電影。 感謝暑假期間cineville的特別活動eurotrip，荷蘭訂閱的cineville可以到到其他國家使用，難得有機會在旅行的時候順便看電影，非常有趣！雖然不能提早訂票，只能在開演前一小時到電影院買票（免費的可以說是買票嗎）但基本上不太會售完。這次在開演前一天到電影院詢問是否能先購票，櫃檯人員不知道是不是因為看我是亞洲面孔，所以問我是不是要看這部，我笑笑說沒錯，她跟我說這個專題還沒有售完過，所以應該不用擔心。實際觀影時雖然人很多，但因為影廳很大，離坐滿還差蠻遠的。只可惜電影院沒有空調，而當天高溫30度前一天甚至來到37度，影廳內真的蠻熱的，影廳外還放了紙扇子，邊搧風邊看電影真的是一個非常特別又荒謬的體驗💀也因為這樣感覺我睡著好幾次應該是熱醒的⋯

Are you fucking kidding me?! Fuck this movie. Now, I won’t lean heavily on the runtime or the pace: it’s long and it’s slow. These are by design and I took them in and went with them. And the fact that Edward Yang also chooses to keep essentially an entire village of people at a distance to us and provide no introductions, no data outside of the mundane discussions of normal life with which to follow anyone or anything along… this is somewhat unique and certainly intentional and I went with it too (even though I barely understood who was who — and often didn’t — or let alone grew to be able to care about them in any significant way)… But all this “showy-by-feigning-unshowiness” nonsense just to suddenly in the final minutes try justifying murder and gain sympathy for a murderer?! Are you fucking kidding me, Edward Yang?! At LEAST have the decency to let your foreign fucking audience (who already have to work overtime piecing together your history and customs) in on your intentions a little by keeping the Chinese Translation* instead of changing it to something fitting of JOY and innocence! You fuck! Fuck this movie. *Literal Translated Title: The Murder Case of the Youth on Guling Street (Like I inferred, perhaps you the reader, knowing it is about a senseless murder from the outset of its four-hour, coming-of-age, sweet-but-troubled framework, will benefit through proper foreknowledge! I’ll never know, because I ain’t doing this a third time. First time, 7 years ago, I got 1.5 hours in, didn’t connect with it, and decided to abandon it. This time I wasn’t willing to back down or make excuses.) That said, in reiteration: it’s not the length, the pacing, the detached framing, or even the senselessness of tragedy that’s my issue… (and in its runtime are several vignettes which are indubitably memorable)… it’s framing the tragedy in sorrow for the killer while having just framed the victim in petty blame, and then doing nothing further to condemn that — essentially creating fictitious details upon a real-life murder, and placing all onus on the victim, the village, and anything but the culprit. Fuck off!

I was not a fan of this one. I respect its place in cinematic history, but I found it underwhelming and disappointing. I’m cool with long runtimes, but this feels indulgent, tiresome, and tedious in a way that Yi Yi never does. The pacing feels flat, and the film overall feels dull and quite boring. Fanny & Alexander by Bergman is 5 hours long, 1 hour longer than ABSD, and it does not feel this tedious. I’m cool with slice of life movies, I’m cool with movies that wander, as long as I care about the characters and feel engaged. But it felt very unfocused. I’m not left caring deeply about anyone or anything in particular. The characters didn’t feel very fleshed out or developed. The film stuffs so many characters in one that it’s hard to truly connect with anybody. Also, some of Yang’s weakest writing for his female characters. Not as egregious as Mahjong, but the women here are bland afterthoughts. Disappointing compared to the fullness of his female characters in A Confucian Confusion and That Day, On the Beach. Overall, the film’s size doesn’t match the size of emotion and connection that it elicits. It’s an investment with minimal returns.

the thing i often find the most frustrating about writing, especially writing fiction with intention of having it published, is the inability to compress the totality of your work and what you're trying to say into something that could hook others in a few minutes as effectively as staring at a canvas or listening to a song. all art forms have a relation to space and time, and how they are engaged with by others in space and time, but differ in the amount of control they have over either or both of those things: a sculpture informs a space, and remains in time, but it can't control if someone walks past it without looking, or the lobby it's located in decides to carve it into pieces and stash it in a warehouse; movies and songs have a completeness of time given that the time it takes you to engage with it is set by the artist, and while movies ideally inform the made-for-purpose space of the theater, and music finds intention of space in both the recording studio and the concert hall, nowadays with device proliferation both lack of control over the space where one watches or listens to it, and often have to share space with the "real" world beyond them; books are finite objects, but have no concrete power to exercise over you when it comes to how long it takes you to read them, where you read them, the quantity of sessions it takes to read them to completion and if you even finish them at all. with some new friends i took a trip to the noguchi museum the other day, which was in the final week of a special exhibition about the works of isamu noguchi specific to new york city, most of which were unrealized, destroyed or altered public works projects. i hadn't found a special exhibition that moving since the gustave caillebotte one at the art institute of chicago , mainly due to how starkly it contrasted with the solemnity and quiet and inscrutability and general rick-owens-runway-backgrounding of the permanent arrangement of the sculptures downstairs: here was a man who committed himself deeply to a city and believed in the transformative potential of labor, only to be rejected in most of his attempts to engender some productive change in his city vis a vis of planned public parks, playgrounds and general art spaces, a lifetime of fighting past this frustration informing the difficulty in "getting" the works downstairs without aide of museum copy, and the intention behind the bespokeness of the museum itself as noguchi's "final gift" to the city. on the train back home one of these new friends (all three of which being musicians, historically the type of artist bonnie is the farthest pole away from in terms of mutual understanding about our art practice and the mechanics behind it) expressed her own frustration at how noguchi's sculpture, and sculpture/museum works of visual art in general, stand so immediately and completely for themselves in a way that music doesn't, to which i laugh and said something to the effect of, "you musicians can achieve something for someone in three minutes what writing would take in three hours!" this was to be the first time i watched a brigher summer day in one continuous sitting (the first time i turned it on too late i got too tired after the first hour, and my first complete viewing was broken up with some pauses here and there), and in a theater, so given the profundity of the day prior at the noguchi, i was expecting to have another totality of artistic experience with a movie already quite dear to me, but four hours came and went and it never fully clicked into place for me, my favorite shots (the lacquered door, honey's entrance, the parallel bike walks between father and son, ming and si'r in the wheat fields, etc) seeming fixed and static. i found myself thinking about nashville , something with a similar quantity of moving parts that fall into place in a final act of public murder, and how the first time i saw nashville in a theater, also a rewatch, my heart could not stop pounding knowing someone was going to die soon and the fact it wouldn't be a surprise this time made it wrench the gut all the more, but a frustration i had with this the first time around that compounded even more here is that the development in si'r's character as acting on a capacity to kill someone is an exponential incongruity compared to the otherwise steady downs and rebounded ups and again downs of the narrative. yang in general is a historical example of mine of a male director with a great sensitivity towards fully realizing female characters, but the women in brighter summer day , despite the gender roles of the point in depicted space and time they occupy, are mostly instrumental and fall in and out of the narrative as needed. granted, this more than any of yang's other films is a Movie About Boys, and certain choices are smart ones, like how ming maintains a strong presence despite a lot of the information presented about her being skewed hearsay from boys and men who are invariably in love with her (beyond the retroactively-revealed-to-be-her flashlighted kiss at the start, we never actually see her *do* any of the fooling around the boys constantly claim of her), but, in the film paced like a three-hour gang epic with an hour rider of bildungsroman family drama at the end, her death, and the perceived necessity of it as a cementing of sir's arc, is perhaps the most senseless in a movie where a handful of teenagers die by the circumstance of samurai sword in near-total darkness. brighter summer day still remains to me one of yang's three works that achieve objective perfection in their filmmaking ( yi yi and a confucian confusion the other two), which i think only makes the flaws to its airtight seals all the more compelling. there has to be a critic out there who's said it better than me but i believe as some sort of universal law that as an artist gets older their work only becomes more and more about their art form of choice itself. consider the next-door movie studio here: it's certainly a space of frustration—the color of the dress is wrong, the actress isn't good enough, ming doesn't find si'r up in the rafters looking back at her—but the scenes here bookend the film in a way, given that si'r's decision to steal the flashlight is what ends up catching sly in the act, which many characters labor to tell si'r as the thing that started the whole mess, and si'r's decision to leave the flashlight back where he found it and replace it in his waistband with the knife the thing that kills ming, kills himself and the narrative in essence: film itself brings this story into existence, and ends it just as suddenly. ( jonathan rosenbaum's piece on yang writes about the flashlight better than i and reading it on the way to the screening really clued me to look out for it in all scenes like a video game key item.) it’s almost like in precisely mapping out every inch of the screen, in taking four years to prepare the filming of such a calibrated machine, yang took it to the limit only to find himself at the fundamental frustration that a limit is something you can never pass beyond; you can only keep making more things and infinitely continue to move forward. brighter summer day 's glass half-emptiness certainly leaves almost no way out for most of its characters—ming and honey are dead, ma loses his best friend, cat's tapes are trashed, si'r is jailed, si'r's father is reduced to a paranoid wifebeater with no promising future employment, si'r's mother is left with an absence she can never fill despite how close she holds it to herself, lao er is without hopes or dreams, even the reverend of the church to which si'r's middle sister devotes herself seems to hold her in some minor disdain—but the one character who seems to have it good in his final scene, uncle fat, is in high spirits because of how si'r saved his life, regardless of si'r's prior expressed want to hurt him. i don't think si'r is particularly a stand-in for yang, as it's based on a real event he had some proximity to in his schoolboy days, but maybe si'r is a version of yang with a similar childhood interest in and proximity to a film, but a version of yang who could not overcome his frustrations, unaware to the fact that regardless of his possible intention to hurt uncle fat that night, something he did saved his life, and uncle fat has a renewed lease on life because of it. so regardless of how frustrating writing is for me, regardless of how frustrating it is to ever make anything, or even do anything, we only do it, we always do it to help someone live just a little longer.

Criterion Challenge 2026 by Letterboxd user Ben #1: Random Number Generator The Criterion Challenge is back and this time I am revisiting a film I don't like but am willing to give it a second go. Set in 1960 Taiwan. Chinese families moved to Taiwan in order to avoid Chinese communism. We see the life of a teenager who is in the middle of a gang war between teenagers who create gangs to survive, a girl who is involved with another person, and finally his family caught in political turmoil. That was what I was able to gather in this four hour flick by Edward Lang. I know nothing about him. I tried watching this film three years ago while being sick. I did not like it at all and I could not concentrate on it. Now that I know what's going on, I can say it's better than I thought, but only slightly. The film's real problem is that it drags constantly. There are many scenes of nothing happening. I am familiar with this approach but the pacing needed to be tighter. The film does succeed in cinematography and setting. Taiwan was experiencing a cultural shift with the emergence of rock n roll. The film thankfully ties it's political backdrop, and cultural shifts with the rise of rock n roll very well  The main character is somewhat interesting. The film is based on a real murder that happened around that time. The film follows his rise and fall from aimless adolescent to teenage criminal. It works somewhat. The film does have its highlights. I like the stuff with the gangs and I like the issues surrounding the political and rock n roll connections coupled with a touch of identity. But the film is so long that trying to focus on them is difficult. Overall I'm glad I saw it and appreciate it a little better. But I still found it slow, overly long, and off focus. I need to see this again to fully understand it. But I'm glad I was able to at least start to appreciate it. I need time on this one. 6/10

I don't really feel like going along with the delusion that this isn’t just unnecessarily long. Given the brief synopsis, I expected a 4-hour run time to give us a plethora of experiences. Instead, we get repetition. Repetition and repetition. Extraordinarily little character growth and slow, ultimately meaningless expansion on the same few themes. It's well made. You are drawn in by the emotion. If you are looking for more of an experience than a movie, then, yes, this is up in that 4+ star range it seems overstuffed with. The point is the grinding, slow despair and after 4 hours you are one with the characters. I don't think 4 hours were needed to make the ending impactful. Many movies can do the same in less than 2. I'm just not here for that experience and the story itself could be effortless wrapped up in 90-120 minutes. There are multiple storylines that are completely unnecessary in any reasonable interpretation of the story, such as the filmmaking one. I didn't dislike this and the run time didn't elicit any negative reaction, probably because I watched it over quite a few installments. I just think, again, there was so much that is unnecessary. I won't say self-indulgent, because I don't think that's what they were going for, I think it's to draw you in to what the filmmakers and characters lives were like, as I said. An OK, but not enthusiasic rating from me.

For my hundredth film this year, I wanted to choose something special. I thought for a long time - maybe I should watch something iconic that I missed or haven’t gotten around to yet, or something that has been on my watchlist for a long time. But in the end, I decided to find a list of the longest films that are a must-watch. I don’t know why, but my eye fell on Edward Yang’s “A Brighter Summer Day” . And it seems to be the most monotonous multi-genre movie ever created . I read how people admire this film and call it one of their favorites. I read about where the idea for the film originally came from and what its main theme is. There are few answers, the movie is indeed not easy for an evening watch. The four-hour runtime really feels like four hours . It’s not entertaining, more like something meditative, thanks to its beautiful locations and shots. But at the same time, I got tired of it - tired of the changing subjects, of not understanding why I’m watching this now, why this person sits silently at a table for two minutes and I’m just observing. The film often references War and Peace (about three times), and we know Tolstoy is famous for his long descriptions of nature and so on, and while that is interesting and necessary in the novel, here it could be done without. The story itself is unsurprising despite the loglines and headlines, about the murder of a girl and a KGB investigation. Because of the slow pace, I don’t feel any emotions, they just show me events as if silently, and I take note of them without much surprise or sympathy. Usually I really do love long films, but I want the length to be justified, and here I didn’t notice that. Maybe I’m not smart enough to see the uniqueness and importance of this film, but it just didn’t resonate with me.

Wanted to connect with this the way I did with Yi Yi , but alas. Regardless, it’s a thorough restoration from Criterion that does justice to Yang’s vision. The guy was a creative visionary, no doubt about it. This epic pushes 4 hours with a focus on the lives of the Taiwanese children of Chinese expats/refugees fleeing mainland China after the Civil War. Though one could be mistaken in thinking the gang ‘turf war’ is only nominally a “war”, Yang disabuses us of that notion as he captures dramatic scenes of street violence, targeted hits on youth leaders and juvenile delinquency of all forms. The kids are abused and neglected at home, and they re-assert familiar power structures in the *playgrounds (*the tennis court, the music hall, the restaurant). Yang’s only music comes in diegetic form via ‘50s Western rock ‘n roll hits and sappy love ballads from Ricky Nelson to Elvis whom the characters adore. It’s a tapestry of a specific place during a specific moment in time under unique political circumstances, but for me, Yang seems unable to bridge the knowledge gap with the audience enough to make me care, especially given this runs at a punishingly languid pace.

This is a beautifully shot and undeniably impressive feat of filmmaking that a younger version of myself might have tried to find a way to love more than I actually did, but I've recently become a lot more cynical of these long, slow arthouse classics and I simply didn't emotionally connect with this one at all. I couldn't really find enough to latch onto in terms of story or character, and without those things you really start to feel every minute of the almost four-hour runtime. Gorgeous visuals alone weren't enough to make me love it.

My hot take? This is Burning but worse and in double the time. (Okay, I know that's being pretty reductive about both films, but that's my immediate reaction now the credits have finished and this is my crappy Letterboxd account so I'll do as I please.) While technically outstanding, I can't say I especially rate A Brighter Summer Day . Many seem to praise its sprawling, “novelistic” style but I'm in the minority here saying that works against the film, which would be much better served with a sharper focus. Praise the 100+ speaking parts all you want, but three hours in my partner and I were still saying things like, “Which boy is Airplane again?” There are too many little distractions taking away from what's really important. On that note, the card at the start telling you that youths are starting gangs because of a lack of identity and security does a lot of heavy lifting, because Yang doesn't show any of that. I know the director has more filmmaking talent in a speck of his dandruff than I do in my entire body, but I still think this is a failing of his and the film. (The kids singing songs in English doesn't scream identity crisis for me, sorry. People all around the world enjoy songs not in their native language – you could probably draw a historical line from Italian and Germanic operas all the way to K-pop to demonstrate this point – so this argument doesn't hold much weight for me, sorry.) Lastly, I have issues with both S'ir and Ming that affect my view of the film. It's tough to discuss without spoilers but I was shaking my head at both come the end. I think we're given too little insight into S'ir's interiority to really, let's say, “appreciate” what comes at the film's climax. Perhaps Yang wants us to be shocked/frustrated/confused by A Brighter Summer Day's seemingly irrational outcome, but without sufficient context, it lacks impact.

The first director that makes me think of the word auteur. This is only the 2nd film I've seen apart from YiYi and you can really tell that he focuses on bringing a slice of life structure to the screen. Instead of telling stories where you can make a decent guess on where it's going and where it'll end up, he brings you smack in the middle of their messy reality and have you be an observer to a slow basic day in the life or a tense, highly emotional wave of feelings. This had a twist I wasn't expecting in the slightest and I enjoyed every moment.

I don't know why I was surprised given the subject matter throughout the film but the darkness of the concluding act of this film really devastated me. Maybe it's just because Yang's style is so disarmingly peaceful, with the whole film being wrapped in this daydreamy, nostalgic, hang-out movie glaze, or maybe it's because the film captures this feeling of an ephemeral period of time, with most of its subjects unjustly victimized by their era and circumstances, but regardless, it's extremely moving. You really get to live and breathe with his characters and even though there's this sort of transitory feel to their presence in the film, with fairly important characters being introduced or leaving with very little warning, you feel the time passing very clearly and experience the deep intensity of their growth and losses. That's why the ending just sucks you in, because by that point, you're not ready to leave these people or this troubled yet beautiful period in time. I wouldn't say that this was my favorite of the few Edward Yang films I have seen so far but to be fair that's a pretty high bar and this is still a remarkably beautiful film and definitely worth the time investment.

A brighter summer day is a 4 hour coming of age film that uses the gradual unfolding of life to build an emotionally resonant picture of adolescence. Set in a societally tense environment, it follows a boy named Si’r as he navigates school, family, and relationship pressures. The film is never driven by twists or turns, but driven by small parts that gain weight and accumulate into a grander picture. Interactions in the classroom, uncomfortable moments of authority, and shifting dynamics within cliques all lead into a sense of unease throughout the film that is bordering the line of subtlety. The overarching structure to embodies life, with a messy, indirect, and shaped directly to what’s expressed. You see the character of Si’r change but you only notice when he’s changed to much as he’s molded by the environment around him instead of dictating his own path. One of the themes of this story is the school system and how it shapes crucial events within the story, as well as being a microcosm for society in Taipei as a whole. It is shown to be rigid, hierarchal, and impersonal, prioritizing discipline over growth. The students are meant to follow standards, yet never receive guidance to becoming “functional”. Themes like generational divide are reinforced with teachers being authority figures that are often disconnected from the realities of these kids lives. It all comes together into the point of the school system being a source of pressure rather than an empathetic system meant to help children find meaning and support. It supports power over the needs of the youth, and is a critique of institutions focused on control. This films depth emerges naturally from the multitude of events that occur. It builds off the idea of loss of innocence, portrayed not as a quick shift, but a slow almost unperceived process that can’t be recognized until it’s too late. Si’r progresses through the story with his experiences gradually destroying any sense of simplicity within his life, and instead replaces it with constant conflict. This connects with themes of identity as the characters are constantly in a fight to find themselves within an environment that prioritizes expectations over personal desire. Everything around them tells them what they should be in differing ways which causes a constant pull that will eventually break them. Another key theme is social pressure and environment. It insinuates that behavior can not be separated from its context. Societal instability, and peer dynamics all play a role in shaping actions and thought, emphasizing the importance of environment in what we do. It is further deepened by the political and cultural uncertainty which although subtle, they seep into the background of the story and create constant tension. The filmmaking is impeccable with how these themes are portrayed. Edward Yang uses a very restrained, and observational style to allow the story to unfold with a sense of patience. The consistent use of long takes with minimal editing allows an almost hypnotic engagement, with constant details in the back for viewers to catch and draw conclusions from. It allows for a sense of authenticity that deepens the impact of the experiences. Visually this movie is a marvel, as it reinforces its themes with characters framed in crowded or enclosed spaces that emphasize confinement, and lack of freedom. Even in the open the camera work makes characters feel small which help allude to the idea of larger forces in play. The camera never gets personal, and instead stays at a distance where you are able to observe, reinforcing the feeling of isolation. The lighting is also used in very unique ways to highlight moral and emotional ambiguity, such as highlighting a face partially to represent a kind of “gray area”. The sound design is also impeccable as it reinforces realism with constant silence, and ambience instead of a typical score. It allows the film to breathe and gives weight to dialogue and performances by the actors. When the music is present however, it is introduced naturally as a part of the world rather than being imposed onto the film. Performances by the actors as well were exceptional at capturing its feelings of isolation, as well as vulnerability without ever feeling exaggerated or underplayed. This film seamlessly brings everything together into one cohesive and immersive story. It never offers easy answers or explanation, but instead presents a picture of growing up in an age of uncertainty and pressure that allows you to discover everything contained within it. Its length (although daunting) is iffy at times imo, but is absolutely necessary to establish connection the characters, and the story’s themes which helps make the impact feel earned. All in all this films stands as a powerful exploration of youth and the forces which shape it. Through its masterful direction it captures the often invisible struggles of adolescence that feels prevalent to not just the period, but the modern day as well. It’s a work that doesn’t stay in your mind due to spectacle, but instead relies on its honesty, patience, and ability to reveal complexity within the ordinary. An absolute masterpiece that must be watched even if the first few hours can be tough.

Only Edward Yang could make four hours feel like the only honest length for a movie about growing up under martial law, and it's a little maddening that "long" is still the first word people reach for. Yes, it's long. It's also a movie about what happens to a kid's sense of time when every institution in his life, school, family, the state, has already decided how his hours get spent without asking him. Almost none of the men in this film have real power, only fear, handed down from above and taken out on whoever's below. Fathers get interrogated by the state, then come home to interrogate their sons. I recognized this machinery of surveillance and disappearance from recent Brazilian films, Secret Agent and I’m Still Here , working through their own military dictatorship, state fear turns out to look remarkably similar no matter the hemisphere. The pattern runs all the way down until there's nobody left for Si'r's generation to pass it to, so the kids turn violence on each other instead, rebuilding the same hierarchy inside their own gangs. Which is where the baseball bats come in. The school starts requiring them to be registered, specifically because kids keep using them as weapons, the kind of fix that solves the object and ignores the reason for it. Yang's camera treats all of this the same way— at a remove. Wide shots, kids staged deep in the frame, whole scenes lit by a single bulb or a flashlight. The distance reads as cold and observational, but that's exactly what lets you see clearly, the mundane texture of these kids' daily lives sitting right next to state violence and gang violence, filmed with identical detachment. The gangs, for their part, have the full James Dean thing going, Americana rock and roll swagger borrowed wholesale from Elvis and imported into 1960s Taipei. But the look is aspirational Americana, and the weapons, when they finally show up, are something else entirely, real Japanese swords stashed in the attics of houses these families inherited from the Japanese occupiers. The thing these kids escalate to killing each other with isn't homegrown at all, it's leftover colonial hardware from an entirely different empire, discovered by accident in the walls of their own homes. The irony writes itself. Kids performing an American identity, fighting with Japanese steel, inside a Taiwan still trying to work out an identity distinct from mainland China. And caught in the middle of all of it is Ming, who barely gets to exist as her own person in this movie. Every boy who orbits her, Honey, Sly, eventually Si'r, reads her as a scoreboard rather than a human being, proof of standing. It's hard to watch in 2026 without thinking of Adolescence and the vocabulary that show put into wide circulation, boys taught to experience a girl's independence as a personal insult, her attention as a debt she owes rather than a gift she gives. Sixty-some years and a different hemisphere apart, and it's the same rot: take away a boy's sense of power everywhere else, and he'll go looking for it in the one place he's still been told he's allowed to have some. Si'r doesn't start the film as one of those boys. He ends it as exactly one, and the tragedy isn't that he snapped, it's that everything around him had been building toward that ending all along, a blow meant for someone else finding Ming instead. It didn’t move me the way Yi Yi does, but that's a high bar for anyone, including Yang himself. And yet, this is a spectacle on the scale of Leone's Once Upon a Time in America , the kind of thing very few directors can actually pull off.

Edward Yang captures 1960s Taipei and a huge ensemble with an almost unbelievable level of detail. After a while, the film stops feeling like a reconstruction of the period at all. The night school, street gangs, family homes, friendships, rivalries, romances and American pop songs do not merely provide a backdrop. They form an entire society that these children are trying to understand while the adults around them are still struggling to find their own place within it. Taiwan is changing, but nearly everyone seems caught between worlds. The parents carry the insecurity of having fled mainland China, and their children inherit that anxiety without fully understanding its source. They turn toward Elvis, movies, romantic fantasies and gangs, borrowing identities wherever they can find them. Some of the things the teenagers say sound startlingly mature, but it never feels written for effect. They have simply been forced to absorb the disappointments, fears and contradictions of the adults around them far too early. At almost four hours, the film is enormous without feeling inflated. Yang gives every relationship enough time to develop until even a passing interaction seems connected to something larger. When violence arrives, it is not exciting or cathartic. It is sudden, confused and frightening, often obscured rather than displayed. It is about as far from stylized, Tarantino-like spectacle as violence can get. It hurts because Yang has spent hours making these people and their world feel real. What happens near the end left me stunned. Learning that Yang based the film on a murder he remembered from his own childhood made it even more heartbreaking. Beneath the epic scale is the story of young people shaped, and eventually destroyed, by forces they barely comprehend. This is Edward Yang at the height of his powers, and a very close second to Yi Yi for me.

"In the heat of the summer You're so different from the rest" One of the most immersive movies I have ever watched, also a very challenging one. The movie is such a slow burn and a devastating one at that. The characters feels so real with their own behaviours and actions living in a world that doesn't seem to give them a sense of security and was forced into a environment that forces them into becoming child soldiers of their own life, of their own destiny... What I really love about this movie is the way it is filmed and the how realistic it is. It feels more like a documentary rather than a movie at times. The viewer becomes more like a witness than a mere spectator. There're no close up shots anywhere in this movie which gives you this distant you get with the characters. But weirdly enough it is this distance that makes you connected with the characters even more. There's this intimacy that the camera brings to the table that not a lot of movies was able to archive!!! The movie reminds me of City Of God but with a twist both from the editing perspective and the main characters, whereas Rocket never belongs in gang and in the movie actively trying to get out of the situation he's in, Si is tragically influenced by the violence surrounds him. City of God uses Rocket's narration to tell the story whereas A Brighter Summer Day leaves the viewer up to interpretation and let us decide how we feel about the characters... The end of summer is here so I picked this movie to finally check it out and somehow it gives me the upmost comfort but at the same time the most discomfort I've ever felt

Never have I watched a film so naturalistic. Never have I watched a film with such contrast between the hopeful, and the bleak. This film is like reading a novel. Each character has a perfect, and fully fleshed out arc. It shows how war can cause lasting social predjudices, and hatred that bleeds through the population - in this case through the youth in 1960s Taiwan. Brilliant masterpiece, but not better than Yi Yi. I belive that Si'r and Sly have juxtaposing character arcs. Whilst Si'r begins with an inate benevolance, and is slowly in moulded by the hatred surrounding him, Sly begins his arc as the main source of hatred, the antagonist for the first half of the film if you will. Sly better's himself, abandoning his life of chaos, and his arc culminates with a resounding sense of honour. This is an absolute masterpiece.

The effect of war didnt stop in the battlefield. It breeds hate, sense of secure and violence throughout generations. A brighter summer day showed war from the innocent people prespective. The nuance is somehow quite and peaceful, yet the impact is growing inside each individual.

I don't know what it is about stories involving middle school kids being impacted by failing institutions or what exactly makes them so captivating. All I know is that both this film and Season 4 of The Wire are my favorite forms of media to ever fit in that category, even if they feel completely different from each other. I guess what makes A Brighter Summer Day stand out is that while it predates The Wire with taking a strictly blunt and more objective approach in showing how children are being funneled into criminal behavior, it still treats warm nostalgia, yearning and innocence as huge parts of its identity. All while still tackling such a disturbing real-life story involving middle school kids. It makes for such a harrowing, yet beautiful contrast throughout the movie. All in all, A Brighter Summer Day was a very emotionally heavy film, especially given its 4 hour run time. It didn't make me cry, but it left me feeling cold and empty by the end. It taps into a unique point in our childhoods, a point in time in our youth where we become more aware or privy to the grimmer parts of everyday life. It weighs in on that weird feeling where we realize the world isn't quite what we thought it was and how experiencing that at such a young age can have rippling effects throughout our lives. I'd like to believe that's what Edward Yang wanted to aim for when making this film, especially when he grew up around the same time and political climate that the film depicts. Apologies if I sound like a huge downer, but you know a film is special when it takes you to places like this and you just feel like talking about it. Overall, I loved A Brighter Summer Day. A powerful film all the way through. Pretty much my 2nd favorite Edward Yang flick after watching Yi Yi. Listening to Angel Baby is gonna feel a whole lot different from here on out.

I had seen a few of Edward Yang’s films and remember catching his magnum opus, Yi Yi, back in the early 2000s. For years, I tried to get a copy of A Brighter Summer Day, but it was only available in bad prints or terrible VHS transfers. So when the American Cinematheque screened a 4K restoration in Los Angeles, I jumped at the chance to see it on the big screen - and it paid off wonderfully. This film packs a punch. Its ending is terrifying, surprising, and deeply affecting. Despite its nearly four-hour running time, it leaves you wanting more. The main character is a teenager attending night school - I’m terrible with character names - but the movie’s true subject is the entire community around him: his family, including a father, mother, and older sister who each leave a strange and lasting impression; the members of his gang; and, naturally, the lovely teenage girl at the center of his world. I won’t spoil what happens, but the ending is so shocking that it leaves you breathless. The narrative sprawls, yet every part of it feels incredibly calibrated. There are no catchy lines, but there are countless indelible moments that stay with you long after the credits roll. Near the midpoint, a terrifying sequence of violence makes you think the film has reached its climax—but it’s only the midpoint, a choice that reveals just how masterfully the narrative has been constructed. Do yourself a favor: watch this film. Start it early, and watch it in one sitting. It’s a transformative experience.

Edward Yang consegue captar com perfeição a decadência não só de uma juventude, mas de uma nação inteira traumatizada pela história. Xiao Si'r é o protagonista perfeito para mostrar a situação de Taipei nos anos 60, é um jovem inocente, porém não é um jovem perfeito, principalmente na escola, isso leva ele à sua relação com as gangues e à violência local. Quando Xiao Si'r conhece Ming, isso acaba mudando um pouco ele, tenta focar em protegê-la, porém Ming é uma pessoa instável, ela procura se relacionar com diversos homens, mentindo várias vezes a Xiao Si'r, logo isso se torna um motivo para ele adentrar mais a esse mundo, e tudo o que ele passou culmina na violência se alastrando mais e mais, tanto em Xiao Si'r quanto nas pessoas em sua volta. Um exemplo disso é seu pai, que durante todo o filme tenta educá-lo, mas aos poucos percebe que seus esforços não são suficientes e que já perdeu o controle sobre o filho. Essa relação entre pai e filho também representa muito bem o conflito entre uma geração traumatizada pelo passado e outra que está crescendo em uma sociedade completamente diferente. No fim, A Brighter Summer Day é uma joia do Novo Cinema Taiwanês, um filme que de longe pode ser apenas um longa adolescente, mas é um filme extremamente pesado sobre a violência e as consequências dela em uma geração assolada por seu passado.

Si’r, do you remember this song I recorded? Guess who I sent it to. Elvis! He even replied to me. He was surprised to know that his music is so popular on this small unknown island. 99/100 17th greatest film ever made (in my top 150 ) best film of 1991 ( each year's best ) An ambitious work that tells the story of a country through a highly important social commentary (actually, through MANY social critiques). Set during a period that the director personally lived through, it feels deeply personal. With one of the most impactful ending s ever, it is not only the greatest coming-of-age film, but also, probably, the best film of the 1990s . That is why, with his fourth feature film, Edward Yang further refines his style, creating what is probably his magnum opus (although I still have to see Yi Yi ) and making A Brighter Summer Day (1991) one of the greatest masterpieces in the history of cinema. His mainly long shots direction and framing style couldn't have been more impactful, making the view even visually beautiful. Probably thanks as well to its cinematography , with the yellow and ochre tones that characterize many very long films in which viewers can immerse themselves in the characters, the audience develops a particularly strong emotional connection with all these teenagers and all the people we see in 1960s Taipei. The film's critique is probably aimed at the Americanization of the country, but not in the sense of moving away from one's roots; rather, in the sense of pretending to be someone you are not. There are many factors that lead to the loss of hope; many factors that push a young boy into the world of adults , while also bringing the viewer into that world alongside him. my own interpretaton - *SPOILER* Through the character of Ming being also a bit of an actress, I saw a meta-cinematographic intention. As Si'r tells the director he didn't understand Ming, he's also saying the viewers the same thing. This was also during the final extreme climax, giving us a back-shot of Si'r powerfully rapresenting his crysis, as very few films did so well in the history of cinema. *SPOILER ENDS* Even though its imposing length, and the fact that I wasn't understanding right the subtitles, which forced me to go back and becomes nervous, I completely recognized the greatness of the work, leading me to almost cry in the last scene. favorites 🥇 1990s each year's top 4 🥇 Taiwan 🇹🇼 each country's top 4 each genre's top 4 5th best ending good looking 4th longest I watched

Four hours long, yet it feels less like watching a film and more like living inside a city, a family, and a generation. Edward Yang turns one boy's story into a portrait of an entire society caught between history and modernity. Every scene seems ordinary until you realize, hours later, how much it has revealed about loneliness, violence, love, and growing up. Few films feel this vast and this intimate at the same time. By the end, you don't feel like you've watched a movie, you feel like you've lost a place that briefly became part of your life.

Why is it 4 hours long? The pacing never felt bad, tedious, it never felt dragged, but I’m just wondering why the picture had to be four hours long. It’s like, how do you determine what scene is worth putting into the film and what’s not? So, for example, the grocery store guy gets a heart attack, that’s a scene, or a plot point. Si’r helps him. In return, grocery store guy helps Si’r’s dad get an interview with a new business person. They go out for the evening, mom and dad with the new potential business partners. Si’r takes the opportunity to take a girl out on a date. He steals his mum’s watch so that he can pawn it for some money for the date. Father comes home, finds out about the stolen watch, and beats the elder brother thinking that he’s the culprit. Si’r comes home to the sight of his father violently beating his innocent brother. This seems to be the final straw of injustice for Si’r. After this, Si’r commits to seeking ‘justice’ — revenge. Imagine that, a heart attack that occurred maybe an hour prior also has its pay-off. Let’s try another scene: Ming does a screen test and cries really naturally on camera. Near the end of the film, the director wants Si’r to help them find Ming cause she’s such a great actress, but she seems to have changed addresses. In the scene just prior, Si’r finds out that Ming has fallen in love with other guys and not just him. So Si’r feels cheated. So yes, he believes she is a great actress. Anyway, I didn’t explain that well, but even in four hours I don’t think that there is a scene that is not important. Sly comes back a changed man. Si’r gets more and more philosophical: “it’s comforting to know that people can change”. If Sly can change then he is hoping that he can change Ming. Something about War and Peace . The objects in this film are very important. The flashlight, the knife, the tape recorder, the radio, and every time has its own narrative arc, a completion. Again, nothing seems to be unimportant, everything seems to be a detail. Very, very, very impressive. A Brighter Summer Day: Cat loved to sing and kept chasing that bug. He got violent there for a bit but kept mostly to singing. He sang a cover of an Elvis song and sent Elvis the tape. Elvis got back to him and even sent a gift. It’s like, Cat made it out of this cycle of violence. You don’t have to get trapped. But Si’r did. The film being a reference to this idea — that one can escape — is ironic and painful because Si’r doesn’t manage to escape, and it’s easy to see how he got trapped.

عد 1771 فلم THE CLOUD- CAPPED STAR مخرج Ritwik Ghatak فلــــــم من بنگلادش، جميل ناحيه التصوير والدفئ الذي يخلق الاسود والابيض للمـــــــشهد والمُشاهد من عشاق افلام الاسود والابيض، قصه الفلم جمــــيله ولكن تطور الاحداث بهذه الصيغه المبالغ بها يجعلك تنفر من الفلم، كـــذلك (خبطه الاداءالمسرحي) للممثلين من ضمن عيوب هذا الفلم، واذا هناك حســـــــنه فيه فهي تصويره الرائع والزوايا التي تستقر فيها الكاميــــرا. وانقل لكم كلمه من محب للسينما شاهد الفلم فقال: كل شخص محب للسينما ولم يتابع هذه التحفه فهو يحمل عار!!!!! ولا ادري اين العار في عدم مشاهدتي لفلم اغلبه مبالغه غير مقنعه سواء للحدث او الاداء. يحــــكي فيلم "Meghe Dhaka Tara" القصة المأساوية لابنة جميلة لعائلة لاجئة من الطبقة المتوســـــــــــطة من شرق باكستان، تعيش في ضواحي كلكتا في ظـــــل ظروف متواضعة، تضحي نيتا بكل شيء من أجل أســـرتها، بما في ذلك سعادتها الشخصية، وأموالها، وصحتها، بينما نادرًا ما يتم الاعتراف بإنجازاتها من قبل الأشخاص من حولها. فلم THE CLOUD- CAPPED STAR مخرج Ritwik Ghatak انتاج 1960 وقت 126 دقيقه تمثيل Supriya Choudhury، Anil Chatterjee جائزة 1 ترشح

Indian Neo-Realism mixed with melodrama. It's a combination of identifiers that sends shivers down my spine, and the film doesn't disappoint. It's a sluggish, 2-hour-long social drama (with some horrible musical influences) that never redeems itself, but only gets worse as it progresses. A relatively well-off family flees from their home and ends up in the slums of Calcutta. The daughter of the family does her very best to improve the situation for her family, even sacrificing her own life and happiness to do so. For all the sacrifices she makes though, her family doesn't seem very appreciative of her efforts. A film about self-sacrifice where things just get worse for the lead character. The performances aren't that great, the cinematography is very basic and the drama piles up endlessly. The music was pretty grating too, making the 2-hour runtime a real obstacle. Not my type of film, I really disliked this one.

Two hours of misery porn. Never really embeds itself in Nita's point of view the way it would need to for it to hit as hard as it should, or in her family's point of view the way it would need to for it to feel slimy and awful. In trying to balance the narrative, it removes a lot of the emotional depth. That, and I just find it really hard to connect with Indian cinema in general, with a couple of exceptions. Stylistically it's not for me, the forlorn poetic musical interludes in this one are especially irritating to my taste.

La cinematografía es tan pero tan buena que ha hecho creer a la gente que la película es extraordinaria. Sinceramente no es nada más que una telenovela ramplona; si la historia se desarrollara en México no sería más que un capítulo de Lo que Callamos las Mujeres , o de Mujeres Casos de la Vida Real, o de La Rosa de Guadalupe. ¿Acaso tiene trama la historia? Digo, porque ver a la protagonista ser una abnegada magdalena que sufre y sufre por espacio de dos horas no es nada interesante. El problema de Ritwik Ghatak es que si quiere hablar del papel de la mujer dentro de una sociedad misógina, lo termina arruinando porque romantiza el sufrimiento de la protagonista; si Ghatak quiere hablar de los efectos socioeconómicos de la infame Partición, pues no entiendo porque no lo aborda en lo absoluto y la película fácilmente puede prescindir de eso. Todos los personajes son caricaturas. Muchos admiran la actuación de Supriya Choudhury, pero, para mí, no tiene nada de rango y se nota rumbo al final cuando a su personaje le da tuberculosis (aparte de todo lo que la familia y novio le hacen le da tuberculosis; nada más faltó que regresaran los británicos y la hicieran esclava o algo así) y ella está re-tiesa. Bastante decepcionante trabajo si pensamos en lo que también estaba haciendo Satyajit Ray en ese entonces.

This is one of those infuriating melodramas that spends two hours documenting the suffering experienced by a saintly young woman with a drab personality. She is surrounded by selfish monsters who don't bear any resemblance to actual human beings and the screenplay works overtime to make us feel pity for the idiotic masochist at the centre of the story. They presumably intended to craft this tale into a feminist parable about the horrors of a sexist society but it ends up falling prey to all sorts of misogynistic clichés. It's telling that every single female character who is presented is an unsympathetic light is willing to push back against social boundaries. The only woman that we are asked to admire is a pushover who actively chooses to become a martyr. I'm sick of watching supposedly tragic dramas that tell stories about characters who suffer from inertia.

Upon my initial viewing of Ritwk Ghatak’s The Cloud-Capped Star last year, I wrote extensively about this film’s larger role in analyzing the socio-economic contexts in which the film emerged out of and how these factors, although never expressly called out in the film, convey a theme of industrialization and modernization as a method of disrupting the personal lives and social intimacies of those in society. While this is an analysis that I still stand by and continue to be proud of, I do want to highlight another aspect of the film that I neglected on my first watch; this being a review of the film itself. The Cloud-Capped Star is a difficult film to sit through both due to its themes and the structure of the film itself. This is a film that is poorly structured and paced causing it to be monotonous to watch given its over two hour runtime. Due to the language barrier I cannot attest to the quality of the performances, but there is an aura of over-exaggeration to the way characters move around their environments. This makes the performances feel very stilted and performative, which comes across as soap operatic rather than melodramatic. This is certainly a by-product of casting mostly non-actors however that doesn’t make it any less jarring to watch. In the end, The Cloud-Capped Star is a film which I appreciate for its narrative scope and underlying societal critiques more than I appreciate it as a film to watch and enjoy in its own right.
