The Betrayal of the Horse: When a Horse Becomes a Verdict “This is my horse!” Mikolka cried, bringing the shaft down with a heavy blow. “Beat her to death! Why don’t you beat her?” someone shouted from the crowd. Mikolka raised the shaft again. The wretched horse collapsed on her haunches, then struggled up and tried once more to pull the cart. Six whips lashed her from every side. The shaft fell again, then again, with a terrible rhythm, as Mikolka, almost mad with rage, seemed determined to kill her in a single blow. The scene comes from Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment. Before Raskolnikov acts on his theory of the “extraordinary man,” he dreams of himself as a child watching a horse beaten to death. He runs to her, embraces her bloody head, kisses it, then clenches his small fists and throws himself at the man who has killed her. The dream is one of the novel’s great flashes of moral revelation. It exposes the compassion in Raskolnikov that theory has not yet destroyed. It also announces that his path will not end in the cold triumph of an idea, but in guilt, suffering, and redemption. History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

I tried watching The Turin Horse , and I didn't get anything out of it. So I then listened to Jonathan Rosenbaum's audio commentary. hoping it might offer something I had missed. Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.

Oh boy. There is perhaps an argument that Béla Tarr is one of the most predictable filmmakers in contemporary cinema. The film is going to be in black and white. It’s going to feature extremely long takes. Seconds will turn into hours. Characters’ speech will sometimes sound as if they’re reading straight from an intimidating philosophical treatise or hard-line manifesto. And it’s going to be one of the grimmest things you’ve ever seen in your sorry little life. With this movie, Tarr and Hranitzky amply follow through on all of these predictive suppositions, and just to add even more spice to proceedings, there is no dialogue for the first 30 minutes. There’s a short introductory voiceover, and then…no one speaks. At all. For half an hour. Meanwhile, a string refrain that sounds like Phillip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi score under the influence of heavy sedatives repeats over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Only after death, if I find myself in hell. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".

Nietzschean nihilism is a ground zero of nothingness. The lethargic decadence of once elite history makers allows for the virulent power grab of outside forces, that then deterritorialize the structures of society. This film hones in on the former (nothingness, zero, pure the dread of pure potentiality) while giving us only a glimpse of the latter (the takeover of the other), even though one cannot be without the other. I come away from this thinking there are two possible reasons for this decision by the filmmaker. Either: 1) he doesn’t fully grasp the dynamic nature of Nietzsche’s thought or 2) he focuses on nothingness because it gives him a reason to make a drab and slow movie. Maybe it’s a little bit of both, but either way, the idea here is secondary to the technique. And that for me is a disingenuous way to make a movie. You don’t make slow, motionless films because you want to make one, you make it because it’s a way to convey something. The cart is before the horse; this man just wants to show us he has the capacity to make a long, slow movie. A massive waste of time.

Bunlar büyük metaforlar gibi girip bırakiyor. Sadece “bak her şey sönüyor” diyor. Eee tamam sönüyor da bu bana ne düşündürüyor? İzleyiciye alan açmakla hiçbir şey kurmamak arasında fark var, bunda ikincisi var. Zaten en başından beri hayat mekanik bir tekrar. Dolayısıyla yok oluş bir çöküş gibi değil uzatılmış bir hiçlik gibi. Tempo meselesine gelirsem evet uzun planlar düşünmek için alan açıyor ama bir noktadan sonra aynı şeyi defalarca izlemek derinlikten çok durağanlık hissi yaratmış. Hareketsizlik de bilinçli bir tercih evet ama bu kadar da amaçsızlık izleyiciyle kurulan bağı zorlamış. Tanrı meselesi de çok kararsız. Eğer mutlak bir hiçlik anlatılıyorsa kuyunun taşla dolması ve ışığın sönmesi ilahi bir cezalandırma değil mi? Tanrınının yok olduğu bir evren yerine terk edilmiş ama hala bir düzen tarafından kapatılan bir dünya hissi var. Bir diğer aklımda kalan soru da zaten başından beri ölü doğmuş bir hayatı izliyorsak bunun çöküşünü neden bu kadar uzun izliyoruz? Unutulmaz mı? Evet. Ama benim için etkileyici olduğu kadar karakter, anlam ve dönüşüm kurmaktan tembellik edilip yok oluşu sadece biçimsel bir tekrar olarak izletmesi yüzünden çok itici. Görüntü güzel, atmosfer güçlü ama bir yerden sonra bu da yetmiyor çünkü zihinsel temas kuramıyorsun.O yüzden finalde tamamen karanlığa gömüldüğümüzde bir şey hissetmek yerine şükür sonunda bitti dedirtiyor. Bu filmi izlemek sinirlerimi çok bozdu. Bir de mal insanlar çıkıp “abi slow sinema, sanat sineması” falan deyince daha da çileden çıkıyorsun. Yavaşlık amaç değil araç olmalı. O kadar açık fırsat, o kadar detay ve potansiyel varken filmin yaptığı şey ise dümdüz tekrar ve sadece yavaşlık. Sürekli bir şeyin anlam ifade edeceğini ima edip hiçbir şey yaptırmamasının daaa bu kadar tutarsızlık bu kadar kaçırılmış fırsat ve izleyiciye bir bağ kurdurmayan bir filmin bu kadar övgü almasının da ta  AMINA KOYAYIM.

La película empieza poderosa, en medio de la tempestad, un hombre con su caballo intentando que el viento no se los lleve, una música ensordecedora y te meten una cita de Nietzsche en una transición igual de magnífica que el comienzo. Esos son los primeros cinco minutos de película, parecía pometedor y luego ves al hombre entrando en su rutina, se mete a casa y... empiezan a comer papas. Toda la película es un hombre levantándose de la cama, comiendo papas y volviéndose a acostar. Hay un trecho enorme de la película donde el hombre solo se la pasa comiéndose unas malditas papas. No pasa nada, no pasa más nada. Bien, me quieres vender la cotidianidad, pero, ¿me tenías que hacerme tragar la rutina de varios días del mismo hombre comiéndose unas papas? Más o menos a mitad de película llega un sujeto a la casa y dije: finalmente se dignaron a que pasara algo. Pero no, el sujeto era una herramienta al espectador para darnos contexto de toda la situación, pero la actuación es pobre y es una inmediata verborrea con toques líricos y poco destellos narrativos. Ahí dije: suficiente. No pude seguir viendo más, sé que pasa algo al final, pero no importa. Creo que estamos acostumbrados a que pase algo, sé que el director es así, la otra vez hizo tragarme 15 minutos de una persona caminando, pero la película duraba sus seis horas, quince minutos eran un pestañeo, pero aquí... esa grandilocuencia del inicio no se concreta con el hombre comiendo papas y menos con ese final que pareciera más el empate del inicio. Perfectamente la película se pudo haber terminado con el hombre comiendo papas y hubiese sido la misma basura. Decepcionante, aburrida y muy pobremente escrita. Que no se me malentienda, amo el cine somnífero, pero hay límites que simplemente no se pueden cruzar.

They say that "Brevity is the soul of wit" so I guess this is the funniest movie of all time. In all seriousness though, this was too slow and artsy even for me and I try to have an open mind about there kinds of films. It has some nice cinematography and great blocking. The mood is very on point as well. But in general it felt like a real chore to get through. I doubt it was the directors intention but it felt somewhat cathartic to watch such a slow film in a time when one is constantly bombarded with visual and auditory stimulations. During the movie, I started to think and to reflect about several things in my life the same way I do when going for a walk in nature.

Unrelentingly bleak. Monotonous, but not necessarily repetitive. Personally, I think Jeanne Dielman is a better examination of the mundane patterns of life, though its interests are individual and physiological. This is more concerned with mythos and humanity as a whole. I fought of sleep so many times that I ended up making paper crafts while watching just to stay awake. Yes, I got bored.

I dip into slow cinema once every six months to challenge myself by going out of my comfort zone but this is my last detour in my journey to watch all of film canon. A father and daughter survive a storm which could be interesting if it was an hour shorter. There are only so many ways you could show a man peeling a potato before you send the audience running back to their phones. More than the slow pace I am bothered by the lack of narrative. I have mentioned in other reviews – The decision to let the visuals do the heavy lifting does not work for me in spite of some beautiful, painterly images. Cinema is not just a visual medium it is a visual storytelling medium. That is not a difference in semantics but in function. The slow pace is an invitation to think but the movie does not give me much food for thought. Arthouse films peaked in the 60s with the likes of Fellini, Bergman, Antonioni and Rohmer. All of them are on the slower side but they ask incisive questions about sex, religion and creativity. They reward thinking you have to ponder about the character motivation to get most out of them. On the other hand slow cinema from directors like Tarr, Claire Denis or Abbas Kiarostami has one-note characters who never give the impression of having rich inner lives so thinking about them adds nothing to the experience. They are just badly paced, thematically empty and unabashedly self-indulgent. I am not fond of either extremes – I hate both Fast and Furious and its ilk, and slow cinema. Neither has any semblance of story and to enjoy them one has to either stop thinking or give into overthinking.

Derzsi János szavaival élve: Fuhbazdmeg Borzasztóan szikár és rideg film a Torinói ló. Olyan, ami szánt szándékkal antagonizálja a nézőjét annak érdekében, hogy ne csak átadja, de fizikailag éreztesse is üzenetét. Amit itt kapunk, az nem a végnek a kezdete, hamem már a végnek is a legvége, a teljes nihil. Mindezt Tarr Béla azzal éri el, hogy gyakorlatilag egy végtelen, kilátástalan loopba helyez minket. Öltözés, krumpli, pálinka, öltözés, krumpli, pálinka, öltözés, krumpli, pálinka. Az első óra után már könyörögtem a szereplők feje fölött lógó apokalipszisért, hogy végre kikerüljünk a körforgásból. Szándékos ez a rendező részéről? Persze, kibaszottul. Kétségtelen, hogy rommá trollkod minket az öreg és amikor már hatodszorra nézeti végig, hogy az apát felöltöztetik, szinte látom a lelki szemeim előtt, ahogy a markában röhög, hogy "na, elég volt már a létzésből, vagy még hetedszerre is felöltöztessük". Adom! Mindez dícséretes, de ez nyílván magában hordozza, hogy nem egy "fun watch", hanem inkább kínkeserves hosszútávfutás. Nem viccelek, amikor azt mondom, hogy antagonizáló. Olyan a Torinói ló, mint amilyennek szerintem a laikusok elképzelik, hogy milyen lehet egy Tarrbéla film. Csak éppen nem ilyen szokott lenni általában, de most tényleg olyan! Épp ezért ez nyolcórásabbnak érződik, mint a Sátántangó. Kicsit olyan érzés, mint amikor a Dark Souls híres lett arról, hogy kurva nehéz, ezért a Dark Souls 2-ben unfair és élvezhetetlen szintekre tekerték a nehézséget.  Senkinek nem ajánlom első Tarr Béla filmjeként, ahogy a Dark Souls 2-t se ajánlanán első Dark Souls játéknak.

Just to avoid any misunderstanding: I’ve watched thousands of films in my life, and I consider myself capable of sensing any kind of idea or philosophy even in simple actions and stillness. I  get that this is Béla Tarr’s style, but if you still find a film heavy even after watching most of it at 2x speed, if nothing pulls you in, then something isn’t working. I watched an old man eat a potato for three minutes in the most “interesting” way possible. The entire film probably has less than 30 lines of dialogue. I knew the story about Nietzsche and the horse, so I expected a different pattern, a different flow. Honestly, if Nietzsche rose from his grave and watched this, he’d probably break down all over again. I just don’t understand how this has a 7.7 on IMDb. I can’t help thinking that the artsy crowd didn’t genuinely enjoy it but rather enjoyed saying they enjoyed it.

Film jest ładny ale męczący jak cholera. W tle powiedzmy że jakaś wizja końca świata ale jakoś tego nie czuję. Po prostu przez 2 i pół godziny dwójka ludzi wstaje, ubiera się, je i dogląda gospodarstwa a na dworze szaleje wiatr.

I'm on vacation and I decided to sit down for a rewatch of this one, with company this time. The first watch was unbearable to me, like a fucking endurance test. So I wanted to see if my experience would be the same. My rating went up a point, but still, this movie is the most torturous thing I've ever watched. I also have to clarify that I'm a big Nietzsche fangirl, but I guess I'm kinda dumb too because I could only understand the movie after reading countless reviews or explanations to get it. Anyway, I appreciate this movie a lot, especially the cinematography and its message. But it's still one of the most torturous things you can make me watch. And don't get me started on those potatoes..

''Werckmeister harmonies aura été d'une incroyable incroyable accessibilité en comparaison de ceci'' J'apprécie beaucoup le cinéma contemplatif, lent ou sans beaucoup de réels dialogues. Si ce n'est que l'expérience dans ces cas là passe souvent en priorité par la mise en scène. Si on place par exemple Terrence Malick à ce niveau sur une extrémité de ce spectre avec une mise en scène extrêmement dense et foisonnante, je pense que l'on peut placer Bela Tarr à son autre extrémité. C'est L'austérité pure. Une maisonnette isolée durant une tempête et de la répétition à tout les niveaux : Des plans fixes interminables, un thème musical unique rejoué en boucle une douzaine de fois, un vent qui souffle pendant deux heures trente, de la gestuelle répétée. Cela n'a même pas le sens que cela peut prendre chez Jeanne Dielmann. Bela ne nous donne rien et on doit faire avec. Qu'est ce qui fait que je ne ressens rien, que ça été une expérience extrêmement sensorielle agressive et éprouvante pour moi par rapport à tant de personnes qui ont aimé. Ça me semble plus intéressant comme réflexion que de trouver un sens au film en lui même.

Y'know, I can handle slow cinema. I watched Sàtántango with next to no issue. But it wasn't the bleakness of the film itself that made me want to die, IT JUST KEPT GOING. Took a couple Ibuprofen as the old man banged around to pack for what is ultimately a fruitless journey, and now I'm convinced Béla Tarr was a sadist.

I seem to remember Werckmeister Harmonies as one of the least enjoyable film experiences I’d had up to that time. I have, however, since then acquired a taste for slow films in which nothing happens. In other contexts at least - usually Asian. So I’m hanging out with Bela Tarr again to test my cineaste bonafides, and it’s slightly better this time, but still not for me. A father and daughter living in a small shack in the countryside is subject to unexplained misfortunes - they wake up one day and their well has dried up. The horse stops eating and working. Apocalypse surrounds them, as gales howl, and it appears that nature is abandoning them, humble as their life is. It’s all shot in this transcendent style, with long takes and slow moving cameras, and a beautifully deliberate use of zooms and framing. The black and white photography is lovely. The glacial pace is arguably appropriate in depicting this slow death of a family. Trust me, I get it. It’s just not particularly enjoyable, edifying, or enlightening. Only in small moments do the images suck you in to a point of flow. You’re never out of analysis mode. (When we observe the cart outside the house, we know in advance that Tarr is going to make us watch the entire thing be unloaded). If there’s a lack on my part, I guess that it’s not because I don’t understand it, or that I’m a Tik-Tok-addled millennial, but I’m simply not at a level of Zen not to let thought take over in the long scenes of people eating potatoes. There may come a time when I’m capable, but not yet. Still to come is all 400-so minutes of Satantango .

Olha… The Turin Horse é aquele tipo de filme que você respeita mais do que gosta. Dirigido por Béla Tarr, ele tem uma proposta claramente artística e até fascinante em teoria, mas na prática, pode ser extremamente cansativo. A rotina repetitiva do pai e da filha, comendo batata e encarando o vento infinito, até funciona como metáfora no começo. Você entende a ideia: o esgotamento da vida, o peso da existência, o mundo “apagando”. Só que chega um ponto em que o filme parece preso nessa mesma repetição e não evolui o suficiente pra sustentar o interesse. Visualmente, o filme é lindo. O preto e branco, os planos longos, a atmosfera pesada… tudo muito bem construído. Mas ao mesmo tempo, o ritmo é tão arrastado que acaba afastando mais do que envolvendo. Em vez de te puxar pra experiência, ele pode simplesmente te cansar. E aí fica aquela sensação: você entende o que o filme quer dizer, mas não necessariamente sente vontade de continuar ali. No fim, é um filme com intenção, estética e conceito fortes, mas que sacrifica demais o envolvimento em nome da proposta. Pra alguns vai ser uma obra-prima contemplativa; pra outros (como no meu caso), uma experiência interessante… só que arrastada demais pra realmente marcar. Bonito, simbólico e cheio de significado mas também excessivamente lento e pouco envolvente. Um daqueles que você admira mais do que gosta!!

Une pesanteur insoutenable. Les silences, le vent, la poussière, les couleurs chromatiques, la longueur... Tout donne à croire que le film souhaite faire souffrir son spectateur pour pouvoir refléter la folie et la névrose de Nietzsche.
The Naked Island walked so this could crawl. And it crawled at such a pretentious pace that it ended up getting absolutely nowhere. I really hope those potatoes were amazing, though.

I always love Béla Tarr movies for about 20 minutes. Then I realize that I'm not getting much more than a fairly immersive mood-piece. Absolutely gorgeous to look at, with interesting symbolism, but everything there is to be gained from it is already apparent from the get go. The longer it runs, the more you notice all the small issues. Acting isn't great and all the repetition wears out even the aspects that I was initially really into. The music itself has a very nice tone, but it's repeated to such an extent, it's completely ruined after some point. I like a lot of what it's going for and there is a lot to analyze thematically. Béla Tarr is damn good at capturing the feeling of human suffering, but the experience of watching it is often frustrating in ways that don't seem intentional.

Very slow cinema, I struggled with it. Has some really cool long takes. It's better than jeanne Dielman, this is real suffering and nightmarish existence. Unlike the other film mentioned. This is the most bleak depressing film I've ever seen I think. Too long though. Have to be in the right mood.

I adore Bela Tarr’s filmmaking style!!  The Turin Horse makes monotony profound too, which is really hard to do.  This film is quite tedious to sit through, so I’d be lying if I said I enjoyed my time with this movie.  It’s got gorgeous cinematography though and there is a deep message to be found as well.  Probably not coming back to this in the future to be honest

Une histoire en six jours. Je savais dans quoi je m’embarquais cette fois-ci en lançant un film de Béla Tarr . J’ai attendu le bon moment pour le faire, et effectivement, ça change l’expérience et le ressenti. Le narrateur en fond et le séquençage en chapitres journaliers sont une plus-value pas négligeable dans mon appréciation. La musique de Mihály Víg apporte beaucoup à cette lenteur et accompagne parfaitement l’histoire. Ce film, dans sa lenteur et sa simplicité, contient en réalité beaucoup.

Even by Bela Tarr standards this was very slow. I can appreciate what this film represents, but it was kind of mind numbing to actually watch. I don't think I'd get much from coming back to this, unlike a lot of Tarr's other works.

The Turin Horse stands as an unapologetic, uncompromising monument to apocalyptic nihilism. Opening with the famous anecdote of Friedrich Nietzsche’s mental collapse after witnessing a cabman whip a stubborn horse in Turin, the film shifts its gaze away from the philosopher to focus instead on the horse, its aging owner, and his daughter. Over six days, Béla Tarr meticulously tracks the slow, relentless unraveling of their basic existence. Shot in stark monochrome, the film is a mesmerizing work of pure atmosphere—its hypnotic rhythm and austere visuals immersing viewers in a vision of existential collapse. Unyielding in its artistic conviction, The Turin Horse offers a rare, uncompromising meditation on the futility of human struggle. It is a work that will resonate deeply with purists of extreme slow cinema, commanding respect for its bleak beauty and unwavering dedication to form.

در ژانویه‌ ۱۸۸۹، در یکی از خیابان‌های تورین، فریدریش نیچه صحنه‌ای دید که شاید برای همیشه چیزی را درون او شکست. صاحب اسبی حیوان را به شلاق می‌بست. اسب دیگر توان کشیدن بار را نداشت، ایستاده بود و از حرکت بازمانده بود. نیچه خودش را به حیوان رساند، گردنش را در آغوش گرفت و گریست. پس از آن فروپاشید و دیگر به زندگی عادی بازنگشت. سال‌ها بعد، بلا تار از همان صحنه آغاز می‌کند؛  البته نه از فیلسوفی که در خیابان‌های تورین فرو می‌ریزد، از اسب. می‌پرسد بعد از آن چه شد؟ و پاسخش یکی از تلخ‌ترین، عجیب‌ترین و خاص‌ترین فیلم‌های تاریخ سینماست. پدر و دختری در خانه‌ای دورافتاده زندگی می‌کنند. صبح از خواب بیدار می‌شوند، لباس می‌پوشند، آب می‌آورند، سیب‌زمینی می‌پزند، می‌خورند، اسب را به کالسکه می‌بندند و شب می‌خوابند. روز بعد دوباره همین اتفاق می‌افتد. و روز بعد. و روز بعد. هیچ حادثه‌ی بزرگی در کار نیست. کسی کشته نمی‌شود، شهری منفجر نمی‌شود، جنگی آغاز نمی‌شود، ابرقهرمانی برای نجات نمی‌آید، فقط باد می‌وزد. اسب یک روز دیگر حرکت نمی‌کند. آب کم می‌شود. غذا از دهان می‌افتد. چراغ خاموش می‌شود و جهان، بدون آن‌که اتفاق مشخصی برایش افتاده باشد، آرام‌آرام تمام می‌شود. شاید ترسناک‌ترین شکل نابودی همین باشد؛ اینکه جهان با یک انفجار تمام نشود، فقط کم‌کم دلیلی برای ادامه دادن باقی نگذارد. این همان جایی است که نیچه دوباره به فیلم بازمی‌گردد. نیچه از زندگی سؤال ساده‌ای نمی‌پرسید. نمی‌پرسید چگونه می‌توان خوشحال بود، چگونه می‌توان رنج کمتری کشید یا چگونه می‌توان زندگی راحت‌تری داشت. مسئله‌ او بسیار بی‌رحمانه‌تر بود: آیا می‌توانی زندگی را همان‌طور که هست بپذیری؟ نه زندگی‌ای که آرزو داری داشته باشی. نه زندگی‌ای که اگر گذشته را اصلاح می‌کردی ممکن بود به دست بیاوری. همین زندگی! با تمام شکست‌ها، تحقیرها، تنهایی‌ها، فقدان‌ها ، اشتباهات، بیماری‌ها، عشق‌های نافرجام و لحظه‌هایی که آرزو می‌کنی هرگز اتفاق نیفتاده بودند. اینجاست که ایده‌ هولناک بازگشت جاودانه ظاهر می‌شود. نیچه در حکمت شادان از موجودی سخن می‌گوید که در خلوت‌ترین تنهایی، سراغ انسان می‌آید و خبر می‌دهد که زندگی‌ای که اکنون داری، باید بارها و بارها، تا ابد، دقیقاً به همان شکل تکرار شود. هیچ چیز تغییر نخواهد کرد. هر درد، هر شادی، هر شرمندگی، هر بوسه، هر مرگ و هر صبح دوباره بازخواهد گشت. تصور کن تمام زندگی‌ات را یک بار دیگر زندگی کنی. بعد یک بار دیگر. و یک بار دیگر. و هیچ راه فراری وجود نداشته باشد. حتی کوچک‌ترین جزئیات هم تغییر نکنند. همان خانه، همان آدم‌ها، همان خیانت‌ها، همان اشتباهات، همان اضطراب‌ها؛ همان روزی که کسی را از دست دادی. همان حرفی که نباید می‌زدی. همان لحظه‌ای که ترسیدی و عقب کشیدی. همان عشقی که به پایان رسید. همان فرصتی که از دست دادی. همان صبحی که با بی‌حوصلگی از خواب بیدار شدی و نمی‌دانستی چرا هنوز باید از تخت بیرون بیایی. و دوباره همه‌ آن‌ها . برای همیشه. نیچه نمی‌خواست صرفاً یک نظریه‌ عجیب درباره‌ ساختار جهان ارائه کند. ارزش این ایده در جای دیگری است. بازگشت جاودانه از انسان می‌پرسد: اگر قرار بود همین زندگی را بی‌نهایت بار تکرار کنی، آیا می‌توانستی آن را دوست داشته باشی؟ اگر پاسخ نه باشد، مسئله فقط آینده نیست. مسئله همین اکنون است. شاید به همین دلیل بازگشت جاودانه از مرگ هم ترسناک‌تر است. مرگ دست‌ کم وعده‌ پایان می‌دهد. می‌توانی تحمل کنی چون می‌دانی این درد، این تنهایی، این شکست، روزی تمام خواهد شد. اما در بازگشت جاودانه، پایان وجود ندارد. هیچ نجاتی در آینده منتظرت نیست. قرار نیست روزی از این زندگی عبور کنی و به زندگی دیگری برسی. قرار است دوباره همین را زندگی کنی. و این پرسش، آرام‌آرام آدم را از درون می‌خورد: اگر قرار است همه‌چیز دوباره اتفاق بیفتد، پس من با این زندگی چه کرده‌ام؟ نیچه برای این وضعیت واژه‌ای داشت که شاید یکی از سخت‌ترین خواسته‌هایی باشد که یک فیلسوف از انسان مطرح کرده است: آری گفتن به زندگی. نه آری گفتن به زندگی وقتی همه‌چیز خوب است. این آسان است. آری گفتن به زندگی وقتی زندگی به تو خیانت کرده است. وقتی چیزی را که دوست داشتی از تو گرفته است. وقتی فهمیده‌ای بسیاری از امیدهایی که سال‌ها به آن‌ها  تکیه کرده‌ای، فقط راه‌هایی برای تحمل کردن امروز بوده‌اند. وقتی می‌فهمی گذشته قابل اصلاح نیست و آینده هم هیچ تضمینی ندارد. آری گفتن به زندگی یعنی پذیرفتن تمام این‌ها، بدون اینکه مجبور باشی آن‌ها  را زیبا جلوه بدهی. نیچه نمی‌گوید رنج خوب است. زندگی اسان است. شکست زیباست. نمی‌گوید باید به هر آنچه بر سرمان آمده لبخند بزنیم. مسئله عمیق‌تر است؛ آیا می‌توانی آنچه را اتفاق افتاده، بخشی از زندگی خودت بدانی، بدون این که تمام زندگی را به خاطر آن نفی کنی؟ در این معنا، انسان نیچه‌ای کسی است که اجازه نمی‌دهد رنج، تمام معنای زندگی‌اش را تعریف کند. اما اسب تورین درست در نقطه‌ مقابل این امکان ایستاده است. در فیلم، زندگی آن‌قدر تهی شده که دیگر حتی چیزی برای آری گفتن باقی نمانده است. تکرار دیگر سرچشمه‌ معنا نیست. تبدیل به زندان شده است. صبح می‌آید، چون همیشه صبح آمده است. غذا خورده می‌شود، چون همیشه غذا خورده شده است. آب آورده می‌شود، چون همیشه آب آورده شده است. و ناگهان اسب می‌ایستد. شاید اسب اولین موجودی باشد که در این چرخه دست از تظاهر به ادامه دادن می‌کشد. انسان‌ها  هنوز تلاش می‌کنند همان کارهای همیشگی را انجام دهند. اسب دیگر نمی‌تواند. انگار بدن حیوان چیزی را فهمیده که ذهن انسان هنوز از پذیرفتنش فرار می‌کند؛ این‌که ادامه دادن به خودی خود دلیل نیست... ما انسان‌ها استاد ادامه دادن هستیم! گاهی سال‌ها در رابطه‌ای می‌مانیم که دیگر چیزی در آن زنده نیست. سال‌ها در کاری می‌مانیم که از آن متنفریم. سال‌ها رؤیایی را دنبال می‌کنیم که دیگر حتی نمی‌دانیم چرا زمانی برایمان مهم بوده. سال‌ها مخفیانه کسی را دوست داریم که می‌دانیم حتی دیگر ما را به یاد نمی‌آورد. سال‌ها صبح از خواب بیدار می‌شویم، کار می‌کنیم، پول درمی‌آوریم، غذا می‌خوریم، می‌خوابیم و دوباره از ابتدا شروع می‌کنیم. بعد اسم این تکرار را می‌گذاریم زندگی! شاید یکی از تلخ‌ترین کشف‌های انسان این باشد که می‌توان سال‌ها زنده بود، بدون این که واقعاً زندگی کرد. و در اینجا پرسشی پنهان شده که شاید نیچه هرگز نتوانسته باشد به طور کامل به آن پاسخ دهد: اگر زندگی آن‌قدر سنگین شود که دیگر نتوانی به آن آری بگویی چه؟ صدرا خرازی- مرداد 1405 بازبینی فیلم اسب تورین

ok i think i have let my shock and confusion pass me by and im more able to articulate my thoughts on the film. the film is beautifully shot and the score is amazing. both of these put together really do add to the dread and misery that the film is able to perfectly encapsulate. The film was a perfect pick for the bleak week festival as it is an incredibly miserable thing to experience. this movie is not enjoyable at all and i think i would rather be shot than have to rewatch this movie again. the utter redundancy of watching the father and daughter perform the same chores everyday with slight variations for 2.5 hours is absolutely grueling and makes you feel like finishing this movie is the equivalent to carrying out a prison sentence. HOWEVER, the sequences with the horse are greatly moving, representing the last of the father and daughters hope the horse soon goes from a strong animal carrying heavy loads to one that mopes around all day while refusing to eat and drink, the storm outside totally shattering its will. The horses refusal to even live shows that there is no hope for the farmer and his daughter to continue, even with the slight hope that the monotony of their daily routine gave them that too is eventually taken away as the well runs dry and both father and daughter stop eating resigning to their fate. TLDR: monotonous life sucks balls, try to make a change before you become resigned to your fate

I don't know that slow burns are for me. Or maybe i shouldn't watch them so late. Besides that, the film is beautiful, bleak, and timeless. Tarr was a master at turning a frame into a painting. I actually did enjoy how the film wrapped up despite it essentially being almost 3 hours of people just living life, but it definitely felt like it went on 20-30 minutes too long. I think we see the old man get dressed 6 or 7 times. Of the 30 shots 6 of them were getting dressed! But I still walked away fairly satisfied, glad I watched it, and much more interested in Tarr's stack of work.

Um espelho invisível Da minha vida e seu peso: Um nada. Levo comigo O retrato de mamãe. O vento se foi, E meu estômago continua Vazio.
My boy Bela always knows how to bring the fun. This is a beautifully photographed film. Pause it at any moment and it's going to be an absolutely gorgeous frame. But Jesus Christ, Bela, I get it.

The Turin Horse is immaculately composed, weighing with apocalyptic finality in every shot from its austere opening horse ride to its final scenes of mundanity amid despair. The film isn't desperate so much as it is purely hopeless, offering no solace or commiseration for its protagonists but rather luxuriating in their suffering. While I found the films interiors and landscapes alike to be stunning in their obsessive emptiness and despair, I struggled to find much substance in this commitment to a single, uncompromised evocation of pain; even if The Turin Horse feels like the work of a great artist, its lack of particularly mixed feelings is not very interesting or thought-provoking.

I'm glad this is my first Bela Tarr film. I also tried watching Satantango but I gave up after 2 hours, slow cinema is not for me. Frankly, I did not enjoy it. It was incredibly boring but at the same time, I can't take my eyes off the screen. It's like watching football for me. The only difference is that the latter is fast paced. But the feeling of uncertainty and anticipation makes it so similar.

i watched a baked potato get eaten without a utensil in black and white at least five times in 155 minutes— this movie is like watching paint dry… but oh! what paint! and why does it dry like that.

Penso di aver avuto l’illuminazione per l’interpretazione di questo film. Qualcuno potrebbe interpretarlo come nichilismo trito e ritrito ma questo non è il caso. La frase “Si può portare il cavallo alla fontana, ma non lo si può convincere a bere” vi dice qualcosa? Esattamente … questo film è solo l’espressione fisica della citazione kenyesiana. Interrompete le vostre elucubrazioni da uomini con il pesce in mano e guardate la realtà, è tutta una metafora economica. E poi è uguale ad un meme che ho visto un mese fa su una pagina di schizoposting.

They Shoot Pictures, Don’t They? Unseen 79/360 Movie Century Challenge 1/100 Impressed by the horse acting and the wind, felt nothing for the humans. The aim was to produce existential dread but the ascetic remove and intentional tedium resulted in sporadic engagement and a desire for the end to come sooner. RIP Bela, we'll always have Satantango.

Incomparable à n'importe quel autre film par son rythme presque désespérant. C'est extrêmement lent, mais l'ennui est presque accompagné d'une frustration envers une fin inévitable et la confrontation avec une impuissance frappante. C'est brutal, monotone et gris (le format noir et blanc n'aide pas). Difficile de savoir si c'est l'influence d'un biais inévitable après avoir lu autant d'éloges sur ce cinéaste et cette œuvre mais j'ai quand même l'impression de comprendre un peu où tout le monde voit un génie. Tarr transmets parfaitement sa vision mélancolique de la vie humaine, de cette famille complètement misérable dans une tempête omniprésente. On comprendrais presque que la valeur d'un film n'est pas définie par l'expérience de visionnage. Dommage, je dois être un peu trop jeune encore.

Le Cheval de Turin est un film qui semble d’abord réduit à une sensation : le vent. Un vent incessant, presque agressif, qui empêche toute respiration et finit par envahir tout le film. À part cette force naturelle, il ne se passe presque rien, et c’est précisément ce “rien” qui déroute. Le quotidien se répète, les gestes s’épuisent, le monde paraît se vider de son sens. Béla Tarr ne cherche pas à raconter une histoire mais à faire ressentir une fin, une extinction lente, silencieuse, sans explication. C’est un film difficile à commenter parce qu’il refuse le discours : on ne le comprend pas vraiment, on le subit.

Tak jak śmierć Davida Lyncha w zeszłym roku zmotywowała mnie do nadrobienia jego filmografii, tak odejście Béla Tarra sprawiło, że postanowiłem obejrzeć "Koń turyński". Niestety nie znalazłem wielu innych jego dzieł z polskimi napisami. Koń, którego niegdyś Nietzsche ocalił przed cierpieniem ze strony woźnicy, zaczyna niedomagać - odmawia jedzenia i pracy. Film opowiada też historię woźnicy i jego córki. Zdziwiłem się, że opowieść László Krasznahorkaia, którą obecnie czytam, stała się zaczątkiem dla ostatniego filmu węgierskiego mistrza kina. To było bardzo długie, 155 minut mojego życia. Nie jestem pewien, czy to nie był najmniej dynamiczny seans, jaki widziałem. Musiałem obejrzeć go w dwóch częściach, bo za pierwszym razem zasnąłem. Dlatego wydaje mi się, że próg wejścia jest bardzo wysoki dla przeciętnego widza. Ja ledwo przez niego przebrnąłem. To ponury, surowy i smutny obraz o wyraźnie apokaliptycznym klimacie. Jednocześnie urzekły mnie zdjęcia Freda Kelemena. Bohaterowie wykonują codziennie te same czynności, popadają w rutynę. Prawdopodobnie na długo zapamiętam odgłos wiatru, który towarzyszy nam niemal cały czas. Z jednej strony było to mocne, niezwykle pesymistyczne doświadczenie, w którym przez sześć dni świat powoli się kończy. Z drugiej, nie był to najciekawszy seans w moim życiu. Nie wiedziałem, że końcem świata będzie codzienne zajadanie się pulkami. "Koń turyński" to film, który imponuje artystycznie (atmosfera, zdjęcia), ale jest naprawdę ciężki w odbiorze, i to nie musi być wadą, lecz jego charakterem. Czy w Polsce mogę gdzieś obejrzeć inne dzieła tego reżysera, najlepiej z napisami polskimi?
A very challenging watch, barely got through it. I liked many scenes-striking black and white images created a sense of bleakness and unyielding emptiness. Rip Béla Tarr

Truthfully, I didn't stop making films because... It's because there's nothing more to say. I mean, when you're talking about death, what else is there to talk about? Death is not like the apocalypse, which is a big TV show with horsemen and all that. Silence. Life simply runs out silently day by day. You think you're doing your daily routine, but each day you're a little older and a little different. By these little daily differences, you're exactly that much closer to the point when you simply... There's no noise; there's nothing. It all simply went away. Now, fuck it. How do you deal with this? So, should I make another movie? About what? I can't. There's no reason to. So, what happens next? That's all. -BÉLA TARR

Potato skins contain concentrated amounts of fiber, iron, potassium, B vitamins, vitamin C, and antioxidants. Key Vitamins and Minerals: - Fiber: Ounce for ounce, the skin contains a large share of the potato's fiber, providing about 2 grams per ounce to support digestion. - Iron: “The skin of a whole baked potato provides 88-percent of the total amount of iron.” - Potassium: This essential mineral helps regulate blood pressure and supports heart and muscle function. - Vitamin C: Acts as an antioxidant and supports immune health. - B Vitamins: Includes vitamin B6 to aid in red blood cell formation and metabolic health. - Antioxidants: Rich in plant compounds like flavonoids, phenolic acids, and anthocyanins (especially in red and purple varieties)

in a lot of ways it feels almost pointless to ascribe a rating to this. because how do you properly rate a quasi-arthouse installation that's nigh-hyper focused on testing your time. making you feel the same kind of dreary hopelessness in a world devoid of love and hope i guess in that way, this movie should be a perfect 10/10 because it absolutely achieves the kind of mood it sought out to capture. the heaviness of human existence, the perspectives of man where one sees barbaric cruelty and another sees the only way he can afford to continue surviving in a world that has given him no rope. but i guess when it comes down to it, this simply didn't connect with me on an emotional level the way damnation did that film similarly feels entirely committed to its vision of a world devoid of god, where hell is the dreary rain and aching pain with which all of our hollow bones are constructed. but damnation gripped me by the soul and never let go, every torrential downpour, muddy flailing limb, glowing neon light; it depicted a world i could vividly and tangibly connect with. the turin horse, while having no less an enrapturing world, ultimately felt like i was watching it from the outside in. that there was a lens, a window, between the harrowing, grueling experience it captured and the emotions i wished to feel from witnessing such an event still a very worthwhile experience, one that again informs the nihilistic viewpoint tarr captures through his apocalyptic visions of man's own barbarism and the aimlessness of such a life. rife with moments not just of harrow but moments of fervor and almost beauty; moments that trick you into thinking this world is worth salvaging. but ultimately, i found my connection to it much more fleeting than i would have liked

The sheer economy of action of this movie is amazing. The reframing of shots was brilliantly executed. It really nailed the cinematographic minimalism concept. I think that the theme is the heaviness of existence and the inevitable decay that eventually comes after countless struggles with an anticristian vibe on top with the reversion of the christian creation. Probably the most nihilist film one will ever see. Worth a watch if you are not depressed.

The harsh winds, the gritty film grain, the dread filled score, some days it feels like the main constants of our life is its nothingness. Some days it feels like the fruitlessness of our actions is always in a perpetual rebirth, always fitting into whatever context it is placed in whether it is the start of the world or now (the world’s end).

My first Bela Tarr joint. Incredibly visually striking in this richly-textured black and white, minimalist in a way that forces you to pay attention to cloth and fur and rock and wind. Watching it, your brain shifts gears into a different mode of film-watching. After spending the first day with the two peasants, watching them go about the routine of their days like a perfectly choreographed dance, wordlessly moving in tandem, the repetition of the second day had me gleaning for anything new. I found myself fascinated by how differently the daughter eats a potato from how the man does, given that I couldn't see her eating the first day. By the time a group of traveling Romani show up on the fourth day, five or so people talking at once feels overstimulating. Watching a week of Genesis play out in reverse, the world getting smaller and smaller until even light finally goes out, seeing the daughter near the end quietly pull out and work on some mending really got to me.

stark fatalism that pulls u along its fierce elemental whirl; a world crying in pain -- on its last breath -- yet more terrifying than its roaring winds is its silence... and the darkness. hypnotic and immersive from its initial strenuous marching scene to its final extinguished image.

مبدئيا كده انا متفرجتش على فيلم انا لعبت يوجا و لازم تكون ده اللي عامل حسابك عليه لو ناوي تخوض التجربه ديه، لأنه ده اول فيلم اشوفه بيوصللك معنى العدميه  بأنه يعيشهالك كأنك قاعد مع نيتشه ذات نفسه . ده مش معناه انه الفيلم ممل، لأنه ده مش فيلم، ده علاج مر . من خلال أب عجوز وبنته عايشين في بيت حجري معزول، وسط عاصفة لا تهدأ، بيحطنا المخرج بيلا تار قدام حياة تخليك مصدوم: ازاي أبطالها وصلوا للدرجة ديه من بتتكرر كل يوم، ومع كل مرة نشوف نفس الأفعال بنبدأ نحس إن الزمن عندهم مش بيتقدم، لكنه بيلف حوالين نفسه. وده بيترجم في مشهد عبقري: كادر واسع جايب الغرفة كلها، الأب قاعد قدام الشباك على الكرسي بيتأمل في A film nem tartalom, hanem morális állásfoglalás. Tarr élete során ezt az elvet követte. Ez talán ebben, az utolsó filmjében mutatkozik meg igazán. Ahogy a Partizán potcastben is elmondta, a filmművésznek el kell döntenie hogy művészet marad, vagy inkább a szórakoztató ipar részévé válik. Hogy cgi szuperhősöket akarunk nézni, vagy kulturálódni. Tarr mindog a művészet mellé tette le a voksát, és talán itt éreztem ezt a legjobban. Nem fogok hazudni, ezt a filmet fájdalmas volt végignézni, az utolsó fél órára már elfáradtam, és ezt úgy mondom hpgy Tart Béla az egyik kedvenc rendezőm. Ez a film két és fél óra semmi. Béla szavaival élve "kozmikus semmi". És ez nem egy rossz dolog! Nem kell elvárnunk egy filmtől hogy kiszolgáljon, hogy szórakoztasson. Ez a film gondolkozásra késztet. Gondolkodsz közben, de nem más dolgolról, hanem a filmmel együtt gondolkozol. Amiket mi látunk ebben a filmben azok véglények. Ez nem élet. Ez életben maradás. Élet ez egyáltalán? Nem. Ez csak létezés. A motorikus képességeik tartják őket életben, rutinból élnek. "Sokan 25 évesen meghalnak, de csak 75 évesen temetik el őket"- Benjamin Franklin Ppntosan ugyan ezt látjuk. Ők csak léteznek, de nem élnek. Főleg az apuka, a lányban maradt még egy csepp, ő törődik a lóval, nem csak a saját életbenmaradásához szolgaló ezközként tekint rá. Ebben a filmben ha egy szó se lenne, az se lenne baj. Ahogy az apuka kapkod a krumplihoz, gyorsan leszedi a bőrét, összezúzza és gyordan befalj miközben levegőt vesz hogy hűljön, mindent elárul. Ez nem étkezés, ez táplálkozás. Csakis életbenmaradásról szól. A lány viszont fogja a krumplit. Itt látszódnak az apró különbségek. Azt hiszem ez történik ma kicsiben minden emberrel. Tarr látott mindent.

Canto de cisne del gran realizador y maestro húngaro, última obra formal de ficción con la cual anunció su retiro –mismo que terminó siendo parcial pues en 2019 presentaría Missing People, una incrustación al cine extendido a manera de  documental/instalación a solicitud expresa del Wiener Festwochen Festival de Viena– una brutal epístola de partida en la que encumbre y reviste con profundidad y parsimonia (cual fue su costumbre) los temas y acercamientos existenciales que manejó durante su filmografía; cruenta esquela que en su afonía y sosiego explora el devenir humano y su efímero y encarnizado paso por la experiencia de la vida. En esta edificación la contemplación y el silencio se presentan portentosamente como un retablo de los tiempos universales, no marcando o caracterizando una época o un tiempo (o región), sino que perfilan y definen nuestra propia naturaleza. El propio Tarr llegó a mencionar sobre esta, su última impresión, que trataba sobre la pesadez de la existencia humana. Basada en la ya mítica anécdota donde Friedrich Nietzsche defiende a un caballo de feroces azotes y que, según el consenso general, marca el preámbulo de su hundimiento mental; esta postal que increpa el origen del filme mantiene a su vez una inquietante relación con un paraje de la excelsa Crimen y Castigo de Fiódor Dostoyevski (publicada apenas un par de décadas atrás); donde el protagonista Rodion Raskólnikov se sueña de niño viendo como es violentamente golpeado un caballo, como él lo intenta defender con todas sus fuerzas sobre un llanto profundo, pero al final todo resulta inútil. Sumando una capa más a este soporte discursivo que dialoga entre memorias históricas e interpretaciones ontológicas y morales, Béla Tarr se apoya de László Krasznahorkai (Nobel de Literatura 2025) –quien no le es nada ajeno; adaptó algunas de sus novelas como también colaboró directamente con él en otros guiones– para acoger la peripecia ya afamada y sortear el camino más común: el hombre (el sabio, el ilustrado), y así poder enfocarse en un lindante temático de la misma importancia: el caballo. De esta forma, siguiendo al vejado jamelgo es como la trama nos lleva a un acampado solitario –y que en parte nos recuerda al mejor  Bergman– para así cercanos en linderos de apatía, en un confinamiento que intenta ser rutinario pero que pronto habrá de develar la decadencia del todo. El recorrido trazado es el de una agonía, pero su tratamiento no es apuntalado en lo agónico, es en cambio en el de la quietud; un dolor que abraza y se acepta cual destino. No es que no se pueda luchar contra él, es tan sólo que es ese el punto común donde todos habremos de encontrarnos finiquitados; allanados en un mutismo voraz que nos explica y nos despliega. Le inexistencia como parte de. El Caballo de Turín de Béla Tarr parte, entonces, de una nota al pie de la filosofía y rompe las membranas de las horas y los años, de los segundos y los lustros. Se anida en la promesa de un pozo siempre proveedor y se enfrenta a un viento sempiterno que devela al agotamiento al tiempo que anuncia el borde y el corolario. Es una venta atroz pero sincera. La voz con que Béla Tarr construye –y construyó– su despedida es apenas audible, es sutil, pero tiene una potencia enorme: un agreste campo, perturbador como sugestivo donde la turbación y la calma no se disputan o enemistan sino simplemente se dan la mano.

Entré en la filmografía de Béla Tarr con cierto respeto, siendo consciente de que lo hacía, probablemente, por su obra más radical. Es una película bellísima, austera y minimalista, de un precioso blanco y negro. Apenas hay diálogos, pero resulta completamente comprensible; por momentos, parece que estuviéramos ante cuadros hiperrealistas en movimiento. Partiendo de aquel episodio que, según parece, llevó a Nietzsche a la demencia, la película nos enfrenta a la deprimente monotonía de una pareja (padre e hija) de granjeros. La repetición de sus rutinas, el viento incesante y la desaparición de todo a su alrededor convierten la película en una experiencia casi hipnótica, que desemboca en una profunda desolación.

Two months ago i watched Hu Bo's An Elephant Sitting still (2018). A few days ago i rewatched Tarr's own Werckmeister Harmonies (2000) . Both these films lacked something. That something... dread..? The monotonous hellscape? The brutality of the elements? I can't put it into words, but that something is present within this monolith. God created the world in 6 days, Says one religion. Tarr takes this absurd belief and makes a film where a small world is destroyed by the relentless abuse of the elements, all captured in slow, monochromatic fashion. A bleak dystopian reverse genesis.

On January 3rd 1889, renowned German philosopher Fredrich Nietzsche acted in opposition to the very philosophy he had spent the entireity of his adult life preaching. Upon witnessing the brutal whipping of a horse in Turin by a carriage driver, overwhlmed by empathy and sadness, he rushed over to the aforementioned horse and hugged it, preventing it being beat any longer. He sobbed greatly and was eventually removed by a friend of his, and transported back to his quarters, where he would remain in a delirious sleep-state for 2 days. This marked his profound mental breakdown, under which he would remain for the next 10 years of his life, cared for by his mother and his family before his eventual passing. Tarr begins The Turin Horse with a narration that essentially summarises these events. Yet, Tarr's introduction also ends with the line "yet no one knows what happened to the horse." That is the story that Tarr wants to tell, the story of the horse after this infamous incident. Bela Tarr's The Turin Horse is an apocalyptic tale of death. Not just the death of human or animal life, but the death of life itself, in a profoundly existential way, life as a force itself. We follow this family of two, a father and a daughter, as they carry out their monotonous daily routines, repeated over 6 days. Their lives are spent mostly in silence, the two hardly involve themselves in many conversations with each other, and they carry on with a deep resignation. A resignation of life, of meaning and an eventual submission to suffering and death. It is one of the bleakest narratives I have seen; a completely painful experience as the inevitability of death and meaninglessnes takes over, a complete dissolution of the human spirit. I will not claim to know or have read much of Nietzche's works, but it's clear Tarr employs Nietzsche as more than just a narrative prologue to the begin his story. He turns Nietzsche's concepts of nihilism and stasis into a daily routine for these protagonists, mirroring the empty hopelessness of their lives. The repetitive sequences mirror his idea of eternal reccurrence. I'm sure there's even more meaning that I may not have picked up in relation to Nietzsche's philosophy because of my lack of having read his work, but what all I could pick up is extremely alluring and brilliant. Furthermore, there is the elemental nature of this film that embodies its own spirit. The howls and the shrieks of the wind act as tertiary characters in the scenes between the daughter and her father, further contributing to the despair echoed by the screenplay. The wind, to me, acts as nature's own response to its exploitation and mistreatment by humans. Just like the titular horse's own decision to stop working on the second day, the wind's aggression is in a way its own revolution, its own protest to humanity's exploitation, a theme that is echoed by a very brilliant metaphorical monologue by a neighbour later on in the film. The film de-centers the man from the collapse of the world, here Tarr is less interested in the suffering of humanity, but the suffering of the environment itself. The Turin Horse is apocalyptic not because it depicts some radically terrifying future, but because of its profound vision of environmental collapse, leading to humanitarian collapse. Any anthropological sympathy is lost; this is the destruction we caused, and we must pay the price for it. There is hardly a filmmaker who can capture so much meaning within a single shot like Bela Tarr. His movies can be seen as boring, pretentious, over-wrought with metaphors and a grueling, monotonous exercise in patience testing. This may be true, after all all art is subjective, yet I find Bela Tarr and his long-winding and patience testing narratives to be incredibly heavy and rewarding. Thematically rich and still somehow, incredibly relevant to this day. I have only seen one other film of his (Werckmeister Harmonies), but I am already confident his filmography will be something I will adore. Loved nearly every second of this.

Béla Tarr didn’t just make a movie about the end of the world; he filmed the world slowly dying of exhaustion. The Turin Horse feels like an anti-Genesis. Instead of watching a universe come into existence over six days, we watch one methodically and quietly shut down. There are no explosions, no aliens, no grand apocalyptic spectacle. Things simply begin to stop: the horse refuses to work, then refuses to eat; the water disappears; escape becomes impossible; and eventually, even the light goes out. At the center of it all are an aging cabman, his daughter, a stubborn horse, and a relentless howling wind that seems determined to erase them from existence. This isn't a film you simply watch; it’s one you endure. Across its two-and-a-half-hour runtime, Tarr strips cinema down to its barest essentials and turns repetition into philosophy. Getting dressed. Tending to the horse. Fetching water. Eating potatoes. Again and again. And somewhere in that repetition, you begin to feel the physical weight of existence itself. How much of life is really driven by meaning, and how much of it is simply habit? We keep going because yesterday we kept going. Perhaps the horse is the only character wise enough to finally say, in its own way: No more. Fred Kelemen’s camera doesn't merely observe this dying world; it glides through it like a ghost. Every frame looks like a charcoal drawing smudged by the dust of a dying universe, while Mihály Víg's hypnotic, looping score plays like a funeral march for existence itself. Bleak, hypnotic, exhausting, and strangely beautiful. The Turin Horse demands immense patience, but surrender to its rhythm and it becomes an overwhelmingly profound experience. This isn't just a film about the end of the world. It feels like watching the world quietly decide that it has had enough of us. A soul-crushing, breathtaking masterpiece and one hell of a final statement from Béla Tarr.

The fear of just doing the same thing all over again until it's all over. I remember spending time in a birdwatching observatory in Jurmo island during winter. There were these insane snow storms that hurt your skin like hell and sometimes electricity died inside. The storm in this film reminded me of that. Makes you appreciate modern luxurys. But the fate we all have in the end remains the same so you best make best use of it. Possibly the most silent theater I can recall. The Turin Horse has power that is hard to explain.

When the very last meaning of survival is stripped away, that raw silence becomes unbearable to endure. As you watch, something inside just hollows out. No dramatic tears, no final farewells only a creeping, silent darkness accumulating piece by piece. A numbing silence washes over you before you even realize it. This film forces you to feel what happens when the final urge to live completely flickers out.

Es de esas películas únicas y raras que te apartan un poco del lado racional y que ves solo con los sentidos. El plano secuencia de apertura es hipnótico. Algunos desorientados la tachan de pretenciosa, cansina o aburrida. Puede serlo para quien concibe el cine solo desde una perspectiva puramente narrativa. Los planos largos y repetitivos son la forma en la que podemos acercarnos a la monotonía, a esa clase de aburrimiento que incluso se asemeja más a la paz de no esperar nada. La película es el concepto mismo del eterno retorno: una misma vida condenada a repetirse infinitas veces. Es un recorrido por la pérdida de la voluntad y del sentido.

В этой огромной дыре человеку бесполезно кричать, ведь его щуплый голос никогда не будет по-настоящему услышан в бездне его же творения.

In Turin, on January 3rd, 1889, Friedrich Nietzsche steps out of the door of number six Via Carlo Alberto, perhaps to take a stroll, perhaps to go by the post office to collect his mail. Not far from him, or indeed very far removed from him, a cabman is having trouble with his stubborn horse. Despite all his urging, t he horse refuses to move, whereupon the cabman... Giuseppe? Carlo? Ettore? ...loses his patience and takes his whip to it. Nietzsche comes up to the throng and puts an end to the brutal scene of the cabman, who by this time is foaming with rage. The solidly built and full-mustached Nietzsche suddenly jumps up to the cab and throws his arms around the horse's neck, sobbing. His neighbor takes him home, where he lies still and silent for two days on a divan until he mutters the obligatory last words, "Mutter, ich bin dumm," and lives for another ten years, gentle and demented, in the care of his mother and sisters. Of the horse, we know nothing. Cut to horse. If that premise moves you, watch The Turin Horse . Whatever you think about Nietzsche, the idea that one of the most preeminent (prominent, at least) thinkers of our time had his brain melted into infancy for ten years by this singular, relatively normal event, is so thought-provoking that I still can’t stop thinking about it. To then execute on the concepts of divinity, humanity, and suffering over the course of the film is an artistic miracle. Gorgeous score, and some of the best photography ever put to screen; made possible by masterful camera operation. Sparse, meaningful, efficient dialogue highlights the nuance of our understated, weary characters. The ONLY problem I have is the chewing, but the chewing is the point, so I’m scratching that one. Thank you Bela Tarr, and rest in peace.

Essa sensação de desespero, de desesperança, de que nada vai melhorar e de que tudo só tende a piorar... é horrível. Tenho enfrentado isso. Não sei se reassistir um filme com esse tom me ajuda muito, mas acho que confrontar que esse sentimento é real e é mais comum do que eu imaginava é chocante. O Cavalo de Turim é, provavelmente, um dos filmes mais depressivos já feitos - e, definitivamente o mais depressivo que o Béla Tarr dirigiu na carreira dele. Com uma sequência de desventuras que só desmotivam os personagens, somos lembrados de que morrer não é repentino: é algo gradativo, que acontece conforme vamos notando que esse é o destino fatal para o corpo e a mente humana. Quanta filosofia num filme de 2h35 aparentemente monótono e que carrega tanto simbolismo, né?

"The Turin Horse" by Béla Tarr is undoubtedly a masterpiece that deserves each of its 5 stars. From the first frame, the film captures you with its minimalist aesthetic and its slow but deeply evocative narration. Tarr’s direction is a hypnotic journey: each carefully composed frame conveys an almost mystical solemnity , transforming everyday life into an almost spiritual experience. Personally , I was impressed by the director’s ability to make silence speak, which almost seems like an antagonistic character. The long sequences, although seemingly endless, are an invitation to reflect on the meaning of life and the human condition, transforming every moment into a work of art. The photography, austere but at the same time poetic, and the impressive and very evocative soundtrack, merge to create an atmosphere that envelops and transports the viewer through the film. This film is not only a visual experience, but also an emotional one: it is a work that requires patience, attention and an open mind, and pays off with a wealth of sensations hardly comparable. In conclusion, "The Turin Horse" not only embodies the best of cinema, but also demonstrates how simplicity, combined with a mastery of impeccable technique, can give life to a deeply universal story. A film that I highly recommend to those who are looking for a cinema that knows how to excite and make people think.

Братья Стругацкие хотели чтобы экранизировать свою повесть,  Алексею Герману, режиссер решил снимать «Трудно быть богом» еще в 1968 году, через 4 года после выхода книги. Вместе с Борисом Стругацким они написали первый вариант сценария. В августе Герман получил разрешение на съёмки, но вскоре началась операция «Дунай» — вторжение в Чехословакию войск СССР и других стран Варшавского договора, поэтому режиссеру не разрешили снимать фильм. Производство картины затянулось по причине трудностей с финансированием и сложности озвучания. Когда же финансирование нашлось, снимали картину в 2000 году и закончились в 2006 году. С тех пор, Алексей Герман работал в основном над звуком. К сожалению, он умер в феврале 2013 года, не успев доработать звуковую составляющую. Завершали работу над картиной его сын, Алексей Герман мл., и Светлана Кармалита. Самих же братьев тоже уже не стало. Сама же картина вышла в 2013 г., долго делали эту картину, очень долго, но стоило ли овчинка выделки? А вот и нет, то что Стругацкими использовалось редко и умело, в фильме гипертрофированно до немыслимых масштабов и превратилось в самоцель, идея здесь исключительно одна, мол, все люди коричневая субстанция, коричневая субстанция на них, вокруг них и внутри них, субстанцией люди были всегда и навеки им и останутся, ибо такова их природа, так себе мысль конечно, но это как говорится  “У кого что болит?” Однако донести свою точку зрения можно куда менее блевотными способами, чем строить трёхчасовой фильм вокруг одной банальной идеи залитой литрами жидкой грязи и коричневой субстанцией, иногда вообще закрадывается крамольная мысль, что целью режиссёра как раз и было заснять тонны грязи и коричневой субстанции, чтобы потом посмеяться с того, как люди будут находить в этой смрадной клоаке космической глубины философский подтекст. Разумеется тут же нашлись толпы не быдла объявившие картину гениальной, мол, всё так и есть, только они такие волшебные выходят на улицу, чтобы прикупить очередной IPhone или баночку фуагра, как их тут же окружает грязное вонючее быдло, само собой сами они при этом себя такими не считают, пусть эти товарищи продолжают искать жемчуг в море поноса хоть до скончания времён, нам же как это странно не звучало нужны внятный сюжет, логика, нормальная игра актёров и приемлемая картинка, а не сферичная шизофреничная блевотная ерунда, какой именитый режиссёр её не снимал и сколько бы лет он на это не потратил, король то голый Господа. Адекватной экранизации Трудно быть Богом попросту не существует, если фильм 1989 г. был унылой коричневой субстанцией, то картина Германа это просто коричневая субстанция, причём с большой буквой “Г”, больше сказать нечего и вообще лучше помыть руки, после работы Германа возникает знаете такое неодолимое желание. “I’d rather be happy over liking Hard to Be a God.” - COOP, 2025 I watched this movie almost three years ago and called this dreadful, uncomfortable, and drawn out figurative “snuff film” a masterpiece. Then I never watched it again, and I deeply regret not revisiting it sooner. I have to ask… what the hell did I even see in this movie? A deep character study? Clearly something. I know that not every great film is supposed to be “enjoyable”, but I don’t think a good movie should give me absolutely nothing to enjoy at all, like this one does. Seriously, I could barely even finish it. The only good thing I can say is that the cinematography reflects the movie's tone perfectly. It’s very atmospheric, but that can’t salvage how genuinely uncomfortable it made me feel throughout. And not even in a good, thought provoking way. I got to a scene in the dungeon with only 35 minutes left and just decided to skip to the end… which I know is cheating, but how am I supposed to stay invested in something I already hate watching? Watching this movie again was legitimately one of the most dreadful viewing experiences I’ve ever had. The first time I saw it, I was 15, at a point in my life when I wanted to be a “true cinema nerd” and get into more “absurd cinema.” In doing so, I guess I convinced myself that I loved this movie way more than I actually did. Okay fine; that’s the understatement of the century. The worst thing you can do as a movie fan is convince yourself that you like something you really don’t. I really do want to love these kinds of movies, okay? I think movies like “Stalker” and “Werkmeister Harmonies” are very thought provoking, and masterfully made films that were made with a greater intention than to be slow and enduring for the sake of it. They’re also movies I haven’t seen in a while, but can confirm I’ve seen more than once in less than three years,  and have taken actual time to think down. But this one just feels like an endurance test and never feels like it has anything meaningful to say. It’s nothing more than one big drag of a watch.

This is likely the most disgusting film I’ve had to endure with little to no reward for it. It’s as though the director instructed everyone to act as vulgar and as uncaring as possible at every given moment regardless of what their character motivations were. Never is an opportunity missed to spit everywhere, physically abuse someone, smear crap on someone’s face, cough up mysterious substances, etc. The main character seems to have no motivation and uses his lethargy to essentially torture those around him and slog through his mud-caked surroundings aimlessly. The movie appears to abandon its premise almost immediately, instead favoring endless grotesque set pieces to test the audience’s endurance. There is a somewhat interesting plot underneath it all and some genuinely impressive cinematography and set design despite how disgusting it is, but digging through the filth just isn’t worth it.
