Every watch is just more fully appreciating how this movie’s DNA is scattered through any movie about space made ever since. It’s wild how singular the vision for every single little detail in this movie is before we had even been to the moon, and how all of the beautifully rendered and dynamic CGI of Interstellar, or even the ambitious and groundbreaking VFX of Star Wars pales in comparison to a matte painting and a rotating miniature with unidirectional lighting when composed just right, with the proper intention and ambience. Same with the BCU of Hal’s red dot, same with all the monolith shots and the dawn of man looking better than the best nature documentary. 2001 is the monolith Kubrick sent us from the future to teach us a new form of art we weren’t ready for yet and still aren’t for the most part.

a mind-bending sci-fi spectacle that completely redefines space exploration. pengalaman nonton alur awalnya yang minim dialog beneran bikin garuk-garuk kepala , keheningan luar angkasa yang dipadu musik klasik terasa hypnotic tapi sekaligus bikin gelisah. visual pesawat sama stasiun luar angkasanya kelihatan ahead of its time buat ukuran film lawas, walau tempo pergerakannya kerasa lambat banget pas bagian awal. the early sequence setting up the ancient monolith creates a deeply mysterious atmosphere. konflik pas komputer kapal mulai bertingkah aneh itu bagian paling mencekam , intrik antara astronot lawan sistem AI yang dingin kerasa unsettling . suasana sepi di dalam kapal malah nambah rasa takut yang pelan-pelan menteror pikiran. the subtle psychological battle against an unfeeling machine keeps the tension at its absolute peak. visual trip pas perjalanan antar dimensi beneran pamer efek visual gila , bentukan cahaya sama warna-warninya kerasa trippy parah sampai bikin pusing sendiri. ga ada penjelasan gamblang soal apa yang sebenarnya terjadi di layar. the surreal visual overload leaves you utterly stunned while trying to process the strange imagery. ending-nya yang penuh simbolisme misterius bikin mikir keras seharian , filosofi soal evolusi manusianya kerasa mind-blowing walau rada abstrak buat dicerna sekaligus. tontonan yang emang butuh kesabaran ekstra tapi ninggalin kesan yang susah hilang. the final scene wraps everything up in a hauntingly ambiguous note that invites endless interpretations. an unmatched masterpiece of sci-fi cinema that offers a truly unforgettable journey.

SPOİLERR Şimdi filmin asıl konusu, uzaylıların kendi dilleri aracılığıyla insanların zaman algısını değiştirip geçmiş, gelecek ve şimdiyi aynı anda algılamamızı sağlaması. Louise onların dilini çözdükçe beyninin zaman algılama şekli değişiyor ve böylece ilk sahnelerde kızının ölümünü gösterdiği yerlerin geçmiş değil, aslında gelecekten kesitler olduğunu anlıyoruz. Sonrasında Louise geleceği, kızının öleceğini ve çok büyük bir acı yaşayacağını bildiği halde geleceği değiştirmiyor. Ian ile yine evleniyor, Hannah doğuyor, hastalanıyor ve ölüyor vesaire. Yani bu hayatı yaşamayı seçiyor. Sonunun kötü olacağını bilse bile bu süreçte yaşayacağı mutluluğu seçiyor ve kaybedeceğini bilerek kızıyla geçirdiği her anın tadını çıkarıyor. Özgür irade ile kader arasındaki bağlamın ortadan kalkması ama Louise’in özgür iradesiyle yine aynı kaderi seçmesi bence filmin verdiği en güzel mesajlardan biri. Çünkü gelecekte ne olacağını bilmek, o hayatı yaşamaya değmez hale getirmiyor. Ama ben filmin bunu yansıtış biçimini ve olay örgüsünü hiç beğenmedim. Bilimkurgu işin içine girince beklenti de ister istemez artıyor ve film sonunda bende biraz fıss çıktı. Özellikle uzaylı temasının kullanılışını çok sevmedim. Bazı yerlerde mantık hataları ve zorlama çözümler olduğunu düşündüm. Çin bakanının fikrinin değişmesi falan da bana aşırı saçma geldi. Yani anlam bakımından gerçekten çok güzel bulduğum bir film ama bunu işleyiş şekli bana göre değildi. Bence verdiği mesaj çok daha farklı ve çok daha etkileyici bir şekilde işlenebilirdi. Bu yüzden filmi anlam bakımından beğensem bile genel olarak çok overrated olduğunu düşünüyorum.

As vezes pra ver um filme estadunidense você tem que ignorar a "estadunidensice" por trás dele, mas dessa vez ficou difícil afetando a experiência. Arrival dirigido por Denis Villenueve é uma obra de ficção científica, que trata da chegada de uma especime alienígena que tenta contatar a humanidade em diferentes regiões do mundo, o filme visualmente falando, é lindo, sua fotografia é selo Denis Villenueve, lindíssima. Queria dar ênfase também no desing dos aliens desse filme que são um dos mais criativos que vi Agora sobre o enredo, pessoalmente imaginei que focaria no estudo de uma língua alienígena, com eles tentado decifrar cada gota da linguagem dos Heptadotes, coisa que foi resolvida em 50 minutos, e talvez essa ideia tenha me decepcionado um pouco ao passar da obra, o problema inicial começa no que disse anteriormente: "diferentes regiões do mundo", logo tem geopolítica, e como é um filme do E.U.A, a China é estereotipada como o mais extremista em relação aos aliens, a Rússia como uma ditadura que mata seus pesquisadores por revelar informações, e cara, isso só dá a impressão de ser pura propaganda(e pasmem, é), com a "américa" sendo a mais racional e calma dos 3(sim, mesmo que eles tenham sido também relativamente agressivos, isso não foi tão demonstrado no filme, tanto que não nomearam nenhum superior estadunidense, só general Shang Shang e Shang). O motivo do general chinês mudar de ideia é idiota, e isso se encaixa no segundo ponto, que é mais pessoal O filme começa uma coisa e termina uma completamente diferente, isso não é ruim na maioria dos casos, mas aqui em específico só me frustrou, sair de um filme de tentativa e erro de comunicação para o plot principal envolvendo uma visão não linear da história não me agradou ou me envolveu, com esse sendo um dos pontos para o general chinês largar sua postura agressiva, parece uma solução extremamente vaga pra um problema que foi mostrado durante o longa inteiro. No fim o filme é bom, só me desagradou

Arrival: Villeneuve's (failed) Space Odyssey Look, I'm not going to come out and say that this is a bad film, because it clearly isn't, but I would hesitate to say that it's a good film as well. Day by day, my feelings that we as a species should have retired the sci-fi drama genre after Solaris (1972) grow. To be perfectly frank, I felt nothing from this film, one that definitely earned the description of, "a mile wide, and an inch deep." It attempts to tackle so many things at once that it eventually lacks any true identity and fails to separate itself from similar pictures of the 2010's. Even starting the film, I was immediately hit with a rushed, melodramatic sequence of our protagonist and her daughter all throughout her life, which ended before I could even form a thought. Why even include it? Does it serve any purpose besides telling me, "You are going to watch a drama. This will be sad. Feel sad for this person." I will give credit where it's due. The cinematography is obviously gorgeous and is by far my favorite aspect of the film. The sound design and score are both ominous and melancholy. However, I don't love the production value as a whole, because the incredibly dull color palette is a bore to look at. The set design of the military base was also quite bland. The alien itself was without a doubt beautifully surreal, and the scenes of Banks/Donelly attempting to communicate with them are easily my favorites in the film. Even the concepts alone are quite fascinating and even well-executed at times, but I can't help but get the feeling that I've seen this film before. There are so many aspects that are completely run-of-the-mill, such as Banks' "tragic backstory," which we learn later in the film is actually after the main events. Yes, I thought the "recalling the future" concept was quite cool, but it ultimately accomplishes nothing but feel emotionally manipulative yet cold at the same time. Seriously though, how many characters are there in the sci-fi genre that are nearly identical to Banks? A lonely, alienated melancholic genius that gets brought in to "solve the mystery," while everyone else distrusts her and treat her with hostility. She really fits right in with the crowd. I just can't stand the execution of so much of this film. The exposition was actually quite intriguing, but I got to the second act of the film and was fighting the urge to fall asleep. Was it trying to bore me on purpose? I enjoyed the third act much more than the second, as that's when the stakes really raise and we get a bit of well-done suspense. It sucks, because that's when I really felt how much potential this film had! The ending montage didn't do it for me though. Every science fiction film nowadays does this to make it seem "emotional," but it ends up just feeling extremely forced. Without a doubt my least favorite from Villeneuve at the moment, but you never know... perhaps a rewatch could boost it all the way to the top, and I realize how it's secretly a masterpiece. But then again, perhaps not. Not a bad film, but not an especially good one either.

Το Arrival είναι ακριβώς το vibe που γουστάρω σε τέτοιες ταινίες, έστω κι αν σε κάποια σημεία νιώθεις ότι πάει λίγο αργά. Το πιο δυνατό του χαρτί είναι ότι βγάζει εντελώς από το κάδρο τις κλασικές χολιγουντιανές φόρμουλες. Δεν έχει ούτε λέιζερ, ούτε εκρήξεις, ούτε τον πλανήτη να σώζεται στο παραπέντε. Είναι μια ταινία που εστιάζει καθαρά στο πώς στο διάολο καταφέρνεις να επικοινωνήσεις με κάτι που δεν έχει καμία λογική σχέση με την ανθρώπινη φύση. Οπτικά και ηχητικά η ατμόσφαιρα σε πλακώνει. Αυτά τα τεράστια, μονόλιθα σκάφη που απλά αιωρούνται σιωπηλά και ο απόκοσμος ήχος στο background χτίζουν μια συνεχή ένταση, χωρίς να γίνεται τίποτα υπερβολικό στην οθόνη. Εκεί που πραγματικά με κέρδισε, όμως, είναι στο πώς χειρίζεται το θέμα του χρόνου. Παίζει με την ιδέα του ότι η γλώσσα που μαθαίνεις αλλάζει τον τρόπο που αντιλαμβάνεσαι την ίδια την πραγματικότητα, και τελικά το χρησιμοποιεί για να σου ρίξει ένα πολύ βαρύ ψυχολογικό χτύπημα. Αντί για κάποιο φθηνό plot twist με εξωγήινους, η ταινία καταλήγει να σε βάζει να σκεφτείς κάτι πολύ πιο ανθρώπινο: αν θα επέλεγες να ζήσεις μια ιστορία από την αρχή, ξέροντας ακριβώς πώς και πόσο άσχημα πρόκειται να τελειώσει. Ναι, ο ρυθμός του είναι αρκετά αργός και θέλει λίγη υπομονή, αλλά ο τρόπος που κουμπώνουν όλα τα κομμάτια στο φινάλε σε αποζημιώνει στο εκατό τοις εκατό.

Louise: What is your purpose on Earth? Abbot: Offer Weapon Everyone's reaction to that is such a good example of people's interpretation of things can lead to problems that aren't even there. My first thought was, they're offering humanity a weapon to protect themselves. But somehow they thought it meant, a weapon to use against each other. How would anyone even get to that conclusion? What the weapon or gift turned out to be, is the last thing I was expecting. I'm still not fully sure I understand. Obviously Louise was brought in to translate the aliens language, so she had the most time to study them and their gift. But wouldn't others around the world also be studying it? So she shouldn't be the only person who gets to "use" the gift. Like the other films I've seen from Dennis Villeneuve, there's not much excitement to Arrival. But I'm glad I finally found a movie of his I like. Because the whole thing is definitely interesting. I'm curious from the start what is happening, and once it was over I still had a lot to think about. As soon as Louise mentioned how Kangaroos got their name, I paused the movie to find out if that was true. Turns out it's considered a myth, which if I'd waited at least another 30 seconds I would have found out. But it sounded believable, and apparently hasn't completely been disproved.

The main idea had potential, don’t get me wrong, but I feel like the execution undermined the story a lot. There's a lot of interesting presentation here, but in my opinion not really that many interesting ideas. Like Interstellar, this film seems to me to hide its lack of focus with a fog of pathos. If Villeneuve's idea was for the viewer to make their own interpretation of everything but the most basic truths about the film, sure, he achieved that. But I could have done that equally well without seeing the film. I dunno, I just don't think the idea of non-linear time is all that fascinating. Dune delves a lot into this to, predestination, genetic memory, time literally going in cycles etc etc. To me, it's either depressing or absolving of responsibility. All the actual science is just for show, the linguistics is just a framework. My most charitable interpretaion of the real message seems to be simply "dont let the past form your future, always look to new possibilities for happiness". And I mean, that's not a bad message. Just like this isn't a bad film. Just a bit shallow perhaps. Also, why is everything so grey and overcast?

Ekranda aynı görüntüler duruyor ama hepsinin üzerindeki anlam tamamen kırılmış durumda… Hikaye gökyüzünde öylece duran devasa gemilerle, ne olduğu belirsiz bir gelişle başlıyor. Ne saldıran var ne de ne yapacağını anlatan, sadece oradalar. Filmin bütün havasını kuran şey de bu sessizlik. Uzaylıların gelişi bir aksiyon malzemesine dönüştürülmemiş yani dünyaya inen şey bir savaş değil, doğrudan bilinmezliğin kendisi.İnsanlığın buna verdiği tepki ise fazlasıyla..tanıdık. Önce isim koyulur, sonra kategorilere ayrılır,en sonunda ise bir tehdit olup olmadığını çözmeye çalışırız.Anlamadığımız bir şeyin karşısında öylece durmak bize yetmez; mutlaka onu tanımlamamız, sınırlarını çizmemiz gerek çünkü ne olduğunu bilmediğimiz her şey, korkunun en sevdiği malzemeye dönüşür.. Louise in hikayedeki varlığı bu yüzden çok değerli. Kendisi bir asker değil, elinde silahı olan ya da dünyayı kurtarma iddiasındaki bir süper kahraman hiç değil. Onun elindeki tek şey kelimeler. Film bize, insanlığın kaderini bazen bir silahın değil, doğru zamanda sorulmuş doğru bir sorunun değiştirebileceğini gösteriyor. Amy Adams ın Louise i oynama biçimini özellikle çok realistik buldum. Öncelikle yaşadığı duyguları seyircinin gözüne sokmaya çalışmıyor.Yüzünde sürekli tartıp biçen, konuşmadan önce düşünen bir hal var. Sessiz kaldığı anlar boşluk hissettirmiyor, aksine rahatlıkla zihninin içine girmemizi sağlıyor. Jeremy Renner ın Ian karakteri ise bu ağırlığın yanında daha rahat nefes alabildiğimiz bir alan açıyor ve aralarındaki bağ da filmin genel kasveti altında kaybolup gitmiyor. Böylelikle bu uyumu biri kelimelerin anlamına, diğeri sayıların düzenine bakan iki insanın birbirini tamamlama çabasıyla izliyoruz.Ama Louise in asıl sınavı heptapodlarla başlıyor.İlk temas sahnelerinde camın iki tarafındaki iki türü izlerken aralarında sadece birkaç metre var gibi duruyor. Oysa aradaki mesafe bundan çok daha büyük. Onların dünyayı nasıl gördüğünü, hatta dil dedikleri şeyin bizim bildiğimiz dille aynı şey olup olmadığını bile bilmiyoruz. Louise in yaptığı şey karşı tarafa kendi kurallarımızı öğretmek değil de onların dünyayı nasıl okuduğunu anlamaya çalışmak.Filmin güzel yerlerinden birisi de tam olarak burası: Bir dili gerçekten öğrenmek, sadece kelime ezberlemek değildir. Dünyayı, başka bir düşüncenin cümleleri içinden görmeye başlamaktır.Heptapodların dili çözüldükçe Louise in zamanı algılama şekli de değişiyor ve film o ana kadar bize gösterdiği her şeyi baştan diziyor. Başta Hannah yı Louise in geçmişinde kalmış bir anı sanarken onun henüz yaşanmamış bir geleceğin parçası olduğunu anladığımızda sadece hikayenin sırası karışmıyor aynı zamanda da Louise in verdiği kararın ağırlığı da bambaşka bir yere oturuyor.Çünkü Louise ne yaşayacağını biliyor.Gelecekteki acıyı, kaybı, yaşayacağı o büyük ayrılığı görüyor.Ve yine de o hayatı seçiyor. Beni asıl etkileyen şey geleceği görebilmesi değildi. Gelecekte ne olacağını bildiği halde oradan kaçmamasıydı.Biz çoğu zaman seçimlerimizi bilmediğimiz için yapabiliyoruz. Birini severken bizi ne zaman bırakacağını bilmiyoruz. Bir yola çıkarken sonunda neyle karşılaşacağımızı bilmiyoruz. Bilseydik, belki de o kapıların çoğundan içeri hiç adım atmazdık. Louise in hikayesi ise bize başka bir ihtimali gösteriyor: Bir şeyin nasıl biteceğini bilmek, yaşandığı anın değerini yok etmez..Bir gün biteceğini bildiğin bir şarkıyı yine de keyifle dinlersin..Son sayfasına geleceğini bilerek bir kitaba başlarsın..Hayatında kalıcı olmayacağını bilsen bile bir insanı fazlasıyla sevebilirsin. Denis Villeneuve zamanı geçmişten geleceğe giden düz bir çizgi olmaktan çıkardığında, yaşadığımız anların anlamı da değişiyor. Louise için çocukluğu, anneliği, kaybı ve sevgisi birbirini takip eden kompartımanlar değil, hepsi aynı anda var olan tek bir bütünün parçası.Bu fikir bir yandan da çok sarsıcı..yani gerçekten sonunu bilseydin, o hayatı yine de yaşar mıydın? Louise in cevabı oldukça netti zaten:) çünkü bazı şeylerin sonunun gelecek olması, onları hiç yaşamamış olmaktan çok daha kabul edilebilir. Acıyı yok etme imkanı varken onu da hayatın bir parçası olarak kabullenmek, bana kalırsa korkakça değil, inanılmaz derecede cesurca bir duruş. Filmin arka planındaki politik taraf da bu felsefeden bağımsız değil. Farklı ülkeler aynı olayla karşılaşıyor ama ortak bir dil kurmak yerine birbirlerinden şüpheleniyorlar. Bir kelimenin yanlış anlaşılması, güvensizlik, korkunun büyümesi… Filmdeki en büyük tehlike hiçbir zaman uzaylıların ne yapacağı değildi. insanların anlamadıkları bir şeyi kendi korkularıyla tamamlamalarıydı. Villeneuve bütün bunları anlatırken filmin atmosferini de aynı sadelikte tutmuş. Gri gökyüzü, sis, o geniş ve soğuk manzaralar…JJ in müzikleri de görüntüye sonradan eklenmiş gibi değil, sanki filmin kendi sesi gibi arkadan akıp gidiyor.(en sevdiğim<3) Arrival ı bu kadar sevmemin nedeni de bu olabilir..büyük bir uzaylı istilası gibi başlayıp insanın zamanla, kayıpla ve seçimleriyle kurduğu ilişkiye kadar inmesi..Sonunda elimizde uzaylılardan çok daha soyut bir şey kalıyor..kendi hayatımız.Bence bir şeyin nasıl biteceğini bilmek, başlangıcını anlamsız kılmaz. Bazen sonunu bile bile yürürüz o yolda..Bazı hikayeler sonları yüzünden daha az değil, tam tersine sırf o son yüzünden çok daha değerlidir.

One of the most human sci-fi’s i’ve ever seen. my fascination with linguistics actually made this movie so much more of an interesting watch. I learned about the sapir-whorf hypothesis which essentially is the idea that language can fundamentally alter the structure of thought and even your perception of reality. the movie then takes this incredibly intellectual concept and turns it into something so human. Louise knows the beginning, the middle and the end simultaneously. she knows she will have a daughter she loves beyond comprehension, she knows she will lose her, she knows her marriage will fall apart partly because of the choice she makes but she still chooses that life. Her choice wasn’t solely because “love is worth the pain.” But does something ending tragically make the happiness that precedes it any less real? if you knew exactly when and how you would lose someone, would loving them become meaningless? or would knowing how temporary it is make every moment with them infinitely more precious? The ultimate choice was choosing to live the entire experience, regardless of its ending. there’s something so beautiful yet terrifying about accepting your life as a whole rather than judging it solely by where it leads. Can’t stop thinking about this movie. Would I  willingly walk into the greatest grief of my life just to experience the love that comes before it? Thank you for the existential crisis villeneuve incredible.

Human Kind of Sci-Fi. Arrival moves through these calm currents of emotion throughout. There’s anxiety, sadness, curiosity and this constant sense of unease, yet somehow it remains incredibly peaceful at the same time. It’s strange to feel so emotionally engaged while also feeling completely at ease. Amy Adams gives such a quiet performance, but underneath that stillness are these huge waves of emotion. Like watching an ocean that looks completely calm from the surface, while everything underneath is constantly moving. She was perfect for this role. The score adds so much to that feeling, giving the film this almost meditative quality that carries from beginning to end. I genuinely felt at peace watching this. Everything about Arrival comes together so naturally. The direction, Amy Adams’ performance, the score, the writing. Nothing feels out of place, and everything adds to the same feeling. This might even be a perfect movie.

If someone asked me the question Louise puts to Ian, my answer would be different. Choosing it on behalf of others is a different moral question.

Eu adoro filmes que conseguem pegar uma ideia de ficção científica e, em vez de usá-la apenas como espetáculo, transformar essa ideia em uma discussão sobre algo profundamente humano. A Chegada faz exatamente isso. É um filme sobre alienígenas, linguagem, comunicação e uma possível ameaça à humanidade, mas, no fundo, é muito mais sobre tempo, escolhas e a maneira como lidamos com aquilo que sabemos que vai acontecer. A linguagem é o verdadeiro coração do filme. Conforme Louise aprende a se comunicar com os heptápodes , percebemos que não estamos simplesmente acompanhando alguém traduzindo palavras. Ela está tentando compreender uma forma completamente diferente de enxergar o mundo. A ideia de que a língua que falamos pode influenciar a maneira como percebemos a realidade é fascinante, e o filme leva isso até uma consequência muito maior: e se aprender uma nova linguagem significasse aprender uma nova maneira de experimentar o próprio tempo? É aí que A Chegada deixa de ser apenas um filme de primeiro contato e se transforma em algo muito mais emocional. A maneira como o filme apresenta as lembranças de Louise é genial porque, durante boa parte da história, acreditamos estar vendo o passado dela. Aos poucos, percebemos que aquelas imagens não são exatamente memórias. E quando a verdade finalmente se revela, várias cenas anteriores mudam completamente de significado. O mais doloroso é perceber que Louise passa a conhecer o futuro e, mesmo sabendo que determinadas coisas vão acontecer, decide vivê-las. Ela sabe que haverá amor, felicidade, mas também sabe que haverá uma dor enorme. E mesmo assim escolhe seguir em frente. Isso transforma a pergunta do filme. Não é mais “se você pudesse conhecer o futuro, tentaria mudá-lo?” , mas “se você soubesse que algo maravilhoso terminaria em sofrimento, ainda escolheria vivê-lo?” E acho essa uma das ideias mais bonitas e tristes que um filme poderia explorar. Louise não escolhe porque não entende o que vai acontecer. Ela escolhe justamente porque entende. O sofrimento não apaga o valor de tudo aquilo que veio antes. Também gosto muito de como o filme utiliza a própria estrutura narrativa para fazer o espectador experimentar, de certa forma, aquilo que Louise está experimentando. O tempo deixa de ser uma linha simples de começo, meio e fim. Informações que pareciam pertencer ao passado ganham outro significado quando descobrimos que pertencem ao futuro. É um daqueles filmes em que a segunda metade não apenas explica a primeira: ela transforma a primeira. E visualmente A Chegada acompanha perfeitamente essa proposta. Os ambientes são enormes, silenciosos e quase contemplativos. A presença dos alienígenas causa estranheza sem precisar transformar tudo em espetáculo. A trilha de J óhann Jóhannsson também contribui muito para essa atmosfera de mistério e melancolia. No fim, A Chegada me pega porque utiliza a ficção científica para fazer uma pergunta extremamente humana: se pudéssemos conhecer toda a nossa história antes de vivê-la, escolheríamos vivê-la mesmo assim? E a resposta de Louise é ao mesmo tempo devastadora e bonita.

Anytime I ever had the thought of doing a Pixar deep-dive, which I've been thinking about doing for a while now, the thought usually came to a halt once I remember this franchise's existence. I had the misfortune of being dragged along to see this when it was in theaters and I was in high school, and it just feeling like one of the most devastating viewing experiences of my life up to that point. Not just because it's a terrible, painfully unfunny movie with an insane premise that makes less sense the more you think about it, but because I was seeing Pixar, a film studio I respected, fully become Disney-fied, making corporate slop designed to boost merchandise profits and basically nothing else. I guess the Pixar "golden era" technically ended with Toy Story 3, but at the very least, their golden streak ended here. The main reason this was their first bust was because it has no real idea to it. "What if the world were cars" is not an idea that resonates the way their other premises did up to this point. And I really try not to be CinemaSins and just poke holes in weird premises and plots. I'm more than happy to take a fantasy at face value if it's appealing enough, or has an internal logic to it. But I cannot get behind this world at all. If this were just a zany, cartoony comedy, the dumb premise might be totally fine, discounting the fact that the jokes in this movie are painfully bad. But it's not, and quietly the worst part about this is the air of Pixar prestige it has that's in all their movies, because it dares insinuate that the "what if cars were people" movie is worthy of standing on the same pedestal. Pathetic. Well, I hear Cars 2 is supposed to be deranged, so I have that to look forward to, I guess. Can't believe this is Paul Newman's final movie, I think I need to buy a couple jars of his salsa to make this up to him.

Carros é, com folga, o trabalho mais preguiçoso, conceitualmente bizarro e cheio de fórmulas batidas de toda a história da Pixar. Em vez de entregar a genialidade emocional ou a ousadia dos grandes trabalhos do estúdio, a animação parece uma propaganda gigante para vender brinquedo de plástico, embrulhada em uma Jornada do Herói tão burocrática, previsível e sem graça que beira o insuportável. O grande erro da narrativa está na tentativa de aplicar a clássica jornada do Joseph Campbell a um protagonista raso e mimado como o Relâmpago McQueen. Ele começa como o típico babaca egocêntrico e arrogante que precisa passar por provações para se transformar, mas o roteiro conduz essa redenção de forma tão robótica que nada ali convence. Ao se perder a caminho da Califórnia e destruir a rua da esquecida Radiator Springs, McQueen é forçado a ficar preso no interior, onde encontra o batido arquétipo do mestre recluso no Doc Hudson e o alívio cômico caipira na figura do Mate — que mais irrita do que diverte. A dita "transformação espiritual" dele ao descobrir o valor da vida simples não parece fruto de uma tomada de consciência orgânica, mas sim de uma imposição das circunstâncias, fazendo com que a lição de moral no clímax da corrida final soar puramente piegas, forçando a barra para transformar um esportivo vaidoso em santo de uma hora para outra. Além dessa estrutura dramática capenga, a própria lógica do universo é um buraco negro de absurdos. É impossível se importar de verdade com um mundo feito puramente de lataria, onde a existência de portas, janelas e calçadas não faz o menor sentido pela ausência total de seres humanos. Para piorar, a direção se perde em um segundo ato extremamente arrastado, parando a história para mostrar piadas infantis de carros assustando tratores e romances sem química nenhuma entre dois automóveis. Carros pegou a estrutura mais nobre da narrativa universal e a reduziu a uma história rasa de cidade grande encontra o interior, trocando a profundidade poética da Pixar por um amontoado de clichês comerciais.

(Movie description in bold at the bottom) By the time The Incredibles (2004) came out, I was beginning to get too old for Pixar movies. I was a teenager and wanting to start enjoying more older fare. With this being said, I stopped watching a lot of Pixar films after Incredibles . Cars was the first one I didn't see, and now, on the 20 year anniversary of the films release, I feel like I really didn't miss much. Cars feels like Pixar's first real cynical movie; making a movie that feels like it was done as a vehicle (pun unintended) to sell toys first and a good movie second. This is odd considering this is the company that made the Toy Story franchise. Between world mechanics that get too confusing, and a story that just isn't interesting, Cars feels like the first real wiff in Pixar's history of great quality films. While the car mechanics can get confusing, there are aspects of the world design that are kind of nice. Examples include Sally Carrera's (Bonnie Hunt) hotel which are shaped like traffic cones (you just have to forget that this is influenced by Native American teepees) and a doctor's office being just a car mechanic shop. There are also some really nice landscapes of the American desert, which look really good. Cars are meant to take us from point A to point B. Cars asks if this go go lifestyle is really that good. It pines for the old days when experiencing life was part of living. This is done through Route 66, which traveled in a maundering way that worked with the land, instead of through it. When the interstate was built, it bypassed Radiator Springs, and car travel became simply about the destination. Cars is bringing up points that were explored in media like Fahrenheit 411 , where people travel so fast they can't see the world around them. The message of the film does work overall, and is a saving grace for the movie. The problem with the movie is the world of the Cars. As I watched the film, I got more frustrated as to what is considered a car thing and what is a take on human things. Why does Lightning McQueen (voiced by Owen Wilson) have a human-like tongue? What is Mack (voiced by John Ratzenberger) being bullied by a bunch of punk cars a parallel to in human form? Do all these cars have the life expectancy of people? By the time the movie got to the halfway point, I settled into just going with the fact that sometimes the cars are just car stuff, and the human stuff is just human stuff that the movie is doing. However, the fact that my mind was consumed with these questions as I was watching the movie is a bad sign for the movie. The cast is overall good in this movie, and it was nice to hear Paul Newman, in his last appearance in a non-documentary, but this movie does one thing that is unforgivable. It establishes a forever legacy for Larry the Cable Guy. Larry as Tow Mater is by far one of the most annoying characters ever put to screen. His southern twang and just overall annoyance was something I just never got used to. Cars 2 has the reputation of being the worst Pixar film, or at least the first truly bad Pixar film, and since it features Tow in a bigger role, I can see why. A little of Larry goes a long way, but for me I wish Larry would go far away and never come back. This movie is just boring. I really didn't care about Lightning, or any of the characters. They are all so boring and add so little. This was a movie solely meant to sell toys. I guess it worked, since this was the first non Toy Story movie to get a sequel, but for Pixar I think we all expect better than a concept that seems more fit for a Saturday morning cartoon show than a feature length film. Then again, Transformers (2007) would come out the very next year and be one of the most profitable films of that year, so what do I know? In a world populated by anthropomorphic race cars, Lightning McQueen (voiced by Owen Wilson) is one of the best race cars in the world. After finishing in a three way tie with Chick Hicks (voiced by Michael Keaton) and Strip "The King" Weathers (voiced by Richard Petty), the three cars must go to California to race in a tiebreaker. On the way west, Lightening gets lost and finds himself in the decrepit town of Radiator Springs. After damaging the towns main road, Lightening must begrudgingly repair the road as he complains and gets more annoyed with this failing town. I have this recurring dream. It’s the dead of night. I’m walking down a street on the way from the station towards my old house. There’s a field to one side of me and the road to the other. The only light I see is the flickering orange light of the dim street lamps. The only sound is my feet touching the worm and dashed concrete. Suddenly I hear the distant noise of tires on tarmac. I am not nervous, not really, but I can hear that it’s going to drive passed me. I can hear it coming closer until I know it’s on the same street as me. I turn as the car passes me and I glance at it. It is a car and it isn’t. It’s a live car. There’s no driver and the car has a face. The face stares back at me. I hope to never see that face outside of a dream. The thing slows down and smirks at me. It is matching my pace as I try to turn away from it. The last thing I feel is its tire feet mount the curb and the last thing I hear is the car whispering something that sounded like the noise of lightning. Then I wake up.

|EN| Cars John Lasseter , 2006 Cars is one of those movies that does exactly what it sets out to do, without ever managing to leave a particularly deep impression. Lightning McQueen's story is simple and fairly classic: an arrogant protagonist completely focused on success is forced to stop and experience a world completely different from his own, eventually learning to value the people and things he used to overlook. His redemption arc is predictable, but it works. Whenever the film wants to be emotional, it actually manages to get there, especially through the relationship Lightning builds with the people of Radiator Springs. It does not try to complicate its story, and that is probably one of its strengths. The screenplay is simple, straightforward, and well written, with plenty of humor and a pace that keeps the film enjoyable. The world of Cars is also a lot of fun to spend time in. Turning a universe entirely inhabited by cars into a kind of American road movie is a simple idea, but Pixar manages to build a coherent world around it, filled with memorable and likable characters. Still, the film never left me particularly impressed. Its themes are the familiar ones of growing up, humility, friendship, and rediscovering what really matters, but they are not explored in a way that feels especially original to me. It is a good animated film, entertaining, emotional when it wants to be, and perfectly suited to the audience it was made for. But, for me, that is pretty much where it ends. Nothing wrong with it, nothing extraordinary either: a solid film, but nothing more. |IT| Cars John Lasseter , 2006 Cars è uno di quei film che fanno esattamente quello che promettono, senza però riuscire a lasciare qualcosa di particolarmente profondo. Not sure why this was such a childhood staple for me, it’s good but not great. This universe does contain many unanswered questions which are more fun to ponder than actually watching the movie itself. The first racing sequence is honestly pure body horror where like 15 people die in a pile up and then lightning mcqueen breaks both of his legs and tries to drag himself across the finish line. Then he visits a tent full of rusty cars which he treats like lepers and I don’t understand what the filmmakers intention was. are we supposed to agree that rust is gross? Are these sickly, dying people? Or are they simply unwashed? My friend who is a WGA winning writer has a theory that the cars universe represents an AI/advanced alien takeover of the planet, which is then trying to re-create humanity and the human experience but with cars. I must say that I fully agree with him, and when the film is watched through this lens it becomes thoroughly horrifying and a thousand times more interesting. Like for instance, at one point a husband and wife are going on a road trip and they accidentally wind up in radiator springs, but because both of them are car people they’re taking this road trip together as two cars rather than a husband and wife together in one car. it is nonsensical and ridiculous and something that only an extremely advanced (but far removed from humanity) alien AI race in the far future could think makes any sense. Another horrifying aspect of this movie is the caste system that is inherent to the universe and which each individual is born into. If you were born as a tire changing little car thing, that is your destiny. Same as if you’re a race car, a tow truck, or a semi truck. Your career is predetermined, and there is never hope for self actualization in this society. Sally appears to belong to an elite caste, and because she’s a porsche she gets to be a lawyer, but it’s unclear if that’s directly related or if maybe luxury cars have the privilege of going to college and choosing their careers. Race cars are the gladiator caste and must subject themselves to complete disfigurement and unimaginable pain on a regular basis. Tractors are for some reason not people but instead livestock, though it’s never explained why farming is taking place. For whom is wheat being grown?? This is a good example of the AI theory. Also flies are also cars but they don’t appear to be sentient. What does it all mean???

Yes I do have quite a soft spot for this movie, I've seen it undoubtedly more times than any other movie over my entire life, and even still that doesn't make this a perfect or even great film for that matter. It carries echoes of John Lasseter's actual masterpiece, Toy Story 2 , yet stumbles through some weaker jokes and cheeky references, most of which I still have an affection for, but contrasted against 3 all-timer voice performances, this movie walks a tight line between generation-defining spectacle and reminders that this is still at its core an animated kid's movie from the 2000's. Hearing Paul Newman is the most obvious standout, bringing his classic charm to kids like me for the first time to drive home a simple yet timeless moral. Owen Wilson is a perfect other half to the main mentor/student dynamic, yet I can't shake the underlying discontent his character spends the first two acts reckoning with, especially with the context of his suicide attempt the following year. His career history of comedic roles aren't a crutch for this role, and instead the occasional vulnerability he shows makes this a surprisingly interesting undertaking for an otherwise straightforward narrative. Michael Keaton still consistently amazes me as the unforgettable asshole Chick Hicks, a role that proved to me how even Keaton's most random or commercial work has a special place in my heart existing long before I ever saw Birdman . As I get older I'll inevitably continue to love the dialogue of nostalgia and accepting change this movie presents even though the words themselves will never change, sometimes thats just what I want from cinema and this movie provides a window into my childhood like no other. Also why did Sally poop on McQueen when they were going for a drive that is just so strange.

El desempate se decide en una semana, McQueen quiere llegar primero pero se pierde en un pueblito, donde hace un desastre y para que le permitan irse tiene que arreglar la carretera. Durante ese tiempo ahí se hace mejor amigo de Mate, amigo del resto y se enamora de la Porsche (yo también, obvio, es una Porsche AZÚL). Doc, como el representante del pueblo, es un antiguo campeón de la copa pistón, quien le dice a McQueen que solo es una copa vacía. Termina la carretera, pero se encariñó con todos así que duda en irse, cuando lo encuentran y vienen por él y va a la copa Pistón. En la carrera, está desconcentrado, viviendo en los recuerdos, cuando escucha la voz de Doc y se da cuenta que todos sus amigos están ahí, se concentra y cuando tiene la delantera, el segundón hace una jugada sucia y hace que el rey tenga un accidente, McQueen para frente a la meta y deja que el otro gane la carrera porque entiende que no solo se trata de ganar, ya no piensa en sí mismo y entiende que es la última carrera del rey, así que le ayuda a terminarla. McQueen rechaza el trato que siempre había querido y se quedó con quienes lo apoyaron desde un principio, vuelve al pueblo y hace sus oficinas allí.

yo no entiendo, entonces al final quién mata al padre? Mira me vi la película ayer, y lo que veis arriba fue mi reseña pero, es que sinceramente, está es mi cuenta de Lettterboxd y pongo las reseñas que yo quiera y voy a ser completamente transparente con lo que opino sobre esta supuesta obra maestra, ya que no comprendo, porque "tengo que poner una buena reseña", cuando nadie le importan realmente. Primero, partiendo de la base que viendo solo la sinopsis ya me pude imaginar de que iba a ir la película, y lo que lleva de trasfondo (la crítica social), por lo que dice la gente de ella (que es una obra maestra), y sobre todo por el contexto. Primero decir, que entendiendo su contexto me parece que se siga considerando una obra maestra me parece una barbaridad, su guión sinceramente me dio la sensación de ser bastante simple y predecible, no sé si es que he visto películas con grandes plot twist o que, pero es que no me sorprendió lo masss mínimo. A ver, estuve pensando durante toda la película, por lo menos espero que al final, digan quién mato al padre realmente y sea un giro de guión, pero no sé porque me esperaba eso. Ya se que el punto de la película no es desmantelar al asesino, si no la crítica al sistema judicial estadounidense, pero honestamente gente, cuando yo vi que 12 hombres ajenos a todo eso, iba a decidir sobre un joven si iba o no a la silla eléctrica, me pareció cuánto menos una barbaridad, y no me parece nada transgresor lo q los personajes discuten. Me esperaba unas reflexiones más interesantes, profundas sobre la vida y etc. Pero es que es tan superficial. Los "marcos de personaje" son cuanto más aburridos, osea pienso en Wes Anderson y como el lo hace tan bien con los suyos, que al ver una película suya, como the Royal tannebauns, cada uno evoluciona y se nota la función que cumplen y etc. Esto me parece patético, es que es tan obvio lo que cada uno va a responder. Es entonces cuando aquí entra lo que más me interesa, me sentí literalmente en un mansplaining continuo de un tío "noble" que usa el sentido común, que cualquier mujer hubiese pensado desde un inicio, los típicos pensamientos lógicos que una niña de 14 años lleva pensando toda su vida y un hombre de 40 acaba de llegar a esa misma conclusión, y se cree que ha soltado una verdad aristotélica y que está sentando cátedra, pero es literalmente algo tan obvio, que resulta absurdo lo grandiosos que se sienten. Se le pone la etiqueta de el salvador, el único que piensa que el niño es inocente, hace que todos cambien de opinión, honestamente es lógica pura y dura, y repito en su contexto vale, pero que hoy en día se siga aclamando como una de las mejores películas de la historia? Solo pensad que hubiese sido de esta película si hubiesen sido 12 mujeres (q si, que por el contexto a ella no sé les tenía en cuenta, blah blah blah) pero solo imaginénlo, saben que ?? QUE DIRECTAMENTE NO EXISTIRÍA PELÍCULA, porque a la conclusión que llegan de q el niño viene de un barrio marginal y no sé que, es lo que cualquier mujer hubiese pensado desde el primero momento, saben ustedes porque??, porque las mujeres hemos sufrido esa represión toda nuestra vida y llegar a esa conclusión es nuestro día a día, pero claro que un tipo blanco con dinero se lo llegué a plantear: menudo salvador, un aplauso por favor, ha usado su cerebro. Dicho esto, no me gusta ser así, pero a veces me sacan de mis casillas porque a quien cojones le importa lo que 12 hombres blancos con dinero tengan que decir?? NADA

É um bom filme. mas sinceramente achei um pouco superestimado.a ideia é excelente e é impressionante como conseguem sustentar praticamente o filme inteiro em uma única sala, dependendo quase que unicamente dos diálogos e das discussões entre os personagens. A tensão funciona e a forma como os argumentos são construídos é satisfatória. Mas talvez eu tenha assistido com expectativas que não foram atendidas. Dado a reputação que o filme carrega, frequentemente aparecendo em rankings de melhores filmes de todos os tempos, eu esperava uma experiência mais marcante e impactante talvez. Reconheço completamente sua relevância para a história do cinema em si pois acredito que o contexto histórico e o fato do filme inteiro se passar dentro de uma única locação e sendo sustentado por 12 homens conversando era uma demonstração impressionante de inovação na escrita e direção. Ainda assim, é fácil entender por que virou um clássico. Só não entrou pra mim nesse nível de “obra-prima intocável” que tanta gente coloca.

Makes sense why this is regarded as one of the best films of all time, so good! Pacing is so good and you jump into the plot right away. For better and worse this movie created a whole legal drama genre that has real life impacts on the justice system. This movie was made 30 years before DNA and I think it’s a stronger movie for the reason that there is no DNA to think about. Juries actually over rely on the presence of DNA (and other iffy Law and Order type science like bullet casing marks) when deliberating a verdict. Get into the nitty gritty! Think about how could one witness hear a scream if the other witness said the train was passing at the exact same moment. This movie is a liberal fantasy that relies on one person insisting on considering the opposing view point, in this case a verdict of not guilty. But, I actually that’s a strength of this movie rather than a weakness. We have to suspend disbelief all the time for a films to be impactful, so why not choose to believe that despite known social and peer pressure someone can voice their disagreement. Devils advocate is usually a negative instigator but it’s fun to watch someone play out that line of argument in a way that is actually worth considering. The justice system is racist. The people making arrests, prosecuting, and deciding criminal cases are racist. The backbone of “justice” should not depend on one good man doing the right thing. Nothing is ever truly objective, which is especially true of the law despite all the language that hopes to make you think it is. I think I’m probably the prime audience for this movie and loved it! Put me on a jury!! I’d be so ethical!!

I genuinely believe this to be a pillar of not only filmmaking but story telling. The script, is perfect as well as the screenplay. The film tskes place in one room for the majority of its duration, so how do you keep it interesting? You craft the perfect script. Perhaps the most important aspect to really carry the script is the acting. The acting must be independent, each character must be written as though they are the first to be so. 12 Angry Men is built around identity. Each man comes from a unique walk of like with unique experiences and unique opinions. The point of 12 Angry Men is the men coming together. The crux of the story is development, every character changes in some way. The men, despite their unique outlooks, upbringings, and actions must come to a civic and unanimous decision to determine the life of a young man. In order to convey said developments there must be a identity to each character thst is their own entire, and they must be played perfectly for those characterizations. Juror 1, the "leader". He directs the room, but he does not lead it. He is no dictator or supreme leader of thr room, but he has the clipboard, he must declare a vote, he must deliver the decisions. He is not the toughest man in the room, he, more or less, just guides the men. He has his own opinion and he states it clearly. But juror 1 is not stern nor is he Stark. Juror 2, the newbie. Juror 2 has never been on a jury. He doesn't exactly know the directions of debate, but he knows the inner workings of the court. He knows how the court plays and he knows the evidence rather well. He doesn't know how to use his voice clearly over the elders at first, usually being pushed around and silenced. His opinion isn't the clearest either. He says the boy is guilty "just because he is" he's nearly unsure of his own stance, meek in his closed answer. But over time he starts to find his voice. He establishes his knowledge and his eventual confidence. He's inexperienced, coy, and easily pushed around. But he eventually finds himself to reslly prove and get his opinion out. Juror 3, the antithesis. Juror 3 is even labeled by 8 a sadist, which isnt false at all, but his character is deeper than that. He's experienced, older while still having mobility, confidence, and a voice to shout with. He has his definite opinion upon the evidence and he stands by it. He has a solid opinion, he has a genuine belief and he sticks right by it. At his core, he blames the child more than anything. Being a stern father of a son he hasn't seen in two years, he blames the defendant. He knows of his living condition yet he blames the society, he blames the child himself for the possibility of the murder. His pent up rage of his own life pours out in the room, in his opinion. He knows his interpretation of the facts and he knows his opinions, but he is not understanding. He sees his words as the definite truth, he screams and antagonizes and he belittles. He does not work in the view of justice, he works in the view of punishment and of competition, of winning some kind of game of being the 'right one'. Above all else, the man is shadowed by his own life, especially his life with his son, who he in a way blames for their divide. On the same side of the coin, his ultimate anger at the end after he is now the lone juror unleashes and is what ultimately makes him see the error of his ways. He bursts out in an angry monologue. How could anyone, let alone everyone, oppose his definite fact. He takes the photo of his son from his wallet and after seeing what has been the anchor of his rage, rips it to pieces. As soon as he does, he realizes this error, maybe he really is the problem, maybe the boy isn't to blame, maybe it isn't a fact, but it is possible. Juror 4, the statue. Similarly to juror 3, he nearly sees his opinion as fact, but where they differ is approach. Juror 4 knows the evidence well, he knows well upon his own interpretation and opinion, but he is calculated, he is thoughtful in the court system. He does not see this as a game or a competition. He hopes to find whatever Justice he truthfully believes, he is opinionated but he is tolerant in a way. He nearly never sweats and he nearly never moves. As all the men do, he gets angrier as the heat increases and as the temperature rises, but he is clear and concise in his approach. He wants an end, but a right one. He knows his truth but, perhaps begrudgingly, he listens to the other side of the story, and through hearing that he coukd possibly be wrong, he sees the error and realizes that he could possibly be wrong. Juror 5, the experienced. Juror 5 grew up in the same conditions as the defendant. He knows the conditions of the slums, what it can do to a person and how they can operate. Because of his experience, he is particularly sensitive to the prejudices of the other men. He has his beginning opinion but he is nearly embarrassed and certainly unsure of it from the beginning, choosing to pass when asked why he initially votes guilty. He sees the prejudice of the room and he applies his own personal experience with the defendants upbringing and sees that there may be a chance that the boy did not do it. Juror 6, the working man

Por vezes, alguns dos considerados "cânones" do cinema são ainda mais fascinantes do que sua fama tende a sugerir. Assisti 12 Angry Men (1957) com uma noção abstrata prévia, mas realmente não estava esperando que o filme fosse ser tão intrigante e instigante. Não atoa é um filme tão aclamado, é uma obra tão meticulosa em cada um de seus aspectos — sobretudo sua blocagem e encenação — que chega a ser gratificante um filme que se preocupa tanto em trabalhar o cinema numa premissa tão teatral. Ele exemplifica bem, inclusive, a relação que estas duas artes tem. Desde a criação do cinematógrafo, o cinema extraiu muito de sua base no teatro como também em outras artes. Conceitos como mise-en-scène, por exemplo, são emprestados. Mas justamente dessa raiz que a sétima arte se ramificou. No teatro, o olhar vem de amplas perspectivas. Organizar atores, cenários e objetos é um trabalho cuidadoso que oferece um guia em comum a cada pessoa em cada acento. No cinema, essa organização é voltada a um único olhar: o olhar da câmera. Ela permite um close-up em qualquer detalhe que tanto a pessoa da primeira fileira como a última irão observar com perfeita nitidez. Mas também, quando o diretor confia no uso da profundidade de campo em seu filme, ele ganha uma liberdade e oferece um direito ao espectador para olhar o que lhe chama mais atenção no plano — seja no primeiro quanto no segundo plano — .  Num filme de ambiente pequeno e fechado como este, o uso desta ferramenta pode não parecer em primeiro momento, mas é tão relevante quanto o close-up. Quando se há uma visão dos jurados na mesa, o espectador tende a prestar mais atenção naquele que mais lhe gera interesse ou intriga. Conferir por conta própria um pequeno detalhe na interpretação de cada ator na mesa (independente dele ser ou não o principal foco naquele instante). Quando um dos jurados começa a ser abertamente racista e cada um sutilmente se retira da mesa/desvia o olhar/vira as costas, o plano aberto junto a profundidade do campo montam diante de nossos olhos quase que uma pintura. Quando um dos jurados tira a faca do bolso e crava na mesa, a forma como o choque de todos gera desorganização ainda é organizada pela maneira como cada um está presente na imagem de acordo com sua própria expressividade. São inúmeras cenas marcantes. O filme se declara humanista, independente dos fatos. Neste sentido ele é metalinguístico: Independente da verdade, as perspectivas subjetivas são inevitavelmente manipuladas. Votar pela inocência do réu é algo que fere egos, pisa em tabus e preconceitos, indaga convicções, nenhum deles nem o espectador estava na cena do crime. Eles encenam, simulam, deduzem, o cinema é a verdade simulada do mesmo modo. E a indagação que a obra faz segue sendo fundamental sobretudo numa geração tão insensível e  apática quanto a nossa. Cinco minutos é tempo para decidir por uma vida sem pensar em sua realidade, seu contexto, sem se por no lugar? Mais do que a verdade, é isto o que importa para o filme, e para a arte, a única verdade é a de quem reflete a obra.

It wasn't a bad movie, but honestly, I didn't find it as profound or impactful as everyone makes it out to be. I liked the atmosphere the rain, the cool color palette, and that sense of suffocation and anxiety but at times, it felt like the film was trying too hard to appear dark and serious. The core premise intrigued me more than the execution itself: when your child goes missing, the law fails you, and no one can help just how far are you willing to stray from your moral boundaries?

Once I saw that the movie is set in 2013, I let out an exhausted sigh because the only forgivable scenario of this movie working is if it took place in the 60s or 70. The movie takes itself seriously - you are forced to take it seriously as well, but when you do, all of it aggressively falls apart out of the sheer stupidity of... everyone. What a headache.

Hard to say something about it because I really liked some of the aspects about it: the performances which are great, the premise which is very interesting, the cast is talented and the beginning had potencial but along the way the movie just falls apart, things just don't make much sense. Keller doesn't stop to think that a mentally disable guy that has a 10 IQ and a mind of a child is the prime suspect of what happened with his daughter, but that doesn't have any logic since the police already confirmed after interrogating the guy that he is innocent, the guy also doesn't seem to be able to do anything other than just mumbling some nonsense that only him understand. He is not responsible for the crime commited against those two families but the MC keeps brutalizing and destroying him anyway, making a victim of kidnapp and abuse to be kidnapped and abused again is terrible. He is just a kid, functionally. But Keller doesn't care anyway and his methods couldn't help him to do shit in the whole process. The truth was discovered by detective Loki without any of Keller's actions and when Loki got to the place was almost too late. Fortunately, he was able to save Keller's girl, which also doesn't make any sense since he couldn't even see straight while driving under a heavy rain. Feels forced and hard to believe someone in that situation was able to save another person while being injured and with almost no time at all. Girls were both saved without any permanent scars or wounds, which also is unbelievable and stupid, since the serial killer abused and killer so many other kids before. Why those two were already alive and well after days being dissapeared? Why maintain them well and with life? How keeping them well that long around was a good idea? Nothing makes much sense. 0 internal logic and the whole story pushes forward the idea of "the end justifies the means", a dangerous, problematic and toxic message to the audience and the public in general. The guy tortured a kid to find his own kid while praying to God, how hypocrital is he? How insane is the director? Not right make a character like Alex suffer what he had to endure and then be saved off-screen, after being explicited tortured for so much time. Could you do the same in his place? Would you have the guts to do what is "necessary" for save who you love? Whatever it takes can cost another life, can take you push your own limits, but the movie the never makes you criticize the dark and violent things the protagonist does, it actually makes you empathize with the violent father more than with the victim of all the torture and abuse. The film wasn't written well enough to make you care for all the victims, only with a portion of them, a couple of kids you know nothing while the ones that suffered the most are just treated as the monsters. Really a shame. Could have been much better in so many ways. The more I think about the less I like it. It's only a fine movie. Appreciated to see Jackman and Gyllenhaal acting together, not appreciated as how mentally ill people are portrayed and how violence and tortured are excused as "the only way" to save someone else, when the victim isn't even the real criminal. I feel more bad about Alex than I feel about that two girls. Sorry. And what was that ambigous ending? 2 hours and a half to make a open finale? Seriously? This is so disrespecful and stupid with the audience. Open endings can work with some movies but this piece of media is definitely NOT one of them. The real prisoners are my expectations that got locked away from a true good experience. And they won't be free. 4 out of 10. 2 ☆☆

“You wasted time following me.” All I hear and see are good things about this movie, and this was a good movie. The movie was masterfully shot, every scene gorgeous in their own way. The acting, of course, was great. I can fawn over every actor and say what an amazing job they did but this is such a stacked cast I don’t think I need to. What I will say is Terrence Howard gave a surprisingly good performance. In fact, I wish we saw his character way more. It’s just so funny to me that this guy, who can apparently act really well, also created Terryology. #1x1=2 . What I didn’t like is how needlessly convoluted the film is. I love nuanced characters and complex stories and layers upon layers, which Prisoners has, but Prisoners had no good symbols or meaningful side characters. Every symbol in this movie seemed like an afterthought and the way to make all these symbols work with each other was to add a string of characters who were shells of actual human beings. The story just seemed silly at times. Especially the last piece of the puzzle which just fell utterly flat. Like, I can just imagine this last piece of the puzzle lying supine on the ground with the mobility and width of a pancake.

Two young girls disappear in broad daylight.  The family doesn’t believe the detective is doing enough fast enough, just like every other kidnapping story ever written.  Given that cliche as a premise, what would you do if it was your daughter?  Take drugs to sleep the hours away?  Lean on others?  Pray?  Or torture innocents? The acting by Jake Gyllenhaal and Hugh Jackman is excellent. The cinematography is great.  I hesitate to downgrade its rating for those reasons, but the story just doesn’t break any new ground.  It’s very formulaic.  There are stereotypes and inconsistencies that made me cringe.  And it’s unbelievably slow.  It does not need to be 2 1/2 hours.

Prisoners is one of those films that is genuinely great but also makes you feel miserable for basically the entire runtime. It’s incredibly intense, Hugh Jackman is terrifying in a way that still feels believable, and Jake Gyllenhaal gives Detective Loki this constant exhausted, obsessive energy that somehow makes the whole thing even more stressful. Paul Dano is also so unsettling here that I can absolutely see how he eventually became the Riddler. Different film, same deeply uncomfortable aura. My only real issue is the ending. I know the ambiguity is the point, and I know the whistle suggests Loki probably finds Keller, but after everything that happened I honestly just wanted a more definite win. Let him save the girl, get found, and give me five minutes of relief. Excellent film. Horrible time.

Lived up to my expectations. Denis Villeneuve’s Prisoners is a very well crafted thriller that undoubtedly needs to be watched at night to fit the vibe of the movie. Crime thrillers are one of my favourite movie genres so i was bound to enjoy this. Hugh Jackman in my opinion has his best ever performance in this film. His character Keller Dover is the father of one of the kidnapped children and as the movie goes along, day by day you can see his rage increase and his reliance on humanity fades. In many scenes you can hear his voice break and your dragged into his broken psyche. This performance was stellar. Jake Gyllenhaal played Detective Loki, a detective who boasts his history of solving every crime he has previously met. However the one he is about to tackle, challenges and eats away at his mind. In many ways his mind is imprisoned in the maze of the case mystery. Paul Dano plays the kidnapper suspect and watching this film, it makes absolute sense why Dano was chosen to play the Riddler. Such a chilling and subtle creepiness he brings to the screen. David Dastmalchian was a suprise addition to the cast and he was a treat to see. He aswell fit the creepy and dark vibe of his character. The final third of the film was goddamn great. A plot twist that really makes you locked in on what happens next. And question what you previously watched. Bravo Denis Villeneuve 👏

This film might be one of my most favourite films of all time. It is so creative. The movie follows a father whom is played by Hugh Jackman, the film is centred around his daughter and her friend being kidnapped/going missing. He takes matters into his own hands to find her or gather any information/evidence on her whereabouts so he gets closer to figuring out what happened to her. Detective Loki, played by Jake Gyllenhaal, is the main detective who is put on this case. Each performance in this film is all done extremely well. There’s so much depth and meaning in each and every character. This might be one of Hugh Jackman and Paul Dano’s best performances. The story is also very interesting and well written. “Prisoners” is highly praised feature that portrays the concept of a profoundly unsettling, emotional, and suspenseful investigation of a missing child in such an incredible and distinctive way. It portrays the anger and rage of a dad who is just trying to find his daughter and the feared feeling towards the suspected with unique story telling. It reveals the plot twist in a way that is quite unpredictable and many first-time watchers would not be able to figure out. The acting from each actor/actress is in done in an oscar worthy performance. Hugh Jackman absolutely stands out in this film because of how well he shows the realistic anger of a parent whose is daughter was kidnapped and he’s just carrying the pain of almost losing a child. Paul Dano feels more and more unsettling everytime he’s on screen because of how insane his character is and the brilliant performance he put on as a truly mind-twisted antagonist. The pacing is very important in this film and it really shows it with how well directed this film is. It’s a film that doesn’t necessarily have any confusing scenes and is easily understood. In terms of violence and gore in this film, there’s more than a few scenes that contain some gore but it actually makes sense and it’s properly placed. The cinematography stays true to the plot and every scene is well filmed. The ending itself is a major plot twist that is understandable because it gives the viewers a sense of what had happened after the film’s ending. Denis Villeneuve did quite well with the directing of this film. I have watched this film more than once and it just gets better after every rewatch.

A little disappointment for me. I am not a huge fan of classic police thrillers, even though I have watched many of them, and Se7en is in line with stereotypical American thrillers. Indeed, it’s about two investigators conducting an investigation into a crazy serial killer, except there is nothing original here; it’s too bland. Moreover, all the cases are foreseeable and expected, as the killer openly shows the detectives that his victims represent a specific deadly sin. It seems as if David Fincher wanted his thriller to be a global success, as he adds all the easy elements for his film to be broadly appreciated. Moreover, Brad Pitt doesn’t play that well here, according to me. The setup and the first act are also way too long. How many scenes of small talk do we have to undergo before the plot starts to get exciting ? Nevertheless, the turning point, although late, is good. The final confrontation is also decent but not that shocking or surprising for the spectator. I can’t help comparing Se7en with Prisoners . I think that Prisoners is a textbook example of what a thriller should be: it’s refined, visually soothing, and the plot is just perfect. On the contrary, Se7en is weak. To conclude, the “seven deadly sins” that John Doe follows aren’t from the Bible, as many could think. The concept traces back to Evagrius Ponticus, a Christian monk living in the Egyptian desert in the late 4th century. He wasn’t trying to build a moral code for everyone, he was writing practical guidance for monks trying to master their own minds during long stretches of solitude and temptation. He identified eight “evil thoughts” that troubled the ascetic life (he added “sadness,” which was removed later). Dante's Purgatory cemented the seven deadly sins in Western moral imagination. In the poem, Mount Purgatory is shaped like a mountain with seven terraces, one for each sin, stacked in order of severity (worst to least severe). Souls climb the mountain, working through one terrace at a time, purging themselves of that particular sin before moving up to the next. The order is : Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth, Greed, Gluttony, Lust.

Tengo opiniones bastante encontradas con Se7en porque realmente me gustó muchísimo el desarrollo de la película, la investigación, las pistas y la forma en la que vamos conociendo a John Doe, me parecía que la película estaba construyendo algo con muchísimas posibilidades narrativas y durante gran parte de ella sentía que cada detalle tenía una razón para estar ahí. Doe claramente quería que alguien lo encontrara y que alguien pudiera observar su obra, incluso cuando Somerset y Mills llegan a su departamento se siente que Doe está impresionado por haber sido encontrado y que realmente existía una construcción alrededor de la investigación que me parecía excelente. El problema para mí aparece principalmente en el final y no porque no entienda lo que la película quiere hacer, de hecho entiendo perfectamente la intención de que Mills termine representando la ira y que Doe construya las condiciones necesarias para que Mills termine matándolo. El problema es que siento que la película justifica el final pero no lo desarrolla de la mejor manera posible. Para mí existe una diferencia muy importante entre que un acontecimiento pueda ser justificado dentro de la historia y que realmente haya sido construido narrativamente para que ese acontecimiento sea una consecuencia natural de todo lo anterior. El caso de Tracy es el ejemplo más importante. El plan de John Doe comenzó antes de que Mills fuera asignado como compañero de Somerset, por lo que Mills aparece dentro de la historia de una manera bastante circunstancial y posteriormente Doe adapta su obra alrededor de él. Contextualmente se puede justificar que Doe envidia la vida de Mills, que ve en él aquello que él mismo no tiene y que por eso decide convertirlo en la representación de la ira, pero narrativamente siento que la película no construyó suficientemente la relación de Mills con Tracy para que su muerte tuviera el peso que necesitaba tener. Tracy termina siendo fundamental para el final pero durante gran parte de la película no existe un desarrollo suficiente de ella como para sentir que estamos llegando inevitablemente a esa tragedia. Por eso también me parece extraño cuando Doe habla de su “obra maestra” como si todo lo que ocurrió hubiera estado construido específicamente alrededor de Mills, cuando realmente la película nos muestra un plan que existía antes de que Mills estuviera involucrado. La explicación existe, pero siento que aparece principalmente para poder justificar el desenlace que la película ya necesita. Para mí una revelación puede ser algo que jamás vi venir, pero cuando finalmente aparece debería poder mirar hacia atrás y pensar que todo estaba ahí, que las acciones anteriores de los personajes y las circunstancias de la historia produjeron naturalmente ese resultado. En Se7en yo no tuve completamente esa sensación, tuve más la sensación de que entiendo por qué Doe decidió hacerlo pero no siento que la película haya construido suficientemente las condiciones para que tuviera que hacerlo de esa manera. También me sucede algo parecido con Somerset durante la escena final. Somerset entiende perfectamente lo que está ocurriendo, intenta convencer a Mills de que no mate a Doe porque sabe que hacerlo significa que Doe gana, pero la forma en la que responde durante la escena me parece extraña respecto a su propia motivación. Si realmente quiere impedir que Mills lo mate, esperaba una reacción mucho más desesperada y física, intentando acercarse a él, detenerlo o ponerse entre ambos, porque Mills tiene varios segundos para tomar una decisión mientras Somerset simplemente intenta convencerlo. No digo que solamente exista una manera realista de reaccionar, pero dentro de lo que la película había construido de Somerset, su comportamiento me pareció demasiado conveniente para que Mills pudiera llegar exactamente al resultado que la historia necesitaba. Y esto es lo que más me decepciona porque la tesis de la película me parece excelente. El problema no es el nihilismo, ni que el final sea oscuro, ni siquiera que Doe consiga ganar. El problema es que siento que la tesis está mucho mejor construida conceptualmente que dramáticamente. La película sabe perfectamente qué quiere decir con Mills convirtiéndose en ira, pero siento que tuvo que acomodar algunas decisiones de los personajes para poder llegar a esa conclusión. Para mí la profundidad narrativa está mucho más relacionada con la relación entre la motivación de un personaje y las acciones que produce esa motivación. Un personaje tiene determinados valores, deseos, miedos y circunstancias, y a partir de eso debería tomar decisiones que produzcan el desarrollo de la historia. Cuando ocurre así, el final no solamente se justifica, sino que se siente como una consecuencia de todo lo que vimos. En Se7en siento que en algunos momentos ocurre lo contrario, que el final necesita que determinados personajes hagan determinadas cosas y posteriormente la película encuentra una explicación para que esas cosas tengan sentido. Me hubiera gustado muchísimo más que la película desarrollara a Mills como el protagonista central, que conociéramos mucho más su vida, su relación con Tracy, su personalidad y sobre todo su obsesión con demostrar que puede ser un buen detective. Que la investigación de Doe fuera progresivamente convirtiéndose en una obsesión personal y profesional, que Mills comenzara sacrificando aspectos de su vida por resolver el caso y que finalmente esa obsesión terminara produciendo la pérdida de Tracy y su transformación en ira. De esa manera la muerte de Tracy no sería solamente el elemento necesario para completar los siete pecados, sino la consecuencia de una relación que nosotros ya conocemos y que hemos visto desarrollarse durante toda la película. Incluso siento que Somerset podría no haber sido necesario como protagonista secundario si la película hubiera profundizado mucho más en Mills. Su presencia funciona muy bien para contrastar dos formas de entender el mundo y la investigación, pero al mismo tiempo divide el protagonismo y hace que Mills no tenga todo el desarrollo psicológico que para mí necesitaba tener para que el final realmente me destruyera. Se7en es una película que me parece muy buena durante gran parte de su desarrollo y cuya idea final me parece incluso excelente, pero para mí existe una diferencia entre tener una conclusión interesante y construir perfectamente el camino hacia ella. El final se puede explicar, se puede justificar y tiene una tesis muy clara, pero siento que la película no consiguió desarrollar todas las condiciones necesarias para que yo sintiera que ese final era una consecuencia inevitable de los personajes y no solamente la conclusión que la historia necesitaba alcanzar. Me hubiera gustado ver una película donde la profesión, la obsesión, la familia, el sacrificio y finalmente la pérdida de Mills fueran construyendo poco a poco su transformación en ira. Creo que con ese desarrollo Se7en podría haber sido una de mis películas favoritas, porque la investigación de John Doe y la tesis que plantea tienen muchísimo potencial, pero para mí la construcción narrativa del final se siente demasiado impuesta y eso termina quitándole profundidad a una película que conceptualmente tenía muchísimo más para desarrollar. Gracias

To say the least, I was a little bit disappointed after having heard really good reviews about the movie. I was going into this movie expecting to watch a deeply psychological murder mystery like what it portrays itself to be. Although, after finishing the movie I don’t think they really quite hit the mark with that. My main issue with the movie is the fact that it seems like things just happen. For instance, though Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman are both detectives/investigators, I felt as though they did very little detective work to figure things out. Majority of the movie is them showing up to the crime scenes of each “sin” (after other personnel have already investigated) and then it’s Morgan Freeman stating the obvious fact that the killer is using the pattern of the seven deadly sins. All of the “detective work” that is done just seems predictable and superficial just to progress the story. Another example of this is the fact that Pitt and Freeman don’t even actually catch the antagonist; he voluntarily turns himself in. Granted, they were on his trail at a point, I just think it’s lazy writing to have him turn himself in, especially after just running from them a few days ago. Even still, the best part of this movie was by far the main antagonist who is only really present for the final 3rd act of the movie. I think Kevin Spacey does a really good job portraying an emotionless, psychotic serial killer though he lacks a proper script. I really enjoyed the dynamic and tension between Spacey and Pitt, but I just couldn’t help but question why? I’m not sure if I just missed that part of the movie, but why did Spacey choose Pitt. What was his motive? Not only that, but, not to sound heartless, are we as the audience supposed to care about the final twist in the end with the package? It didn’t really feel like they built much on Pitts personal life outside of work, so why would we care about Pitts’ significant other? I don’t know I think overall the movie just felt a little undercooked.
