Se7en is a film which attempts to wear many hats. On one hand you have attempts at a highly interesting and flashy serial murder case which operates as the major stopping points of the story. Each of the murders is extreme and profane, crafted with this kind of blunt detail that’s certainly entertaining, but ultimately surface level and less well thought out than they likely intended. On the other you have an extremely standard buddy cop framework between the two main characters which makes no real attempt at straying away from convention. Both of these central building blocks are joined together by this phenomenal, nearly noir, presentation which sets up the film as something which is both easily entertaining and contains more for those who are willing to seek it out. Unfortunately, I found Se7en ultimately ends up confused in this crossroad of seriousness and entertainment, ultimately ending up lingering at the surface level and only utilizing these bigger ideas as window dressing rather than something which builds towards something greater. Unfortunately the signs are there from the beginning. The characters in this film are prototypical to a degree which ends up being serviceable but lacking both in terms of story progression and intrapersonal drama. Brad Pitt plays a standard hotshot new detective, willing to prove himself and reeking in overconfidence by his supposed credentials. Rather than demonstrating his actual abilities, Pitt prefers to crack one liners and sneer at his partner’s persistence to do his job properly rather than quickly give up the moment he faces the first sign of abstraction. Likewise, his partner, Morgan Freeman, is his polar opposite. An old blood detective who just wants to retire out of the force because of the toxic apathy of society which has eroded his sense of goodwill. He’s ultimately pragmatic about his job and knows that their efforts are more likely than not to be pointless in the grand scheme of things. This is about as standard of a setup as you can get, but the film never really causes it to head in any sort of meaningful direction. Pitt and Freeman very rarely actually interact for the first quarter of the film, and due to the extremely short timeframe of the plot, their inevitable destination as uncommon allies mere days later is unnatural and unconvincing. The two of them lack chemistry, and their lack of substantial interaction makes the buddy cop presentation lose traction as a whole. Pitt’s more than willing to speak his mind, and the film is more than willing to utilize him as the main source of entertainment, but because Freeman isn’t willing to ever give him an inch these moments end up falling flatter than they had to. This is representative of how the film handles the crux of their characters as well. Pitt and Freeman represent opposite ends of the same coin. Being detectives and thoroughly entrenched in the toxicity of low society, Pitt’s optimism and Freeman’s pragmatism could represent some kind of clash of ideals. But instead, Se7en chooses to merely float these ideas rather than tackle them directly. This is most blatantly presented in a scene in a bar about halfway through the film. Freeman is telling Pitt about how he’s fed up with all of the apathy of society, how people are so willing to take the easy way out rather than work through their problems, which ultimately is the source of their misfortune. Society does not care about itself and so Freeman does not care about society. Pitt rejects this idea, not for any actual stated reason or counterargument, but merely because he cannot accept this line of thought. He states that Freeman himself is also taking the easy way out, which is true, but does little to shift his perspective in any meaningful way. This idea remains a loose thread rather than being properly explored, and this trend can be observed with much of the rest of what Se7en aims to accomplish. The other core principle of Se7en is, of course, the murders. This aspect is where the film really shines. Se7en is already a visually impressive film, perfectly capturing the kind of grime which makes up this low society by operating primarily with low blues and greys. This is a very dark film, but the main attribute I would give the visual quality is dirty. The murders primarily take place in these low income locations, even the apartment buildings are worn down and damaged. Despite the primary weather condition being rain this ends up reminding me of mud more so than dirt being washed away. This translates to the murders perfectly. Each of which are immensely brutal and highly creative, making use of the sin motif more as a suggestion for a gory creative artpiece than anything. My favorite ended up being the first of the murders, representing gluttony you have this obese man who was forced to eat himself to death, but not before cutting off an entire pound worth of meat off his body. This is far and away the most visually stimulating of any of the murders, and perfectly builds up the case as something which is equal parts sadistic and incredible. While grotesque, the visual quality makes it more entertaining than disgusting, and the absurdity of the murders themselves adds to this feeling. Of course, the problem lies with how these murders are presented. For the first half of the film, the duo is convinced that the murders are inspired by famous literary works such as The Divine Comedy and The Canterbury Tales due to them representing the titular seven sins. The film spends a significant amount of time showcasing them researching and discussing these ideas leading you to believe that these would be significant details to the case. Unfortunately, this ends up being nothing more than a wild goose chase, and these details are nothing more than window dressing than any kind of greater idea. Once you reach the halfway point, the film is more than willing to abandon this idea and pivot back towards the cops stumbling in the right direction rather than solving the murders from their own ideas. Of course, the books do end up being brought up again as a key plot point, but it’s only done so to a superficial degree rather than being an integral aspect of how the murders are conducted. This wouldn’t be so much of a problem had the film not spent as much time as it did during the set up period showcasing these works and explaining how they relate to the case. It makes their investigation seem even more like a wild goose chase rather than an intellectual process, a feeling which is only amplified as the film progresses as they never manage to make it off the back foot. Much like the murders, the person who’s leading them along is equally disappointing. John Doe’s reveal in the finale of the film is nothing short of abrupt, and what he actually manages to accomplish once he reveals himself is middling at best. While the ultimate climax, the psychological destruction of Pitt’s character, is certainly very entertaining (and brought forth one of the most iconic lines in modern cinema) John leaves a lot to be desired in terms of actually being a villain. He comes across as a caricature of Hannibal Lecture but without the raw intimidation or presence. He speaks in this very monotone and vague way as a way of demonstrating his control over the situation, only truly losing his temper when he begins to speak about his victims and their respective sins. Unfortunately, he offers little additional support to the foundation of the murders, only confirming that they were executed for superficial means rather than any kind of actual greater purpose or meaning. It’s easy to see that, yes, the people he murdered are representations of the seven sins in some way, but they aren’t carried out as a result of any sort of conviction or greater purpose, but rather just as a means of “higher punishment” administered through his own means. Pitt rightfully calls him out on this, but due to the shallow nature of his character he’s unable to capitalize on this point, mirroring his lack of ability to counter Freeman. My issues with Se7en are not due to a lack of entertainment. The movie excels when it comes to simply fun, the basic nature of its core elements, which are elevated due to the higher quality of its premise, is enough to make sitting through the film worthwhile. However, the film insists that it includes higher ideas in an attempt to nudge itself into something more without properly committing. Each of its greater elements: the character’s opposite personalities, the higher purpose of the murders/how the murders are actually solved are merely thrown out and left unresolved for the viewer to take at face value rather than leaving much room for thought. The ideas being unresolved isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but they end up feeling cheap because of how little foundation they’re given, rather than the lack of a concrete conclusion. Se7en seems to present itself as a movie which is more than your standard buddy cop serial murder mystery film, but while it’s certainly higher quality than your run of the mill flick it just can’t seem to escape its simplistic roots. In the end, it chose entertainment over truly committing to what it wants to say, it takes the easy way out, though I can’t blame them for it.

The atmosphere is great, it’s dark without being boring, surprisingly funny at times, and I loved all the literary references and the whole seven deadly sins concept. BUT I genuinely don’t understand why people talk about the ending like it’s some insane plot twist 😭 John Doe is literally just some random guy we’ve never seen before. Of course I didn’t guess who the killer was, HOW COULD I?? He wasn’t a character 😭 And the more I think about his “perfectly planned” master plan, the less sense it makes. Mills literally JUST moved to the city. John Doe had supposedly been planning these murders forever, but somehow the grand finale of this extremely elaborate seven-deadly-sins plan depends on a detective he basically discovered three days ago?? Why is he suddenly obsessed with him? How did Mills and his wife become such an essential part of a plan that was already in motion before he even knew they existed? I get the symbolism, I get what the ending is trying to do, and the final scene is definitely disturbing and memorable. But I kept waiting for that moment where everything would click and I’d realize “OH MY GOD, THAT’S WHY.” Instead it was more like “oh… so Kevin Spacey is just some guy and he really hates Brad Pitt for some reason.” Great vibes though.

A movie that spends seven days reminding us that humans are f**ked up, and somehow still manages to feel a little empty !! This is definitely well-made or the most artistic film of Fincher’s direction, the gloomy cinematography, the production design and that constant feeling of rain-soaked misery all work perfectly together. Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman are great, and the film knows exactly how to create an uncomfortable atmosphere without constantly throwing cheap jumpscares at you. The philosophy behind the film is interesting too, especially its idea of how deeply corruption, violence and human nature are connected, but I don't think it explores those ideas as deeply as it could have. The problem is the screenplay. The concept is brilliant, but the actual mystery and investigation never felt as gripping to me as it should have. A lot of the film feels like it is building toward that famous ending rather than giving us an equally engaging journey to get there. I also predicted the ending, or at least where it was more or less heading, which made it much less impactful for me. And yes, the ending is disturbing and memorable, but one great final act can't completely save a film that feels unnecessarily slow and repetitive in the middle.

Pretty enjoyable for the first three quarters, though I'm a fairly easy guy to please. Some scenes were drawn out, Brad Pitt's performance was disappointing, but the case was engaging and the kills were pretty gnarly, love to see it. The ending was pretty disappointing, right from the moment the van rolls in. I have no problem with the idea of John Doe setting up his final kills in this meeting, nor any problem at all with Doe himself being one of his targets, but I can't help but feel he would've been far better suited as the representation of wrath over envy. That "I've always admired you" shit was such an ass pull. I don't even mean in the script itself, he'd said it plenty of times before in the movie, even though I think setting up a twist like this by just repeating a line a few times is kinda lame. No, this is an ass pull in the context of Doe's character. As far as we can tell, Doe's admiration of the two detectives came from when they found his apartment. Cool. You're telling me that Doe's master plan, years in the making, ended with him deciding he fit the bill for envy because he was impressed by a couple detectives a few days before? It just seems a little impulsive for this criminal genius. I understand that John Doe is crazy, of course he is, he's a serial killer. But I can't help but feel that he would've been a far more interesting character if he saw himself as the embodiment of wrath. If he was more self aware about his work, and more aware of his role in it as the wrath of what he sees as the divine, I think the ending would've been way stronger than him fucking over Brad Pitt over some nonsense about envy. I guess it was a solid film overall, I'm just very disappointed with the ending.

É muito fácil entender a temática degradação moral/social, não só porque o filme comunica isso por si só (fotografia, niilismo dos personagens - diálogos sobre apatia social etc), mas precisa vir alguém mais de uma vez pra explicar como aquele mundo é corrompido o suficiente pra permitir o mal retornar a ficar solto. Ao mesmo tempo que me pega muito o lance de que nem todos os assassinatos são mostrados com frieza suficiente como outros, sendo que claramente cada morte poderia tocar em mais pontos mais profundos, mas são descartados ou por falta de desenvolvimento, ou uma aceleração proposital da montagem. Mas além do que eu já mencionei, esse corte ainda é muito coeso como apenas investigação, já que a relação dos personagens funciona muito bem por todo o filme, e os minutos finais são realmente de grande impacto. The premise is too horrific and too impracticable for me to buy into. A corporation acquires a baby, imprisons him for 30 years, deliberately traumatizes him by staging his father’s death, manipulates every intimate relationship he has, prevents him from leaving through phobias and coercion, and broadcasts his entire existence for profit. I get that it's a satire. But there’s a realism problem. This isn’t merely exploitative reality television. It’s a human-rights atrocity happening in public. Where are the protesters? Lawyers? Governments? Religious groups? Journalists? People trying to break into the dome? Sylvia is essentially the only person behaving the way you’d expect millions of people to behave. The movie wants the audience to make the comparison to celebrity/Hollywood/reality TV -- but for me that was asking too much. I don't think celebs or reality tv stars are victims. Truman is. The logistics also become ridiculous if you think about them for 30 seconds. The number of people required to sustain this conspiracy, the legal structure permitting it, airspace, utilities, medical care, education, sex and reproduction, emergency situations, Truman’s legal identity, outsiders getting in, employees never exposing it, governments allowing it—the movie simply says, essentially, don’t think about that. I get that people love this movie for its message and the satire. It just wasn't for me.

A fun and interesting delve into the human psyche influential enough to the point where we use it in everyday dialogue to describe any sorts of weird coincidences. Jimmy Carrey as always is a thrilling watch, even in a more serious role than he is usually given. It takes a brilliant actor to carry a film in which only one character experiences the plot and develops throughout it. The supporting cast does their work but i can't help but find them slightly underwhelming in comparison to Carrey's starpower, even if that fact comes with the nature of the role. Unfortunately, I believe this is one of those films where the concept and premise far surpasses how it is actually presented on screen. The whole plot feels like a rush to get Truman to discover the truth, rather than spending time with this pre-established world that could present a unique dynamic between characters. The execution picks up massively once the shift happens but I think the first half of the film suffers massively through it lack of eventfulness. Culturally influencial but not the masterpiece it is often told to be. 6/10

דרמה, מתח, קומדיה, מסתורין. לפני שנים רבות, ארבעת הז'אנרים חיו בהרמוניה, אבל הכול השתנה כשהכניסו אותם לסרט של שעה וארבעים דקות. צחוק בצד, איזה קונספט מטורף לסרט. אפשר לעשות איתו כל כך הרבה וללכת אותו לכל כך הרבה כיוונים. הבעיה שלי היא שהרגשתי שכל פעם אני מקבל לגימה קטנה של משהו מעניין, רק בשביל שישר יעברו לדבר הבא. התחלנו בקומדיה סאטירית, ואז עברנו לבלשות ומסתורין, ואז דרמה על בן אדם שכל החיים שלו הם שקר, ואז לחרדה וקלסטרופוביה, ואז לאקשן עם הרבה הומור פיזי. ואז, טוב, די, אתם מבינים מה אני אומר. כל כך הרבה דברים, כל כך הרבה רעיונות, אבל הסרט פשוט לא נתן לי לשקוע בשום דבר. מה שגרם לסרט של שעה וארבעים להרגיש כמו שלוש שעות. בצורה מצחיקה, אולי אם הסרט היה קצת יותר ארוך או יותר ממוקד, הסרט היה עובר בצורה חלקה. ושלא תבינו אותי לא נכון, אני מבין למה כולם אוהבים את הסרט. יש כל כך הרבה מה לאהוב ולהעריך פה: המשחק נהדר, הקונספט מדהים, ויש סצנות נקודתיות שמבוצעות מעולה. אבל כמכלול, לא עבד לי. לסיכום, חפרתי.

Muy buena, introduce en la vida de un hombre atrapado desde su nacimiento en una jaula de cristal donde el aspecto más feo no radica únicamente en la megalomanía de su creador sino en la complicidad de una sociedad capaz de ignorar el abuso sistemático y la privación absoluta de la libertad de un ser vivo con el único fin de mantenerse entretenida exponiendo un egoísmo social absoluto donde lo que no les afecta de forma directa no tiene relevancia para la mayoría. Esta falta de empatía colectiva funciona en mi opinión como un espejo de cómo se normaliza el cautiverio en nuestra propia realidad. Si bien a nivel legal una de estas cosas es impensable en el mundo real por al valor que le damos a nuestra propia especie, el concepto se vuelve real si pensamos por ejemplo en el encierro que sufren los animales en los zoológicos. Al igual que el protagonista ellos tienen formas de comunicación, pensamientos y emociones, no decidieron nacer en entornos artificiales ni convertirse en el espectáculo de nadie. The Truman show. Dirigida por Peter Weir. (1998) La película sigue a Truman Burbank, un hombre que descubre que su vida es un programa muy popular de televisión, pero debajo de esa premisa hay una película bastante inquietante sobre la libertad, la identidad, el control y nuestra necesidad de sentir que nuestra vida nos pertenece. Seahaven es prácticamente perfecto; es una pequeña isla con calles limpias, vecinos amables y casas bonitas. Todo eso está diseñado para que Truman no tenga motivos para querer irse de Seahaven. Prácticamente está encerrado por una rutina, y la manipulación constante. Su miedo al agua, por ejemplo, fue creado deliberadamente para impedirle abandonar la isla. No necesitan poner una pared delante de él si consiguen que él mismo crea que no puede atravesarla. •Al igual que Christof no se considera un villano. Él cree que le está dando a Truman una vida segura y auténtica dentro de un mundo diseñado exclusivamente para él. Y ahí está una de las partes más interesantes: Christof confunde conocer completamente a una persona con tener derecho y control sobre ella. Decide quiénes son sus amigos, quién será su esposa, dónde vivirá, qué verá y qué temerá. Incluso controla las circunstancias de sus relaciones. Es una forma extrema de paternalismo: "Yo sé qué es mejor para ti, aunque tú no lo sepas." •Sylvia es fundamental porque ella le dice, de alguna manera, que aquello que considera normal no es normal. Ella se convierte en la primera grieta de su realidad. La segunda fue sin duda la repentina aparición de su padre, el cual, en su historia, estaba muerto. En resumen. The Truman Show no trata solamente sobre un hombre que descubre que vive dentro de un programa de televisión. Trata sobre atreverse a cuestionar la realidad que nos entregaron. Y o sea fuera del tono serio, que miedo. Él realmente pensaba que se estaba volviendo loco. ¿Cómo podrías comprobarte a ti mismo que no estás alucinando cuando todos te dicen que es la realidad? Tipo, su mejor amigo desde los 7 años seguía un guión. Ay no, literalmente podría ser un episodio de black mirror. "In case I don't see ya. Good afternoon, good evening and good night" -Truman.
"We accept the reality of the world with which we are presented, it's as simple as that.” What an absolute brilliant way to display rich themes that are even more relevant in 2026.

Jim Carrey's bombastic positivity matched with Ed Harris' flat-cap-wearing cruelty make this war over a world ...nearly enchanting. The Truman show is a rare thing, in that it gives itself away immediately, the wool is pulled back for the viewers so we, on our couches, are in step with all the characters and viewers slobbering on their couches within this world. The meta-handshake happens the moment we cue this one up. But don't be fooled, this is a film about cruelty, torture, and deception on a scale the likes of which too many of us might fail to notice hits too close to home. It is good art in the sense that this is a film that comments on something we were headed for... and now live within. Its relevance came to us, over time. So much of so much of this film is ubiquitous at this point. We watch it and shrug and fail to see that Carrey looking at himself in the mirror, ought to be us looking in the mirror. We watch him, watching himself... but the smoke and mirrors movie magic of it all is that it is us he is talking to, not himself - he is calling out for us to break out of the world we've been presented with, to question the nature of the system we live within. It doesn't hurt that he is willing to die to find the truth, a new reality, to push back against the status quo. But my lord, when you realize that he is walking into a world which has gleefully watched him be caged and lied to for a lifetime, that that is the choice he chooses... you begin to see that the overlord's offer is a better deal than its surface might suggest. This one ends where it should, before you see Carrey see people who love him vicariously, who want to meet him, who care for him as the celebrity of their own twisted obsessions to see people controlled. But maybe love is enough to blind him to reality? But once the gig is up, once the cruelty has transformed and lost its juice, us, just like those parking cops at the end, turn the channel to see what else is on.

“In case I don’t see ya, good afternoon, good evening, and good night!” What would you do if you found out that your entire life was fake? Every person in your life an actor dedicated to keeping you from discovering the truth. Every waking moment of your life broadcast to an audience that you don’t even know exists. Every aspect of your existence, from your job, to your marriage, even your birth; all meticulously scripted by an unseen hand with the intention of garnering ratings and views. It’s a profoundly existential concept, fit for an equally existential film. Jim Carrey’s best roles are ones where he can be emotional, yet still have moments that allow him to go off the rails when its appropriate, and his performance in this is a toss up with Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind as a career best. Even though we the audience are privy to the fact that Truman’s life is an illusion from the very beginning, it still doesn’t make it any less devastating as Truman’s reality begins to unravel around him, thanks in no small part to Carrey’s fantastic performance. It’s no wonder he won over the hearts of so many viewers. Obviously everyone already knows about the brilliant commentary this film has on reality TV and celebrity culture, but this film is so rich with thematic depth that that’s only the tip of the iceberg. One could easily point out the film’s criticism of mass surveilance, which is more topical now than ever with Flock cameras popping up on every street corner. Coinciding with that, The Truman Show (the fictional show, not to be confused with the movie about said fictional show) is really an idealized vision of the long-outdated American Dream. As a child, Truman dreamt of exploring the world and taking in everything that life has to offer, but his dreams were shot down by the authority figures in his life. Now he lives in a copy-pasted suburban house, working a 9-5 cushy desk job day after day, returning home to a bland loveless marriage and a mortgage that will likely never be paid off; living in blissful ignorance of the world outside of his little pocket of suburbia. It’s a role that, as Americans, we’re expected to fill no matter what, and any deviation from that role is tantamount to heresy. Coupled with the constant bombardment of product placements and advertisements throughout his life, it’s clear that Truman’s false reality is a picture-perfect snapshot of life within a capitalist/consumerist system; a safe and comfortable existence, but one that is ultimately neither fulfilling nor sustainable. And yet, Truman still yearns to follow his heart and do what gives him joy and meaning, and so he must break free from the confines of the system, and in doing so find that meaning and fulfillment he’s been searching for his whole life. With Truman questioning his place in both society and the world at large, it’s no surprise that his breaking of the status quo incur wrath of both the systemic and divine variety. Christof, (whose name is emblematic of another certain religious figure) is not just the voice of the corporate backers of the show, but also the literal god of Truman’s reality. He’s also an enigmatic control freak with a god complex, and brought to life by a great performance from Ed Harris. Similarly to his presentation as a god-like figure, he also represents a concept not too dissimilar to 1984’s Big Brother; a controlling force dominating society with an all-seeing-eye (or in this case, moon) that eliminates any individual’s sense of privacy. Truman’s defiance against him is not only an act of rebellion against authority, but also metaphorically and literally standing in defiance of his god, Christof, whose divine edicts boom down from the heavens. Truman chooses not to follow the path chosen for him in Christof’s divine plan, but to carve out his own story and forge his own destiny, a concept that Christof, simply cannot fathom, and therein lies his folly. The scene in which these events take place has got to be one of my favorite endings to a film. I mean, you’ve all seen the shots by now, they’re just incredible. We may never know what happened to Truman. Maybe he reunited with Sylvia, and the two sailed off into the sunset, bound for Fiji. Maybe he lived a life constantly oppressed by paparazzi, as so many celebrities of his status are. Or maybe he just faded into obscurity after being cast out of the limelight. We’ll never know, but the point isn’t the story itself, it’s the concept of not following a story written for you, but to write one for yourself.

I know I’m probably in the minority with this one, but The Wolf of Wall Street just didn’t work for me. On paper, it has everything going for it: Martin Scorsese behind the camera, an incredible cast and a larger-than-life true story about greed, excess and corruption. Unfortunately, I never really connected with the film’s central character, and that made the whole experience feel like a very long slog. Leonardo DiCaprio is exceptional as Jordan Belfort, completely throwing himself into the outrageousness of the character. Jonah Hill is equally memorable, while Margot Robbie makes a huge impression in one of her breakthrough roles. The performances across the board are strong, and there’s no denying that everyone is giving it their all. My problem is that I simply didn’t care about Belfort or his journey. The constant partying, drugs, money and excess become repetitive rather than entertaining, and with a runtime of nearly three hours, that repetition really starts to drag. There are some genuinely funny and memorable moments, but they were never enough to keep me invested in the story. I can appreciate what Scorsese was trying to do, and I can absolutely see why this film has such a huge following. The performances are outstanding and the filmmaking is undeniably impressive. But for me, it’s a case of admiring the film more than actually enjoying it. Perhaps the biggest problem is simply that The Wolf of Wall Street never grabbed me. When a film is this long, you need to be invested in its characters or story, and unfortunately I was neither. A technically brilliant film with some fantastic performances, but one that just wasn’t for me.

Mano, que loucura. Esse filme é uma enorme bagunça. É gigantesca a quantidade de informações que ele te empurra de uma vez, acho que eu tô até meio sobrecarregada. Caralho. No começo você pensa: “Nossa, é um filme interessante sobre ações e bolsa de valores.” Mas, quando você percebe, já está no meio de uma coisa completamente louca, cheia de esquemas ilegais que, sinceramente, nem eu entendi direito. Mas é verdade seja dita: esse filme sabe como prender o telespectador até o final. E outra: puta que pariu, o Jordan é muito burro. Não só ele, como a maioria dos seus parceiros. Pra mim, o ponto alto desse filme é a Margot Robbie. Sinceramente? Que mulher.

“The wolf of wall street” is a movie that doesn’t take its subject matter seriously . It is rather insensitive, pretentious and empty . The fact that this movie is told from Jordan Belfort’s POV logically explains why some of the scenes are depicted the way they are, I wasn’t expecting this to be a moral awakening or a repentance type of movie, but I sure as hell did not expect this to glorify Jordan Belfort’s hedonistic lifestyle & crimes. I fail to see the so called “satire” in this film when the criminal & asshole himself makes a cameo in the film . The “wolf of wall street” is a film in which a criminal who managed to steal and send more than 1500+ working class/middle class people into financial hardship and debt can proudly boast and promote the film discussing his crimes as if it was a movie discussing the life of some scientist or humanitarian. The tone of the film mishandles the severity of the subject, which is probably the main reason why Jordan Belfort felt so comfortable endorsing this film and promoting it. This movie doesn’t depict Jordan for the flawed opportunistic greedy character he is , and even when it does attempt to show that, it is plainly “comedic” and it is not something to be criticized, it is something to be endorsed, it is just being “ambitious”, it is just being “smart”, it is just “wanting the best for yourself”. Being greedy, self-serving and opportunistic is alright and even good because then you get to have endless sex, do endless drugs, and afford everything from lavish parties to lavish trips . This film showed all “the good and the beautiful”, the beautiful women, the parties, the drugs, the trips, but when it came to the consequences of Belfort’s actions, we are shown practically nothing of use . In a way, watching this film you might even get the impression that even if you ended up doing everything that Jordan did you would manage to get away with a slap on the wrist, basically unscathed . We saw no real serious effects or consequences of his drug and sex addiction, no real or serious consequences of his crimes, we only see him playing tennis at jail . In this glorified romanticized piece of media, everything is lavish and extravagant, even jail time is portrayed as something that is not far away from pleasurable or hedonistic . This film intends to criticize hedonism while ironically taking a part of that same hedonistic lens that it is trying to argue against .

the wolf of wall street was INSANE 😭 i knew it was supposed to be chaotic, but actually watching this was a whole different experience. the entire movie is just one ridiculous thing after another, and somehow Martin Scorsese makes nearly three hours of absolute insanity fly by. For me, Inception is a puzzle, not cinema; a film that mistakes complexity for depth and substitutes its engineered calculations for cinematic experience. Nolan does not create dreams; he engineers them. Dream and the unconscious are reduced to a set of rules, layers, timings, instructions, and computational ticking clocks. Nolan is incapable, within the work, of allowing the real madness of dreams to take shape. Nolan does not set the unconscious and dreams free; Nolan writes a rulebook for the unconscious. The dream is not free; it has rules. The unconscious is not instinctive; it is calculable. Nolan wants to create the unconscious, but his unconscious is under control. As a result, because of Nolan’s misunderstanding of the uncontrollability of the unconscious and dreams, neither is actually created in the film. That is why the more the film talks about dreams, the less it creates dreams; the more it talks about the unconscious, the less it resembles the unconscious. As the film moves forward, more and more pieces are placed on the table: the first layer, the second layer, the third layer, time... and instead of dreaming, the viewer becomes a solver of a puzzle. As a result, watching the film is less like experiencing a world and more like solving a puzzle, and Christopher Nolan fails both at creating dreams and at creating the unconscious. Then action arrives in the film and devours everything: gunfire, chases, explosions, falling, an assault on the snowy fortress, and... as if even the unconscious in Nolan’s world cannot breathe without turning into an action sequence; a world that resembles a video game or a rule-bound action film more than a fluid and unpredictable unconscious. The visual effects are technically impressive; but being impressive, for me, is not form. The rotating hallway, the folded city, and the play with gravity, rather than becoming sensory experiences, are more like the film’s engineering calculations. It does not reach feeling and form, and does not turn into meaning. This chain does not take shape for me in Inception . Even the repeated close-ups of baby-faced DiCaprio’s face do not save anything for me. The camera repeatedly moves in close to Cobb’s face, but DiCaprio’s emotionless face remains incapable of saving the film. On the other hand, the film’s emotional center is also crushed beneath the weight of its engineered calculations. Cobb and Mal are supposed to be the heart of the film, but their grief and love often become fuel for that same mechanical narrative machine. In fact, feeling does not live within the image; rather, it has to move the puzzle forward. Feeling, instead of springing from within the image, is often a device for advancing the film’s mechanical puzzle. And this is where, for me, the film collapses. The film wants to engineer feeling. But feeling cannot be engineered. For me, cinema begins where the image can create feeling, build form, and arrive at meaning without relying on an instruction manual, but in this film, the puzzle becomes more important than the image, conceptualism moves ahead of feeling, and technique does not reach form. Ultimately, in Inception , I am faced with a work that explains dreams instead of dreaming; controls the unconscious instead of creating the unconscious; and architects the pieces of a puzzle with skill, without necessarily transforming these pieces into a living cinematic experience for the viewer. Nolan engineers the puzzle in Inception ; but in the process of engineering the puzzle, he loses cinema.

Que filme estéril. Eu realmente pensei que fosse gostar mais, até porque, como não gostei de Paprika, não ia ficar naquele nhenhenhê de “é uma cópia mal feita”. Mas é realmente uma cópia mal feita. Como alguém pega um conceito tão fértil quanto sonhos e mente e faz algo tão pouco imaginativo? Os sonhos parecem mapas de uma missão de espionagem, e não o teatro da nossa mente e dos nossos desejos mais profundos. A premissa deveria abrir espaço para o absurdo, para o subconsciente, para coisas que não obedecem à lógica, mas o filme parece ter sido feito por um executivo lendo um livro de autoajuda. É extremamente elaborado, mas quase nunca parece fértil. Estamos literalmente entrando na cabeça dos personagens, mas é difícil ter alguma simpatia por eles. Os sonhos não revelam nada profundamente particular, e todos parecem existir dentro da mesma estética fria e genérica de blockbuster. O inconsciente acaba parecendo um ambiente corporativo. E os personagens também não ajudam. Achei difícil me importar com quase qualquer um deles, e o drama do protagonista e da mulher me pareceu muito mais funcional para a trama do que realmente emocionante. A única parte que me tocou foi a do DiCaprio precisar aceitar que não pode continuar vivendo preso à imagem da mulher que perdeu, porque, de alguma maneira, isso é identificável para todo mundo. A ideia de esquecer alguém, ou, pelo menos, aceitar que a memória dessa pessoa não pode continuar controlando sua vida é genuinamente bonita. É uma pena que o filme precise de tanta maquinaria em volta para chegar a algo tão singelo. A primeira metade foi insuportável. Muito chata e sem graça, parecendo só um filme de espião com uma ideia mais interessante. A segunda metade melhora bastante, porque finalmente existe alguma tensão e a estrutura dos sonhos começa a produzir consequências de verdade, mas ainda fiquei com a sensação de estar vendo um conceito extraordinário sendo utilizado de maneira infrutífera. O final, porém, é instigante, porque finalmente existe alguma ambiguidade de verdade. Se ele está sonhando, é nota 8. Se não está, é nota 4. Como não sei, fica no meio-termo: 6/10. Porque nos sonhos, estamos juntos.

Rewatching this after almost 10 years and here are my thoughts, 1.  It’s a strange feeling giving a lower rating to something that probably helped shape my taste in movies in the first place. As a teen, I thought this was one of the best films ever. Not my experience today. 2. It is still a brilliant concept and lots of masterful cinematic moments,  but once you know where everything is going, you really notice how much of the movie is people explaining the movie. 3. It spends a lot of time explaining the rules instead of just letting you dream. There are stretches where characters are basically explaining Inception to you. Younger you might have loved learning the rules; now you might notice how much dialogue exists purely to make the mechanics understandable 4.Hans Zimmer’s score might have aged better for me than the film itself. 5. Fischer’s storyline hit me differently this time. Arguably some of the most human material in the film belongs to the person they’re manipulating. 6. Cobb still works for me, but most of the crew feel more like pieces of the heist than actual people. 7. For something about dreams, everything feels strangely organised. 8. Folding Paris is still one of those scenes that reminds me why I fell in love with this movie. 9. The ending is still very well done, leaving it to interpretation and ambiguity. Still one of the best endings to a movie in my opinion.

Inception is a film made for the big screen. I remember it being exciting, new and so much fun on first viewing, so awe inspiring in theatres.  The movie falter a bit on repeat viewing, (there’s an emptiness that peaks its head out every once in a while), but it does hold up. I love that Christopher Nolan just decided to retro-fit this sci-fi story onto a heist narrative.  It works well! The team assembles, they all get their moments to shine, and they scatter with a knowing nod at the end of the robbery. This film has a LOT of things going on, it really walks a tightrope without managing to fall onto the hard pavement, although there are some close calls.  As is normal with a Nolan film, it’s too long. I think some of that could have been dealt with in the editing, but I’m not entirely sure what I would cut. It’s not really a detriment to the film, but why does Nolan insist on weird names like Ariatne? I get that there’s a literary reference there, but it’s a hard word for half the cast to say comfortably. But that ending is a corker! The spinning top.  The great musical swell by Hans Zimmer.

I slept on Inception, no pun intended, for quite a while before finally checking it out.  I was aware of the metaphor for filmmaking and such and some complaints that for a world set in dreams, it's rather unambitious in dealing with the unreal.  And while I'm sure more could have been done to make something more challenging and experimental, the film as is acts as a fantastic ride while being a metaphor for being Christopher Nolan, a man whose work probably keeps him from his kids. But I think part of the reason I forgive the lack of being overtly fantastical in the way that a Nightmare on Elm Street might be is that because it is about filmmaking, it is a fun heist movie exploring the idea of using the pieces and ideas a viewer already knows and how when properly utilized can be a way to bring in a new idea to the viewer.  If anything, I feel this is not what Nolan thinks he does specifically but also aspirational, in hopes of being the man who can put in a new idea.  And like a thief it needs to be done with tact so eventually the "target" and become a part of the same side, with your defenses overcome in the face of an idea baked in emotion. But if this was all "idea" it wouldn't work.  The way it works is that Nolan is a tactful and even fun filmmaker, even if the films aren't big on laughs.  It's easy to think of Nolan as a maker of blockbusters that feel more "dour" but he is actually an expert ride-crafter where the goal is to make a blockbuster that still wants to explore ideas but are also a blast to watch.

Rewatched Inception to put my thoughts in which film I thought was better- Paprika or this. Getting the record straight: Inception, despite being an exposition-heavy/slow paced film, is better overall in comparison to Paprika. My opinion why is this: First off, Inception has that sort of style in which everything is difficult, yet fairly easy to understand. It may be slow, but there are multiple visually pleasing scenes/intense action sequences that keep the audience in put, also with more actually innovative narrative that just begged to be seen. Second, paprika? One can’t deny the possible influence it had on Inception, but you also can’t deny the fact that Paprika relied more heavily on a style-over-substance approach and “dream logic” to patch up its obviously weak narrative. Many that love Paprika usually trash Inception without ever knowing that Inception at least has something to hold bound to instead of what’s basically a art-showcase. There’s too much going on to even care, especially when Paprika is already slow as hell. In a simple summary, Inception may have copied Paprika- we’ll never know, but it surely became superior to it and told a much more engrossing story than Paprika will ever be. 8/10.

Desde el principio presenta una idea muy original: entrar en los sueños de otras personas para obtener o implantar información (como es el caso en esta película). Es un concepto complejo, pero la película logra desarrollarlo de una forma que se vuelve cada vez más interesante conforme avanza la historia. Lo que más me gustó fue precisamente el concepto de los sueños, las actuaciones y los giros de trama. La forma en que Nolan construye distintos niveles de sueños y hace que todos funcionen al mismo tiempo es algo que pocas películas han intentado hacer. Leonardo DiCaprio hace una gran actuación como Cobb. Además de liderar al equipo, consigue transmitir el peso emocional que carga durante toda la historia. También me gustó mucho la dinámica que tiene con los demás miembros del grupo, ya que hace que la misión se sienta más real y que te intereses por lo que les ocurre a todos. Mi escena favorita fue la batalla final. Es un momento lleno de tensión, acción y emoción donde todas las piezas de la historia comienzan a encajar. Además, la forma en que se conectan los diferentes niveles de sueños hace que la secuencia sea aún más emocionante. La música es otro de los puntos fuertes de la película. Ayuda a crear una sensación constante de misterio, urgencia y grandeza que encaja perfectamente con la historia. Algo que también me parece destacable es el uso de efectos prácticos. Nolan evitó depender completamente del CGI y utilizó escenarios reales, efectos físicos y cámaras IMAX para muchas secuencias importantes. Esto hace que escenas como los pasillos giratorios o los cambios de gravedad se sigan viendo espectaculares incluso años después de su estreno. Fight Club (1999) Fight Club: Violence in Place of Understanding Human Alienation On its surface, Fight Club is a film about the alienation of modern man: alienation from work, from the body, from objects, from the crowd, from the self. My thesis is that instead of building a machine for understanding this alienation, the film builds a machine for discharging it, and that this discharge is substituted for analysis through an aestheticization of violence. Contrary to the common reading that treats the film as a critique of late-twentieth-century consumerism (a reading I'll address below and show to be insufficient), my argument is that the film's formal structure, at a level deeper than the characters' explicit dialogue, presents violence not as an object of examination but as the very telos of liberation. The choice of an unreliable narrator is, at first glance, a classic device for representing the subject's internal rupture, a tradition running from The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari to Taxi Driver . The key difference, however, lies in how the camera positions itself relative to that rupture. In the scene introducing Tyler on the airplane, Fincher uses a low-angle medium shot that places Tyler in a position of visual authority from the very first moment, before the narrator himself even understands his relationship to this man. This choice, unlike Scorsese's treatment of Travis Bickle, where the camera deliberately maintains a cold, alienated distance from the subject, invites the viewer into identification from the outset. The film's form makes the audience fall in love with Tyler before the narrative ever discloses that he is a hallucination. This formal-narrative contradiction is where the problem begins: the final revelation (that Tyler and the narrator are one) is shocking at the level of story, but at the level of form it has already been neutralized. The camera has been complicit with Tyler from the start, not with the narrator. Comparing two key fight scenes, the narrator's first brawl with Tyler in the parking lot and the narrator's fight with "Angel Face," reveals the film's editing pattern. In both scenes, the cutting rate accelerates as the fight continues, and the sound design shifts from realistic effects toward exaggerated sonic design (heartbeat, echo), a pattern nearly identical to the escalation used in genre action sequences. The contrast with something like the fight scenes in Scorsese's Raging Bull is instructive: there, slow, repetitive editing turns violence into an experience of attrition and meaninglessness; the blows repeat until pleasure is drained away. In Fight Club, by contrast, the editing builds toward a rhythmic climax that completes pleasure rather than dissolving it. This formal choice is not incidental; it is meaning-making. At the sensory level, the audience experiences violence not as crisis but as resolution, precisely reproducing the same psychological pattern the film claims to be exposing. The most significant objection to this reading is the common argument, made by critics such as actor Edward Norton and in academic readings including those of Ruben Austin and Henry Giroux, that the film is a self-aware critique of toxic masculine ideology: the final scene, in which the narrator shoots Tyler and stands beside Marla, is read as a symbolic rejection of the fantasy of violence. This reading is defensible at the level of plot, but it fails at the level of form. Visually, the closing scene is accompanied by a triumphant score (the song "Where Is My Mind," with its melodic swell) synchronized with images of the towers collapsing, a combination that evokes liberation and grandeur, not warning or catastrophe. If the film truly intended to reject violence, its final sound design and editing should have conveyed a sense of emptiness or horror, not an inspirational musical crescendo. In other words, the explicit language of the plot (the rejection of Tyler) contradicts the implicit language of form (the celebration of destruction). In cinema, form always has the last word. In the film's framing system, Marla is almost always shown in tight shots, from angles that place her at the margins or behind the narrator. For example, in the support-group scenes, the camera focuses on the narrator's reaction to Marla's presence rather than on Marla herself as a subject with an independent crisis. This consistent framing choice reveals that within the film's formal apparatus, alienation is understood not as a universal human problem but as a specifically masculine crisis, whose resolution is sought through the reclamation of the male body via pain. This can be contrasted with a film like Kieślowski's Three Colors: Blue , which builds a crisis of identity through a woman whose relationship to loss is tied not to the body and violence but to silence and quiet reconstruction. The absence of such a possibility in Fight Club is not accidental; it reflects the limits of the film's formal imagination. Fight Club is a film of considerable technical skill, but that skill, rather than serving an understanding of alienation, serves to aestheticize a violent solution. The contradiction between the explicit language of the plot (which claims to critique violence) and the implicit language of form (which celebrates it) is exactly what turns the film not into an analysis but into an unconscious complicity with its own subject matter. For this reason, I give half a star to a film that has put formalist craft in the service of a dangerous thesis: the replacement of understanding with violence.

é um daqueles filmes que parecem ter conquistado um status quase intocável na cultura pop, mas pra mim, essa fama é muito maior do que seus méritos. o filme é frequentemente tratado como uma obra profunda e revolucionária, porém acho uma narrativa que, apesar de começar com uma proposta interessante, termina se rendendo a um espetáculo vazio. nos primeiros atos, a história parece caminhar para uma crítica ao capitalismo, ao consumismo e à alienação da vida moderna. até há espaço para imaginar uma discussão mais complexa sobre o sistema e sobre como ele molda a identidade masculina. mo entanto, essa possibilidade logo é abandonada e em vez de aprofundar suas críticas, o filme transforma esse discurso em um pretexto para cenas de violência, caos e ação, esvaziando boa parte do potencial que havia construído. outro aspecto que me incomodou foi a forma como os personagens são apresentados. Achei todos profundamente antipáticos e difíceis de acompanhar. a impressão é de que o filme espera que o espectador admire figuras que, na prática, são dominadas pelo ego, pela agressividade e por uma visão bastante limitada das relações humanas. me parece um filme pensado prioritariamente para um público masculino. sua reflexão sobre masculinidade é quase inteiramente construída a partir da violência, da destruição e da necessidade de reafirmação do homem. falta sensibilidade para explorar outras dimensões dos personagens ou das pessoas afetadas por suas ações, o que torna a experiência emocionalmente distante. sei bem que o filme possui uma direção marcante, um ritmo envolvente e um desfecho que surpreendeu muitos espectadores. ainda assim, esses elementos não foram suficientes para me convencer. Para mim, trata-se de um filme superestimado: começa sugerindo uma crítica social promissora, mas termina reduzindo suas ideias a um espetáculo de violência que parece muito menos inteligente do que acredita ser.

J'avais détesté ce film quand je l'avais vu ado. Le revoir maintenant n'a pas fondamentalement changé mon opinion. Formellement c'est très bien exécuté, c'est du Fincher à son prime (quoique cette surabondance de numérique verse un peu parfois dans le too much). Quoiqu'un peu trop verbeux. Cornélius ne nous laisse aucun répit avec ses pensées, ça aurait été bien de suggérer plutôt que de réciter. Avec le recul c'est un peu le point faible de Fincher, c'est un très bon illustrateur, mais tous ses films sont d'une froideur clinique - bien que, d'une certaine façon, ce soit assez adapté au sujet, un peu de subtilité sur l'exposition aurait été bienvenue. En revoyant le film en connaissant le twist, on décèle en effet les quelques indices qui sont disséminés ici et là passé la moitié. Mais ça ne me réconcilie pour autant pas avec cette fin qui reste à mes yeux une fin de petit malin. Pour moi le film tient difficilement avec ce twist - je comprends l'allégorie, le message, mais j'ai du mal à accepter tout ce qui se précède. La névrose est trop forte notamment dès qu'il est en public. Ça fait partie de ces films où l'allégorie, l'exercice de style, prime sur la narration ("qu'importe la cohérence, c'est la manière qui importe"). Admito que no me quedé mirándola fijamente la verdad, pero si la deje de fondo y la ví gran parte del tiempo, no me salte escenas, pero si le quite atención a varias porque honestamente los diálogos eran bastante incómodos y desagradables, aunque también entiendo que está hecho mayormente para provocar y tambien como una visión a toda esa vida callejera, a las adiciones de Marla y a la dinámica que llevaban entre ellos, las peleas y demás, pero no significa que a mi personalmente me haya gustado, entiendo el mensaje, pero fue un disgusto tanto las escenas como varios diálogos. El mensaje de la película como tal no me parece malo, es un buen concepto utilizar a un alter ego para simular la libertad que anhela el protagonista, también es buena la crítica y esa visión a como es la dinámica de los hombres, siempre luchar por quien es mejor y vivir demostrando cosas que no son por simple aprobación, aunque es una lástima que la sátira no haya llegado del mejor modo y los hombres lejos de reflejarse y buscar cambiar esos patrones de la sociedad o dejar de reprimir ciertas cosas solo por querer aparentar hombría, terminaron tomándose la película como un ejemplo, viendo a Tyler como un idolo, admirando las peleas, cuando el verdadero objetivo que busca la pelicula es criticar eso y no tomarlo como referencia, pero buenooo cada quien. A mi perspectiva la escena que más vale es la del final, el soundtrack es buenísimo y hace buena referencia, la escena es memorable por todo lo que significa y representa, si soy honesta ya estaba a nada de ponerme a ver otra cosa, pero me quedé ahí solo para ver ese final. Y en cierta parte eso le quitó emoción a lo que pudo ser mi experiencia viendo la película porque solo estaba esperando el final por una escena, la historia ya me parecía bastante corriente y no se, nunca le ví ese punto fascinante. Con esto no quiero hacerme la más cinéfila ni insinuar que son películas comunes y corrientes, solo que personalmente no la disfruté como la mayoría, pero no quita que sea una película de culto y con un mensaje bastante fuerte y significativo Por cierto, esta buenísimo el coso que aparece cuando reseñas la película JAJJAKAKAKAK ya me dio culpa porque voy a romper las reglas

|EN| Fight Club David Fincher, 1999 David Fincher is a director I consider very competent, but rarely one who truly excites me. With Fight Club , however, he certainly manages to bring the film home, helped by remarkable source material: Chuck Palahniuk's novel already provides a story with considerable impact. I think Fight Club has to be judged in two different ways: through the first viewing and through every viewing that follows. On a first watch, the film works extremely well. It captures your attention, builds its world, and successfully deceives the audience until the reveal. The production is excellent, the cinematography is distinctive, and the sound effectively supports the story. Its themes — consumerism, alienation, identity, and masculinity in crisis — also contribute to its enormous cultural impact. The problem comes with subsequent viewings. Once you know the trick, the castle slowly begins to collapse: forced elements and narrative inconsistencies become more visible, making the whole mechanism much less solid than it initially appears. This is where, for me, it loses something compared to other thrillers built around a revelation. The Usual Suspects , for example, becomes more fascinating and precise with every viewing; Fight Club , on the other hand, loses some of its magic once you already know the trick. It still remains a cult film of enormous importance, one that has left a deep mark on contemporary culture. But its cultural impact alone is not enough, in my eyes, to make it a masterpiece. A powerful first viewing, culturally hugely influential and very well made, but ultimately less solid than its reputation might suggest. |IT| Fight Club David Fincher , 1999 David Fincher è un regista che considero molto competente, ma raramente capace di entusiasmarmi davvero. Con Fight Club , però, riesce sicuramente a portarsi a casa il film, anche grazie a un materiale di partenza notevole: il romanzo di Chuck Palahniuk offre già una storia di grande impatto. Credo però che Fight Club vada giudicato in due modi: attraverso la prima visione e attraverso tutte quelle successive.Alla prima visione il film funziona molto bene. Cattura l'attenzione, costruisce il proprio mondo e riesce a ingannare lo spettatore fino alla rivelazione. La produzione è ottima, la fotografia è riconoscibile e l'aspetto sonoro accompagna efficacemente la storia. Anche i suoi temi — consumismo, alienazione, identità e crisi della mascolinità — contribuiscono al suo enorme impatto culturale. Il problema arriva con le revisioni. Una volta conosciuto il trucco, il castello comincia lentamente a crollare: emergono forzature e incongruenze narrative che rendono il meccanismo molto meno solido di quanto sembri alla prima visione. È qui che, per me, perde qualcosa rispetto ad altri thriller costruiti attorno a una rivelazione. I soliti sospetti , per esempio, diventa più affascinante e preciso a ogni visione; Fight Club , invece, perde parte della propria magia quando ormai conosciamo il trucco. Rimane comunque un cult di enorme importanza, capace di lasciare un segno profondo nell'immaginario contemporaneo. Ma il suo impatto culturale non basta, per me, a trasformarlo in un capolavoro. Un film potente alla prima visione, culturalmente importantissimo e ottimamente realizzato, ma meno solido di quanto la sua fama possa far pensare.

Antykonsumpcjonizm drugiego roku studiów, nastoletni nihilizm i diagnoza męskości wychowanej przez kobiety - Fincher wie, że to bełkot, ale nie umie tego dobrze pokazać. Krytyka siedzi w dialogach, egzaltacja w kadrze, a kadr zawsze wygrywa. Po demontażu Tylera zostaje tylko trzymanie się za ręce przy walącym się mieście. Twist czytelny co najmniej od końca pierwszego aktu, wyjaśniany jak rewelacja, więc kotara opada w ciszy zamiast w zdumieniu. Pewnie lepiej rezonuje z samotnymi facetami - to nie był zamysł Finchera i najlepiej dowodzi, że bardziej od satyry wybrzmiewa pozorna egzaltacja. Przy okazji - animacje fatalnie się zestarzały. Zostaje parę trafionych satyrycznych obserwacji, niezłe kreacje i czarny humor, który czasem gra. Warsztatowo ładnie: brudne zielonkawe zdjęcia, montaż na bit Dust Brothers, meblowanie mieszkania. Ale dwie godziny mielenia tego bigosu bardziej męczą, niż ekscytują. Muszę złamać pierwszą zasadę Fight Clubu w sieci: nie oceniamy nisko Fight Clubu.

ce film m’a vraiment fait réfléchir sur l’identité et sur cette envie de devenir quelqu’un qu’on pense être incapable d’être. le narrateur vivait presque comme une machine : une routine, un travail, des objets, et très peu d’émotions qu’il arrivait réellement à exprimer. puis Tyler apparaît comme tout ce qu’il n’osait pas être : libre, impulsif, en colère, sans peur des règles. mais au fond, Tyler n’est peut-être pas seulement une autre personne. il représente tout ce que le narrateur avait enfermé en lui. et c’est justement ce que j’ai trouvé intéressant dans la fin. quand il comprend enfin ce qui se passe, j’ai l’impression qu’il retrouve une partie de lui-même qu’il avait complètement perdue. pour la première fois, il ressent vraiment : la peur, la colère, l’amour, la douleur. même si tout ce qu’il a vécu était destructeur, il n’est plus cette personne vide et programmée qu’il était au début. j’ai beaucoup aimé cette idée que parfois, on peut tellement vouloir devenir quelqu’un d’autre qu’on finit par créer une version de nous-mêmes qui semble plus vivante que notre vraie vie. et puis cette fin… impossible de ne pas rester devant l’écran à essayer de tout remettre en place dans sa tête.

Yes I gave this movie 5 stars. Yes I understand the underlying themes and criticisms of toxic masculinity and consumerism portrayed in the film. Yes, I understand that Tyler Durden is not supposed to be some kind of role model, and that the entire point is to criticise the exact people who idolise him. Yes, I understand that Fight Club fans who completely miss the point are basically the living embodiment of the film’s criticism. Yes, I know that liking a movie does not mean I agree with every single thing it portrays. Yes, I am aware that the film has been discussed in approximately 47 million video essays explaining why its fans are stupid. “ It’s only after we’ve lost everything that we’re free to do anything ” Wow. Rewatching fight club after 2 months of letting it marinate and it again reminds me why Fight Club is my favourite movie. To me, Fight Club was about a false sense of what freedom is to the Narrator. We spend 2 hours to see the Narrator in a life he hated, trapped in an endless cycle of insomnia and emptiness. We then see him introduced to a character that embodies his dream of what freedom looks like, Tyler Durden. He offers the narrator a  completely different perspective on what life truly is about, however slowly taking over his life and his sense of control and freedom. Rewatching it, I genuinely felt as if I was watching an intertwined masterpiece unfold where dots were connecting from two ends of the movie and I’ve never felt that way with another movie before. The hidden meanings, subtle themes and a raging philosophy of what life actually means, represented by two very opposing personas is just so beautiful. I also adore the unstable narration where follow the Narrators perspective throughout the movie so we don’t seem to question whether the things that are happening should be happening. However during the final act, where the big plot twist is dropped on us, the rest of the movie, the narration shifts in a way where we view his actions from a third party perspective and there we realise how mentally ill the narrator actually is. On the second watch, expecting the plot twist, I was able to see so much more and the subtle clues that they hinted throughout the movie. Conversations and dialogues that involved the two main characters were SO much more fascinating to follow. Also, I find Tyler Durden to be just a piece of art and his ideology and perspective on certain things is truly fascinating, especially compared to the society we live in today. For example, he states that “ the things you own end up owning you ” and when I really sat down and thought about that, it was just so refreshing to see things like that in a completely different perspective. Another example was when he had tortured and threatened an innocent man, all so that the next day onwards, that innocent man will never try harder in his life to achieve his goals of becoming a veterinarian. All in all, Fight club somehow gets better on the second watch, David Fincher IS the goat and @danyaalkhalid just doesn’t understand peak yet but maybe 1 day 😌

Le film — ou plutôt les critiques — m'ont bien dupé. Mais qu'est-ce que c'est que cette bouse, sérieusement ?! Comme d'habitude avec Christopher Nolan, il n'est pas vraiment réalisateur mais plutôt écrivain : il passe son temps à expliquer ce qui se passe à l'écran au lieu de nous laisser le découvrir par nous-mêmes. Déjà, je crois que je n'ai jamais vu un plot twist aussi ridicule de ma vie. Si je résume globalement l'histoire : des magiciens trouvent comme par magie des doubles d'eux-mêmes et les tuent. Voilà donc l'incroyable chef-d'œuvre dont tout le monde me parlait. C'est du foutage de gueule. Comme d'hab, Nolan nous balance son projet sans réelle construction. Il utilise ses personnages comme décor et son décor comme personnage. Tout est artificiel et prétentieux. Le film se croit incroyablement intelligent et intellectuel alors qu'il nous propose énormément de choses absurdes. Le jeu d'acteur, les dialogues complètement débiles, les rebondissements qui s'enchaînent avec un ridicule alarmant... Tout semble vouloir nous prouver à quel point le film est intelligent, sans réellement réussir à le démontrer. Et puis le film passe son putain de temps à tuer tout le monde au lieu de réellement nous balancer de la magie. Maintenant, si tuer des personnes et faire apparaître des doubles, c'est ça la magie, mieux vaut que je ne dise rien. L'histoire est complètement tirée par les cheveux, parfois même nanardesque. Et même la présentation du film est mensongère : on nous vend quelque chose de mystérieux et spectaculaire, alors qu'on se retrouve surtout devant un mélodrame surjoué avec des acteurs en double, présentés comme si c'était le miracle du siècle. Et le pire, c'est cette impression de recyclage permanent. Le film reprend des idées déjà vues auparavant et nous ressort exactement le même délire de merde que dans Inception : un concept compliqué, une narration qui veut absolument paraître intelligente et des explications qui prennent le dessus sur l'émotion et le spectacle. Et on va vraiment me dire que ce film est captivant ?! Je préfère regarder des films sous-cotés. Au moins, je suis sûr de ne pas être déçu, parce que les chers cinéphiles me conseillent des grosses daubes qui servent strictement à rien. Bon, tout n'est pas à jeter. Les passages avec Tesla sont probablement parmi les plus intéressants, notamment lorsqu'on découvre le fonctionnement de certaines expériences. Le développement des règles du tour de magie est également plutôt bien construit : le film respecte finalement assez bien l'idée qu'un tour doit avoir un principe, une méthode et une réparation derrière lui. Mais à part ça... Tout est digne d'un film qui se fout royalement de votre gueule. Un film qui se croit intelligent alors qu'il ne l'est pas. Un film qui te balance des rebondissements totalement débiles à chaque scène. Et cette fin... C'est clairement le complot poussé jusqu'au ridicule le plus alarmant. J'étais à deux doigts de l'arêter avant la fin... Nolan n'a décidément pas fini de me décevoir. Mais bon, je regarderai quand même ses autres films ultérieurement... De la merde...

What I think is fascinating is truly how every aspect of this film exemplifies the idea of failed seriousness but because it was made by a posh autistic British man we are meant to think of it as elevated. The way it tells you the plot in the first minute (and also that it follows a very classic narrative three part act because that’s what films are!), the performances and the accents are insanely over the top, the terrible wigs and prosthetic hair pieces, it’s all just very silly. But it treats this silliness with the utmost seriousness which I think is really funny but it also saps any Levity out of it. It’s a dour, very heavy handed drama for Harry Potter adults that, ironically for the subject matter, almost compulsively tells rather than shows you. I think there is something inherently so telling about choosing to make a film about prestidigitation where all magic is “logical” or at least scientific. Because those type of magicians are ontologically opposed to the idea of natural magic, predicated on the need for explanation. I think this film prefigures so much of the current horrors with its damn flashbacks, the way everyone constantly announces their intentions and how women are nothing but plot contrivances (Rebecca Hall you deserved better than this and the second you appeared on screen I instantly got sad for the unceremonious way you were ineluctably doomed to get fridged) I think I will just never understand why people revere Nolan, I find his filmmaking so clunky and laden footed and I can’t really understand this obsession with making everything so self serious even though you pick quite silly themes or subjects but hey! Wow this is such a weird film bc I went from mad abt the ending and honestly hating it to realise how much of a masterpiece this film is like it’s such a weird one. I thought it was rlly cool how that’s why he didn’t love Sarah all the time that was rlly cool. I also loved Olivia I honestly felt bad for her too bc I don’t think either man (Freddy and Angier) truly loved her like she was done dirty too. Overall, I was a bit bored throughout, and it was like the sixth sense when I was like waiting for the twist, but I didn’t rlly love the twist. Nunca entendiste cuál era el fin. El publico sabe la verdad. El mundo es simple, miserable, es despiadadamente real. Pero si podías embaucarlos sólo un segundo, se hacian preguntas. Entonces conseguías ver algo especial. Esa mirada atónita en sus caras Me considero una persona muy interesada en la magia y a la cual le gusta ver trucos e intentar descifrarlos. Esta película más allá de usar ciencia ficción, también usa y revela trucos que se han llegado a hacer en la vida real y eso siento que enriquece mucho a la obra. Una vez más, se trata el tema de la obsesión y de querer ser el mejor o el más reconocido en un ámbito. Y, como ya es sabido, estos comportamientos no suelen acabar bien. En cuanto a la rivalidad entre los magos, me ha gustado mucho. Hay un motivo verdadero y de peso por el cual terminan así el uno con el otro. A partir de ahí, es un sinfín de manipulaciones el uno al otro, hasta que llega a su fin de un modo u otro. Centrándome un poco en la narrativa, a pesar de haber visto este recurso anteriormente de manera continua, siento que a esta película en concreto le viene muy bien. Hasta el último minuto de la película he tenido preguntas que se han resuelto en ese mismo momento y que me han dejado asombrado. En general he disfrutado bastante de esta película y estoy más que satisfecho. Aunque me hubiera gustado haber visto algún truco de cartas que conozco.

The Good This was only my second watch, and I was impressed to find I liked it even more this time. The first time you watch The Prestige, Nolan pulls off a fantastic trick. He places the audience in essentially the same position as Angier. You become fascinated by Borden's secret because Angier is fascinated by it, and Nolan controls what you see and when you see it beautifully. And the reveal works so well, with the cost of obsession and sacrifice hitting all at once. The second time, the balance almost reverses. The ending may not hit the same, but the rest of the film works even better. You know the cost from the beginning, and suddenly every interaction is carrying something it couldn't quite carry the first time around. You’re watching Angier’s grief, bitterness and obsession knowing exactly where it's going to take him, and Hugh Jackman is fantastic here. There’s a desperation to him that develops so gradually that you can see him disappearing into it. But it's Borden who changed most for me on a second watch. Knowing his secret means you can see the cost of it written across virtually every interaction. Borden and Fallon, Borden and Sarah, the moments of apparent inconsistency, the distance, the things he can and can't remember, even the moments of genuine love followed by something that suddenly feels completely different. None of this was absent the first time. The reveal makes you understand it retrospectively. On a second watch, you get to live with it as it's happening. And there’s a wonderful symmetry between the two men. Borden gives up an entire life for the trick and can never let anybody know. Angier ultimately does something even more horrifying, all in pursuit of a version of the trick that, to the audience watching it, isn’t actually any better. That’s the beautiful punchline. He can finally be the man who appears at the back of the theatre and takes the applause himself. That’s it. Nobody in the crowd knows or cares what he had to do to achieve it. The difference only matters to Angier. Both men have sacrificed everything for something whose true cost can never be appreciated by the people applauding them. The Bad We’re scraping around here. One thing that bothered me slightly was Borden insisting that he doesn’t know which knot he tied when Julia died. Obviously, once you know the secret, there’s an explanation for why one Borden genuinely might not know. But surely the brothers talked about it? It’s such a monumental event in both their lives that the idea they could maintain uncertainty between themselves feels a little difficult to swallow. There’s perhaps an interesting reading where their identities have become so blurred that even responsibility is becoming shared between them, but I’m not entirely convinced the film earns that. There’s also some fairly aggressive plot convenience around Borden being convicted of Angier’s murder. He’s found at the scene, certainly, and Angier has constructed the situation to incriminate him, but everyone becomes awfully confident awfully quickly that Borden murdered him. In a film absolutely stuffed with doubles, deception, disappearing men and people whose entire profession involves making things appear to happen that didn’t, there isn’t a great deal of appetite for another explanation. It works because the plot needs it to work. And the meh... This was my second watch, and it leaves me wondering what happens on the third. The first time is a marvel, the second is richer. So what does a third watch give me? I had a similar thought after revisiting Inception. There’s always the possibility that once you've experienced the revelation and then experienced the film again with that knowledge, you've exhausted the major ways it can change beneath you. But my suspicion with The Prestige is that it will keep giving, because it's simply too rich beneath the mechanics of its trick. The secret isn't a replacement for the human story. It's the thing that reveals just how much of that human story Nolan had hidden in plain sight. And second time around, I could see it everywhere.

🍃Everything about this held up on a rewatch. I love how uncharacteristically (Nolan-wise) gritty this was. The London streets feel grimy and atmospheric while they host our main characters in an inescapable feedback loop of ambition and depravity. Bale’s performance is just unreal on a rewatch. The subtle physicality and expression work done to distinguish between the twins is crazy work. Jackman is also great, giving one of his best performances. The entire supporting ensemble is similarly excellent. The Root stuff stretches credibility for me and there is a moment halfway where the film feels slightly repetitive but I remained completely engrossed.

Nolan is a master at twists, not because they’re surprising or obvious but because they’re both.  He lays breadcrumbs that lets the viewer figure it out before the big reveal, but it’s subtle enough so that when it is shown the buildup still carries the weight.  This movie is no different.  It’s essentially Spy vs Spy but they’re both asshole magicians and its amazing.
