Um breve comentário... Revisitando "Django", descobri que possuo uma série de incômodos com esse filme. Não consigo afirmar que é um filme ruim, muito menos que é brilhante. Mas há algo aqui que me incomoda profundamente. E acredito ser a maneira como Tarantino dirige sua violência. Não sua eloquência estética que jorra para todos os lados. Mas as escolhas feitas para a construção do ódio sobre os donos de escravos. Em "Bastardos Inglórios", Tarantino não precisa recorrer aos atos de barbárie da segunda guerra para construir a imagem dos nazistas ou alocar a faixa de "esses são os vilões". Pelo contrário, os atos de barbárie apenas recaem sobre eles (com exceção da introdução de Shosanna), e assim somos levados por toda a história. Mas, aqui? Existe um tratamento com o corpo negro que me causa náuseas. Não só a colocação de Django, em alguns momentos, como um sujeito inocente, infantil, incapaz e que precisa de tutela, mas as introduções de Broomhilda serem sempre pautadas pela transgressão de seu corpo. Sua personagem é uma passageira da agonia frente aos nossos olhos. E aí, o tratamento de ventríloquo que Tarantino dar a seus personagens prejudica a própria substância que os constitui. Broomhilda é apenas uma boneca que está sendo torturada durante todo o filme. Apenas esperando a morte ou a surpresa de seu salvador. É engraçado esse filme vir logo após bastardos. Principalmente pelas decisões tomadas de reconstruir cenas de violência ao corpo negro, quase que com o intuito de fazer com quem o telespectador compre a ideia que o dono de escravos é o "homem mal". Como se ser DONOS DE ESCRAVOS já não fossem suficiente, da mesma maneira que ser nazista. Não falo se a escolha do diretor é certa ou errado, se devia ou não estar ali, mas das sensações que provoca ao telespectador. E sim, acho engraçado que em um filme ele não recorra a barbárie ao povo judeu, mas a corpos negros ele dedica tanto tempo e estilo para isso. Sim, DiCaprio rouba o filme pra si. Sim, a sequência de sua morte e o show de sangue é catártico, como muitos filmes de Tarantino NÃO conseguem ser. Mas até chegarmos a esse ponto, somos levados a uma exploração da violência sobre o corpo negro que me causa náuseas.

I think this is just not for me, even on a rewatch I think while there are undeniably great aspects to this film its just so messy as a whole I struggle to get behind anything it puts down. The performances here are probably the biggest detractor, aside from Walz they lack any sort of finesse or styling they are just these over-acted messes I think Leo is the biggest casuality here, Candy at his core feels like he could be a great character but because of Dicaprio's one note performance his character misses any nuance or any quality that would make it stick in my mind for any amount of time. Jamie Foxx feels similarly shallow offering nothing but an attempt at a commanding presence that never feels all that intimidating or striking, and SLJ just kind of flails around. I think because I'm such a huge western fan this one would've have been really special to make it in for me but Tarantino's hodge podge just feels unbalanced insensitive and unfunny. It feels more like a parody of the genre without any understanding what makes the tropes of the genre interesting. Focusing more on reference value and showing the viewer that it is in fact a western than creating something more a cheap roller-coaster ride that certainly has some highs but also makes me reach for the paper bag more than once. The way the film tries to make any sort of a message is baffling to me. Its as if Tarantino got out a balancing scale and was like if I put in loads of goofy and comedic elements but mix it in with loads of edgy, "cool" and violent moments it'll somehow balance out, but to me it just feels disjointed. The film tries to balance the racism it explores with no accountability, there is no justice for D'artagnan just a fuckload of n-slurs. And while the oppressors are brought to justice by the end the way its just handled with zero weight or magnitude makes it all feel worthless by the end. That being said I believe the film really has some fantastic scenes in isolation, the scene where Django shoots his first bounty with Schulz or the one where they're at the dinner table in candy land are still genuinely tense and the opening is really fun, but it's overall tonal dissonance and general feeling of lack of weight make this a dud for me. Not bad just not for me.

Something about it feels a bit contrived and artificial. I absolutely loved Inglorious Basterds, which shares many similarities to this; it's a soft remake of an earlier action/exploitation movie, but in that case I think it far exceeds its source material, with a much more convincing story and emotional ties to the characters. I have not watched this in a long time. This was picked at random from my shelf as a background watch. Honestly I thought/hoped I had reviewed this already. I was hoping to not have to reevaluate this. There was a few years there when the general consensus was that this was a top 3 Tarantino movie and was genuinely beloved by most people I knew and talked movies with. This is one of those movies I remember very specifically the first time I watched it. It was at a Debate tournament my school was hosting and I was probably supposed to be helping with something. Instead I watched this on some guys laptop with the other boys who weren’t good enough at debate to be closely supervised or noticed as missing. At 16 I thought this movie was cool as shit. I’ve seen it a handful of times since that, but it’s been at least since like 2019 that I watched it I’m pretty sure. I really just don’t have the same relationship with Tarantino I had back then. Some of the scenes in this are really tough to watch. There’s a lot of hard r’s dropped and it’s weird when you remember that a white dude is going to this level to show the brutality of slavery. It feels like he’s trying to get away with being racist by having it be a revenge exploitation, but he doesn’t have the connection for that to be his rage. Seems to me like he just wanted a setting to allow him to write white racists and have cool action scenes. The funniest scene is literally Jonah Hill making jokes as a klansman. That’s too humanizing for the KKK imo. That said it does capture the evils of slavery regardless of intention and it feels good seeing those racists die. The big fights is one of the best action sequences Tarantino has made. It’s also one of the best movies for his unique shade and volume of blood. The image of the red-orange blood on a white horse goes pretty hard. I love this as a Jamie Foxx movie. He’s a great movie star and incredible in this. I don’t like all of the Tarantino of this but I love all of the Jamie Foxx of this.  Good performances from the other big names here as well but D’Jango is the movie. 3/5 it’s good but a tougher Tarantino watch for me and just not one of his I revisit as often. Some parts of it do hold up and parts don’t. I definitely view it a lot definitely than I used to before I really developed my taste.

Que FILMAÇO! Meu primeiro filme do Tarantino e, cara, é tanta coisa, tantas mensagens que te pegam. Uma hora esse filme te faz sentir raiva, outra hora você ri, outra hora fica eufórico. E, nossa, quantas sensações diferentes em um filme de faroeste. Quanto a uma crítica, não vou tentar me estender muito, mas esse filme facilmente daria uns 20 parágrafos. Bom, o filme é dividido em três arcos muito bem definidos, e eu gostei bastante dessa divisão. É bem explícita a ascensão do Django, a missão para resgatar a Brunilda e, por fim, o clímax. Cada uma dessas partes é muito divertida e cheia de críticas à época da escravidão, ao tratamento dado aos negros, ao racismo e etc. Todas essas críticas são ridiculamente bem escritas e cirúrgicas, justamente por serem secas e te deixarem com raiva daquilo que está sendo mostrado (ou, pelo menos, é isso que deveria acontecer). Ao mesmo tempo, em alguns momentos você consegue rir da situação, seja pelo absurdo, seja pela graça mesmo. As atuações são estupendas. Os três atores principais roubam a cena: Jamie Foxx, Christoph Waltz e Leonardo DiCaprio. Principalmente o DiCaprio. Minha nossa, que vilão bom. Ele é acompanhado por um subvilão, interpretado pelo Samuel L. Jackson, que a todo momento consegue te deixar com raiva. Minha nossa, que raiva desse personagem. O Waltz e o Jamie Foxx também têm uma química que funciona desde o minuto 1 do filme. Os dois são muito bons juntos e conseguem carregar boa parte da história com uma naturalidade absurda. Uma coisa que achei muito interessante foi a evolução do Django. Graças ao roteiro, é perceptível o desenvolvimento dele por meio do letramento e do pensamento individual. É muito satisfatório acompanhar isso e ver como o personagem vai mudando ao longo do filme. A cena da KKK, de longe, é uma das coisas mais engraçadas do filme. É tão idiota que acaba sendo genial, e a cena termina de uma forma espetacular. Pra terminar, só apontar a única (única mesmo) coisa que não gostei: o ritmo do começo. A diferença de ritmo entre o primeiro terço do filme e o momento em que eles conhecem o personagem do DiCaprio fez com que o início demorasse um pouco pra mim. Mas talvez seja só meu cérebro derretido pelo TikTok, enfim, fica aí o comentário. Que filme maravilhoso. Fica a dica.

Leonardo DiCaprio was absolutely hilarious, especially every time Rick started crashing out over his career. Brad Pitt was also fucking perfect as Cliff. Dude just shows up, does whatever the hell he wants, and somehow looks cool doing it. The movie is definitely slow, but I honestly didn’t mind it. I loved the whole Hollywood setting and how it felt like Tarantino was showing his version of what Hollywood used to be. And then that ending… HOLY SHIT. I wasn’t expecting it to go that way at all, and seeing the whole Manson situation get turned into one of the most insane endings was peak Tarantino. The flamethrower scene had me fucking crying. Not my favorite Tarantino movie, but there’s just something about this movie that I really enjoyed. It’s basically three hours of hanging out with two dudes in Hollywood, and somehow I’m completely invested.

Embora, a morte de King tenha sido o estopim para que Django pudesse resgatar sua esposa e assim traçar todo o plano de explodir a Candyland, gostava que ele tivesse ficado vivo para desfrutar da Candyland em chamas no fim de tudo. I am so very split on this movie. On the one hand, it brought me to tears, it is empathetic, it is beautifully shot. On the other, it is exploitative, ignorant, reductive. It presents one of the most violent, most disturbing, most saddening scenes and then undermines itself by needledropping a Radiohead song, playing it as safe as imaginable for a presumably western audience. Throughout the movie I was wondering, what country is this even about? I thought I missed an explanation and was trying to connect the dots, people speak Arabic, there is some kind of civil conflict in the 70s and 80s, there is a "Christian right" in conflict with a presumed (is it ever even made explicit?) left resistance. Why not make explicit that this is about the civil war in Lebanon? Clearly, the movie's relation to politics is as timid as Villeneuve's early attempts at making the landscape a character, conveying emotion purely through filming these very wide shots, but it always draws back before really going anywhere, seemingly afraid it would offend an audience's sensibilities. If the central hypothesis of Deleuze and Guattari needed any more confirmation, it is here that we find it: The main character's real life inspiration (Soha Bechara) was a communist soldier, the assassination attempt that landed her in prison was committed on a reactionary South Lebanese army general. But the movie stays fundamentally incurious about her motivations, about the motivations of the Lebanese armed forces, it has no interest understanding how people get so racist they commit these atrocities and it is especially afraid to be seen "taking a side". What the movie instead opts to do is write an oedipal drama; it is all about *family*. Politics, religion, personal convictions, historical situations, they all collapse into a backdrop to what really matters: Love, trauma, anger, all happening within the theatre of the oedipal triangle, mommy - daddy - me. I can't deny that said oedipal story did work on me and hit me emotionally, even more though I think it is a real shame how close this actually gets to being earnestly good and thoughtful. It wouldn't have needed much, all it would take is that this movie is less afraid of "politics", of "taking sides" and that it dares actually embrace a perspective on something instead of avoiding that by any means necessary.

Ce film aurait pu montrer les horreurs commises dans les deux camps, tout en mettant en évidence l'absurdité de ces conflits et de la haine qu'ils engendrent. MAIS… Il ne faut visiblement pas brusquer le monde du cinéma. Alors, plutôt que de mettre les deux camps sur un pied d'égalité, on va s'attaquer à ceux qui ne disent rien. Je vous laisse deviner ? ( NON ) Les Chrétiens. On a donc un film qui imagine un pays, qui suggère l'appartenance musulman de l'un des camps ( Clairement inspiré du Liban) mais qui, pour l'autre, n'hésite pas à multiplier les références chrétiennes : la Vierge Marie sur AK47 après avoir abatue de sangfroig un bus entier d'innocent, des croix montrées à plusieurs reprises, des discours chrétiens entre deux scènes de torture, etc. Alors oui, le film montre des atrocités commises par différents camp. Mais pourquoi insister autant sur l'iconographie chrétienne lorsqu'il s'agit de représenter la violence ? à force, cela mes un noms simple a retenir sur ces atrocité " Le christianisme ". Et c'est justement ce qui me dérange : si le but était de dénoncer les horreurs d'une guerre de religion, pourquoi ne pas donner la même place aux symboles et à l'identité religieuse des deux camps ? Pour votre gouverne, 4849 chrétiens ont été tués dans le monde en 2026, dont 93% en afrique, selon les chiffres d'Open Doors. Ce film aurait dû faire beaucoup plus de bruit. Edit : 4800 comme le nombre de personne qui on mis 2 etoile a ce film ;)

Por sí sola, es una buena película. Habiendo leído la obra, no tanto. Sé que es tedioso escuchar críticas del tipo “la adaptación no es 100% fiel al libro” pero en este caso, me parece que pese a ser una obra, el texto original parecía hecho para el cine y no requería modificaciones. Entiendo que los cineastas toman ciertas decisiones, pero suprimieron partes muy importantes y agregaron cosas nuevas que no aportaron mucho a la historia. Casi todos los personajes perdieron gran parte de su profundidad: Nihad, Simon e incluso Nawal, todos parecían estar al servicio de la trama y girando en torno al “plot twist” y no se sintió el esfuerzo de desarrollarlos con humanidad.  Lo que más me indigna es que dejaron por fuera la historia de amor adolescente entre Wahab y Nawal, una parte tan natural, cruda y paradójica de la historia. Y ni hablar de la eliminación del personaje de Sawda: sin ella Nawal no hubiera cantado, y fue una lástima no ver ese vínculo tan puro y profundo. Reitero, todo estaba al servicio del plot twist. Enfin, es una buena película, pero si quieren sentir todo a un nivel más visceral y conocer una historia más humana, lean la obra de Wajdi Mouawad. (Odio que la gente piense que la historia es de Denis Villeneuve)

該怎麼說呢，火燒車與結局確實震撼，但整體敘事卻感覺綁手綁腳，沒能更好地用鏡頭傳達，但也確實讓我很好奇原劇作的呈現，應該會比電影精彩很多吧？ 本片多次在觀眾試圖解讀影像之前率先透過某人講出媽媽發生什麼事，忽然失去探索影像的主導權，身為電影觀眾不免對此有些反感，且講完了還要再給你看事發當下的鏡頭，感到多餘的同時馬上瞭然不過是因為劊子手的臉很重要，觀眾要先看到他，後面才能產生劇本想要的震撼效果，但這種目的性極強的鏡頭手法卻讓人有點難以忍受。 火燒車那場戲的震撼度仍然是全場最佳，也確實帶出極有說服力的轉捩點，但下一幕就接到另一個時空女兒來到媽媽家鄉悠閒散步的觀光客模樣，又讓我惋愕怎麼能就此放掉火燒車場面的後座力，轉而把觀眾的情緒切斷？ 而全片都在用這種七零八落的平行敘事，看完後除了瞭解事態全貌與結局的震撼感外，在反思層面與鏡頭語言上卻蒼白得嚇人，無從得知媽媽後來是怎麼克服仇恨與兩個小孩相處的？知道真相後的媽媽是如何從震撼掙扎到寫出那兩封信的？小兒子是帶著怎樣的心情與思考後不小心脫口而出「畢竟我有那種基因」的？ 總之本片拋出了極其龐大的議題卻在影像上處理得零零落落、捉襟見肘，身為觀眾都不免為導演緊張得要命，也搞得「1+1=1」這種台詞像是用完即棄的震撼彈，炸完了什麼也沒能留下。

Wow, I really don’t know what to say. Villeneuve is easily one of my favorite directors, and he creates such an expertly crafted story of family, war, and grief. The landscapes and visuals pull everything together so well, with static and lingering shots that really make you feel the emptiness and harshness of the world. It takes you through a multigenerational story, slowly unwinding the truth behind so much mystery. The first hour broke me, and I was out of tears for a while, but I assure you I would’ve had more if possible. Radiohead being the only songs in this is kinda hilarious, but it also works. As soon as the first song began I instantly recognized it and thought, “how does Denis have the audacity to play this after what just occurred.” It’s such a gruesomely real look into the world of war and how that shapes people. The narrative structure and time jumps, combined with the immense amount of travel, also help show the determination and desperation the characters have. It always gives you enough to understand and feel what’s happening without overloading you or cutting anything short. I do think the third act loses some momentum, and the ending itself is really emotionally deep but also a bit too coincidental and almost feels forced for impact. However, that really didn’t take away from the experience of watching this. It’s truly incredible and definitely something I have to rewatch. Wouldn’t be shocked if it rises to a 4.5 or even a 5.

While often enshrined as a cinematic masterpiece, The Battle of Algiers reveals itself upon closer inspection to be a technically flawed work of state-sponsored propaganda that priorities political utility over artistic integrity. It is profoundly shallow in character observation and attempts to substitute the hollowness of the narrative with the heaviness of the topic (colonialism). As this film was commissioned by the Algerian government and produced by an FLN commander, the impact of other Algerian resistance movements are completely ignored and instead the film is to function as a seemingly authentic origin story propaganda. The film’s celebrated documentary aesthetic is revolutionary, but is undercut by multiple weak formal aspects. The lighting in particular is jarringly inconsistent, often featuring blindingly bright front-lighting in scenes where no logical light source exists. Even between cuts of the same scene, the front-lighting persists into the new perspective, resulting in continuity errors and shifting shadows that shatter the very immersion the film claims to cultivate. This is compounded by an uneven sound design that lack consistency in dynamic and integration. Furthermore, mechanical cuts stitch scenes together without transition or narrative juxtaposition. As a result, the film feel like a collection of in-cohesive fragments that lacks vision. As mentioned previously, the film disguises narrative depth by the weight of its topic rather than by the quality of its writing. Despite the film's attempt to imitate observational realism, characters are treated as hollow ideological devices rather than real humans beings. The much applauded non-professional actor, Brahim Hadjadj, performs an Ali la Pointe that is painfully one-dimensional and mechanical, providing no window into the character's psyche (to the point that it is difficult to even recognise him as the protagonist). Ironically, the "villainous" Colonel Mathieu is given more complexity and range, feeling slightly more like a real individual instead of just a hollow political vessel. The film’s most egregious flaw is its poorly executed mechanical emotional manipulation from its sound and visual language. Death and suffering of Algerians are accompanied with religious scores and manufactured tears to evoke sanctity and martyrdom. In contrast, the death of European innocents are treated with cold, percussive score and lack of emotional outburst (even from themselves) to trivialise the tragedy. Disregarding the intent, the ostentatious and un-serious execution results in theatricality that ends up losing emotional grounding. Ultimately, The Battle of Algiers is less a work of art and more a technical manual for insurgency. It fails the "show, don't tell" rule with its paradoxical, dry narration and expositions that explains the how of the conflict while speaking little on the historical why. Concerningly, the film also directly proclaims the effectiveness of terrorism as a mean to gain UN support as well as the potency of torture (despite many research indicate otherwise). In the film's final scene, the irony of shouting for independence in the language of the coloniser is perhaps the film's most profound and most honest observation about the lasting scars of imperialism, yet unsurprisingly this is a depth that clearly escapes the interest of the film.

my "remedial film school" project — catching up on the movies that most frequently turn up on greatest-of-all-time lists — has sometimes led to disappointments, but few have been as much of a struggle for me as this one. Admittedly it wasn't ideal viewing circumstances, pulling it up in fits and starts and consistently tuning out, such that it took me three or four sessions to make it through these two hours. I think it's just so unlike any film that I've seen before that I genuinely didn't know how to watch it, and the film was not in a hurry to teach me. Probably my biggest barrier is that it seems so disinterested in the humanity of everyone on screen — we don't follow hardly any characters consistently enough to get a sense of who they are as people, with the weird exception of Colonel Mathieu. Yes war dehumanizes everyone, but that doesn't mean the film needs to help the process along. Brahim Hadjadj plays Ali La Pointe as a sullen-faced silent type, which makes a certain amount of sense for his situation but makes him unengaging as the lead of a film. And the movie's weird dispassionate documentary-style tone means that I spent the whole time waiting for a moment of connection that never came. Time passes, people die, a series of events is shown, with little sense of causality or logic. But I suppose maybe frustrated restlessness is the desired effect after all?

Not sure what all the fuss is about with this one. I give it credit for retelling actual events that went mostly untold and a nice large scale spectacle at the very end. Ultimately though this is a slog and entirely unremarkable, my partner even fell asleep. We follow the events of an attempted revolution headed by the Algerians against the occupying French forces. That's all that happens the entire runtime. Every single character that we follow has zero depth and all we know about them is they must kill the French imperialists or kill the people killing the French imperialists. There is almost zero weight given to the importance of this revolution, we don't really see how the French occupation negatively effects the Algerians, we do however see how the French was effected via the numerous terrorist attacks, but it's hard to sympathize with the French victims as they shouldn't be there to begin with. This isn't some deeply nuanced and enlightened approach to make us think critically about the cost of revolution, it's simply a shallow reshowing of events that don't deliver much emotional bearing. This movie spends all of its time on the failed revolution, and shoe horns in the successful revolution in the last 10 minutes. Battle of Algiers doesn't even hold up well from a film making perspective, as previously mentioned, the characters are surface level and the performances match. It's scenes of violence and "action" are very noticeably fake, removing all chance of viscera. This is a film that does not succeed on a story telling level other than to create a document of history, albeit even then only painting a minuscule fraction of the picture.

Got so excited because the music in this is used in Inglorious Basterds [45] On the technical level in regards to the psychology, camera-work, and thematic weight the depictions in this hold, this is an astoundingly well-done film. It has quite literally been used by both resistance fighters and militaries to gain insight on how these movements can be ran, it was written by someone who was a member of the FLN (National Liberation Front), contained actors who had lived through the accounts detailed, and was shot on location where the events occurred. There are of course some historical inaccuracies, but by and large this is a frighteningly accurate depiction of this event, and furthermore it makes you feel like you're there. It's also important to note that both the French authorities and FLN did even worse things in real life. Specifically the French, as this really cannot capture the breadth of killings and abuse they inflicted on Algerians to get their way (also highlights how useless the UN is and has always been). And there's one specific scene in this movie that is absolutely the highlight for me where Colonel Mathieu claims they cannot be fascists or oppressors as many of them were part of the resistance movement fighting against the Nazis ( cough couch Israel cough couch ). But this line is just wonderful, and for me it beautifully illuminates the uncomfortable reality of brutality humans are capable of; if our worldview justifies it we can be just as capable of the evils we decry. And this also gets into the meat of the question this film is proposing: what is justified in my fight for freedom? We are definitely on the side of the FLN in terms of perspective, but the film never tries to state that they are the good guys (and while I think we can come to the conclusion that comparatively they were, they still weren't "good" guys). It inherently puts the question to us when we are watching them bomb places with civilians of "is this justified?" Personally I don't know, I would like to say they could've instead bombed military targets or done some other thing, but the reality very well may be that this was the only way to make effective change (and when you are trying to change the fact that you are being brutally oppressed by colonizers, that effective change is pretty darn important). It's also interesting as they are fully willing to shirk things such as Sharia Law to wage this war (such as the women disguising themselves as French women) when the aim is to be able to reinstate that law once they have gained their independence (a whole other decision that I believe would warrant a whole new version of FLN to fight against the oppression that that brings). In the end I think this is wonderful at making you have to weigh what is right in your own mind, and hopefully reassess your own beliefs. At the very least this movie shines a light bulb on an event (and an issue) that deserves to be known and talked about. France still hasn't issued an apology to Algeria (just how the U.S. hasn't to Vietnam about things as basic as the effects of agent orange, or Japan to China about Nanjing, nor Britain to India, etc. etc.) and while I do believe the status of the world is much better today, it takes a simple Google to see this is still occurring all over. And I believe the biggest part that makes it overwhelmingly depressing is that it is truly completely manufactured by humans to a degree that is mind-numbingly pointless. So why am I giving this such a review after going over all that which I have gleamed from the movie? Cause I didn't really enjoy watching it that much. While all of the above are true, I never found myself caring about the events of the story. Characters are barely fleshed out, and they jump from person to person so quickly it's impossible to truly get invested in any particular aspect. The bag drop off scene is easily the best as it gives enough room to breathe and let you ruminate with the emotions of the characters, but outside of this it is purely the analytics of what is being done and the loud declaration of why (which is of course always for a free Algeria or because France doesn't want to give up Algeria) with no real inspection into the characters and deeper motivations. It sets me at a removed distance from what is going on, and I unfortunately could care little less what would happen to everyone. Of course I am sad when innocents die, but that is because innocents died, not because of anything the film was doing to invest me. Freedom isn't free, but what cost are we willing to pay, and what does free even truly mean to us?

While this film may seem like an almost shattering statement meant to invoke a sense of injustice within you as it details the wrongdoings of the government and the dangers of colonization, for me, it just seemed like pro-revolutionary propaganda, which, while that is a movement I completely think is justified, propaganda tends not to have much of anything beyond its purpose of making you say that's bad and that's good. I would've preferred a more introspective look into the lack of morality that revolution warrants in order to work, and the sacrifices that need to be made in order to continue it. This highlights, particularly, the oppression, racism, and the cruel generalization of the Arabs due to them only demanding that they want their home given back to them. It's reminiscent of Palestine's genocide, just on a smaller scale. The Battle of Algiers may be more of an exposition of what occurred in Algiers, with the intent of making the revolutionaries seem like heroes and the army look like an empire, which is why it is nowhere near my favorite film. Much like the many flaws OBAA had regarding its lack of any actual reflection or any sense of more abstract themes for me, both are still great films that only suffer from what they're missing. The film seeks to document the actions and the wrongdoings of the rebels and the army. It's not really followed by a plot, but rather an escalation of means as the rebels begin attaining more and more authority over the people of Algiers, and as they become a more prominent, symbolic force of hope for the people. What I did find more interesting was the French civilians' response to the rebels' attacks. The generalization and the prominent racism committed by them, while an understandable response to the rebels' terrorist attacks, is in no way excusable, and it's a concept I would've preferred to have seen more insight into. The army begins to employ "interrogation tactics" that in reality, are just glorified torture, and due to these, the entire rebel group begins to lose men. The film ends with them being wiped out from the map with the death of what I would say is the protagonist of the film. The best part for me was the ending, which was the insurrection of the Arabs against colonization by the French, and how the revolution serves as a catapult for them to join their efforts and unite. No longer were they going to be saved by a group of heroes; rather, they must be the heroes themselves. The film's themes are kind of empty. It's more about what the film shows you rather than what it indicates, which is my main issue with it. I hoped for some deeper statement on how revolution needs to be carried out with the disregard and the savagery that the oppressors have always fought with, and how that means that instead of being heroes or rebels in the most indicative sense, it would be redundant, and instead you must become something far darker, something far more immoral and soulless. You must echo the same brutality shown to you by the enemy so that you may prevail for your cause. Your intention may be different, but the consequences of your actions will be the same. Death in the name of a symbol; just that one is more hopeful and useful than the one employed by the opposition. This was nowhere to be found in the film, and while I understand that this film serves more as a documentation or a version of the story meant to entertain us, well, it lacking this kind of reflection really did a number on me because I like to think about films after watching them, and I felt almost nothing concerning this film's final statement. This is just personal preference, I suppose, and it has to do with the fact that I personally have more emotional connection to abstract themes rather than to evocative statements, so I guess you could say this just wasn't for me. The film's production was kind of insane now that I think about it? There are some explosions that really kind of surprised me due to the sheer impact of their force, and it makes me wonder if they actually did blow up buildings with people inside them. Anyways, the cinematography and the visuals obviously take a step back, considering this is a film that is heavily focused on telling its plot rather than being a good film. I think it's interesting how some parts were filmed, but in the visual department, I didn't find anything that really blew me away. The acting was also kind of disconnected from me because I think that the characters felt incredibly 1-dimensional and taken aback. It's more of a story in which the ideologies are the protagonists and the actual characters are just plot devices, which is not something I'm particularly fond of. The pacing was also incredibly long, and the entertainment value was just something that I didn't find, since it's a film that is stripped of any actual cinematic qualities. I'd like to say that it is an absolutely iconic reminder of the time and that its importance does not falter, but that also does not negate its qualities, which I didn't necessarily prefer.

+ : Le film évite le manichéisme et montre que les deux camps ont eux recours à des méthodes brutales et contestables pour atteindre leurs objectifs (sans avoir peur de déconcerter son public en montrant des attentats ou la torture) Le colonel Mathieu est le point fort du film. C’est un  ancien résistant et vétéran d’Indochine qui connaît la logique de la guérilla. A chacune de ses apparitions son intelligence et sa compétence sont mises en avant, que ce soit lors des briefings , lors de ses interactions avec les journalistes puis avec sa victoire militaire à la fin du film. C’est également dingue de ce dire qu’un des acteurs algérien fut un combattant pendant le conflit - : La Mise en scène du film a très très mal vieilli. De plus le fait que la plupart du cast soient des amateurs se voit avec un jeu d’acteur pas dingue. Puis il y’a une grosse disparité de qualité entre la première heure très pauvre avec un rythme plutôt lent et la deuxième heure qui est beaucoup mieux.

The premise described on letterboxed doesn’t start until nearly 50 minutes in. Prior to that, all we’re watching are radical extremists blowing up random civilians, which eventually comes together into some measure of purpose by the end. The sparse but thoughtful lines of dialogue illuminate the different narratives we use to try to justify our actions. The torture, tricks, and escalating tactics can be effective at times, but the film is ultimately at odds with itself. It wants to depict the mechanizations of revolution without sympathetic characters, only sympathetic factions. That’s admirable, but then it relies on excessive crash zooms and close ups on random crying people, a cheap, easy way to get the viewer enraged. Though I shouldn’t say random because they’re almost always the radicals, who by the end, are just terrorists gunning down pedestrian women. The film is not as impartial as it wants us to think it is, and unfortunately, I found myself kinda siding with the colonists who by and large followed some kind of ethical code (even if random grunts broke it on occasion). The radicals, by contrast, were so conniving that it really did feel like the colonists had every right to be suspicious of them. I think we’re naturally drawn to side with the underdogs because we know that their options are far more limiting, but I also think if they’d focused on actually targeting the French military, instead of regular people, or otherwise did anything that showed them rustling with the moral lows they were stooping to, it would have revealed their humanity in a way that shoving a camera into someone’s face doesn’t.

La bataille d'Alger est un film incontournable sur la guerre d'Algérie, il est même le plus connu internationalement. Le film se déroule durant une période précise de la guerre que l'on appelle « la bataille d'Alger », période qui a duré de 1956 à 1957. Durant cette période, Alger devint un véritable champ de bataille où le FLN et l'armée française se sont livrés à des combats sans merci. Les deux camps ont fait preuve d'une extrême violence, notamment lors des attentats commis par le FLN contre des innocents ou encore à travers les tortures pratiquées par l'armée française. Cette violence, que l'on ressent tout au long du film, est caractéristique des régimes coloniaux, mais surtout des débuts de révolutions. En effet, Frantz Fanon , dans Les Damnés de la Terre , explique que la violence est une étape nécessaire pour que le colonisé, privé de toute initiative et de libertés intérieures et extérieures, retrouve ses droits. La violence extrême est donc nécessaire, mais elle constitue seulement la première étape de la révolution, elle n'est pas la révolution en soi. Cette étape de la révolte et de la lutte armée est la forme infantile de la révolution, c'est-à-dire qu'elle constitue le premier mouvement nécessaire, mais qu'ensuite tout le travail reste à faire. La révolte permet d'arriver à l'indépendance dans le cas de l'Algérie, qui devient officiellement indépendante le 5 juillet 1962. Ce mouvement d'insurrection fut impossible à canaliser pour l'armée française, malgré sa supériorité militaire, c'est pourquoi De Gaulle conclut progressivement qu'une Algérie française n'était pas durable. C'est donc par la violence et le courage que l'Algérie devint indépendante. Comme le souligne Fanon , le plus dur dans la révolution est l'après-révolte : une fois que les opprimés ont gagné, que faut-il faire ? Comment s'organiser ? En Algérie, Ben Bella fut le premier président en 1963, mais il fut renversé en 1965 par un coup d'État. C'est ensuite Boumédiène qui prit la relève en renforçant le poids de l'État dans l'économie. Des politiques d'industrialisation (Industries industrialisantes ou modèle Feldman-Mahalanobis) furent mises en œuvre, mais avec un succès limité, car cette stratégie d'industrialisation est autocentrée et nécessite donc une forte demande intérieure. Or, en Algérie, la population représentait alors moins de 40 millions d'habitants. Cependant, grâce au pétrole et au gaz (95 % des recettes d'exportation algériennes), l'État a pu financer certains projets tout en restant fermé au tourisme et à une grande partie du commerce extérieur. Aujourd'hui, les relations franco-algériennes sont tendues. L'affaire Boualem Sansal en est un exemple. Il existe toujours des frictions entre les deux États, notamment autour du Sahara occidental et du passé colonial français.

What impressed me most is that the movie refuses easy heroes. Both sides commit brutality. Both sides justify brutality. The French military often wins tactically. Raids, arrests, intelligence gathering, interrogations. The Algerian independence movement wins strategically. The film’s central point is devastatingly simple: An insurgency is not defeated when its fighters are defeated. It’s defeated when its cause loses legitimacy. The French win battles. Then lose Algeria. One of the rare war films that feels more interested in power and politics than victory.

Watching Black & White Movies #5 Twentieth-century evil for me is embodied in the terrorization of militaries operating brutally, efficiently, and without remorse. Yes, Mathieu embodies this threat. But don’t Ali La Pointe and Saadi Yacef Djafar as well? In that sense, the film is careful to show that history’s judgment depends on which side of it you occupy (eg. maybe French colonialism is bad and the french suck!) What the film captures exceptionally well is the terror created by war, portraying both sides in meticulous detail. The reason I rated it so low is that this documentary-style approach leaves Mathieu as the only substantially developed character. As a result, I find it difficult to see the film as a full exploration of its subject; it’s a documentary-esque sequence of events, but not a “complete” examination of the conflict. Its nuance is incomplete. Rather than offering a truly comprehensive portrayal, it presents a focused account that inevitably privileges certain perspectives over others. Italian neorealism is not particularly my thing either and this is a rare Morricone score miss. At the very least it is completely impossible to dislike the Mathieu discussing Sartre scene love you Sarte.

Un excellent film où le cinéma d’action moderne est né. Un film politique du réalisateur italien Gillo Pontecorvo. La manière dont le film est produit est juste glaçante, même radicale. Basé sur la lutte pour l’indépendance algérienne, c’est un film qui brûle la rétine et le cœur du spectateur, assistant à cela jusqu’au point d’éveiller les consciences. Les acteurs sont bien choisis et ciblés de manière très précise. On ne cherche pas de grandes stars hollywoodiennes mais des visages de haine marqués par cet épisode colonial, qui retransmettent leur identité de combattant au téléspectateur. Les décors également, on veut de l’authenticité jusqu’au bout. On tourne dans la vraie Casbah d’Alger où, quelques années auparavant, des guérillas avaient véritablement eu lieu. Les plans également sont aussi un chef-d’œuvre. La caméra, tenue par Marcello Mastroianni, jette toutes les règles et tous les codes du monde du cinéma, filmant à portée de main pour nous introduire dans le monde réel qu’a vécu l’Algérie durant cette conquête coloniale. Il filme comme on court dans la Casbah, comment on se cache, comment on respire ainsi que l’on combat. Des cadres parfois instables, flous, mais totalement choisis pour l’immersion la plus totale, avec un vrai style tremblant de réalité. En conclusion, un film d’une expérience hors norme, nous faisant vibrer tout au long du visionnage, en comprenant la vie des algériens durant 132 ans de conquête coloniale sanglante menée par la France.

What a setting to watch this film for the first time. The AFI Fellows audience was deathly silent throughout the whole screening. There is so little levity of any kind to hold onto. Yet, all of us were captivated from start to finish. We experienced a world with a beating heart, where every character we followed felt authentic and purposeful. Every time I felt I could justify one side's view, the film deliberately introduced a more complex perspective, forcing me to reconsider. I think THE BATTLE OF ALGIERS represents a small miracle. As powerful as the story is, I am more inspired and impressed that this story was allowed to be told in the first place. In the end, I especially related to the occupied citizens of Algiers, especially those who sacrificed everything for the cause of freedom. When it comes to war, there are no winners. My fundamental belief is that when we turn to violence, the consequences are far too many and complex to understand, let alone decide a victor. But the Algerian people deserved their freedom, and witnessing their drive for that cause lights a fire in me. This is what great movies do! I hope to use this battle cry in my own ventures into storytelling.

It’s a classic for a reason. There’s something so awe-inspiring about how visceral The Battle of Algiers comes across. From the gritty black and white, newsreel style filmmaking to the passion of the Algerian citizens, most of them reeling from  the real life events, all of them non-actors, there is a tangibility that only neorealism at its most effective can create. The plot mostly drags, I expected that, but there are so many things to admire. I especially loved that it didn’t shy away from the less pretty stuff and the gorgeous score from Ennio Morricone.

A lot of my favorite movies, their very existence is a miracle. ‘The Battle Of Algiers’ is no exception, with both the uphill backstory of the FLN driving France out of their country and, as people with no experience in film making, producing a movie about this series of historical events. “Can you separate the art from the artist?” okay sure but can you separate the art from history? Before getting into that, in a vacuum this is a thrilling movie that succeeds in filling its viewer with on-the-edge-of-their seat uncertainty of what’s to come. Just like when one watches ‘Titanic’ we know how it ends but we still get wrapped up in what’s happening. It would be impossible to spoil ‘The Battle Of Algiers’, no series of words can summarize the experience of watching, feeling. The sequence leading up to the first explosions in civilian areas goes toe to toe with the most well made suspense/thrillers. Of which, one of the biggest strengths of ‘The Battle Of Algiers’ is how it portrays its subjects. Obviously we are meant to empathize with the FLN fighters, but it doesn’t stop there. The “bad guys”, the French, aren’t shown in a two dimensional villainous manner. (which is in stark contrast to the recently released ‘I Am Cuba’, two years prior.) Even the main antagonist Colonel Phillippe Mathieu is shown as intelligent, cunning, capable. Maybe emphathize is the wrong word, “humanize” might be better. But what are we supposed to think when there’s emphasis on a baby licking an ice cream cone moments before the explosion that will brutally maim, kill them? In the same breath, we see the uncertainty (?) of the women before erupting carnage. There is a depth here that is absent in nearly all movies built around these types of events. Especially made in the U.S. where all terrorists are painted with evil brushes. No matter where you lie politically, ‘The Battle Of Algiers’ is a must watch that will either add to your perspective or straight up twist it into something different. I can see why the Black Panthers used to screen this for each other. (Or why it was included in ‘One Battle After Another’ as a way for Leonardo Di Caprio’s character to relive his days of fighting the forces at large.) This rewatch has cemented the film in my Top 10 Of All Time. It is a miracle of film making no doubt.

TOP 28 LETTERBOXD! FULL REVIEW! Where other war movies fall short at showing the full brutality of war, this shows it in the most extraordinary way, unlike anything you'll ever see. Gripping, intense, and suspenseful; it feels so realistic that you'll be tricked into thinking that some of these scenes come from found footage. In The Battle of Algiers , they show that during wartime, humans forfeit their morals and jurisdiction to achieve their goals by doing whatever it takes. But they show it from both sides: the Algerian rebellion and the French government. What’s even more interesting is that the Algerians are played by actual Algerians, all non-professional actors, some of whom had actually fought for the FLN. They show the injustice and oppression the French brought upon them. French law enforcement murder innocent people and use bombs, to the point where the Algerians can’t let it pass anymore. So they use the same violence as a form of retaliation. We get a peek at how rebels actually fight against their oppressors, and we root for them because of it. There isn’t a main character, but that’s not even necessary because the message, story, and plot are what’s important. We see multiple characters who get their moments, and we actually care for them in such a short span of time. When they execute a plan, we’re glued to the screen because of the intensity. Ennio Morricone’s music sounds like a ticking time bomb during those suspenseful moments. There is no melodrama: this is the real thing. What’s intriguing is that Algerians are depicted not as one-dimensional characters, but as the centre of the story. They terrorize, but we get to see their motivations beforehand: oppression, over a century of colonialism, and innocent people being murdered. French laws and repression created the conditions for the rebellion, and the Algerians give the French a taste of their own medicine, but the French come back even more fiercely. This is the story of what has been happening throughout history, and what is still happening today. That’s what makes this movie so timeless and important. Dangerous people grab power and start wars for their own personal gain, but lead their own people astray by distorting their viewpoint. Like Vladimir Putin, for example: a clever and dangerous man with an enormous amount of power, willing to go to war against Ukraine in pursuit of Russian power and influence, while justifying it through distorted arguments. Colonel Mathieu (Jean Martin) represents those dangerous men with enough power to break through all morals and laws. When we get introduced to Colonel Mathieu, we can already tell: this guy is bad news. This is a person who is dangerously clever and is there to stop the terrorists by whatever means necessary... After watching Lawrence of Arabia , I thought:' What can top this masterpiece? Will I ever be as baffled by a movie as I was with this?' The Battle of Algiers did it for me. This is the greatest movie I’ve ever seen. 10/10! Greatest movies OAT: boxd.it/XjeOk

the movie was off to a good start, with the music, animation, and plot, even the setting taking place in 1929, pre-WW2, and within the timeframe of Italy joining Germany, all aligning well and coming out beautifully. i’ve questioned Ghibli writing a misogynistic lead and limiting men to brainless, women-obsessed creatures, as Ghibli is widely known for tender love, genuine connections, and respect amongst all genders, but it came to serve the greater good of proving the lead wrong and showing women gaining respect over and over again. a nice way to deliver an idea, until it wasn’t. Gina and Fio are truly the stars of the movie. even with how few scenes Gina got, she still showed up during the climaxes of the plot, often solving things herself. and then there’s Fio, the 17-year-old girl with ambitions to design airplanes and see the beauty of the world. i loved Fio so much. she’s ambitious, well-spoken, brave, and talented. i always love seeing a hardworking, decision-making woman in media, let alone when she’s young and charming too. the plot follows Marco, a pilot who has lost hope in humanity due to all the torture and pain he’s seen during the war, which left him with nothing but survivor’s guilt. as he’s seen “all the good ones die,” he turned into a pig, which people theorize is a way of showing him detaching from the pain of being human, experiencing loss, love, and joy. he gave up on who he once was and became an aimless pig, no longer who he was before and unsure of who to become. but being surrounded by Fio’s charm and heartwarming personality restored his faith in humanity, allowing him to leave Porco behind and become Marco again. hence the sentence, “Porco never showed his face again.” the airplane by Gina’s island also suggests she won her bet, and that the night visitor reciprocated her love, which he wouldn’t have done before due to his low self-esteem and guilt. he thought she deserved any of the pilots who died, but not him. he doesn’t even know why he survived that day. moving on from that fear of unworthiness, he flies higher than ever and loves Gina how she wants to be loved. it’s a beautiful view of the movie that really makes sense. but here comes the elephant in the room... the kiss. it’s important to note that Fio is 17 years old, and Marco is in his 30s, if not early 40s. they connect as family, whether that’s shown through familial banter and fights or even encouragement and support. Fio notes throughout the movie that she’s similar to Marco when he was her age, showcasing the experience gap between them. she’s just starting, and yet she kisses him in a way relatives shouldn’t kiss. whether that’s a hint towards Gina-Fio-Marco engaging in polyamory, or just to show the genuine, impulsive joy and love Fio feels, and how her love for Marco came from him allowing her to experiment, i genuinely don’t care. that was completely unnecessary. if anything, most people were confused as to why it would happen. if Gina were the one who kissed him, it would’ve helped the plot immensely. it would’ve made sense. but the writer(s) found a semi-incestuous way of making it work, and it completely ruined the movie. which is why it gets one star. pedophilia isn’t a good plot.

non riesco a mettere più di due stelle perché il modo in cui è rappresentato il legame tra Marco/Porco e Fio, per me, “overshadows” l’intera trama. ho guardato il film al cineforum del left camp, carico di mille aspettative accumulatesi negli anni (perché ne ho sempre sentito solo parlare bene), per poi ritrovarmi completamente spiazzato da quella dinamica di cui nessuno mi aveva mai proferito parola. da quando Marco/Porco mette piede nella Piccolo SRL, per me è stato un crescendo di disagio e disgusto, che per tutto il film mi ha fatto pensare “ma ora questa dinamica si smonterà, vero?”, per poi non smontarsi mai e anzi, peggiorare con il finale! ma dico io: che bisogno c’era di rendere la ragazzina 17enne l’oggetto della bramosia di decine di uomini adulti per tutto il film, senza rappresentarlo in modo critico? erano necessari i commenti sui suoi fianchi e sul suo sedere (!!) , o il modo in cui viene costantemente trattata come una ragazzina innamorata di un 36enne (Marco/Porco), che vuole a tutti i costi le sue attenzioni (anche chiedendogli di poterlo baciare, per poi pure farlo alla fine del film)? e ci tengo a mettere bene in chiaro una cosa: sono perfettamente consapevole del fatto che il film sia ambientato nel 1929 e pubblicato nel 1992. ciò non toglie che la dinamica tra i due personaggi potesse essere scritta in mille modi diversi da questo. il fatto che Fio abbia 17 anni e il legame con Marco non sia di tipo padre-figlia, bensì dipinto come un “rapporto speciale” più ambiguo, è una scelta DELIBERATA di rappresentazione della classica narrativa in cui “l’ amore di una ragazza candida e innocente, che vede il mondo con occhi diversi, è l’elemento salvifico del troubled man adulto di turno”. Porco letteralmente viene SALVATO dal bacio (sulla bocca) che gli dà Fio. ogni elemento, ogni scena che caratterizza questo lungo pattern che si dipana per tutta la pellicola, non è casuale, ma è lì per un motivo. simboleggia una rappresentazione ben precisa. e non è che il film è semplicemente “invecchiato male”, è che la cultura di base da cui parte non vede la problematicità di questa narrativa. e a questo mi collego a una critica più generale: è davvero impressionante vedere come queste narrative (che rimandano a ideali di p3dofilia, mi dispiace ma va detto: il pattern è lì, è visibile, gli elementi sono tanti e non è un semplice evento che si verifica una tantum nel film) siano sempre state così normalizzate, cioè viste come normali, da tanti, tantissimi uomini nell’industria cinematografica, così come in tutto il mondo. inutile dire che sono rimasto molto deluso da Miyazaki (anche se, alla fine, è sempre un uomo di una certa età…), e che penso non riuscirò a guardare i suoi film per qualche breve tempo. sono molto amareggiato, perché “la Principessa Mononoke” era entrato nella mia top 4 film di sempre, e ora francamente non mi sento molto a mio agio e a posto con me stesso nel metterlo lì. penso che lascerò quel posto ancora vacante per un po’. in conclusione, voglio dire che metto comunque due stelle anziché una perché, per onestà intellettuale, ci sono tante altre tematiche nel film che vengono trattate bene e che si meritano di non metterlo nella spazzatura dei film da una stella. ma qui si apre la riflessione su quello che più di tutto mi fa stare male: come è possibile che per anni ne avessi sentito soltanto tessere le lodi in giro, e davvero nessuno avesse pensato di muovere prima qualche critica riguardo a questo tema presente nel film? per me è un inferno vivere in un mondo in cui questo film è osannato (specialmente negli ambienti “compagni” e di sinistra, solo per quella cazzo di quote sull’antifascismo), soprattutto se acriticamente. mi fa sentire ancora più alienato nel mio disagio. spero che in futuro, se mi capiterà di guardare film in cui noto nuovamente questo tipo di dinamica/narrativa, questo succeda in compagnia di persone che hanno la mia stessa sensibilità su questo tema.

i never liked this miyazaki as much as i did the other ones when i was younger, and didn’t understand why until rewatching it at an older age. now i realize it was likely because of the pervasive and needless misogyny littered throughout the film. i may not have had the vocabulary to label the prejudice in this movie when i first watched it, but that does not make the seed planted in my young mind that my girlhood made me inferior somehow any less harmful. in other miyazaki films (spirited away comes to mind), women and girls are treated and presented simply as humans while in Porco gender is emphasized and stressed almost constantly. i was almost uncomfortably hyper-aware of my own existence as a woman and how i would be an outsider if present in this film. if i was an engineer, i would be doubted. if i threw a wrench, my arm would be insulted. little me likely didn’t catch the underhanded, unnecessarily sexist, and borderline predatory commentary in this film but, whether fortunately or unfortunately (i haven’t decided yet) big me caught it like a ball in a mit. i wish i could go back in time and tell little me to pay no mind to the line “you throw like a girl,” but rather to remember only “all middle aged men are pigs.”

I love Ghibli films, but after rewatching Porco Rosso, I think it has major structural flaws. The film suffers from severe tonal whiplash—it tries to explore heavy themes like PTSD, survivor's guilt, and the anti-fascism, but constantly undercuts them with plain silliness. For instance, the sky graveyard scene is a haunting depiction of war trauma, but its emotional weight is completely undone by placing it alongside goofy slapstick and cartoonish pirate fights. Porco's transformation into a pig is clearly a metaphor for self-loathing, yet the movie treats his condition as a punchline far more often than a psychological burden. Furthermore, the treatment of Fio is deeply uncomfortable and unnecessary. She is introduced as a brilliant 17-year-old engineer, yet the plot constantly reduces her to an object of male desire. The climax literally turns her into a prize to be won in a fistfight between two older men, which completely strips away her agency. Finally, the film's politics feel superficial. Porco’s iconic line, 'I'd rather be a pig than a fascist,' sounds great, but his actual stance is just passive avoidance. He doesn't resist fascism; he just retreats to a private island to work as a mercenary. Using anti-fascism as an aesthetic backdrop without engaging in actual resistance makes the slogans feel empty. Also this film was catered towards middle age men — it started off as a short in - flight film for airlines. So just by this alone it makes the whole Fio thing worse. I could rate it lower, but there’s worse movie out there. It has some charm in like the animation/art.

To this day, I still can’t quite say where I should place Porco Rosso amongst the other Ghibli films. On the one hand, it’s a visually stunning film with plenty of aviation action, beautiful scenes set on the island and out across the sea, and a great deal of heart. But on the other hand, the story is actually very simple and centres on a feud between two pilots and the road to their ultimate showdown. Just between the lines, Porco Rosso repeatedly offers bits of information that add depth to the world and its characters. However, these are very rarely explored in any real detail. Porco Rosso is definitely worth a watch for fans of the studio, but it’s more of a light-hearted slice-of-life film that’s great fun whilst you’re watching it, yet doesn’t leave much of a lasting impression the days after.

a cena do "cemitério de aviões" é arrebatadora. daquelas que deslumbram, mas, ao mesmo tempo, te devoram. para mim, é uma das melhores de todo o estúdio. as sequências de voo também são impressionantes. nelas, dá para ver a paixão de miyazaki pela aviação em cada detalhe de capricho. sinto que "porco rosso" é quase como sua carta de amor aos aviões. porco é um homem que deixou de ser humano em um mundo cada vez mais desumanizado. trata-se de uma amálgama metafórica entre a visão que ele tem de si mesmo por carregar a culpa de ser um sobrevivente no pós-guerra e o abismo que se cria entre ele e a sociedade. ele voluntariamente se transforma em uma figura socialmente indesejada, pois prefere abdicar de seu status e de sua própria forma humana a se curvar e servir a um regime autoritário. fica evidente como, para miyazaki, o ato de voar sempre foi a representação máxima da liberdade e da beleza humana. os céus, antes ocupados por "aviadores românticos", agora passam a ser uma mera ferramenta de propaganda militar. mas, ainda assim, não consegui deixar de me incomodar com a relação entre porco e fio. a audácia e o otimismo inabalável dela na humanidade são as forças responsáveis por fazer com que marco, posteriormente, comece a fazer as pazes consigo mesmo. enquanto marco, engolido pelo nacionalismo vazio, escolhe se isolar em seu pessimismo e acreditar que "todos os homens bons morreram", fio representa o amanhã, incorporando a juventude que carrega o espírito revolucionário de recusa à imutabilidade que aparenta estar posta. em um primeiro momento, tudo isso me pareceu meio nebuloso e senti que a mensagem perdia força com essa relação ambígua entre os dois. ao mesmo tempo que se constrói uma postura quase paternal quando ele repreende as atitudes dos homens ao redor que a objetificam constantemente, o filme reforça a atração que ele sente por ela em diversas vezes. essa dubiedade estética e narrativa me impediu, inicialmente, de comprar a dinâmica entre os personagens e de me cativar por eles por completo. mas mudei de perspectiva quando soube o que o próprio miyazaki falou sobre a obra. sabendo que ele declarou que todos os homens de meia-idade se transformam em porcos, e que projetou no protagonista suas próprias frustrações, passei a ver essa dubiedade com outros olhos. percebi que ela reflete uma escolha de sobrepor o embate ideológico limpo a uma autocrítica muito crua da masculinidade. marco é um herói político firme, mas moralmente rústico e impregnado pelo cinismo de seu tempo. esse contraponto é evidente até na vida real. nem mesmo os nossos heróis históricos estavam limpos dessa sujeira da época em que viviam. ao escancarar as contradições do personagem em vez de poupá-lo, a obra nos lembra que mesmo as figuras mais avançadas politicamente carregavam pontos cegos, e revela como é fundamental para as novas gerações encarar e superar essa herança ultrapassada por dentro dos próprios movimentos de mudança. antes eu ia dizer que não tinha gostado tanto, mas agora sinto que gosto do filme. preciso rever com outros olhos para me decidir por completo.

8.5/10 i just know somebody in the studio said “until pigs fly” and miyazaki went “…say that again?” Out of all the Ghibli movies I’ve seen so far, this one is definitely the funniest and most unique in tone. We got the antiwar central theme— classic Ghibli stuff— but to put it in both a comedic lens and put it in a minimum fantasy historical-fiction-feeling setting and tone is inspired . I truly did not expect the wildly different directions this movie went in, and it’s so tightly written that it’s able to pull it all off both believably and emotionally . I will say— and this may be a product of this being set in the 1930s— the romance is written a bit questionably . I won’t say much for the sake of preserving the impact of certain character details, but what I will say is Porco Rosso and Fio’s mentor and apprentice relationship is sweet. I’m very glad that it does not extend any further than that . End of sentence. Not groundbreaking in terms of Ghibli, but still very much up to their standards of guud . It’s nice to see Studio Ghibli’s range! They do whimsical magic and wonder very well, but they can also change up the tone and their approach to magic in ways that make for very different and still good movies.

My thoughts on his curse even being on how he stays in the swine form due to his constant self perception of himself as a pig. The cast in the film is great too, I quite enjoyed the many designs of the pirates in the film but the highlight to be for characters has to be Gina and how her singing is portrayed in the film. I’d rather be a pig than a fascist This iconic line rings true today more than ever. As we are once again entering an era where world leaders are clamoring for power and dismantling democracy left and right. We are once again entering an era where young men and women are shipped off to war, and genocide is allowed to take place on full display. There are two main themes or thoughts, I guess, that stick with me from this film. And I’ve always enjoyed this commentary from the film. But re-watching it now for the first time in at least 15 years these hit so much harder: First off, the horrors of war and their impact on a person. There’s a famous quote that goes something along the lines of “no one ever survives a war, the person who returns is not the same one that left”. Porco Rosso himself is a LITERAL allegory for this, he is no longer a man but a pig. He is forever detached from reality, which impacts himself put also the people with whom he had previous relations. Secondly, this film about sea plane pilots on the Adriatic coast gives off many similar vibes to various westerns and films about pirates. The value of freedom is tremendous in a world which is shrinking, to the point where being broke (or literally being a pig) is a price worth paying. But this freedom is threatened by rapidly encroaching imperial movement. I really like the parallels between the airplanes in this film and the ships in media such as One Piece or Pirates of the Caribbean. What a ship is, is freedom. I be yearning for some sort of vessel where I can vanish over the horizon, capturing my freedom. This film is also very interesting due to Miyazaki's personal ambivalence and kind of embarassment to this film. He has many times called the film "foolish" and deemed it very self-indulgent and targeted at the wrong audience. A personal goal of Miyazaki's when making film is said to be to create worlds of escapism and childlike wonder. Where his works can, and often do, handle quite real and dark themes, but at the core there should be hope and childlike wonder. Porco Rosso however contrasts this, as there is no real "happy ending". Rather it leaves off quite melancholic and ambiguous, he doesn't become human and get the girl. As well as the meat of the story focusing on our grumpy middle-aged protagonist.

Porco Rosso é o filme mais melancólico e adulto do Miyazaki, e é justamente por isso que ele funciona tão bem. A premissa é absurda, um piloto da Primeira Guerra Mundial que foi transformado em porco, mas o filme trata isso com uma naturalidade que faz você esquecer a estranheza em minutos e simplesmente aceitar que aquele homem escolheu ser um porco porque o mundo dos humanos o decepcionou demais. A beleza do filme está nas coisas que ele não diz. A guerra, o amor não resolvido com Gina, a recusa de Marco em voltar à forma humana, tudo é tratado com uma leveza que esconde uma tristeza profunda, e é nesse contraste que o filme brilha. As cenas de voo são lindas, a animação é impecável e a atmosfera do Adriático te transporta de um jeito que poucos filmes conseguem. A ressalva é que o filme é mais contemplativo do que narrativo, e quem espera um arco dramático mais definido pode sentir falta de uma resolução mais clara, já que Miyazaki prefere deixar tudo em aberto, como a própria vida... No fim, Porco Rosso é um filme sobre desilusão e sobre a escolha de se isolar quando o mundo já não faz sentido. É leve na superfície e pesado por baixo, e é exatamente isso que o torna especial. E eu amo de fato, esta frase abaixo. "Eu prefiro ser um porco a ser um fascista."

Malcolm X had his phones tapped, was stalked by the FBI, and had informants surround him under the COINTELPRO program. MLK Jr. had the FBI sending him anonymous letters blackmailing him and telling him to kill himself. Not 30 years later, they greenlight movies portraying these people in tailored, Hollywood lights. You tell me what's more plausible: that America had a radical ideological shift in a couple of decades, or that they decided it would be more effective for them to hijack these incredibly nuanced movements borne of blood and bones, and turn them into just another story of revolution. We normally only make movies for and tell the stories of revolutionaries who had their visions come to life. Those who failed are forgotten; they'll probably have their name uttered for the last time by a family members a few decades after they're buried. Is this the world Malcolm X imagined? Malcolm X failed, as admirable as he may have been. America is the only place where the dead bodies of revolutionaries are exhumed, dressed up, and paraded around as if their visions have come to life. America is the only place where they can get away with not changing by making their revolutionaries dance on stage, dead or alive, to make it seem like something has changed. They put them through the school curriculum criterion. Rosa Parks didn't give up her seat? She's through. MLK had a dream? Let him through. Nat Turner led an incredibly violent slave rebellion? Nah, make him wait 2 centuries instead of 2 decades before we give him a story; he did too much. It is because of this facade of change that I have an inherent mistrust of anything that comes out of Hollywood. The American film industry has become a monster of unfathomable proportions, and it would be crazy naïve not to entertain (or accept entirely) the idea that it is used to push whatever political narrative Western civilization wants perpetuated at that specific point in time. I love this movie. It is amazing, but I would rather approach it with a cautious hate than with open arms just to be one of the many victims seeded with America's culture machine. (Texto en español e inglés) Of the 202 minutes that Malcolm X runs, approximately 202 of them are unnecessary. Few films achieve such a feat: to be a masterclass in how to attain such a degree of formal mediocrity that, after nearly three and a half hours, one can barely come up with a dozen memorable shots—and perhaps not even five. It is also a masterclass in cynicism on Spike Lee’s part: nothing says “we have thought deeply about representation” quite like placing a group of Black girls among the crowd worshipping Malcolm X at the end, a character whose misogyny the film seems far too busy aestheticizing to bother actually confronting. P.S. The dance scene in which Malcolm meets the white girl is, in itself, one of the greatest examples of failed technical showmanship I can remember since the explosion of the Challenger space shuttle. ——————- De los 202 minutos que dura Malcolm X, le sobran aproximadamente 202. Pocas películas consiguen semejante proeza: ser una clase magistral de cómo alcanzar tal grado de mediocridad formal que, después de casi tres horas y media, uno apenas puede rescatar una decena de planos memorables —y quizá ni siquiera cinco—. También es una clase magistral de cinismo por parte de Spike Lee: nada dice mejor «hemos pensado profundamente en la representación» que colocar, al final, a unas niñas negras entre la multitud que venera a Malcolm X, un personaje cuya misoginia la película parece demasiado ocupada estetizando como para molestarse realmente en problematizarla. Posdata: la escena del baile en la que Malcolm conoce a la chica blanca constituye, por sí sola, uno de los mayores ejemplos de alarde técnico fallido que recuerdo desde la explosión del transbordador Challenger.

I found this film interesting but also quite frustrating. Despite the long runtime, I came away with only a vague understanding of his political and religious views. I also found it strange that the Civil Rights Movement is barely mentioned because it feels like an important part of understanding Malcolm X and his place in American history. For someone who doesn't already know much about him, the film doesn't always provide enough context. His evolution as a person is interesting but I wanted the film to explore his ideas and contradictions in more depth. Denzel Washington gives a very strong performance and he is definitely one of the best things about the film. The production is also impressive and the historical atmosphere feels convincing. It's an interesting film but I found it too long and not informative enough about such a complicated historical figure. A well-made but frustrating historical drama.

I really wanted to like this more, especially given the subject and Denzel Washington’s presence, but honestly? This was a frustrating watch. Way too long and overexposed — it drags itself out for over three hours and somehow still feels like it’s just hammering you with information instead of guiding you through a story. It’s less of a movie and more like someone decided to do a Wikipedia reading session, page by page. There’s barely any emotional depth. It doesn’t feel like a character study or a lived experience — just a checklist of events with Denzel stepping in and out of different time periods while the editing makes sure you’re never quite sure where you are. The way it cuts between scenes, especially the flashbacks, is genuinely jarring. There were moments I didn’t even know if what I was watching was part of the present timeline or a narrated memory. It just throws you into transitions with no finesse, and it constantly undercuts any potential momentum. It’s like a photograph with the saturation maxed out — everything is pushed to the extreme without any room for nuance or subtlety. Just messy, loud, and overstuffed. There’s no breathing room. And that’s probably the biggest missed opportunity: with a figure as complex as Malcolm X, you expect depth. But this just overwhelms instead of connecting. Not even Denzel Washington could save this one for me. I’d give it a 2/10 — more exhausting than impactful.

His disillusionment with the Nation of Islam should be the climax of the movie, but there isn't any buildup or warning signs. To be fair to Lee, and I think Baldwin vocalized this suspicion as well, a Malcolm movie is probably undoable: how can one conceivably imagine  Hollywood allowing a movie to do justice to Malcolm, as an individual life and a microcosm of black life and revolutionary politics in America, in an honest way? This movie is a perfectly fine drama if one wants to ignore the history or the political significance of its subject, but it’s bad history, and not even in a pedantic, fact-checking sort of way. It’s predicated on a book which itself failed to capture Malcolm’s politics or the changes he underwent toward the end of his life (see George Breitman’s excellent 1967 The Last Year of Malcolm X, or the excellent collection Malcolm X Speaks , as a corrective to the Haley autobiography which came out before the script for this movie was even finished). This script was itself famously lambasted by Baldwin as a terrible white Hollywood bastardization of his vision (the movie literally includes a scene Baldwin attacked as an egregious distortion of his vision in a co-writer’s “revision” of his work, instead of the scene Baldwin envisioned. Nell Irvin Painter and Gerald Horne have spilled enough ink on how the script and Lee distorts Malcolm’s historical legacy and political significance. While I won’t go so far as to fully endorse Kwame Ture’s harsh judgement that Lee is a “petit bourgeois who took the choice of selling out of his people for a fistful of dollars” by failing to show that “Malcolm X was a revolutionary”, I think it’s fair to say that Lee doesn’t capture what Baldwin saw in Malcolm, the revolutionary spirit, what he called “a virile impulse long since fled from the American way of life”, a virility which neither Lee’s skillful direction nor Denzel’s tremendous performance evoke. Aside from the formal skill in the movie’s direction, and the great acting, Lee is refreshingly bold in connecting Malcolm to ‘92 at the beginning of the movie, and it’s a shame the rest of thet movie isn’t animated by that same polarizing political charge: Malcolm was a political revolutionary, and by the end of the movie he ceased to be a calculating, political man and is elevated into a depoliticized symbol of Black cultural pride. He counts for color and attitude—for a temperament, much as King and Malcolm represent dueling temperaments at the end of Do the Right Thing— without the substantial content of his political trajectory (e.g. we could also take Karenga’s complaint of the lack of engagement of Malcolm with Africans in the movie, i.e. his internationalism, one of the vital elements of his later political evolution). You can’t capture everything in a life, but to capture someone truthfully , one must engage with the essential aspects of one’s life and work. This movie was all over the place. It did a terrible job getting his political views across and failed to show how his upbringing shaped who he became. Malcolm X was a self-critic. He constantly challenged his own beliefs and was humble enough to admit when he was wrong. He was nicknamed Satan during one period of his life, before joining the Nation of Islam and later converting to Sunni Islam. He disagreed with many of Martin Luther King’s views and shared a well-known friendship with Muhammad Ali (then Cassius Clay). Before he entered the criminal world, he frequented music gigs and rubbed shoulders with some of the major blues musicians of the era. The film touches on none of this. It could have focused on one chapter of his life and explored it with real depth. Instead, it scatters across everything and lands on nothing. The film does show his Hajj, and to its credit, the pilgrimage sequence is depicted with some care. But it fails to follow through on what the Hajj meant. The transformation it triggered — his rejection of the Nation of Islam’s racial theology, his embrace of Sunni Islam, and his decision to challenge Elijah Muhammad — is barely explored. That’s the consequence that put a target on his back, and the film treats it as background noise rather than the pivotal turning point it was. The film also completely flattens his relationship with Martin Luther King. Malcolm was openly critical of the civil rights movement’s direction. He argued that political movements tend to get whitewashed, diluted, and commodified. The film makes it seem as though the two men were broadly aligned. They weren’t, and that tension matters. If you’re watching this to understand Malcolm X and his politics, skip it and read the autobiography instead. If you want to watch Denzel Washington play Malcolm X, this is your film because his performance is genuinely excellent. But as a portrait of the man? Three hours, and they left out almost everything that made him who he was.
