Avec Malcolm X, Spike Lee signe un film qui se veut à la fois ambitieux et nécessaire. Il est évident que ce projet lui tient à cœur et que son importance pour la communauté afro-américaine ne fait aucun doute. Le film est complet, documenté, et témoigne d’un véritable engagement. On comprend pourquoi il a été réalisé et pourquoi il est considéré comme un jalon du cinéma engagé. Pourtant, malgré la force du sujet et l’évidence du travail fourni, le film peine à captiver. Trois heures de récit font parfois sentir le poids de la longueur, et le rythme manque de dynamisme. À certains moments, on a l’impression de parcourir une encyclopédie visuelle plutôt que de vivre une expérience cinématographique. Les séquences s’enchaînent avec fidélité aux événements historiques, mais sans toujours offrir de point de vue nouveau ou d’élan dramatique capable de captiver le spectateur non averti. Le problème n’est pas le sujet, qui est passionnant et chargé d’une intensité politique et humaine indéniable, mais la manière dont il est traité. Malcolm X ressemble parfois à un biopic « Wikipédia » : tout est là, rien n’est oublié, mais la narration peine à provoquer l’émotion ou à stimuler l’esprit. On ressent une impression de distance, comme si le film voulait tout raconter plutôt que raconter quelque chose. En résumé, Malcolm X est un film important, admirable dans son ambition et sa sincérité, mais qui, pour moi, échoue à captiver pleinement. La richesse du matériau historique ne suffit pas à transformer le film en une expérience cinématographique fascinante. Mon jugement repose moins sur le fond que sur la forme : malgré tout le respect que j’ai pour le sujet, je me suis ennuyé, et le film ne m’a pas accroché.

At the outset, it seemed that this biopic was going truly commemorate Malcom X as a leader and represent the African American struggle for liberation without commodification for the white audiences. As Denzel Washington's voice echoed in the cinema, charging the white man with what has only now been declared as the greatest crime against humanity by the UN (of course Argentina, the US and its favourite ally voted no and the EU and UK abstained), I beamed, watching the American flag burn. And with it, the facade of the 'American Dream' and the freedom and 'unity' the flag represents. In less than 3 minutes I was reduced to tears as X's 1964 speech on the "American nightmare" played over footage of Rodney King being brutally beat by police only year before the release of this film. The fact that Warner Bros. objected to include any of this being included is insane. It all went downhill from here. I felt a lot of the film that chronicled Malcom's earlier hustler lifestyle was unnecessarily long and overdramatised to appeal to a crossover audience (it did, people would not stop laughing). Lee did not need any acting role in this biopic at all, even if he may have not intended it, it seemed disrespectful to Malcom X's autobiography. I loved Denzel Washington performance in this film, its sadly ironic that he lost the Oscar to a white actor. However, I will say Washington's Malcom X lacked the rage, resistance Malcom X possessed, necessary for black militancy. The remainder of this film felt very cherry picked. Not once was Malcom X's condemnations of capitalism and colonialism included. The scariest part is I almost did not realise this until Bobby Seale and Nelson Mandela made a cameo and Angela Davis and the Black Panthers appeared in a montage for a split second. Unfortunately, yet again, Lee projects his Madonna-Whore complex unto his depiction of Malcom X and his relationship with women in this film (his educated progressive sister was simply just not included). (This is all just constructive criticism, I enjoyed this film) I just think that Washington's Malcom X at the end of this film was not the Malcom X who advocated for black liberation, self-defence and militancy and died for it.

I read bell hooks' critical essay about this film right after watching it, so I might be biased toward criticism here. But I think her points are important. She points out that key details of Malcolm's story have been changed, such as the role of his siblings in his conversion to Islam. She also points out that (Black) women in general are portrayed rather superficially, as "either virgins or whores, madonnas or prostitutes— and that’s Hollywood". And that Malcolm's criticisms of colonialism and capitalism are almost absent from the film – likely to make the film more palatable to white audiences. That said, it's still a powerful biopic. It's beautifully shot and powerfully acted. But it's also too Hollywood for its own sake.

skillsで鑑賞。リアペの課題が出ていたのでそれを添付 I watched the movie “Malcolm X”, and I was surprised and impressed by the way Malcolm’s identity changed over time. In his early life, his identity was deeply shaped by racism. However, in the end, he came to see himself as he truly was, without viewing himself through the lens of skin color. In this essay, I will discuss this transformation through three aspects that his name, institutional discrimination, and his experience in prison. Firstly, I was surprised that his name, Malcolm Little, is actually the named from white plantation owner. This was revealed when Malcolm was in prison and taught about black is not wrong via many things. His name, “Little” was not Malcolm’s family name, and it was taken from the name of his ancestor’s plantation owner. I think this was shocking because it shows how slavery took away people’s identity as they did not give the name from the very beginning, and it continues after many decades. Secondly, I was surprised that there is some invisible discrimination. When I hear “discrimination problems,” I always come up with some violent problems. Of course, Malcolm was a victim of physical violence due to discrimination, such as his father being killed by white people, but he was also affected by more subtle, mental discrimination. For example, he was a good student at school, despite being the only colored in his school, and he dreamed of becoming a lawyer. However, when he told his teacher, he was discouraged simply because he was Black. Another example, he always tried to straighten his curly hair to look more like a white person. He thought this made him better than other Black people. But later, he realized this way of thinking actually showed how much he had been influenced by white standards. This part was very interesting to me because there are some examples of invisible discrimination. Lastly, I was surprised that he finally found himself in “prison”. I had no expectation that an important figure like Malcolm X had once been a criminal, and it was also during his time that motivated to learn and proud of being black. He started to read some books and knew that words related to “black” had negative meanings while words related to “white” had positive ones, or that the first humans on Earth were in prison. These discoveries made him prouder as a black and triggered him to see himself without the perspective of white. In conclusion, Malcolm X’s story shows that identity can change through experience, knowledge, and reflection. Through his name, his experiences with discrimination, and his time in prison, he gradually freed himself from the influence of racism and came to understand his true self.

Дружба Малкольма Х и Мухаммада Али как показатель братства, и причем здесь "Нация Ислама". Нация Ислама и Малкольм Х Нацию Ислама создал Уоллесон Фардон Мухаммад в 1930. Данная религия продвигала измененный под афроамериканцев Ислам. Где они были божественным видом, а Аллах там считается черным. Малкольм Х - самый яркий бывший представитель "Нации Ислама". Он продвигал идеи религии и боролся за права афроамериканцев. Зарождение дружбы. Мухаммад Али тогда ещё Кэссиус Клей был восходящей звездой в боксе. С сильным характером и сильной агрессией к расизму. Малкольм ходил на бои Клэя, так они и начинали своё знакомство. Братство Кэссиус и Малкольм стали лучшими друзьями. Х помог Клэю обрести политический голос и найти Бога в "Нации Ислама". Элайджи Мухаммад дал имя Клэю - Мухаммад Али. Больше у него нет рабского имени. С того момента Мухаммад начал вести активную политическую жизнь с продвижением своих взглядов, взглядов "НИ" и борьбы с расизмом. Малкольм был наставником великого боксёра. Они были неразлучны. Уход Малкольма из Нации Ислама и единственное, а также главное сожаление Мухаммада Али. Посетив Мекку Малкольм понял, что Нация Ислама это обман и вышел из этой организации в истинную веру и стал настоящим мусульманином. Впредь Х выражал взгляды настоящего Ислама и осуждал "НИ". За это организация множество раз пыталась убить его, и у них это вышло. В тот момент Мухаммад перестал дружить с Малкольмом, он отрекся от него считая предателем. Вскоре после смерти Малкольма Мухаммад никак не отреагировал. Но когда умер лидер "Нации Ислама" Элайджи Мухаммад Али впал в депрессию и последовал за его сыном. Вскоре Мухаммад Али стал сунитом, тобишь проповедовал истинный Ислам. В одном из интервью Мухаммада Спросили, о чем он сожалеет. Он ответил, что только об одном: Он отвернулся от своего лучшего друга - Малкольма Х.

It could ostracize white audience members but Lee proudly, painstakingly details the process of hot-comb straightening and it is one of several esoterica that I'm elated was incorporated. As a non-religious film I did have a hard time accepting them refuting one brainwash for another... but that's here nor there. There are great moments within, iconic either because of the historical iconography or because the film made it so (I'm not sure) and some amazing performances within, particularly by Denzel Washington and Angela Basset. However, even though the script has some great moments... a personal favorite is Malcolm X telling a white woman "nothing" is what sympathetic whites can do for the movement... the script also leaves out a lot of personal character building and showing transition from criminal to born again cultural leader. He's pretty awful and unlikable in the first 30 or so minutes, threatens to beat women for challenging him, robbing a house, cheating the only guy who saw any potential in him. He suddenly becomes a saint after going through a prison montage and finding a new religion. It's hard to understand what in him truly changes, felt repentance, was wanting to be better. Credit due to the latter half of the movie, in more comfortable ground, as it shows how his pilgrimage softens his stance on all white people being evil devils. By that time, it seems, he had burnt too many bridges even among his own leadership. The movie doesn't sugarcoat how people felt about him, but it also doesn't really show what was so magnanimous about him over the many other people also saying similar messages of "enough is enough". So once again, with a Spike Lee Joint, I'm trying to bridge the message he thinks is so obvious with my non-understanding (maybe I can't truly understand as a non-black person... idk). I wanted the message to be a little more solid, but this was the person who we are given as the deliverer of this message. Blame history I guess. It's muddled and changes. Perhaps this is because the real man was gunned down in his prime, or because he changed stances many times. That's fair...  but it's not a great person to make this strongly messaged movie about. I feel like it says a lot less than a 3 hr movie should. For a clearer message, with a person who also encountered racism but didn't go to crime, watch Ghandi.

Watched this for my spring of 2026 college course: cinema director: Spike Lee (think that was the course name). Theme/Subject: transformation Cinematic aspect: cinematography One expressive cinematography is the three different color pallets to paint the historical transformation Malcolm X had. Each color pallet reflects the three acts in the film. The first one (Act I) is shown to be warm and rich which represents his youth and his drug addiction since there was a crack epidemic ravaging  the black population. Then we move to Act II which contains one cool shade color that represents Malcolm X’s time in prison. When serving his time in prison Malcolm found his faith, Islam, and we get to Act III which is to be seen as more of the earthy type of color to represent him joining the National of Islam (NOI) and eventually Malcolm X left and went to Mecca he took the name of el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz. Each color shows different stages of his life. I think the opening montage really sets the mood for the film. It was an interesting way of incorporating history of violence against the black population mixed with the audio of Malcolm X along with the American flag slowly burning up and turning into the letter X. Right there and then you get a sense of what the movie will be about. When reading the textbook (pg 203-207) it was important that Lee wanted to shoot the Middle Eastern scenes in Africa rather than New Jersey. “It was a life-changing experience for Spike” (pg 204). Lee felt an instant connection where he saw the pyramid and the sphinx for the first time and thought those were his ancestors who built them. Scientists to this day don’t know how it was built. That scene in the film was the turning point for Malcolm X where he wanted to express more of an internationalist and anti-racism perspective. And truly without one of Lee’s associate producers, Fernado Sulichin, that scene and Lee’s experience wouldn’t have happened. Sulichin did not take a no for an answer. Heck “he [even] went to the high Islamic court again and again, until they finally agreed to allow for the first time a 35mm motion picture camera in the city of Mecca during Hajj” (pg 204). Even though the film was long (which I did not expect) I thought it was put together beautifully. I mean Denzel Washington was phenomenal. Of all of Spike Lee’s films we were going to watch this semester, this film was the one I was most excited to watch because of Denzel’s performance and the man he delivered.

Truly one of the greatest, most committed lead performances maybe of all time. Yet, biopics — obviously! — are almost always so reverential and venerational, so totally mythologising in their vision of the biographic object, that I sometimes struggle with the form. I have previously had a very hard time finding some well-recognised, highly lauded biopics even worth finishing. I did not per se have that problem here; the life story is far too engaging, as are Malcolm X’s ideas and the stunning charisma with which Washington portrays him. Angela Bassett’s performance as Betty Shabazz also makes the film so gripping, as she insistently demands that his family life be taken as seriously as his public life, that the two combine to create the man. However, I also can’t say that this is my favourite kind of film, or that I could ever find a biopic a truly great Work Of Art. Perhaps a me-problem. (Obviously I recognise it’s completely deranged to watch a film this Big on a plane, but here we are)

Scavenger Hunt #138 Film 1 of 30 Category: A film about activism. The Film *Malcolm X* is not simply a biography of an important man. It is the story of a person repeatedly destroying an old version of himself in order to become someone greater. Spike Lee refuses to present Malcolm as though he entered the world already prepared to become a leader. We see his anger, vanity, criminality, discipline, faith, pride, mistakes, and eventual willingness to reconsider beliefs that once defined him. The different names he carries represent those transformations. Malcolm Little is the child born into a family terrorized by racism. Detroit Red is the young man attempting to bury that pain beneath style, excitement, and crime. Malcolm X rejects the name inherited through slavery and replaces it with the unknown history stolen from him. El Hajj Malik El Shabazz emerges after Mecca with a larger understanding of humanity. Each name belongs to the same man, but none contains him completely. The early scenes are energetic and entertaining, but that energy hides enormous insecurity. Malcolm straightens his hair, changes the way he dresses, and performs a version of himself designed to survive and feel powerful. The conk becomes more than a hairstyle. It shows how racism can teach someone to reject features of his own body before he even realizes he is doing it. Prison becomes the place where physical confinement produces intellectual freedom. Malcolm begins reading, questioning language, and recognizing how history has been written by people with the power to define everyone else. Education does not merely give him information. It gives him a new understanding of himself. He discovers that controlling language means controlling the boundaries of what people believe is possible. The Nation of Islam gives Malcolm discipline, purpose, and a community, but the same organization that helps rebuild him eventually attempts to control him. His devotion to Elijah Muhammad is sincere, which makes the betrayal deeply personal. Malcolm realizes that replacing one form of dependence with another is not true liberation. He must be willing to question the person who taught him how to question everything else. His journey to Mecca becomes the film’s final great transformation. Malcolm does not abandon his understanding of racism in America, but he recognizes that his previous beliefs about race were incomplete. What makes him extraordinary is not that he was always correct. It is that he was willing to change publicly after building his identity around certainty. Many people would rather protect their pride than admit that experience has expanded their understanding. The Direction Spike Lee directs the film with the scale and confidence of an epic while keeping Malcolm’s personal evolution at its center. The opening immediately connects Malcolm’s life to the America that continued after his death. Images of the American flag burning into the shape of an X are combined with footage of Rodney King being beaten, making it clear that this is not a safely contained history lesson. The conditions Malcolm confronted did not disappear with him. Each period of Malcolm’s life has its own visual identity. The early sequences are colorful, playful, and alive with movement. Prison removes that freedom and replaces it with hard lines, shadows, and confined spaces. As Malcolm becomes a public figure, the compositions grow larger and more controlled, reflecting the authority he has developed. By the final section, that control begins collapsing under surveillance, threats, and betrayal. Lee never allows Malcolm’s speeches to become interruptions in the story. Speaking is the action. The film understands that Malcolm’s voice was his greatest instrument because he could transform private anger into a shared political consciousness. The crowds do not simply admire him. They recognize experiences that society repeatedly told them to endure quietly. The march to the hospital is one of the clearest demonstrations of his power. Malcolm controls the movement of an entire crowd with small gestures, revealing the discipline behind his leadership. The police see danger because they are witnessing a Black man exercise authority that does not depend upon their permission. The final movement carries an unavoidable sense of dread. Malcolm knows that death is approaching, but he continues speaking because fear can no longer determine the value of his work. The famous shot of him moving toward the ballroom makes him appear almost separated from the ground, as though history is carrying him toward a fate both he and the audience already understand. At more than three hours, the film is long, but that length mostly feels earned. Malcolm’s transformation would lose its meaning if any major stage were treated as a brief montage. Some supporting relationships are compressed because the film has so much history to contain, yet the overall scale allows Malcolm to feel like a full human being rather than a collection of famous speeches. The Acting Denzel Washington gives one of the greatest performances ever placed in a biographical film. He does not simply imitate Malcolm’s voice and physical mannerisms. He captures the intelligence, humor, anger, confidence, vulnerability, and constant mental movement beneath them. His performance changes with every stage of Malcolm’s life. Detroit Red moves with youthful arrogance, constantly trying to appear larger than he feels. The imprisoned Malcolm becomes quieter as his mind awakens. The public speaker controls rooms through rhythm and precision. The later Malcolm appears calmer but also more exposed because he is no longer protected by the certainty or organization that once surrounded him. Denzel is especially powerful during the speeches because he communicates why people followed Malcolm. The words are important, but so is the feeling that every sentence has been sharpened by personal experience. Malcolm does not speak about racism as an abstract political subject. He speaks as someone whose family, childhood, body, opportunities, and identity were all shaped by it. Angela Bassett brings strength and emotional clarity to Betty Shabazz. Betty is not merely the supportive wife waiting outside Malcolm’s public life. She understands the danger surrounding him and the cost his mission places on their family. Bassett shows the love between them while never pretending that loving someone with a historical purpose is easy. Delroy Lindo is also excellent as West Indian Archie, particularly when Malcolm encounters him years later. Archie’s decline becomes a vision of the future Malcolm escaped. Albert Hall gives Baines the calm authority necessary to make Malcolm’s religious transformation believable, while Al Freeman Jr. portrays Elijah Muhammad with enough warmth to make Malcolm’s eventual disillusionment feel genuinely painful. Conclusion *Malcolm X* succeeds because it refuses to freeze Malcolm into a simple symbol. He was not one thing for his entire life. He was a man capable of growth, contradiction, anger, tenderness, discipline, and change. The film respects him enough to show the journey rather than only celebrating the final image. His evolution does not weaken his legacy. It is the legacy. Malcolm teaches that identity does not have to remain confined by the name, history, or beliefs handed to us. A person can examine himself, reject what no longer serves the truth, and continue becoming someone new. The assassination is devastating because Malcolm dies at the moment his understanding is becoming widest. He has separated from the institution that once gave him power, broadened his view of humanity, and begun building something independently. The tragedy is not only that a great man was killed. It is that we will never know what his next transformation might have become. The final sequence expands Malcolm beyond one body. When people across generations declare themselves Malcolm X, they are not claiming to replace him. They are recognizing that his struggle for dignity, knowledge, and self definition belongs to everyone denied the right to define themselves. Spike Lee created something far greater than a standard biopic. He made a film about the courage required to confront the world and the even greater courage required to confront yourself. Malcolm’s power did not come from never changing. It came from refusing to stop.

Ouvrir sur le défrisage de ses cheveux n'est pas un détail anodin. Ça dit déjà tout de la difficulté à s'accepter en tant que noir dans une société où ton identité semble être un problème. Denzel Washington incarne Malcolm X dans toute sa complexité et ses contradictions politiques et spirituelles qui en font une figure humainement fascinante. Spike Lee associe chaque période de sa vie à un langage visuel différent. La chaleur de la pellicule pour la nostalgie de sa jeunesse, la froideur et la rigidité des cadrages pour les années de dogme comme une doctrine qui l'enferme, jusqu’à des plans larges presque de péplum, quand s'ouvre enfin son esprit. On ne suis pas une statue d’un leader politique ou un prophète né avec une ligne claire, mais un homme en mutation permanente, dont la pensée se redéfinit à mesure qu'il se cogne aux réalités du monde qui l’entoure. Cette mue fait de lui un penseur tragique. Il est assassiné précisément au moment où sa pensée atteint sa maturité la plus vaste, la plus nuancée, et donc la plus dangereuse pour le système.

Religion is regarded by the common people as true, by the wise as false, and by rulers as useful. I don't know about the first two lines, but the last one still feels true even today. Religion can absolutely become a useful tool for rulers or people in power. In today's world, we call them politicians or sometimes even religious figures who claim to be God's servants. When you follow them blindly, you are praised as a devotee. But the moment you start questioning them, that's when the real problem begins. You don't get answers. Instead, hate is thrown your way. That only deepens your suspicions and slowly makes you realise what kind of world we live in --> where someone dictates what's right and what's wrong based on beliefs that have been planted into people's minds for years. I think Spike Lee tries to say something similar through Malcolm X . Religion or any faith, should guide a person into becoming a better version of themselves than they were yesterday. It should help you become a better human being who recognises everyone as equal. But when religion is used to build rage, spread hatred and discriminate against others based on race or colour, then it stops being a solution and becomes another problem added to an already existing one. Once hatred is passed down through generations, it isn't easy to erase. Even when the truth is right in front of you, accepting it means accepting that everything you've believed your whole life could have been a lie. That's not easy for anyone. When you can't question your beliefs and you can't accept the truth either, that's when blind faith takes over and blind faith only creates more hatred towards the people who dared to question it. When you don't question anything and simply follow blindly, consequences will always follow. By the time the truth reaches you, you won't even be ready to comprehend it. Brainwashing, whether done over generations or even over years, makes it much easier to hate, discriminate against and diminish another person than it is to love them. Love , Love is something every human being should possess. But people in power find it much easier to awaken hatred than compassion. People blindly follow them, become victims themselves and end up hurting both themselves and the people around them. That's exactly why Malcolm X's journey is so fascinating. He was once consumed by that blindness. He hated others based on race, colour and religion. He blindly followed those principles, preached them to others and built an entire movement around them. But the moment he started questioning everything and finally discovered the truth, his entire worldview shattered. He realised how wrong he had been and saw the damage his own words had caused to the people around him without ever knowing it. And look what happened when he finally chose to question that blind faith... What a pitiful world we still live in, driven by hatred in the name of race and religion. A faith built upon fear and hatred has brought this world far more wars than peace has ever known.

MALCOLM X *SPOİLER* Önce kendisinin hayat hikayesini anlatmakla başlayalım. Malcolm'un babası daha Malcolm 6 yaşında iken öldürülür ve annesi ise yaşananlardan dolayı akıl hastanesine kaldırılır. Malcolm ise koruyucu ailede kalır. 20 yaşında hırsızlık ve diğer suçlardan hapishaneye girer ve orda "İslam Ümmeti" adlı harekata katılır ve Müslüman olup kendi yolunu çizmeye başlar. Malcolm harekata katılmadan önce de dünyanın nasıl işlediğinin farkındaydı ve kendisini film de siyahilerin ne durumda olduğunu en baştan söylüyordu. Harekata katıldıktan sonra ise en başta inandığı yoldan ilerledi ve hakkı yenen tüm siyahilere ses oldu. Ancak ilerde işler sarpa saracak ki kendisi idol aldığı *Elijah Muhammed* tarafından ihanete uğrar ve onlarla yollarını ayırır. Burada kendisinin söylediği şu sözü yazmak istiyorum; -"Ölümü anlarım ama ihaneti anlayamıyorum..." Malcolm çıktığı yerden dolayı ölümden korkmayan birisi olarak biliyoruz ancak kendisi bu yaşına kadar böyle sağlam bir ihanete uğramamıştı. Hem de dost dediği insanlardan gelen bu ihanetin sebebini kendisi o zaman bunu sorgulamış ve Allaha dua etmekten başka bir şey yapamamıştır. Peki neden Malcolm X? Kendisi bunu şöyle açıklıyor: -"Malcolm köle tacirlerinin verdiği bir isim X ise bilinmeyeni temsil ediyor aynı matematik de ki gibi. Kendi ana vatanımıza döndüğümüzde bu X anlamını kaybedecek ve bilinmeyen kalkacak." Malcolm kendi yolunda giderken aynı zamanda Hacca da gitmiştir ve gittikten sonra önemli bir bilinç kazanmıştır. **Irk eşitliği** bu bilinç ile amerikaya geri dönen Malcolm ırkçı olmadığını ve herkese kucak açtığını söyler. Her müslümanın yapması gerektiği gibi. Buradan sonra ise Malcolm artık diğer harekatçılar tarafından baskı görmeye başlar ve ölüm tehtitleri alır. Malcolm ise bunları umursamaz ve kendi davasından vazgeçmeyerek yoluna devam eder. En sonda ise yaptığı seminer konuşmasında suikaste uğrar ve orada can verir hem de kendi ailesinin yanında. Malcolm bu yola çıkar için başlamadı o sadece siyahilerin en doğal haklarından mahrum kalmasına karşı çıktı ve İslam'ın da buyurduğu gibi haksızlığa karşı çıktı. Bir Müslüman olarak ona Allah rahmet eylesin demek düşüyor bize, onun gibi insanlar bu dünya da çok az bulunuyor ve çoğumuz bize söyleneni yapıyoruz. Bunu yaparken de sorgulamıyor, internette ne dolaşırsa inanıyoruz. Bu biyografi eserine 10/10 puan veriyorum gerek anlatım olsun gerek duygu olsun her şekilde karşıladığını düşünüyorum özellikle *Denzel Washington* burada harika oynamış diyebilirim. *Spike Lee* ise muhteşem bir iş çıkarmış. Benden bu kadar bu tarz filmlere merakınız varsa izlemenizi kesinlikle öneriyorum bu tarz filmler size çok şey katar. Filmi izleyeceklere iyi seyirler diğerlerine de iyi günler dilerim.

Once in a generation biopic? Once in a generation film? Once in a generation artistic achievement? I could hyperbolize about Malcolm X forever and I still would not be able to put into sufficient words just how monumental Spike Lee’s scrupulous account of this man is. No other visual rendition of a public figure can even approximate the effect of its testament to the significance of not just this individual life, but every individual life. It magnetizes with its ambition only to pull the viewer in further, further into its sweeping crevices that envelop the harrowing volatility of souls. Still so early in their illustrious careers, Denzel Washington and Spike Lee demonstrate a drive here that it’s difficult to say they ever had again (if anyone else has ever had it at all); their particular fortitude, courage, confidence, and determination as artists harmonize perfectly with their subject. From the first crackles of the smoldering Stars and Stripes, they reach for the limits of their capabilities and we are witnesses to an actor and his director refusing to deliver anything to the screen except undiluted inspiration. Just please watch this movie.

From the uncomfortable, unappealing, ugly jig of the film's head-scratching overlong opening to the contradictory and incoherently paired quotations by MLK and Malcolm X at the end, this is an in-your-face obnoxious mess that has no clear idea of what it wants to say but is utterly convinced of its own grand importance. The film consists almost entirely of babbling losers spending the whole day aimlessly wandering back and forth on a small stretch of road. Almost without exception these are not characters but thinly drawn racist stereotypes of purposeless black idiots who are hell-bent on getting themselves into trouble but are too stupid to know how to do even that. What is supposed to pass for acting is way-the-hell over-the-top mugging by everyone except the bland and stilted phoned-in performance of the film's wannabe auteur director/screenwriter/producer Spike Lee as well as two fine performances by two of the film's three major white actors, the always excellent John Turturro and Danny Aiello. Lee loves his grandiloquent soliloquies, which consist either of lists or of outright plagiarism (or "homage," as he would dishonestly put it). There is a short montage of several actors one by one looking directly into the camera and each insulting a particular race; the insults consist of lists of nouns and adjectives; they are predicates without propositions. There is a gratuitously long list of popular black American musicians rattled off by Sam Jackson's radio host; the sole purpose here is to provide evidence that, despite what we see depicted in the film in terms of black people's behavior, many black Americans have been very successful in music; yes, that is as much of a non sequitur as it seems. Also shoehorned into the film is identification by name of to that point (1989) every black American political activist, politician, entertainer, and athlete; it is just a product placement-like in-aggregate information dump intended to serve the same purpose as the radio host's annoying list. The plagiarism is in the form of one mostly mute knuckle dragger's beat-by-beat reiteration of Robert Mitchum's love/hate soliloquy from The Night of the Hunter; it makes no sense that this individual would be familiar, certainly to the extent of memorization, with this cultural reference. This individual's sole mission is to be as irritating as possible by blaring his loud radio at everyone to provoke a response. It is all just back-and-forth yelling until a white character smashes the radio, giving this dude his pretext for attempted murder and Lee his pretext for showing the cops killing the provocateur and the mob its pretext to engage in wanton destruction. At this point the loosely knit mob of miscreants unites in its fulfilling its collective purpose of attempting to murder whitey, burning his business to the ground, and attacking the emergency responders when they arrive. These violent black thugs trying to commit suicide by cop invoke the names of real-life violent black thugs (Michael Stewart and Eleanor Bumpurs, misspelled as "Bumpers" in the end-credits dedication) who in real life did get themselves killed by the fault of their own similar recklessness. Is this hateful, insidious wreck of a movie really positing the perspective that these arsonists and would-be murderers are, or believe themselves to be, oppressed by the genial owner of the one place where they each go multiple times per day to purchase food, namely slices of pizza? What does "fight the power" (a phrase repeated about a million times in this movie) mean if not that? At the same time are we supposed to respond sympathetically when a violent mob of "fucking niggers" (to use Spike Lee's obsessively repeated choice phrase) attempt to murder the white man and then burn the place to the ground before turning on the Korean shop owner across the street and threatening him with the same fate for no reason other than that he is not black? The race riot scene is a sadistic fantasy of a racially inverted recreation of the Howard Beach incident (the mob in the film chants "Howard Beach"), the mythical attack of a black man by a white mob outside of a pizzeria in New York a few years before this movie came out. The myopic libs of 1989 America, and worldwide, were too busy drooling all over themselves and each other in competitive heaping of praise upon this work of fiction to notice or care about the world's largest democracy movement in generations, which was ongoing by the film's May 19 Cannes showing and which was weeks past its bloody finale by the film's June 30 wide release. This film's revolution around interpersonal bickering takes on a sobering context in light of the PLA's massacre of thousands, albeit thousands of miles away. The point is not that the film should be criticized with respect to an unrelated contemporaneous political event, but rather that the inordinately high critical appraisal derives not so much from a considered assessment of the film on its merits as from a conflation of the film's social consciousness with its artistic value, this conflation based in a paucity of perspective of the extent of that consciousness. At one point the graffiti'd phrase "TAWANA TOLD THE TRUTH!" appears very prominently, to put it lightly. Is this a commentary on the credulity of those who were still clinging to their desperate gang-rape fantasy, or is it a statement of sincerity? Just before the end credits why do we have MLK telling us (namely, black Americans) to be non-violent but then Malcolm X exhorting "us" to violence? Is the senseless violence depicted in the film supposed to give its community of perpetrators a sense of accomplishment for having driven out one of the vanishingly small number of businesses operating in their ghetto neighborhood? How does it make any sense that this decent guy would be an oppressor of any sort or part of "the power" to fight? The film has no idea about any of this. Like the rioters leaning in to their true calling of vicious hooliganism, Lee has heard of the names of some high-profile black people, many accomplished, some criminal, and wants to make a movie having something vaguely to do with them, but he got too wrapped up in the aimless wandering to care in the slightest about what his original objective was or where he was going, if he was ever going anywhere at all.

I was honestly prepared to give this half a star. Then the Martin Luther King Jr. quotation appeared at the end and, for a moment, I thought the film had managed to redeem itself. Two stars, perhaps. Then came the Malcolm X quotation, and I was back down to one. For me, this is a confused and frustrating film, muddled in its broader argument. The performances are strong, and the actors do what they can with the material, but the dialogue often feels artificial and overly constructed. Rather than emerging organically, the story often feels as if it has been built around a thesis the film itself has not fully worked out. My issue is not with the film’s anger at racism, police brutality or the marginalisation of black communities. Those are urgent and historically entrenched issues. My issue is with the way the film frames its central conflict, particularly around Sal’s pizzeria. Yes, it is an Italian-owned business in a Black neighbourhood, and that context matters. But it is still an Italian-American pizzeria. The demand that Sal place black public figures on his Wall of Fame is presented as a question of representation… but, representation cannot simply mean overriding the cultural identity of a space because it happens to exist within a different community. Yes, in the 1980s, the lack of black representation in American public life is a serious problem. But is the wall of an immigrant-owned pizzeria really the battleground on which that struggle should be fought? The film becomes even more troubling in its final act. Radio Raheem’s death at the hands of the police is unjust and horrifying. The police are clearly responsible for that death. But the escalation that precedes it is not morally simple either. A group enters Sal’s pizzeria aggressively, tensions rise, Sal reacts poorly, violence erupts, and then the police arrive and kill a man. That killing is the central injustice. But does that automatically make Sal responsible for what the police did? Was his business the correct object of retaliation? Spike Lee has said that only white viewers tend to ask whether Mookie “did the right thing”, arguing that the real issue is the difference between property damage and the death of a black man. I understand that distinction, and it is obviously true that a human life is worth infinitely more than a shop window. But that does not, by itself, settle the moral question. Property damage and state violence are not equivalent, but nor does the horror of one automatically justify the other. The question is not whether Sal’s window matters more than Radio Raheem’s life. Of course it does not. The question is whether destroying Sal’s pizzeria was a meaningful act of resistance, an act of misdirected rage, or something more ambiguous. This is where I find the film, and Lee’s later commentary on it, frustrating. There seems to be an almost absolute certainty about what “the right thing” is, yet the film itself ends with two quotations that appear to be in philosophical mismatch with one another. If the answer is supposed to be so obvious, why close the film with both Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X? Why invite that contradiction and then treat the central moral question as if it should not be asked? I would probably have appreciated Do the Right Thing more had I known less about Spike Lee’s own interpretations of it, and less about some of the troubling accounts surrounding his behaviour on set. Taken purely as a film, it has energy, anger and some visual confidence. But as a political statement, I found it far less persuasive than its reputation suggests. The film would be stronger if it allowed more room for doubt, rather than presenting moral certainty as though it were the same thing as moral clarity. The strongest version of this film would have understood that.

The cinematography also helped show the conflict, between the characters. During arguments Lee uses close up shots to show people’s faces, which made their emotions easier to see. Every frame is turned up to eleven, the heat, the sweat, the sound design, the racial tension simmering into rage and by the midpoint it stops feeling like a story and starts feeling like a lecture. The film is soaked in anger from start to finish, and while I understand that's the point, it makes for a genuinely draining watch rather than an illuminating one. The ending with dueling quotes from Malcolm X and MLK, capped with the message that violence is bad. Thank you ….Groundbreaking. But important" and "enjoyable aren't the same thing, and for me, this one stays firmly in the first category….

Spike Lee's film Do the Right Thing was a very good film that combined many different themes to convey an important message. Lee chose to film the story on one specific block in New York during one of the hottest days of summer. The way he kept everything in one neighbourhood makes the movie's racial tensions feel very personal. In this movie, I noticed Spike Lee uses a lot of close-ups to show characters raw and true emotions. In some scenes in the film, Lee has the characters break the fourth wall and speak directly to the audience. This makes the audience feel their anger, makes the emotions seem up front and raw, and helps us experience the frustration some of the characters might feel during similar events. I noticed the heat in this film doesn't create every problem on the block, but it does help bring out existing anger, racism, and frustration. As the day gets hotter, these things start to get worse. I also noticed Lee adds louder music to intensify certain situations. Da Mayor definitely stood out to me because he was always very wise and cared about others even when he was judged. Throughout the film, my opinion about him stayed positive because, no matter what, he always tried to fix and solve problems in the neighborhood. He is a bit of a complicated character because he drinks, but he is still always kind, and he always regulated the chaos with his calmness throughout the film.

Watching Do the Right Thing was honestly pretty interesting because I liked how the movie slowly built up the tension throughout the day. At first, the neighborhood just felt like a normal place where everyone knew each other and had their own things going on. But as it got hotter, everyone seemed to get more annoyed and angry. I noticed how Spike Lee kept showing people sweating, drinking water, using fans, and trying to stay cool. The bright colors and strong lighting also made everything feel even hotter. I also liked the cinematography during arguments because Lee uses close-up shots and low-angle shots to make the characters seem more aggressive and intense. The camera also moves around the neighborhood a lot, which made me feel like I was actually there with everyone. I think the heat didn't really cause all the problems, but it made everyone get angry super easily because I think it made everyone already in a pretty annoyed or bad mood. The character I found most interesting was Mookie because he seemed like someone who was just trying to stay out of everything, but he eventually got pulled into the conflict. I also started to see Sal differently as the movie went on because I didn't think he was completely good or bad. The scene where Radio Raheem gets killed was probably the biggest moment for me because everything went from people arguing to complete chaos. After that, Mookie throwing the trash can through the window felt like a huge turning point. I still don't know  why Mookie did that and that is one of the many questions I have about the movie. I also am wondering my Sal payed him after Mookie basically was the reason his store got destroyed. I liked that the movie didn't really tell us who was completely right because it made me think about the situation myself. At first I thought the movie might be be bad because there is no true plot line, but by the end I realized that the slow build up was important because it made the ending feel way more real because we knew so much about all the characters

I genuinely loved the cinematography in this movie. Spike Lee does such a good job making the heat feel like it is everywhere, even when we’re inside. I really loved the lighting in Mookie’s house when he lays on top of his sister. The way the room is lit, combined with the way everyone is sweaty and uncomfortable, it made me feel the heat through the screen. I also loved how Lee uses sound to make the heat feel even more intense. When the kids are yelling at Da Mayor, everyone is screaming over each other, and the scene gets so loud and chaotic that it almost feels physically hot. The heat doesn’t cause all the problems on the block, but it definitely brings out everything that was already there, like racism, frustration, and anger. As the day goes on, the neighborhood goes from feeling energetic and friendly to feeling increasingly tense, which made the ending feel even more shocking. Mookie was probably the most interesting character to me because my opinion kept changing about him. At first I saw him as pretty chill and someone who was just trying to get through his day, but by the end I was really confused about his choices. I also became more sympathetic toward Da Mayor because everyone treated him like he was a bum, but he genuinely seems like a nice guy and like he cares about the people around him. The ending was probably my favorite part because Lee doesn’t make it easy to decide who actually “did the right thing.” Mookie throwing the trash can through Sal’s window is understandable after everything that happened, but it also leads to so much destruction. That made me realize that Lee isn’t really asking us to pick a side. He’s making us think about how anger builds up, how racism affects a community, and how one decision can have consequences that go way beyond what someone intended. By the end, I wasn’t thinking about who was right or wrong as much as I was thinking about how complicated the idea of “doing the right thing” really is.

Reflecting on the movie Do the Right Thing, the elements that stood out and affected my experience were definitely color, community, and the conflict. Seeing how much color was involved in the film, I feel like I could feel the heat as well. In a way, I would say I felt the heat, and the movie was moving slowly because of how hot it was. I felt the element of community and conflict when the passerby accidentally scuffed up Buggin Out's shoe. Quickly, a group formed behind him, and they were yelling at him and everything. Elements like those made me feel included in a way.  The heat brings out all the tensions that have been brewing day after day. The people of the neighborhood have become irritated and confrontational. We see the neighborhood and its characters change throughout the day; we see this because, in the beginning of the film, it feels somewhat normal. Everyone is going about their business, working and having normal conversations with one another. As the day continues and the heat rises more, the atmosphere becomes more uncomfortable. People try to escape the heat, and one way we see them do this is when they unscrew the fire hydrant and have fun in the water. The afternoon is full of them becoming more hostile. We see many altercations break out in Salś. We see when Buggin' Out talks to Sal about the Wall of Fame and Radio Rahim with the boombox. By night, the whole community has changed; it has become violent and divided. Sals pizza restaurant is now destroyed and on fire, and Radio Rahim died to the cops. In my opinion, the most interesting character in the movie was Da Mayor. To me, he is such an easy character to like. Throughout the movie, he was the most ¨normal/sane¨ person throughout the film. He tries to be nice to Mother Sister and gives her flowers. He also saves the kid from getting run over by the car. Personally, I don't think that the movie ¨didnt¨ have a story; it was a story about a very hot day in the Bronx. But I do think that there was a very loose plot. We jump from person to person and dive into their life. Many of these people's stories don't really mean much for the progress of the story, but for understanding what they are like, and the day I think it works.
I enjoy the message and themes but this could've been cut down quite a bit. The last half hour is great but so much of the rest is a bit too meandering

“Dago, wop, guinea, garlic-breath, pizza-slingin', spaghetti-bendin', Vic Damone, Perry Como, Luciano Pavarotti, Sole Mio, nonsingin' motherf-cker.” Do the Right Thing didn’t impress me as much as I thought it would. Generally, the film was just uncomfortable for me. While the culture and themes of the story are masterful, I don’t think I’d ever revisit it. The cinematography and mise en-scène stood out to me more than anything. The performances were decent, and it dwells into complex racial tensions without pointing to a single moral lesson, which left me feeling confused. The Dutch tilts represent and perfectly show the escalating tension and how everything is breaking down. They skew the perspective, reflecting the reality of a world going out of control, while putting the viewer up close and often low to sense the fear and power of a character. They do this with Radio Raheem the most as he is the biggest and sort of the most powerful presence in the neighborhood. The lower angles execute and signify power, giving a threatening presence and making one character look larger than life and imposing to another. Many people say you can feel the heat shown on screen and really blend into the environment around the characters, but I didn’t relate to that. The combination of reds, oranges, and yellows paired with the New York on location filmmaking produces this heat and atmospheric feeling. Cinematographer Ernest Dickerson applied this color scheme and avoided the use of most spring colors, while much of the production crew painted and redid the neighborhood to make it feel fresh, vibrant, and hot. These visual techniques communicated the idea of putting the viewer into the discomfort of the cast, but I felt like I was watching it and not really experiencing it. As the day moves on and the sun sets, the tension increases and the shots become more zoomed in and close up. Each shot slowly closes the viewer in as the day progresses. A few people have argued that Spike Lee’s performance as Mookie was the best, or that Bill Nunn as Radio Raheem was the best, but between all the performances in this ensemble cast, nothing came close to Danny Aiello’s performance as Sal. Not to be a hater, but most of the performances in this film felt unnatural and didn’t work for me. The way the film portrays the raw essence of a neighborhood and its environment through these performances is neat, except it’s not entertaining to sit through for me. I am a major fan of films that deliver a bleak and honest view of life, but this didn’t do that for me. An example that really annoyed me while others were impressed was Smiley, played by Roger Guenveur Smith . He was intriguing to have in the film, but the dark comedy he brought didn’t work for me. I felt wrong for laughing at him, so I never did. Amidst the chaos, his character is seemingly important, but for me it was just another reason to be uncomfortable and gave me a sense of blankness when it came to breaking down and analyzing the film. A particular moment that stood out to me was shortly after the riot, when Sal’s is burning to the ground and Smiley pins up one of the photos of Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. to the wall so that the community can have representation. This was one of the few Smiley moments that impressed me and actually followed his character through while serving a purpose, because mostly throughout the film he was just interesting to me. What I’ll credit the film for, and what I think is brilliant, is its themes and Spike Lee’s bravery to tell the truth in a way that very few people were willing to at the time. He forced America to witness and face the raw racial tensions that were a massive issue, and Hollywood preferred to avoid the subject and matter of these issues, but Spike Lee decided to prove them wrong. In the end, it became his magnum opus and a landmark piece of cinema for the future. Answering the question of what characters “did the right thing” in the end is complicated because after selecting through all of these characters, no one really did what was right. You could argue that Mookie throwing the trash can into the window was the right thing, and that’s what I thought at first when seeing the scene. But as the ending went on, nothing felt right about choosing either side or any character for that matter. What mainly brought the film to an uplifting and sort of rewarding piece for me was the final moments and conversation between Sal and Mookie. Talking about money, family, life, and sort of giving their last farewells really brought what the rioting and destruction came to an end. It felt like a peace treaty being acknowledged between every character even though the conversation was just Mookie and Sal. The film doesn’t give an easy answer to who did the right thing, and I think that is part of what Spike Lee wants the viewer to confront. The heat doesn’t create every problem on the block, but it brings everything already underneath the surface out into the open. Overall, Do the Right Thing has exquisite mise-en-scène and cinematography that portray the raw essence of the neighborhood, but between the uncomfortable performances and the lack of an actual story, it wasn’t interesting to watch. I never found it humorous other than with the three men sitting out in the sun once or twice, I never “liked” a single character, and while the music was good and the way the film is loud at all times was great, this isn’t a film I’d revisit. I need to read a big breakdown and have someone explain why this film is supposedly so masterful because aside from the immaculate themes and bravery in filmmaking, it’s average to me. After watching this film the thing I wanted the most, that I actual felt the heat in, was the scrumptious looking pizza.

Mi interpretación de Do The Right Thing : Buggin Out y Pino representan dos caras de una misma moneda enfrentadas entre sí, ambas radicalizadas, agresivas y buscando problemas donde no los hay. Esto es apreciable en que, por un lado, Buggin Out podría haber disfrutado de su pizza tranquilamente sin enfrentarse con Sal y, por otro lado, Pino podría haber tratado a Smiley de la misma forma en la que lo trata su padre en lugar de empezar un conflicto (en el caso de Pino hay muchos más ejemplos pero este me pareció el más significativo). Pese a estar enfrentados, comparten la característica de su incesante odio y búsqueda de conflicto. Dicho carácter es probablemente una consecuencia de la frustración que sienten estos personajes, puesto que Pino detesta el lugar en el que trabaja, Buggin Out considera que el mundo es odioso e injusto, etc. La agresividad compartida de estos dos personajes enfrentados entre sí irradia una serie de tensiones cuya explosión se recoge en la última media hora de la película. Estas tensiones terminan derivando en una espiral de violencia con grandes pérdidas como resultado. La mayor de las pérdidas es la vida de Radio Raheem, víctima de la violencia policial. Le sigue la pérdida del negocio de 25 años de Sal. Tras esta amarga conclusión, al final de la película se muestran dos citas con dos mensajes contradictorios: una de Martin Luther King en contra del uso de la violencia y otra de Malcolm justificando la violencia cuando esta sea empleada como defensa. Do The Right Thing no aporta ni pretende aportar ninguna conclusión sobre qué es esta Right Thing ni sobre cuál de las dos citas es correcta . ¿Acaso ha logrado algo la violencia de ambas partes? Una ha perdido una vida y otra ha perdido su propiedad más preciada. El final de la película se siente vacío de significado. ¿A quién debemos hacer caso, a M. L. K. o a Malcolm? Mi principal problema con Do The Right Thing es que esta disyuntiva está muy alejada de lo que vemos en la película. La decisión de Mookie de lanzar el cubo de basura a la ventana no es un acto de lucha contra el sistema, es sencillamente una mala decisión cegada por la furia del momento, ni siquiera dirigida a su verdadero enemigo y causante de la muerte de Radio Raheem, el policía que lo estrangula, sino a su jefe Sal. En la decisión de Mookie no se refleja la disyuntiva entre no violencia (M. L. K.) y violencia defensiva (Malcolm), es una decisión completamente irracional que no merece el revestimiento que le da la película preguntándose si hizo o no la right thing . La única conclusión que puede sacarse realmente de Do The Right Thing es "ojo por ojo diente por diente no conduce a nada", si bien esta cuestión y enseñanza lleva a mi parecer resuelta ya bastante tiempo. Creo que la ejecución de la espiral de violencia a la que conduce el odio, representado por la dicotomía Buggin Out - Pino y continuada por la confrontación Mookie - Sal, no es la mejor de las posibles. Existen varios ejemplos de películas similares que desarrollan esta temática de una mejor manera como es el caso de La Haine o incluso La Batalla de Argel . A pesar de ello, he de decir que me ha encantado la caricaturización de la comunidad cultural de Nueva York que hace Spike Lee y considero que es donde reside la originalidad de la película. Personalmente lo que más me ha gustado. El mosaico de personajes que la componen es interesantísimo y la película lo expone de la mejor manera posible a lo largo de los primeros 90 minutos. Esto es solo mi opinión y entiendo que haya personas que lo vean de un modo completamente opuesto. Igual estoy criticando la película más por lo que yo quería que fuera que por lo que es. Película altamente sobrevalorada, que hace más de 30 años fue relevante y aunque el tema siga presente, se siente aún más superficial. No la disfruté, me pareció que tenía una o dos historias lineales cohesivas y un montón de relleno con monólogos, o escenas de montaje de un programa educativo o de SNL que mete de manera torpe las ideas contra la gentrificación, comunidad o el "portate bien" del título de la peli, siendo incongruente (o quizás no) con la repetitiva frase Fight the power, sonando en la radio de la víctima que molesta a toda la calle a todo volumen. Aunque pudieran agradar algunos personajes, resultaron teatrales y unidimensionales. El final no sorprende, ya que el polvorín alebrestado por la ola de calor lo indicaba, y me pareció que aunque confusa como las revueltas suelen ser, se presta a que no sea entendida como se supone que el mensaje al final desea. Francamente no creo que cambiara formas de pensar en su momento, solo hizo que fuera políticamente correcto y aplaudible,  hablar de esta película como si fuera la panacea como lo hizo Kim Basinger saliendose del guión y asegurando que era la mejor película del año y que la Academia la había pasado por alto. Siendo aplaudida por el Spike Lee reconociendo su valentía. No deseo ser malinterpretada, el cine es político y para premisas importantes, merece mejores realizaciones. Solo creo que la instrumentalización de esta película supera su calidad. Definitivamente creo que hay mejores películas sobre el tema. ​

Spike Lee wants it both ways where "these are just characters, and this is how they act" and the point is in the discussion of what audiences pick out from their interplay; but he does so while also thinking the movie has an unambiguous clear answer—as the guy who wrote it. I think that description correctly diagnoses the issue holding it back from being good as that thumb-on-the-scale aspect. In that it's said to be a character/ideas-heavy thing where fun stylized characters (more negatively caricatures) exaggerating specific aspects of real world people creates a play space of idea exploration, but it ends up not working out as anything actually explored because its got a message to tell. But then framed that way, as a movie with something to say, it essentially wastes its entire runtime not saying it (and indeed never saying it, as other reviews show people leave the movie having not heard anything at all, talking about how everyone is bad or over-focused on Sal and what he did or did not deserve). And even if it were more openly explicit, it spends no time showing, justifying, or defending the message because of the aforementioned interplay/audience discussion format it wants to be.

A large portion of movies could just as easily be books. You can read through the story and dialogue, and the images you visualize in your mind would be a decent approximation of the movie. Then there are movies like this: so overwhelmingly visual, illustrative, and stylized that it feels impossible to imagine them existing in any medium other than film. It’s not just what is said, but how it’s said; not just what happens, but how every shot is composed and presented. The visual language is so essential to the experience that trying to translate it into another medium would fundamentally lose something.

Ventiquattro ore nel microcosmo di un quartiere di periferia nero della fine degli anni ‘80. È una giornata afosa e Samuel L. Jackson nei panni di un conduttore radiofonico pacifista che inneggia al C-H-I-L-L ci accompagna in un viaggio attraverso le semplici vite dei vari personaggi che animano l’incrocio principale del quartiere, tra una pizzeria italiana e un ventiquattrore coreano: il vecchio ubriacone soprannominato Da Major, la mother prioress, tre buontemponi che vivono sotto un ombrellone, un ragazzo autistico che vende per due dollari fotografie di Marthin Luter King e Malcom X, un omone che porta sempre con se’ il suo stereo, un iperattivo ossessionato dalle sue Jordan, l’italo-americano Sal proprietario della pizzeria con i suoi figli Vito e Pino. Il protagonista, Mookie, è osservatore di questa bomba a orologeria (non a caso è interpretato dallo stesso regista). Troppo impegnato a cercare di vivere una vita dignitosa, non si schiera né con i bianchi né con i neri, cerca di salvarsi la pelle e di porre fine agli inutili battibecchi razziali che avvengono alla pizzeria, dove lavora. Man mano che la giornata va avanti capisce che deve prendere in mano la situazione e fare la cosa giusta. Divertentissimi i dialoghi anche grazie a una regia irriverente che cita i videoclip rap di quegli anni, montaggio serrato che non lascia spazio alla metabolizzazione. Lo spettatore cerca di restare a galla in un vortice di cose che succedono una dopo l’altra, proprio come il protagonista, finché la situazione non gli sfugge completamente di mano, e necessita di una scelta netta. Meno realista pessimista e più ispirante del suo fratello parigino La Haine, Do the Right Thing riesce a trasmettere tanta insofferenza verso la questione razziale con due ore che volano via grazie a un ritmo sostenuto e dei dialoghi - ripeto - divertentissimi (altra differenza rispetto al film di Kassovitz, in cui la narrazione viene arbitrariamente interrotta per dare spazio a dei “vuoti” cosmici, a dei piani statico-estatici che mettono in risalto un ulteriore momento in cui è scandita la vita dei personaggi: la noia). Per Mookie non c’è spazio per la noia. La sua vita è frenetica, americana, una miccia innesca un esplosione di violenza nel senso opposto.

I think what makes me truly love this one; putting aside the obviously very prescient and thought provoking social commentary, is how chill it is. Which sounds odd given how harrowing the final explosion of hatred and violence is. But for the whole run time before you’re just spending time with the characters on the block watching their interactions. You see the old drunk with a heart of gold slowly win over the wise maternal figure, the local shit-talker try to start fights, kids playing, regular people just hanging out on a summer day. You get to fully feel the community before it’s wounded deeply. And with such style too. Bill Lee’s jazzy OST sets the mood perfectly and Spike’s classic Hollywood-esque stylization in color and camerawork ensure you’re fully locked in for the ride despite the slow-going nature. On a personal relation; having delivered pizzas in a community not as fully urban but also not far unlike the one in the film certainly helps in feeling the mood.

This joint is perfect , it is, I swear, I couldn’t believe it at first but it’s just the most important, interesting, relevant, pure hearted and heartfelt film I’ve ever watched, and that list goes on! I mean, really, this shit is awesome. Every performance here could be taken out and considered the most charismatic and, most importantly, real . Radio Raheem’s speech about love and hate explained as a boxing match or, even, a street fight. I can’t get enough of this movie, it’s one of the few examples where there wasn’t a moment where I wanted it to end, all though by the end, Spike Lee brought us everything he had to say without even saying it because, just as Da Mayor said, "Those that’ll tell don’t know, and those that know won’t tell". Everyone has something to say, and those who say they don’t are liars. But more important is not if you say the right thing, but if you do the right thing . As I already mentioned, this film’s character cast might just be the greatest I’ve ever witnessed. Mookie, Da Mayor, Radio Raheem, Mother Sister, Buggin Out, Tina, ML, Sweet Dick Willie, Mister Señor Love Daddy, you are interested in everyone. It’s not like any other movie where every character just mixes in one big mass. A wise old man that is treated like a joke, his love, the host of the neighbourhood’s radio show, or even just a guy with a boombox, everyone’s important, no one blends in and no one’s ashamed of themselves. I also really enjoyed Radio Raheem blasting Public Enemy’s "Fight the Power" following the events the entirety of the movie, representing the endless battle against the oppressors and becoming the final straw before the culmination at the end of the movie. This movie really inspired me to want to  think differently, try more, be smarter, be stronger and of course, once again, reform my t4 and maaaaaaybe even myself. I think what really shows a movie’s greatness and if it’s really deserving to be you favourite is how hard it is to find the right words to explain your feelings for it, and believe me, I’ve got my shit tangled up so much, I can’t even think clearly, but the only thing that’s important is that this movie is perfect, and no one’s words will ever change that. This for sure was a Spike Lee’s joint.

Et en même temps on sent un film de début de carrière qui expérimente, qui est maladroit car pas encore dans une grande maîtrise. De nombreux personnages, situations qui m’ont dérouté car je n’arrivais pas à deviner la suite (plutôt bon signe quand il ne s’agit pas de faire la peinture de la bourgeoisie qui s’emmerde au pieux). On est vraiment dans les images temps qui ne dépendent pas de la narration linéaire. Le vitalisme fluide est partout mais la vague de chaleur dans laquelle l’intrigue s’insère annonce que les flux vont se heurter  à la nécropolitique raciale. One of the worst movies I’ve ever seen. I wish I were exaggerating, but I’m not. I went in ready to tear it apart for my own reasons, but I was first surprised and then devastated by the sheer incompetence of that hack, Coogler. Hideous cinematography—the DP was a total disaster, giving us the first IMAX movie that looks like an iPhone Pro Max video. Pitiful, heavy-handed writing; Jordan overacting to pull off his dual persona—especially the "Smoke" side... Conversations that make absolutely no sense at times... Deeply ridiculous... Not even "so bad it's funny," just ridiculous. When you have family producing the film, there are obviously no safeguards... It’s completely off the rails. Abysmal quality... I won't even get into the gratuitous *Django* scene—so gratuitous it could only have sprung from a sick mind desperate for some kind of catharsis. Peele is toxic; Coogler is nothing but a stain. I’ll stop there—the list could go on forever, and I don’t want to deal with the BLM crowd, who seem to have such thin skin. The only saving grace is the music... though even that is marred by mocking white people, portraying them as the inbreds from *Deliverance*... The film is just pathetic, more than anything else.

Neither does the Native American stuff, or the KKK stuff, other than the shootout that feels so detached from the rest of the film it may as well have been a deleted scene. Is it meant to be a post-modern genre piece? The film plays with film form a bit (changes in aspect ratio, that one time travel music montage, the long post credits sequence) - but to what end? They may as well have made every third scene play out in black and white, it would be just as "interesting" and nonsensical as what they did do. Is it just a fun horror romp with a twist? If so, what was that first hour all about? Just watch From Dusk Til Dawn, or Shaun of the Dead, or Suspiria or something. And even the Oscar-winning best parts of the film fell flat for me. Michael B Jordon plays two versions of the same character, except one wears a blue hat and the other wears a red hat. The music is okay at times but laughably bad at others - with the ultra intense electric guitar licks sounding like something straight out of Lethal Weapon. And I get it - it's hard for a film to live up to the hype. But I saw Obsession way after the hype and I loved that film

• This film was a major disappointment to me. There were three dimensions where I think it had to succeed. First, the period piece about African Americans in the Jim Crow south, second, the horror or monster movie, and third, the interplay between these two themes. Unfortunately I don’t think it did well enough on any of these dimensions. • The twins are not interesting characters to me, they are caricatured as exceptionally masculine, aggressive, and competent. • The action sequences were boring and the special effects relating to the vampires and violence were inconsistent, which was distracting. • The scene where Sammy performs in the clubhouse and brings forth music from all times, past and future, is quite powerful and well done. • In my opinion, there should have been more subtlety in the way race was handled in the film. The white people are the monsters, they have corny music, and they turn out to be Klan associates. Once converted, they offer the remaining black people the chance to live forever, as a single (race-blind) community, but they have to forfeit their souls to do so. • I didn’t like the writing, which further detracted from my experience

Shallow Depth of Field, Soft Focus and Anomorphic Blur. The actual Hollywood cultural zietgeist. The modern fad of movies today is new filmmakers and directors trying to inject their films with that enigmatic juice that makes something cinema, that unexplainable feeling of the movies, ironic as most of these new directors are doing everything but making their films feel like cinema. The biggest victim of this new ideology is the visual department, most films are entirley filmed in shallow depth of field, which to put it simply is enhancing a subject and basically leaving the entire background out of focus and blurry (anomorphic blur) this is also called soft focus, when only the subject is in focus. Before today where its now considered normal to shoot 80% of your film in soft focus, movies used alot more deep focus, where subjects are crisp but the backgrounds where enriched with detail, visible detail and not indescrible blurry backgrounds. Now there are positives to using soft focus, it's not like a new technique that suddenly has been founded, filmmakers have always used soft focus, but in moderation, restricting to key character moments when all that is important in a scene is the character. Nowdays soft focus is used to film every scene, it removes world building and the distinct personality of the film. And it's not always a filmmaker problem, this issue has stemmed from studios becoming too lazy to fund and budget set designs properly, and will encourage shallow focus to paste over the cracks of the image being built and spin it as a "cinematic" effect. It's one of the worst trends in todays industry. Sinners is far from the only movie that falls victim to this terrible trend, but it is by far one of the most notable and consequential. 16 academy award nominations were granted to this movie, that is the MOST ever, what does that tell studios and aspiring filmmakers? that movies should be like this? that is a very dangerous precedent to set. This is considered good cinemtography? this WON best cinematography? for what? is soft focus spam considered good cinematography now? no regard for the image as a whole anymore? and I realize that not every shot in Sinners uses soft focus, most of the establishing shots are deep focus (although those are far and few) this constrics world building to images and shots that do not involve the character, which is extremly restricting, the movie feels so trapped in its own misguided idea of visual mastery. Another issue I have with Sinners is Ryan Coogler, more specifically his direction, quite frankly it is pathetic here, characters stand in the middle of the screen speaking to eachother back and forth, clearly Coogler doesn't care about blocking or elevating his written material whatsoever, every scene is just the same regurgitated directing technique, besides the showstoppy "I Lied to You" scene which is really well crafted, which disappoints me in further, because you can do that? but then the rest of the movie is just empty character standing still back and forth dialogue sequences. Coogler seems more trying to copy Tarantino (the Dusk Till Dawn and Django influences are very very prevelant) than to add any real social commentary, his misguided use of the blues in which he completley disregards it's mythic attributes that have shaped its prevelant inimitability in american culture in favour of a hollywoodized cynical use of the blues to pander towards millenials. Michael B Jordans performance is acceptable but replaceable, supposedly the face of dual performance now that the academy have decided to award him with the prestiged best actor award, Peter Sellers must be rolling in his grave, and im sure when Jeremy Irons isn't trying to cancel himself on the internet by miscommunicating his opinions on gay marraige he's asking himself "how the fuck did I not win for Dead Ringers". Obviously Michael isn't to blame for this, it's this new stage academy which so ignorantley percieves any sort of social commentary however true or misguided as "progressive cinema" that they flourish it with every award under the sun, I mean Wumni Mosaku? seriously, but that's what the oscars is now, it's a marketing game who's willing to pay the most money for facadical confectionaries. And it's no surprise that Coogler is returning straight back to Marvel (post credit scene whaaaaa) to finish his Black Panther trilogy, after Warner Bros chucked a ludicrous amount of money at Sinners (ironically which is seemingly outing their own depravity) Marvel now are chucking even more money in Coogler's direction to film whatever softfocusmaxxing project he ends up doing.

‘Sinners’ got a lot of hype and everybody was posting it to their Letterboxd Last Four, so I thought there must be something more to it. However, turns out it was a bit overhyped—certainly not worthy of 18 Oscar nominations. It’s basically a big-budget horror film with some not-so-subtle metaphors for cultural and human exploitation. I certainly appreciate the intent of the film to reach a mainstream audience with a political message delivered by way of an allegory. Unfortunately, it’s not a particularly clever plot or a smart script. There are moments of artistry—the blending of multiple anachronistic musical genres into one scene, for example—but all that smarts gets overtaken by the conventional horror story plot points. My first complaint is, everything feels phony. The period wardrobes feel too new and perfect. The art direction looks too theme park. There are backdrops that are obviously CG. Compare the look of this film to ‘Hamnet’ or ‘Days of Heaven’, and you’ll know what I mean. The past was dirty and messy. Then there’s the camerawork. I keep saying this, but beautiful photography and precise movement isn’t everything. The camera should tell the story without drawing attention to itself. I felt like I was always noticing the camera’s movements instead of following the characters. Most disappointing was the script, which not only spells out the metaphor—in case you didn’t get it—but it also reduces the characters to stereotype gangster tough guys and any true relationships to either sex or violence. That’s just not reality. There’s also the lack of logic. How would people in the ‘20’s before the 100 years of popular vampire films all inherently know all the methods of dispensing with vampires? They exist during the say but burn up when exposed to sunlight? It’s okay if you don’t think about it, I guess. I’m rating it a 6 because it’s decently produced and semi-entertaining, but man, the insight and the poignancy were lost in the traditional horror and gore.
