this film fails on every single level. it immediately begins with its corny, over the top message right in your face dialogue. i accept it. maybe it's because it's translated from German. seriously, it's very obvious this was written for people who are not very smart. i don't care about a single character sincerely. they all seem like empty dolls to die. why should i care if they do, honestly. i hated paul so much when he died i started clapping, because i was going to be actually mad if they didn't kill him. not because war is hell or whatever but because he's so unlikeable and dumb and boring. he's the placeholder for a human but this isn't a video game. why do i care about anything this stupid, boring, annoying man goes through. i don't. all of the cinematography was a blatant ripoff of 1917. not a single element of the original (1930) film is to be seen here. the most memorable parts of that movie aren't even Frankenstein'd into this mess they're just forgotten. the hands on the barbed wire. them in the trenches for days at a time, shaking in the overwhelming noise of the constant bombing and shelling. the crosses going over the young boys who we learned to know and watched march to their deaths. nothing here is memorable or even likeable. there are stupid horns that sound like dubstep sometimes and it honestly feels disrespectful to the actual victims. I've never once hated a soundtrack so much to feel like it was disrespectful to real life, but this feels like it is. all of the characters lack basic common sense and don't even act like human beings. i don't think any of them are even trying to survive (understandable). daniel bruhl pisses on his shoe at one point. a dude stabs himself to death with a fork. there is no humanity to be found here. the ending marches the soldiers to their deaths post cease fire just in case you didn't understand war is meaningless. the main character stands up and dies awkwardly in what is supposed to be a cinematic shot or whatever and then a boy takes his dog tags like he did at the start. subtlety is dead. i guess they thought perhaps we were too stupid to understand basic metaphors, human dialogue or anything that isn't shoved down our throats. the scene that left the biggest mark on me from the first film was when a soldier steals his dead friend's boots, simply because he needs them to continue on. it made me weep. the scene which is arguably the climax of the film were the main character kills a French soldier in a trench and then regrets it is so overdone and bland here that i didn't even cry (i easily cry at any and all films). this film tortures you so much all i felt was tired, but it still didn't convince me war is hell. i can see it now, a little boy who was swayed by internet opinions and happens to idolize the Germans actions watching this and still thinking it was worth it, and that the main character died fighting with honor. it fails at every single possible thing. the beginning is supposed to be school boys naively joining the army and then showing us the reality of the brutality of war but this film is so eager to start it even butchers that by giving us a beginning sequence which screams the messaging in your face before the actual film has even started. they could've just left that as a short film and left me alone. this was a completely useless jerkoff fest made by people who can't understand the themes of a very simple book. there is a complete lack of empathy for any of the soldiers in this film which is hilarious because that's seemingly the entire point of it (for you to empathize with the German soldiers who died for an evil and wrong cause). i do have plenty of empathy for the fact that these were just people but somehow the film is simultaneously too nice to them and too uncaring at the same time. it doesn't understand its own message and neither do i. the only part of this film i enjoyed is the trench sequence right next to when the French's tanks showed up and a little after that, i enjoyed around 30 minutes of this film. the rest of it is a complete mess.

I had read some of the notoriously negative German reviews of this when it released with a few calling it war kitsch and one review even saying it's retroactively a right wing film in how it leans into the stab in the back theory that was so popular amongst post WW1 right wingers. Needless to say my expectations where low and in the intervening time I'd read the book which I had enjoyed. I was utterly shocked with how dull and flatly shite this film is. It's main fault is a vague timbre of genericism that pervades every part of it, non descript music, flat acting, dull pacing and many war tropes combine to create a totally banal experience. The only point I really liked was the opening sequence where a dead soldiers tunic is scavenged, repaired and handed to Paul, our protagonist. The film however goes downhill from here, it removes the crucial section from the 1930 film and book where Paul returns home and meets his ever jingoistic teacher and adds in a truly useless subplot following a German politician negotiating the armistice and a grim general desperate to fight to the bitter end. Both storylines take up crucial time from Paul and his comrades, time which in the wonderful 1930 film added levity and camaraderie, a thing that barely exists here. In fact in some ways this film is orgisatically obsessed with grimness and violence,.it does so with the same shlocky gore that Hacksaw Ridge revelled in, another shite war film. It would be forgivable I'd the battle sequences where well done but they have rigid and unrealistic quality to them that detracts from their effect, the French use flamethrowers at point blank range whereas in reality they would have been used at a further distance, tanks fight without infantry support. This is coupled with the disjointed nature of the film due to the added storylines and the setting around the last week for the war the film tries to add a Dunkirk/Nolanesque countdown clockwork mechanism that is just daft and a far cry from the leviathan feeling of the book and original film where time moves over the course of years as Paul grows rougher, more weary. Here we have a rushed opening sequence after which most of the movie takes place around the last week with Paul being stabbed by a Frenchman at 11 o'clock as the war ends. It's so crazy and dumb in fact that after the soldier pulls the bayonet from Paul's body and the blood pours out we hear another Frenchman outside say, "It's 11, stop fighting!" FUCK OFF LIKE. That is something a child writes and this movie won four Oscars. The book and original film rather end with Paul being banally shot by a rogue sniper with the backdrop of an otherwise quiet frontline. I think it is obvious which is more effective. The real sadness of this film is all the people that will watch it and revel in it and enjoy it and will never watch the original and actually experience just how good that film is and how superior it is. A totally dull affair and not worth any time

I genuinely wonder if I watched the same movie as everyone else. There’s a lot here that I can appreciate. The cinematography is beautiful, the production design is incredible, and when the film actually throws you into the brutality of the war, it can be genuinely horrifying. Technically, this is an extremely well-made movie. But for something depicting one of the most horrific wars in human history, this felt strangely emotionless to me. I understood what I was supposed to feel, but the movie rarely made me actually feel it. The characters never felt developed enough for me to become attached to them, so when tragedy came, I was watching something devastating happen without feeling devastated by it. There’s brutality everywhere, but brutality alone doesn’t create an emotional connection. That’s why seeing a 4.1 average rating throws me so much. I can absolutely see the craftsmanship everyone is praising. I just don’t understand where the emotional connection is supposed to come from. Beautifully made and brutal when it needs to be, but for me, it lacked far too much everywhere else.

Nouvelle adaptation du roman d’Erich Maria Remarque, le film d’Edward Berger entend faire éprouver physiquement l’horreur de 14-18. Tranchées, boue, mutilations, agonies, rats, chevaux morts : rien n’est épargné au spectateur, tandis que le contraste avec le confort des états-majors souligne l’inhumanité du massacre. La démonstration est techniquement impressionnante, mais son insistance finit par en révéler la limite. À force de mouvements de caméra étudiés, de raccords spectaculaires et de compositions soigneusement travaillées, Berger esthétise précisément la violence qu’il prétend dénoncer. Cette fascination formelle introduit une certaine complaisance dans un propos antimilitariste par ailleurs fort peu neuf : un siècle après les faits, fallait-il encore deux heures trente pour nous apprendre que la Grande Guerre fut une boucherie ? L’ampleur de la production impressionne davantage que son regard. Un film de guerre puissant dans sa fabrication, mais dont le spectaculaire finit paradoxalement par affaiblir la dénonciation.

Impressive movie, but they absolutely miss the key themes of the book and turn the plot into what it wasn’t meant to be, a showing of the epic huge loud battles and brutality. The clue is in the name here, this movie misses the mark. The biggest betrayal is the omission of the key scenes of Paul returning home, and how he is treated by those around him versus who he has become and how he feels. The focus is put on parts of the war that, although essential, are not the focus of the book, which is what makes the book so special in the first place! I’m sure if I’d seen the movie first I’m sure I would have enjoyed it much more. My first dislike is the focus on the idea of them being young boys and inexperienced. In the book, there is no confusion that the boys are young, but by this point they were the older group, and this is again so important to the book. To make them young and inexperienced is to take away the fact that they are young and yet they have so much experience and are numb to everything now. My other problem is the omission entirely of the Catholic hospital recovery scenes. I understand that you must omit things, and so normally I wouldn’t have a problem with the omission of such a scene for times sake. But they omitted these scenes so they could focus on the war and battle aspect of the movies, which again IS NOT MEANT TO BE THE FOCUS. The changing of the scene with the French soldier makes no sense to me, while of course still emotionally devastating, to begin the scene with Paul moving across the crater to stab the man I feel removes the desperation element of the act, and makes the remorse feel less genuine. Furthermore, they change not only Paul’s ending, instead of dying on a normal day he dies minutes before the armistice in an epic battle. I can’t understand why they did this (well I can, blockbuster drama) but I really hate it, the way he dies is meaningful and integral to the feeling you get after finishing the book. Finally, they include armistice discussions which are not at all mentioned in the book. This is just a mind boggling decision, as again I might remind you, the name suggests the book is about the everyday life on the front NOT ABOUT THE WAR ITSELF. There are enough movies about the politicians who ended the war, but the reason, again, that this book is so important is that this is emitted. Those on the front had no idea these talks were going on, had no idea what tomorrow would bring let alone and were forgotten and abandoned by those in power, purely cannon fodder to continue and unnecessary and futile war. Basically, if you want a good movie about life as a German soldier in World War I watch this movie, but you like the book, do not watch this movie. It cuts out important parts of the book that make it a masterpiece  in favour of nothing special. There are so many movies out there that do exactly what this movie does, most do it better, but there are no books that do what All Quiet on the Western Front does. I could go on and on.

I appreciated what the film was trying to do more than I appreciated watching it. War movies usually have one of two failure modes. The first is accidentally making war look exciting. The second is spending three hours insisting that war is bad, as though the audience arrived expecting a TED Talk titled “Actually, trench warfare seems underrated.” All Quiet on the Western Front mostly avoids the first trap, then walks straight into the second. Every scene is calibrated toward the same conclusion: young men are chewed up by institutions that barely notice their existence. This is true. It is also established about thirty minutes in. The remaining two hours mostly increase the fidelity of the suffering rather than the depth of the argument. The craftsmanship is undeniable. The cinematography is gorgeous in a way that feels almost inappropriate. The sound design is relentless. The performances are excellent. But I kept waiting for the movie to tell me something about the psychology of war, nationalism, courage, fear, or even ordinary survival that I didn’t already know. Instead, it kept turning the volume up on a point it had already made. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe war really is just endless repetition punctuated by arbitrary death. But a movie isn’t obligated to reproduce the experience of its subject. Sometimes it should interpret it. Beautifully made, emotionally exhausting, and ultimately less interesting than the history that inspired it.

Première fois depuis les Hunger Games que je vois un film juste après avoir lu le livre donc je vais me faire plaisir. Les images, les décors et les grandes scènes d’action sont vraiment très bonnes. Le plan d'ouverture, puis de fin, est peut-être l’une des plus belles manières d’exposer la futilité de la guerre dans un seul dialogue, juste un simple plan fixe sur une forêt. Néanmoins, le film prend le parti de suivre les négociations de l’armistice en parallèle de l’histoire des protagonistes. Or, dans le livre, c’est justement l’absence totale de point de vue autre que celui de Paul qui rend le récit si tragique. À chaque instant, la guerre pourrait s’arrêter dans 2 minutes ou dans 10 ans, ça ne fait aucune différence pour les soldats engagés. Pire, le film introduit à la moitié cet espèce de compte à rebours avant l’armistice pour rajouter de la tension, décision qui dessert totalement son propos. Autre parti pris décevant, l’incarnation d’un grand méchant par le général allemand. “Regardez comme c’est dommage, tout les gens aux autres postes de commandement étaient bien intentionnés, c’est juste un seul méchant monsieur qui cause la mort de tout ces jeunes”. Encore une fois, dans le livre, personne n’est nommé comme responsable de la souffrance des soldats. Toute l’horreur repose là-dedans : des gamins de 20 ans, pris dans un engrenage bien au-delà de leur échelle, et aussi inutile qu’implacable. Une réalité beaucoup plus nuancée et dure que le sosie de Dr Eggman qu’on retrouve. En bref, un film qui incarne visuellement très bien les horreurs de la guerre, mais qui omet totalement les éléments narratifs les plus essentiels du matériel de base. Un film de guerre qui fait coquille vide ?? Chokbar (non)

O cineasta François Truffaut possui uma frase popular: “não existe filme antiguerra”. Em sua tese ele conceitua e discorre sobre a linguagem sensual e entretida do cinema, isso leva a conclusão que não importa o quanto você faça um filme sobre guerra, mostrando inúmeros lados horríveis deste acontecimento horrível, o cinema sempre vai romantizar isso, não por que os criadores quiserem muito das vezes, mas por que é assim que a sétima arte se depõe em nossos olhos e signos. Dito isso, a obra de Edward Berger anda em um liminar tão amedrontador, com um visual tão profundo e melancólico, criticaram as esferas de mais privilégios as bases mais sofridas de uma guerra que por um momento parece que a súmula de Truffaut se equivoca aqui, mas tudo isso para demonstrar que às vezes a maior busca por um sentimento antiguerra traz o amor a guerra. O diretor resolve adicionar a essa obra de trilhagem tão interessante e obscura, com retoques de profundidade de símbolos inclusos como é o exemplo da raposa e das florestas, para no fim adaptar de certa forma uma espécie de jornada do herói. O começo do filme é didático em mostrar um dos melhores acertos do filme, a guerra aqui é trabalhada como produto, como venda. Os soldados morrendo, as costureiras refazendo uniformes, as substituições… tudo aqui mostra um tom legível de repetição e precificação da vida de cidadãos, atitudes essas que realmente acontecem em tempos de guerra. E quando o filme volta para essa leitura é quando ele mais acerta na minha opinião. Todavia, o filme ainda não se desprende totalmente de uma leitura protagonista, jornada e inclusive tem ate mentor. Esse ponto não necessariamente é ruim, tendo em vista que muitas vezes são esses laços que passam a mensagem de humanidade em um cenário de morte, porém é perceptível que na maioria dos filmes grandes de guerra, aqui não diferente, neste posso de sujeira, sangue e morte há um quê de realismo, sempre tem, “o meu filme de guerra tem mais tons de real e de verdade” e quando se tenta sair na contramão da citação que falei no começo deste texto é quando se dá conta do tom persuasivo e nada antiguerra de um filme. O protagonista aqui possui laços, possui dor e temos medo de perder os amigos dele, e isso é um romance de guerra no final das contas! é ruim? É bom? É o cinema persuadindo nós mais uma vez. __dantas

I just watched All Quiet on the Western Front, and, okay, I didn't fully watch it. I actually DNFed it. I didn't finish it. And it's not because it's a bad movie. This movie won four Oscars, and I can't complain about the visuals, the acting, the screenplay, or really anything about how the movie was made. The only thing that made me DNF it is that I just couldn't get into it. I tried. I genuinely tried sticking through it, and I just couldn't. Here's the thing for me. I just wasn't able to develop any kind of connection to the characters. Paul, to me, just felt like another young man and another character. I can't remember for the life of me who the other four people are, whether they're his friends, his higher ups, or whatever. And because I couldn't develop that connection with any of them, it became really hard for me to root for them. I know that sounds horrible, but I just found myself not being able to get into it. I couldn't sit there for more than ten minutes without eventually looking around my room or getting distracted, and that's sort of a deal breaker for me when I'm watching a movie. I think a lot of people are probably going to be disappointed with my take on this. I'm sure some people would tell me that I don't know what I'm talking about or that I just don't understand the movie, but I genuinely tried to give it a chance. I mean, I made it about three fourths of the way through the movie before finally giving up. I just couldn't find myself rooting for Paul or really any of the other characters. Obviously, when they're in battle, I'm rooting for Paul and his buddies to survive and make it through, but there wasn't that deeper emotional connection where I genuinely felt attached to them. I think one of the reasons this movie still gets three stars from me is because it does an incredible job of showing the horrifying reality of trench warfare during World War I. And if I'm being so honest, I was really interested in seeing more of that side of the war. I'm not going to say I wanted to see trench foot, but trench foot was a massive part of the horrible conditions soldiers experienced during World War I, and I was interested in seeing more of those details. I'm glad I got to see the flamethrowers, the tanks, the actual trenches, and just how brutal and terrifying that kind of warfare was. Those parts were genuinely interesting to me. But even with all of that, I just couldn't get into the actual movie. I don't know what it is. Sometimes a movie just doesn't connect with you, and this one didn't connect with me. So I'll give All Quiet on the Western Front three stars out of five, and that's really only because I couldn't get into it. This movie isn't bad whatsoever. The visuals aren't bad. The acting isn't bad. The storyline isn't bad. The screenplay, the cinematography, the coloring, all of it is incredibly well done. I can completely understand why other people love this movie and why it won the awards that it did. It just wasn't for me. That's it.

Bleak as hell, but pretty damn effective. I really liked how completely this strips war of any grandeur and reduces it to mud, panic, exhaustion, and young men being fed into this enormous machine for objectives that become increasingly abstract and meaningless. It’s huge in scale without ever confusing scale for heroism, and I think that distinction is where the movie is strongest. The brutality lands because it rarely feels ornamental; it’s constantly reinforcing the idea that war functions through attrition, reducing individual lives to bodies, numbers, and territory gained or lost. I never connected with the characters quite enough for it to completely devastate me, but the human cost still registers, especially in the quieter moments where all the military rhetoric falls away and you’re just left with frightened people trying to survive. Really well made, appropriately miserable, and impressively committed to its anti-war perspective. It didn’t hit me on some profound emotional level, but I admired a lot of what it was doing, particularly how effectively it makes the entire machinery of war feel both enormous and completely fucking senseless.

Forging your parent's signature for a field trip is good.  Forging your parent's signature to join an ongoing war is bad. The 2022 adaptation of Erich Maria Remarque's seminal anti-war novel isn't what I'd call a remake of Lewis Milestone's Best Picture-winning film from 1930 (or the Delbert Mann version which was made for television in 1979) but rather another interpretation of the story.  It's the same sentiment I have regarding the new Sense and Sensibility coming out.  Rather than remaking the Ang Lee one, it appears to just be the next go-around of filming Jane Austen's book. Director Edward Berger goes all in on the "war is hell" imagery here.  His tasteful eye, combined with the astonishingly great cinematography by James Friend, allows All Quiet on the Western Front a certain visceral heft that may not have been possible given the constraints of its earlier predecessors.  Nothing in the film is particularly new if you've seen its contemporaries but it still manages to achieve its purpose emotionally, thematically and cinematically. Just to get my negative out of the way, I don't get why Volker Bertelmann snagged the Oscar here.  Those three notes sound too much like dubstep for my taste.  Anachronistic scores can work but it took me out.  That said, Bertelmann's other compositions in the film are quite effective but maybe I'm bitter that Justin Hurwitz's Babylon score, easily one of the decade's most memorable film soundtracks, lost to this.  Then again, considering the same branch didn't even nominate Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross for Challengers, I can't say I'm surprised. Felix Kammerer gives a remarkable debut performance.  His face screams someone whose pure innocence will be decimated by the brutality of war, not unlike the young boy from Come and See.  Albrecht Schuch is great too as Kat.  He was a highlight from that Berlin Alexanderplatz in 2020.  Daniel Brühl is easily the most recognizable actor here, lending credibility as Matthias Erzberger, a German politician instrumental in the armistice that ended the war. I was mesmerized by Berger's command of the camera.  He puts you down and dirty in those trenches.  It's a harmonious mixture of some phenomenal production design by Christian M. Goldbeck, seamless integration of visual effects and some awesome makeup that cakes our actors in mud to resemble the horrifically obscuring conditions that it takes to engage in this level of combat.  There's a reason Paul goes from smiling and chipper at the start to absolutely stone-faced by the end. The assembly line nature of the youth as they enter their regiments is frightening.  A batch of young soldiers dies only to be replaced by younger soldiers whose eyes can't fathom the terrifying things they're about to inflict and be inflicted upon.  The scene of Paul engaging in a one-on-one with the French soldier is devastating because it's a fight or flight scenario while also an acknowledgement of how war encourages the loss of our humanity little by little until we can't even comprehend the actions we commit. Paul is one of many millions of people who were indoctrinated into thinking that what they were doing was a good thing and that the future tales of heroics will far exceed anything on the battlefield.  Meanwhile, the people with the power to the end the war only did so when it mathematically didn't make sense to continue and even still there were those who pridefully refused to concede, thus dragging on the war.  You just become numb to it all, senseless to the feeling that you're a pawn, an eventual casualty in a long list of obituaries. If the Germans pulled a Reynolds Woodcock and simply sewed the names into the fabric it'd make the whole recycling uniforms thing easier.

I tend to be cynical about the effectiveness of propaganda in entertainment media, so it’s still easy for me to imagine the cohort of young German men/boys who would watch this and say: “yes, that’s terrible, but only because we lost. As a movie though, I appreciated this more than the original. The tone and pacing were more consistent. Ed Berger’s remake also benefits greatly from modern filmmaking techniques, from VFX to sound design. All Quiet on the Western Front is one of a small group of Netflix original movies that is both impressive to look at and actually worth watching. Sure it isn’t a particularly unique story, instead essentially playing as a remake of a remake, but if you’re looking for a brutal and striking depiction of war then you’ll be hard pressed to find better. What fascinates me about war is that despite every distinct conflict being inherently awful, each of them are terrible in their own unique way. You’ve obviously got the raw numbers with WW2, the insanity and trauma of Vietnam and the boredom of the Gulf war, but I honestly don’t think anything can ever top WW1. It’s kinda the perfect culmination of everything awful people associate about war. It happened at a time when people still thought fighting and dying for your country was honourable, so you had poor recruits thinking they were going on an adventure and generals who thought any problem could just be solved by throwing bodies at them. You’ve also got undoubtedly some of the worst conditions in any modern conflict with the trenches and their mud, disease and rats, on top of the insanity element thanks to spending years fighting for a few extra metres and watching your friends get blown to pieces. Truly as far as picking a bad experience to live through, I think you’d be hard pressed to find anything worse than ‘The Great War’ and All Quiet on the Western Front really excellently captures that vibe. What this movies really excels at is getting across how every soldier as an individual was treated like absolute dirt. They were given hammy down clothes from the last lot who had been slaughtered and then sent to die in the mud just so some stuck up boffins could pat themselves on the back and eat a fancy pastry. Their lives were viewed as completely without value besides dying for their country, despite each of them being people in their own right with families and hopes. The fact that this story is told from a distinctly German perspective further helps manifest that idea, since ultimately every young man in every country during the war got the same speech about how righteous they were and how they will bring glory to their fatherland. They couldn’t all be right and realistically none of them were. It’s easy to solidify yourself in the ‘us vs them’ mindset when looking at historical conflicts, hence why stories like this one are so important. That scene in the mortar crater really gets the point across. Everyone was told to hate and kill each other, but looking in the eyes of another innocent young lad and taking his life away remains genuinely one of the most horrific things you could be forced to do. Scenes like that are used effectively throughout All Quiet on the Western Front and really draw into question the inhumanity that was rife during WW1. The other aspect of All Quiet which is undoubtedly great is how terrific it looks. Maybe it’s because I’m used to the green screen/volume vibe of most straight to Netflix movies, but this movie really blew me away from the visuals. The cinematography is gorgeous with its use of colours and its framing of the central events, sometimes heightening the tension like with that tank sequence and sometimes contrasting the chaos with more quiet, tender moments. I wasn’t expecting this movie to be as Terrence Malick as it is, but it’s quite a nice homage to movies like The Thin Red Line whilst further helping demonstrate the shear chaos unleashed by the war. On that note, the gore in this movie is also excellent. It doesn’t pull any punches, with bodies just lying everywhere, often missing parts, all whilst being framed with such a blasé and unfazed perspective. It’s an essential aspect of capturing the vibe of this conflict, given that soldiers at the time had to live around decaying corpses rife with disease all whilst never knowing if they or their mates would be next. All Quiet honestly gets pretty dark at times and I really appreciate it. It’s absolutely not afraid to delve into the traumatic and damaged mindset of the German soldiers, making the movie overall all the more effective. All that glazing being said, I had heard claims that this was an easy contender for ‘the best war movie ever made’ and I just don’t know if I’d agree. It’s very good don’t get me wrong, but it feels like it’s missing something that the best of the genre absolutely aren’t. I can’t help but get the feeling that the ending of this movie and the emotional stakes would have been much more impactful if the first half an hour wasn’t so rushed. I haven’t seen the original in completion, but I understand that a big part is dedicated to introducing the characters and seeing them be all excited and giddy before they go off to war. In this version, it kinda feels like the filmmakers were anxious to get them straight into conflict and as a result only left maybe three scenes of the characters before they become damaged (maybe the Netflix influence creeped in there). Whilst I do think that their descent into nihilism is portrayed effectively, I would have liked to get to know the characters a bit more before they became broken. Some war movies can get away with having bland characters because they frame their stories as something that could have just happened to anyone, but All Quiet definitely feels like it’s trying to zoom in and tell a personal story and I’m not sure it’s done as well as people say. I couldn’t really name any of the characters other than Paul, and even then I can’t say I related to him personally, outside of his situation which everyone else around him was also in. I feel like if I really liked him and his mates as guys, then that ending scene would have been brutal, but as is I was almost indifferent. Their fates were quite predictable and at the end of the day they were all probably better off than if they were forced to continue their suffering. Something like Saving Private Ryan for example always leaves me shattered since I love those characters so much, but the same doesn’t really apply to All Quiet. Maybe another little thing, and this is more of a personal problem than an objective complaint, but the scope of the story just didn’t particularly strike me. All Quiet kinda feels like it’s running the gamut of WW1 things, and whilst they’re all done very well individually, the way they are all connected together to produce the final narrative felt a little lacking. It’s just Paul running from battle to battle trying to survive without any particular goal in mind. It’s a tough complaint for sure, but in such an overplayed genre where every major conflict has been covered by a dozen famous movies (in this case also the exact same story multiple times)  I think All Quiet feels a little bit lacking in what it has to offer. Even if the ideas are very strong, they have absolutely been covered elsewhere and have been occasionally done just as well, which in my eyes makes this movie feel a tad more generic than it probably should. A very good watch all and all. It’s probably one of the few foreign language films that you could convince your dad to watch and there is absolutely a reason for it. Even if it isn’t the most original or character driven story, it would be pretty hard to execute this narrative much better. Maybe that means we won’t get a fourth go at it, but with how creatively bankrupt executives are nowadays I honestly wouldn’t be surprised. Watch this space.

In my line of work, we often omit the usage of the word “remains” — if nothing has changed, it should be left unsaid. But “remains” can mean a lot of things. What hasn’t changed, the splintering of bodies, what is left behind. The main audial motif of the movie is titled “remains”, and the audience is almost berated with it, like the relentless barrage of artillery fire, again and again and again and again. Its scenes feel almost post-apocalyptic in its delivery of the past. What was once memory is now history. History tends to mysteriously vanish, a case of the universal forgetting. The lessons learnt are what remains. But nothing remains at all except remains. Even that is buried on unmarked soil. And to think that, after humanity has gone through so much in a little over a century, it has learnt nothing. Perhaps nothing has really changed, and that is the most upsetting of all.

There’s a sort of irony that, despite being a beyond exceptional technical directing talent who only gained the assistance of even more exceptional technical directing talent along the way, Iñárritu is by far the most graceless, hollow showboater Hollywood has seen in decades, arguably even more than someone as derided for showboating as Michael Bay. He’s a monkey’s paw curse made man: born with both divine technical ability and the worst possible thematic and narrative instincts those technical abilities could be paired with. Derivative, overly-literal macho faux-art nonsense. Historically irresponsible, burdened with clunky attempts at spiritualist visual metaphor and just way, waaaaaay too long. Lubezki can light and shoot snow-covered forests and babbling brooks all day but he can’t save a movie that, at its core, has nothing of any worth to say. Nothing truly relevant or engaging happens between those beautifully composed frames, save for a final shot that attempts to add deeper subtext the narrative itself does not attempt to possess. If you're after a “man fights nature/masculinity” movie set in a lot of snowy forest wildernesses that’s actually good, Joe Carnahan’s “The Grey” is a daring masterpiece.

Leonardo DiCaprio gehört zweifelsohne zu den besten  US-amerikanischen Schauspielern der Gegenwart. Lange musste er trotz einer beeindruckenden Filmografie auf den längst verdienten Oscar als Bester Haupdarsteller warten. Umso trauriger, dass er mit diesem für  den Rachewestern "The Revenant" ausgezeichnet wurde. Von der großartigen Schauspielkunst DiCaprios ist hier hinter seinem Bart und unter dem Schnee leider wenig zu sehen. Seine Leinwandkollegen Tom Hardy oder die Grizzlybärin können diesen auch nicht übertreffen. Der von DiCaprio verkörperte Hugh Glass und der Pferdekadaver sind auch kein gutes Leinwandpaar. Dass DiCaprio sowie Regiesseur Alejandro González Iñárritu für diesen Film jeweils mit dem Oscar ausgezeichnet wurden, bestätigt noch einmal die Blut, Schweiß und Tränen-Ideologie der Academy.  Survival-Challenges oder dass man als Vegetarier rohe Bisonleber verspeist, scheinen wohl Merkmale guter Schauspielkunst zu sein. Es wirkt, als sei dieser Film vor allem gemacht worden, um bei der Oscarverleihung 2016 abzuräumen. Sieht man mal von den Schauspielern ab, hat der Film weder oberflächlich noch inhaltlich etwas zu bieten. Die Handlung ist banal und die Landschaftsaufnahmen erinnern eher an den Windows-Sperrbildschirm als an großes Western-Kino. Die Suche nach Spiritualität wirkt aufgesetzt, um der Handlung künstlich Tiefe zu verleihen. Es hätte ja ein interessanter Film sein können, der das Verhältnis von Mensch und Natur und die Themen und Fragen des Western-Genres aufgreift und neu verhandelt. Doche solche Fragen und Genre-Motive sind hier eher lose Assoziationen als bedeutungstragende Elemente des Films. Möglicherweise wird "The Revenant" nur dafür in Erinnerung bleiben, dass Leonardo DiCaprio für diesen Film seinen bisher einzigen Oscar als Bester Hauptdarsteller gewann.

The script is simple: revenge after injustice. The movie is built around the pain and suffering of Hugh Glass, who has his stepson killed by Fitzgerald after their settlement is attacked by Native Americans. A premise like that demands great performances to make an impact, and that's what holds the entire movie together. DiCaprio delivers it pretty well. It isn't one of his best performances, but it's a good one. Unpopular opinion: I believe Tom Hardy is the standout of the entire film! I don't usually expect much from him, and that's exactly why his performance is so impressive. Maybe the best character he has ever played. The whole time he is on screen, he grabs your attention. Simply as that. We've all seen dozens of revenge movies, but DiCaprio and, mainly, Hardy make this one stand out. The direction is great, and the scenes are raw, bloody, and aggressive. The soundtrack is subtle but works well. In short: the movie is simple, well-paced, and well-structured, and Hardy's performance makes it even cooler. OBS: DiCaprio has played several characters better than this one. It's kind of sad that "The Revenant" was the role that finally won him the award in 2016.

I did it! I watched The Revenant! What did I get out of the experience, you ask? First things first: Naughty Dog and Rockstar should be bending their knees to Iñárritu after ripping off their respective climactic fights from this film. The Revenant: probably in the upper echelon of "films I've never seen despite my age and preferences in actors and Oscar history." I remember watching the commercials before its release, but I was too young at the time to go see it (or at least too young to want to witness Leo crawl into the belly of a stallion). I have fond memories of the "Leo has never won an Oscar" memes, and endlessly watched WatchMojo's incessantness in crowning him in the number one spot for Oscarless movie stars. Despite my desire, the half-face Leo staring into the lens of the camera poster never caught my eye enough on streaming services to warrant a click (the 150-minute runtime doesn't help either, but this is also the guy who watched Oppenheimer 6 times, so take that claim with a grain of salt). Thank god HBO Max decided to blow the dust off of their Digger-related media this month. I've already watched Birdman, and I've started The Last Samurai (which doesn't look to be passing the Woke-ometer based on the first half hour). I'm taking the opportunity given to me and consuming myself with all the knowledge I can before the first of next month, when my most anticipated movie of the year comes out (It's Verity). A decade of buildup, the final episode when I finally watch the movie- does it live up to the hype I've built up in my mind... Um... Eh. Remember in The Last Jedi when they act like they're going to kill off Leia, and give her this really beautiful swan song scene, only to have her survive the attack and then never speak again throughout the rest of the trilogy. Like, yeah, that was all good and dandy, but what's the point? That's how I feel about The Revenant. Sure, Leo gives a great performance, the camera work is electric, and the cinematography is beautiful, but what does any of it amount to other than meeting those specified criteria? Why does The Revenant exist? Is it commenting on some greater cultural theme that 2015 audiences could resonate with? I don't see any. Is it trying to be an Odyssey-esque revenge story for Leo to shine in? I guess, but it doesn't do anything particularly unique besides replacing the Cyclops with a bear. I just see no reason for this movie to exist other than to watch people's eyes open in bewildered awe as you explain to them the basic plot points of the film. Happy for Leo, worried about Digger.

Revisiting this almost ten years after I first reviewed it, and my impression hasn't budged: same admiration, same reservations, same grade. This is a film that demands something from you, and the rewatch was every bit as punishing as I remembered. Not a flaw, a design. The cold, the length, the sheer physical exhaustion of Glass dragging himself back to life all become something you endure rather than simply watch. On the technical side it is close to flawless. Iñárritu's direction is staggering, and Lubezki shooting on nothing but natural light gives you images you don't forget. DiCaprio throws his whole body into a nearly wordless role and finally got the Oscar he'd been chasing, with Tom Hardy just as good as the treacherous Fitzgerald. The lifelike makeup seals the immersion. Everything you can point a camera at, or build in front of one, is working at the highest level. Where it falls short is the script. The pacing sags in stretches, and too many scenes seem to exist for their visual force rather than any real narrative weight, beauty that doesn't always serve the whole. It's a monumental thing to behold and a hard one to sit through, and I respect it more than I love it. A survival epic that earns its greatness and makes you pay for every minute of it.

"The Revenant" es la película modelo que deberían seguir todos los directores si quieren conseguir que su actor principal gane un Óscar. Para empezar, la trama es emocionantísima y deja momentos de una tensión brutal, como la pelea con el oso, en la que de verdad estás sufriendo mientras la ves. Además, a medida que avanza la historia, se va haciendo cada vez más evidente la diferencia entre los personajes que rodean al protagonista y el propio Hugh Glass, que acaba dejando escenas que quedan para la memoria. Más cosas que quiero reseñar de esta cinta son: • La actuación: Leonardo DiCaprio, dando vida a Hugh Glass, está brutal. Es una actuación de Óscar y está a un nivel estratosférico. Consigue transmitir muchísimo prácticamente sin necesidad de palabras y hace que sientas todo lo que está viviendo el personaje. El resto del elenco también está muy bien, aunque algunos aparecen durante tan poco tiempo en pantalla que no tienen suficiente margen para demostrar todo su potencial. • La dirección: Alejandro G. Iñárritu es un genio absoluto de la dirección. La manera en la que utiliza los planos consigue que el protagonista luzca todavía más y que cada momento tenga una fuerza visual enorme. La cámara está constantemente encima de los personajes y hace que vivas las situaciones prácticamente desde dentro, demostrando el enorme talento de Iñárritu detrás de las cámaras.

I forgot how truly amazing The Revenant really is; I truly believe it’s a masterpiece. Leo gives one of the best performances of his career as Hugh Glass; he barely has any dialogue throughout the entire film, but he doesn’t need it. The way he portrays anger, grief and (above all) pain just from facial expressions and motion truly captures the horror his character goes through. Tom Hardy’s performance is the complete opposite; visually he’s almost completely emotionless, but he builds his sneering, disgusting character through how he delivers his dialogue. The film is visually stunning; the way AJI and Emmanuel Lubezki contrast the natural beauty of the frontier with the harsh brutality of living and going to war in such an environment, truly captures frontier life in 1820’s America. The brutality sticks out in particular in The Revenant ; the bear attack scene looks so real that it’s actually difficult to watch - Rachel was nearly in tears. The makeup and prosthetics applied to Leo, combined with his performance, seems so so genuine, and the fight between Hugh and Fitzgerald at the end feels so real and human and not choreographed at all (like when he axes his fingers off!!!). Some people say it’s slowwww, or boringgggg or poorly written but they’re all incredibly wrong. It’s a harrowing, brutally realistic tale of survival and revenge and I think it’s perfect.

Una d'algunes de les que tenia pendents i ni m'ha impressionat ni m'ha decebut. No considero que sigui una obra aclaparadora perquè no té res que la faci sorprenent més enllà d'una història trepidant i excel·lentment narrada. Intueixo que això és el que provoca sensacions. Spielberg agafa la biografia de Frank Abagnale , un precoç estafador estatunidenc que causaria impacte a la societat nord-americana amb la seva habilitat per l'engany. Una cosa és tenir un bon material de fons i l'altra saber portar-lo a la pantalla gran d'una forma completament brillant. Em congratula veure que Spielberg ho aconsegueix i, aparentment, sense cap mena de dificultat. Com a espectador no necessites reflexionar en excés o estar atentíssim per no perdre't el mínim detall. És una pel·lícula que es gaudeix sola: té un ritme lleuger, molt viu i extremadament agradable. La crònica no és monòtona i presenta uns girs i ocurrències que traspassen el predictible. M'agrada pensar que tota història està precedida d'un missatge de fons, d'una intenció clara independentment de l'entreteniment. Aquí se'm complica més identificar-ho, no perquè no hi sigui, sinó perquè crec que se li dona menys importància. La inevitabilitat del protagonista per deixar de mentir és un tret que pot abordar certes reflexions, però per mi no arriba a una profunditat digna de menció. Frank Abagnale (un genial Leonardo DiCaprio ) fa de la mentida patològica el seu modus operandi, un comportament persistent i compulsiu que forma part de la seva identitat. Una característica visiblement present també en el seu pare (interpretat per un grandiós Christopher Walken ) que ens deixaria una metàfora molt il·lustrativa que després heretaria el seu fill: "Two little mice fell in a bucket of cream. The first mouse quickly gave up and drowned. The second mouse, he wouldn't quit. He struggled so hard that eventually he churned that cream into butter and crawled out." Frank Abagnale Sr. viu constantment en un món envoltat de fantasia, s'obliga ell mateix a viure en un ordre construït per les seves autocomplaences i vol sempre anar per un camí que no li correspon i no es pot permetre. Quan la realitat se li fa evident l'única cosa que sembla aprendre és traslladar les responsabilitats als seus perseguidors. La metàfora li serveix per arrossegar al seu fill amb el niu de l'adoctrinament. Projecta el seu ego i deixa de fer-li de pare per fer-li d'animador quan les seves decisions són notòriament reprovables. Aquest suport fa que Frank Abagnale Jr. sigui una versió "millorada" del que és el seu pare. Ell ja no menteix per benefici, menteix perquè li proporciona plaer i fa que la resta de mortals l'admirin. Utilitza constantment als qui l'envolten com a mers instruments a punt per ser manipulats. Tot això l'acaba convertint en un home exteriorment idíl·lic, però interiorment desert. Un narcisisme que, poc a poc i amb l'ajuda d'un agent de l'FBI (Tom Hanks), aconsegueix gestionar. Sí, és un relat de superació personal. No obstant l'anterior, la conclusió, amb tot el que comporta, és el postre en aquest menú de Spielberg .

They say truth is stranger than fiction, but I sometimes think that what makes a true story interesting is precisely the fact that it really happened. When it comes to the simple pleasure of a well-crafted story, fiction still has the edge. First time watch. Charming, enjoyable. Mostly false. Probably won't rank among my favorite Spielberg films, but as always, the display of technique is impressive. Effortlessly crafted cinematography and blocking. Sharp editing. Top-notch performances across the board. A script that could easily work as a masterclass in setup and payoff which all builds to a highly satisfying ending. A better film, still, than most directors can pull together on a good day. I'll admit however, searching for details about the real Frank Abignale has soured my enjoyment somewhat. The film does only say it was "inspired" by true events. However, it's still a common misconception that the film is or was at least based on a true story, when many of Frank's claims have been disputed as far back as the late 70s. Meanwhile, his real exploits include allegedly impersonating a doctor to sexually assault Pan Am flight attendants. The film not only supports his lies, but glorifies and exonerates him to an almost comical degree. The real Frank even gets a cutesy cameo. Unlike another, similarly false movie based on "true" events, "21", this film doesn't even give Frank an alias to allow any reasonable separation. It concludes with a wall of wrap-up text to update the audience on his career and assure us that Frank and Tom Hanks' fictional FBI agent remained good friends. Somewhat suspiciously, when it comes to his check fraud, the film goes to great lengths to explain the mechanics of how the scheme works. When it comes to his lengthy impersonations, the film largely glosses over these. As if impersonating a head pediatrician for a year is too ludicrous to even portray. We never see him in an operating room, a cockpit, or a courtroom for more than a minute each. Much of it seems to rely of a lot of adult women being easily manipulated or too horny for this 17 year old to see through him. I don't know if the book cares to elaborate further, but I have my suspicions. Still, it's a highly entertaining, if not slightly frustrating film to engage with.

Some surprise actors: Had no idea Christopher Walken, Ellen Pompeo, Jennifer Garner, or Amy Adams would be in this! Most notably, Amy Adams plays Brenda, the mousy, sensitive, nurse Frank works with. I thought her performance in this was heartbreaking and impactful. That said, I didn't think this was Tom Hanks' best movie. Tom Hanks plays Hanratty, the cop that is chasing Frank. I'm not sure if it was just from the script or seeing so many other Tom Hanks' movies, but it was difficult to place him here. I thought his standout moment was when he finds Frank in Montrichard, and this takes awhile to get to. Christopher Walken, on the other hand, is charismatic and intriguing throughout. Spielberg brilliantly sets the tone of Frank’s exploits as a game show, appropriating the very silly, very American craving for attention and flair for the spectacular(ly convoluted). I wonder how early on he knew it was all a ruse. A film about this self-fantasising myth-making as a craving, about the paradigm of greatness bringing out from deep beneath your soul a self-defeating, poisonous desire of making yourself seem larger than you really are - a mania quite indistinctive from America’s fascination with itself that naturally manifests in the entertainment industry. “Knock knock.” I've had many conversations with composers & friends about how much they were struck by John Williams’s opening credits music. The very first time at the cinema, I recall beaming at the screen – feeling the love for the Pink Panther movies & Henry Mancini. Instead of deploying his usual massive, brass-heavy orchestra, Williams curated a lean, intimate chamber ensemble focused on precise textures, including: - Solo Alto Saxophone: Played by renowned session musician Dan Higgins, the saxophone acts as the primary "voice". Its slinky, fluid lines mimic the nimble movements of Frank Abagnale Jr.. - Mallet Percussion (Vibraphone & Marimba): The vibraphone provides the characteristic mid-century jazz shimmer, while the woody timbre of the marimba anchors the lower rhythms. They frequently play interlocking triplet patterns together. - Tactile Sound Effects: The arrangement famously integrates finger snaps & human "shushes" directly into the percussion mix, instantly grounding the track in the jazz-club aesthetic of the era. Williams deliberately channelled the style of his own musical youth - when he was known as a jazz pianist named "Johnny Williams" - while paying homage to 1960s movie music masters like Mancini. And then this is my favourite Tom Hanks performance in a Spielberg movie. Hanratty is a straight man in a straight career, crunching numbers on criminals who have created new ways to crunch numbers. He is the perfect opposite of Frank. Hanks has physicality, but it’s a contained performance – all in the accent, stiff jaw & posture. “Next slide, please. Next slide, please.” Also have to give my respects to the twinkle in the eyes of Christopher Walken. The father/ son tale at the heart of this is pure Spielberg tragedy. Quite adjacent to the real-life tale, as is much of the movie – but those random restaurant meetings are just heart-breaking to watch. Thank goodness they never filmed his Central Station death as was planned. DiCaprio’s raw pain at learning about the death after-the-fact is pain enough. I haven’t loved anything by Spielberg as much in the quarter decade since. Part of my ‘Spielberg Phase’ of a LetterBoxd Review Catch-Up. Viewed courtesy of the Home Library

Where are you going, Frank? The thesis of this film becomes so many things about what we do when our dreams are crushed or we feel like we are put in between a rock and a hard place. The opening scenes feel so vividly like real memories I have of proud moments in my parents lives and moments when I idolized my parents relationship at a young age. The immediate subversion of this idolization into an unhealthy view of how to “win” at life and how to cheat everyone around you I think is what always attaches me to Frank early. I  have this deep sadness when I witness moments where parents do things for their kids, make sacrifices or life change, and the child doesn’t understand and becomes ungrateful or upset. I don’t know why making it by the best a person can just hits me deeply but this and Pursuit of Happyness are examples of movies that stick a shovel in my gut. Selling the families car and pancakes on birthdays from Frank Sr transform into christmases alone and literal prison time for Frank Jr. The movie paints these mirrors and patterns so wonderfully as personal and emotional moments coming from Frank and his reactions to these situations, it’s not just the consequences but the quiet sadness of the facade shattering. I think that’s what makes Frank Jr so engaging, his granger feels so fantastical and impossibly silly but simultaneously desperate, unexplainable, and tragic by the end. It’s never a hero story, but one where we try to understand him in his lows and highs. There is so much of Spielbergs real life in this family routine, his mother cheating specifically became very familiar.  But most importantly this movie is very obviously not a biopic about Frank Abagnale, it’s a movie about a man who stays a kid for much too long and pushes his luck because he’s scared of conflict. And as much as I’d love to say I don’t relate to that, this movie feels uncomfortable in its lies because i have tried to avoid so many scary things in my life, and im still very early at learning that it won’t kill me to go through things, not around. I think something else interesting here is how Frank and Carl both start as outsiders. People who have to make concessions to those around them to gather favor. They are not so different. We get these conversations between them full of acusations and and jabs because they are both insecure about the same things. It’s a wonderful structure of the ring spreading out and then closing back in on each of them. Visually, this movie more than any Spielberg makes me feel all of its wider lenses. The prevalent use of hand held camera in this movie also emphasizes this effect, scenes ending with an empty room that feels round and swimming, and the blocking feels that much more like a dance than shapes passing. I saw this movie very early in my life and it is still such a rich little roller coaster I like to hop on sometimes. It always surprises me.

Guns, explosions, and monster trucks. Is this what's considered "entertainment"? Thrown into a post-apocalyptic world, we are shown dynamics between governor and governed that are simply laughable, as if hoarding all the water from the population wouldn't cause an immediate uprising and lead to a proto-communist society. Scenes made purely to get a confused or indignant reaction from the spectator, making each ridiculous moment appear even more senseless than the prior. Despite having really gorgeous cinematography and color grading, everything else is as close to horrible as possible. Editing, VFX, and acting (by some charactes), are all lackluster, something that is amplified by the fact that the film has no real story to tell. I believe this is even more unengaging than Maze Runner 2 — my first one star review on Letterboxd— which at least had a malformed concept of a plot going on from the first movie of the saga, unlike what I've just watched. I don't enjoy these post-apocalyptic, survival action stories, with the sole exceptions being both The Last of Us games (so far), but I went into this film without any expectations whatsoever; so being met with with the most mindless, generic, action (sub)plot I've seen made me irritated from the start. I genuinely cannot understand how this can be so famous and well received as it is, do the people really live for the idea of turning off their brains for two hours and accepting the most wacky shit the director and writer could think of after snorting moldy chalk? Infuriating. Fuck this!

Reminds me a lot of Star Wars Episode 1 in the way the film is focused on self-important lore and world-building above all else, turning its back on the fizzy melodramatic fun of the original works. None of the characters are engaging, little of the action is exciting, everything is so transparently in service of delivering lame jargon and iconography, which all has a smug 1960s hippie vibe to it that I find totally insufferable. The extent to which it is impossible to give a shit about Max or Furiosa is remarkable, they're not cool, charming, funny, self-reflective or in possession of any other potentially humanising traits, just relentless grim stoicism. Perhaps if the film were not saddled with one of Tom Hardy's most moronically misjudged performances and Max had some kind of charisma, like Mel Gibson achieved without sacrificing intensity, the viewer would have had some kind of way in to the film on an emotional level, shame no one reigned him in. Also remarkable is how unexpectedly slow it is, both dialogue and action scenes dragging terribly - take the scene where Max first holds Furiosa and the wives at gunpoint, it goes on so long with so little of any significance happening that it starts to become awkward, the characters just standing and looking at eachother. This absolutely feels like it was directed by a 70 year old and edited by someone with no prior action film experience. Of course there's a lot of spectacle, but you mainly consume it with a dispassionate appreciation of the scale and detail of the production design and the work that must have gone into realising it, rarely approaching the edge of your seat. Miller just isn't a good enough action director to cope with the scale he's aiming for here - within the huge road-fleets there's no real sense of where the active characters are in relation to eachother, of who is in which samey vehicle or where the danger will be coming from, so the feeling that the baddies are just popping into existence to fulfil a quota for action within an artificial entertainment becomes too nagging. Would also help if this hadn't aimed for a PG-13 rating, more graphic violence would at least provoke a visceral reaction to what's happening on screen that you don't get when the film is constantly shying away from the reality of people getting shot in the head or blown up or crushed by huge trucks. A lot of people seem to be very passionate fans of Fury Road and yet the follow-up was a huge financial flop, so why didn't they turn up for it in droves? I think the reality is that it's easy to make this film sound conceptually cool on paper, but on a more nuts-and-bolts level it is let down by weak direction - the idea of the film is better than the reality.

A ver, primero que nada: no llegué a terminar la película. Pero si soy completamente sincera, los primeros 40 minutos fueron suficientes. Para muestra, basta un botón. Igual voy a ser buena y darle una oportunidad y terminarla, porque sé que tiene una cantidad absurda de críticas positivas y probablemente haya algo que todavía no estoy viendo. Pero si tengo que sacar una primera conclusión es que me está resultando muy difícil tomarme en serio lo que estoy viendo. No porque la propuesta sea exagerada (esa es parte de su identidad) sino porque muchas de las situaciones me resultan poco verosímiles incluso dentro de la lógica que plantea la propia historia. Lo que más me llama la atención es que se nota que tiene muchísimo presupuesto, pero pareciera que se olvidaron de ponerlo en el guion. Desde el principio me hice millones de preguntas sobre la lógica de esta peli: decisiones sin sentido, situaciones que parecen contradecir las propias reglas que plantea la película e inconsistencias de los personajes. Y creo que ese es mi principal problema: No logra hacerte entrar en su mundo. Es una distopía en la que casi no hay agua, el sol parece querer quemar a todo el mundo y solo lo mas importante para mostrar es como una sociedad decide resolver sus problemas manejando vehículos a toda velocidad por un desierto. Esta premisa puede ser completamente delirante, es justamente por eso q necesitás construir muy bien la trama y las reglas de ese universo para que el espectador diga “okay, esto está loco pero tiene sentido dentro de este mundo” y pueda empatizarrr. Además todo ocurre a una velocidad tan frenética y fría que lo hace todavía más difícil de procesar y así de apoco deja de impresionarte lo que ves. Todo está puesto al servicio de la acción, mientras que la trama y los personajes principales quedan bastante relegados. Y hablando de personajes, tampoco están tan buenos. El protagonista: tipo sensillo, fuerte, misterioso, sarcástico, antihéroe, con pasado trágico y prácticamente todas las características clásicas para que un hombre conecte. El villano es una cosa cochina no se que más decir. Y después están los personajes femeninos. Acá me costó mucho comprar el supuesto mensaje de empoderamiento. Tenemos un grupo de mujeres que son literalmente modelos, todas extremadamente atractivas, vestidas con muy poca ropa, ingenuas e indefensas. Incluso mantienen una actitud cariñosa con una persona que les hizo daño. Hay un personaje femenino que sí se presenta como fuerte y capaz, pero incluso no termina de despegarse de ciertos clichés. Visualmente la película es espectacular. Probablemente sea lo que más puedo rescatar hasta ahora. Tiene una estética muy original y extremadamente reconocible. Todo es exagerado y artificial, pero creo que justamente esa artificialidad es parte de su identidad. El mundo se siente quemado por el sol, los colores son súper contrastantes, los vehículos y personajes tienen diseños increíbles y cada plano parece pensado para ser visualmente muy impactante y llamativo. La música también acompaña muy bien toda esta locura. Si querés una película superficial, no tenés ganas de analizar demasiado la lógica de lo que estás viendo, querés acción prácticamente constante, paisajes increíbles, personajes visualmente muy llamativos y poco interés por el lore o la construcción del mundo, probablemente esta sea tu película. Pero bueno, en cuanto a la trama, se podría haber hecho y aprovechado muchísimo más (y sin hacer falta sacrificar acción) Hacer una película de 2 horas que básicamente trata sobre vehículos peleando en un desierto es una idea muy arriesgada. Para que funcione, hay que saber atrapar al espectador y hacer que le importe lo que está pasando no solo entretenerlo con explosiones y colores. Igual, voy a terminarla. Capaz dentro de una hora vuelvo acá a borrar absolutamente todo esto. Ojalá...

Mad Max Fury Road (2015) von George Miller, erzählt von einer Verfolgungsjagd durch eine postapokalyptische Welt. Der Film hat in erster Linie sehr starke Actionszenen zu bieten, welche gehäuft auftreten und atemberaubend sind. Die inszenierte Welt weckt aber kaum mein Interesse. Sie wirkt auf mich überinszeniert und wenig kohärent. Diese Überinszenierung erzeugt bei mir eher Distanz als Faszination. Zudem finde ich abgesehen von Furiosa und Nux kaum einen Charakter interessant. Besonders die Antagonisten wirken eher wie groteske Symbole, die sehr einprägsam sind, aber für mich keine interessanten Figuren darstellen. Auch Max weckt kein besonderes Interesse bei mir. Oft sieht man Rückblicke, welche bei mir eher unbeantwortete Fragen aufwerfen als Interesse am Charakter. Dass die Charakterentwicklung auch über die Action geschieht, ist mir bewusst, dennoch kann ich mich damit nicht anfreunden. Der Film hat eine sehr simple Handlung, die aus einer Verfolgung besteht, was ich auch als eine der Stärken sehe. Es wird nicht versucht krampfhaft etwas Komplexes erzählen. Dass Start und Endpunkt derselbe sind, ist nett inszeniert gibt dem Film meiner Meinung nach aber auch keine besondere Tiefe.

A film with a detailed world and impressive sets but just another standard non stop action movie. This is my first Mad Max film simply because I haven't been very interested in the series. I do however play games in my free time and after playing Mad Max on the Xbox I thought maybe I should give some of the films a go. Considering Fury road had some extremely positive reviews and starred Tom Hardy I had high hopes. I would have probably been better to assume the worst and be pleasantly surprised though. While it has some things going for it, overall I found it just another average action movie. The set design, world building, costume and sets are impressively immersive and the creators have done an impressive job creating a genuinely unique and believable world. The desert landscapes look incredible and are paired with some excellent cinematography that really brings the world to life. The costume design really brings the characters to life and when paired within the immersive environment it genuinely feels like the world has its own culture and history. Another great element is that it does actually feel like a non stop action film. I personally found the endless action a bit monotonous but if you are a fan of action films this is certainly something you will enjoy. Once the characters hit the fury road, the violence and intensity just keeps hammering away right until the bitter end. I wouldn't say I didn't enjoy the film at all, but for me the endless action didn't allow for any character or story development at all and at times it felt completely exhausting personally. It's just not enough for me to consider it a great film, it is however action paced, immersive and fun. It's also visually stunning and has some incredible stunts and vehicle sequences that offer a unique experience. Mad max is a simple and streamlined action film that's genuinely fun and is complete non stop action. While it has an excellent and immersive world I did find the action became a bit exhausting and did at times wish they spent more time offering viewers any sort of depth or character development. A genuine action film but nothing you haven't seen before from the genre. 6 / 10 Dave Kaye (Bilbo Bagsy) 13/09/2026

Sem contar na falta de realismo com a humanidade em si né, em tão pouco tempo a humildade não iria criar uma cultura e modo de viver totalmente novos sem lembra de nada do seu passado ao ponto de consideramas sociedades antigas um mistério, cultura levam varios e vários anos para ser feito, e estamos falando de poucos anos entre os filmes, tipo no primeiro filme ainda havia leis, estados, policiai, direitos, tecnologia, remédios, comércio e comunicação, em 30 anos tudo isso ser apagado e ninguém lembrar de nada é loucura. Rzemiosło nie do podważenia: praktyczne efekty mają fizyczny ciężar, pościgi są czytelne co do kadru, a uniwersum - specyficzne, polaryzujące, ale ciekawe - niesie mitologię, w której Nux dostaje pełny łuk niemal bez słowa. Mój problem z tym filmem jest taki, że to wszystko, co ta cysterna wiezie. "Who killed the world" i reszta warstwy tematycznej to hasła wypisane na ścianie, nie tezy, z którymi film cokolwiek robi. Cały ładunek siedzi w kinetyce, więc kiedy ta przestaje brać - a po godzinie repetycji naprawdę przestaje - nie ma z czego czerpać: ciche fragmenty są tematycznie puste, a logika bywa zbywana movie magic naiwniej, niż bym chciał. Reputacja głębi chyba wzięła się stąd, że precyzję formy pomylono z bogactwem treści. Car chase: the movie - świetnie zbudowany rig, z ładnym V8 - ale po przejechaniu połowy trasy przez pustkowia ma się ochotę wysiąść i przejść pieszo.

Well folks, here's a smidgen of controversy for you.....I wasn't blown away by Fury Road! I mean it's a great chase movie, it has insane stunts, amazing vehicles, machine gun editing, it's playful with film speed, it features the legend that is Hugh Keays-Byrne, Toecutter from the very first movie, as Immortan Joe in his final film role, fun bad guys, Tom and Charlize snarling at each other, and and and...so much is going on!! And I'm exhausted. I just can't see this being the best Mad Max film as some do. It's all a matter of personal taste I guess. And my personal taste, also controversially, still rates the OG Mad Max as the one that means the most to me. I watched it on first release in London with my old man, and it was of course unlike anything I'd seen before. So bleak, such an unfamiliar backdrop, as I'd basically only seen Hollywood or old British movies up to then, such a scary film. And no familiar actors to feel safe with. I also have a soft spot for number 2, the Road Warrior, a great follow up. And like many I was deeply disappointed with Thunder Dome. Fury Road is a definite improvement over that last entry, absolutely no doubt. But call me an old reactionary or simply a fuddy-duddy, I need something more than an extended chase to wow me, however frenetic or visually resplendent. I appreciate great stunts, but I miss the days when CGI wasn't a thing, however much it 'enhances' the action. And lastly, as much as I usually love Tom Hardy he's no Mel Gibson, he's not the Max I grew up with, he's completely different, and I'd have less problem if his character had not been named Max. For most of the running time he wasn't even the main character, and Furiosa was so much more dynamic. I'll stop there. I did honestly enjoy Fury Road, but I found it good rather than great.

Nou de bsm filmafdeling sloeg weer toe, dit keer op de mooie zondagavond bij gastheer Jelmer (& thijme). Na er achter te zijn gekomen dat het rad wel eens bijgewerkt mag worden is uncut gems eruit gekomen als winnaar! Deze film had maar liefst een rating van 4,0 vele prijzen gewonnen en is in mijn ogen waarschijnlijk een van de weinige goeie en serieuze films van Adam sandler( als we voice acting niet meetellen tenminste, love hotel transylvania). Zoals u aan de rating kan zien heeft de waarschijnlijkheid zich niet geopenbaard en was adam zoals vanoids weer een teleurstelling. De hele film is een soort marathon van een persoon die een bepaalde eindtijd wil halen maar die helaas niet getraind heeft, laten we die persoon voor het gemak even het compleet fictieve personage jesse noemen en die persoon heeft een bijzonder matige conditie, een peuk- en gokverslaving, en een bijzondere woordenschat en manier van debken zal ik maar zeggen maar tegelijkertijd is het een zeer amicale en gemakkelijk lullende gozer. Er zit constant spanning( en daarbij behorende zeer spannende en epische muziek onder) op en er is constant chaos en wat aan de hand en soms moet er even aangezet worden om vervolgens even de vuilnisbak te legen en dan vervolgens denkt de film weer van oh het is een marathon en hij heeft geld nodig, gooi er maar weer wat doms tegenaan. Tempo zit er wel in maar er gebuert telkens wel heel veel, onnodig veel. En net zoals bij marahtons moet het tempo hier wat beter gedoseerd worden. Aan het begin moet je nooit te veel rennen en dat is orecies wat hier wel gebeurt het was nog wel begrijpelijk maar gewoon onnodig. Daarna js de hele film eigebkijk wat ik al zei. Een soort jesse die een marathon onvoorbereid gaat lopen. Hij denkt telkens oomh ik kan wat aanzetten maar dat ging toch niet, dan loopt hij weer tegen een van eerdere benoemde problemen aan en en ziet ie na wat creatieve,idiote en wat bizarre problemsolving  later weer een gokkast( of gaat ie dus weee sneller lopen, of hij heefr nieuwe schoenen gekocht en maakt verkoopt er 1 hlaverwege) en creëert ie weer een nieiw probleem of het oude komt bovendrijven. Ondertussen een heleboel fucks maar het is gewokn debiel dat je zo een marathon gaat rennen, ik heb ooit een filmpje van streetLabs gezien en daaruit concludeer ik dat dat geen aanbeveler is, zo ziet u ook hier in dit metafoor! De oplossingen, logica, voorspelbaarheid en de hele situatie zijn idioot en na een paar keer bijna omvallen komt jesse er zelf achter dat ie het helemaal neot leuk vind en vervolgens gaat hier toch weer verder waar ie mee bezig was. De toeschouwer aan de zijkant gaat hete chter vervelen en haakt helaas af bij deze absurde poging tot een goede prestatie. Het vermaak is weg de prestatie zelf qas al niet goed en zijn avond was ( deels ) geruïneerd! Jesse zelf is als een mongool doorgegaan tot de finishlijn en js over ds lijn gekropen na heel veel moeite met een zelfvoldsne uitdrukking op zijn gezicht loopt hij naar de medaillestand om er daar achter te komen dat de goede prestatie voor niks is geweest. Zijn zendertje met de bijbehorende tijd is per ongeluk verwisseld met die van iemand die te laat over de finishlijn is gekomen en die dus niet gefinisht is waardoor zijn euforie verdwijnt als sneeuw vork de zon. Tot overmaat van ramp heefr fit slechte nieuws geleidt tot een hartaanval ( al kan dit ook beïnvloed zijn door de levensstijl) en moest jesse het leven laten. Wat is nu de moraal van het verhaal? Uncut Gems suit Howard, un bijoutier new-yorkais constamment à la recherche du prochain coup qui pourrait enfin tout arranger, alors même que chacune de ses décisions ne fait qu’aggraver sa situation. Le film réussit parfaitement à installer une tension quasi permanente. La mise en scène des frères Safdie est nerveuse, étouffante, presque agressive, et Adam Sandler est excellent dans ce personnage incapable de s’arrêter, même quand tout lui échappe. Le problème, c’est que le début est tellement chaotique qu’on a parfois du mal à réellement s’attacher à Howard. On observe surtout sa chute comme une suite de mauvaises décisions plutôt que comme quelque chose qui nous touche. Et pourtant, la fin fonctionne justement parce qu’elle donne enfin tout son sens à cette fuite en avant : Howard semble incapable de vivre autrement que dans le risque, comme si gagner importait finalement moins que le besoin de continuer à jouer. Une fin réussie, qui rend le personnage plus tragique qu’il n’en avait l’air.

• I really enjoyed this one. It had a very independent-movie feel, with an edgy introduction and immersive (but disorienting) sound editing which tries to get you in the city and in the jewelry store. • Adam Sandler is excellent as an eccentric Jewish NY jeweller with patterns of erratic behaviour. Kevin Garnett was a surprising strong point in the movie too; he acted well. • I enjoyed living with Adam Sandler’s character in his hectic life and his bad decision-making. • The movie surprises you at times, and the ending is not gratuitous. • Initially I gave this 4/4 stars. Upon a rewatch in 2026, I’m downgrading it because I simply don’t appreciate this kind of movie as much anymore. I can see why it really appealed to me as a younger man. It has a frantic pace and a claustrophobic atmosphere that sets it apart from other Hollywood productions that you would see Sandler in. It’s funny, often at Sandler’s expense, because he puts himself in these catastrophic situations over and over. There is an element of fantasy to his affair with Julia Fox, the very attractive younger woman who is seemingly head-over-heels for our old, funny-looking, ambitious protagonist. And yes, the gag at the beginning is very good and the ending is punchy. But as a 30 year-old, I didn’t enjoy being in this world quite as much, with sleazy jewellers, bookies, groupies, and the like. Also, having seen a lot more independent cinema by now, it wasn’t as interesting or groundbreaking as before. However I can still appreciate that it’s well-crafted and does incredibly well at what it sets out to do.

This film helped me understand the Safdie brothers’ directing style a lot better, as it feels quite similar to Marty Supreme. The movie starts abruptly and keeps you in constant tension until the very end, with barely any moments to breathe. One thing that especially stands out is the overlapping dialogue in many scenes. That was probably my main issue with it, though i needed the pace to slow down a little at some point. The third act is easily the best part, showing how well the Safdies can handle a three-act structure. They also manage to bring out Adam Sandler’s talent beyond comedy. The way he talks and moves makes you forget that he is primarily a comedic actor and pulls you deeply into his character.
