A big dumb movie like Top Gun deserves a big dumb sequel,  otherwise the entire endeavor doesn't seem worthwhile. Maverick doesn't go far enough in that direction. I'm of the mind that most of this is fine, if uninspired. However, Kelly McGillis not returning, and rather slotting Jennifer Connely into a new character role, is a terrible choice that feels retrofitted around the absence of the romance from the first movie. Like many late career Tom Cruise romances on film, it feels perfunctory at best and carries no weight. Similarly, Miles Teller unfortunately lacks the charisma of his onscreen deceased father,  Anthony Edwards/Goose. Disappointed in the young recruits' call signs: Playback; Hangman; Rooster; boring.I wish they'd have gotten weirder with it: Doghat; Flip-Flop; Groundswell; etc There's nothing as interesting as Iceman, here. All of the new recruits mostly feel like hollow proxys of characters from the original, most glaringly Glen Powell. It's bad criticism to say what you'd prefer the movie to be about rather than what it is,  and I'm anti-deaging effects in onscreen generally, because they seldom look good, but the opening of this movie,  Tom Cruise flying mach 10+ in a fancy future jet,  made me think that a plot where he accidentally flies into the past, back to the 80s, and saves a de-aged Anthony Edwards from death, maybe even bringing him back to the 2020s, would rule. Overall lacking the blissed out stupidity of the original.  Disappointing it doesn't lean harder into some legacy aspects, namely musically. Kind of insane not to do a Danger Zone needledrop. Possibly just in need of a Tony Scott infusion that is sadly no longer possible. Jets are very cinematic.

A movie that only gets more disappointing the more you watch it. Maverick completely lacks the nuance and beauty of the original film. All the love has been drained out in favor of vague foreign threats and fancam fodder. Every time the story is presented with the opportunity to do something interesting, it decides instead to go in the most bland direction possible. In Maverick grief is smoothed over and easily forgotten. In the first film, our heroes were fallible - grief forced them into their own personal reckonings. Not even the US government can save men from their feelings, and that creates a compelling and relatable narrative. In Maverick, the heroes exist only to kill faceless bad guys and always make it out alive. Freedom fighters can never die. There is no questioning the protagonists and no sympathizing with the antagonists. When nothing bad can happen, the franchise cannot be anything more than a spineless advertisement with facist undertones, and I truly believe it has the capacity to be more than that. The more friends ask me to watch this movie with them, the more I find it hard to ignore its glaring faults. I’d just rather be watching the original. I love Tom Cruise and I love action movies; I know that they are capable of more.

Mini-collab with Dan (who also convinced me to watch the OG, kudos to Dan) Watched literally right after rewatching Top Gun , and I know I'm in the minority here, but I did not like this as much. The magic of Top Gun is gone. What made the OG special was its coming of age story. The focus was on Maverick. Of course the sequel's title is Maverick , but the thing is, Maverick got his arc in the first film. Instead of passing the torch on to the young generation, the film doesn't dare do so, instead rewinding and resetting Maverick's major arc beats. This is as per course of a series, but it still makes it no less lazy, especially when Cruise is pushing 60. Maverick's very much an outsider and he needs a new romance which adds even less to the sum than the original (while absolutely trashing McGillis's Charlie by not even giving her a passing mention from anyone , I'm not even going to pretend Maverick is in any way hung up on her after so many years, so they could've had anyone mention her). Sure, there's new blood, Rooster and Hangman (Glen Powell was a mix of Iceman and Maverick somehow for me), but the spotlight's still on Maverick. Glen Powell didn't have enough screentime, but then again, he wasn't the most important of the recruits, but even Miles Teller's Rooster felt side-lined. It's telling that the focus of training was Maverick. Can the recruits outmanoeuvre him, can he simulate bombing (Iran-- ahem-- I mean--) an unnamed nuclear enrichment site under the deadline? The visuals match the OG at the beginning, but gradually slip into ugly modern lensing. The music is nostalgia bait and not as strong. Even the greater focus on the mission with its target specifics lent a darker tone. At a point earlier on, Maverick makes a comment to Jon Hamm's character that he's going to train the kids to return only to be met with an incredulous stare. The connotation was clear. They're training pilots for suicide missions. Meeting the objective is the most important and only goal. The original film was an entirely different vibe. Maverick felt modern in the worst ways for me, including sacrificing character and connection for plot beats and seriousness. Basically, I don't think the sequel brought anything fresh or better; it was entirely of its 2020s generation. I suppose I got to watch Glen Powell in another film. Yay?

Assorted moments that stood out to me while watching: - Actually having a flashback to Goose dying in a fiery explosion during 'Goodness Gracious Great Balls of Fire' was awesome. - Maverick literally throwing the rule book into the trashcan on his first day as a teacher. And in that opening shot in the hangar, he does the Riker Maneuver on his chair! He's not like a regular teacher, he's a cool teacher. - The enemy is never named or specified, they just have old planes and a red bird symbol. I could write a whole essay about this (which usually means I like something?). - Big Military Propaganda, huh? Sort of just a Navy recruitment ad, pretty weird to watch while I was abroad in New Zealand. I felt like I should have to stand at attention while the national anthem plays over the credits or something. - Wet denim football < short shorts volleyball - Miles Teller was delightful in the secret third act when he got to do something other than resent his dad stand-in. Just yelling "holy shit" at every crazy fucking thing Cruise did was very fun. - None of the dialogue/advice in the secret third act could be anything other than stuff we've already heard before (don't think, just act; it's not the plane, it's the pilot; etc.) which I think is smart screenwriting, but it was funny to notice because whenever a character needed a pep talk, it was like you had a word bank and could just slot in whatever motif fit the best at the time. - I think there was a throwaway line about Bob not being short for Robert but being an acronym. But there was no payoff!! I wanted him to be Big Ol' Balls. He always will be in my mind. - I begged for a Hangman redemption, and we got it. - Seriously this movie feels like a script you'd pull out for a screenwriting class, very neat and by-the-book, which is brilliantly conservative for a sequel 20 years later which I expected to be a mediocre cashgrab. - A very straightforward, very sincere nostalgia trip to a place and time I have no nostalgia for. Pairs well with popcorn.

É um ótimo exercício de marketing, com cenas de caça que tiram o fôlego. E só! A sessão nostalgia tem agradado muito ao público nos últimos anos. Filmes que fizeram sucesso nos anos 80, 90 e até no início dos anos 2000 estão ganhando cada vez mais remakes, reboots ou, como neste caso, continuações. Há muitos críticos dizendo que Top Gun: Maverick é “maravilhoso”, uma “correção do passado”. No caso das cenas de voo, eu até concordo. São impressionantes e, sem dúvida, o grande destaque do filme. Mas todo o restante acaba sendo prejudicado pela repetição de trilha sonora — com exceção da música-tema, que continua linda —, de cenas e até de um contexto muito semelhante ao primeiro filme, tudo cuidadosamente pensado para manter os saudosistas encantados. Assim como no primeiro Top Gun , não temos um roteiro muito elaborado. Em alguns momentos, a história se mostra confusa, enquanto os personagens são explorados de maneira superficial. O próprio nome Maverick faz jus ao filme: tudo gira em torno dele. O maior destaque é, mais uma vez, Tom Cruise. Parece que o filme foi concebido também para mostrar que, mais de 30 anos depois, ele ainda consegue tirar o fôlego do público com suas performances — seja na moto, no caça ou simplesmente demonstrando um vigor e uma energia que continuam sendo sua marca registrada. Top Gun: Maverick entrega um espetáculo visual impressionante e cumpre muito bem a missão de despertar a nostalgia. Mas, quando retiramos todo esse aparato, sobra pouco além de uma continuação que se apoia demais no passado para funcionar no presente.

Eine weiterführung des Films aus den 1980ern. Wir begleiten wieder Maverick, der immer noch Captain der Navy ist bei seiner Arbeit. Er hat nun eine Stelle als Testpilot für die Navy und testet eine neues Flugzeug, das den Überschallflug revoluzionieren soll. doch das Militär will die teure Entwicklung eines solchen Flugzeugs nicht mehr unterstützen. Um zu beweisen, dass das Flugzeug es wert ist, dass daran weitergeforscht werden darf riskiert er den ersten Flug mit Mach 10. Als er aber noch mehr aus der Maschine herauskitzeln will passiert es. Das Flugzeug gerät ins Schlingern und stürzt ab. Da er nun seine Job verloren hat, wird er erneut dem Top Gun-Stützpunkt, diesmal als Trainer zugeteilt. Hier soll er die jungen Wilden auf einen tödlichen Einsatz vorbereiten. Unter den Piloten ist auch der Sohn von Goose, dem Co-Piloten, der damals bei einem Einsatz mit Maverick ums Leben kam. Der Film glänzt, wie schon damals mit unglaublich guten Bildern, die das amerikanische Militär nur von seiner besten Seite zeigt. Das versucht der Film aber auch nicht im Ansatz zu verheimlichen. Die Musik lässt einen sofort wieder izurückerinnern an das Original. Ein Film, der nur so von Testosteron strotzt, das Original hochhält und weiterführt.

“you know, lost souls are not that different from those in the zone. the zone is enjoyable, but when that joy becomes an obsession, one becomes disconnected from life.” you have to admit to dissect the nature of the afterlife and telling it through an older, childless, single, black man is awesome… but to tell a story about a dead black man who lives in black communities in america, reaching the pearly gates of the great beyond, and then doing all that while not mentioning jesus once is some backbreaking gymnastics that it’s almost impressive. and, despite that, it still feels like they kept their cards too close to their chest. it still feels like spirituality and heaven by committee. how do we include the least religion possible here? how do we make the movie about dying but keep our tail so far between our legs that you can’t see it? make every dead person on the travelator an old person who is ready to die, that rings true doesn’t it? how do we make the movie about jazz in black communities, have almost exactly half of it, and then ignore the rest of those spaces? how do we cover our arse by saying the great before and beyond is a hypothetical place, even though we’ve seen and made a more interesting cultural depiction of death before in ‘coco’? there also some funny nitpicks i have, things you only really realise once you think too hard. let me just go for the throat, there’s no point in wasting time: if this movie declares that people have personalities before they’re born, does this movie inadvertently say that life begins at conception? what are you doing? why would you put yourself in a position? i don’t hate this movie! if you watch it you’re gonna get a visually arresting and a beautifully animated film here, with specific touches like accuracy on musical instrument performance, some nice film grain, diversity, and mood lighting that will absolutely knock your socks off. ‘soul’ is a very impressive and slick piece of visual production. this movie is about adulthood careers as opposed to childhood dreaming which cuts to the heart of something honestly quite mature. this movie might not be the highlight of your week, but it would be a night well spent.

It felt like it was trying to be ‘inside out’. Like why did they make the type A counter evil? What I wanted more of was the grit, the tears, the pulling of the heart strings - a calling to why we are here in the first place. I wanted to leave this movie inspired to continue following my dreams but left muddled thinking that no one has a ‘spark’ - we just tell that to ourselves, and that we’re here to experience. Feels like one of those Pixar films that displays so much potential in the first 20 minutes in setting up some poignant message about grappling with our own sense of mortality, and Reznor and Ross' soundtrack accompanied with Jon Batiste is a worthy companion. But the movie stumbles over its own footing as it gets lost trying to narrow down and convey what exactly the underlying message of its story is. Is finding your "spark" supposed to be about realizing that your lifelong passion isn't actually lucrative and you should find something more sustainable if you can't make a living off it? Or is it about coming to terms with the idea that your lifelong ambition isn't always what it turns out to be and it's okay to just start anew? Or that your life still has purpose even if you feel like you haven't fulfilled what it is you thought you were meant to do? It becomes so convuluted by the end and these questions still go unanswered, so the emotional baggage you're left with doesn't feel nearly wrapped up as well as it could've been. Ultimately comes off as a visually and sonically captivating Pixar installment (still thought the "Great Beyond" looked and sounded cool af) but with a lot of unfulfilled potential in its central storyline and main character arc — coupled with an antagonist that's honestly not very memorable either. I liked it enough to stay entertained on my flight, but given the overall content and musical appreciation prevalent throughout its runtime, I do wish I ended up loving it more.

One of the most visually stunning Pixar movies that they've ever made, but when you watch it, it kind of begs the question: who is this for? In the 90s, Disney went chasing Oscars with Pocahontas and Hunchback of Notre Dame, and made movies that were too silly for adults and too serious for kids, so they ended up being mostly for nobody. Although Soul is a superior film to those two examples, this movie certainly has the same vibe. Soul has a lot of talk about Jazz theory and the astral plane, so it has a lot of stuff that's going to go over kids' heads; but it also has a talking cat and a lot of pratfalls, so it feels too unserious for adults. It's a movie about a sad middle-aged guy who dies but gets stuck in an ethereal plane and has to learn about the beauty of a mundane existence. But, you know, for kids. The movie is beautiful to look at and has an amazing score. This is one of those movies where a guy has to prove that he's amazing at playing an instrument and the times that he plays ACTUALLY sounds amazing. But ultimately that movie has a crazy mishmash of different tones. One of the climaxes of this movie involves calming down a little anxiety demon who keeps repeating, "I'm not good enough," which is something Pete Docter does again in Inside Out 2, only better.
Although I had to cry and love the theme/topic and characters and the music. I cried harder watching Coco and that sits at 4 stars. So naturally there has to be a bit of a gap between these.

Un film molto delicato, spirituale nel messaggio, come premesso dal titolo. Forse anche troppo per un bambino, perché il messaggio è sottile e complesso da cogliere anche per un adulto, e arriva nel finale, trasformando tutta la narrazione in un percorso dell’anima. Sarebbe bello far capire ai nostri figli, fin da piccoli, che la scelta migliore è trovare prima di ogni cosa serenità ed equilibrio dentro di noi, far la pace con noi stessi e godersi la vita come un grande dono, e non renderla bella o brutta a seconda se si raggiungano o meno i grandi obiettivi. Che ci aiutano a vivere una vita piena ma che non dovrebbero essere il senso unico dell’esistenza. Un messaggio delicato e difficile da trasmettere, e da rendere credibile, soprattutto dopo che le generazioni precedenti hanno costruito un mondo dove tutto ruota intorno al mantra capitalista “live your best life”… «Per che cosa vorresti essere ricordato al mondo?».

Fuckass movie In all honesty, I've been going through a rough path for a couple of months now and I’ve been feeling a lot like 22 at the beginning of the movie. Everything about life is just « meh », I’ve slowly been loosing passion for my hobbies and passions, just kinda stopped caring overall about everything, becoming more cynical by the minute. I was just thinking about what I wanted to do in the future and how once I get to that point I’ll be fine and life will finally be great. When Joe stands on the sidewalk after the performance - the one he always wanted, the one that would change everything - he simply appears normal, or rather empty. His life isn’t changed like he always said it would be. It’s still pretty much the same overall, even if he achieved his dream. He achieved his « purpose », so what’s next? As he plays the piano all by himself in his dark apartment, he remembers the joyful moments of his life and yes music and jazz is there, but that’s not all there is. It’s the mundane things of everyday life. I also really liked the story of his barber friend, how he wanted to be veterinarian but bc he needed money for his daughter hospital bills, he took up barber lessons and he’s now the best there is. Becoming a barber wasn’t in his plans, as he said so himself, but he’s still happy being one bc isn’t that the whole point anyway? The message of the movie isn’t anything revolutionary per say, it isn’t the first time I’ve heard it, but I did need to hear it once again lately. Life is all about the small moments between the big events, that’s when you are truly living. My big events will come, but that doesn’t mean I have to sit here and do nothing in the mean time, I can live a little.

Très bien, et vraiment beau. Joe Gardner est professeur de musique à New York et ne vit que pour le jazz. Le jour où il décroche enfin le concert de sa vie, il tombe dans une bouche d'égout et se retrouve dans l'au-delà. Il refuse d'y aller, et se retrouve associé à une âme qui, elle, refuse de naître. Ce qui rend le film remarquable, c'est son sujet. Pixar demande si une vie qui ne réalise pas sa vocation est une vie ratée, et répond non. Le film déplace la question de la passion vers celle de ce qui nous anime vraiment au quotidien, et c'est un propos rare pour un film familial. Docter matérialise des concepts abstraits avec une aisance hallucinante. Le Grand Avant, le Grand Bazar, l'océan des âmes égarées, et ces entités en charge de l'au-delà représentées par de simples traits en mouvement. On reproduit l'exploit de Vice-versa. La musique fait énormément, et le film a deux univers sonores : le jazz de Jon Batiste pour la Terre, ce sont ses mains qu'on voit jouer, rotoscopées  et les nappes éthérées de Trent Reznor et Atticus Ross pour le monde des âmes. Ma réserve : il y a quelques égarements scénaristiques au milieu, notamment le long passage dans un corps de chat. Premier Pixar avec un héros de couleur. Oscars du film d'animation et de la musique.

Öncelikle, filmdeki o yaprakla ortaokulda görsel sanatlar için bir proje yapmış olmanın gururunu çok net yaşadım. 22’yi filmin ortalarında çok bencil ve hatta biraz rahatsız edici buldum. Fakat filmin sonuna doğru, aslında ona ne kadar benzer hissettiğimi fark ettim. Hayatta hep bir amacımız olması gerektiği düşüncesi, gerek üzerimizdeki baskılar gerekse içinde büyüdüğümüz kültür tarafından sürekli önümüze konuyor. Bir şey yapmak, bir “purpose” bulmak zorundaymışız gibi hissediyoruz. Ama filmin de çokça vurguladığı gibi, “purpose” ve “passion” aslında sandığımız kadar önemli olmayabilir. “A spark isn’t a soul’s purpose.” Hayatta yaparken bizi gerçekten mutlu eden, heyecanlandıran, yaşadığımızı hissettiren şeyler var. Film bunlara “spark” demiş. Fakat bu spark’ın illa ki hayatımızın amacı olması gerektiğini düşünmek, bence çok yanlış bir kalıplaşmış düşünce. Bunu bu filmi izledikten sonra asıl fark ettim. Hayatta ne tek bir amacımız var, ne de sadece tek bir spark hissedeceğimiz şey. Bazen en sıradan şey bile ruhumuza çok derinden dokunabilir. Belki de mesele bir purpose bulmak değil, o küçük spark’ların kendisini yaşayabilmek. Sonuçta hayat sadece tek bir şeyin peşinden gitmek ve bunu bir amaç haline getirmek için çok kısa :)

I was honestly surprised when I went back to Letterboxd and saw that this was a 4.4. It’s far off that for me. I know I started watching this when I was younger and stopped it. At the time, I think it was just for the gore, but maybe it was also me already knowing that I wasn’t going to like what the movie was. Also, clearly, my parents had absolutely no control over what I watched. But anyway. There were a few things I liked: Christoph Waltz’s performance, the colour choices, and… that’s pretty much it. I really didn’t like the pacing. There were so many scenes that felt unnecessarily prolonged and, to me, added very little to the story. And there are so many storylines that felt unfinished or underdeveloped. Honestly, I would have found the story of how the propaganda machine worked, how they turned Zoller into this heroic figure, made a movie about him, and used cinema as propaganda, so much more interesting. Or even Shosanna’s story: how she got the cinema, how she planned her revenge, and what she was actually trying to achieve. There was so much potential in both of these storylines. Instead, Zoller’s storyline becomes this weird thing where he seems almost harmless, even though he killed 300 enemies, randomly falls in love with Shosanna, and then, in the final moments, you actually see who he really is. I just kept thinking there was so much more that could have been done with these characters and their stories. And then, of course, the bane of my existence in movies: American soldiers coming to save the world. I’ve always hated that concept and I will always hate that concept. Apart from that, one of the things that annoyed me the most was how much time is spent building Hans Landa up as this terrifying and intelligent character, only for his story to end the way it does. He’s obviously a horrible character, but after all that build-up, I expected a much more ba-bam ending. Shout-out to Christoph Waltz, though. He was the main reason I kept watching, so naturally I was even more annoyed by how his character ended. And probably the biggest problem for me is that the movie felt childish at times, especially when it was trying to be funny. A situation like this is not funny to me, and some of the comedy completely took me out of it. The buongiorno scene that everyone seems to love, apparently peak comedy? I was just sitting there thinking, really? And cringing so much. Even the music, which I thought could have saved the movie a little bit for me, sometimes felt wasted. There were moments where I felt like it wasn’t being used at the right time, and some of the tension could have been so much better. Something about the pacing, the music, or simply the way the scenes were handled just didn’t get me there. The movie felt like it was lacking so much of its potential, and I think that was most obvious during those scenes. Maybe I’m missing something, but for a movie that is so highly rated and so highly praised, I spent a lot of it thinking: this is it?

BASTARDOS INGLÓRIOS Extremamente fraco, mal dirigido e, para mim, um filme ruim e até desrespeitoso. O maior problema é a maneira como Bastardos Inglórios trata a Segunda Guerra Mundial. A guerra e o horror nazista são transformados em uma espécie de fantasia estilizada, quase como se tudo tivesse sido construído para ser divertido e satisfatório. Para mim, isso tira muito do peso do período que está sendo retratado. E o humor também não funciona. É um filme para maiores de 18 anos, mas em vários momentos parece ter sido escrito para adolescentes que acham violência e palavrão automaticamente engraçados. Algumas cenas parecem existir apenas para virar uma edit no TikTok. A única coisa que realmente consigo elogiar é Christoph Waltz. Hans Landa é disparado a melhor parte do filme, e Waltz entende perfeitamente o personagem. Ele consegue fazer o sujeito ser carismático sem deixar de ser repulsivo, e sua atuação realmente merece todos os elogios que recebeu. Fora isso, não consegui encontrar muita coisa que me interessasse. Os personagens são pouco envolventes, o roteiro se apoia demais no estilo e eu pessoalmente não gosto da maneira como Tarantino dirige seus filmes. Violência estilizada e aquela necessidade constante de transformar tudo em uma cena “icônica” simplesmente não funcionam comigo. Talvez eu seja uma das poucas pessoas que realmente não entende todo esse amor pelo filme. Para mim, Bastardos Inglórios parece muito mais interessado em ser cool do que em dizer alguma coisa sobre a guerra que está retratando. -P.F. Prado

For how much people seem to enjoy this it felt somewhat lacking in substance, in terms of the humor, it was mildly funny and got some laughs out of me. Beyond the humor and some of the more tense scenes being well done, the film felt like a jingoistic overidealization of what the US actually contributed in WW2. Next to nothing about the film does much to display the nuances of WW2 and the sacrifices made by other countries such as the Soviet Union, China, or Poland beyond vague statements about other countries and treats the US like the primary operator within this war. In addition the alternate ending to WW2 as a whole just feels like a disservice to it's role as a war film and gains it nothing meaningful beyond swift justice to all the Nazi leaders under an ironic premise, the problem of it all is that no conflict is as clean-cut as Inglourious Basterds makes it seem. Overall if you're really itching to watch this whole film then knock yourself out, otherwise it wasn't much worth watching beyond a couple laughs.

Overall a pretty decent watch. It was action-packed through the end with Tarantino’s quintessential parallel plot-lines intersecting through Hans and converging on the final theatre explosion. The filmography was excellent and the use of the explosive nitrous content in the films was clever. And in particular, I love the underground tavern scene because it aptly depicted the escalation of tension between the parties involved. But a few things felt amiss to me. Firstly, given Hans’ extremely calculative nature, it seems absurd to me that he could not have anticipated the double-cross coming at the end when he made the deal. While some argue that it was because he already foresaw the Allies winning and wanted to save himself or that he was too indulgent with post-war fame, neither of these facts were clearly established in the film or about his character. This, to me, is the biggest plot hole that comes off as a convenient ex-machina for the Basterds to emerge victorious. Secondly, I’m surprised that Mimieux and the Basterds’ paths never crossed, which felt like a loose end to me especially because the Basterds didn’t even appear surprised when the cinema caught fire even before their own dynamite had gone off. Nonetheless, it was still an exciting watch I would recommend especially for action lovers!

Um breve comentário de sensações... Recentemente falei com um amigo a respeito da sensação que eu tinha ao ver algumas séries. O exemplo era relacionado a série "Reacher".  A sensação em questão era a de que eu não conseguia "sentir" que aquilo era uma série, mas um grande filme cortado em 8 partes. Não sei se é necessariamente um demérito para a produção, afinal ela me agrada em alguns aspectos (outros nem tanto). Mas, acho engraçado pensar que eu sinto o completo inverso ao me deparar com "Bastardos Inglórios". Não um filme, mas uma série. São 13 anos de diferença entre as produções de mídias completamente divergentes. Mas, não sei se é, também, um demérito do filme está sensação. Na verdade, ele trás algumas consequências para a organização daquele mundo. Recentemente eu pude ler o texto "Da vida das marionetes" de Matheus Cartaxo. Um texto que se apresenta como notas a respeito da carreira de Tarantino. Algo que me chama atenção para esse punhado de notas é a organização de Cartaxo a respeito do como Tarantino transforma seus personagens em bonecos que estão ali para que a sua imagem (não mensagem) se potencialize. Ele fala a respeito do ventríloquo que "brinca e se diverte com as aventuras desses bonecos, contanto que eles não carreguem o peso da realidade ". Isso me faz pensar nessa sequência de filmes especificamente. Uma sequência que eu vejo como um grande parque de diversões do Tarantino. Me refiro a "Kill Bill" (2003-4), "Death Proof" (2007) e, agora, "Bastardos Inglórios" (2009). Vejamos se eu consigo organizar isso. Tarantino organiza este mundo em três frentes. A história de Shosanna, a dos Bastardos e a dos nazistas, com um pequeno foco em Hanz Landa. As três vão se entrelaçando por coincidências (algo que ele faz brilhantemente em "Pulp Fiction") até o ponto de choque: o cinema. Esse grande palco de contar histórias. Histórias que estão necessariamente no passado e que através da interferência tecnológica, se apresentam no presente instante. O que Tarantino faz aqui não é, nem tem esse objetivo, de ser um filme histórico ou educativo. O que ele faz é tirar da embalagem os seus Max Stell e colocar todos em um grande ringue. Não atoa seus personagem são desprovidos de sentimentos. Não frios, caricatos, indo em direção ao grande combate sem sentir peso algum dos acontecimentos. Até mesmo Shosanna, que talvez fosse a personagem que "deveria" carregar consigo um peso dramático, se mostra uma personagem fria. É uma personagem que tem uma tarefa a cumprir nesse grande tabuleiro com que seu Deus brinca. É, talvez, algo que me remeta a criação de Grant Morrisson frente ao seu run do "Homem-Animal". Um grande Deus, um autor, criando, deixando morrer e deixando viver quem ele quer. Traçando os atos mais perturbadores frente as imagens para produzir uma peça de entretenimento. Não deveríamos esperar educação, redenção, conscientização... não deveríamos esperar nada na verdade. Ela é o que é. Uma organização de imagens que contam uma determinada história que, talvez, tenha como objetivo nos provocar algo. E esse algo, sim, deveria ser o que poderíamos moldar e, talvez dali, construir algo. Então, "Bastardos Inglórios" não é um filme histórico. É mais um dos brinquedos disponíveis do parque de diversões de Tarantino. Mérito? Demérito? Isso cabe ao julgamento de cada um, perante sua experiência. Particularmente não vejo como demérito. Mas é engraçado que, os três filmes que citei, são os que menos me agradam, até esse recorte de 2009. Eu poderia colocar "Cães de aluguel" (1992), mas esse eu não gosto mesmo. Os demais, apenas não me despertam nada, apenas alguns raros momentos de brilhantismo do diretor. Depois que Tarantino faz seu grande filme, - falo de "Jackie Brown" (1997) - filme que vem após um outro grande momento de sua carreira, "Pulp Fiction" (1994) - algo parece mudar. O autor encontrou seu estilo? Ele consolidou suas percepções de cinema frente ao público? Ele se provou algo? Ele nos provou algo? São questões que me passam pela cabeça a pensar o quão profundos são os personagens de Jackie e as coincidências que amarram a teia de Pulp. Dentro do recorte que fazemos aqui, esses dois filmes parecem ser o grande ápice do diretor. E após esse ápice, ele se permite gozar, desequilibrando tudo, que eu poderia dizer (por achar isso), que estava equilibrado. Tanto "Pulp Fiction" quanto "Jackie Brown" parecem trabalhar de maneira organizada aquilo que molda o cinema de Tarantino. As coincidências que constituem sua teia dramática. Bem como, a constituição de tensão que explode em violência. Não necessariamente gráfica, ao exemplo de "Jackie Brown", que é seca e crua. A partir de "Kill Bill" isso parece mudar. Não que exista uma maximização do sentimentalismo de seus personagens. Mas, na verdade, existe uma ausência de sentimentalismo. O sentimento de seus personagens, parecem ficar presos em uma caixa, fazendo com que eles sejam bestas imbatíveis. Raros momentos como o choro de Uma Thurman ao final de "Kill Bill" ou a diálogo do Sheriff a respeito do gozo do personagem de Kurt Russell em "Death Proof". "Bastardos Inglórios" parece fazer isso com seus personagens. Os únicos que parecem ter algum tipo de sentimento, que se parecem ser mais "humanos", são justamente os nazistas. Hitler e Goebbels são sentimentais; frágeis; sensível; algo que dentro do cinema de Tarantino parece ser a demarcação da morte. Suas caricaturas, como a de bebês chorões, parece ser à grande ofensa que as imagens de Tarantino dirigem a eles. Um outro personagem, nazista, é o pai de Maximillian. Preso no banho de sangue do bar, tudo que aquele homem quer é ver seu filho que acabou de nascer. Tarantino humaniza os nazistas, mesmo assim os trucida (graças a Deus"!). Cria um jogo próprio onde seus personagens "do bem" não podem ser humanos, pois são suas marionetes que vão realizar seus desejos plásticos. É violência por violência cinematográfica. Pelo prazer de criar belas imagens e de explodir em catarse. O problema é que Tarantino, aqui, não cria belas imagens e muito menos catarse.

This is such a mixed bag of a movie. Every scene in which Hans Landa is in, is near perfect for me. He has such a gravitas to him that it feels like he is always in control and knows just a bit more than he should. For me that opening scene hits all of the points I wanted it to, perhaps as a standalone scene one of my favorites ever. The implications of being entirely powerless, not even having the bigger pipe, in your own home are so terrifying, especially since the one that had power over you can absolutely destroy your entire life. For me at least his menacing presence and the dark shadow that he casts over every scene he is in, is exactly what I want from a WWII movie. Landa shows how brutal and thorough the Nazis could be. But on the other side of that coin you have the Bastards. Most of their scenes are almost cartoonish, with slapstick gratuitous violence, and quippy remarks. All of the scenes with Hitler are no different. It's really hard to find him at all intimidating when he's portrayed as a whiny helpless child. It felt strange that every other Nazi on screen was more threatening than one of the most powerful, charismatic dictators of all time. Having seen a few other Tarantino movies, this feels like often the tone that he sets. But it's hard to overlook that first scene and the feeling that he could make a compelling story about the horrific and frightening aspects of the Holocaust, without the goofy nonsense. I feel like I could get behind this movie being a straight up comedy if it didn't have brilliant dramatic sequences that were just so much more compelling to me than the comedic ones. All that being said this was extremely well made. The set design, acting, cinematography, and direction, are all so well done. I especially enjoyed the shot composition. Every time that there was a close up of Landa while he's interrogating is so so good. And that shot in the opening looking out the doorway, is incredible. I just wish that all of the excellent technical aspects were backing up a more focused movie.

The second film in my staring-Brad-Pitt-and-also-semi-nihilistic double feature. While Inglourious Basterds has many impressive elements, I am left wanting. It looks great, sounds great, and acting is good. Pitt and Waltz and particularly enjoyable. But a film about revenge fantasy is not compelling to me. And the commentary on the manipulation of history through cinema and other retelling is fine, but not in a way that I found beneficial.

Although i really enjoyed watching it, it hasn’t ruminated the best, especially in light of Quentin’s recent viral meltdowns and outbursts. The primary issue with the film is moreso in how the movie progresses, as a movie that starts strong and gets worse isn’t normal and this movie suffers from that second half slog. Extraordinary and iconic opening scene with masterclass acting transitions into a waiting game with an occasionally funny gag. Ending is decent, but that last fourth just makes the movie lesser. Excellent performances, especially from Christoph Waltz who is easily the highlight of this film, and awesome and memorable scenes like the bar scene are excellent but it just doesn’t alleviate the sluggish nature of the film.

The idea that differences in language become the key to the story, and the tension created in the scenes that grow out of that idea, are both fascinating. But as a story set against this historical tragedy, the movie felt a little too playful overall, and I found myself somewhat resistant to that tone. What’s more, that very “resistance” feels like a rather dangerous trick. Normally, after enjoying a violent movie, I’m left with a certain uneasiness over the fact that human beings, myself included, seem to have an instinct for enjoying violence. But this movie prepares that sense of “resistance” in advance, allowing us to walk away with the illusion that we ourselves are resistant to violence. In that sense, you could argue that the movie actually makes violence easier to enjoy, and in a way, makes for a much more purely entertaining experience than a fictional violent movie. What an irony.

Que dire???? Ce n'est pas le meilleur film de Tarantino... Mais il est quand même vachement bien. Les séquences d'ouverture et de fin sont assez spectaculaire, mais avec une inversion totale des rôles, qui clou le film assez magnifiquement. Alors moi, vu que j'aime pas trop la violence gratuite et préfère les films d'auteurs (même si j'adore Tarantino), le coup des scalps m'a gêné, et j'étais dubitatif sur la pertinence de la chose, mais au final, ma mère m'a expliqué que c'était les indiens qui faisaient ça, donc j'aime bien la ref à la colonisation. J'ai adoré voir hitler criblé de balles quand même. Ca me gène toujours un peu ce côté jouissif, mais bon c'est des nazis, donc ça reste moral je pense. Y a quand même pas mal d'idées de mise en scène intéressante, même si le format utilisé m'a perturbé, et j'ai pas compris le but. Comme il aime le faire, Tarantino utilise des chapitres, ce qui est sympathique, même si je n'en sais pas trop l'utilité, c'est plus scénaristiquement esthétique qu'autre chose à mes yeux. J'ai trouvé le film un peu long, mais ça passe quand même, et puis la plupart des séquences étaient intéressantes. La séquence où les nazis crament est quand même superbe. Il y a clairement un jeu d'ironie (Ils sont dans un four géant en quelque sorte). D'ailleurs il est assez présent, autant avec ça, qu'avec l'inversion des rôles du début à la fin, qu'avec le fait que les nazis se fassent cramer dans leur avant première de films avec un peu moins de 300 morts causés par eux, sachant qu'ils sont 350. Mais enfin voilà Tarantino en fait des caisses, mais sait bien en faire des caisses. Après j'ai pas grand chose à dire, en même temps j'ai beaucoup aimé ce film, en même temps, il ne m'inspire rien..... et je le trouve peu pertinent et intelligent dans sa construction.

Sering kali kita dijejali dengan petuah moral yang berbunyi, "Orang lemah membalas dendam, orang kuat memaafkan, orang cerdas mengabaikan." Di atas kertas, itu adalah konsep yang indah. Namun, di medan perang, ungkapan tersebut runtuh seketika dan kehilangan daya magisnya. Membunuh bukanlah sebuah urusan kecil. Tidak banyak keyakinan moral atau doktrin hukum yang mampu mengurus urusan cabut-mencabut nyawa ini secara jujur dan detail. Di sinilah Quentin Tarantino masuk dan menampar realitas tersebut. Ia mengajarkan satu taktik peperangan yang paling menakutkan yaitu bercerita. Lewat Inglourious Basterds, ia membuktikan bahwa cara menghancurkan lawan fasis tidak harus melulu dengan agresi militer terbuka. Terkadang, penghinaan paling brutal justru dilakukan dengan menciptakan panggung media di mana sang lawan justru terhibur saat narasi itu sedang membakar mereka hidup-hidup. Di dalam semesta fiksi historis ini, tata kelola kuasa dibagi ke dalam tiga yurisdiksi yang saling berbenturan. Pertama, mesin birokrasi Nazi yang diwakili oleh Kolonel Hans Landa sebagai sosok penegak sistem yang oportunis dan menjadikan kekejaman sebagai prosedur administrasi. Kedua, otoritas barbar dari unit gerilya pimpinan Letnan Aldo Raine yang beroperasi di luar konvensi perang demi menebar teror psikologis. Ketiga, keadilan senyap dari Shosanna Dreyfus, seorang penyintas yang menggunakan infrastruktur propaganda musuhnya sendiri (sebuah bioskop) sebagai ruang eksekusi. Ketiga faksi ini tidak sekadar bertarung memperebutkan wilayah, melainkan memperebutkan narasi tentang siapa yang berhak menulis akhir dari sejarah. Sebagai seorang arsitek emosi, Tarantino tidak pernah terburu-buru. Penceritaan dengan tiga sudut pandang ini berhasil dirajut dengan sangat rapi, ditopang oleh manajemen tempo (pacing) yang luar biasa kejam sekaligus elegan. Tarantino menguasai betul seni membangun ketegangan lewat percakapan di ruang tertutup, mulai dari peternakan susu LaPadite hingga kedai minum bawah tanah, sebelum akhirnya meledakkannya. Eksekusi ini dihidangkan tepat pada bagian akhir film dengan sangat megah. Penonton seolah diantarkan pada sebuah ujung cerita dengan cara yang sangat sopan. Kesopanannya menjadikan kita seolah disambut sebagai tamu kehormatan dengan ungkapan, "Anggap saja rumah sendiri," persis sedetik sebelum rumah tersebut dibakar habis. Jika kita membedah anatomi film ini menggunakan kacamata kebijakan, Inglourious Basterds adalah sebuah kritik telanjang terhadap bagaimana institusi mengelola propaganda. Joseph Goebbels menggunakan sinema (Nation's Pride) sebagai instrumen negara untuk melegitimasi pembunuhan massal dan mencuci otak massanya. Namun, logika sistem ini diaudit dan dibalik secara mematikan oleh Shosanna. Ia menyadari bahwa sistem fasisme yang begitu angkuh memiliki satu kelemahan fatal yaitu kecongkakan mereka sendiri. Dengan mengunci para petinggi Reich Ketiga di dalam bioskop yang memutar film mereka, Shosanna mengubah kebijakan propaganda menjadi ruang gas bagi para pembuat aturannya sendiri. Lebih jauh lagi, karakter Hans Landa adalah potret sempurna dari busuknya sebuah tata kelola kediktatoran. Kesetiaan pada ideologi hanyalah ilusi. Ketika kapal mulai tenggelam, sang birokrat tertinggi akan dengan mudah melacurkan seragamnya demi jaminan kekebalan hukum. Tarantino pada dasarnya tidak sedang membuat film sejarah, melainkan sedang menyusun sebuah peradilan alternatif. Inglourious Basterds adalah fantasi keadilan (poetic justice) ketika realitas hukum dan pengadilan perang (seperti Nuremberg) dirasa terlalu birokratis dan tidak pernah cukup untuk menebus dosa sejarah. Pada akhirnya, film ini meninggalkan satu peringatan struktural bagi kita. Senjata paling mematikan dari sebuah rezim bukanlah senapan, melainkan layar sinema. Dan ketika medium penipuan itu direbut kembali, api yang menyala tidak hanya membakar tubuh para tiran, tetapi juga meluluhlantakkan warisan sejarah mereka.

I saw Joker in IMAX on October 3rd for the Thursday night preview. My initial reaction to this movie was not an appropriate level of cringe, but a blatant shame & facepalming for Arthur Fleck. I find no similarity towards. I know people are going to see it differently because Joker is the story of your passed over struggling man. He has to draw more focus for civil service because of a traumatically abusive upbringing. Growing up I did have a strict, disciplined childhood, but that order sharpened me overtime instead of degrading any sense of cognitive development. However, Joker is the story of a man who never quite has the lucidity of a “real world” because of a broken mind coping with the traumatic past of a violent mother. It's abhorrent to figure out his whole life and inspiration to make the big time like “King of Comedy” is nothing more than a farce to keep Arthur going despite the constant maintenance of a bed-ridden mother. Arthur is deeply flawed and that makes it tough for any well-adjusted audience to really sympathize and I mean sympathy in the sense of “this is a character I want to see succeed.” As we see him try to cope with his ongoing inadequacies, he snaps violently at anything he deems deeply inhuman inhabiting the slums of Gotham. My rating for this movie is not a reflection of the story, but really the characterization of the “struggling neurotic male”. We the audience are given an unreliable narrator that makes the world out to be this apathetic society of malevolent individuals as opposed to a series of inner-city mingling bearing the depth of a mentally disturbed trauma victim, Arthur. The saving grave of this whole charade is Fleck's cathartic violence to everyone that was culpable in his downfall.

Le film paraissait beaucoup plus deep quand j'avais 13 ans... On voit que Todd Phillips a essayé de faire un film intelligent mais tous les thèmes sont abordés de manière superficielle. Le film montre un mouvement de révolte populaire mais sans jamais montrer les raisons de leur colère, leur idéologie, les dynamiques entre les classes sociales. Ils se battent contre "le système" sans jamais nous dire quel système sûrement parce que le réalisateur avait peur de faire un film trop politique. La maladie mentale est aussi représentée de manière ultra caricaturale, Joaquim Phoenix en fait trop, il se sent obligé de sortir des phrases ultra dramatiques ("Are you having negative thoughts 🤔? All I have are negative thoughts 😈") + musique triste pour bien nous faire comprendre qu'il va pas bien. Ducoup au lieu d'avoir un film intéressant sur l'intersection entre la pauvreté et les problèmes de santé mentale qui montrerait un vrai mouvement social avec de vrais revendications on a juste un film sur un mec qui se venge des gens qui ont pas été gentils avec lui parce qu'il est trop dark.

This films manages to show, through the eyes of an outcast, how mad and sick our society is. The clown aren’t those who comes to light, accepting the label other attribute to them, but those who hide their true identity for the sake of their reputation and of their privileges. A society where everyone was born free, each one and the same measure, but where some cannot afford even the bare minimum to live with dignity, while others plan to buy a spare mansion for summer… A society where the weaker who asks for a better treatment is seen as a fool, someone to make fun of, and the mighty go on undisturbed, craving for more. ‘Joker’ is set in the ‘80, but it shows us a truth we still live nowadays: “we are all equals, but some are more equal than others”.

我滿喜歡瓦昆•菲尼克斯(Joaquin Phoenix)選擇以一種纖細、敏感的人格特質來詮釋小丑這個角色，也喜歡導演把電影的重心放在到底是什麼樣的社會與生命經驗，才會讓一個破碎之人一步步成為一個瘋狂惡徒。 這部電影看似是在描繪一個邪惡之人的誕生，乍看之下也為小丑最後的種種惡行安排了許多可以在某種程度上同理他的原因，例如精神疾病、童年虐待，以及強烈的階級剝奪感。 但有趣的是，為什麼我們通常不太會因此認為這部電影是在明顯替暴力行為辯護？而有些牽涉到種族或性別議題的電影，卻常常會引起不同立場的群體之間的爭議與論戰呢？ 我自己猜想，或許是因為相較於一些至今仍存在許多不同理解與爭論的社會議題，「殺人是不對的」在現代社會的日常道德判斷中，已經具有相對穩固的共識。 因此，電影即使花了很多篇幅去描繪一個兇手是如何形成的，觀眾仍然會很清楚：理解一個人為什麼變成這樣，並不等於認同、也不等於正當化他所做的事情。 也正因為這個底線幾乎不需要再特別說明，電影才有餘裕把注意力放在人性的複雜面、灰色地帶，以及人與社會之間可能存在的共同困境。 而這也讓我想到，或許其他仍然存在許多價值衝突的社會議題，也不一定只能透過明確的道德立場來呈現。 當然，一部電影選擇表達某種價值主張，或甚至直接挑戰某些既有的社會觀念，絕對沒有問題。電影可以是抗議、揭露、批判，也可以試圖說服觀眾。而且對於某些仍然存在現實不平等的議題，我完全能理解創作者為什麼希望透過作品去挑戰既有的觀念。 而我比較好奇的則是：除了告訴觀眾「什麼是對的」之外，是不是還能進一步往人的生命經驗裡去探索？ 例如那些衝突如何在複雜的現實中進入一個人的生命，以及它可能造成的孤獨、人際關係撕裂、家庭矛盾、經濟與社會壓力，以及對人性基本尊嚴的追求。 我想，我喜愛的其中一種電影，可能是這樣的： 它不只是關注某個社會議題，也不只是替某種立場發聲，而是更進一步描繪一個真實的人，如何在這個充滿矛盾與複雜衝突的世界裡存活。它不急於把人物變成立場的代言人，也不急於給觀眾一個明確的道德標準答案，而是願意把人性的複雜、荒謬與希望，一一溫柔地攤開在我們面前。

"É impressão minha ou o mundo está ficando mais maluco?" Esse filme é simplesmente fantástico. Todd Phillips apresenta uma visão mais humana e profunda de um dos maiores inimigos do Batman. Em vez de mostrar apenas o Coringa como um psicopata que espalha o caos, acompanhamos Arthur Fleck, um homem fragilizado, solitário e constantemente desprezado pela sociedade, até sua transformação no símbolo do caos que conhecemos. Gotham é sombria, suja, violenta e decadente, uma estética que combina perfeitamente com os temas de desigualdade social, abandono e saúde mental abordados pelo filme. Joaquin Phoenix entrega uma atuação impecável, mergulhando completamente na complexidade emocional de Arthur e transitando entre fragilidade e violência. A história também mexe muito com a cabeça, lembrando Taxi Driver, com momentos desconfortáveis e situações que fazem o espectador questionar o que é real. Apesar do ritmo lento e da duração extensa, é uma experiência muito interessante. O roteiro, a cinematografia e a atmosfera são espetaculares, e o filme consegue fazer refletir sobre sanidade, realidade e a forma como a sociedade trata aqueles que são constantemente negligenciados. No fim, Coringa vai muito além de uma simples história de origem: é uma obra complexa, desconfortável e que realmente fica na cabeça depois dos créditos. Nota: 8/10

It's as if Ritchie wrote losing my edge but he was being serious about everything. The movie has this generational divide thing, that the old boys are the last ones left with any valor, and the kids are growing up all wrong. This combined with a lot of self reference - Hugh Grant's script where's he monetising a true crime story happening before his very eyes, and familiar Guy Ritchie locations, twists, turns of phrase are played out with this divide in understanding between generations. But is Ritchie doing that much wrangling with his past? I feel like he could be leaning into parody with the back and forths and the race gags and the self congratulating boomer humour of an older guy getting the upper hand on the stupid youth. It could explain The Jam at the end - That's Entertainment as an ironic lashing out at the portrayal of youth crime in media, a deconstruction of his own influence on crime film and his declining cultural relevance. There is not nothing there, given who saves the day in the end... But the SA scene and the sneering scene with the junkies are both enormous miscues that make me think he probably isn't reflecting, that the boomer humour isn't parody So the choice of That's Entertainment, a truly beautiful work of art about urban decay and working class perseverance, to close his film that instead of reckoning with his own legacy or making some gesture bigger than itself instead just plays the hits and pats itself on the back, feels very ugly and very hollow. Also Mccounaghey is clearly miscast, it's all too bright and clinical and looks bad and the framing device is fine but doesn't work with how flat the rest of the movie is dramatically

Could Guy Ritchie be considered as a “one-movie wonder” director? This is the fourth film of his that I’ve watched, and it’s impressive how none of them come close to the originality, humor, energy and entertainment value of Snatch. This one is just another generic crime movie. The famous “dad movie”, the kind of movie that an older guy who only watches action and crime films will watch and say, “What a masterpiece.” It has a great cast and good performances, especially from Matthew McConaughey, Colin Farrell, and Hugh Grant, who manage to save the film at certain moments. But Guy Ritchie relies way too much on events without truly good writing and throws in countless twists at the end just to keep the audience interested. I think there are at least five twists in the final act alone, seemingly to mask the pathetic writing of the film and characters. Btw this movie has many failed attempts at humor also. Anyway, it has some entertainment value, a good pacing and in certain moments Guy Ritchie directs well and gives us flashes of his originality, but there are very few of them. At one point, you might even think the film is going to take a good direction, but then it goes right back to its mess. Overall, it’s just very generic. It’s a movie to watch to kill some time, because it manages to keep the audience entertained throughout its two-hour runtime, but its content is cheap, a premium generic action.

I wanted to like this film, I really really did, and while there are some very good attributes, this film suffers from building into something ambitious and not being able to neatly tie that ambition up by the end. Let me start off with the positives. This film has some really great cinematography that helps to build tension, and some very solid editing that makes sure this film doesn't ever drag. It's not the best I've seen, but it does it's job very well for the film. The costumes are 100% a standout of this film, telling you everything you need to know about a character's personality before they actually become fleshed out. The ensemble of this film, led by an excellent Matthew McConaughey, is also very solid, very comitted to the bit, and very good at really making the most of the material. Where this film struggles though is the writing and direction by Guy Ritchie. The screenplay is a big issue in my opinion, because it has good moments, namely the first act being a great setup and an excellent hook for a movie. The second act drops a little bit but is pretty solid overall. Where this film really ends up falling off a cliff is the third act. After setting up several characters, a very odd framing device, numerous character relationships, and very briefly mentioned ideas and other minor characters, the film seems to realize it only has about 30 minutes to tie all of it up, and I was dissapointed to find it done in a very messy manner. What happens is a very quick succession of strange plot twists, thrusting supporting characters that haven't been seen for upwards of 45 minutes into large, plot-essential roles, and even going as far as to introduce a new operation behind the scenes of characters we haven't met that are related to a character that was quickly killed off and used as a gag. Some of these suddenly important characters I really didn't have a strong connection to at all due to the fact that they were simply underwritten. There is so much exposition, that maybe cutting a few plotlines would've tightened the ending up a lot better. As for the direction, it struggles to decide whether this is supposed to be a campy serio-comedy, an intense crime thriller, or an all-or-nothing high stakes action film. There are so many jokes and odd inclusions that don't quite seem to line up with anything else in the film. Personally, the campy crime thriller seen in the first act of the film is where this really shines, and where it's performances feel the best. I really wanted to like The Gentlemen, but unfortunately, the film felt too ambitious to ever catch up to itself.

J’ai beaucoup apprécié le style de Guy Ritchie dans Snatch et on retrouve énormément d’éléments similaires dans le montage de The Gentlemen. Malheureusement c’est quitte ou double. Ici, je n’ai pas été pris dans l’histoire et j’ai trouvé le film très long. Si dans Snatch j’ai le sentiment que le style de Guy Ritchie sert vraiment l’histoire, que ce soit avec le montage nerveux, les changements de rythme ou les dialogues qui contribuent à rendre le film dynamique et à maintenir l’intérêt, à l’inverse, dans The Gentlemen j’ai plutôt eu l’impression que le style prenait toute la place au détriment de l’histoire. Le montage et les effets de mise en scène sont toujours très travaillés mais comme je n’ai pas accroché à l’intrigue, ils ont plutôt renforcé cette sensation de longueur. C’est dommage parce que le casting joue très bien et que le film en lui-même est assez élégant.

The Original Gangsters Also gut Freunde, es kann ja nicht immer nur Spaß und Spiele geben, ab und zu muss man auch arbeiten, also: Erst die Arbeit, dann das Vergnügen, deshalb beginnen wir unsere zweite heutige Kritik mit etwas theoretischem Unterricht zum Thema Film (keine Sorge, ihr kennt mich hoffentlich mittlerweile, allzu trocken wird es nicht), tauchen wir also etwas ab in das Werk des Guy Ritchie (aber nur etwas): Guy Ritchie hat Zeit seines Lebens Filme über die Art von Menschen gedreht, der er sich selbst zugehörig fühlt: Den jungen Rebellen, die der alten Generation, die denkt, ihr würde alles gehören, ordentlich in den Arsch tritt und dabei eigentlich auch meist Erfolg hat. Bloß war das in den 90ern, und die Zeiten ändern sind. Damals war Ritchie ein junger Mann, ein junger Rebell, doch nun gehört er selbst zur alten Generation mit der Vormachtsstellung, gegen die er einst nach allen Regeln der Kunst (im wahrsten Sinne des Wortes) rebellierte und revoltierte, und da ist es nur angebracht, dass Ritchie sich endlich sein Alter eingesteht und dementsprechend endlich ein Alterswerk abliefert. The Gentlemen ist nun dieses Alterswerk, der zwar die Ritchie-typischen Themen, aber aus einer Ritchie-gänlich-untypischen Perspektive, und dennoch in jeder einzelnen Sekunde der zwei Stunden Ritchie. Mickey Pearson (Matthew McConaughey) ist zwar Amerikaner, aber dennoch hat er in England ein erfolgreiches Gras-Imperium aufgebaut. Doch da da Cannabis kurz vor der Legalisierung steht erkennt der intelligente, charmante Drogenbaron, dass das ein legales Geschäft, verbunden mit seinem Namen und Ruf, niemals erfolgreich sein kann, weshalb er, mit Unterstützung seiner Frau Rosalind (Michelle Dockery), den Verkauf an seinen Konkurrenten, den jüdischen Entrepeneur Matthew Berger (Jeremy Strong) vorbereitet. Doch zugleich bleiben für ihn und seinen loyalen Consigliere Ray (Charlie Hunnam) noch genug Probleme, die beseitigt werden muss, etwa der arrogante Dry Eye (Henry Golding), ein Mitglied der Triaden in England und Stellvertreter von Lord George (Tom Wu), der ebenfalls Interesse an dem Imperium zeigt, die jungen Boxer des Coach (Colin Farrell), die eine Grasplantage überfallen und der schmierigen Privatdetektiv Fletcher (Hugh Grant), der im Auftrag des Zeitungsverlegers Big Dave (Eddie Marsan) in Pearsons Angelegenheiten und vor allem seinen kreativen Akitivitäten herumschnüffelt... Dachtet ihr etwa, der Unterricht ist schon zu Ende? Falsch gedacht. Beschäftigen uns wir nun damit: Womit beschäftigt Guy Ritchie sich in seinen ganzen Filmen (zumindest den ganzen guten Filmen, lassen wir die paar Ausrutscher aus dem letzten Jahrzehnt mal außen vor)? Mit jungen Gangster, die gegen alte Gangster rebellieren, und obwohl sie diesen ich Macht unterlegen sind, am Ende über sie triumphieren oder zumindest überleben, weil sie ihre Unterlegenheit mit genug Gewitztheit wieder wett machen. Eindeutig identifizierte sich Ritchie einst mit diesen jungen Rebellen, sprühten seine Filme doch einst von genau dieser kreativen, rebellischen Energie. Im Alter ist Ritchie nun gemäßigter geworden, aber deswegen noch lange nicht gemäßigt. Deshalb macht es dennoch Sinn, das Ritchie irgendwann die Perspektive dreht, schließlich kann niemand, kein Tarantino und auch kein Ritchie, ewig der junge Rebell bleiben, und so liegt der Fokus hier auf den Silberrücken, den Alteingessessen, den originalen Gangstern, den Gentlemen. Und bereits der Titel sagt alles aus, denn während man von den Figuren in Ritchies früheren Filmen kaum von Gentlemen sprechen konnte haben die alten Gangster hier tatsächlich so etwas wie Ehre und einen Kodex, zwei Dinge, die die jungen nicht kennen, etwas, das ihre Rebellion wesentlich unsympathischer macht, als wir es sonst vom Briten gewohnt sind. Die Altersmilde merkt man dem Werk nicht nur hinsichtlich ihrer handlungstechnischen Ausrichtung oder der zurückgefahrenen Inszenierung an, sondern auch hinsichtlich der Charaktere, die zwar alle weiteren betont cool sind (gerade Colin Farrell, der mit hartem irischem Akzent seine Coolness wohl mit Löffeln gefressen hat), aber denen es an der Ritchie-typischen Skurrilität erstaunlich mangelt. Matthew McConaughey, Charlie Hunnam, Farrell, sie sind alle unfassbar cool, was spätestens klar wird wenn jedem von ihnen sein ganz eigener Moment eingeräumt wird, in dem er mit seiner Coolness glänzen kann. Das mag für den für den Mann aus Hatfield vielleicht nicht ganz typisch sein, aber es erfüllt den Zweck, denn es ist cool (wer hät`s gedacht) und vor allem verdammt unterhaltsam. Vor allem ist das Skript, das Ritchie seit langer Zeit wieder gänzlich allein geschrieben hat, erneut weniger originell denn zweckmäßig. Und heutzutage ist es vieilleicht noch weniger organisch, denn während Ritchie früher das tat, was viele Gaunerkomödien taten, tut er heute das, was er früher tat, nur eben mit verdrehter Perspektive. Die Handlung ist dabei größtenteils vorhersehbar, nur eine Wendung um den Privatdeketiv Fletcher und seinen Versuch, Pearson über Ray zu erpressen, überrascht tatsächlich. Und vor allem beweist Ritchie am Ende eines: Egal wie oft er über den Film den Faden zu verlieren scheint, egal wie oft er sich in einem Labyrinth aus Nebenhandlungen zu verlieren scheint, am Ende findet er wieder ans Licht, entwirrt das an den gordischen Knoten erinnernden Wirwarr und vereint sämtliche Handlungsstränge, wenn auch mehr oder minder gelungen, mit der Haupthandlung. Man merkt dabei durchaus an, das Ritchie höchstwahrscheinlich nichts an dem Film voraus geplant und die Nebenhandlungen deshalb er zufällig entstanden sind, was auch erklärt, wieso Ritchie gegen Ende schon sehr konstruieren und Geschichten gehetzt zu Ende erzählen muss, damit diese Nebenhandlungen rückwirkend irgendeinen Effekt auf die Haupthandlung haben und nicht einfach wirkungslos verpuffen. Die Darbietungen sind allesamt der Handlung angemessen. McConaughey lässt seinen typischen Charme spielen, vermengt ihn mit seiner ihm eigenen Coolness und sorgt so für einige der eindringstlichsten Szenen, wenn  er gerade in zwei Szenen die Beherrschung verliert und seine Gegner bedroht. Doch auch hier verlieht der Texaner nichts wirklich von seiner Coolness, was die Szenen noch während der Sichtung viel eindringlicher machen. Auch Michelle Dockery als seine Frau, Charlie Hunnam als sein loyaler Mann für die Drecksarbeit und Henry Golding als impulsiver Gangster mit Ambitionen können in ihren Rollen überzeugen, lediglich der ansonsten immer gute Jeremy Strong wirkt hier stark fehlbesetzt, weil er seiner Rolle weder die nötige Präsenz verleihen noch überzeugend porträtieren kann. Als Scene Stealer erweisen sich vor allem zwei: Während Colin Farrell mit seinen trockenen, lakonischen Sprüchen, vermengt mit seinem originalen irischen Akzent und ebengalls einer Portion Coolness wohl für einige der lustigsten Szenen des Films sorgt (deswegen unbedingt im O-Ton schauen), überzeugt vor allem Hugh Grant: Der veträumte, zerstreute einstgie RomCom-Held spielt hier einen schmierigen Privatdeketiv und kann mit seiner Mischung aus trockenen Sprüchen, schmierigem Verhalten und schwulen Anmachen auf eine Weise überzeugen, die man vor dem Kinobesuch wohl kaum für möglich gehalten hätte. Insgesamt lässt sich wohl sagen: Wer hätte gedacht, dass Ritchie vom jungen Rebellen zum alten Monopolisten reifen und seinen kompletten Stil umkrempeln muss, um nochmeil einen verdammt ordentlichen Film abzuliefern, der es mit seinen besten Filmen nicht nur aufnehmen kann, sondern diese zum Teil auch übertrifft!

Absolutely incredible, slept on this movie for ages but I’m so glad I gave it a try. This is probably one of my favourites in this genre, an absolute classic imo. The narrative style through the conversation was superb, I was a little confused early on but everything started making sense slowly. First and foremost, the biggest strength is that almost every character in the movie is memorable. It’s hard enough to write one solid and interesting character, imagine how hard it is to write like 8 of them. Mathew McConaughey was solid, he’s always impressive tbh but it was nice to see him in such a dark and gritty British world. It’s also interesting that he accepted to do this since some other actors genuinely do have more screen time than him. Charlie Hunnam as Raymond is one of them, he’s ever present in the entire movie and he is just incredible. Hugh Grant is alongside him in most scenes and he also makes a solid impression. However it was Colin Farrel as Coach who blew my mind, I just loved his character so much and the entire track with him as his students was integrated seamlessly. Now for the only negative I have, Jeremy Strong. I can’t believe I’ve just uttered those words as I’m a massive massive Succession fan and also a die hard Kendall Roy loyalist. But he just did not fit into this world, and tbh he felt even more out of place when we come to know that he’s the main ‘villain’, just did not have the dangerous and cunning feel at all. I just loved it from a plot perspective, it was smart and wacky. The concept of the weed farms itself was solid and the way the story was dealt with was even better, they didn’t over complicate it but the twists and turns definitely did keep things engaging enough. I probably didn’t do a great job at fully expressing my thoughts about this movie but I really did enjoy it a lot.

It’s not a bad watch (pacy, interesting, relatively entertaining), but I’d argue that it is a bad film. This has film school written all over it. It indulges in the assumption that it’s smart. In reality, it’s a simple plot made interesting through the reverse chronology. The stylistic choices were at an eye-rolling level of film school cliche (brooding scenes in black-and-white do not a masterpiece make). Like other Nolan films, I felt no emotional connection to this story. I was very aware I was watching a film, rather than feeling invested in the world of these characters. There’s no emotional intelligence in Nolan’s filmmaking, and so I find myself searching for positives in the technical aspects of his films. But I found the screenplay entirely overdone, almost written like a novel where everything has to be said rather than shown. The sterile acting reinforced the distance I had as a viewer from this film.

I finally watched Memento and it is one of Christopher Nolan's weakest films. Firstly I like the idea of the film, it follows a man suffering from short term memory as he searches for his wife's killer and to help himself piece the puzzle together he makes use of photographs and notes to remember key details. Now this is a fresh idea and something I haven't seen before but the execution was lackluster. The story and editing of the film is non linear. The film drops us into major plot points and goes backwards a couple of moments before that point to show us the events leading up to that major story beat. My issue is how jarring this while watching because you're confused half the time. Something major happens and then you're in a completely different scene that seems unrelated. I understand fundamentally it's to have the user feel like Leonard the main character because he has short term memory loss and throughout the film finds himself in strange situations he has no recollection of being in, but for me it made the film feel disjointed and difficult to comprehend. And the film's structure doesn't help with character introductions or development because the film introduces a character that knows Leonard but as the viewer you only get context of how they met later on, which makes it difficult to understand characters' motivations and why they behave the way they do. Another issue I have are the black and white exposition dumps Leonard gives us; they are misplaced and the black and white filter feels out of place. If the purpose of the film was to make the viewer as confused as the main character I'd say Nolan did a great job. The only positives of the film are Leonard's monologues. Most of the film is spent inside Leonard's head and Guy Pierce does a great job portraying his confusion and the struggles of short term memory loss and having to rely on notes and other people which could easily manipulated which is another aspect of the film I enjoyed. As Leonard tries to find his wife's killer you notice how the notes he makes and the people he talks to are unreliable and how he has to discover the truth when he can't trust anyone or anything. I love Christopher Nolan but Memento wasn't great.

Es decir, no me creo que sea tan metódico para absolutamente todo, pero luego arranque las páginas de su informe policial y tome decisiones enajenado sin poder apuntar las consecuencias después etc, etc. No sé tío, recuerdas todo antes del accidente pero empiezas a sabotearte a ti mismo… Tu mujer no murió, era diabética, estuviste interno, confundes tu historia con la de un cliente que tuviste… Simplemente no puedo comprarte que sea porque el prota necesita una excusa, no después de haberle visto tan metódico durante toda la peli. This movie is amazing. The elements of mystery, and the way by which certain scenes work within the look at Lenny's character really work up. The confusion works because it helps to show how his life really is. This takes the movie to the next level in terms of the story. Christopher Nolan’s directorial genius elevates a linear narrative into a deeply entertaining one. By placing the audience in a constant state of disorientation at the start of every scene, Nolan masterfully forces us into the same fractured mental state as Lenny, keeping us thoroughly engaged. The awe we feel each time we piece together a clue—an ability Leonard is tragically deprived of—is brilliantly executed. We also see that the protagonist is constantly cautious about whom to trust. He suspects he is being used, and while this is true, the only proof he has to back his theories is the anecdotal evidence he has gathered himself. This is a puzzle we, the audience, are also trying to figure out for the majority of the film. Towards the end, we realize that he is indeed being manipulated: by Natalie for arguably pragmatic reasons, and by Teddy, who kills two birds with one stone by giving Lenny a purpose for living while also serving his own personal interests. Because of this shared confusion, the audience is led to believe that Lenny's truth is our truth. However, at the actual chronological end of the story, Lenny subtly reveals that he’s actively choosing to live for revenge. He desperately wants meaning for his actions, or in his own words: "I have to believe in a world outside my own mind. I have to believe that my actions still have meaning, even if I can't remember them." The true tragedy is not what he has forgotten, but what he actively chooses to bury. His inability to move on is not simply because he cannot make new memories, but rather because of his own active choice to forget the ones that don't fit his narrative. Teddy captures Lenny’s state perfectly: “So you lie to yourself to be happy. Nothing wrong with that—we all do. Who cares if there's a few little things you'd rather not remember?" This perfectly reflects the true message of the film: the choices Lenny has made since the incident are ultimately to blame. His willingness to lie to himself leads him to commit terrible tragedies just so he can live comfortably in a fabricated reality. He chooses to ignore everyone's warnings and run from the truth. Despite everything that is revealed, he willfully continues living in ignorance, perfectly punctuated by Lenny's—and the film's—final line: "Now... where was I?" before looping seamlessly back to the opening sequence.

OBRA MAESTRA Antes que nada, mis dieces a Christopher Nolan por sacar adelante un filme así, tan original e inmersivo que, por lo menos a mí, me ha mantenido pegado a la pantalla en todo momento. Si no quitas ojo y prestas atención a TODOS los detalles, esta película es una auténtica joya. Me considero una persona muy observadora, siempre intento que no se me escape nada, y esta película ha sido hedonismo puro. Es increíble como Nolan hace que sientas la ansiedad, el agobio, la tortura y la cárcel mental de no recordar lo que ha sucedido hace dos minutos, rodando la trama al revés. Esa manera tan única de meterte en la piel del protagonista y tan diferente de cualquier otra película: aquí no estás inquieto por saber qué pasará después, si no por qué ha pasado ANTES. Es como si te convirtiesen a ti en el enfermo durante dos horas, y ESO es lo que la hace tan brutal. Es cruda, es misteriosa y su estética me parece sensacional, así como las actuaciones, la fotografía y la voz en off. Todos los detalles y los giros están tan bien elegidos que no puedo sino apreciar y aplaudir el proceso creativo del auténtico rematado de la cabeza que ha ingeniado semejante puzzle. En el ámbito filosófico, moral y reflexivo de la película —película que, por cierto, sigue una línea similar a Shutter Island en su invitación al dilema moral, lo cual, al tener que darle al coco, me encanta— es curioso como los dos personajes, “Teddy” y Natalie manipulan al protagonista para conseguir lo que quieren, así como el protagonista se manipula a sí mismo y se cree sus propias mentiras… y tira para adelante, aun tras asumir la verdad, ¿o no? A destacar la genialidad de Joe Pantoliano —Ralphie en Los Soprano , actorazo de los pies a la cabeza, un virtuoso este señor— a quien tanto cariño tengo. También, por supuesto, a Guy Pierce, se da por entendido. Para que luego parezca que soy hater de Nolan. Reafirmo lo que dije en mi review de Tenet. Donde más brilla Nolan es también donde más flaquea, es como un vaso de agua que a veces se desborda (véase Tenet o la Odisea) y a veces se queda lleno a la perfección (véase The Prestige, El Caballero Oscuro o Memento). ¡BRA-VO!

50 minutes of the worst characters engaged in the most dull melodrama imaginable, followed by 40 minutes alternating between loud barking and shrill screaming. Probably not the worst King adaptation, but the worst one I want to sit through.

Stephen King’s literary works have birthed some of the most iconic horror masterpieces in cinema history. However, the 1983 film adaptation of Cujo represents a staggering failure in narrative execution, stands as a masterclass in bad screenplaying, and serves as an ultimate waste of audience time. What promises to be a tense, claustrophobic thriller quickly devolves into an exercise in narrative stupidity, structural overkill, and profound boredom. The primary catalyst for the film's failure is the sheer stupidity woven into the fabric of the screenplay. For a horror film to maintain tension, the characters must make choices that feel organic, even if desperate. In Cujo, the characters are driven entirely by contrived ignorance designed solely to force the plot forward. The screenplay relies on a series of absurdly convenient oversights: a breaking car that happens to fail at the worst possible location, characters who refuse to communicate basic information to one another, and a complete lack of survival instincts. Because the script fails to establish intelligent stakes, the audience is left rooting against the human protagonists rather than fearing the antagonist. This structural ineptitude leads directly into the film's most egregious flaw: the central conflict gets boring after exactly five minutes. The novelty of a rabid St. Bernard trapping a mother and child inside a sweltering Ford Pinto wears off almost immediately. Once the physical parameters of the siege are established, the film completely runs out of ideas. The audience is subjected to endless, repetitive cycles of the dog barking at the window, the characters screaming, and the dog retreating, only to repeat the sequence moments later. Stripped of psychological depth or escalating tension, the film ceases to be scary and becomes aggressively monotonous. Compounding this boredom is the screenplay's reliance on overkill. Lacking the nuance required to sustain a feature-length film in a single location, the filmmakers substitute genuine terror with relentless, loud overstimulation. The editing becomes frantic, the score shrieks at every minor movement, and the dog is subjected to an absurd amount of cosmetic gore that feels cartoonish rather than frightening. By dialing every sensory element up to eleven without any narrative progression, the film numbs the audience. The overkill exposes the fundamental emptiness of the script; it is a short story stretched violently beyond its breaking point. Cujo is a monumental waste of time. It takes a terrifying, subtext-rich novel about family fractures and domestic terror and flattens it into a dull, repetitive creature feature. The screenplay lacks the wit to engage the mind, the pacing to hold the attention, or the restraint to build actual dread. Instead of delivering a tight, memorable thriller, Cujo leaves its audience trapped in a stagnant vehicle of poor filmmaking, praying for the credits to roll.

Cujo es una crítica a nuestra sociedad actual. El perro constantemente queda en segundo plano para que nos enfoquemos en las dinámicas familiares que se nos muestran en la película, como lo son las familias de Vic y Joe. Por un lado tenemos la infidelidad de Donna y por el otro el maltrato que Joe ejerce sobre Charity. Con esto claro, puedo ver que la película no quiere enseñarnos la historia de un perro asesino infestado de rabia; quiere mostrarnos cómo este tipo de dinámicas tóxicas afectan a los miembros más vulnerables de la familia; como a los hijos, por ejemplo. Ahora, sinceramente esto me lo saqué del fundillo. Yo sí quería ver una película de un perro asesino infestado de rabia, joder, si quisiera ver una película de drama familiar, pues simplemente miraría una de drama familiar, pero este no es el caso. Joder, yo quería mi película de terror, carajo, odio como dejaron al puto perro en segundo plano solo para enfocarse en las misms problemáticas familiares que mencioné solo para burlarme. La próxima vez, si haces una película que a penas trata sobre un perro asesino, no pongas su nombre como título; algunos nos podemos llevar una gran decepción.

This was not great. A hard thing when adapting books to the screen is capturing all that rich internal narrative. Even with human characters, it can be hard to cram all of those thoughts onto the screen in a way that doesn’t feel forced. When the character is a dog, however, it is a much more difficult feat. And here, it shows. The book is full of Cujo’s own thoughts and feelings about what is happening to him. How he is reacting to sights and sounds once the rabies takes hold of him. It’s obviously incredibly hard to do this on screen, so we don’t get any of that. We’re also missing lots of important information about characters that we learn in the book. Lots of background and context for why they act the way they do. I get stuff has to be cut to account for a reasonable run time, but so much was cut here. Performances were decent, I don’t think anyone stood out in particular apart from the dog playing Cujo. Some parts of the plot were changed, and I don’t think they worked particularly well. Overall, quite disappointed with this considering how much I enjoyed the book!
