Um das direkt zu Beginn klar zu stellen: Ich bin kein großer Fan der Buchvorlage von Stephen King, aber dennoch habe ich versucht dem Film eine faire Chance zu geben. Allerdings ist dieser Film so hochgradig langweilig, dass mir das irgendwann einfach nicht mehr möglich war. Denn die Geschichte zieht sich und zieht sich und es hört nicht auf. Sekunden werden zu Minuten, Minuten zu Stunden. Und dann sitzt da dieser Hund vor dem kaputten Auto, in welchem eine Mutter mit ihrem Kleinkind sitzt und es passiert nichts. Selbst wenn der Hund angreift ist das kaum spannend genug, um die Minuten davor und danach noch zu retten. Ich saß knappe 90 Minuten da und habe mir eine Film angesehen, der sich wie 180 anfühlt und versucht, den Zuschauer durch die Langeweile zu erdrücken. Die Handlung fand ich im Buch schon nicht allzu spannend. Vor allem aber auch, da ein Gefühl aufgebaut wird, welches mir nicht gefällt. Dieser Zeitdruck, der geschaffen wird, da die beiden Festsitzenden langsam einfach nicht mehr durchhalten. Im Film war das auch der Fall, aber es war mir ab einem gewissen Punkt einfach egal. Ich wusste was passieren würde, auch wenn der Film in einem Fall den Schwanz einzieht, und dann war es eben so. Die Handlung hat mich einfach kalt gelassen. Den Punkt, den ich "Cujo" aber geben muss, ist der Look und die Inszenierung. Denn der Look hat mich immer wieder an Horrorfilme aus den 70ern erinnert, die einfach dreckig und räudig aussehen. Genau das schafft der Film auch hin und wieder, was mir ziemlich gut gefallen hat. Die Inszenierung ist ebenfalls nicht übel. Diese beiden Punkt habe ich dann doch noch neutral sehen können. Denn das muss ich einfach sagen. Der Film scheitert an der Prämisse und nicht an der technischen Umsetzung, da ich die Kamera und Inszenierung vollkommen solide fand. Insgesamt ist "Cujo" also ein Film, den ich aufgrund des Pacings ziemlich schwer zu ertragen fand. 2/5 Sternen.

A snoozer of a King adaptation as horror that does have a couple things going for it as a family drama. I've also got to give the film credit for its portrayal of the male lead as a father. It's rare to see good dads in movies that aren't explicitly geared as family fare. Dee Wallace's mom character is portrayed far more negatively, the way dads are more often shown, and the script lets her contain multitudes, as she seeks selfish pleasure and ultimately protects her son when she has to. It's pretty refreshing, actually. Cujo himself is a menacing villain, but everything plays out in such a lazy, laconic way that your interest flags. It's also shot with zero panache. Passable in ways, but it lacks the humor of better adaptations like Graveyard Shift and the pure filmmaking muscle of ones like Christine .

When I think of Cujo, one of the first things that comes to mind is what Stephen King once said about the novel: he doesn’t remember writing it. King penned the book while struggling with alcoholism and later admitted that he had no real awareness of the process—he just knew the story came out well and became a huge success. The film adaptation, released in August 1983, didn’t fare as well with critics but was a box office hit. Cujo tells the story of a friendly Saint Bernard who becomes rabid after being bitten by a bat. Donna Trenton (Dee Wallace) has recently separated from her husband following the revelation of an affair. Her five-year-old son, Tad (Danny Pintauro), adores the dog, whose owners—young Brett Camber (Billy Jayne) and his father, a mechanic (Ed Lauter)—don’t mind the visits. One day, Donna and Tad come to see Cujo only to discover that the dog has turned into a violent killing machine and has already attacked one of his owners. When their car dies and they are trapped inside under the summer sun, Cujo’s aggression escalates, and the two must figure out a way to survive with no help in sight. I last watched this film sixteen years ago, and my opinion hasn’t changed. The story is solid, and there are genuinely suspenseful moments, but the pacing drags. The majority of the action takes place in a single location, and the ending is easy to predict. That said, the film is effective in its tension-building, with Cujo appearing suddenly to deliver moments of real terror. The script provides some character development, but the slow progression makes the experience feel longer than it really is. I also read Cujo in high school and, as often happens, the book outshines the film. The novel’s suspense and depth are far superior to the movie, though the adaptation does capture certain frightening moments and presents them in a realistic, well-executed way. Cujo himself is genuinely terrifying at times, and the film does have moments that will make your heart race. Ultimately, while the movie has its merits, it’s a slow burn that doesn’t fully live up to the tension and richness of King’s original story.

It still could have fit in the movie given that it followed the beats of the plot of the book. Maybe in 1983 it was just too much of a downer or maybe the film didn’t have the budget to have the police and ambulance arrive to a Donna who was trying to resuscitate her son for so long after killing Cujo. This adaptation derives its horror from the systematic collapse of domestic security. Rather than presenting evil as an external or supernatural force, the film finds violence within the familiar, transforming the family dog into an agent of biological disorder. Cujo’s descent into rabies is consequently devoid of moral purpose - his violence is pathological, arbitrary and indifferent to human suffering. Dee Wallace gives a notable performance, gradually moving from domestic anxiety towards states of acute psychological and physical distress. Pintauro’s presence intensifies the film’s emphasis on vulnerability and dependence. Teague’s direction is similarly restrained, employing increasingly claustrophobic compositions and restricting movement as the narrative progresses. The automobile becomes both shelter and prison, while heat, dehydration and mechanical failure function as additional instruments of physical deterioration. The film’s fairly austere tone derives from this refusal of melodrama - as Cujo presents terror as a material condition, in which ordinary structures of safety prove temporary, unreliable and ultimately incapable of containing violence. CUJO Kritik Review (1983): Cujo ist ein Horrorfilm, Thriller und Survival-Horror mit Mystery- und Monsterfilm-Elementen und basiert auf Stephen Kings gleichnamigem Roman. Lewis Teagues Verfilmung erzählt von dem zunächst freundlichen Bernhardiner Cujo, der nach einem Fledermausbiss an Tollwut erkrankt und zu einer tödlichen Bedrohung wird. Im Mittelpunkt stehen Donna Trenton und ihr Sohn Tad, die während einer Autopanne auf dem Grundstück der Cambers in ihrem Wagen festsitzen und von Cujo belagert werden. Die größte Stärke des Films ist seine beklemmende Atmosphäre. Cujo braucht erstaunlich wenig klassische Horroreffekte, um Spannung aufzubauen. Besonders die Hitze, die Enge des Autos und das Wissen, dass der Hund jederzeit angreifen könnte, erzeugen ein starkes Gefühl der Ausweglosigkeit. Die scheinbar alltägliche Situation entwickelt sich dadurch langsam zu einem echten Überlebenskampf. Auch Dee Wallace überzeugt als Donna. Sie vermittelt glaubwürdig die zunehmende Panik und Verzweiflung einer Mutter, die nicht nur um ihr eigenes Leben, sondern vor allem um das ihres Kindes kämpfen muss. Danny Pintauro funktioniert ebenfalls gut als Tad, dessen Angst die ohnehin angespannte Situation zusätzlich verstärkt. Besonders interessant ist, dass der Film sich zunächst viel Zeit für das Familiendrama nimmt. Die Eheprobleme zwischen Donna und Vic sowie Donnas Affäre wirken zunächst fast wie eine völlig andere Geschichte. Dadurch entsteht allerdings ein Kontrast zum späteren Horror: Die privaten Probleme werden zunehmend unwichtig, sobald Donna und Tad tatsächlich ums Überleben kämpfen müssen. Cujo selbst ist eine überraschend effektive Horrorfigur. Der Film macht aus ihm kein übernatürliches Monster, sondern einen durch Tollwut gefährlich gewordenen Hund. Gerade diese Bodenständigkeit macht die Bedrohung glaubwürdiger. Der Horror funktioniert dadurch weniger wie Fantasy und stärker wie ein realistischer Survival-Thriller. Auch die Inszenierung von Lewis Teague kann überzeugen. Die Kamera nutzt besonders das Auto als klaustrophobischen Schauplatz und macht aus einem eigentlich kleinen Raum eine zunehmend unerträgliche Falle. Die begrenzte Bewegungsfreiheit der Figuren wird dabei konsequent für die Spannung genutzt. Das größte Problem liegt für mich im langen Aufbau. Der Film braucht relativ viel Zeit, bevor Cujo tatsächlich zur zentralen Bedrohung wird. Das Familiendrama besitzt zwar seine Berechtigung, wirkt aber stellenweise etwas zu ausführlich. Wer hauptsächlich einen Tierhorrorfilm erwartet, muss entsprechend Geduld mitbringen. Auch die Nebenfiguren bleiben teilweise oberflächlich. Einige Handlungsstränge rund um die Familie Camber und Donnas Eheprobleme tragen zwar zur Ausgangssituation bei, erhalten aber nicht immer genügend Tiefe, um wirklich interessant zu werden. Die Horror-Sequenzen selbst sind dafür deutlich stärker. Sobald Donna und Tad im Auto festsitzen, entwickelt Cujo eine wesentlich intensivere Dynamik. Die wiederholten Angriffe könnten leicht eintönig wirken, doch die zunehmende körperliche Erschöpfung und die Hitze sorgen dafür, dass sich die Situation immer weiter zuspitzt. Visuell ist der Film für seine Zeit ordentlich umgesetzt. Die Aufnahmen von Cujo funktionieren vor allem deshalb gut, weil die Inszenierung nicht permanent versucht, ihn spektakulär aussehen zu lassen. Stattdessen reicht häufig schon seine Präsenz vor dem Auto aus, um Spannung zu erzeugen. Auch die vergleichsweise zurückhaltende Darstellung von Gewalt unterstützt den realistischen Ton. Das Erzähltempo ist insgesamt etwas unausgewogen. Die erste Hälfte ist deutlich ruhiger und stärker vom Familiendrama geprägt, während die zweite Hälfte wesentlich konzentrierter auf den Überlebenskampf setzt. Dadurch fühlt sich der Film fast wie zwei unterschiedliche Geschichten an, die erst später vollständig zusammenfinden. Das Finale liefert schließlich einen intensiven Überlebenskampf und funktioniert emotional vor allem durch Donnas Entschlossenheit, ihren Sohn zu retten. Die Auflösung ist wirkungsvoll, auch wenn sie gegenüber Stephen Kings Roman verändert wurde. Fazit: Cujo ist ein atmosphärischer und teilweise sehr spannender Tierhorrorfilm, der besonders durch seine realistische Bedrohung, die klaustrophobische Auto-Situation und Dee Wallaces starke Darstellung überzeugt. Der lange Aufbau, das teilweise ausgedehnte Familiendrama und einige oberflächliche Nebenfiguren verhindern für mich eine höhere Bewertung. Sobald der eigentliche Überlebenskampf beginnt, zeigt der Film jedoch deutlich, warum er zu den bekannten Stephen-King-Verfilmungen der 1980er gehört.

É impressionante que, na época em que escreveu e lançou o livro homônimo, em 1981, Stephen King passava pelo pior momento de sua vida, quando estava viciado em álcool e cocaína. Por causa disso, o autor não se lembrava de ter escrito Cujo. Em sua autobiografia, ele revelou sentir um profundo sentimento de tristeza por não se lembrar de ter trabalhado em uma história da qual gostava muito. A inspiração para criar Cujo veio da vida real. Em 1977, a Harley-Davidson de King quebrou em uma estrada de terra no Maine. Ele levou a motocicleta até o mecânico local, que ficava em uma área isolada. Ao chegar lá, King se surpreendeu ao ver o que considerou o maior cão da raça São Bernardo que já vira na vida. Além de rosnar de maneira agressiva para King, o animal ainda tentou avançar sobre ele. Felizmente, o mecânico apareceu e acalmou o animal, que viria a ser a principal fonte de inspiração para a obra Cujo. A adaptação cinematográfica foi lançada em 1983. Dee Wallace interpreta Donna Trenton, a mãe; Danny Pintauro, Tad Trenton, o filho de cinco anos; e Daniel Hugh Kelly, Vic Trenton, o pai. O maior destaque é a performance visceral de Denise Crosby ao lado do pequeno Danny Pintauro. Destaco também o excelente trabalho com os cães utilizados para interpretar Cujo, o personagem responsável por todo o terror da história, publicada originalmente em 1981. Em "Cujo", o espectador acompanha uma história de drama sobre traição, até que o terror e o suspense tomam conta da trama. O espectador fica apreensivo e imerso no desfecho daquela mãe desesperada, que luta pela própria sobrevivência e, principalmente, pela do filho. A sensação de desespero aumenta com cada aparição do enorme cão raivoso, nojento e implacável, que continua a atacar mesmo em estado de putrefação, devido à raiva transmitida pela mordida de um morcego. Assim, o espectador experimenta um pouco do desespero da mãe e do filho diante de um cenário caótico e isolado, no qual o interior do carro é a única proteção disponível. Acredito que, devido aos seus vícios na época em que escreveu o romance de terror Cujo, King tornou a história mais sombria ao dar um final trágico para a vida do pequeno Tad Trenton. Para "consertar" esse desfecho cruel, o estúdio optou por manter o menino vivo, considerando a morte da criança uma cena muito pesada. Essa mudança foi aprovada pelo próprio King, que admitiu se arrepender de ter matado a criança na história original. Se você está procurando um filme de terror repleto de suspense, que o prenda do início ao fim, o diretor Lewis Teague oferece exatamente isso em uma adaptação cinematográfica que merece ser vista — e até mesmo revisitada. Foi o que fiz antes de escrever esta resenha.

Cujo is not really a film about a rabid dog. That is merely the skin it wears. Beneath the blood, the barking, the dust and the suffocating heat is something far more disturbing: the idea that sometimes there is no monster hiding in the darkness because the darkness has already found its way into the ordinary world. Cujo begins as something innocent. A massive, affectionate St. Bernard whose greatest crime is being a dog. Then a single bite changes everything. Rabies becomes the invisible hand reaching inside an innocent creature and turning love into instinct, loyalty into violence, and familiarity into terror. And that is what makes Cujo so fucking bleak. The dog isn't evil. There is no calculated hatred behind those eyes. No supernatural intelligence. No demonic possession. Just a living thing slowly being stripped of itself until instinct is all that remains. In a strange way, Cujo becomes a metaphor for what happens when something innocent is infected by something it never asked for. But the film doesn't stop there. Donna's crumbling marriage, Tad's childhood terror, Vic's absence, the neglected house, the oppressive summer heat everything feels like it is quietly decaying long before Cujo arrives. The dog is almost the physical manifestation of everything that has already gone wrong. And then comes the car. That fucking car becomes a coffin. Trapped inside it with her son, Donna is no longer fighting some cinematic creature that can conveniently be defeated. She's fighting exhaustion, dehydration, heat, panic and the terrifying knowledge that the thing outside only needs one mistake. The car becomes a tiny island of civilisation surrounded by something primitive. Inside: mother and child. Outside: hunger. And between them is nothing but glass. What makes the film particularly cruel is how little control its characters actually possess. There is no heroic cavalry riding over the horizon. No clever escape. No reassuring sense that the universe gives a shit whether these people survive. The world simply keeps moving. That is perhaps the darkest thing about Cujo. The horror isn't that evil exists. It's that sometimes suffering doesn't require evil at all. Sometimes tragedy is just biology, circumstance, bad timing and a series of tiny failures colliding at exactly the wrong moment. Cujo himself becomes almost tragic in the process. Somewhere beneath the blood and madness is the same dog who once wagged his tail and greeted people with affection. The creature attacking Donna is simultaneously the victim and the threat. And that makes him far more disturbing than a conventional monster. Because you can't hate him completely. You can only fear what he has become. The film's atmosphere feels like a fever dream dry, suffocating and increasingly claustrophobic. The heat isn't merely background scenery; it feels like another predator. Everything is baked, exhausted and dying. Even the silence seems to sweat. And Tad's fear gives the film another layer entirely. To a child, the world is already enormous and incomprehensible. A dark closet can become an abyss. A nightmare can become reality. Now imagine being trapped inside a car while something enormous and violent circles outside. The film understands something deeply uncomfortable about childhood: Children don't need to understand death to be terrified of it. They only need to understand that Mum might not be able to protect them. That is where Cujo sinks its teeth into something deeper than animal horror. It's about helplessness. About watching something you love deteriorate and being powerless to stop it. About the thin line separating civilisation from instinct. About how quickly the familiar can become alien. And ultimately, about survival. There is no grand philosophical explanation waiting at the end. No cosmic meaning behind what happens. Just people desperately trying to stay alive while the world closes around them. Cujo isn't frightening because he's a monster. He's frightening because he was never supposed to be one. He was someone's beloved dog. And perhaps that's the cruelest metaphor of all: Sometimes the thing that destroys you isn't born evil. Sometimes it is simply something innocent that has been infected, broken, starved, neglected or pushed beyond the point where it can recognise itself. A mother and her young son find themselves ensnared in their immobilized vehicle during a heatwave, threatened by a once-gentle St. Bernard now driven insane by rabies. This taut, surprisingly character-driven adaptation of Stephen King’s novel is anchored by a powerful performance from Dee Wallace, who infuses real emotional depth into the role of a woman already grappling with domestic pressures before the horror unfolds. Danny Pintauro is equally compelling as her terrified son, providing the film with a genuine sense of vulnerability. Director Lewis Teague maintains a tight and grounded focus, prioritizing tension over spectacle. Charles Bernstein contributes an effective, unobtrusive score that subtly heightens the film’s mounting dread without calling attention to itself. The canine effects—a combination of trained animals and practical techniques—are executed with precision, and the film never loses sight of the tragedy underlying the menace. The final act is particularly strong, functioning like a pressure cooker that relies on performance and pacing rather than shock tactics. A lean, earnest thriller that transcends its “killer dog” premise due to dedicated acting and a straightforward, no-nonsense approach. It stands out as one of the more emotionally impactful King adaptations of its time.

It's a strange film... ​At first glance, the filmmakers seem to think that the heart of the matter lies in whether the wife of the murderer has been violated or not—except they don't. Justifiably so, as they themselves declare in the movie, since that would still not make the murder permissible. Then they swerve to an after-the-fact plea of temporary insanity on the thinnest of evidence. ​The attorney (Stewart) raises smokescreen after smokescreen regarding the possible rape and the murder victim's character, offering very little to substantiate their central defense claim. This, too, his very character admits. I understand exactly what the film is doing here: it is a deliberate critique of the US legal system and juries, exposing the courtroom as a cynical game where truth takes a backseat to theatrics. ​However, while I get the point, the execution feels far too clinical. Spending nearly three hours meticulously building a courtroom drama only to conclude that the entire system is fundamentally broken—and that the truth doesn't actually matter—almost invalidates the film's own narrative. If the whole process is just an empty sham, watching it play out for that long ultimately becomes uninteresting. Because of this detachment, all the characters remain mere caricatures that we never examine more than skin deep. While the filmmakers likely intended to provoke these exact moral questions, the execution is so dry that it feels like reading a well-argued college essay—intellectually sound, perhaps, but it doesn't make for an engaging film. It's a strange film...

Enjoyable and impressively authentic-feeling courtroom drama, though at nearly three hours it did feel a little long. What I liked most was how procedural it is: you really get a sense of how a defense attorney constructs a case rather than simply uncovering “the truth.” The film never cuts away to show us what actually happened, so we are left with the same uncertainty as the lawyers and jury, weighing testimony, credibility and competing versions of events. That ambiguity is one of the film’s real strengths: the point is not that we eventually discover the truth, but that a legal judgment still has to be reached without anyone (except the accuseds) ever being completely sure of it. Some of the social attitudes are fascinatingly dated, particularly the way Lee Remick’s appearance and sexuality become part of the case. There are also some oddly broad comic touches—the dog, in particular—that felt distracting, and I could have done with less of Stewart’s fishing, law-practice troubles and the subplot involving his alcoholic colleague. The Duke Ellington score is fantastic. Jazz seems like an unlikely choice for a courtroom drama, but it gives the film a distinctive energy and is almost worth the watch by itself. A little bloated and occasionally eccentric, but intelligent, entertaining and unusually convincing.

I was pleasantly surprised by this one, I don't know that I'd agree if someone told me it's almost three hours long in a couple of days from now, it's such a captivating film that it literally feels like it goes by in absolutely no time. I went into it expecting an unforeseen plot twist a la Witness for the Prosecution, and maybe that's exactly why I was pleasantly surprised. The film takes its story seriously and immerses you into a pool of moral quandaries that are hard to get out of precisely because of one's lack of knowledge of the truth. At the same time as it shows you the many societal obstacles there are to the believability and the respectability of women's testimonies of abuse due to social prejudice even within what is supposed to be a serious legal process, it at the same time makes you question not necessarily that the story behind it might be a complete fabrication, but that the motivations for positioning such abuse at the center of it all might actually end up contributing to the further societal incarceration of the woman at the center of it all. I can definitely see why Anatomy of a Fall takes after the name of this one, and, even if I consider that one to be an even more sofisticated version of the educated paranoia that takes over the viewer purely via the uncertainty of judicial proceedings, this is still a very respectable film, one of those everyone should see at least once in their lifetime if that makes any sense.

I think this is one of the very best courtroom dramas ever put to screen. It is a complete dissection of the legal system, the people involved, the external factors, and a balance between legality and morality. A lot of films of the same genre rely on the decision of guilt or innocence to drive the narrative, but this movie is completely different. There is so much more to a case than guilt or innocence, and this movie explores it all. Court is normally presented as this place of structure, but in reality it is a game of push and pull to sway the jury to your side. It is all about theatrics to a point where the facts almost begin to take a backseat. Not only is the legal system in question, but the act itself is, as well. A case that seems so open-and-shut is never so simple. On a different note, Jimmy Stewart is Jimmy Stewart. It was an absolute pleasure to watch him play tug-of-war with George C. Scott and even Joseph Welch for almost three hours.

85/100 El cine clásico americano sobre la justicia y procesos jurídicos es increíble, me está empezando a encantar este género y claramente en Hollywood lo trataban muy bien durante la era clásica del cine. Esta película que se centra en un caso de asesinato no es una cualquiera, porque también expone ciertas circunstancias que pueden dificultar en gran medida el proceso jurídico, y que incluso por eso se pueden llegar a tomar decisiones incorrectas, haciendo que la película se sienta bastante realista. Al inicio pensé en calificarla más bajo por lo que considero el problema principal, la duración, para ser de 160 minutos, varias veces se siente que no se avanza mucho en la historia, pero pensándolo mejor, ese es uno de los principales puntos de la película, llevar a cabo un proceso jurídico casi siempre toma más tiempo del que nos gustaría. Aparte de eso, me gusta también que casi todas sus escenas sean en una corte, dando importancia de por qué en el cine antiguo era tan importante hacer tomas largas y aprovechar los escenarios, a diferencia de hoy en día, que hay constantes cambios de escena. Anatomy of a Murder forms quite an intriguing investigative drama. This confidently serves up what is perhaps the most comprehensive onscreen treatment of the judicial process. Frank matter-of-fact discussion of the main subject matter must've been quite the shock back in the "squeaky-clean" times of 1959. The counselors don't beat around the bush here. They talk about sex, rape, and murder... for lack of better terms. It's striking how relevant that particular aspect rings nowadays, especially in regard to how lawyers, officers, and judicial figures speak about women in cases involving them in any capacity. While inspired by an actual case circa 1952, the film feels ahead of its time in laying out the information to the audience. Otto Preminger's patient, level-headed direction allows what could've been melodrama to instead become a true-to-life mystery... and a fascinating mental exercise. James Stewart reliably offers yet another excellent performance. It's clever how this film plays with the trusted authority type we'd expect him to fill, notably when the trial gets heated. The ensemble cast acquits themselves superbly (no pun intended). Lee Remmick treads the line between desperate wife and seductive femme like the palm of her hand. Ben Gazzarra spiritedly lends intensity and grit into his defendant, fueling the stakes in his position. George C. Scott, Orson Bean, and Joseph N. Welch steal their scenes with such vivid presence (loud or quiet). The strength of all their performances on top of an astute script already warrants a physical media purchase. Preminger takes it further by developing an absorbing style that enables the back-and-forth to be so engaging. Charm, warmth, intrigue, and crackling dialogue foster strong interest well before the defense accepts their client. The additional layer of ambiguity kept me guessing even while I was fairly certain of how the proceedings would play out. Moreover, any viewer can read each beat, detail, and revelation differently to walk away with varying conclusions, no matter the ultimate ruling. Makes for a haunting ending that leaves a silver lining of sorts. Moody cinematography bathes in the noir aesthetic and adds considerable flair to it. Fantastic framing throughout! Some shots move in the right way at the right time, whether a gradual glide or a frantic snap. Duke Ellington delivers a ritzy jazz score that's also willing to be melancholy at points. Really dug the main menu music on the Criterion DVD, which also rules when heard in its proper context. I would advise against watching this late at night, lest you become sleepy and miss a crucial moment. Its slower burn through 2 hours and 40 minutes does accurately convey how it feels to observe a trial. Your mileage will vary there. One side character's odd detour and a couple repetitive motions stall the momentum a tad. Though I can say overall the film's a far more efficient use of time than actual jury duty. After sorting through and analyzing its intricately stitched pieces, I can attest that Anatomy of a Murder stands as a classic. Viewing several of its genre peers earlier this year (from Philadelphia to Coyote vs. Acme ) may have diluted the impact for me. Nonetheless, it's an excellent picture bearing esteemed influence.

La película judicial por excelencia; casi tres horas de duración que no se sienten en ningún momento, donde el guion y las actuaciones lo son todo, cómo se nos va revelando cada cosa para luego usarla en el caso y aun así sorprendernos como a los del jurado, una maestría que pocas veces hemos visto en este género. Quizás no tiene las revelaciones más impactantes de la historia, pero sí uno de los mejores ritmos y guiones en la historia del cine. James Stewart la rompe con, posiblemente, la mejor actuación que le haya visto. Tiene un ritmo fabuloso que se divide claramente en dos: una primera parte recolectando los datos para el caso y conociendo a los personajes, y la segunda con todo el juicio, donde todos los datos y revelaciones que vimos se presentan en la corte. Lo mejor de todo es que logra sorprendernos a pesar de que ya sabemos todo lo que pasó en el asesinato. ¿Y saben qué es lo mejor de todo? Su final tan poético, que critica la basura del sistema judicial. Realmente es uno de esos clásicos del cine que envejecieron como el vino. Como casi todos los clásicos (en mi opinión), ha habido películas del mismo género que han sabido llevar de mejor manera el género en el futuro. Aun así, no podemos olvidar de dónde salieron y sus orígenes. Claramente, Anatomy of a Murder es una de las pioneras. Tremendo clásico del cine que tienen que ver mínimo una vez en la vida, sí o sí.

From Duke Ellington's sizzling noir soundtrack to James Stewart's magnetically folksy demeanor, Anatomy of a Murder has the components to make a legendary motion picture. Despite the big stars, Otto Preminger, led by Wendell Mayes' rollicking screenplay, gives us something darker, critical, yet exquisitely amoral. Anatomy of a Murder does not attempt to proselytize the virtues or failures of the justice system. Instead it parses out the strategies of a defense, accounts for the varying elements relating to unpredictable human personalities and emotion, presentation of the facts and witnesses, and ultimately leads us to Platonic conclusion of how rhetorical, rather than logical, the American legal system actually is. The movie is not intended to make you feel resolved, and the lingering ambiguities remain as mysterious and subject to conjecture as Laura Manion's heeled shoe found in the trash can. Despite the somewhat dreary outlook, the movie is led by a small-town charismatic lawyer Paul Biegler, played by James Stewart, who uplifts the audience through his character's devotion and cunning. Biegler is a realist, but he's not a pessimist. Sure, he is jaded, having lost his re-election bid for district attorney, and a bit resigned, spending his time fishing and playing piano. But he is far from unmotivated. With a witty tongue and laid-back personality, he seems unshaken through most of the film, openly recognizing the weaknesses and strengths of the facts of the case and accounting for the minute factors that tarnish the supposedly fair legal process. His character, along with his steadfast secretary Maida Rutledge and barely sober but loveable Parnell McCarthy, provide a sense of light in the gray. His client, Frederick "Manny" Manion, is recalcitrant and short-tempered. Accused of murdering Barney Quill for allegedly raping his wife, his blatant jealousy and violent acts in the jail do not help the audience believe Manny was justified. Nor would it convince the jury in the film. Manny's wife Laura Manion does not help the picture: for the standards of that time, she is considered a flirty woman who wears her clothing too tight. Biegler is cognizant of how these issues can affect his case. Biegler counsels Laura to dress modestly, not necessarily because he thinks Laura's fashion has anything to do with the murder, but because he knows how this can come off to a problematic, prejudicial jury. What is most intriguing is that Biegler does not seem to care whether Manny was justified and continues to walk a thin ethical line regarding witness coaching. Biegler inveigles Manny into the irrestible impulse defense, not because it is necessarily true, but because it is the only real legal defense available. However, Biegler's sly witness preparation tactics are fire against the procesecution's fire. For example, Claude Dancer insinuates a false narrative regarding an affair between Quill and Laura, something that even if struck from the record, will not be erased from the jury's mind. The matter of rape becomes a part of deliberations, essential to the defense. But evidence, like torn panties, are hotly scrutinized in cross examinations by Dancer. Biegler's courtroom theatrics and fiery objections are matched by Dancer's intensely hostile methods, resulting in a messy, explosive trial. The movie's climax is a stroke of luck more than it is a recognition of good method. Biegler pulls a hail-mary good-faith witness, (a trope that later became common in these types of exuberant legal dramas). Biegler's only power is persuasion: persuading the judge to overcome the often arbitrary legal obstacles; persuading the witnesses to say and do the right thing; persuading the the easily emotionally manipulated jury prone to the prosecution's smokescreens. The turn at the end demonstrates how many factors can be out of your control at trial when all persuasion has been exhausted. Beigler did all he could. He could only pray thereafter. The movie, although morally gray, ends on a light note. Biegler finds Laura's heel among the rubbish, suggesting her and Manny left in a hurry before they had to pay the lawyer's fees. Manny is concretely imperfect: he's an angry, jealous, violent, dishonest person who ditches his obligations. However, it does not seem fair to have seen him behind bars for Quill's murder. The audience is prone to celebration with the defense. And ironically, Biegler is retained by Pilant to execute Quill's estate, bringing some hope that a private practice has now been established. Despite being ethically questionable as an attorney, Biegler is rewarded. I am not bothered by this. I believe Preminger intended to show, objectively, how imperfect the legal process can be. It is subject to partial authorities, discrimination, and emotional appeal. In many cases, only by pushing the limits of the practice can an attorney triumph against the odds. The boundaries between zealous advocacy and guile are blurred.

Chinatown is a beautifully made and highly respected neo-noir mystery, but personally, it didn't work for me. The film follows private detective J.J. “Jake” Gittes as he investigates what initially appears to be a simple case involving a wealthy Los Angeles family. The mystery gradually becomes much darker and more complicated. There is no doubt that the filmmaking is excellent. Roman Polanski creates a fantastic noir atmosphere, the cinematography is beautiful, and Robert Towne's screenplay is considered one of the great screenplays of American cinema. Jack Nicholson is also excellent as Jake Gittes. His performance has plenty of charm and personality, and he fits the private-detective role perfectly. Faye Dunaway is also strong, particularly as the mystery surrounding Evelyn Mulwray becomes increasingly complicated. But despite all that... I was bored. 😭 The pacing is simply too slow for my taste. The investigation takes a long time to develop, and many of the conversations and discoveries didn't keep me interested enough. The mystery itself is complicated, but for me, complicated didn't necessarily mean engaging. There were moments where I was more interested in seeing the movie finish than finding out what happened. The film's atmosphere is impressive, but atmosphere alone isn't enough to make me enjoy a movie. The story also becomes increasingly dark and disturbing, especially towards the end. I can appreciate what the filmmakers were trying to achieve, but emotionally I never connected with it. The ending is undeniably powerful and tragic, and I understand why it is so highly regarded. But again, respecting a film and enjoying a film are two different things. Chinatown clearly has enormous influence and technical quality. It simply isn't my kind of movie. Overall, Chinatown is a technically brilliant and historically important neo-noir, elevated by Jack Nicholson, Faye Dunaway and an excellent screenplay, but its slow pacing and style made it a boring and unenjoyable experience for me. A great film for many people — just absolutely not my cup of tea. 🖤🎬

Ele consegue resolver o caso principal; contudo, sua expressão ao final revela que permeia uma complexidade e uma estruturação política que não podem ser alteradas. Essa fragilidade de tentar mudar algo muito maior que você é o ápice de Chinatown. Aquela região em que nunca se espera algo pior, e quando o pior chega, você já entra em conformidade, é o jeito como Jake e todos lidam com a impotência. Só desgosto que é muito demorado para que essa cadeia de acontecimentos se forme.

Good noir: Intellectually great, emotionally distant This was my first time watching Chinatown, and honestly, the thing that pulled me in the most wasn't the mystery, it was the vibe. The world-building is incredible: the clothes, the cars, the quiet jazz, the heat of 1930s Los Angeles, the backyard scenes, the hats, all of it. Jack Nicholson has this classy, effortless presence, and the film's whole aesthetic feels timeless. Great performance by Faye Dunaway too. But the movie itself is emotionally cold. It's a slow burn, and for most of the runtime, I felt like the film kept a distance from me. The message and themes are definitely strong, but for me, they don't fully hit until the final scene, and that's where I had a mixed reaction. It almost feels like the entire movie was built for that final moment, where everything becomes very obviously "noir" and you see the system's corruption laid out. But the thing is: even without that last scene, I already sensed the corruption throughout the film. It's implicit. It's in the world, the tone, the dialogue. So the movie didn't need to rely so heavily on that final punch for me to understand what it was doing. And maybe that's because we watch the film from a third-person perspective. We see signs of the system's rot throughout the story, long before the main character truly realizes it. If I were in the detective's shoes -if I were seeing things only through his head- it would probably feel more engaging and shocking step by step. But as viewers, we catch the overall darkness earlier, which made the ending feel powerful but also slightly predictable in feeling, even if not in plot. So overall, I loved the atmosphere and the classic detective tone, but emotionally it didn't grip me the same way other classics do. Chinatown doesn't grip emotionally at all. It's more observational. More philosophical. You're meant to watch the world and its corruption, not get pulled into the characters' inner lives.

On my recent movie arc, a natural fulcrum point that you reach is whether the classics are worth visiting. Are you watching them because you'll think you'll like them or because movie buffs say you should like them so you HAVE to watch them? I've never been a huge fan of classical acting, a bane that plagues me with movies from the 40s all the way to the 80s. The style is very different and while understandable and appeals to some, I usually find it to date movies too much, it's dramatic in a more theatrical way. As ironic as it sounds I prefer movies that are a little less theatrical with their character portrayals. I prefer more realistic/grounded performances you find in modern acting or performances that are less like caricatures and more like the person they're supposed to be. But times were different, in bygone times of film-making people weren't looking for relatable they were looking for better versions of themselves. A detective that always has the perfect quip, a damsel in distress that is beautiful but sassy but also mysterious!? While I say all of that, I can't help but notice the bright spots in older movies that shine through every time I watch them. Old movies are time capsules of the past that allow you to see the origins of where the modern films you love came from; their humble beginnings. With little experience with Noir films of the 40s, 50s and 60s its easy for me to overlook just exactly HOW revolutionary this movie was for the genre at the time of its release. How purposefully theatrical the acting was and how much it used plot devices from these films and then subverted them or expanded upon them. Looking at it through that lens, everything started to click for me, and the biggest thing I noticed is that Jake Gittes isn't the typical noir detective he's actually a flawed man that fails to see the dark corners of the world and our "femme fatale" is actually a traumatized woman and a victim of those same dark corners. This movie is THE quintessential Noir film for me. It wears the influences of its predecessors on its sleeve while also influencing decades of films to follow. While carrying out the tropes you typically see in these movies, it, at least at the time, had an ending that made stomachs churn in defeat at the hopelessness that it leaves you with.  I can confirm that never having been spoiled, for me it had the same effect. It follows an intriguing mystery, that at parts is cliche but also provides nuance in strange places. The acting is great, despite my biases towards modern acting (it took me some getting used to). The shots were innovative for the time and its layered with thick metaphors to the corrupt vs life on the surface throughout. AND nearly every scene has a double-meaning or a callback for later. I was thoroughly engaged and it accomplished what I hope to see in any watching of a classic movie according to critics. It MADE SENSE why this movie was influential and considered a classic. Has the formula been improved upon since this film? Probably. Is it dated and completely different from a Noir film that would be made today? Yes.... I mean, noir as a genre itself is dated. BUT! Did I enjoy myself with this film? HELL YEAH! That's all I can ask for, and in my surprise of how much I enjoyed this movie I sometimes caught myself stopping to appreciate what it did at the time it came out. The fact that i'm a big Jack Nicholson fan also helped a tremendous amount.
The phrase "Forget it, Jake, it's Chinatown" is just a cinematic way of saying "The winner takes it all. The loser has to fall." It will be a great TikTok edit with the ending and the song.

THE TRUTH WAS NEVER ENOUGH. Chinatown è uno di quei noir che riescono a essere molto più di un semplice mistero da risolvere. Polanski parte da una storia apparentemente classica, fatta di tradimenti, ricatti e segreti, e costruisce lentamente un mondo in cui ogni risposta apre una porta su qualcosa di molto più grande. Jake Gittes è un detective convinto di sapere come muoversi in quel mondo. È intelligente, sicuro di sé e abituato a pensare di poter arrivare alla verità prima degli altri. Ma più si addentra nella vicenda, più si accorge che non tutto può essere controllato. Dietro il caso ci sono il potere, il denaro, l’acqua e una Los Angeles che sotto la sua superficie luminosa nasconde una realtà molto più sporca. E forse è proprio qui che il film mi ha convinto di più. Gittes non è l’eroe che arriva, risolve il caso e rimette tutto al proprio posto. Fa quello che può, arriva alla verità e prova persino a cambiare il destino di Evelyn. Ma conoscere la verità non significa necessariamente avere il potere di cambiarla. Il finale, per questo, è devastante proprio nella sua semplicità. Non cancella ciò che Gittes ha scoperto: gli mostra semplicemente quanto poco possa bastare, a volte, per fermare qualcosa che è ormai molto più grande di lui. “Forget it, Jake. It’s Chinatown.” Un noir elegantissimo e amarissimo, costruito con una precisione quasi perfetta e capace di lasciare addosso quella rara sensazione di aver assistito a una tragedia che, una volta iniziata, forse non poteva più avere un finale diverso.

El estreno de Chinatown en 1974 no sólo consagró a Roman Polanski, Jack Nicholson y Robert Towne, sino que transformó para siempre el cine policíaco. Es una de esas películas en las que todo parece ocupar exactamente el lugar que debe: el guion, los personajes, la fotografía, la música, la ambientación y, sobre todo, una concepción del mundo profundamente pesimista. No es casualidad que apareciera precisamente en 1974. Estados Unidos atravesaba una profunda crisis de confianza en sus instituciones. Watergate acababa de llevar a Nixon a la dimisión y Vietnam había dejado una enorme sensación de fracaso y desengaño. Chinatown recoge ese clima y lo convierte en ficción: aquí la corrupción no se encuentra en los bajos fondos, sino en las estructuras mismas del poder. Noah Cross no es simplemente un criminal; es un hombre integrado en el sistema, rico, respetado y prácticamente intocable. La película pertenece además, de lleno al Nuevo Hollywood, aquel cine de los setenta que empezó a desconfiar de los finales tranquilizadores y de la justicia poética. Y pocas películas llevaron esa desconfianza tan lejos. Jake Gittes investiga porque cree que, como detective, descubrir la verdad significa acercarse a una solución. Pero cada respuesta sólo abre una nueva puerta hacia algo peor. Su investigación no consigue restablecer el orden: consigue demostrar que el orden ya estaba podrido. El guión de Robert Towne es extraordinario precisamente por esa manera de hacer crecer el misterio. Lo que comienza como un caso aparentemente relacionado con la gestión del agua de Los Ángeles termina conectando corrupción política, intereses económicos y una tragedia familiar monstruosa. La investigación funciona simultáneamente como thriller y como descenso moral: cuanto más sabe Jake, menos capaz es de controlar las consecuencias de aquello que descubre. Y Polanski entiende perfectamente que ese mundo debe estar filmado bajo una luz completamente distinta a la del noir clásico. Chinatown utiliza el color, el Panavision y el sol abrasador de Los Ángeles para construir un auténtico noir a plena luz del día. No necesitamos callejones oscuros ni lluvia para encontrar la podredumbre. Está delante de nosotros, perfectamente iluminada, escondida detrás de mansiones, oficinas, piscinas y hombres respetables. Jack Nicholson está magnífico como Jake Gittes. Su detective conserva el cinismo, el ingenio y la arrogancia del protagonista clásico, pero Polanski le quita la seguridad de saber que al final podrá arreglar las cosas. Jake puede descubrir la verdad, pero no puede controlar el mundo en el que esa verdad existe. Y ahí está una de las grandes diferencias con el detective del cine negro tradicional: no fracasa porque no haya sido suficientemente inteligente, sino porque se enfrenta a un poder que está fuera de su alcance. Faye Dunaway convierte a Evelyn Mulwray en algo mucho más complejo que una femme fatale convencional. Parece inicialmente sospechosa, pero poco a poco comprendemos que ella también es una víctima. El verdadero poder no está en la mujer misteriosa que oculta secretos, sino en el hombre que posee los recursos para decidir qué secretos pueden salir a la luz y cuáles permanecerán enterrados. Y entonces llega ese final. Polanski decidió mantener un desenlace mucho más cruel que el que originalmente imaginaba Towne, y la decisión resulta fundamental para la película. Evelyn muere, Cross consigue lo que quiere y Jake sólo puede contemplar cómo todo aquello que había intentado evitar sucede delante de él. La investigación ha sido correcta; sus conclusiones también. Lo que resulta inútil es pensar que conocer la verdad basta para que exista justicia. “Olvídalo, Jake. Es Chinatown.” Pocas frases resumen con tanta precisión una película. Chinatown no es únicamente un lugar: es una forma de entender el mundo. Un territorio donde las buenas intenciones, la inteligencia y el esfuerzo individual pueden resultar completamente insuficientes frente a estructuras de poder mucho más grandes. Por eso considero que Chinatown no sólo es una obra maestra del cine negro, sino una de las grandes películas sobre la impotencia del individuo frente al poder. Toma todos los elementos del noir clásico —el detective privado, la mujer misteriosa, la corrupción, la investigación, la ciudad— y los conserva para después destruir las expectativas que llevaban asociadas. El detective no salva a nadie. La víctima no obtiene justicia. El culpable no recibe su castigo. Y descubrir la verdad no cambia absolutamente nada. Ese pesimismo, unido a una puesta en escena de una precisión extraordinaria, convierte Chinatown en una película prácticamente perfecta. Un misterio criminal que termina siendo algo mucho más oscuro: el descubrimiento de que, en determinados lugares, la verdad puede ser perfectamente conocida y seguir siendo completamente inútil.

Era uno de los grandes clásicos del cine negro que todavía tenía pendiente de ver, y la verdad es que no me ha decepcionado. Roman Polanski hace un trabajazo en la dirección. Me gusta mucho cómo va construyendo la historia poco a poco, haciendo que el misterio vaya creciendo a medida que avanza la película. Además, los planos y la puesta en escena ayudan muchísimo a crear esa sensación de tensión e incomodidad que está presente durante prácticamente toda la película. La ambientación de Los Ángeles de los años 30 también me parece increíble y le da a la película una personalidad enorme. La interpretación de Jack Nicholson es sobresaliente. Su personaje, Jake. J. Gittes, tiene muchísimo carisma, pero también es bastante cínico y arrogante, y creo que Nicholson consigue transmitir muy bien todas esas facetas. Si no me equivoco, este fue uno de sus primeros papeles realmente importantes en Hollywood, y demostró que podía llevar perfectamente el peso de una película. Y ese final... Uff. Creo que es casi lo mejor de la película. Me parece un cierre brutal, tanto por lo que ocurre como por la forma en la que está planteado. Es de esos finales que hacen que, cuando terminan los créditos, te quedes unos minutos pensando en lo que acabas de ver. Lo dicho, creo que Chinatown es una de las mejores películas policíacas y de cine negro que he visto. Tiene una historia muy bien construida, una atmósfera increíble y un final difícil de olvidar. Una auténtica joya que recomiendo muchísimo. 👌

O filme logo de início te força a pensar que Summer é uma garota ingrata, que consegue as coisas de forma mais fácil e desapega de tudo facilmente (o que não seria ruim, até certo ponto se não fosse a a forma como o assunto é abordado). Achei tendencioso colocarem dessa forma desde o começo, me incomodou. Pareceu mesmo que o diretor tinha algum problema passado mal resolvido com os próprios sentimentos em relação às mulheres. É uma perspectiva bem machista pôr o protagonista como um santo, sendo um homem adulto. O que na verdade era pra me forçar a acreditar na narrativa da mulher monstruosa manipuladora na verdade me fez entender que esse cara é maluco com força. A lenda além de machista (porque só sabia objetificar a Summer), teve a coragem de chamar isso de amor. Ele é egoísta ao ponto de achar que a ela é obrigada a gostar e ficar com ele (nada muito diferente de vários homens por aí). A frase famosa que ele cita estar apaixonado é mais horrorosa ainda, porque ele só sabe citar partes do corpo dela. Piora depois, quando ele tenta justificar ambos serem almas gêmeas por gostarem de uma porra de um prato de comida. A criança que Tom desabafa boa parte do filme consegue ser mais madura que esse doente. Não é muito diferente de um heterotop, a diferença é que ele se faz de coitado pra chamar a atenção. Um dos amigos próximos dele, quase que de forma simbiótica, também não é coisa boa. É possível reparar isso na cena do restaurante, onde ocorre o encontro comemorativo da equipe de trabalho. O filme tem uma pegada muito boba, eu esperava mais. Romance e comédia? isso sim que é uma piada. E porra, do nada um MUSICAL? Era só o que me faltava. QUE TORTURA. E eu finalmente entendi de onde vem a frase mongoloide que um monte de homem usa sobre tatuagem de borboleta. Sério isso? KKKKKKKKKKKK Não gostei do enredo, não gostei dos personagens, não gostei de nada nessa porra. Chamaria de terror não pelo relacionamento falido, mas sim pelo filme ser uma completa bosta. MEU VEREDICTO: Summer não é um monstro nem algo do tipo, foi babaca em alguns momentos sim, mas ela é resolvida emocionalmente. Ela sempre disse as intenções dela desde o começo do filme. Ninguém tá errado por buscar uma relação casual, mesmo que com dúvidas, principalmente quando é deixado bem claro desde o início. Errado foi o Tom por criar muitas expectativas e depois de ter concordado com a relação, culpar o amor e incomodar os outros com suas próprias mágoas. O amor não é culpado por isso. Muito homem critica o filme porque a situação se passa a favor da Summer, uma mulher. Se fosse o Tom com intenções casuais, não teria gerado esse burburinho todo. ''Não existe essa coisa de destino. Nada é para ser'' Nota: Esse filme foi muito estressante de assistir. Só assisti até o fim pra poder trazer uma opinião com embasamento entre extensas aspas porque afinal toda opinião não é imparcial. Não recomendo que ninguém assista.

Like if Harry met Sally but there's no Sally and Harry was kind of a loser. Really that's the main bone I have to pick with this — the guy kinda sucks and everything revolves around him. His loser friends, his faux-precocious younger sister, his boss, his co-workers, and most importantly, Summer, all orbit him and have seemingly no life of their own. Every word they say or action they take is a reaction to Tom's behaviour — or if it isn't it goes brazenly unexplained. Why is Summer so commitment-shy and avoidant? There must be some thing there, some semblance of personal history that we're just not getting a god damn hint of. She tells him of her past boyfriends (played for laughs), she cries at the ending of the graduate (getting there, but you still end up asking why ?), and that's as close as we get to seeing who she is as a person. As an individual. The other thing though is that I don't mind some of what's done here. I laughed out loud a few times at the beginning — there really is some fun to be had, especially when the interests of the main guy are tailored almost a little too specifically to yours. But fuckin' christ Marc Webb, really? Summer's basically a cardboard cutout for your fantasies to get sketched onto, dude. She's not exactly manic, nor very pixie — and even though she is girl (Zooeyy Deschanelll! He llo!) she's mostly dream. The character trait of adamantly defending Ringo Starr as her favourite beatle is some shit I'd come up with in 20 minutes on a throwaway daydream, dude, like c'mon. Put me in a boring two hour lecture and I could whip up some wayyy better shit. Some shit that puts a dumb ass smile on my face. But that's not the point the point is that I'm also kind of a loser and when I put on a rom-com I don't want to see some shit I can outclass in a daydream I want to see real people (♪ and I want to see [real] liiife ♪) that are grounded in their own unique lived experiences and who share their thoughts and opinions and feelings between each other — I want to see people with flaws that are given reason to, I want to see people who both act and react in equal amounts. Or at least I want to see Nora Ephron's name on the writing credits, cause otherwise the com isn't gonna cover up for the rom. Speakin' of the com, which I said I kinda liked before, it actually kinda sucks balls. A lot of it's referential. And that's okay, y'know. But it's just a little too referential. Like you're standing on the shoulders of giants and you feel the need to point that out, and not only point it out but make pointing it out be a large part of what you're bringing to the table? You don't need to be giant, of course, but when you can't be bothered to try and make something feel big or original in your own movie — that's when the nods start to grate on me. I will say the ending is actually really cute but I'm staying strong on this rating. I kept wanting it to be over the longer it went on, and while I'd like to say it was neither here nor there, it leaned towards the there just that tiny, unjustifiable bit more. I mean, fuck me. That Thomas fuckin' Hansen of all guys has to be the poster boy for The Smiths in the modern zeitgeist is nothing short of a tragedy. All that being said, if thirteen year-old me had ever gotten my hands on this I would have fallen completely and absolutely head over heels. What that spells out for the quality of the film, well... take that as you will. Also who's gonna tell him there's only like 365 days in a year what the fuck do you mean 500 days of summer that's like astronomically impossible.

Eu não acho que esse é um tipo de filme que eu amo. Desde o início já sabemos que “esta é a história de um rapaz que conhece uma garota. Mas você deve saber logo, esta não é uma história de amor.” Antes de assistir o filme eu via algumas pessoas comentando sobre a Summer, ser uma menina chata, irritante… e no começo não pensei assim, mas no decorrer da história não fiquei com raiva apenas dela, mas do Tom também. Ambos os lados trazem algo meio tóxico pra história. Do lado do Tom vemos um personagem que vive com extremos, para ele ou é tudo ou nada, mesmo ele tentando disfarçar percebemos que essa relação o incomoda justamente por ele não saber o que exatamente a Summer quer, ou até onde isso vai chegar. Além disso, ele não quer desistir dessa relação e ele não respeita o fato de que ela não o ama: “I don’t want to get over her. I want to get her back.” Por outro lado vemos a Summer, que ao mesmo tempo que deixa claro desde o início que não quer nada sério foi quem levantou as expectativas. Ela que beijou ele na sala das cópias, por exemplo. A questão é, no fim eu fiquei igual ao Tom, meio incrédula, porque como ele mesmo disse: “You never wanted to be anybody’s girlfriend, and now you’re somebody’s wife.” O que nos leva a pensar, ela não queria um namorado, ou não queria o Tom? E a resposta é óbvia, ela não queria o Tom.

Rewatched this for probably the tenth time and it still gets me in a completely different way each time depending on where I am in life. It's such a sharp, unsentimental look at how we construct narratives around people — Tom isn't wrong to feel what he feels, but the film is smart enough to know he's wrong about her, and it never lets him (or us) off the hook for that. The nonlinear structure isn't just a gimmick, it mirrors exactly how memory actually works when you're picking apart a relationship after the fact — the good days bleeding into the bad ones out of order. Zooey Deschanel and Joseph Gordon-Levitt are so good at playing two people who are compatible in every way except the one that matters. The "expectations vs. reality" split-screen sequence is one of my favorite pieces of editing in any romantic film, and the ending earns its optimism without undoing anything the rest of the movie built. A perfect, quietly devastating little movie about the lies we tell ourselves when we're falling for someone.

This is my 4th time watching 500 Days of Summer this year. Of course I’m writing one long ass review again because somehow I always feel the need to write at length about it. I have come to have a quite intimate relationship with this film, maybe more than with any other I’ve ever seen. I just love everything about it and I think it’s a rather underrated cinematic gem. I know it’s a very popular film but I don’t think it receives the appreciation it deserves. For a long time I understood Tom and I related to him, and although I can now see everything with a lot more nuance than I did the first time around, I don’t think he’s the villain, as most people would say. I think that this is the usual progression of someone who watches this multiple times. The first time around you side with Tom, the second time around you see it a bit differently and side with Summer, but then, if you get to rewatch it multiple times, over and over again, you’ll realise that that’s the wrong way of watching it. This film isn’t about Tom or Summer being wrong, although I understand how easily one can fall into that trap. None of them are wrong. They are just… human. They are normal people who are complex and complicated and intricate, as the average human usually is. They both make mistakes and they both fail at truly connecting, but that’s just the reality of relationships. They are, most of the time, messy, complicated and hurtful. It’s hard wanting love and giving or receiving it. It’s not as easy as they show us in the media. I think that the whole discourse around Tom seeing Summer as a manic pixie dream girl is actually telling about most of us. Maybe we don’t want to admit it but we would all like meeting the perfect person that will complete us, the person that will choose us no matter what and who will be easy to love and who’ll basically remain an idea. And of course we don’t feel good when we find out that there’s no manic pixie dream girl or prince charming that’ll be everything we wanted and will love us unconditionally. This idea of perfect romance is so ingrained in our minds that we can’t actually differentiate anymore between what an authentic human connection looks like in reality and how it is portrayed in the movies. When talking about dream partners, Paul says that his wife, Robyn, is better than any dream girl, because she’s real. And I think that accepting the real is a very hard thing to do. We tend to idealise people to some extent and project our fantasies onto them and we stray from the person that’s actually in front of us. Loving someone is not always easy, and your boyfriend or girlfriend will not always live up to the idea you have of them. And you’ll think they’re not the right person, when in reality they might be, but you just prefer the idea you created in your head over what’s right in front of you. We’ve become so obsessed with the idea of a perfect partner that we forget how imperfect and flawed we are. And I think one of the reasons behind this is that we are really hurt and we want to be saved. We want to be chosen and we want to feel like we matter. We want love because everything always leads back to it. It sounds cliche but everything is always about the same thing over and over again. It might not be the best thing that we as people revolve our existence around, but we don’t really get a say in it. For better or for worse, this is what we have to deal with, and Tom and Summer’s story might be someone’s real story. Relationships can look like that and it’s normal, although painful. As I’ve said before, I don’t think there’s someone who’s right or wrong in this film. During their conversation in the car scene, a song by Carla Bruni plays on the radio, while we can hear these exact verses in French: “I am told that destiny is making fun of us. That it doesn’t give us anything and promises everything. It appears that happiness is within reach. So we reach out and we end up going crazy.” I think this sums up Tom’s and Summer’s dynamic. They’re fragile people who both want love, although they approach love differently, either obsessing over it or running from it. One of the saddest scenes in the film, personally, is the opening scene with the montage of them as kids, while Regina Spektor’s “Us” plays in the background. I find it very poignant because it makes me think how both of them were those two little kids, full of hope and happiness and waiting to see all the beauty that the world can bring, and their life experiences sadly led them to defend themselves against relationships with other people one way or another. Who could break those kids’ hearts by telling them what their future will look like? It’s just sad and there’s nothing more to be said about it. I find Summer’s story particularly sad, or rather the way she ended up approaching love, because we don’t learn much about her. I encountered a lot of people with avoidant attachment styles and I had not so nice experiences with some of them, and I didn’t manage to ever understand why they are the way they are, but right now I’ve come to a place where it saddens me. It saddens me to think of these people as kids that went through some experiences that made them develop this strategy of running away from relationships and love in order to stay safe. How heartbreaking is that? After all, both anxious and avoidant people want love deep down. They just learned different ways to protect themselves from disappointment, and although I’m more of an anxious person (although I have some avoidant traits too), I think that the avoidants’ story is more tragic and more poignant. But I think it’s sad in general that life makes us go through all these painful things and we end up developing these defensive strategies that prevent us from being able to connect with other people that maybe truly care about us. Although Tom’s and Summer’s story is not really a love story, maybe it could’ve been in other circumstances. I have some thoughts about the ending too, but I’ll leave that for my next rewatch.

Assisti a (500) Dias com Ela com zero expectativas. Achava que seria insuportável, só mais um filme de romance dos anos 2000 dos Estados Unidos igual a tantos outros, e que eu nem conseguiria terminar. No fim, acabei assistindo a uma obra-prima. Dei 5/5 e, sinceramente, o filme atingiu qualquer expectativa que eu nem tinha imposto e até mais. Impressionante. Tom e Summer são extremamente tóxicos um para o outro, embora de maneiras diferentes. Isso não significa que eu tenha odiado a dinâmica entre eles; algumas atitudes me incomodaram, principalmente porque os dois conseguem ser muito babacas, mas isso faz parte da construção dos personagens e da relação. Principalmente o Tom. As conversas dele com os amigos são extremamente machistas, misóginas e babacas, e eu odiava essas cenas. Fico até na dúvida se isso foi proposital para mostrar o verdadeiro lado do Tom, deixando claro que ele só gostava da Summer quando ela era conveniente para ele e para a visão que tinha dela, ou se ele simplesmente era um babaca covarde cercado de amigos babacas. Desde o início, Summer fala que não quer um relacionamento. Tom, mesmo sabendo disso, fica com ela porque tem certeza de que ela vai mudar de ideia depois, porque vai se apaixonar por ele. Ele cria expectativas porque quer e depois se machuca porque elas não correspondem à realidade. Ele escolheu ignorar o que ela estabeleceu desde o começo e, mesmo assim, age como se tivesse sido injustiçado. Isso fica muito claro depois da briga no bar, quando ele grita com ela e joga coisas na casa dela porque Summer agiu de acordo com aquilo que havia sido estabelecido entre os dois. Ele não consegue aceitar que a relação não é aquilo que imaginava e desconta a frustração nela. E o pior é que, depois disso, Summer ainda vai pedir desculpas, quando ela estava certa em ficar com raiva porque Tom bateu em um cara para “defender” ela. Ela estava literalmente certa naquela situação. Ela não deveria ter que se sentir culpada por estabelecer limites e ficar com raiva quando eles são ultrapassados, muito menos ele deveria receber toda essa compreensão por ter se machucado justamente porque escolheu ignorar esses limites. Isso também mostra como Tom não sabe receber um “não”. Quando acha que Summer não vai querer sair com ele no início, ele imediatamente começa a chamá-la de esnobe, babaca, alguém que só tem um rostinho bonito e acha que é melhor que os outros. É como se, no momento em que ela não corresponde ao que ele quer, ele precisasse transformar isso em um defeito dela. E acho que o maior problema de Tom é justamente esse: ele não gostava da Summer por quem ela realmente era, mas pelas expectativas que tinha sobre ela. Ele criou uma versão perfeita dela na cabeça e passou a se relacionar com essa versão, ignorando tudo aquilo que ela estabelecia quando não correspondia ao que ele queria. Não é culpa dela não ser quem ele imaginou que fosse. Isso fica ainda mais interessante porque Tom é o narrador, e ele não é confiável. A história é contada pela perspectiva dele, então Summer é apresentada quase como a vilã que destruiu seu coração, enquanto, quando você olha além da visão dele, percebe que ela é uma personagem muito mais complexa. A atuação da atriz da Summer, porém, me incomodou MUITO. Eu odiei CADA segundo da atuação dela em tela. Não sei se foi uma escolha de atuação que eu simplesmente não entendi, se foi a dubladora ou se ela realmente atuou muito mal, mas parecia que estava interpretando uma psicopata. Ela quase não demonstrava emoção, fazia umas caras estranhas ou simplesmente nenhuma expressão para determinadas situações. Sorria, fazia cara séria ou ficava com a cara normal, e isso não ajudou em nada a simpatizar com ela, principalmente porque o narrador é o Tom e ele já apresenta Summer de uma maneira pouco favorável. Em alguns momentos, inclusive, ela me lembrou a atuação da Gal Gadot em Mulher-Maravilha, mas pode simplesmente ser uma impressão minha. Mesmo assim, dá para perceber que Summer é uma personagem muito mais complexa do que a visão do Tom faz parecer. E ela também é babaca em vários momentos. Não é simplesmente que ela não queria nada sério: ela não queria nada sério com ELE. Ela nunca teve certeza sobre o que sentia, enquanto Tom sempre teve certeza demais sobre o que ela deveria sentir. Isso fica muito claro quando ela dança com ele mesmo sabendo que ele ainda gostava dela e que ela já estava comprometida, sabendo que aquilo só faria ainda mais mal para ele. Depois, quando ele questiona por que ela fez aquilo, ela simplesmente diz que estava a fim. Quanta falta de consideração com ele. Ela vivia alimentando os sentimentos dele mesmo sabendo que eles não eram recíprocos, então também era extremamente tóxica com ele. Mas Summer nunca pediu para Tom enxergá-la como uma pessoa perfeita. Essa imagem foi criada por ele. Quando ele fala que nunca vai entender por que ela fez aquilo e que não fazia o menor sentido, na verdade faz sentido. Ela não é perfeita. Ela é complexa, contraditória e também é babaca. Ela tem seus motivos para fazer as coisas, mas isso não significa que todas as atitudes dela sejam certas. No fim, os dois são péssimos um para o outro. Tom não consegue enxergar Summer como ela realmente é e insiste em transformar a relação naquilo que gostaria que ela fosse, enquanto Summer também toma atitudes que alimentam os sentimentos dele mesmo sabendo que não sente o mesmo. Eles se machucam, não conseguem se entender e têm expectativas completamente diferentes sobre aquela relação. Não é que um seja o vilão e o outro a vítima: eles simplesmente nunca funcionariam juntos. E o filme deixa indícios disso desde o início. Naquela cena da loja, em que existe a indicação de que aquilo é apenas uma fantasia, já existe uma pista de que Tom está enxergando aquela relação através daquilo que imagina que ela deveria ser. O relacionamento deles já parecia fadado ao fracasso. Tudo isso fica ainda melhor por causa da estética do filme. O contraste de cores é simplesmente genial, um espetáculo. O conceito da estética, a trilha sonora e a forma como o filme apresenta a história são brilhantes. Tudo tem uma identidade muito própria e contribui para a maneira como a narrativa funciona. E o final é simplesmente perfeito. A frase que Tom fala no início sobre como você vai saber quando for amor não é apenas uma frase que o filme retoma no final: o filme inteiro é uma explicação daquela frase. E o mais genial é que ele não prova que Tom estava errado. Ele prova que Tom estava certo, só que ele interpretou aquilo da maneira errada. Tom acreditava que Summer era a pessoa certa e que os dois dariam certo porque sentia aquilo por ela. Só que o filme inteiro mostra justamente que eles eram péssimos um para o outro e que aquela relação nunca funcionaria. A frase dele continua sendo verdadeira: quando for amor, você vai saber. O problema é que Tom achava que já sabia. E isso fica completamente claro quando Summer fala sobre o marido. Ela diz que, com ele, simplesmente sentiu, enquanto com Tom nunca teve certeza. Essa fala é a prova absoluta daquilo que Tom disse no começo. Quando era a pessoa certa, ela soube. Com Tom, ela nunca teve aquela certeza. Por isso, Tom e Summer nunca dariam certo. Não porque a frase estivesse errada, mas justamente porque ela estava certa. Tom passou o filme inteiro acreditando que aquela relação funcionaria porque acreditava que tinha encontrado aquilo que a frase descrevia, enquanto a própria história mostrava que os dois eram completamente errados um para o outro. Quando eles finalmente encontram as pessoas certas, isso deixa tudo ainda mais claro. A relação de Tom e Summer nunca foi feita para funcionar, e o filme passa a história inteira construindo essa ideia até finalmente prová-la no final. E então o timer recomeça. Absolutamente cinematográfico. O filme inteiro foi a explicação daquela frase, e o final é a prova definitiva disso. Tudo que aconteceu entre Tom e Summer serve para mostrar que eles nunca dariam certo, enquanto o que acontece depois mostra exatamente o que Tom dizia que aconteceria quando fosse amor de verdade. Eu simplesmente amei como o filme conseguiu fazer isso. Fui assistir achando que seria insuportável, só mais um romance genérico dos anos 2000, e achando que eu nem conseguiria terminar. E terminei completamente apaixonada pelo filme. Duas horas escrevendo essa avaliação, mais tempo escrevendo sobre o filme do que assistindo, duas horas super bem gastas.

Mein Lieblingsfilm über Liebe, auch wenn es keine Liebesgeschichte ist. Beim ersten mal schauen war ich unendlich traurig und jetzt ist das irgendwie mein Wohl-Fühl-Film geworden. Die Geschichte ist so toll, so ein banger Soundtrack und so viele freie Stilmittel die den Film so interessant machen. Ich mein allein der Anfang vom Film mit den Kindervideos, Summers Vorstellung oder diese "Erwartungen vs. Realität" Passage. Dieser Film ist voller Kreativität und hat keine Angst mit solchen Ideen das Format zu sprengen. Solche Filme liebe ich.
